title: Head-to-Head Comparison of Flortaucipir and MK6240 tau-PET to Detect Subtle Objective Cognitive Impairment in Clinically Unimpaired Individuals
6bbdb7b49c5a399b02dafa06a0b04841c132e504.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Tau-PET is associated with subtle objective cognitive impairment (SOCI) in clinically unimpaired (CU) individuals, but whether the spatial patterns and strengths of these associations differ across tracers remains unclear. We performed a head-to-head comparison of [¹□F]MK6240 and [¹□F]flortaucipir to investigate their associations with SOCI in CU individuals.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>We cross-sectionally assessed CU participants from the HEAD study who underwent both tau-PET scans. Linear regressions examined associations between domain-specific cognition and tau burden using standardized uptake value ratios (SUVR) in regional and voxelwise analyses, alongside regional spatial extent of tauopathy (SEOT) measures. Tau burden was compared across groups representing different levels of SOCI. Models adjusted for age, sex, and education, with additional adjustment for amyloid-β burden. Centiloid-stratified analyses examined associations across amyloid-β burden levels.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Among 297 participants (mean [SD] age, 67.0 [8.4] years; 179 [60.3%] female), higher [¹□F]MK6240 SUVR was associated with poorer memory performance. Greater SEOT with either tracer was associated with poorer memory and showed nominal associations with executive dysfunction. Regional association strengths did not differ significantly between tracers, while SEOT yielded comparable or stronger associations than SUVR. Centiloid-stratified analyses revealed tau– cognition associations primarily at intermediate and high amyloid-β burden. [¹□F]MK6240 showed more spatially extensive voxelwise associations with memory and across SOCI group comparisons. Regional analyses also yielded more statistically significant differences across SOCI groups with [¹□F]MK6240 than with flortaucipir. These differences were predominantly driven by participants meeting actuarial mild cognitive impairment criteria, who exhibited greater tau burden than groups with less pronounced psychometric impairment. Across tracers, SEOT yielded more consistently significant differences among SOCI groups than SUVR.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>
                <jats:sec>
                  <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Both tracers showed associations with SOCI in CU individuals, with broadly comparable regional association strengths despite differences in the spatial extent and statistical significance of their findings. SEOT complemented SUVR by identifying additional significant associations and group differences. These findings suggest that tracer choice and quantification approach may influence the spatial distribution and statistical significance of observed tau–cognition relationships without necessarily altering their overall strength.</jats:p>
                </jats:sec>

title: Sensory processing sensitivity profiles and self-reported mental effort and concentration across pedagogical contexts among social services and healthcare students: a cross-sectional study
container-title: Advances in Health Sciences Education
a16c4fe48360c18b9334893e71317e638d1080c5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Changes in higher education and evolving pedagogical practices have increased the diversity of cognitive, emotional, and social demands experienced by students, highlighting the need to understand individual differences, including sensory processing sensitivity (SPS).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aim</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To identify SPS profiles among social services and healthcare students and examine whether self-reported mental effort and concentration across selected pedagogical contexts differed between the profiles.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A cross-sectional study.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Participants</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>1185 social and healthcare higher education students across Finland.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The data were collected with the SPS Questionnaire (43 items) during 2024–2025. K-means clustering and One-way ANOVA were employed to analyse the profiles of SPS. The associated pedagogical factors were analysed using Chi-square tests. The STROBE guidelines were followed.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five distinct SPS profiles emerged, differing significantly in sensitivity, emotional reactivity, and pedagogical responses. Profiles characterised by higher emotional and physiological reactivity (Profiles 2, 4, and 5) generally reported greater mental effort and more concentration difficulties, particularly in socially demanding and performance-based situations such as group work, oral presentations, and simulations. In contrast, low-reactive profiles (Profiles 1 and 3) demonstrated stable concentration and lower cognitive load across learning contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Pedagogical methods do not influence all students equally. Instructional approaches that involve intense social interaction, performance exposure, or high cognitive demands may disproportionately increase stress and cognitive load for highly reactive learners. Designing inclusive, psychologically safe, and adaptive learning environments that consider SPS-related differences can support student well-being, learning effectiveness, and sustainable professional development in social and healthcare education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Deliberate metaphor as a rhetorical strategy for corporate identity construction
container-title: Review of Cognitive Linguistics
f051d7463426b7ed36de664b94ef6e1ee91d9b2f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Using Deliberate Metaphor Theory and metaphor scenario analysis, this study compares the corporate identities constructed by Huawei before and after the imposition of US sanctions. The results show both convergence and divergence in deliberate metaphors and corporate identities. Although Huawei has long been portrayed as partnership-focused, innovation-driven, talent-valued and law-abiding, the specific identities it has constructed change markedly. In the pre-sanction period, Huawei is portrayed as a confident navigator, a military-style agile organization, a discerning talent gardener, and a vigilant sentinel against organizational decay. In the post-sanction period, it is framed as a resilient and steadfast traveler, a forward-looking strategic force mobilizer in the intelligence era, a storm survivor, and a down-to-earth ecosystem cultivator, reorienting its communication focus from internal optimization to addressing external challenges and accomplishing digital-era missions. This study indicates that corporate identity is a dynamic, context-sensitive cognitive construct which enables corporations to build trust across diverse contexts.</jats:p>

title: Eye-tracking insights into cognitive mechanisms in L2 reading
container-title: Australian Review of Applied Linguistics
78de375a684901490d21194b5a4a58f4c54d4c7e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the differential roles of working memory (WM) and comprehension monitoring (CM) in
					predicting L2 reading comprehension among Persian EFL learners across beginner and advanced proficiency levels. Utilizing a sample
					of 80 participants, comprising 40 beginners and 40 advanced learners, various cognitive measures including a Reading Span Test
					(RST), an Eye-movement Inconsistency Detection Task (measuring gaze durations), and a reading test (RT) were employed to assess
					working memory capacity (WMC), comprehension monitoring, and reading performance. Group differences were examined using univariate
					and multivariate analyses, and a hierarchical multiple regression was conducted using the full sample to examine the predictive
					contributions of WMC and CM and their interactions with proficiency group. The results indicated that while both WM and CM are
					integral to L2 reading comprehension, their relative contributions differ significantly between beginner and advanced learners.
					While WM plays a crucial role in L2 reading comprehension among beginners, comprehension monitoring becomes more predictive for
					advanced learners. Specifically, beginner learners with higher WM capacity demonstrated better reading performance. In contrast,
					advanced learners benefited significantly from effective comprehension monitoring, as evidenced by longer gaze durations
					correlating with higher reading scores. The study offers insights into the cognitive mechanisms underlying L2 reading and highlights the need for proficiency-specific instructional approaches, with implications for theory, practice, and future research.</jats:p>

title: Culture or cognition?
container-title: Review of Cognitive Linguistics
86c8ee25f8897837681e0dcbf21a05ca3407d065.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Gender languages assign nouns to a category, such as masculine, feminine, neuter or common. Gender assignment is
					complicated and difficult to learn, as languages do not have specific rules for assigning a noun to one or the other gender. This
					study looks at gender assignment from the perspective of semantics and lexical semantic evolution, exemplified on the
					Indo-European family. Gender assignment has a semantic core, in which animate nouns are more likely to be masculine, inanimate
					nouns feminine and neuter, nature nouns masculine, and culture nouns feminine or neuter. To investigate how these patterns emerge,
					we study the evolutionary dynamics of these semantic properties on a gender-coded lexical data set for Indo-European. We find that
					masculine is a stable gender that remains in its semantic category and does not change. Feminine is also a stable category which
					may get lost or transfer to masculine. Neuter and common are unstable categories, which continuously alter or get lost in gender
					assignment. In sum, our result shows that the semantic core of gender — affected both by cognitive and cultural factors — remains
					stable and does not vacillate in evolution.</jats:p>

title: The cognitive–digital pathway to sustainable entrepreneurship: examining entrepreneurial mindfulness, digital adaptability and sustainable growth aspirations
container-title: Management & Sustainability: An Arab Review
b5ae3570f7d89b91fbd576e240b0e1d5e6418bae.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how entrepreneurial mindfulness and digital adaptability capability jointly influence opportunity recognition and sustainable growth aspirations. Grounded in Cognitive Appraisal Theory and Dynamic Capabilities Theory, it explores how entrepreneurs' cognitive awareness and adaptive digital capabilities interact to shape long-term growth aspirations in increasingly uncertain and digitally evolving business environments.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study employed a quantitative cross-sectional design using survey data from 238 respondents (N = 238) engaged in digitally enabled entrepreneurial activities. Established measurement scales were used to measure the study constructs, and the hypothesized relationships were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings indicate that all hypotheses were supported. Entrepreneurial Mindfulness significantly influenced Opportunity Recognition (β = 0.566, t = 4.609, p &lt; 0.001) and Sustainable Growth Aspiration (β = 0.400, t = 5.363, p &lt; 0.001). Digital Adaptability Capability positively influenced Opportunity Recognition (β = 0.334, t = 2.560, p = 0.010) and Sustainable Growth Aspiration (β = 0.299, t = 3.689, p &lt; 0.001). Opportunity Recognition also positively affected Sustainable Growth Aspiration (β = 0.317, t = 4.744, p &lt; 0.001).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cross-sectional design limits causal inference, while the use of self-reported data and a sample of digitally active entrepreneurs in Indonesia may constrain generalizability. Future research should employ longitudinal or multi-source designs and examine the proposed relationships across diverse national and digital contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings emphasize that sustainable entrepreneurial growth requires the simultaneous development of cognitive and digital capabilities. Entrepreneurship education, incubators, and business support programs should therefore integrate mindfulness-based decision-making with digital capability development to strengthen opportunity recognition, strategic adaptability, and long-term business sustainability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study provides a conceptually integrated perspective on sustainable entrepreneurial growth by examining the complementary roles of entrepreneurial mindfulness and digital adaptability capability through opportunity recognition. Rather than introducing a new theoretical model, it extends existing entrepreneurship literature by demonstrating how Cognitive Appraisal Theory and Dynamic Capabilities Theory can be jointly applied to explain the cognitive and technological foundations of entrepreneurs' sustainable growth aspirations in digitally transforming business contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: More Than a Coin Flip: Forced-Choice Performance Above the Binomial Mean and Word-Frequency Bias on the Word Memory Test Under Sham Random Responding
container-title: Psychological Injury and Law
773d3cd6ea313ceabe8e1d023452e65f52e5d785.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Below-chance performance on forced-choice performance validity tests (PVTs) is typically interpreted against a binomial model that assumes a .50 probability under uninformed responding. We tested whether this assumption holds for the Word Memory Test (WMT) and whether item-level lexical properties account for departures from the binomial expectation using a sham extrasensory perception (ESP) paradigm to elicit uninformed (i.e., “random”) responding. Fifty-five undergraduates completed the WMT Immediate Recognition (IR) trial without prior exposure to the study list. Total scores and item-level responses were tested against exact binomial expectations. Pair-level lexical contrasts (target minus foil) for log word frequency, age of acquisition, concreteness, and orthographic distance were derived from the English Lexicon Project and examined as predictors of item selection in ordinary least squares (OLS) and generalized estimating equation (GEE) models. Mean IR performance was 24.15 of 40 (60.4% correct), exceeding the binomial mean, t(54) = 8.40, p < .001, d = 1.13. Eighteen IR items deviated from .50 after false-discovery-rate correction, predominantly toward the keyed-correct word. Target-foil word-frequency asymmetry was the dominant predictor of IR item selection (bivariate r = .56; OLS and GEE p < .001); concreteness and orthographic distance were unrelated to IR selection, and age of acquisition did not predict IR selection after frequency was controlled. Under attempted uninformed responding, WMT IR performance exceeded the nominal 50% binomial expectation by 1.31 binomial standard deviations (a magnitude exceeding the minimum threshold for practical significance). Item-level deviations were associated primarily with target-foil word-frequency differences. The findings identify a lexical feature relevant to test construction and forensic interpretation.</jats:p>

title: Mechanisms of change in cognitive–behavioural therapy: implications for clinical practice
container-title: BJPsych Advances
c85d0ca2594dfbf0e6989107d5d63825761e7fed.abstract:
<jats:title>SUMMARY</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cognitive–behavioural therapy (CBT) developed from two traditions: behavioural methods grounded in learning theory, and cognitive models that explain emotional distress through appraisals and beliefs. Contemporary practice integrates both at the level of formulation and technique: behavioural methods such as exposure and behavioural activation can change cognition, while cognitive strategies can support behavioural change. The empirical picture is more complex. Component studies suggest that behavioural interventions alone often produce outcomes comparable to full CBT, while the mediating role of cognitive change remains debated. This article reviews both traditions, describes how contemporary accounts of exposure (including inhibitory learning and expectancy violation) and behavioural experiments integrate them and considers what component and process research in social anxiety disorder and depression reveals about mechanisms of change. We argue for formulation-driven CBT, selecting cognitive strategies, behavioural strategies or both, according to the presentation, patient capacities and preferences, and treatment stage. Fictitious vignettes illustrate this approach, including adapted CBT for people with an intellectual disability.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive biases in nursing students' clinical decision-making: insights from high-fidelity simulation using think-aloud and observational methods
container-title: Frontiers in Medicine
b19bec6a2f903ba13e0f220d0c6b315c0aef16b6.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive biases are systematic errors in human reasoning that can compromise clinical decision-making (CDM) in healthcare. While extensively studied in medicine, nursing research on cognitive biases in CDM remains limited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Aim</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to explore and identify cognitive biases and examine their relationship with nursing students' clinical decision-making during a high-fidelity simulation of a deteriorating patient scenario.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A mixed-methods design was employed, incorporating concurrent and retrospective think-aloud (TA) protocols and observational data.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty-three final-year Bachelor of Science nursing students participated in a high-fidelity, manikin-based simulation involving a clinically deteriorating patient scenario. A catalogue of 12 cognitive biases was developed from the literature and used to code statements from concurrent and retrospective think-aloud protocols and observational data using content analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 166 bias occurrences were identified across all data sources (63 concurrent TA; 51 retrospective TA; 52 observation). Representativeness was the most frequently identified bias overall, particularly in retrospective think-aloud data. Order effect was the most common bias in concurrent think-aloud data, and representativeness and order effect were the most common in observational data. Premature closure and availability were also prominent across all sources of data. Biases occurred proportionally across both Type 1 (automated/pattern recognition) and Type 2 (hypothetico-deductive) decision-making, with notable differences between concurrent and retrospective think-aloud findings. The findings also suggest that simulation may support students' awareness of cognitive bias.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>High-fidelity simulation, combined with think-aloud protocols and observation, provided a useful approach for identifying cognitive biases in nursing students' clinical decision-making. The findings have implications for simulation design, debriefing practice, and nursing education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Selegiline prevents cognitive impairment and hippocampal CA1 excitability deficits induced by repeated isoflurane exposure
container-title: Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience
8d68aeee446d84117264800558ebb188874aa0e5.abstract: <jats:p>Postoperative cognitive dysfunction (POCD) is a common and clinically significant complication following anesthesia and surgery, affecting up to 40% of elderly patients, yet no established preventive therapy is currently available. Although neuroinflammation has been widely implicated in POCD, the electrophysiological mechanism linking anesthetic exposure to cognitive decline remains poorly understood, and pharmacological approaches to prevent this pathological cascade have not been established. To isolate the contribution of repeated anesthesia exposure itself, independent of surgical trauma, we used a repeated isoflurane-exposure mouse model, which we refer to as anesthesia-induced cognitive impairment (AICI). Using this model, we show that repeated anesthesia produces significant impairments in spatial working memory and recognition memory, accompanied by impaired hippocampal CA1 long-term potentiation (LTP). Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings further revealed intrinsic hypoexcitability of CA1 pyramidal neurons in isoflurane-exposed mice, characterized by reduced firing frequency, prolonged action potential half-width, slower repolarization, and diminished afterhyperpolarization. Reduced spontaneous excitatory postsynaptic current (sEPSC) frequency and amplitude further indicated impaired excitatory synaptic drive in CA1 neurons. Notably, pretreatment with selegiline, an FDA-approved selective monoamine oxidase-B (MAO-B) inhibitor, prevented isoflurane-induced cognitive deficits, preserved hippocampal LTP, preserved intrinsic neuronal excitability, and largely normalized action potential kinetics while maintaining sEPSC frequency, although the reduction in sEPSC amplitude was not significantly prevented by pretreatment. In contrast, direct application of high-concentration selegiline impaired LTP induction. Together, these findings identify impaired CA1 neuronal excitability and excitatory synaptic drive as key electrophysiological correlates of AICI and suggest selegiline as a promising pre-emptive candidate for mitigating anesthesia-related cognitive decline.</jats:p>

title: Fear memory expression and reconsolidation depend on hippocampal astrocytic glutamate uptake in male rats
container-title: Frontiers in Cellular Neuroscience
9185a60547959af803d062979730b2c3cc4d340e.abstract: <jats:p>The control of glutamate levels in the synaptic gap is crucial for neuronal communication, as it prevents excitotoxicity from excessive receptor activation. Glutamate transporters GLT-1 are mainly localized in astrocytes and its expression is particularly abundant in the hippocampus (Hp). In this study, we explored the role of GLT-1 in consolidation, expression and reconsolidation of memory, using contextual fear conditioning (CFC) task. Dihydrokainic acid (DHK), a selective GLT-1 inhibitor, was injected into the dorsal Hp of male rats at different times around aversive learning. DHK administration 15 min after a weak CFC training session promoted long-term memory (LTM) formation. However, DHK administration around strong CFC training sessions did not affect memory consolidation. Moreover, DHK infusion 15 min before the LTM test session impaired CFC memory expression. Importantly, if applied 15 min after a reactivation session, DHK impairs CFC reconsolidation. In contrast, the antibiotic ceftriaxone (CFT), which increases GLT-1 expression, did not affect the consolidation or the expression of fear memory. The effects of DHK and CFT on memory were not due to changes in locomotor activity or anxiety-like state of rats. In conclusion, our findings indicate that inhibition of hippocampal astroglial glutamate uptake impairs the expression and reconsolidation of aversive memory without impairing its consolidation, and highlight potential therapeutic avenues for neuropsychiatric conditions, including phobias, post-traumatic stress disorder, and cognitive deficits.</jats:p>

title: Histopathological alterations of deep cervical lymph nodes in Alzheimer's disease and their association with cognitive decline
5007a92e2e0b8a916e78bdeece0bb80541adef03.abstract: Background Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is characterized by progressive cognitive and functional decline with amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau pathology. In addition to abnormal protein aggregation, impaired clearance of brain-derived solutes through glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic pathways may contribute to disease progression. Deep cervical lymph nodes (DCLNs), as major downstream lymphoid structures of central nervous system drainage, may provide a peripheral histological window into the brain-cervical lymphatic axis. However, whether human DCLNs undergo histopathological remodeling in AD and whether such changes are clinically relevant remain unclear. Methods DCLNs were obtained from 66 participants, including 59 patients with moderate-to-severe AD and 7 cognitively unimpaired controls. Hematoxylin and eosin staining was used to assess lymph node morphology and germinal center (GC) abundance. Multiplex immunofluorescence was performed to evaluate Aβ, tau, alpha-smooth muscle actin (alpha-SMA), CD31, and LYVE-1. Cognitive and functional status were assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE), Clinical Dementia Rating-Sum of Boxes (CDR-SB), and Activities of Daily Living (ADL) scores. AD patients were stratified by GC abundance using a cutoff of 4 GCs. Multivariate logistic regression, receiver operating characteristic analysis, decision curve analysis, and 6-month postoperative follow-up were performed. Results DCLNs from patients with AD showed histopathological remodeling, including reduced GC abundance, structural disruption, fibrosis-related stromal changes, altered vascular and lymphatic marker expression, and detectable Aβ and tau immunoreactivity. Compared with patients with > 4 GCs, those with ≤ 4 GCs had worse baseline cognitive and functional status, including lower MMSE scores and higher CDR-SB and ADL scores. In multivariate analysis, higher alpha-SMA mean fluorescence intensity was associated with a lower likelihood of preserved GC abundance, whereas higher MMSE score was associated with preserved GC abundance. Patients with > 4 GCs also showed greater improvement in MMSE, CDR-SB, and ADL scores at 6 months postoperatively. Conclusions Human DCLNs exhibit histopathological remodeling in AD. Reduced GC abundance is associated with greater clinical impairment, fibrosis-related remodeling, and poorer 6-month postoperative improvement, suggesting that DCLN histopathology may have potential clinical and prognostic relevance in AD.

title: Strategic AI Underuse: Effort Incentives, Displacement Risk, and Organizational Responses
container-title: Metroeconomica
17d199c667017c1124b57760e9ef21d359d78aea.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This paper studies how workers' employment concerns can affect the effective use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools after adoption. When productive use of these tools raises workers' perceived risk of displacement, employees may optimally reduce productive effort, trading current earnings against employment security. The baseline represents the first implementation period, when neither side has yet observed behaviour and production under the new technology. The firm evaluates adoption using the observed pre‐AI effort level, while workers forecast the production scale from the most recently observed aggregate output. Strategic underuse can therefore partly or fully offset the productivity gains expected from AI tools and make an initially attractive technology unprofitable after implementation. After implementation, the firm observes the effective effort response, while its organizational options depend on whether it can diagnose the incentive mechanism behind that response and on the cost or feasibility of workforce adjustment. The firm may choose technological reversion, labour hoarding, workforce restructuring through voluntary separations, or employment‐preserving contracts based on negotiated working‐time reductions. Robustness benchmarks show that the displacement‐induced incentive for underuse can persist when firms and workers form more forward‐looking expectations. A Monte Carlo calibration illustrates that all four organizational responses can arise as profit‐maximizing outcomes.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Changes and Brain Structural Plasticity under Long-Term Negative Emotions: Research Progress and Causal Controversies
container-title: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
7104a120c66d2bfa57d7c757c8fbbb60b4c55255.abstract: <jats:p>Depression, fear, and anxiety are typical negative emotions. If these emotions persist for a long time, they can lead to cognitive biases and physical discomfort. Two common clinical subtypes are generalized anxiety disorder (GAD) and major depressive disorder (MDD). Whether these emotions causally affect structural plasticity and neural circuit function—and if so, how—remains an open question. Prior work has combined brain imaging, non-invasive brain stimulation (including Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation), and drug intervention data to map the structural and circuit changes linked to different negative emotions. The prefrontal-amygdala circuit appears central to negative emotion processing, yet the brain changes linked to depression, anxiety, and fear differ. Because cross-sectional studies capture only one time point, they cannot resolve causality—brain abnormalities may be pre-existing traits, or they may emerge secondarily from persistent emotions. Non-invasive brain stimulation and pharmacological interventions can modulate neural circuits, which supports their potential as interventions. A single scan gives only a snapshot. It cannot show whether negative emotions reshape the brain over time, or whether pre-existing brain features shape those emotions. Longitudinal tracking of the same individuals across multiple time points, with control groups for comparison, would help clarify it.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive-Behavioral Couple Therapy for Relationship Distress: How Maladaptive Beliefs Shape Relationship Functioning and Psychological Well-Being
container-title: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
15767c39dcc5d6cb1ad0e453dd47a492b0410bea.abstract: <jats:p>Relationship distress is associated with poorer psychological well-being, including heightened stress, anxiety, and depressive symptoms. Cognitive-Behavioral Couple Therapy (CBCT) focuses on couples' relationship cognitions and interaction patterns; however, few existing reviews have synthesized the effects of specific relationship beliefs and attribution processes on relationship functioning and individual psychological outcomes. This literature review examines how hostile attributions, mind-reading expectations, catastrophizing, aversion to disagreement, and rigid destiny beliefs contribute to relationship distress, and how CBCT may modify these processes. Recent meta-analyses, randomized controlled trials, longitudinal studies, and large-scale relationship research published primarily from 2020 onward are synthesized. The evidence indicates that CBCT-informed interventions can improve relationship satisfaction, communication, and selected indicators of individual well-being. Collaborative communication and reduced maladaptive attributional processing are plausible mechanisms, although causal evidence is still limited. CBCT appears most useful when cognitive restructuring is paired with behavioral practice and communication skills. Clinical interpretation should nevertheless account for cultural variation, contextual stress, unequal access, and the need for safety assessment when coercion or abuse is present.</jats:p>

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence-Assisted Language Learning: Cognitive Mechanisms, Theoretical Tensions, and Ethical Governance
container-title: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
0796b58d89d60973e3d08c8cbd763f0b2a7a0bac.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the environment of language learning, but its theoretical basis and ethical boundaries have not been fully explored. This paper builds a multi-level analytical system for AI-assisted language learning based on cognitive load theory, the zone of proximal development, generative linguistics and the technology acceptance model. AI can help students learn better by reducing extraneous cognitive load and providing easy-to-access support and instant correction; however, due to technological limitations, it may also reduce students' sense of ability and self-management. Generative linguistics and generative AI are not in opposition; rather, the former advocates for data frugality and innate mechanisms, while the latter is characterized by data maximalism and statistical learning; they are in harmony at the level of third factors and the Minimalist Program. According to the above research, chatbots have shown a modest positive effect on language learning; this degree varies depending on the learner's level, interface Design, interaction characteristics, etc. Based on the above, this paper introduces a "Smart Chinese" collaborative learning plugin that integrates ChatGPT with special scaffolding tools for assessment, planning, practice, feedback and community support. Finally, it presents the ethical problems of algorithmic bias, data privacy, over-reliance, and educational gaps, and proposes a multi-level governance system at the institutional, technological and pedagogical levels.</jats:p>

title: A Multimodal Nomogram Predicting the Risk of Cognitive Impairment in Parkinson Disease
container-title: Movement Disorders Clinical Practice
d595cf03da8bc6ae10e4bcc348c84e01f0490af8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Cognitive impairment is the most consequential non‐motor complication of Parkinson's disease (PD), yet no validated tool integrates multimodal data to predict individualized risk trajectories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The aim is to develop and internally validate a time‐to‐event nomogram for predicting 5‐year risk of cognitive impairment in PD using the Parkinson's Precision Markers Initiative (PPMI).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed 1188 PD patients with normal cognition at their first cognitive assessment and up to 13 years of follow‐up. Twenty‐seven candidate predictors across seven domains were evaluated. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)‐penalized Cox regression performed variable selection. Performance was assessed via nested cross‐validation, bootstrap optimism correction, calibration, and time‐dependent area under the curve (AUC).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      During median follow‐up of 3.0 years (interquartile range [IQR], 2.0–5.0), 457 patients (38.5%) developed cognitive impairment. LASSO selected 14 predictors. The Cox model achieved a concordance index (C‐index) of 0.747 (optimism‐corrected: 0.733; nested CV: 0.736 ± 0.042), with apparent time‐dependent AUC of 0.77, 0.79, and 0.83 at 3, 5, and 8 years (held‐out: 0.75, 0.78, and 0.81). A companion model without genetic predictors, for unknown
                      <jats:italic>GBA</jats:italic>
                      status, performed similarly (optimism‐corrected C‐index, 0.729). The strongest predictors were age (hazard ratio [HR], 1.05/year;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001),
                      <jats:italic>GBA</jats:italic>
                      mutation (HR, 2.05;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001), cognitive complaints (HR, 1.67;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.001), and Symbol Digit Modalities Test (HR, 0.98/point;
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.001).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A multimodal nomogram integrating clinical, cognitive, genetic, and neuropsychiatric predictors provides individualized estimates of 5‐year risk of cognitive impairment in PD; after external validation, it may support prognostic counseling and trial enrichment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: In-Memory Computing Architectures for Accelerating Large-Scale Models: Principles, Devices, and System Challenges
container-title: Applied and Computational Engineering
3b90ca40b93160d6590d615a35b21805f5730845.abstract: <jats:p>Memory bandwidth is the binding constraint for large-model inference today. In-memory computing (IMC) addresses this limitation. This paper reviews where the technology stands. It compares analog and digital IMC implementations and find that analog arrays currently lead on energy efficiency, while digital designs maintain a substantial edge in precision and programming flexibility. Then it discusses three device candidates: Resistive Random-Access Memory (ReRAM), Ferroelectric Field-Effect Transistor (FeFET), and Spin-Transfer-Torque Magnetic Random-Access Memory (STT-MRAM). ReRAM offers the highest density but suffers from stochastic filament growth and conductance drift. FeFETs integrate cleanly with CMOS but are limited by ferroelectric switching variability. STT-MRAM is the most durable and stable, yet its modest tunnel-magnetoresistance ratio restricts analog precision. Finally, three limitations are pointed out: device variation under realistic workloads, peripheral-circuit overhead that can erase array-level energy gains, and scalable multi-chip orchestration for trillion-parameter models. IMC will succeed or fail based on cross-layer co-design—not on any single device breakthrough. Materials, circuits, compilers, and algorithms must advance together, and the compiler layer remains underdeveloped relative to device research. This paper provides development ideas for higher performance for IMC.</jats:p>

title: Persistent memory through triple-loop consolidation under stochastic unit turnover
container-title: Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience
22c44da96cd1e37f2e0945ec029727a7e976d101.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Dissipative cognitive architectures maintain computation through continuous energy expenditure, where units that exhaust their energy are stochastically replaced with fresh random state. This creates a fundamental challenge: how can persistent, context-specific memory survive when all learnable state is periodically destroyed? Existing memory mechanisms—including elastic weight consolidation, synaptic intelligence, and surprise-driven gating—rely on gradient computation and are inapplicable to dissipative systems that do not perform it. We introduce
                    <jats:italic>Deep Memory</jats:italic>
                    (DM), a backpropagation-free persistent memory mechanism operating through a triple-loop consolidation cycle: (1)
                    <jats:italic>recording</jats:italic>
                    of expert-specific content centroids during active computation, (2)
                    <jats:italic>seeding</jats:italic>
                    of replaced units with stored representations, and (3)
                    <jats:italic>stabilization</jats:italic>
                    through continuous re-entry that counteracts dissipative drift. We demonstrate that discrete expert routing via Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) gating is required, in the regimes tested, for DM functionality, preventing the centroid convergence that would render stored memories identical. Across 972 simulation runs spanning thirteen experimental blocks, we establish: (i) removing stable context–expert binding removes structural specialization (MI = 1.10 vs. 0.001 under binding destruction;
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    = 91); (ii) DM achieves persistent representation quality
                    <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                    = 0.984 compared to 0.385 without memory (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    = 16); (iii) continuous seeding reconstructs representations after interference (
                    <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>recon</jats:sub>
                    = 0.978; one-shot seeding fails;
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    = 30); (iv) the mechanism operates within a well-characterized (
                    <jats:italic>K</jats:italic>
                    , ρ) envelope with identifiable degradation boundaries (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    = 350); (v) a factorial ablation isolates recording × seeding as the minimal critical dyad (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    = 40); and (vi) six confirmatory experiments—including single-factor causal ablation, mediation analysis, and comparison with associative and reservoir baselines (Hopfield, ESN) under matched turnover—validate what the mechanism requires and how it compares with those baselines (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                    = 370). Results (ii)–(v) rest on pilot-scale seed counts (4–5 seeds per condition); at these counts no paired non-parametric test can reach
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                    &lt; 0.05 whatever the effect size, so we report them as estimates of effect size and direction rather than as confirmatory tests. Within these limits, DM is a falsifiable, bounded mechanism for persistent memory in backpropagation-free cognitive systems. Its relation to hippocampal consolidation is a functional analogy only: DM shares the premise of a store held apart from the computing substrate, but assigns the fast and slow roles in the opposite direction to complementary learning systems theory.
                  </jats:p>

title: Functional food intervention alleviates cognitive impairment by reshaping the gut microbiota and restoring propionate levels: evidence from edible bird’s nest supplementation
container-title: Frontiers in Nutrition
3f83c5a71e8726c3278eb4954a2a154cb9875a86.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Aging-related cognitive decline is closely associated with synaptic dysfunction, neuroinflammation, and alterations in gut microbial homeostasis. Edible bird’s nest (EBN), a glycoprotein-rich functional food, has attracted attention for its potential neuroprotective effects. However, whether EBN has an ameliorative effect on aging-related cognitive impairment remains unclear. This study evaluated the effects of EBN supplementation on memory impairment in a D-galactose (D-gal) -induced aging model and explored the potential mechanisms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Mice were subjected to chronic D-gal administration and treated with low or high-dose EBN or sialic acid (SA). Spatial learning and memory were assessed using the Morris water maze. Hippocampal neuronal morphology, dendritic spine density, synaptic marker expression, glial activation, and inflammatory cytokines were evaluated. Gut microbial composition was analyzed using 16S rRNA gene sequencing, while fecal short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) were quantified by gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC–MS). Correlation analysis was performed to examine the association between gut microbial taxa and SCFA levels.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      D-gal treatment induced marked cognitive impairment in mice, as reflected by reduced spatial memory performance, decreased hippocampal dendritic spine density, and diminished expression of synaptic markers including
                      <jats:italic>Bdnf</jats:italic>
                      (brain-derived neurotrophic factor),
                      <jats:italic>Dlg4</jats:italic>
                      (postsynaptic density protein 95), and
                      <jats:italic>Syp</jats:italic>
                      (synaptophysin). In contrast, EBN supplementation, particularly at the higher dose, significantly improved spatial learning and memory, preserved dendritic spine integrity, and upregulated the synaptic genes. Moreover, EBN effectively attenuated D-gal-induced glial activation and lowered the elevated pro-inflammatory cytokine levels in both serum and brain tissue. Analysis of the gut microbiota revealed that EBN supplementation was associated with a partial reversal of D-gal-induced shifts in microbial community structure, with a pronounced increase in the relative abundance of
                      <jats:italic>Lactobacillus</jats:italic>
                      . Concurrently, fecal propionate levels, which were reduced by D-gal treatment, were restored following EBN supplementation, and propionate abundance correlated positively with
                      <jats:italic>Lactobacillus</jats:italic>
                      . SA supplementation also showed beneficial changes in several measured outcomes, suggesting that SA may contribute to some of the responses observed following EBN supplementation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In summary, EBN supplementation ameliorated cognitive impairment in D-gal-induced aging mice, and this effect may be associated with restoration of gut microbial homeostasis and increased fecal propionate levels. Given that aging is a major risk factor for metabolic syndrome and related cognitive decline, these findings highlight the potential of EBN as a functional food for combating age-associated metabolic and neurological disorders, possibly through modulation of the microbiota-gut-brain axis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Exploratory evaluation of electroencephalogram-derived features for classification of mild cognitive impairment in two independent datasets
container-title: Frontiers in Computational Neuroscience
6088171800f1aadb3d4f5e17e4d7fc6a9703a979.abstract: <jats:p>A proper diagnosis of mild cognitive impairment (MCI) is one of the important challenges in the early detection of dementia. For the classification of MCI patients and healthy controls, some electroencephalogram (EEG)-derived indices were calculated and compared. Some studies have been conducted on the high accuracy classification of MCI patients and healthy controls, but classification may depend on the dataset and recording conditions. In this study, we evaluated EEG-derived indices in the Japanese and the Iranian EEG datasets and examined their classification performance under within-dataset and cross-dataset validation. This classifier had common features but was learned for each dataset. The Japanese dataset consisted of 7 MCI patients and 10 healthy controls. The Iranian dataset consisted of 29 MCI patients and 32 healthy controls. The common 16 EEG data were separated into 5 frequency bands. Power spectrum and SL values by Synchronization Likelihood were calculated as features for classification. These standardized and exponentially transformed indices were also used as features. Furthermore, graph metrics were calculated based on SL values before or after standardization and exponential transformation. Features used for classification were selected from these indices. The high classification accuracies were obtained from the classifier using a 34-dimensional feature subset selected from standardized and exponentially transformed EEG-derived indices for lower alpha band. Accuracies of this classifier were 88.24% in the Japanese dataset and 86.89% in the Iranian dataset. To evaluate classification accuracy while minimizing information leakage and optimistic bias, nested leave-one-out cross-validation was performed. Accuracies were 88.24% in the Japanese dataset and 83.61% in the Iranian dataset using exponentially transformed EEG-derived indices for lower alpha band. To evaluate whether the classifier can generalize to independent datasets obtained under different recording conditions, exploratory bidirectional cross-dataset evaluation was performed. Accuracies were 40.98% (Training data: the Japanese dataset, Test data: the Iranian dataset) and 58.82% (Training data: the Iranian dataset, Test data: the Japanese dataset). These findings suggested that resting-state EEG-derived indices for lower alpha band may contain information useful for classification of MCI patients and healthy controls. However, they suggested that classifier based on these indices may partly reflect dataset-specific characteristics.</jats:p>

title: Association between cardiovascular disease risk and cognitive function in older adults based on the China-PAR model: a cross-sectional study
container-title: Frontiers in Public Health
be39c758f1f67cfffebe030ac2527367962677a3.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To investigate the association between cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk and cognitive function in older adults using the China-PAR model.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study adopted stratified random sampling. A total of 570 older adults were selected from 3,750 health examinations at a community health service station, with sample size calculated by the cross-sectional study formula. We collected questionnaire and physical examination data including demographics, blood pressure and metabolic indicators. Cognitive function was measured by the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA), and cardiovascular risk was assessed via the China-PAR model. All analyses were performed with SPSS 27.0 using Spearman's rank correlation analysis and multiple linear regression analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The mean MoCA score was 25.94 ± 2.71. MoCA scores differed significantly across CVD risk groups and were negatively correlated with CVD risk level (r = −0.56,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      &lt; 0.001). In the primary adjusted Model 2, both the high-risk (B = −0.68,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      &lt; 0.001) and moderate-risk groups (B = −0.31,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.02) had significantly lower MoCA scores than the low-risk group. In the sensitivity analysis (Model 3) additionally adjusting for age and gender, the results were similar (high risk: B = −0.65,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      &lt; 0.001; moderate risk: B = −0.30,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 0.03). Compared with the college group, all lower education groups showed significantly lower MoCA scores. Sensitivity analyses restricted to participants aged ≤ 74 years yielded a similar pattern of findings.

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Higher CVD risk was associated with poorer cognitive function in this study population, with lower MoCA scores observed particularly among participants in the high-risk group. title: Comparative evaluation of ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao responses to patient questions on pulmonary contusion: quality, reliability, readability, and content deficiencies
container-title: Frontiers in Medicine
579500b0e5a0eb1bd6d8eb72770864908bef346b.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To compare the quality, reliability, understandability, actionability, readability, and content deficiencies of responses generated by ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao to common patient questions about pulmonary contusion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Twenty frequently asked questions about pulmonary contusion were identified from Google Trends, common clinical consultations, and relevant clinical guidelines. Each question was submitted separately to ChatGPT, DeepSeek, and Doubao, producing 60 responses. Information quality and reliability were assessed using the GQS, mDISCERN, QAMAI, EQIP, and PEMAT (understandability and actionability). Readability was evaluated with six indices (ARI, FRES, GFI, FKGL, CLI and SMOG). Content deficiencies were classified as omissions, hallucinations, output errors, or outdated medical advice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Significant differences were found among the three models across all quality and reliability measures (Friedman test, all
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                       &lt; 0.05). ChatGPT had the highest median GQS (4.50), QAMAI (26.00), and EQIP (75.00%) scores, whereas DeepSeek had the highest mDISCERN score (18.00). ChatGPT also achieved the highest PEMAT-U score (median 83.50%), and its median PEMAT-A score (80.00%) was equal to that of DeepSeek. Pairwise comparisons showed that ChatGPT and DeepSeek did not differ significantly on GQS, EQIP, PEMAT-U, or PEMAT-A, but both significantly outperformed Doubao (all
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      _adj &lt; 0.05). None of the models met the recommended sixth-grade reading level for public health information. ChatGPT produced the most difficult-to-read responses (median FKGL 16.85). A total of 44 content deficiencies were identified, most commonly omissions (52.27%), followed by hallucinations (25.00%) and outdated medical advice (13.64%). Quality-related measures were generally positively correlated, whereas associations between information quality and readability were weak.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>ChatGPT and DeepSeek generally performed better than Doubao in providing information about pulmonary contusion, although each model showed different strengths. However, none of the models met the recommended readability standards for public health information, and clinically relevant content deficiencies were observed across all three. LLM-generated medical information should be used as a supplementary source rather than a substitute for professional medical advice.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Functional impairment statistically mediates the association between hyperarousal neuropsychiatric symptoms and cognitive decline: a prospective cohort study
container-title: Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience
3fcab360e42dfa090511cc6eb47dcfd0a757276d.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Neuropsychiatric symptoms (NPS) are prevalent in older adults and are associated with cognitive decline. This study investigated the association between hyperarousal NPS (HNPS) and cognitive progression, focusing on the mediating role of functional impairment and its link to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) pathology.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Using data from 1,657 non-demented participants in the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI), we evaluated the Hyperarousal Neuropsychiatric Inventory Questionnaire (HNPI-Q, comprising agitation, anxiety, and irritability), the Functional Activities Questionnaire (FAQ), APOE ε4 status, Alzheimer’s Disease Assessment Scale-Cognitive Subscale 13 (ADAS13) scores, regional brain volumes, and amyloid-β (Aβ) positron emission tomography (PET) Centiloid values. Analyses included Cox and linear regression, mediation analysis, and nomogram development.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      HNPS predicted 5-year cognitive decline (HR = 1.14,
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                      = 2.7 × 10
                      <jats:sup>–4</jats:sup>
                      ), an association attenuated after adjusting for FAQ. HNPI-Q scores were longitudinally associated with functional and cognitive decline. Mediation analyses indicated that functional impairment statistically mediated the association between HNPS and cognition. Notably, the rate of functional decline was strongly correlated with the rate of Aβ accumulation, a coupling that was also evident in participants who progressed to cognitive deterioration. Predictive models based on HNPI-Q and FAQ showed excellent discrimination (AUC: 0.838 and 0.845) and calibration.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>HNPS was associated with cognitive decline, an association that was statistically mediated by functional impairment, which itself co-varies with Aβ pathology. The HNPI-Q stratified the 5-year risk of cognitive deterioration in this cohort, and whether intervening on these symptoms or on functional decline alters the clinical course remains to be further investigated.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Help students construct a hub-and-spoke cognitive structure: a key pathway to reduce burden and improve quality in mathematics classroom teaching
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
b518b8ee84f0cd53e354522080f864174a2387f6.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    The fragmented organization of mathematical knowledge may make it more difficult for students to understand knowledge structures and engage in mathematical reasoning. This study examined a “hub-and-spoke cognitive structure” teaching framework, aimed at promoting students’ formation of a more coherent and structured mathematical knowledge system by optimizing how instructional content is organized. The framework organizes related mathematical content around a generative core concept (the hub) and connects associated knowledge through consistent reasoning pathways (the spokes), thereby integrating knowledge construction and review into a recursive learning process in which prior and new knowledge interact. A two- round action research design was implemented in two parallel Grade 10 classes, using the vector representations of the four centers of a triangle (the centroid, circumcenter, incenter, and orthocenter) as the instructional content. The first round was conducted in Class A (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 61). Based on the problems identified through an immediate feedback questionnaire, student interviews, classroom observations, and students’ written mathematical reasoning, the instructional design was refined by strengthening the derivation of the foundational example, comparing alternative proof methods, optimizing inquiry tasks, reallocating instructional time, and providing differentiated scaffolding. The revised design was then implemented in another parallel class, Class B (
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 60). The results showed that students in Class B gave higher ratings for the clarity of teacher explanations, acceptance of the instructional approach, and their self-perceived understanding and application of the content. Interview data and written reasoning further indicated that some students understood the reasoning pathways underlying the related concepts and attempted to apply them in subsequent tasks. Across the two action research rounds, the hub-and-spoke teaching framework provided a practical approach for teachers to organize related mathematical instructional content around core knowledge and to iteratively refine instruction in response to classroom feedback. The findings also provide exploratory classroom-level evidence of students moving from fragmented knowledge learning toward a more relational understanding of mathematical knowledge.
                  </jats:p>

title: Preserved olfaction unmasks choroid plexus–related cognitive risk in Parkinson’s disease
container-title: Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience
63e6455241e5d2ddbeba83dfd3034be9fb144527.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Choroid plexus volume (CPV) has been associated with cognitive impairment in Parkinson’s disease (PD), particularly frontal-executive dysfunction, whereas olfactory dysfunction is linked to cognitive deterioration and may reflect greater α-synuclein involvement. Whether olfactory status modifies the association between CPV and cognitive outcomes remains unclear.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed 718 participants with early-stage PD followed for up to 10 years. Baseline CPV was derived from structural MRI. Hyposmia was defined as an age- and sex-adjusted University of Pennsylvania Smell Identification Test percentile ≤ 15. Kaplan–Meier and multivariable Cox models were used to examine incident cognitive milestone (CogM), including a CPV × olfactory status interaction. CPV was standardized to 1-SD units. Multiple sensitivity analyses assessed robustness.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Among 709 participants with olfactory data, 502 (70.8%) had hyposmia. Ten-year CogM-free survival was 59.4%. The primary Cox analysis included 680 participants and 173 CogM events. Among participants with normosmia, each 1-SD increase in CPV was associated with higher CogM risk (HR = 1.63, 95% CI 1.20–2.22,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.002). Hyposmia was associated with higher CogM risk at the mean CPV level (HR = 1.91, 95% CI 1.23–2.97,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.004). The CPV × hyposmia interaction was significant (HR = 0.62, 95% CI 0.43–0.88,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.008); the CPV association was absent in participants with hyposmia (HR = 1.01, 95% CI 0.83–1.22,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      = 0.950). Findings were consistent across sensitivity analyses.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Olfactory status modified the association between CPV and cognitive outcomes in early PD. Larger CPV was associated with higher CogM risk in participants with preserved olfaction, but not in those with hyposmia. These findings warrant validation in independent cohorts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Role of Paternal Small Non-Coding RNAs and Dopamine Signaling in High-Fat Diet-Induced Transgenerational Reward Memory
container-title: Theoretical and Natural Science
6c17d9219c5b6caa6a4af57ebe5bfc3dab41d9fb.abstract: <jats:p>Parental environmental exposure can affect offspring through hereditary germline changes without changing the DNA sequence. Ongoing studies show that parental diet can induce heritable molecular changes, thereby affecting offspring metabolism, behavior, and neurological function. However, the mechanism behind these persistent neurobehavioral effects remains unclear. In order to solve this problem, this study explored whether the parent HFD will produce cross-generational memory, thereby changing the reward-related behavior of the offspring. Specifically, it studied the role of dopamine regulation and sperm small non-coding RNA in this process. F0 male mice received a control diet or a high-fat diet before mating, while F1 and F2 male mice maintained a normal diet. Reward-related behaviors will be evaluated through various hedonic preferences and reward learning tests. The functional contribution of dopamine will be evaluated at the molecular, behavioral, and electrophysiological levels by methods such as Neuropixels and high-performance liquid chromatography. Small RNA sequencing will identify persistent sperm small non-coding RNA candidates between generations. Ultimately, this study aims to determine how paternal HFD causes cross-generational changes in reward-related behaviors through dopamine regulation and sperm small non-coding RNA. These findings may contribute to a better understanding of how paternal diet shapes the transgenerational memory of neurobehavior and to identify this genetic causal reproductive mechanism.</jats:p>

title: The Logical Probability Behind Lotteries and Raffles: Chance and Cognitive Bias from a Data Science Perspective
container-title: Theoretical and Natural Science
f2fb5bbafa209ab53b86e3ba6c7c4d48f6b55674.abstract: <jats:p>The entertainment activities such as lotteries and raffles are popular among people, but the cognitive bias of people may result in fluke mentality, leading to social issues like debts, problem gambling and behavioral addiction. This essay focuses on the logic of probabilities behind lotteries and raffles, talking about how data science deal with the chances and misconceptions of them. Our topics include probability, independent events, the expected value and so on. The method is based on overview analysis of previous resources. The study suggests that the huge prize money in lottery does not necessarily equate to high average returns, and past outcomes in independent random events do not affect future probabilities, When faced with low probability and high return events, people's judgments are often influenced by subjective weights and intuition, forming a sense of opportunity illusion. The conclusion of this study indicates that data science can help the public correct cognitive biases, enhance probability awareness and rational decision-making ability through objective probability, expected value, natural frequency, and large sample data analysis.</jats:p>

title: Simple method to reduce the memory effect in microbolometer cameras
container-title: Optical Engineering
80c89142fb8fc504ea046be7427c11b31e672717.abstract: <jats:p>Motion blur is frequently observed in images captured by infrared (IR) microbolometer cameras. This is due to the important memory effect in this type of sensor. Actually, it corrupts the response not only in the presence of relative motion between camera and target object, but also in the event of rapid variations in the temperature of a static target. From a thermal point of view, a microbolometer sensor behaves like a first-order dynamic system. This is why the sensor’s temperature, hence the output signal, retains traces of all past IR radiation events. This memory of past events is fading exponentially with a timescale corresponding to the sensor’s so-called thermal time constant. We propose an image processing method that eliminates, at least partially, the memory effect of microbolometer cameras. It considers each pixel individually and removes from the current signal the influence of incident radiation history that is older than the pixel’s previous reading. Specifically, in any image, the memory of IR radiation events that took place before the previous image can be completely erased. Motion blur is therefore considerably reduced. Thanks to this patented procedure, the microbolometer camera can be considered as having evolved from a time-constant sensor (i.e., with infinite support) to an integration-time sensor (i.e., with finite support), much like cameras equipped with cooled photon detectors. This specific integration time corresponds to the delay between two readout cycles. Given this, it is possible to further reduce motion blur by increasing the camera’s readout frequency. The proposed method does not require complex deconvolution procedures, is independent on the direction of relative motion, is easy to implement, and can operate in real time.</jats:p>

title: Beyond hospitality: unpacking the role of hotel industry in catalyzing tourism-led inclusive growth in Jammu & Kashmir
container-title: Global Knowledge, Memory and Communication
e5e6b5eb12b0d2cef51a3a402060285f6d771259.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to examine the role of the hotel industry in promoting tourism-led inclusive growth (T-LIG) in the tourist destinations of Jammu and Kashmir, India. It investigates how hotels contribute to inclusive growth within the tourism sector and identifies various challenges that affect inclusive outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adopting a qualitative methodology, data were collected through semi-structured interviews with 32 hotel owners and managers, selected using purposive and snowball sampling techniques. Thematic analysis was conducted using NVivo 14 to uncover patterns and themes related to inclusive growth practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The analysis reveals that while the hotel sector generates employment and fosters local economic linkages, these contributions do not automatically translate into inclusive growth. Structural barriers, such as gender inequality, digital exclusion and inconsistent corporate social responsibility (CSR) practices, limit s broad-based participation. Larger hotels implement formal CSR initiatives, whereas small and medium-sized hotels support local communities through informal practices like local hiring and procurement.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study offers a unique hotel-level perspective on T-LIG by examining the hotel industry as a distinct operational node within the tourism sector and identifying the conditions that enable or constrain inclusive growth in the fragile destination of Jammu and Kashmir.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Ordinal Memory for Synchrophasor Reconstruction and Generator Coherency Monitoring Under Explicit Measurement Constraints
b0d43d7a8fb9bc31a5d7583eb6e79acc7e3d11d8.abstract: <jats:p>Phasor measurement unit (PMU) streams in smart grids lose packets in transit, yet compact learning mechanisms for filling these gaps are often compared without separating reconstruction accuracy from the measurements each method may acquire. This study evaluates a finite-memory ordinal mechanism (FMOM) under three explicit measurement contracts: passive packet arrival, paid queries to fixed snapshots and a common downstream generator-coherency tracker. Nine signal families combine public field recordings, generated events and nonlinear generator simulations; four loss regimes and three masks per episode yield 684 matched passive cases across 14 implementations. Under 50% independent loss, the passive ordinal adapter improved on its predecessor, route–offset recalibration (ROR), in seven of nine families but attained no family-level minimum, ranking third of ten primary implementations behind rolling singular-value decomposition and median shift. In the active pilot, five families required at least as many paid measurements as direct reading, and anchored sorting produced comparable errors. In the coherency pipeline, the IEEE 39-bus mean adjusted Rand index rose from 0.8284 (ROR) to 0.8417, while median shift reached 0.8505. Ordinal memory therefore offers useful but restricted gains, and measurement access, fallback state and reference definitions should be reported when smart grid monitoring algorithms are compared.</jats:p>
