title: <b>Understanding the Relationship Between Generative AI Dependence and Students’ Problem-Solving Ability: The Roles of Cognitive Offloading and AI Literacy</b>
container-title: International journal of interdisciplinary knowledge (IJIK)
86e180b1c3280076caacf8c4934f8727e895b5c2.abstract: <jats:p>Today, Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is quickly becoming a staple of university students' work, as it can provide instant answers to information search, writing, explanation and problem solving. While GenAI can aid in learning, overreliance can lessen students' independent thinking. This study explores the ties between generative AI reliance and students' problem-solving skills, focusing on cognitive offloading as a mediation factor and AI literacy as a moderation factor. A quantitative, cross-sectional research design is suggested with a sample of 100 University students. The data will be analyzed using descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, regression, mediation and moderation analysis through SPSS. The conceptual model suggests that students' problem-solving ability may be linked to their degree of cognitive offloading, which could be further linked to their reliance on GenAI. The authors suggest AI literacy as a boundary condition that could affect the relationship between GenAI dependence and problem solving ability. New studies suggest that students' use of GenAI in problem-solving is multi-layered and constructive, as well as thoughtless, and that there are four aspects of AI literacy: knowledge, application, evaluation, and understanding of ethical issues. Thus, the present study is centered on not only students' usage of GenAI, but also how reliance on GenAI can impact their thinking processes when addressing academic challenges.</jats:p>

title: Enhancing the actuation speed of Nitinol shape memory alloy wires via laser-induced surface modification
container-title: Journal of Intelligent Material Systems and Structures
2300de4a3ac68150aaa851e1ded15874d5c8b4f3.abstract: <jats:p>This study investigates laser surface modification to enhance the actuation kinetics of Nitinol Shape Memory Alloy (SMA) wires. Using an optimized 20 W laser power with 1 mm marking pitch, discrete Optical Discolored Region (ODR ∼15 µm) were introduced to modify the thermo-mechanical response. Experimental results demonstrated a 34% reduction in dynamic actuation time and a 57% increase in actuation velocity compared to the unmarked control at low voltage 1.78 V. Under isobaric loading (0.18–0.42 N), the modified actuators exhibited a distinct positive load-dependence, achieving a peak stroke of ∼26 mm at 0.42 N—significantly outperforming the pristine wire which suffered from stroke saturation. Thermal profiling confirmed that surface texturing improved heat rejection, lowering peak actuation temperatures by ∼15%. While cyclic testing revealed a beneficial ∼30% “training effect” in stroke amplitude, it also highlighted a stability trade-off with accumulated residual strain (∼4 mm) at high loads, indicating a need for mechanical pre-conditioning. Thermomechanical hysteresis analysis confirmed that the laser-induced microstructure mitigates blocking stress, maintaining superior energy density under heavy loads. These findings demonstrate that laser patterning is a viable technique for developing high-frequency, rapid-response SMA actuators.</jats:p>

title: No Memory Is an Island: How Social Interactions Transform Autobiographical Memory
container-title: The Neuroscientist
141dd402f7d784a64723b64e1fa3da0c00566853.abstract: <jats:p>Autobiographical memory is not merely a record of past events but a dynamic reconstruction shaped by context, emotion, and social interaction. In this hypothesis paper, we propose that empathic interactions can transform autobiographical memory, altering memory’s content, emotional tone, and integration into the self. We begin by outlining the social foundations of autobiographical memory and the neural systems involved in its transformation, focusing on the hippocampus, prefrontal cortex, and amygdala. We then explore how empathic exchanges may lead to changes in memory specificity and coherence, emotional reappraisal, and self-concept, particularly within psychotherapy and close relationships. Central to our framework is the proposal that interbrain synchrony, neural coupling across individuals during interaction, facilitates the co-construction of meaning and shared understanding. Crucially, we argue that distinct forms of empathic interaction and patterns of interbrain synchrony support different mechanisms of memory change, including contextual binding, emotional regulation, narrative reframing, and self-relevant integration. We discuss how these mechanisms support memory updating through repeated interpersonal engagement. Finally, we offer testable predictions of our model and consider clinical and societal implications. Our framework bridges memory research and social neuroscience and offers a novel, integrative direction for understanding memory as a phenomenon co-constructed through interactions.</jats:p>

title: Social Isolation and the Risk of Cognitive Decline and Dementia: Implications and Prevention Strategies
container-title: Indian Journal of Social Psychiatry
ad9314a0155a46d402f161dfa48ea16e3bb15495.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This narrative review examines the robust epidemiological link between social connectivity and cognitive health, illustrating how frequent social interaction serves as a protective factor against dementia, whereas social isolation and loneliness act as significant catalysts for cognitive decline. The mechanisms driving this association are complex and multifaceted, involving a synergy of psychological, behavioral, and physiological pathways; specifically, social isolation is shown to disrupt neuroplasticity, increase chronic stress responses, and elevate systemic inflammation, all of which accelerate neurodegenerative processes. To mitigate these risks, this paper advocates for a multitiered approach to intervention, emphasizing the integration of social prescribing within clinical practice, the development of national policies that prioritize age-friendly infrastructure, and the implementation of community-based initiatives designed to foster meaningful intergenerational and peer-to-peer engagement. By addressing social isolation as a critical public health priority, we can leverage social participation as a potent, nonpharmacological strategy to preserve cognitive function and enhance the quality of life for aging populations.</jats:p>

title: Data from Matrix Stiffness–Encoded Mechanical Memory Maintains Proliferative Dominance in Metastatic Tumors
a77151bd5ab76d3f363091f2c0abfd5841bfc293.abstract:
<jats:p><div>Abstract
<p>Primary and metastatic lesions share similar biological properties despite existing in different microenvironments. A better understanding of the mechanisms underlying the maintenance of phenotypic homogeneity in heterogeneous microenvironments could help identify strategies for suppressing metastasis. In this study, we found that mechanical memory enabled tumor cells to resist biomechanical stress and sustain malignant traits. Matrix stiffness activated the RhoA–ROCK1 signaling pathway, leading to actin cytoskeletal remodeling and suppression of mitochondrial fission. The dysregulation of mitochondrial dynamics enhanced fatty acid β-oxidation, leading to the accumulation of acetyl coenzyme A and subsequent histone hyperacetylation. The stiffness-mediated epigenetic reprogramming was mitotically heritable, allowing progeny cells to retain a proliferative advantage after detachment from stiff environments. Inhibition of RhoA–ROCK1 disrupted mechanical memory, thereby reducing metastasis. These findings suggest that targeting mechanical memory may be a strategy for preventing metastasis.</p>
Significance:<p>Matrix stiffness induces metabolic and epigenetic rewiring that creates a lasting memory in cancer cells that supports metastasis, revealing mechanical memory as a potential target for metastasis prevention.</p><p><a target="_blank" href="https://aacrjournals.org/cancerres/article-abstract/doi/10.1158/0008-5472.CAN-26-3004"><i>See related commentary by Kilian, p. 5313</i></a></p></div></jats:p>

title: Computational Link Between Motivational Factors and Cognitive Deficits in Depression
container-title: Cognitive Computation
8087338a9d83c515e2ae702ad5e043fdd2d6771d.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cognitive deficits are a common symptom of depression and contribute significantly to the disabling effects of the disorder. Experimentally, they are observed as increased reaction times, increased error rates, and deficient performance adaptation after making errors or receiving adverse feedback, in multiple cognitive paradigms. In the current study we aimed to address the cause of these cognitive deficits from a theoretical perspective. We constructed computational models of optimal resource allocation in two cognitive tasks – Delayed Match to Sample (DMS), and Eriksen Flanker (EF). The models explicitly link performance feedback values and beliefs about task controllability with measures of cognitive performance including accuracy, reaction times, and post-error improvement in accuracy (PIA). We then introduced depression-related motivational changes – altered control belief and feedback values (representing learned helplessness, anhedonic valuation and negative bias) – to see if these factors can account for deficits in cognitive performance. In the DMS task, altered control belief and lower valuation of correct performance accounted for decreased accuracy and decreased PIA. In the EF task, these two factors could explain increased response times, decreased accuracy and decreased error-related negativity (ERN) signal magnitude. Increased valuation of adverse feedback, on the other hand, was linked to increased EF accuracy and increased ERN signal magnitude. Furthermore, in the EF task, different combinations of depression-related motivational factors led to different patterns of cognitive performance, which could offer a basis for stratification. Our study offers a novel perspective on how cognitive deficits in depression can be viewed as consequences of altered motivational factors. The developed models provide an explicit computational and algorithmic bridge between the commonly observed cognitive deficits (increased reaction times, decreased performance accuracy, worse post-error adaptation) and factors such as learned helplessness and anhedonic valuation.</jats:p>

title: Combined therapy with Cortexin and Citicoline for cognitive and astheno-depressive disorders after gunshot-induced spinal cord injury
container-title: S.S. Korsakov Journal of Neurology and Psychiatry
ce733a0ebe1a1738e81e37c7a91c2fc4aff0f09c.abstract: <jats:p>Objective. To evaluate the efficacy and safety of combination therapy with Cortexin and Citicoline in patients with cognitive and astheno-depressive disorders resulting from gunshot spinal cord injury (SCI). Additionally, a comparative analysis of therapeutic efficacy was conducted based on the degree of neurological deficit as measured by the ASIA scale. Material and methods. The «Phoenix» prospective, open-label, longitudinal, comparative clinical study enrolled 60 patients aged 18—55 years undergoing the second stage of medical rehabilitation. Participants were assigned to four groups based on the severity of neurological deficit (ASIA A and ASIA C) and the therapy administered. Outcomes were measured using the MoCA, HDRS-17, asthenic state scale (ASS), HADS, VAS, and MAS questionnaires on Days 1, 15±2, 30±2, and 90±7. The study groups received combined neuro-metabolic therapy: Cortexin 10 mg intramuscularly once daily for 10 days and Recognan (citicoline) oral solution 1000 mg/day (10 mL) for 30 days. The comparison groups received standard therapy, which included pharmacological management of anxiety and depressive disorders as indicated, therapeutic exercises, physiotherapy, massage, and supportive treatment. Results. In patients with ASIA A severity of SCI, by Day 90, the median increase in MoCA score was 2 [1.75; 3.25] points in the combination therapy group, compared to 1.5 [1; 2] points in the comparison group. The decrease in HDRS-17 score was –10 [–12.25; –9] points versus –5 [–5.75; –2] points, and the decrease in ASS score was –33 [–34.25; –31.75] points versus –26 [–26; –25] points, respectively. A clinically significant reduction in HDRS-17 scores (≥50% from baseline) was achieved in 90% of patients in the combination therapy group and 20% in the comparison group. Among patients with ASIA C severity of SCI, the median increase in MoCA score was 2 [2; 3] points in the combination therapy group versus 1.5 [1; 2] points in the control group. HDRS-17 scores decreased by –12.5 [–14; –9] points versus –8 [–8.75; –6.25] points, and ASS scores decreased by –31 [–32; –30] points versus –22 [–23.75; –22] points, respectively. No serious adverse events were reported. Conclusions. Combined neurometabolic therapy may represent a promising component of comprehensive medical rehabilitation for patients with sequelae of SCIs who present with cognitive and emotional impairments.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive functioning and visual perception in patients with schizophrenia
container-title: S.S. Korsakov Journal of Neurology and Psychiatry
a0c6bea4bf6b62eb7aeb5c463b3f6686039b4753.abstract: <jats:p>Objective. To analyze visual perception characteristics in patients with schizophrenia and to establish the relationship between contrast sensation parameters and cognitive functioning metrics. Material and methods. A total of 40 patients diagnosed with schizophrenia and 20 healthy individuals serving as a control group were included in the study. Contrast sensation of the visual system was evaluated using computer-assisted visocontrastometry at low (0.4 cycles/degree), medium (1, 3, and 6 cycles/degree), and high (10 cycles/degree) spatial frequencies. Results. The findings indicate that contrast sensation in schizophrenia patients is statistically significantly lower (p<0.05) across all spatial frequency ranges when compared to control individuals. A positive correlation was identified between contrast sensitivity at high spatial frequencies and motor functions (r=0.405; p=0.009) and executive functions (r=0.321; p=0.042). The severity of neurocognitive deficits was found to be exclusively associated with the perception of high spatial frequencies (p=0.043). Conclusions. The results underscore the critical role of the parvocellular neural system in the manifestation of cognitive impairments in schizophrenia.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Engagement as a Key Mechanism of Cognitive Sustainability in the Age of Generative AI: An Interdisciplinary Framework
container-title: Applied Sciences
eacd36bcb90165310a86aad5ca8ec3f7566b4576.abstract: <jats:p>Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) systems can improve productivity, yet their long-term implications for human cognition remain contested. This article develops an interdisciplinary framework for explaining how different patterns in the distribution and support of cognitive operations between humans and GenAI may shape cognitive engagement and cognitive outcomes over time. The framework draws upon a Neuro-Information-Systems (NeuroIS)-informed approach by integrating cognitive, behavioral, self-report, and neurophysiological perspectives into a multilevel account of how GenAI use shapes human cognition. We argue that cognitive engagement—the depth, persistence, and strategic quality of human processing during AI-supported tasks—is a proposed central mechanism linking the distribution and support of cognitive operations between humans and GenAI to cognitive outcomes. Direct effects on outcomes may coexist with engagement-mediated effects on outcomes. The cognitive consequences depend particularly on whether cognitively consequential operations related to understanding, learning, critical evaluation, and independent judgment continue to involve meaningful human engagement. Specifically, the framework integrates five elements: (1) antecedent conditions (user, task, and GenAI/system characteristics); (2) regulatory processes (metacognition, trust calibration, and motivational/goal regulation); (3) human–AI cognitive work configuration and cognitive engagement (i.e., how cognitive operations are distributed between the user and the AI system and how cognitively engaged the user remains); (4) short- and intermediate-term outcomes (performance, understanding, retention, and agency); and (5) long-term outcomes of cognitive sustainability and cognitive dependence. The article derives design principles for engagement-preserving AI and contributes to an interdisciplinary research agenda for examining these relationships through convergent behavioral, self-report, neurophysiological, and longitudinal evidence.</jats:p>

title: AI Literacy and Innovative Behavior in AI-Assisted Learning: Cognitive and Affective Trust in AI and Creative Self-Efficacy as Sequential Pathways
container-title: Behavioral Sciences
3cc96e5a28b212ed9bd72f581bbddad4ae53b933.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) is increasingly embedded in higher education, yet how AI literacy relates to AI-assisted innovative behavior in learning (IBL) remains unclear. This cross-sectional study examined whether cognitive and affective trust in AI, together with creative self-efficacy (CSE), sequentially linked AI literacy to IBL. A sample of 1173 Chinese college students completed an online survey; gender, age, and AI use frequency were controlled. AI literacy was associated with IBL in total (β = 0.211, 95% CI [0.155, 0.267]), but the direct association was no longer significant once the mediators were included (β = 0.057, p = 0.056); the total indirect effect accounted for 73.2% of the total association. When both trust dimensions were modeled simultaneously, all seven specific indirect pathways were significant. The pathway through cognitive trust (0.093) exceeded that through affective trust (0.057; Δ = 0.036). Re-estimation under a symmetric covariate specification confirmed a modest antecedent asymmetry (Δ = 0.086), whereas the two trust dimensions did not differ reliably downstream. Cognitive trust thus appears to be the more readily mobilized gateway to IBL, whereas affective trust may require relationally supportive design. Single-wave self-reports preclude causal inference.</jats:p>

title: Circular Economy-Based Scenario Planning for Resilient Humanitarian Supply Chains: A Fuzzy Cognitive Mapping Approach
container-title: Systems
a3781264ad1b8abe5b1fc70593df95399379ddd5.abstract: <jats:p>This paper aims to develop a scenario-planning framework that integrates circular economy (CE) practices into humanitarian supply chains (HSCs) to enhance systemic resilience. Specifically, the research seeks to provide a strategic blueprint for humanitarian organizations to transition from traditional linear models to sustainable, resilient ecosystems that maintain high service levels amid extreme uncertainty. The study employs a mixed-methods design to develop and validate a framework for circular, resilient HSCs. The qualitative phase involves semi-structured interviews with experts to identify and contextualize key constructs related to CE and resilience in HSCs. In the second phase, Fuzzy Cognitive Mapping (FCM) models the causal relationships among the identified constructs, capturing the complexity and feedback dynamics inherent in HSCs. Finally, the study conducts a scenario analysis to assess the impact of alternative strategic configurations on overall system performance. The findings demonstrate that CE in resilient HSCs emerges from dynamic interactions among CE practices, adaptive capabilities, and collaborative system structures. Scenario planning further reveals that integrated strategies combining agility, local resource utilization, innovation, and policy support yield the highest levels of system adaptability and sustainability. This study contributes to the HSC resilience literature by integrating CE with scenario planning theory into a unified analytical framework. In practice, the study provides actionable insights for humanitarian organizations and practitioners by identifying key leverage points and strategic pathways for designing adaptive, regenerative, and sustainable humanitarian relief systems.</jats:p>

title: Viral Immunomodulation as a Potential Driver of Trained Immunity: Emerging Mechanisms of Innate Immune Memory and Antiviral Protection
container-title: Viruses
508c53c4210119af2e374f14149270c0507160b6.abstract: <jats:p>The discovery of trained immunity has challenged the longstanding view that immunological memory is restricted to the adaptive immune system. Trained immunity refers to the capacity of innate immune cells to undergo long-term functional reprogramming following exposure to microbial, endogenous, or environmental stimuli, resulting in enhanced responses to subsequent challenges. Trained immunity is mediated by epigenetic and metabolic remodeling, including changes in chromatin accessibility, histone modifications, and cellular metabolism. Recent studies further demonstrate that these memory-like properties can also be established in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells (HSPCs), providing a basis for their long-term persistence. While Bacillus Calmette–Guérin (BCG) and β-glucan are the best-characterized inducers of trained immunity, increasing evidence indicates that viral infections and viral vaccines can also induce durable innate immune reprogramming. Epidemiological studies have demonstrated heterologous protective effects associated with vaccinia, measles, and oral polio vaccines, while cytomegalovirus infection and severe SARS-CoV-2 infection have been linked to long-lasting alterations in innate immune function. Notably, many of these viruses possess potent immune evasion mechanisms that suppress interferon signaling, modulate NF-κB activation, disrupt antigen presentation, and alter myeloid cell function. We propose that viral immune evasion and immunomodulatory strategies may promote trained immunity by triggering compensatory metabolic, epigenetic, and transcriptional reprogramming that persists after resolution of infection. This review summarizes the historical development and molecular basis of trained immunity and examines emerging evidence linking viral infections and viral vaccines to innate immune memory. We further discuss the potential roles of virus-induced autophagy and long non-coding RNAs as mechanistic bridges connecting viral infection, immune reprogramming, and trained immunity. Understanding how viral infections shape innate immune memory may provide new opportunities for antiviral therapies, vaccine design, and broad-spectrum immune protection.</jats:p>

title: Integrating Applied Positive Psychology and Cognitive Prospection into Metabolic Self Regulation Beyond Glycemic Control
4ebee7c0a25a1a5077e7ef1bc85c3108e982418a.abstract: Conventional models of chronic illness self-regulation adhere to pathogenic, risk-avoidant paradigms that emphasize symptom prevention and rigid biomarker thresholds (e.g., HbA1c < 7.0%). Although indispensable for preventing microvascular and macrovascular pathology, this deficit-centered focus paradoxically depletes self-regulatory bandwidth, culminating in decision fatigue and diabetes-related distress. This paper proposes an applied psychometabolic paradigm that synthesizes Martin Seligman’s PERMA framework, Barbara Fredrickson’s Broaden-and-Build theory, and cognitive prospection—the mental generation and affective pre-experiencing of prospective states. We posit that postprandial glycemic volatility acts as an acute neuroenergetic disruptor, impairing prefrontal executive resources essential for emotional equilibrium, forward-oriented planning, and sustained work performance. To empirically ground this paradigm, a 7-day single-subject (N=1) dietary crossover investigation was performed under naturalistic conditions. Continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) interstitial traces were integrated with real-time ecological momentary assessments evaluating executive focus, affective stability, and physical stamina across three dietary regimens: (1) Unsequenced High-Glycemic Intake, (2) Targeted Intra-Meal Nutrient Sequencing, and (3) Microbiome-Directed Whole Foods with Active Ferments. Marked glycemic spikes during Phase 1 (peaking at 207 mg/dL) consistently elicited acute neurocognitive sluggishness, attention fragmentation, and severe collapses in self-rated executive focus (reaching nadirs of 1/10). Conversely, intra-meal nutrient sequencing (Phase 2) attenuated peak postprandial excursion to 124 mg/dL without restricting caloric density, while fiber-rich fermented nutrition (Phase 3) established post-meal recovery at 93.7 mg/dL alongside ceiling-level ratings of executive flow and positive affect (10/10). These observations indicate that somatic metabolic stability constitutes an essential physiological foundation for executive stamina and agentic prospection. Reconceptualizing dietary behavior from a burden of clinical compliance to a proximal driver of mental vitality provides a viable framework for applied positive psychology in health settings.

title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNs for Flexible Working Memory
7bfeefbdb3d57889d30ddf78aec4761cd1a899a1.abstract:
<jats:title>
                  A
                  <jats:sc>bstract</jats:sc>
                </jats:title>
                <jats:p>Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.</jats:p>

title: What Predicts Reading and Spelling in English as a Foreign Language? Cognitive and Linguistic Evidence from Young Learners in Germany
1f74914b60300869dd467e1ef69599821a0c7bce.abstract: This longitudinal study examined which cognitive and linguistic skills predict English as a foreign language (EFL) reading and spelling skills among elementary school children in Germany. A total of 107 learners (Mage = 10.52, SD = 0.64) were assessed at the beginning of Grade 3 on nonverbal intelligence, phonological short-term memory, phonological awareness, working memory, and English grammar and vocabulary. Linear mixed-effects models, with age, gender, and language background as covariates and classes and schools as random effects, predicted six literacy outcomes at the end of Grade 4: reading comprehension, pseudoword reading, oral reading rate and accuracy, and real-word and pseudoword spelling. Nonverbal intelligence and phonological awareness predicted reading comprehension, and English vocabulary made a smaller contribution. Beyond comprehension, other outcomes showed different significant predictors: phonological short-term memory predicted pseudoword reading, L2 receptive grammar and vocabulary predicted real-word spelling, and nonverbal intelligence predicted pseudoword spelling. Phonological awareness, assessed in German, did not uniquely predict decoding or spelling, and no variable predicted oral reading rate or accuracy. The predictors differed across literacy outcomes, suggesting that early EFL reading and spelling components do not rest on a uniform set of skills.

title: Effect of Repetitive Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation (rTMS) on Serum Neurofilament Light Chain (sNfL) and its Correlation to Cognitive Function in Multiple Sclerosis
container-title: NeuroRehabilitation
4779d966e17718fd9952e933394d2942aeea4d01.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is a non-invasive neuromodulatory technique that has emerged as a promising therapeutic intervention for various neurological disorders by modulating cortical excitability and neural plasticity. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic inflammatory demyelinating condition marked by central nervous system (CNS) lesions that can cause significant physical or cognitive disability, as well as neurological abnormalities. We now know that 40–70% of all MS patients have cognitive impairment that impairs their lives. Even in these so-called benign forms of the disease, 15 years after diagnosis, with an Expanded Disability Status Scale (EDSS) score of up to 3, cognitive abnormalities can be diagnosed in half of these patients.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To investigate whether high frequency (rTMS) can modify MS cognition assessed by clinical and serum Neurofilament Light Chain (sNfL).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Forty-five patients with relapsing-remitting multiple sclerosis (RRMS) were randomly allocated into three equal groups (n = 15 each): a 5-Hz rTMS group, an 18-Hz rTMS group, and a sham stimulation group. The treatment protocols were administered daily on five consecutive days weekly for 2 weeks over the vertex and left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (lt. DLPFC). Cognitive performance was assessed using the Brief International Cognitive Assessment for Multiple Sclerosis (BICAMS), comprising the Symbol Digit Modalities Test (SDMT), California Verbal Learning Test–Second Edition (CVLT-II), and Brief Visuospatial Memory Test–Revised (BVMT-R). Serum neurofilament light chain (sNfL) levels were measured as the secondary outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Repeated-measures ANOVA demonstrated significant time, group, and time-by-group interaction effects for sustained attention (SDMT), verbal learning and memory (CVLT-II), and visuospatial memory and learning (BVMT-R) (all
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       < 0.05). Both active rTMS groups showed greater short-term gains in cognitive performance compared with baseline and the sham group, with the greatest gain observed following left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (Lt. DLPFC) stimulation. However, these cognitive benefits were not maintained at the 3-month follow-up. No significant effects of rTMS were observed on serum neurofilament light chain (sNfL) levels. Correlation analysis revealed significant associations between cognitive performance and disability status, with CVLT-II scores negatively correlated with EDSS scores (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">r</jats:italic>
                       = −0.321,
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">P</jats:italic>
                       = 0.031).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These findings suggest that repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) applied over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex or vertex may provide short-term improvements in cognitive test performance, particularly in attention, verbal learning and memory, and visuospatial memory, with larger effects observed following Lt. DLPFC stimulation. However, these effects were transient and were not sustained at the 3-month follow-up, underscoring that any clinical benefit of the present protocol is short-lived rather than durable. By simultaneously evaluating cognitive outcomes alongside serum neurofilament light chain (sNfL), this integrated assessment of cognitive outcomes and sNfL adds a novel translational perspective to rTMS research in multiple sclerosis., this study offers a novel perspective on the possible biological correlates of cognitive change. The absence of significant changes in sNfL despite the observed cognitive changes is a hypothesis-generating observation, rather than direct mechanistic evidence, raising the hypothesis that these short-term cognitive changes may involve functional modulation of cortical networks rather than measurable changes in neuroaxonal injury. Given the exploratory nature and modest sample size of this trial, these findings support further investigation rather than establishing clinical efficacy.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: From “Stolen Data” to “Own Private Tutor”: Reasons of U.S. Higher Education Students’ (Non-)Adoption of ChatGPT
container-title: Journal of Educational Technology Systems
0c63614f5980e30ec8d8e6704f676a456cc9726b.abstract: <jats:p>This study explores U.S. higher education students’ motivations and hesitations regarding the use of ChatGPT for academic purposes. Drawing on a large corpus of open-ended survey responses, we conducted a qualitative thematic analysis of students who reported using ChatGPT and those who reported not using it. Guided by Uses and Gratifications theory, we identify nine themes that capture students’ reasons for use (e.g., learning and tutoring, content generation, brainstorming, expressing ideas, feedback and validation, research support, immediacy and convenience, task management, and exploration and entertainment) and six themes that capture reasons for non-use (e.g., ethical concerns, lack of need or interest, limited awareness, accuracy/privacy concerns, and moral opposition and principled resistance against AI). Findings show that students approach ChatGPT (or not) as a flexible support tool whose perceived value is context-dependent and shaped by academic demands, perceived risks, and values about authentic learning.</jats:p>

title: A Bioinformatics-Integrated Biochemistry E-Module in Problem-Based Learning: Effects on the Cognitive Dimension of Collaborative Problem-Solving Skills
container-title: Florea : Jurnal Biologi dan Pembelajarannya
cf2e8913a3ffd465df8a7c66f918f4d80f131601.abstract: <jats:p>This study aimed to examine the association between a bioinformatics-integrated Biochemistry e-module in Problem-Based Learning (PBL) and students’ cognitive collaborative problem-solving skills. A nonrandomized control group pretest–posttest quasi-experimental design was employed involving 62 undergraduate Biology Education students at Universitas Negeri Malang, comprising 31 students in each class. Both classes received PBL, with the experimental class using a bioinformatics-integrated Biochemistry e-module and the control class using a Biochemistry website. PubChem, KEGG Pathway, RCSB PDB, and PyMOL were incorporated as bioinformatics resources. Data were collected using a cognitive collaborative problem-solving test and analyzed using ANCOVA, with pretest scores as the covariate. Mean scores increased from 70.4 to 88.5 in the experimental class and from 67.2 to 81.4 in the control class. ANCOVA revealed a significant adjusted difference between the classes (F = 26.284, p < 0.001, partial η² = 0.308), with adjusted means of 88.1 and 81.7 for the experimental and control classes, respectively. These findings indicate that the use of a bioinformatics-integrated Biochemistry e-module in PBL was associated with higher cognitive collaborative problem-solving scores than the use of a Biochemistry website.</jats:p>

title: Rodent strain differences in sensory function and gating: implications for cognitive phenotyping and brain disease models
container-title: Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience
ff688bbfc3bd96e0a448c5eee551df526b28ad9b.abstract: <jats:p>Rodent strain differences are well established, yet their implications for sensory-dependent cognitive phenotyping are not always adequately distinguished from effects of substrain divergence, experimental environment, or disease-related manipulations. This review synthesizes evidence that auditory and visual function, sensory and sensorimotor gating, and task-dependent behavioral strategies shape how cognitive phenotypes are expressed and interpreted across commonly used mouse and rat populations. Direct comparative studies reveal strain- and age-dependent variation in auditory thresholds, visual acuity, prepulse inhibition, habituation, and auditory evoked responses. These differences can affect access to task-relevant stimuli and the interpretation of behavioral measures without necessarily indicating deficits in learning or memory. We further examine strain-related differences in hippocampal synaptic plasticity, GABAergic inhibition, interneuron composition, and network oscillations, while distinguishing ex vivo network phenotypes from demonstrated mechanisms in behaving animals. Thalamic reticular nucleus–auditory thalamic and mediodorsal thalamus–prefrontal cortex pathways are considered plausible candidate circuit substrates; direct evidence that they mediate inter-strain cognitive differences remains limited. Studies of genetically modified and brain disease models additionally show that genetic background can amplify, attenuate, or leave unchanged mutation-associated phenotypes, making both strong and limited background effects informative. Within an integrative sensory–cognitive gating framework, we propose a strain-informed approach emphasizing precise population identification, task-relevant sensory assessment, appropriate genetic controls, complementary behavioral readouts, and background validation proportional to the intended scope of inference. This framework serves as a guide to interpretation rather than an established causal pathway, with the aim of improving reproducibility, mechanistic interpretation, and the translational relevance of rodent models.</jats:p>

title: Development and Validation of a ChatGPT-Based Assessment for Conversation-Related Clinical Skills in Occupational Therapy OSCEs
container-title: American Journal of Occupational Therapy
d57747fec4997984a73386d42ed016fea5a107c2.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Importance</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Conversation-related clinical skills are central to Objective Structured Clinical Examinations (OSCEs) in occupational therapy. However, real-time examiner scoring is resource-intensive and may overlook students’ specific skills. Transcript-based scoring with Chat Generative Pre-Trained Transformer (ChatGPT) may address these limitations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To develop a ChatGPT-based assessment for chief-complaint interview OSCEs (G-ACE) and examine criterion validity against expert-consensus ratings, test–retest reliability, and inter-rater reliability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Secondary analysis of de-identified transcripts from 8-min chief-complaint interviews with a simulated patient with stroke during an OSCE.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Settings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A university in northern Taiwan.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Participants</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fifty-eight de-identified transcripts from undergraduate occupational therapy students.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Criterion validity was acceptable for “Primary Symptoms and Related Feelings” and “Impact on Daily Life” items (weighted kappa ≥ 0.60), but lower for “Rehabilitation Expectations” and “Communication Skills” items (0.18–0.59). For domain and total scores, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs) were 0.17 to 0.78 and percentages of mean absolute errors (MAE%s) were 4.6% to 20.7%. Test–retest reliability was acceptable at the item level (weighted kappa = 0.68–1.00), and acceptable to good at the domain and total score levels (ICC = 0.65–0.85; MAE% = 2.3%–9.1%). Inter-rater reliability was acceptable for most domain and total scores (ICCs = 0.52–0.78; MAE%s = 1.3%–12.0%), except for the “Rehabilitation Expectations” domain (ICCs = 0.17–0.30; MAE%s = 1.3%–7.3%).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion and Relevance</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The G-ACE demonstrated generally acceptable test–retest reliability and small absolute differences from expert ratings for domain and total scores. Because some items showed lower consistency with expert ratings, formative feedback should be interpreted cautiously based on transcript evidence.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: White matter injury, brain aging, and cognitive decline beyond amyloid/tau
container-title: Journal of Alzheimer’s Disease
c841eb0fb927e205a78cb1aa86db7730109fad32.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>White matter injury in Alzheimer's disease is etiologically heterogeneous. Brain-predicted age difference (Brain-PAD) may capture structural vulnerability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To test whether T1-weighted white matter signal abnormality burden (T1W-WMSA) is associated with Brain-PAD and whether Brain-PAD predicts cognitive decline and mild cognitive impairment (MCI)-to-Alzheimer's disease progression beyond white matter injury and amyloid/tau (A/T) status.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Harmonized data from the Alzheimer's Disease Sequencing Project Phenotype Harmonization Consortium (ADSP-PHC) were anchored to the cardiovascular-risk baseline. Cross-sectional regression tested associations between cardiovascular risk and T1W-WMSA and between T1W-WMSA and Brain-PAD. Mixed-effects and Cox models assessed cognitive decline and progression. We also evaluated sex interactions and A/T timing. Fluid-attenuated inversion recovery-derived white matter hyperintensity burden (FLAIR-WMH) was examined as a modality comparison.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Among 601 complete cases, cardiovascular-risk burden was not associated with T1W-WMSA (β = −0.0003, 95% confidence interval [CI] −0.0470 to 0.0463; p = 0.989), whereas T1W-WMSA was associated with higher Brain-PAD (β = 6.95 years per log-unit, 95% CI 5.71 to 8.19; p < 0.001). Among 369 participants, higher Brain-PAD predicted faster memory (β = −0.0244 per year; p < 0.001) and executive-function decline (β = −0.0153 per year; p < 0.001). Among 201 participants with MCI, Brain-PAD predicted progression to Alzheimer's disease (hazard ratio [HR] = 1.268, 95% CI 1.191 to 1.351; p < 0.001). The association persisted in the pre-outcome A/T-adjusted subset (HR = 1.333, 95% CI 1.203 to 1.477; p < 0.001). No prespecified sex interaction survived false-discovery-rate correction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>White matter injury was associated with older-appearing brain structure but should not be interpreted as exclusively vascular. Brain-PAD provided prognostic information complementary to A/T staging and white matter lesion burden.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Metabolic memory in fruit ripening: bidirectional crosstalk between metabolism and epigenetic regulation
container-title: Frontiers in Plant Science
a6522cf8cd1026da00899ea1d244d3df9583c2d7.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Fruit ripening is a complex developmental process traditionally viewed as being regulated by hormones, transcription factors, and epigenetic modifications in a largely unidirectional manner—with epigenetics acting upstream and metabolism downstream. However, emerging evidence challenges this linear paradigm, revealing that key metabolic intermediates function not merely as outputs of ripening but as critical inputs that shape the epigenetic landscape. This review synthesizes recent advances demonstrating that S-adenosylmethionine (SAM), acetyl-CoA, and NAD
                    <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                    serve as core metabolic “fuels,” with ethylene and polyamines acting as downstream branches and feedback amplifiers within the SAM hub that directly modulate the activity of DNA methyltransferases, histone acetyltransferases, and sirtuin deacetylases, while epigenetic marks may reinforce metabolic states through positive feedback loops. Recent studies have further revealed that metabolic intermediates function as nexus points bridging phytohormone signaling and epigenetic regulation, with SAM, acetyl-CoA, and NAD
                    <jats:sup>+</jats:sup>
                    serving dual functions in both hormone biosynthesis and epigenetic modifications. We propose that this metabolic–epigenetic bidirectional crosstalk may constitute a “metabolic memory”-like mechanism that contributes to the irreversibility of fruit ripening, rather than providing a fully established explanation. In this review, we operationally define fruit-ripening metabolic memory as a self-reinforcing regulatory state in which metabolic intermediates alter epigenetic marks, and these marks persist beyond the initial metabolic signal and feed back to stabilize metabolic and ripening gene expression programs. Recent transgenic tomato studies engineered to overaccumulate spermidine and spermine provide evidence consistent with this model: metabolic activity was revived even at late developmental stages, with reactivation of cellular programs underlying nitrogen: carbon signaling, energy and glucose metabolism. However, we distinguish direct mechanistic evidence, functional evidence, and correlative evidence throughout the review, and we present the integrated model as a testable framework. By integrating findings from tomato, strawberry, apple, banana, peach, and grape, we present a unified framework in which metabolism and epigenetics operate as an interconnected regulatory network rather than as separate hierarchical layers. We also identify critical knowledge gaps and outline future directions, including the need for real-time metabolic flux analysis coupled with epigenomic profiling, single-cell resolution studies, and exploration of transgenerational inheritance of ripening-related metabolic memory.
                  </jats:p>

title: A Multilevel Dataset on Productive Cognitive Friction and Responsible AI-Augmented Business Judgment Under Two Active GenAI Conditions
container-title: Data
6c6bdbe9e8966d3a2f8b94444553927da27f2d35.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can expand analytical support but may encourage premature acceptance and insufficient verification. This article presents a multilevel, multimethod dataset generated during a five-week study within ten-week undergraduate courses at a private university in Mexico. The study involved 120 students in 24 pre-existing teams across four sections and two disciplinary contexts. Teams were assigned within sections to two active GenAI conditions: strategic analysis and executive recommendation, or a productive-cognitive-friction condition adding structured uncertainty, simulation, role-based scenarios, stakeholder and ethical analysis, temporal-emotional reflection, and accountability safeguards. Of 118 consenting participants, 114 met the main quantitative-analysis criteria. The release includes de-identified pre/post responses to the 16-item responsible AI-augmented business judgment (RABJ) instrument; neutral individual performance independently assessed by two evaluators; original and neutral team rubric ratings; expert content-validity ratings; numeric qualitative codes; fidelity and assignment metadata; processed data; aggregate outputs; and reproducible notebooks. Technical validation covers integrity, missingness, reliability, interrater and intercoder agreement, content validity, exploratory structure, cluster-aware reproducibility, and disclosure risk. RABJ is a provisional multidimensional framework, not a validated four-factor construct. Direct identifiers, student-generated text, submitted work, and institutional linkage keys are excluded.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive Regulation in Generative AI Use: A Network Study of Anxiety and Dependence Among Foreign Language Majors
container-title: Journal of Intelligence
aa0297df2ca3706ca2352b70e2f90bebdd206d70.abstract: <jats:p>Anxiety accompanying students’ reliance on generative AI has been linked to appraisals of their own competence and to comparison with peers, two complementary routes usually modeled separately. This study asked which nodes retain conditional associations with AI-related anxiety and dependence when both routes are modeled together. Survey responses from 283 foreign language majors formed a 17-node regularized partial correlation network, supplemented by written responses from 21 students. Social-comparison anxiety was the only anxiety node connected with dependence (partial r = 0.177, 95% bootstrap interval [0.077, 0.280]); exploratory facet analyses located it mainly in fear of falling behind or missing out, less consistently in peer competence pressure, and not in upward comparison. The three measured self-appraisal nodes, which assessed broad confidence, were unrelated to anxiety conditionally and at the zero-order level. The dependence association was modest, had no resolved direction, and was retained only in the fourth-year network; no cohort difference was established, and study year was confounded with collection period. Written responses did not corroborate this association but revealed integrity boundaries, guilt, and redefined language competence, which the survey omitted. The findings identify candidate correlates of reliance that require replication in independent samples, and content missing from AI anxiety instruments.</jats:p>

title: Development of Cognitive Processes in L2 Reading Comprehension: A Longitudinal Bayesian Knowledge Tracing Study of Chinese EFL University Students
container-title: Journal of Intelligence
fe0e0e47ef26d7a5fd1956d47f11294310ee092f.abstract: <jats:p>Understanding how the cognitive processes underlying second language (L2) reading comprehension change over time is crucial for characterizing reading development among English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. Guided by Kintsch’s Construction–Integration (C-I) model and Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST), this study examines the development of four cognitive processes in reading comprehension in terms of longitudinal changes in their estimated mastery: extracting explicit information, interpreting and rephrasing information, making inferences, and synthesizing information across text. Data from 303 undergraduate EFL learners across three semesters were analyzed using Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT), with item difficulty incorporated to improve the estimation of process mastery. The results showed differentiated trajectories of estimated mastery across the four processes. Extracting explicit information and making inferences showed increases in estimated mastery, whereas interpreting and rephrasing information and synthesizing information across text changed more slowly. Cluster analysis further identified four learner profiles based on estimated mastery changes (Early Decliners, Moderate Maintainers, Imbalanced Performers, and Advanced Achievers), highlighting substantial variability in EFL reading development. These findings advance understanding of L2 reading comprehension by showing that component cognitive processes follow differentiated and heterogeneous trajectories over time, and also demonstrating the utility of BKT for tracing process-level changes from longitudinal item-response data.</jats:p>

title: Q-Matrix Completeness for Multiple-Choice Items in Cognitive Diagnosis
container-title: Psychometrika
062910f00f72f74dbc6704f4e2b660bc59f8867a.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Research in the development of cognitive diagnosis (CD) methods for multiple-choice (MC) items has advanced. However, some key statistical properties of the Q-matrix for MC items remain unexplored. One such critical property is completeness, which, when satisfied, ensures that all possible attribute profiles in the data can be identified. An incomplete Q-matrix may result in the misclassification of examinees, leading to distorted interpretations of results and misguided pedagogical interventions. Moreover, a complete Q-matrix is a fundamental assumption in several important areas of CD research, such as model identifiability. In light of these undesirable consequences, this study aims to establish sufficient and necessary conditions for determining the completeness of the Q-matrix for MC items. However, this problem is not a simple extension of the corresponding one for binary items, because an MC item may contain additional diagnostic information through its coded distractors. Consequently, conditions that are sufficient and necessary for completeness in the binary setting may no longer be necessary in the MC setting. To support the proposed theorem, a lemma is developed, followed by corollaries that enhance its applicability. All theoretical advancements are rigorously justified through formal mathematical proofs. Subsequently, a simulation study is conducted to illustrate the implication of the proposed theorem.</jats:p>

                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Surgical technologists must increasingly anticipate surgeons’ needs and develop cognitive understanding of surgical procedures to support intraoperative performance. However, limited evidence exists on integrating cognitive task analysis–based simulation as a pre-class activity within flipped classroom models for surgical technology students. This study evaluated whether a Touch Surgery–based flipped classroom improves knowledge, cognitive performance, and motivation compared with a conventional flipped classroom.</jats:p>

                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This randomized controlled trial (pretest–posttest design) was conducted from February to May 2026 with 67 surgical technology students at Ardabil University of Medical Sciences. Participants were randomly allocated to an intervention group (Touch Surgery simulation-based flipped classroom) or a control group (flipped classroom with narrated PowerPoint materials). Data were collected using a demographic questionnaire, a researcher-developed knowledge and cognitive performance test, and the Course Interest Survey (CIS).</jats:p>

                    <jats:p>
                      Both groups showed significant improvements in knowledge and cognitive performance from pre-test to post-test (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                       < 0.05). While no significant between-group difference was observed in post-test knowledge scores (

                       > 0.05), the intervention group demonstrated significantly higher post-test cognitive performance compared with the control group (
                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>

                      <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>

title: Psychometric Properties of a Patient-Centered Quality of Life Questionnaire After Subarachnoid Hemorrhage: A New Approach
container-title: Cognitive and Behavioral Neurology
ecfb61070b085c49601506f88d6a5eea40ddc93f.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) is a severe condition associated with high morbidity and mortality. However, many individuals classified as having favorable functional outcomes still report persistent cognitive deficits, fatigue, emotional disturbances, reduced social participation, and impaired return to work. Standard tools used to assess health-related quality of life (HRQoL) after SAH, such as the Medical Outcomes Short-Form Health Survey and the Stroke-Specific Quality of Life scale (SSQoL), may not fully capture these individual perspectives.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To evaluate the reliability and construct validity of the Patient-Generated Index (PGI) for HRQoL assessment after SAH.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Individuals who experienced SAH completed the PGI. We then tested construct validity by correlation with the SSQoL. We tested reliability through intra- and interobserver intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs). The International Classification of Functioning, Disability and Health framework (ICF) was used to classify reported health-related issues.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The PGI showed moderate correlation with the SSQoL (r=0.53) and excellent intra- and interobserver reliability (ICC = 0.91; ICC = 0.94). ICF linking identified 146 categories, mainly in Participation (55), Body Functions and Body Structures (52), and Activities (27). Emotional and behavioral challenges, such as fear, fatigue, and difficulty with work and social roles, were prominent. Immediate family was the only environmental factor cited.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The PGI is a valid, reliable, and patient-centered tool for assessing HRQoL after SAH, offering valuable input for rehabilitation planning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Role-Aware and Type-Aware Hyper-Relational Knowledge Graph Completion
container-title: Big Data and Cognitive Computing
fb18000519f4eb606f9323bae8a7cf98709a8786.abstract: <jats:p>Knowledge graphs are foundational to structured knowledge representation and drive the evolution of artificial intelligence from data-driven to knowledge-enhanced paradigms. Hyper-relational knowledge graphs employ hyperedge structures to overcome the expressive limitations of conventional triple-based schemes in modeling complex multi-entity facts with intricate dependency constraints. However, prevailing completion methods prioritize global structural patterns while neglecting entity role dependencies and type-level semantic priors, rendering them vulnerable to data sparsity and semantic noise. This study proposes RATA, a hyper-relational knowledge graph completion model that integrates role-aware and type-aware mechanisms to mitigate these drawbacks. The model uniformly encodes hyper-relational facts through hyperedge representations and captures global semantics using a bidirectional node–hyperedge attention module. It leverages role-aware sequence modeling to explicitly represent entity semantic roles and incorporates entity type priors to construct hierarchical semantics for aligning instance- and type-level information, thereby fusing structural, role-semantic, and type-prior knowledge. Evaluations on JF17K, WD50K, and WikiPeople show that RATA achieves competitive performance on entity and relation completion tasks. Ablation experiments validate the effectiveness of its hyperedge global encoding, role-aware modeling, and type-aware representation learning modules, indicating that RATA provides viable technical support for complex hyper-relational knowledge graph completion.</jats:p>

title: Feasibility and Acceptability of a Nurse-Led Active Music Program for Older Adults with Cognitive Impairment in Long-Term Care: A Pilot Quasi-Experimental Study
container-title: Healthcare
6453710acec2642eb7a22f128859979d662a486d.abstract: <jats:p>Background/Objectives: Older adults with cognitive impairment living in long-term care facilities are a vulnerable population with complex cognitive, emotional, and social care needs. This pilot study evaluated the feasibility and acceptability of a structured, nurse-led active music program and explored preliminary changes in cognitive function, depressive symptoms, and session-based engagement. Methods: A single-group quasi-experimental pre–post study was conducted in one long-term care facility. Eleven residents were enrolled, and nine completed an eight-session, four-week group intervention led by a registered nurse. Feasibility was assessed through retention, attendance, and intervention delivery, and acceptability through satisfaction and willingness to participate again. Cognitive function and depressive symptoms were assessed using the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA) and the 15-item Geriatric Depression Scale (GDS-15), respectively. Participation, sustained attention, and social interaction were recorded during each session. Pre–post changes were analyzed using exact Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results: Retention was 81.8%. Among participants who completed the intervention, attendance was 100% (72/72 scheduled participant-sessions). Satisfaction was 5.00 ± 0.00, and all participants reported that they would be willing to participate again. Engagement scores were moderate to high across sessions. MoCA scores increased from 22.89 ± 2.20 to 23.89 ± 2.03 (p = 0.016), whereas GDS-15 scores showed no significant change (6.33 ± 1.00 vs. 6.00 ± 1.00; p = 0.250). Conclusions: The nurse-led active music program showed favorable feasibility and acceptability indicators in this long-term care setting. Preliminary findings regarding cognitive function warrant further investigation in larger controlled studies, whereas no measurable change in depressive symptoms was observed.</jats:p>

title: Governing Highly Capable Human–Machine Systems Through Authority, Memory, and Consequence
container-title: Information
9565ad73645f0edfd8d7af9018823b2f5ede2c0b.abstract: <jats:p>Increasingly capable AI systems can generate proposals, invoke tools, and create institutional commitments. Their cognitive performance does not establish their authority to act. This conceptual systems article develops governed systemic intelligence as an assurance framework for human–machine systems, rather than redefining intelligence to include governance. It distinguishes capability, epistemic justification, operational authorization, and normative legitimacy. A structured synthesis of intelligence, augmentation, cybernetics, computer security, provenance, and AI oversight motivates eight architectural requirements: ratified purpose, capability–authority separation, bounded authorization, authoritative memory, consequence closure, ratified learning, governed continuity, and external verifiability. A unified traceability matrix connects each requirement to an evaluation criterion, evidence artifact, and omission counterexample. Predicates over an explicit system model separate governance conformance from measured augmentation and from the stronger claim of domain-superhuman performance. A worked hypothetical prior-authorization episode illustrates all eight requirements, while a numerical coherence-debt example makes unresolved discrepancies and missing outcomes visible. Mindful Machines and a conventional policy-and-workflow stack provide alternative implementation mappings. Previously reported implementations support component feasibility and governance-path execution but do not establish complete conformance, scalable oversight, or superhuman capability. The contribution is an assurance-case pattern that composes authority, memory, continuity, and correction obligations into testable claims, with explicit limits under adversarial behavior, institutional capture, and incomplete consequence observation.</jats:p>

title: The Displacement Journey of Armenians from Artsakh (Nagorno-Karabakh): Social Space, Memory, and Experiences of Survival
container-title: Societies
b5953cc2aad795bc20948defc31dad31cdb7d7aa.abstract: <jats:p>A growing body of forced-migration scholarship recognizes the journey as a socially consequential phase of displacement, yet less attention has been paid to how mobility, political control, social relations, vulnerability, and memory-making intersect during rapid collective displacement. This article examines the September 2023 displacement of Armenians from Artsakh (Nagorno-Karabakh) through the Lachin Corridor as a social, political, affective, and mnemonic space. Drawing on 60 semi-structured interviews conducted across Armenia between March 2024 and March 2026, it analyzes how displaced people experienced and subsequently narrated the journey. The findings show that the route was structured by scarcity, waiting, surveillance, and unequal mobility while also becoming a temporary social world sustained through family coordination and cooperation among strangers. The article develops mobile solidarity to describe temporary relations of reciprocity, care, cooperation, and informal authority generated through forced movement, and compressed traumatic space to describe the concentration of insecurity, loss, and uncertainty within a restricted route and period. It further conceptualizes the Lachin Road as an emergent mnemonic landscape, shaped partly through anticipatory remembering during departure. The article advances the displacement journey as a distinct analytical category linking mobility, power, social relations, vulnerability, and memory.</jats:p>

title: Chronic kidney disease as a natural model of accelerated cognitive ageing: mechanisms and novel therapeutic directions"
container-title: Clinical Kidney Journal
23e73b47a1403bc5cbd1e5f6d94d7e9b9f4f2ba4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Cognitive impairment is common in chronic kidney disease (CKD), affecting approximately 40% of patients and increasing sharply as kidney function declines. CKD accelerates many pathophysiological mechanisms shared with brain ageing, with implications for, rather than any equivalence to, the neurodegenerative diseases associated with dementia, notably Alzheimer’s disease and Lewy body dementia. Furthermore, CKD introduces distinct injuries that further amplify these pathways. The convergent mechanisms include cerebral small vessel disease, chronic neuroinflammation, blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption, accumulation of neurotoxic uraemic solutes, gut-brain-kidney axis dysbiosis, and impaired glymphatic clearance; superimposed on these, haemodialysis imposes repeated episodes of acute cerebral haemodynamic stress. Recent evidence also highlights the kidney’s failure to clear circulating aggregation-prone proteins, such as amyloid-β and α-synuclein. Because these processes develop earlier and progress more rapidly in CKD than in the general ageing population, they effectively create a ‘time-compressed’ version of age-related cognitive decline. In this review, we propose reconceptualising CKD as a prevalent clinical model of accelerated cognitive decline. We examine converging evidence from epidemiology, neuroimaging, and molecular studies to support this hypothesis. Finally, we discuss how emerging therapies—ranging from targeted adsorbents and Klotho replacement to microbiome modulation and preventive immunology—are testable hypotheses in CKD, with possible relevance for dementia in the wider ageing population.</jats:p>

title: Association between frailty and cognitive performance across healthcare settings
73767be4fcf467a0d058151141ced0d9847db0a2.abstract: Objective: To examine the association between frailty and longitudinal cognitive decline in older adults across different healthcare settings. Methods: This is a multicenter longitudinal cohort study. A total of 1,440 individuals aged ≥75 years from five European countries were recruited from four clinical settings: geriatric inpatient wards, geriatric outpatient clinics, primary care, and nursing homes. Cognitive outcomes were assessed using the Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) and the Clinical Dementia Rating (CDR) at baseline and after 1-year follow-up. Frailty was evaluated using eight instruments: the Frailty Phenotype, FRAIL scale, SHARE-FI, 3-item Frailty Trait Scale (FTS-3), 5-item Frailty Trait Scale (FTS-5), 35-item Frailty Index (FI-35), Gérontopôle Frailty Screening Tool (GFST), and the Clinical Frailty Scale (CFS). To explore the association between frailty and cognitive decline, we used linear regression (MMSE), and logistic regression models (CDR). All models were adjusted for age, sex, and Charlson Comorbidity Index and stratified by clinical setting. Results: Among the 1,440 participants included from five European countries, most frailty scales were significantly associated with cognitive decline and clinically significant cognitive impairment. Particularly the FI-35 [△MMSE β (95%CI) -2.00 (-2.32, -1.69); CDR OR (95%CI) 4.81 (3.78, 6.13)] and FTS-5 △MMSE β (95%CI) -2.02 (-2.37, -1.66); CDR OR (95%CI) 4.49 (3.40, 5.93) scale, showed the most consistent associations with both cognitive outcomes. Although the magnitude of associations varied across healthcare settings, frailty measures remained significant predictors in several environments, particularly in hospital-based and institutional settings. Conclusions: Frailty is strongly associated with cognitive decline in older adults across different care settings. Incorporating frailty assessment into routine clinical practice may facilitate earlier identification of individuals at risk of cognitive decline and support the development of targeted preventive strategies.

8d1c44e4a254c4cacbcd550dd03ae93f61f33462.abstract: <jats:p>Impairments in balance, stepping and executive function are apparent in many neurological conditions. To address these key risk factors for falls, we have developed an interactive cognitive-motor training program (SmartStep), integrating fast, multidirectional stepping in response to cognitively challenging stimuli. We are now investigating its effectiveness in cancer survivors with chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) (CanSTEP trial) and in people post stroke (SmartStepStroke trial).More than 30 % of cancer survivors are affected by CIPN at six months post neurotoxic chemotherapy treatment. CIPN manifests in sensory and neuromuscular impairments, which in the lower limbs lead to balance and mobility deficits. Despite the ever-increasing burden of CIPN-related disability in cancer survivors, current management is inadequate. There is evidence from small-scale trials of the benefits of exercise, particularly balance training, on neuropathy symptoms in cancer survivors. No studies have examined the effect of exercise on cognitive performance, which is another common complaint raised by 20 to 30 % of CIPN patients and attributed to cancer and/or its treatments. Yet people with CIPN show cognitive-motor function deficits, evidenced by slow and variable stepping response and movement times in tests of choice-stepping reaction time (Menant et al., 2021). The CanSTEP randomised-controlled trial will determine whether four months of the SmartStep training can reduce neuropathy symptoms and improve balance and mobility, compared with usual care (wait-list controls), in people with CIPN. This multi-centre trial is ongoing (n= 106 of target 178), involving adults at least six months post-completion of neurotoxic chemotherapy treatment for cancer, with CIPN symptoms affecting lower limbs.Stroke is a leading cause of long-term physical disability, with over 12 million stroke incidents occurring worldwide each year. Many stroke survivors face balance and mobility challenges and functional dependency due to impaired lower limb muscle strength, control, and coordination. Traditional rehabilitation methods, like repetitive task training, can improve mobility and balance. However, they often require frequent visits to rehabilitation clinics and involve monotonous exercises, making it difficult for people to adhere to the recommended routines, thereby limiting functional improvements. Exergames are increasingly being used in stroke rehabilitation, as they are designed to be enjoyable and to encourage continued participation. However, most programs to date have been centre-based (Lapanan et al., 2026). Hence our pilot trial aims to investigate the effectiveness of four-months of home-based SmartStep training, versus usual care (wait-list controls), balance and mobility, in people with chronic stroke. The trial is ongoing (n=37 of target 86), involving adults at least six months post-stroke reporting balance and mobility difficulties.I will first give a brief overview of our recent research findings that demonstrated the effectiveness of home-based interactive cognitive-motor step training on falls in older adults (Sturnieks et al., 2024) and stepping performance in people with multiple sclerosis (Hoang et al., 2024). I will then present baseline data from both trials highlighting participants' physiological, cognitive and psychological determinants of their impaired functional mobility. I will also discuss potential mechanisms underlying the hypothesized benefits of this intervention on balance and mobility in these clinical groups, based on recent research.</jats:p>

title: Temporal cortical gray matter volume relates to symptom improvement during cognitive behavioral therapy for depression

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is a first-line treatment for depression, yet treatment responses vary considerably. Understanding neurobiological factors associated with symptom improvement may help elucidate mechanisms underlying therapeutic change. This study investigated whether baseline cortical gray matter volume (GMV) is associated with reductions in depressive symptom severity during CBT. Therefore,
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 52 patients with unipolar affective disorders and at least mild depressive symptoms (according to BDI-II) and
                    <jats:italic>n</jats:italic>
                     = 42 healthy controls underwent clinical assessments and structural MRI at baseline; depressive symptom severity was reassessed after six months of outpatient CBT. Multiple regression analyses examined associations between pre-treatment cortical GMV and reductions in depressive symptoms under false discovery rate (FDR) correction. Additional models included anxiety, perceived stress, and childhood trauma as predictors. Compared to controls, patients exhibited significantly higher depressive symptom severity at baseline and greater symptom reduction over time (all
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                     < 0.001). Within patients, baseline GMV of the right middle temporal gyrus (MTG) was significantly associated with symptom reduction (baseline–follow-up; β = 0.55,
                    <jats:italic>p</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sub>FDR</jats:sub>
                     = 0.033). Right MTG volume accounted for additional variance in symptom reduction beyond established clinical variables (Δ
                    <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                    ² = 0.15). Group differences in GMV did not remain significant following FDR correction. These findings suggest that temporal gyrus GMV is associated with symptom improvement following CBT in unipolar depression, extending the focus beyond traditionally emphasized limbic regions.
