title: Green AI for Sustainable Agriculture: An Explainable-AI (XAI) Perspective on Energy-Efficient Crop Intelligence
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
88212f3988da8ca8d548c2cfd044d37d838996f1.abstract: <jats:p>In modern agriculture precision forecast crop yields, diagnose plant disease and schedule irrigation systems rely on machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL). Cost of training and deploying these models is weighed their accuracy. Two research threads have far developed largely in parallel. Green AI, which treats computational and energy efficiency as a first-class evaluation criterion alongside accuracy and Explainable AI(XAI) uses technology like Shapley additive explanations(SHAP), LIME and Grad-CAM to open the “black box” models so that farmers , and policymakers can act on their predictions.This paper synthesises recent literature (2017–2026) at the intersection of these threads as they apply to agriculture, covering crop-yield prediction, plant-disease detection, and soil- and irrigation-modelling studies that report either energy-efficiency measures or explainability analyses, or both. The synthesis identifies a specific and consistent gap: while explainability is now common in high-performing agricultural ML studies, almost none of them report the energy or carbon cost of training the underlying models, and the one purpose-built Green-AI agriculture framework identified in the review explicitly leaves explainability as future work rather than integrating it. Building on this synthesis, the paper proposes a unified Green-XAI methodological framework for agricultural ML that couples resource-appropriate model families – tree-based ensembles such as Random Forest, XGBoost and LightGBM, alongside a compact CNN architecture for imagery – with SHAP-based interpretability and continuous energy/carbon instrumentation across the training and inference lifecycle. The paper details the proposed dataset scope, the governing model equations, the SHAP computation, and an accuracy-versus-energy evaluation protocol, and positions the framework against a comparative synthesis of the performance figures reported by prior studies</jats:p>

title: The Role of AI in Graduate Admissions: Results From the Fall 2025 ETS/NAGAP Survey
container-title: ETS Research Report Series
441e7e8de8fd308cf96d6a4ec93745b07c7bc0cd.abstract:
<jats:p>As artificial intelligence (AI) continues to gain prevalence, its use is gaining acceptance in graduate enrollment management (GEM), as professionals begin to think beyond its use for chatbots or recruitment materials to imagine how it can increase efficiency. At the same time, AI’s effects on how GEM professionals perceive traditional application components are beginning to become clearer. GEM professionals have begun to question the value of the traditional personal statement essay and indicate that other elements of a holistic admissions process may consequently gain significance moving forward, including interviews, campus visits, and proctored writing samples under controlled conditions. Here we detail results from the Fall 2025 ETS/NAGAP survey of graduate enrollment management professionals, sharing their experiences of AI’s impact on graduate admissions processes, and conclude by looking forward to how processes and practices are likely to change based on emerging norms and consensus on best practices.
Suggested citation: Gooch, R. M., & Haviland, S. B. (in press). The role of AI in graduate admissions: Results from the Fall 2025 ETS/NAGAP survey (Research Notes). ETS.</jats:p>

title: Algorithmic Authority in Practice: Generative AI, Decision-Making, and Accountability in Public Administration
container-title: Digital Government: Research and Practice
6291947077e9efdb21bd80154ec49341dcbca7e3.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI (GenAI) is reshaping public sector decision-making, yet empirical understanding of how it reconfigures governance remains limited. Drawing on 24 semi-structured interviews with public officials in Kenya, this interpretive qualitative study examines how GenAI reshapes decision-making authority, accountability, and trust in human-centred governance. The findings identify three interrelated mechanisms: the concentration of epistemic authority in generative outputs, strongest among officials lacking the technical or situated knowledge to interrogate them; a structured pattern of default compliance and selective override, where organisational norms place the burden of justification on deviation rather than compliance; and a diffusion of accountability through system-based attribution for co-produced outputs, reversible where organisations maintained clear review and documentation. GenAI’s fluent, narrative outputs, unlike the scores and flags of earlier systems, appear to lend a persuasive authority we interpret as theoretically significant rather than formally demonstrated. Officials perceived that resulting opacity and diffused responsibility could strain institutional trust even where performance improves, reflecting their accounts rather than direct evidence from citizens. The study contributes a process-oriented, GenAI-specific analytical framework, empirically grounds hybrid discretion in organisational practice, extends emerging accounts of GenAI-specific accountability entanglement, and offers a theoretically informed account of officials’ perceptions of GenAI’s implications for institutional trust.</jats:p>

title: Exploring the Adoption of AI-Enabled Human Resource Management in Bangladesh’s Government Institutions

<jats:p>Purpose: 
This paper explores the implementation of artificial intelligence (AI) in human resource management in the Bangladesh government sector. The study uses survey data of 400 government officials in the public organizations of Bangladesh and utilizes qualitative insights to assess institutional readiness, perceived obstacles, and possible implementation strategies.  Study Design:  The study follows a quantitative approach by conducting descriptive statistics, regression, and correlation analyses. A questionnaire is developed to measure the variables of the study through a survey.  Findings:  The results indicate moderate levels of readiness in data systems, leadership awareness, and critical gaps in human capacity, data quality, and ethical governance. Although there is great evidence of the benefits of AI, there are still major infrastructural and regulatory hurdles. The regression and correlation analyses provide confirmation that both awareness of readiness and barriers play a significant role in the implementation of AI, which suggests integrating AI in human resource management by following step-by-step, government-based, and capacity-based strategies, aligning with national policy goals.  Value:  This study shows the pathways and opportunities for policymakers of Bangladesh’s law enforcement agencies to introduce AI-driven human resource management practices by obtaining clear and fair perceptions of law enforcement professions</jats:p>

title: Secure Communication and Coordination System for Military Operations Using AI and Real-Time Monitoring
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Multidisciplinary Research and Studies
c53ffd5e2c250b9c36603665c85769cd6df781e4.abstract:
<jats:p>Effective military coordination, information management, and operational decision-making hinge on secure and reliable communication. Unfortunately, systems that depend on fragmented channels and manual processes often face delays, limited visibility of information, security risks, and challenges in coordinating activities among authorized personnel. This paper introduces a Secure Communication and Coordination System for Military Operations that leverages Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Real-Time Monitoring. Our proposed system features secure user authentication, encrypted information exchange, role-based access control, centralized communication management, and real-time activity monitoring—all within a single digital platform. By integrating AI, we enhance capabilities like message classification, information prioritization, anomaly detection, and spotting unusual communication patterns. 
The research follows a design-oriented approach that includes requirements analysis, system design, implementation planning, and thorough functional and security evaluations. Our architecture prioritizes confidentiality, integrity, availability, accountability, and controlled access to sensitive data, while ensuring human oversight of AI-generated recommendations to mitigate risks tied to automated decisions. Ultimately, we aim to provide a structured framework that boosts the security, timeliness, and organization of military communication, facilitating better coordination among authorized personnel. To validate the effectiveness of this system, practical implementation and systematic testing under realistic operating conditions will be essential.</jats:p>

title: Students’ Positions towards Generative AI Technologies:  Strengths and Challenges in Higher Education
container-title: Journal of Educational and Social Research
0e92692b1ed4305609b5bc62447b9cd15693ce42.abstract:
<jats:p>The current study examined the attitudes of Arab students toward generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in higher education, focusing on their self-reported awareness of its limitations and risks, readiness to use these technologies, concerns, and recommendations for effective integration into teaching and learning. The study employed a mixed-methods design involving 337 undergraduate and postgraduate students from a teacher education college in Israel, recruited through convenience sampling. Data were collected using an online questionnaire comprising closed-ended and open-ended questions. Quantitative data were analyzed using descriptive statistics, correlation analysis, and independent-samples t-tests, while qualitative responses were analyzed thematically. The findings revealed an overall mean of 2.91 (SD = 0.783) for students’ self-reported awareness of GenAI limitations and risks and a mean of 3.53 (SD = 0.865) for readiness to use these technologies. Readiness was positively correlated with previous use (r = 0.408, p < 0.001), but not significantly correlated with self-reported familiarity (r = 0.031, p = 0.571). Male students reported significantly higher readiness than female students, t(335) = 2.326, p = 0.021, whereas no significant difference was found by academic level. Students’ concerns had an overall mean of 3.06 (SD = 0.872), with the potential negative effects of overreliance on generic skills emerging as the highest-rated concern. Concerns did not differ significantly by previous-use group, gender, or academic level. The qualitative findings showed that students recommended using GenAI to support research and academic tasks, integrating it into courses and learning activities, verifying the accuracy of generated information, and providing appropriate training and instructor guidance. The findings highlight the importance of a balanced and responsible approach to GenAI integration that combines practical support with critical evaluation, academic integrity, and the preservation of independent thinking.

title: Self-Efficacy as a Mediator between Passion for Using AI Applications and Internet Addiction among Egyptian University Students:  A Structural Equation Modeling Approach
container-title: Journal of Educational and Social Research
a18a3df85e87f08687155b23d6ba56af971791e0.abstract:
<jats:p>The study aimed to examine the mediating role of self-efficacy in the relationship between passion for using artificial intelligence applications and internet addiction among university students using structural equation modeling. The study sample included two independent samples, selected from students of the Capital University in Cairo, the psychometric verification sample (N=653) and the main sample (N=730). Participants completed three main scales to assess passion for using artificial intelligence applications, self-efficacy, and internet addiction. The results showed a negative effect of harmonious passion for artificial intelligence applications on internet addiction, both directly (?= -0.111) and indirectly through self-efficacy (?= -0.240). The results also indicated a positive effect of obsessive passion for artificial intelligence applications on internet addiction, both directly (?= 0.164) and indirectly through self-efficacy as a partial mediating variable (?= 0.273). The structural model demonstrated a high fit with the data, and all hypothesized correlations were statistically significant. These results generally indicate that the two types of passion for using artificial intelligence applications (harmonious – obsessive) are associated with changes in internet addiction, whether an increase or decrease, either directly or indirectly through their relationship with self-efficacy as a partial mediating variable. This study contributes to deepening the psychological understanding of how artificial intelligence applications influence the emergence of internet addictive behaviours. A harmonious and balanced passion for artificial intelligence applications reduces digital addiction when there is strong self-efficacy among university students.

title: Data Protection Readiness for AI Proctoring  in Albanian Higher Education
container-title: Journal of Educational and Social Research
7a96f615c159f5d443122845d9ebc6bda2b0611c.abstract:
<jats:p>AI-based proctoring has become a contested instrument for safeguarding examination integrity in higher education, yet it processes extensive personal data, including video, audio and potentially biometric data. No publicly documented deployment of AI-based proctoring in Albanian universities was identified, although digitalisation and European Union accession make future adoption plausible. This article therefore asks whether the Albanian data protection framework is ready for that prospect. It applies doctrinal analysis to the Albanian-language text of Law No. 124/2024 “On Personal Data Protection”, the Constitution and the higher education legislation, benchmarks them against the General Data Protection Regulation and the EU Artificial Intelligence Act, and draws on decisions from Italy, the Netherlands and the United States as evidence of foreseeable legal risks. Hypothetical deployments are assessed in terms of legal risk, with attention to legal basis, the validity of student consent, special-category data, automated decision-making, impact assessment and proportionality. The analysis finds that Law 124/2024 would make the most intrusive designs, such as automated facial matching, home scans and solely automated sanctions, difficult to justify. It also finds that the legal basis for monitoring in public universities remains uncertain, that no dedicated AI legislation is in force, and that supervisory practice is untested. The article concludes with conditions under which less intrusive designs could potentially comply.

title: AI-Enabled Teaching Capability and Sustainable Education  Practice among Teachers in Mountainous China:  The Roles of OER-Enabled Pedagogical Capacity  and Institutional Digital Support
container-title: Journal of Educational and Social Research
e9ac88522149f7771089c9d7d784e109dbc4f7ee.abstract:
<jats:p>This study examines how teachers' artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled teaching capability and open educational resources (OER)-enabled pedagogical capacity are associated with sustainable education practice in mountainous areas of China. It also assesses the indirect role of OER-enabled pedagogical capacity and the moderating role of institutional digital support.The study describes a cross-sectional quantitative survey of 462 teachers from 54 schools in 18 mountainous counties across Yunnan, Guizhou, Sichuan, Gansu, and Qinghai, using a 24-item questionnaire and partial least squares structural equation modelling with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The analyzed results report positive associations between AI-enabled teaching capability and sustainable education practice (? = .331, p < .001), between AI capability and OER-enabled pedagogical capacity (? = .550, p < .001), and between OER capacity and sustainable practice (? = .390, p < .001). The indirect association is .215 and the interaction with institutional digital support is .134. The R² for sustainable practice is .475. The prediction claim is limited to predictive relevance within the cross-validation procedure, not demonstrated performance in new schools across different locations.This study integrates AI literacy, OER-enabled pedagogy, education for sustainable development, and socio-technical support in a teacher-centred model for geographically constrained schooling. Its conceptual contribution separates AI-related capability, open-resource adaptation, and institutional conditions. The proposed priorities combine teacher capability, openly licensed low-bandwidth resources, responsible AI governance, technical support, and professional learning communities.

title: Efficiency of   Project-based Learning Model Empowered  by AI for Pre-service Primary School Teachers

<jats:p> This paper explores the potential of artificial intelligence (AI) to enhance Project-Based Learning (PBL) and evaluates the effectiveness of an AI-powered PBL model for pre-service primary school teachers. Integrating AI into PBL represents a promising direction in teacher education by combining the hands-on, inquiry-based nature of project-based learning with the opportunities created by the digital transformation of education. AI enhances project-based instruction by making the learning process more efficient, personalised, and engaging. To evaluate the model’s effectiveness, the authors conducted a pedagogical experiment involving knowledge tests and project presentations to assess the knowledge and project-related skills of pre-service teachers in the experimental and control groups before and after intervention. The findings indicate that the AI-supported PBL model can significantly improved the project competence of pre-service teachers in the experimental group. The authors conclude that the proposed model is as an effective tool for preparing future primary school teachers, fostering their critical thinking, collaboration, and ability to integrate AI into classroom practice.

title: Personalized Mathematics Teaching Supported by AI Chatbots  to Enhance University Students’ Mathematical Problem-Solving Competence in Vietnam
container-title: Journal of Educational and Social Research
c224c5ca08f4e83b0c4eecb67f01a3737d307f67.abstract:
<jats:p>This study examines the effectiveness of personalized mathematics teaching supported by AI chatbots in enhancing university students’ mathematical problem-solving competence in Vietnam. Focusing on first- and second-year undergraduates enrolled in "Applied Statistics" and "History of Mathematics" courses, we conducted a mixed-methods quasi-experimental study (N = 200) to evaluate the impact of AI chatbot-supported prompt-engineering training on problem-solving competence. Using a quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design with control and experimental groups, we measured learning gains through adapted PISA/TIMSS-based assessments and examined relationships among prompt-engineering skills, AI-related attitudes, and problem-solving performance using regression analysis. Quantitative results showed that the experimental group achieved higher post-test problem-solving scores than the control group, with a large standardized mean difference (Cohen’s d = 1.36). After controlling for pre-test scores, the ANCOVA also showed a statistically significant group effect F(1, 197) = 91.76. Qualitative interviews with 20 students suggested that structured prompting helped students improve confidence, clarify mathematical concepts, and recognize the need to critically evaluate chatbot-generated responses. The findings provide initial empirical support for structured prompt-engineering training in AI chatbot-assisted mathematics learning in higher education. The study offers practical implications for integrating prompt-engineering instruction into AI-supported mathematics teaching and contributes to research on technology-enhanced learning in Vietnamese higher education.

title: EcoShield: AI-Powered Safety Companion
container-title: International Research Journal on Advanced Engineering and Management (IRJAEM)
b184b9524381a54be93df961f06f5e6068b3f6a6.abstract: <jats:p>As rising crime rates and delayed emergency responses continue to pose serious threats to personal safety, especially in urban and semi-urban regions, the need for intelligent and reliable safety systems has become a major concern. Conventional personal safety solutions often depend on manual user interaction, stable network connectivity, and continuous location availability, which can reduce their effectiveness during real-world emergency situations. This project presents EcoShield, an AI-driven personal safety platform designed to enhance emergency responsiveness, situational awareness, and user protection. The proposed system integrates real-time location tracking, geospatial crime data visualization, and voice-based emergency detection to automatically trigger alerts during critical situations. By leveraging mobile sensing technologies and intelligent automation, EcoShield ensures timely communication with emergency contacts even when precise location data is partially unavailable. The system provides a secure and user-friendly interface that supports proactive risk awareness through danger-zone mapping and safe route guidance. Experimental testing and simulated evaluations demonstrate noticeable improvements in alert reliability, response time, and overall system effectiveness. This project contributes toward improving personal safety solutions and establishes a foundation for extending intelligent safety systems to broader smart-city and public security applications.</jats:p>

title: Design and Prototype Implementation of a Modular AI ModelOps Platform for End-to-End Machine Learning Lifecycle Management
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
eb2bc31e68041c9dd49cbf5475934233a8de0724.abstract: <jats:p>Machine learning models are often developed through experiments and notebooks, but moving them into reliable production systems requires coordinated data management, experiment tracking, model versioning, deployment, and continuous monitoring. Disconnected tools and manual release steps can reduce reproducibility and make model updates difficult to govern. This paper presents the design and prototype implementation of a modular AI ModelOps Platform that brings key lifecycle operations into a common system. The platform combines a React and TypeScript dashboard, FastAPI-based control-plane APIs, PostgreSQL application metadata, Redis-backed background services, MLflow experiment tracking and model registry, a model router, and Docker-based model serving. Its delivery workflow uses GitHub Actions for validation and image building, GitHub Container Registry (GHCR) for versioned artifacts, and a pull-based staging release checker on an Ubuntu host. Before promotion, a candidate image is checked for source and version metadata and tested through health and prediction requests; rollback safeguards preserve the previous deployment when validation fails. Functional verification has confirmed a staging prediction from the registered demo-classifier model version 5. Drift analysis and governed retraining are included in the intended lifecycle feedback design, while fully autonomous retraining is treated as an extension requiring further validation. The paper presents the system architecture, implementation workflow, related research, evaluation limits, and future development directions</jats:p>

title: Applications of Generative Artificial Intelligence in Marketing: A Research Review and Future Prospects
container-title: Financial Economics Research
148e1986296fc80c4c7c67c8067c839c2db4ad52.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is turning marketing content into an abundant resource with near-zero marginal cost, but related research is highly fragmented. This paper thematically integrates Chinese- and English-language literature published from 2019 to 2026. The findings show that gains from GenAI marketing are “stratified along the funnel”: evidence of improvements at the attention and interaction stages is sufficient, whereas the effect on final conversion is weak; consumers’ evaluations of content are decoupled from evaluations of the “artificial intelligence (AI) source” label, and disclosure of the AI source significantly suppresses transactions; only 13% of the literature examines moderating variables. Accordingly, this paper proposes a five-stage integrated framework of “technical characteristics → marketing applications → psychological mechanisms → consumer responses → moderating boundaries” and a future research agenda.</jats:p>

title: AI-Based Real-Time Worker Safety Monitoring and Alert System
container-title: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
3a6e7970661569e0e5df5eb2d8b8e46415a7e623.abstract: <jats:p>Construction and industrial work often involve hazards that can be reduced when personal protective equipment is used correctly and safety concerns are reported quickly. Manual observation remains important, but a supervisor may not be able to watch every worker continuously. This paper presents a prototype for real-time worker safety monitoring using computer vision. The system uses a custom-trained You Only Look Once (YOLO) object-detection model with a webcam feed to identify workers and visible personal protective equipment categories, including helmets, goggles, gloves, boots and vests, as well as selected non-compliance classes. OpenCV is used to process camera frames and display detection boxes and a safety-status panel. When configured violation classes are detected, the prototype displays an on-screen warning and produces a voice alert. An SMS notification workflow is also demonstrated through a phone notification screenshot supplied from the project test. The current evidence confirms that the application can display selected safety alerts and that an SMS-style notification was received during the reported demonstration. However, this paper does not claim a measured detection accuracy, a validated reduction in accidents or a measured SMS delivery time because a controlled quantitative evaluation has not yet been documented. The prototype is intended to support, rather than replace, trained safety personnel. Its practical value and limitations are discussed, together with the testing required before deployment in a real worksite.</jats:p>

title: Space-Based versus Land-Based AI Data Centres: A Comparative Environmental Assessment Centred on Google's Orbital Compute Programme
container-title: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
f3021bf1101386f103c9f1752ae4ec6917705980.abstract: <jats:p>This paper compares space-based AI compute against terrestrial hyperscale data centres across six environmental parameters, using Google's published research programme on solar-powered TPU constellations in dawn-dusk low-Earth orbit as the reference case (Arcas et al., 2025). The comparison uses a dual functional unit — 1 MW-year of delivered IT power, and 1 MW of IT power over 1-, 5- and 10-year missions — under a cradle-to-grave boundary that includes launch and re-entry for the orbital case. Three findings emerge. First, the carbon result is functional-unit dependent: per kWh of energy delivered to the payload, orbital systems are 1.5–1.95× more carbon-intensive than terrestrial ones (52.1–66.3 versus 34.0 gCO₂e/kWh) (Ohs et al., 2025); but per MW of IT capacity against real-world grids, launch-phase emissions of 1,032–2,585 t CO₂e are repaid within the first year and amount to only 5.5–13.7% of five years of terrestrial operation at the 395.65 gCO₂e/kWh global data-centre average (Vries-Gao, 2025). Break-even occurs at grid intensities of 21.6–54.1 gCO₂e/kWh over five years. Second, water and land are where space wins categorically: no evaporative cooling, and no terrestrial land conversion of the tens-to-hundreds of hectares a hyperscale facility requires (Hlabisa, 2025). Third, the binding physical constraint in orbit is not compute silicon but radiative heat rejection — 33–67 cm² of radiator per watt of waste heat, or 3,333–6,667 m² per MW (Vicente, 2021) — which converts thermal inefficiency directly into launch mass and launch carbon.</jats:p>

title: Engineering Reliable Agentic AI: Decision-Making in Real-World Deployments
container-title: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
fff86d91ed8939ecca2c00fb727704e6bf3282be.abstract: <jats:p>Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed to give everyday guidance whose correctness depends on rules that users do not know and on personal facts that the agent must first elicit. At each turn, such an agent must choose whether to ask a clarifying question, act through a tool, answer, or decline. This paper presents Rikanverse®, a Proactive, Multilingual, Voice-Native Agentic AI Application, built on a reasoning-and-acting (ReAct) architecture and designed, built and deployed end-to-end solo by the Author. Rikanverse® serves both sides of the market: tenants describe their needs by voice or text and receive matched listings with practical guidance, while landlords register listings by speaking instead of completing forms. The agent treats clarification as an explicit action, acts through a small, typed tool set, maintains persistent session state, and checks every draft answer before release, declining when it cannot answer reliably. The paper describes the system, reports preliminary user evidence from a survey of 30 respondents, and proposes an evaluation protocol in which the trade-off between correct answers and declines serves as the central measure of reliability. The work shows how agent design choices about asking and abstaining can be made explicit and measurable in a deployed system.</jats:p>

title: Negotiating Authority at the Margins: Tribal Women’s Political Empowerment, Capacity Deficits, and AI-Enabled Governance in Jharkhand’s Panchayati Raj Institutions
container-title: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
d59122f1046ac709e82bf9b2d338daee013e08b7.abstract: <jats:p>The Constitution of India (73rd Constitutional Amendment) requires that women be reserved a place in Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs), but there is a huge disparity between women representation and political power, especially for the women of STs who are marginalised on two fronts – gender and ethnic. This paper records the major fieldwork done from June to November 2025 in Mandar Block, Ranchi district, Jharkhand. The study focuses on the quality of political participation of the elected tribal women leaders of Oraon tribe (Mukhya, Up-Mukhya and Panchayat Samiti Members), constraints faced by them in exercising political role, role of information and communication technologies (ICTs) in their political functioning and how their political role has changed over time. These women are afforded the ability to exercise substantive agency (to do their own development work, to campaign for their administrative rights and to challenge the implicit assumption of proxy leadership) but their power is invariably constrained, both because they enjoy limited formal education and because of time poverty, mobility barriers, bureaucratic gender bias and the rising digital divide. The study also shows that the traditional governance system – parallel, which is perceived as non-conflictual, allows the community to work together. Given the results of this study, this paper recommends that AI tools built with a genuinely co-participatory, vernacular-based approach can have some real value as a capacity development tool that can lessen the literacy barrier to access to digital governance; and can provide low-stakes, confidence-building spaces. The implications or ethics of using AI in this case are discussed.</jats:p>

title: PmiREN3.0: a multi-omics integrated and AI-assisted encyclopedia for plant microRNA research
container-title: Nucleic Acids Research
ebea4e08a47e1c5170e5d57141d150ab01cb50a7.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are key post-transcriptional regulators in gene regulatory networks (GRNs). Comprehensive research on miRNAs increasingly requires the integration of large and heterogeneous datasets, together with more efficient approaches to knowledge exploration. Here, we present PmiREN3.0, a major update of the Plant MicroRNA Encyclopedia. Compared with PmiREN2.0, species/subspecies coverage increased from 179 to 340, adding 22 orders, 51 families, and 108 genera. Using the same standardized workflow and annotation criteria as previous releases, high-confidence miRNAs were identified from 5319 small RNA sequencing (sRNA-seq) datasets, with miRNA loci increasing from 39 751 to 87 667 and miRNA families from 7838 to 18 389. Resources and tools from previous releases were extensively updated, while six new modules were added for primary transcripts, DNA methylation, RNA modifications, stress-responsive expression, metabolic pathways, and core GRNs. PmiREN3.0 also introduces miRai+, a knowledge service powered by artificial intelligence (AI) that combines a language model fine-tuned on miRNA knowledge with retrieval augmented generation. Evaluation yielded scores of 0.910 for answer relevance, 0.965 for faithfulness, and 0.906 for factual correctness. Together, PmiREN3.0 provides an expanded plant miRNA dataset and an integrated platform combining multi-omics data and AI-assisted knowledge services for plant miRNA research. PmiREN3.0 is available at https://pmiren.com/.</jats:p>

title: Offloading Thoughts to the Bots: How Generative AI Access Influences Cognitive Reflection
container-title: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
89abf0f54d025ddf7e06b07b896cddba60561ff9.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly used to support reasoning and decision-making, raising questions about how AI influences reflective cognition and trust. This study examined how AI pedigree and reliability influenced cognitive reflection performance, cognitive load, trust, and performance overestimation during a verbal Cognitive Reflection Test (CRT-V). Participants (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">N</jats:italic>
                     = 148) were assigned to a no-AI control condition, a low-pedigree AI condition, or a high-pedigree AI condition. Participants in the high-pedigree AI condition demonstrated significantly greater trust and CRT performance than participants in both other conditions while also exhibiting lower performance overestimation. AI access did not significantly reduce perceived cognitive load, although greater cognitive load predicted poorer CRT performance overall. Importantly, trust interacted with AI condition such that greater trust predicted lower CRT performance in the low-pedigree AI condition but not in the high-pedigree AI condition. These findings support theories of calibrated reliance rather than indiscriminate cognitive offloading.
                  </jats:p>

title: How Will the Food and Drug Administration Regulate Generative AI–Enabled Medical Devices?
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
a300a6094322797af5544e9a5fe281f4bd6372e9.abstract:

<jats:p>
                    The global shift toward cultivating students’ AI literacy requires teachers to reconceptualize curricula and pedagogical practices. However, research has focused primarily on teachers’ use of AI tools, overlooking their readiness to integrate AI literacy as a learning goal, particularly in mathematics education. In response, this study developed and validated the AI-Literacy-Integrated Teaching Acceptance and Readiness Scale for Mathematics Teachers (AILTAR-M). The instrument was theoretically organized around two domains: (1)
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Acceptance</jats:italic>
                    , comprising four constructs adapted from the Technology Acceptance Model (Perceived Usefulness, Perceived Ease of Use, Attitude toward Use, and Behavioral Intention); and (2)
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">Readiness</jats:italic>
                    , encompassing Perceived AI Literacy as a self-reported cognitive dimension and Teaching Self-Efficacy as a motivational dimension. Psychometric evaluation with 549 mathematics teachers in China supported a 29-item, six-factor structure. Exploratory factor analysis (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                    = 174) yielded a six-factor solution explaining 69.7% of the variance, and confirmatory factor analysis (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">n</jats:italic>
                    = 375) demonstrated acceptable model fit (CFI = .938, TLI = .931, RMSEA = .063, SRMR = .038). The instrument exhibited strong internal consistency (α = .899– .943) alongside satisfactory convergent and discriminant validity. These findings provide initial psychometric evidence for using the AILTAR-M to examine mathematics teachers’ acceptance of and readiness for integrating AI literacy into mathematics instruction.

title: AI-Driven Automation for Safety Monitoring in the Chemical Industry: A Review of Hazard Detection, Anomaly Detection, and Predictive Risk Assessment
container-title: International Journal of Innovative Research in Engineering
6ba4818de60cd0bc749813e4939c8326f08d314b.abstract: <jats:p>Chemical and petrochemical plants work with hazardous materials and complex equipment, so small changes in operating conditions can sometimes signal a serious problem. These early signs may appear across several sensors and may not immediately trigger a conventional alarm. For this reason, researchers have explored artificial intelligence (AI) for gas-leak detection, visual hazard recognition, process anomaly detection, fault diagnosis, predictive maintenance, and risk assessment. This review discusses research across these areas, including industrial sensing, deep learning, explainable models, anomaly detection, foundation models, digital twins, and AI-assisted hazard analysis. The reported results are promising within the settings in which they were tested. For example, one pipeline-leak study reports 96.88% classification accuracy, a Tennessee Eastman Process study reports 92% prediction efficiency on an external test set, and a run-level diagnosis study reports macro-F1 values near 0.95 [12], [15], [16]. These figures come from different tasks and test designs, so they should not be treated as directly comparable. Across the studies, recurring concerns include dependence on simulated benchmarks, limited testing of difficult faults, scarce labelled incident data, changes in operating conditions, false alarms, and a lack of validation across multiple sites. The review discusses a layered architecture that connects plant sensors and control infrastructure with validated AI models, evidence-based alerts, and operator decisions. AI may strengthen monitoring, but it should not replace independent protective systems or the judgment of qualified process-safety personnel. Field validation, uncertainty reporting, cybersecurity, traceability, and ongoing oversight remain essential.</jats:p>

title:
Theorizing affective chronopolitics of
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    in higher education: A multi‐level analytical framework
container-title: British Educational Research Journal
8b54c3ab1a16bd01e3322c20a29946013d7f2196.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    This conceptual paper extends existing theorization of
                    <jats:italic>affective chronopolitics</jats:italic>
                    to examine how AI technologies become implicated in the governance of educational subjects, institutions and imagined futures in higher education. In particular, we argue that AI‐mediated temporalities may involve different manifestations such as immediacy, anticipation, acceleration or delay, while their affective dimensions may encompass anxiety and fatigue as well as relief and hope. Building on scholarship on chronopolitics, affect and educational governance, we develop a multi‐level analytical framework spanning the micro level of lived experience and subject formation, the meso level of institutional organization and responsibility and the macro level of policy imaginaries and governance. The framework foregrounds how AI technological capacities become translated into affective‐temporal norms and how their benefits and burdens are unevenly distributed in higher education. We suggest that this framework offers a heuristic for empirical research into how AI reorganizes affective and temporal arrangements in higher education.

title: Mediating Role of Artificial Intelligence Usage between Secondary Mathematics Teachers’ Knowledge of Human-Centric AI Pedagogy and Lesson Planning Skills
container-title: QualiSearch Journal of Educational Research and Practice
b6a575169a03f974de38ea5d95c9bf5f581371c8.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) usage among mathematics teachers has become an increasingly important part of their professional practice, including the planning, implementation, and assessment of instruction. As AI becomes more widely used, it continues to pose the challenge of maintaining ethical standards in its use and safeguarding human-led instructional planning. This study examined the mediating role of AI Usage in the relationship between Human-Centric AI Pedagogy (HCAP) Knowledge and Lesson Planning Skills among the 107 Junior High School mathematics teachers in Congressional District II of Valenzuela City. A descriptive-correlational research design with a mediation approach was utilized. Data were collected using validated instruments measuring HCAP Knowledge, AI Usage based on the four ILAW core elements, and Lesson Planning Skills, and were analyzed using descriptive statistics and mediation analysis with bootstrapping. The findings showed moderate levels of HCAP Knowledge and AI Usage, while Lesson Planning Skills were at a high level. Human-AI Collaborative Knowledge obtained the relatively lowest result among the HCAP domains, while Ways Forward obtained the lowest results in both AI Usage and Lesson Planning Skills. AI Usage significantly mediated the association between HCAP Knowledge and Lesson Planning Skills, indicating partial mediation. The findings highlight the need to strengthen teachers’ capacity to use AI as a collaborative and reflective support for instructional decision-making, leading to the development of a Targeted Mentoring Plan for Mathematics Master Teachers.</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Smart and Precision Agriculture: Smart Sensors, IoT, Deep Learning, Computer Vision, and Decision Support: A Comprehensive Survey
container-title: Open Research Africa
09901c89c9aa579fea1a3ee0981e0610b9fe1f60.abstract: <ns5:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated with smart sensors, Internet of Things (IoT) networks, machine learning, deep learning, and computer vision to support site-specific agricultural management. However, strong performance on computational benchmarks does not necessarily translate into reliable decisions, effective field interventions, or measurable improvements in agricultural productivity and resource efficiency. This comprehensive narrative survey critically synthesizes advances in agricultural sensing, IoT architectures, data processing, multimodal sensor fusion, predictive modeling, computer vision, decision optimization, and automated actuation. Particular emphasis is placed on the relationships between measurement reliability, model generalization, decision feasibility, intervention accuracy, and verified agricultural outcomes. The reviewed literature demonstrates promising capabilities in crop monitoring, yield prediction, disease and weed recognition, precision irrigation, and selected automated operations. Nevertheless, heterogeneous evaluation protocols, limited independent field validation, sensor calibration challenges, distribution shifts, interoperability barriers, and deployment costs constrain operational reliability and generalizability. To address these interconnected challenges, the survey proposes a literature-informed reference architecture linking agricultural observations, data integration, AI inference, constrained decision-making, physical interventions, and outcome feedback, supported by uncertainty assessment, human oversight, and cross-layer assurance. The proposed architecture is conceptual and has not been empirically validated. Future research priorities include reproducible field evaluations, representative agricultural datasets, uncertainty-aware and explainable AI, resource-efficient computing, interoperable infrastructures, and economically inclusive deployment. The review concludes that the practical value of AI-enabled precision agriculture should be evaluated through reliable interventions, sustainable resource utilization, and demonstrated agricultural outcomes rather than predictive performance alone.</ns5:p>

title: Generative AI in Gamified Learning: A Systematic Literature Review on Student Motivation
container-title: Research in Education, Technology, and Multiculture
96476196bfcfd1c9cf2c5a871d3b5fbc8b73ae94.abstract: <jats:p>This Systematic Literature Review (SLR) synthesizes how Generative Artificial Intelligence (Generative AI) is implemented in learning environments, with and without gamification, and what studies report about students’ motivation and engagement. Following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines, structured searches in Scopus, IEEE Xplore, and ScienceDirect identified 792 records, and 116 full-text reports were assessed. Sixty-nine peer-reviewed journal articles were included: 21 on AI-supported gamified or game-based learning and 48 on Generative AI and motivation or engagement without gamification. In the gamified subset, four implementation forms appear (AI characters and role-play partners, LLM feedback and adaptive difficulty, AI-generated assessment items, and Generative AI as a game design tool), and all eight comparison studies reported higher or favorable motivation, engagement, or related outcomes. Across the whole corpus, two meta-analyses and one systematic review report positive overall effects of ChatGPT and Generative AI on engagement or motivation, with moderators and mixed emotional evidence. Individual studies are not uniformly positive: one found that videos outperformed a Generative AI assistant on knowledge gains and curiosity, one found no significant effect on behavioral engagement, and one found that Generative AI use may reduce active learning and motivation. The evidence is concentrated in higher education (48 of 69 articles) and in 2025 (52 of 69); the most frequently stated limitations are small or single-context samples (20 articles) and short interventions with novelty effects (12), and the most frequent recommendations are longer studies (18) and larger and more diverse samples (17). Future research should isolate the AI component's contribution and test it over time. Keywords: Generative AI, Gamification, Gamified learning, Student motivation, Systematic review of literature.</jats:p>

7114b93de07102fe5beba192054534d1040b9db6.abstract: <jats:p>Bagama’t maraming pag-aaral ang tumalakay sa impluwensiya ng midyang panlipunan at mga beauty filter sa pananaw ng mga gumagamit sa pisikal na anyo, limitado pa ang pananaliksik na sumusuri kung paano binibigyang-kahulugan ng mga mag-aaral sa kolehiyo sa kontekstong Pilipino ang mga katangiang biswal ng AI face filters at ang papel ng mga ito sa konstruksyon ng pamantayan ng kagandahan sa kulturang biswal. Layunin ng pag-aaral na kritikal na suriin ang mga katangiang ginagamit ng mga mag-aaral sa pagtukoy ng mga larawang binago gamit ang AI face filters, ang kahulugang iniuugnay nila sa mga katangiang ito, at ang papel ng mga filter sa paghubog ng pamantayan ng kagandahan. Gumamit ang pag-aaral ng kwalitatibong disenyo sa pamamagitan ng Visual Elicitation Technique (VET) at semi-structured interview. Limang (5) mag-aaral na may edad na labingwalong taong gulang pataas mula sa Don Carlos Polytechnic College ang lumahok sa pag-aaral. Ipinakita sa kanila ang dalawampung (20) larawan na binubuo ng sampung orihinal na selfie at sampung bersiyong binago gamit ang AI face filters. Sinuri ang mga nakalap na datos sa pamamagitan ng thematic analysis. Ipinakita ng mga resulta na ginagamit ng mga kalahok ang pagkawala ng likas na detalye ng balat, proporsyon ng mukha, at kabuuang pagiging makatotohanan ng larawan bilang mga palatandaan ng paggamit ng AI face filters. Iniuugnay nila ang mga katangiang ito sa idealisadong kagandahan, digital na presentasyon ng sarili, at pagkakaiba ng artipisyal at likas na anyo. Lumitaw din na nakikilahok ang mga filter at midyang panlipunan sa pagpapalaganap at normalisasyon ng pamantayang nakasentro sa makinis, simetrikal, at tila walang kapintasang mukha. Gayunman, kinikilala ng mga kalahok na hindi ganap na itinatakda ng teknolohiya ang kahulugan ng kagandahan. Ipinahihiwatig ng pag-aaral na ang AI face filters ay hindi lamang kasangkapan sa pagbabago ng mga larawan kundi bahagi rin ng kulturang biswal na nagtataguyod ng mga ideyal na anyo, habang nananatiling mahalaga ang kritikal na interpretasyon ng mga gumagamit.</jats:p>

title: From E-Commerce to AI Commerce: Rethinking the Consumer Journey in the Era of AI Agents
container-title: Journal of Theoretical and Applied Electronic Commerce Research
9efa0e22711e12b8be2d6da2f8925fe5ba43d5d3.abstract: <jats:p>The emergence of increasingly autonomous Artificial Intelligence (AI) agents is reshaping how consumers search for information, evaluate alternatives, and make purchasing decisions. While existing consumer journey models have incorporated AI primarily as a decision-support technology, they provide limited conceptual guidance for understanding situations in which AI agents perform purchasing activities on consumers’ behalf. Drawing on consumer journey theory, AI-enabled commerce, and human–AI collaboration research, this conceptual paper adopts a theory-adaptation approach to examine how established frameworks may be extended to account for emerging forms of delegated decision-making. We propose the Human–AI Collaborative Consumer Journey, a framework that conceptualizes purchasing as a collaborative process involving consumers and consumer-authorized AI agents across different stages of the journey. Its central contribution is the concept of Delegated Consumer Agency (DCA), defined as the configuration of authority consumers grant AI agents to perform cognitive or operational purchasing activities within predefined goals and constraints. The framework highlights how human and AI participation may vary across purchasing contexts and identifies implications for consumer autonomy, decision-making, and e-commerce management. Finally, six research propositions and a future research agenda are presented to guide empirical investigation.</jats:p>

title: Edge Guard AI: An Intelligent Real-Time CCTV Surveillance and Smart Security Analytics Framework Using Local Edge Processing
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
c3b88198f25fc4995fe9030777cacd1bd2f69de6.abstract: <jats:p>Conventional CCTV systems record continuous video, but identifying important incidents often depends on a person watching feeds or reviewing recordings after an event. In this work, Edge Guard AI, a proposed intelligent CCTV analytics framework, is presented for adding automated, locally executed video analysis to existing camera infrastructure. The system receives live video from CCTV cameras, IP cameras, webcams, or DVR/NVR streams and processes frames on a desktop or laptop computer, reducing the need to send complete video streams to cloud servers and addressing bandwidth, latency, cost, and privacy concerns. YOLO detects persons, weapons, and other predefined security-related objects; MTCNN detects and extracts faces; and FaceNet generates facial embeddings for comparison with registered records. Detected persons and events are classified as familiar, unknown, missing-person record matches, or law-enforcement watchlist record matches, with additional trained models supporting masked-face and suspicious-activity detection. Events are assigned Normal, Warning, or Danger alert levels, and significant events trigger image capture, short event-specific video recording, timestamping, and notification through a connected application, with a searchable event history. Role-based Admin, User, and Police modules manage records, alerts, and evidence. The framework is at the proposal and design stage; the capabilities described are objectives to be implemented and evaluated, not completed test results</jats:p>

title: Controlling AI Self-Evolution: Balancing Usefulness, Safety, And Human Oversight
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
7862a25fd6d8f9eed5d4a3d28f3fbe9665a87458.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly capable of adapting to new information, improving task performance, modifying operational strategies, and assisting in the development of more advanced computational systems. These capabilities provide significant opportunities for innovation, productivity, scientific discovery, and decision support. However, they also raise concerns regarding the extent to which AI systems should be permitted to change their own behaviour, expand their operational capabilities, or influence the processes through which they are evaluated and controlled. Unrestricted or inadequately supervised adaptation may introduce unintended consequences, including specification gaming, reward manipulation, degradation of previously acquired knowledge, unexpected changes in system behaviour, and reduced human control. The present study examines how AI self-evolution can be controlled without unnecessarily restricting its usefulness. The study adopts a qualitative secondary-research methodology based on published scholarly literature, established AI safety research, technical documentation, international governance principles, and regulatory frameworks. Existing approaches are compared across six dimensions: capability development, human oversight, objective alignment, operational restrictions, accountability, and continuous monitoring. The literature indicates that AI safety cannot be achieved through a single technical intervention or a one-time evaluation. Instead, effective governance requires coordinated controls throughout the AI lifecycle, including development, testing, deployment, adaptation, monitoring, and retirement. Human oversight mechanisms, corrigibility, risk-based evaluation, controlled access to tools, documented change management, and independent assessment provide complementary safeguards. Nevertheless, existing approaches present limitations. Excessive restrictions may prevent beneficial adaptation, while superficial human supervision, incomplete documentation, and reliance on benchmark performance may fail to identify emerging risks. The study therefore proposes a conceptual governance approach based on bounded self-evolution, in which routine and reversible improvements may proceed within predefined limits, while significant changes require additional evaluation and explicit authorization. The proposed approach also emphasizes independent monitoring, rollback capabilities, incident reporting, and clear assignment of responsibility. The study concludes that preserving AI usefulness and maintaining human control should be treated as complementary objectives rather than competing priorities. Although the proposed approach synthesizes existing methods rather than experimentally validating a new technical system, it offers a structured basis for future research into responsible AI adaptation, organizational governance, and the long-term management of increasingly autonomous systems.</jats:p>

title: A Study of Prompt Engineering Techniques for Improving Generative AI Performance
container-title: International Journal of Advanced Research in Science Communication and Technology
b2c79a43653c0775ed92d8beb30ade0adbc160eb.abstract: <jats:p>Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has transformed the way users create content, retrieve information, write code and solve problems. The quality of outputs produced by Generative AI systems depends not only on the underlying model but also on the instructions supplied by users. Prompt engineering is the process of designing, structuring and refining inputs to guide an AI model towards relevant, accurate and useful responses. The present study examines the role of prompt engineering techniques in improving the performance of Generative AI systems, with particular attention to Zero-Shot Prompting, One-Shot and Few-Shot Prompting, Role-Based Prompting, Contextual Prompting and Chain-of-Thought Prompting. The study adopts a descriptive research design and is qualitative in nature, relying on secondary data collected from academic research papers, conference proceedings and published surveys. The literature indicates that carefully structured prompts can improve task alignment, response relevance, reasoning performance and output consistency. However, prompt effectiveness varies according to the task, model, context and evaluation method. The study also identifies limitations such as hallucinations, sensitivity to wording, prompt injection risks, bias and the absence of universally effective prompt templates. It concludes that prompt engineering is an important method for obtaining more reliable results from Generative AI, but should be combined with verification, clear evaluation criteria and responsible AI practices.</jats:p>

title: A Study on AI Digital Competency and the Perceived Need for AI Utilization Education among Physical Therapy Students

f8b52f591df875ac1c2019dd4f4b18ce9752e66d.abstract: <jats:p>Purpose This study aimed to examine AI digital competency and the perceived need for AI utilization education among physical therapy students and to analyze the relationship between the two variables. Methods This crosssectional correlational survey was conducted with 232 physical therapy students at S University using an online survey. Data were analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation analysis. Results The mean score for AI digital competency was 3.48±0.57, with communication and collaboration showing the highest score at 3.84±0.62 and digital content creation showing the lowest score at 3.03±0.71. The mean score for the perceived need for AI utilization education was 3.91±0.71. AI digital competency was positively correlated with the perceived need for AI utilization education (r=0.320, p<.001). Conclusion These results suggest the need for systematic educational support to help physical therapy students effectively use AI in majorrelated learning and clinical problemsolving.</jats:p>

title: HYBRID FEDERATED LEARNING ARCHITECTURE FOR PRIVACY-PRESERVING AI IN GREEN HYDROGEN ENERGY SYSTEMS: A REVIEW
container-title: International Journal of African Sustainable Development Research
7658450ec240730ecffa038cc235234571c1d5f6.abstract: <jats:p>The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI), Internet of Things (IoT) technologies, and smart grids into green hydrogen energy systems creates opportunities for improved energy forecasting, electrolyzer optimization, predictive maintenance, and operational efficiency. However, the interconnected nature of these infrastructures introduces significant challenges relating to data privacy, cybersecurity, commercial confidentiality, and organizational compliance. This review examines the potential of a hybrid federated learning architecture for privacy-preserving AI in green hydrogen energy systems. Drawing on literature concerning green hydrogen technologies, federated learning, differential privacy, blockchain-enabled security, Privacy Calculus Theory, and the Selective Organizational Information Privacy and Security Violations Model (SOIPSV), the review synthesizes existing approaches and identifies unresolved technical and governance challenges. It conceptualizes a six-layer architecture comprising edge and local processing, privacy calculus, federated learning, secure aggregation, organizational governance, and global intelligence. The proposed architecture integrates privacy-risk and benefit assessment, decentralized model training, cryptographic protection, and policy-oriented accountability to support collaborative intelligence across distributed hydrogen production facilities and smart grid networks. The framework remains conceptual and has not undergone empirical validation, simulation benchmarking, or real-world deployment. Its predictive performance, computational overhead, privacy guarantees, and scalability remain unverified. The review identifies future research priorities, including formal privacy accounting, adversarial testing, standardized benchmarks, governance operationalization, and pilot implementation. This synthesis provides a foundation for developing and evaluating trustworthy, privacy-aware AI architectures for secure and sustainable green hydrogen infrastructure.</jats:p>

title: Nurses’ Attitudes and Experiences With Generative AI in Clinical Practice: Qualitative Systematic Review
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
86fd6e8d39ee5d7b8d9f5992ff17e4580e39e69d.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The rapid advancement of generative AI (GenAI) holds transformative potential for clinical nursing practice, yet its integration also brings significant risks and uncertainties. Despite growing discourse on AI in health care, frontline nurses’ firsthand experiences, perceptions, and practical needs regarding GenAI remain largely under-synthesized in the existing literature.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This systematic review aimed to synthesize qualitative evidence to clarify the core themes related to clinical nurses’ perceptions, experiences, obstacles, and requirements when using GenAI in real-world clinical settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic search was conducted across 10 electronic databases (PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Web of Science, Cochrane Library, ProQuest Dissertations and Theses, China National Knowledge Infrastructure, VIP Information, SinoMed, and Wanfang) for records published between January 2018 and June 2026. Eligible studies included qualitative and mixed methods studies involving registered nurses that explored their perceptions and experiences of GenAI in clinical practice. Two independent reviewers (MMW and CYZ) performed study selection, quality appraisal, and data extraction, with disagreements resolved by consensus. Quality was assessed using the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) Critical Appraisal Checklist for Qualitative Research. Extracted data encompassed study characteristics, participant demographics, and GenAI-related contextual factors. Data synthesis followed Thomas and Harden’s 3-phase thematic synthesis: initial inductive coding generated descriptive themes, which were subsequently integrated with the Technology Acceptance Model for Artificial Intelligence in Nursing (TAM-AIN) framework to develop higher-order analytical themes. Certainty in the evidence was evaluated using the GRADE-CERQual (Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation-Confidence in the Evidence from Reviews of Qualitative Research).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Of the 4350 initially identified records, 13 studies from 6 countries (China: n=6; Saudi Arabia: n=3; United States, Singapore, Australia, and South Korea: n=1 each) met the inclusion criteria, encompassing qualitative data from 234 registered nurses. Three main themes emerged: patterns of nurses’ engagement with GenAI (ranging from passive observation to proactive integration), multidimensional perceived threats to adoption (functional, professional, and accountability-related), and the moderating role of organizational readiness, which influenced whether these threats hindered or facilitated GenAI uptake in practice. The GRADE-CERQual assessment showed moderate to high confidence in all findings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nurses’ engagement with GenAI ranges from passive observation to proactive integration, accompanied by legitimate concerns about functional reliability, professional role displacement, and accountability ambiguity. The moderating role of organizational readiness further highlights that training, tool optimization, and institutional governance remain critical yet often unmet. These findings necessitate coordinated efforts across workforce development, technological design, and regulatory frameworks. Future research should prioritize the development of clinically validated, context-aware GenAI systems that incorporate human-in-the-loop oversight, ensuring that efficiency gains do not compromise the delivery of compassionate, person-centered care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A dual-domain shapelet-guided conditional generative framework for imbalanced bearing fault diagnosis
container-title: Engineering Research Express
48dd31af472500c232f66eee2c6d19a8f53f14c5.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In bearing fault diagnosis, the scarcity of fault samples creates severe class imbalance and makes minority fault distributions difficult to learn reliably. Existing data-level methods mainly rely on interpolation, neighborhood relationships, or distribution modeling strategies to synthesize minority samples, which may fail to preserve complex temporal structures and fault-related local patterns. Although GAN-based methods provide flexible distribution modeling capabilities, their conditioning mechanisms often lack explicit representation of class-discriminative local patterns across temporal and spectral domains. To address these limitations, we propose ShapeGAN, a dual-domain shapelet-guided conditional generative framework for minority fault sample augmentation. Specifically, ShapeGAN first discovers class-specific temporal shapelets from minority and majority samples and derives the spectral representation of each retained segment using the discrete Fourier transform (DFT). A Conditional Mixing Module samples these paired representations, which are integrated by a bidirectional cross-attention generator. Training then proceeds from single-shapelet to multi-shapelet conditioning through the proposed Two-Stage Mixed Training strategy. Experiments on 24 imbalanced bearing fault scenarios show that ShapeGAN achieves the highest average Macro-F1 and G-Mean with the MLP classifier, while its average AUC remains comparable to that of the strongest baseline. With LSTM and ResNet, ShapeGAN achieves the best average performance across all three metrics, demonstrating the effectiveness of the proposed augmentation method across different downstream classifier architectures.</jats:p>

title: Epistemic Risks and a Framework for Critical Generative AI‐Mediated Reading
container-title: Reading Research Quarterly
2e0c7730eff79c1ef8dddf722e65bcc22ac3b8bf.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used to explain, summarize, and generate information, yet these activities are rarely framed as reading practices. This conceptual paper examines GenAI‐mediated reading, in which readers engage with responses generated by large language models (LLM) during inquiry and knowledge construction. GenAI frequently presents fluent and synthesized responses whose evidentiary basis, source relations, assumptions, and limitations may remain opaque. This paper identifies three epistemic risks: (a) fluent language may be misrecognized as truth, (b) algorithmic authority may encourage the outsourcing of epistemic judgment, and (c) responsive generation may weaken readers' critical monitoring through confirmation, sycophancy, or automation bias. To address these risks, the paper brings together critical reading and critical literacy and proposes the Critical Generative AI‐mediated Reading (CritGAIR) framework. The framework includes three recursive dimensions: (a) reading the response, (b) reading the system, and (c) reading the self. These dimensions direct attention to evaluating claims, evidence, and source credibility; interrogating authority, sociotechnical conditions, representations, and power; and reflecting on readers' prompts, trust, and uptake, respectively. Guiding questions and a hypothetical reading example illustrate how scrutiny can be calibrated to task purpose and consequences of error. The paper outlines educational applications and directions for investigating readers' evaluative processes, judgment quality, and the effort required for critical engagement.</jats:p>

title: Effect of Application-Based Learning Using Generative Artificial Intelligence on Information Literacy of First-Year Medical Students in Yunnan Province
container-title: Interdisciplinary Academic and Research Journal
ae5fca122b81c702af4a0f5001bbeece73180306.abstract:
<jats:p>Background and Aims: This experimental research aimed to 1) compare students’ information literacy before and after learning through Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence, 2) compare students’ information literacy after learning through Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence with the determined criterion set at 70%, and 3) assess students’ satisfaction after learning through Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence.
Methodology: The research instruments were lesson plans, students’ information literacy test, and a satisfaction questionnaire. The appropriateness of the lesson plans overall was at a very high level (M=4.62, SD=0.49). The students’ information literacy test had an IOC between 0.67–1.00, item difficulty (p=0.43-0.60), item discrimination (r=0.25-0.50), and KR20 equal to 0.76. The students’ satisfaction questionnaire had an IOC between 0.67 and 1.00 and a reliability index of 0.85. The statistics used to analyze data were mean, standard deviation, t-test for dependent samples, and t-test for one sample.
Results: 1) students’ information literacy after learning through Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence was higher than before at statistically significant level of .01 (t29=18.53, p=.000), 2) students’ information literacy was higher than the determined criterion of 70% at a significance level of .01 (t29=6.00, p=.000) and 3) students’ satisfaction after learning through Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence overall was at a high level (M=4.14, SD= 0.85).
Conclusion: The knowledge gained from the research is that a six-step learning management system using Application-Based Learning using Generative Artificial Intelligence (ABL-GAI), which represents an innovative instructional framework that systematically integrates human-AI co-creation into information literacy education. The most significant steps for enhancing students’ information literacy are step 4: Practice the skills + GAI, and step 5: Apply & create + GAI. Furthermore, this method has been shown to boost students' interest in learning and enhance their proficiency in core information literacy competencies, including information definition & planning, seeking & access, analysis, synthesis & communication, and reflection & self-evaluation.</jats:p>

16c15870fda1fa60be6333161abb4514f456ec4d.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) has increasingly shaped the landscapes of production since the early 2020s. This report reviews the scholarly debate on geographies of production and includes further developments in the spatiality of digitalisation. It draws on literature on firms that develop and offer AI as a product innovation (geographies of production
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">of</jats:italic>
                    AI) and firms that implement and use AI (geographies of production
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">with</jats:italic>
