title: Dynamical effects of herd behavior and constant harvesting in a Leslie-type predator–prey model: A bifurcation analysis
container-title: International Journal of Biomathematics
d435537ce7218c9910dff2fc3d988cc548440c89.abstract: <jats:p>In this paper, we investigate a Leslie-type predator–prey model with prey group defense and constant predator harvesting. First, we establish conditions for the existence and stability of all feasible equilibria of the model. We then derive a critical harvesting threshold for the existence of interior coexistence equilibria. A detailed stability analysis of the positive equilibrium shows that the two species can coexist persistently for appropriate parameter values and initial conditions. Furthermore, we systematically analyze the saddle-node and Hopf bifurcations exhibited by the model. The direction and stability of the Hopf bifurcation are determined by computing the first Lyapunov coefficient. By constructing a universal unfolding near the cusp point, we further prove that the model undergoes a codimension-two Bogdanov–Takens bifurcation. Finally, numerical simulations are performed to illustrate our theoretical results.</jats:p>

title: Propagation dynamics in a predator–prey Model with harvesting and hyperbolic mortality
container-title: International Journal of Biomathematics
796f934946488d6509c5576374a7b383f8eda60e.abstract: <jats:p>In this study, we consider a diffusive predator–prey system with hyperbolic mortality for predators and nonlinear harvesting for prey. First, the existence of traveling wave solutions is established by applying the method of upper and lower solutions together with the squeeze technique, which connects the predator-free constant steady state and the coexistence steady state. Second, using Hopf bifurcation theorem, we also prove the existence of small amplitude periodic traveling wave trains. The obtained traveling wave solution suggests that the predator invasion results in periodic oscillations in the population coexistence domain.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive correlates of diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space index in amnestic mild cognitive impairment: a preliminary study
container-title: Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology
1e1bf996cda945b0527e40176b2aa62fdc1d4c7d.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index is an imaging-derived metric related to perivascular water diffusion and has been reported to correlate with global cognitive performance in dementia. However, its associations with specific cognitive functions in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) remain underexplored. This study aimed to characterize the cognitive correlates of the DTI-ALPS index in individuals with amnestic MCI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cross-sectional study, 57 participants with amnestic MCI underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging and a neuropsychological assessment battery. Correlations between the DTI-ALPS index and performance across the assessed cognitive measures were examined before and after adjustment for age, sex, education, and Fazekas score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prior to adjustment, the DTI-ALPS index showed significant positive correlations with global cognitive measures, episodic memory retrieval, and semantic verbal fluency. After controlling for potential confounders, only the correlations with episodic memory and semantic verbal fluency remained significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The DTI-ALPS index remained significantly associated with episodic memory retrieval and semantic verbal fluency in amnestic MCI after adjustment, suggesting a possible link with frontotemporal network-related cognitive functions. Further studies incorporating multimodal imaging and disease-specific biomarkers are warranted to clarify the biological significance of the DTI-ALPS index and its potential clinical relevance in early cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The effect of parenting interventions to support language and literacy development in 3-7-year-old children in low- and middle-income countries: Systematic review and meta-analysis
container-title: Child Development
401b55bab284f0dcf9e1ce3f039d7338fef1c902.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Children in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) often have limited access to the structured home learning experiences that support language and literacy development during the critical years around school entry. We conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of parenting interventions targeting children's language or literacy in these settings. Twenty-six experimental and quasi-experimental studies from 15 countries involving 6,264 children aged 3–7 were included. Dependent effect sizes were synthesized using random-effects models with robust variance estimation. Parenting interventions were found to be associated with positive pooled effects on language (k = 21, g = 1.35, 95% CI [0.62, 2.09]) and literacy (k = 19, g = 0.94, 95% CI [0.56, 1.33]). Estimates were similar when restricted to the subset of 23 randomized controlled trials. Heterogeneity was substantial for both child outcomes. Exploratory moderator analyses suggested larger effects for both language and literacy in contexts with morphosyllabic script and, for literacy, in interventions that included shared book reading. Risk of bias was judged to be moderate, principally because most studies lacked prespecified analysis plans. We conclude that parenting interventions can support early language and literacy development in LMICs, although some uncertainty remains concerning the magnitude of effects, especially for language.</jats:p>

title: Level-2.5 large deviations and uncertainty relations for self-interacting jump processes: Tilting constructions and the emergence of timescale separation
container-title: Physical Review E
2254032434ab11e26a4641ec6d0fb73b09d929e6.abstract: <jats:p>Self-interacting jump processes (SIJPs) describe systems with non-Markovian stochastic dynamics in which transition rates depend on empirical observables of the process, which gives rise to long-range memory and feedback. We derive the “level-2.5” large deviation (LD) principle governing the joint fluctuations of empirical occupation measure and the flux matrix for a broad class of SIJPs with general functional dependence on an empirical observable. The derivation is based on an exponential tilting construction and reveals a separation between a faster timescale of the microscopic dynamics and a slower timescale of the memory-driven evolution of transition rates, which is expressed through an exponentially discounted LD rate functional. Using this variational framework, we derive kinetic and thermodynamic uncertainty relations that extend classical Markovian bounds to non-Markovian systems and illustrate their performance with simple examples.</jats:p>

title: Comparative Assessment of Orofacial Myofunction, Strength, and Quality of Life in Children With and Without Anterior Open Bite: The OMBIT Study
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
f0cf73444508fa39d6a33cf86e260930b11c82a4.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Anterior open bite (AOB) is a multifactorial malocclusion frequently associated with nonnutritive sucking habits (NNSHs) and orofacial dysfunctions. However, little is known about the specific orofacial strength and endurance profile in affected children. This study evaluated myofunctional history, orofacial myofunctional status, orofacial strength, and oral health–related quality of life (OHRQoL) in children in the mixed dentition stage with AOB, compared to controls without AOB.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Sixteen children with AOB in the mixed dentition stage (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">M</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>age</jats:sub>
                      = 8.2 years) and 16 age- and gender-matched controls participated in this cross-sectional study. Dental and orofacial histories were collected through parental questionnaires. Palatal and occlusal morphologies were assessed using intraoral scans. Orofacial function was examined using the Orofacial Myofunctional Evaluation with Scores (OMES) protocol and ultrasound imaging. Maximum isometric pressure and endurance of the tongue and lips were measured using the Iowa Oral Performance Instrument (IOPI). OHRQoL was assessed using the Child Oral Health Impact Profile–Ortho (COHIP-Ortho).
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Oral habits (e.g., nail biting, lip licking) were more frequently observed in the AOB group, and parental reports indicated that persistent open mouth behavior was reported more often in children with AOB. Two thirds of the participants had a history of NNSH, with similar prevalence across groups; however, AOB was associated with NNSH cessation at an older age. AOB was associated with higher anterior tongue endurance. No other significant differences were found in tongue or lip strength or endurance, OMES scores, or COHIP-Ortho scores.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The absence of group differences in orofacial strength and most endurance measures suggests that, in this sample, mixed-dentition AOB was not accompanied by generalized orofacial strength deficits. These findings support early functional screening and suggest that function-focused orofacial myofunctional therapy, rather than strength-based training, may be a relevant approach in children with AOB.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Hubbard U -dependent electronic structure and curie temperature of monolayer NiCl 2 : a combined DFT + U and spin-S Ising model study

                  <jats:p>
                    The electronic and magnetic properties of monolayer NiCl
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>

                    <jats:italic>U</jats:italic>
                    combined with a spin-S Ising model and Cellular Automaton simulations. Increasing the Hubbard
                    <jats:italic>U</jats:italic>

                    <jats:italic>U</jats:italic>

                    <jats:italic>U</jats:italic>

title: Stability transitions and Neimark–Sacker bifurcation in a predation model with fear induced delay: a discrete-time analysis
container-title: Physica Scripta
0e21bbe7ab1beb5fee50664b0e104e0fc5bd0e35.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Discrete-time dynamical systems frequently exhibit complex and realistic behaviors, particularly in biological contexts. In this work, a continuous-time predator–prey ecosystem is discretized using the Euler discretization method, and the variation in system stability with different parameter values is investigated. Analysis of the fear-induced system addresses the persistence of populations and their mutual influences. Fear restricts prey foraging activities, thereby limiting predator–prey interactions and eventually leading to increased intraspecific competition among predators. Fear significantly influences the system behavior when there is no delay, and it can also be utilized as a chaos control parameter to stabilize the system. For the delayed case, stability switching and the existence of Neimark–Sacker bifurcation are examined. The findings indicate that fear can destabilize an otherwise stable system and conversely, stabilize an unstable one. The primary result showed that a low level of dread exerts a considerable psychological influence on the prey population, thus benefiting the predator population. However, as fear is increased further, its effect plateaus, and additional changes in population dynamics are minimal. To verify the theoretical conclusion and offer more understanding of the dynamics of the system, numerical simulations are carried out.</jats:p>

title: Between Artifice and Enlightenment: Queer Critique, Insecurity, and the AI Large Language Model
container-title: Insecurity and the Eclipse of Enlightenment
eb93d5dc2a9e17c6e89c89b29ec656faaa8e39e1.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Over several decades, machine learning systems—often described with the double metaphor “artificial intelligence”—have become indispensable computational tools in the flow and mediation of economic and social capital. These systems can, on the surface, appear to deepen the dialectic of enlightenment identified by Horkheimer and Adorno by enabling ever greater domination over natural systems and human agency. They therefore generate widespread concern that computational advances endanger the security and autonomy of human subjects, especially in the sphere of production and exchange. Contemporary social theory offers conceptual tools that go beyond received categories of domination and autonomy, however, to provide a reanalysis of machine learning systems and their implication in social dynamics and economic relations. This chapter focuses on the ways large language model (LLM) systems demonstrate complex affinities with theories of mimesis and simulacrum, and therefore how such systems and require a rethinking of performativity and artifice. Recent queer critique—in which reflection on computational systems and simulacra is proliferating—and contemporary social theory, when read together, thus reveal how rhetoric about LLMs demonstrates slippages between agency, performance, reproduction, representation, and meaning that must be unpacked historically and conceptually before metaphors of the “artificial” and “intelligence” can carry analytical weight in addressing today’s socioeconomic relations. Ultimately, this theoretical-conceptual reading highlights the stakes of the problem of truth in systems where artifice manifests both socially and computationally.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive-affective functions, neighborhood opportunity, and social functioning in youth with neurofibromatosis type 1
container-title: Journal of Pediatric Psychology
2cb14b067c0eae9b7de70db16716ce2cc29c074b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated associations between social functioning and cognitive-affective functions (CAF), including executive function, face processing, and theory of mind, and neighborhood opportunity, in youth with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Youth with NF1 (n = 37), ages 8–14 (M = 11.8 years), with no prior autism diagnosis, completed assessments of CAF and peer relationships. Parents completed questionnaires on executive function skills, social impairments, and peer relationships. The Childhood Opportunity Index national composite score quantified neighborhood opportunity. Correlation and hierarchical linear regression analyses evaluated associations between social functioning, CAF, and neighborhood opportunity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Executive functioning and neighborhood opportunity were significantly associated with parent reports of social impairments and peer relationships. Executive functioning and facial expression recognition were correlated with self-reported peer relationships, but were not significant in regression models. Facial identity recognition was significantly correlated with social impairments and parent-rated peer relationships. Theory of mind was not associated with any outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings underscore the interplay between CAF, neighborhood opportunity, and social functioning in children with NF1. Case conceptualizations should integrate social determinants of health with measures of cognition and behavior. Longitudinal research is needed to understand mechanisms driving variability in social outcomes and inform equitable care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Emotional Sustainability Through Childlike Visual Language and Soft Visual Technology for Generation Z in “The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse”
container-title: Negotiating Faith, Fact, and the Future of Higher Education
35d2c1aea398f93b24063b1eeffe762c469b8346.abstract: <jats:p>This study examines childlike visual language in The Boy, the Mole, the Fox and the Horse and explores its potential as soft visual technology for supporting emotional reflection among Generation Z. Using a qualitative approach, the study applies Roland Barthes' semiotic analysis through denotation, connotation, and myth, supported by Focus Group Discussions with eight Generation Z participants and expert interviews in animation and psychology. The findings show that childlike visuals can communicate meanings related to vulnerability, belonging, comfort, courage, and self-reflection. Audience responses also varied according to personal experience and familiarity with mental health topics. Based on these findings, soft visual technology is discussed as a non-clinical visual approach that may support emotional reflection through aesthetic and symbolic experience, while emotional sustainability is used as a broader perspective for understanding meaningful visual design.</jats:p>

title: Teaching for Truth and Pluralism
container-title: Negotiating Faith, Fact, and the Future of Higher Education
8b018e18f17505ad800683cc03f7e7e7a81d7f54.abstract: <jats:p>In the past, higher education has been seen as a citadel of truth, critical thinking, and intellectual integrity. Nonetheless, in modern society, the identity of institutions of higher learning and their quest for truth has been questioned by the increase in tension levels. Due to polarization in politics and academic ideology, a market model in higher institutions of learning, and the ever-growing phenomenon of misinformation, it has become increasingly difficult to distinguish truth from opinion and ideology. There is increasing pressure on higher learning institutions to comply with numerous external demands by governments, corporate institutions, social movements, and so forth, which may affect the research and teaching agendas in a higher learning institution. On the other hand, students have to deal with numerous narrative constructs on online platforms, and it is becoming harder to explain the difference between scholarly writing and appealing but unsupported assertions.</jats:p>

title: Towards an Inclusive Educational Model in Tourism and Commerce
container-title: Inclusion and Diversity in Business and Tourism Education
72cf280f00cf891438c3363f0173397c9c5c41b8.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of universal accessibility and inclusive design into university education in tourism and commerce has become an ethical, social, and competitive priority within the framework of the 2030 Agenda. This chapter analyzes a Teaching Innovation Project conducted at the Faculty of Commerce and Tourism of the Complutense University of Madrid in 2025 to assess the feasibility and relevance of integrating accessibility as a cross-curricular component in undergraduate and postgraduate programs. A mixed-methods approach combined curriculum review with surveys of teaching staff and students. The findings reveal a clear gap between perceived relevance and curricular integration: almost all students value accessibility training for their future careers, while more than half of the teaching staff do not address it in their courses and report limited technical knowledge. Nevertheless, most lecturers show strong interest in further training. The chapter proposes curricular mainstreaming, adapted teaching guidelines, and strength accessibility-related competencies.</jats:p>

title: Beyond “Just Bullying”
container-title: Preparing Pre-Service Educators for Diverse Learners and Communities
7c52d60b425e9541aa2c318a59f9d04a312828d8.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how preservice teachers can be prepared to respond effectively to discriminatory language in K–12 classrooms. Drawing on practitioner evidence from a district-level culture and diversity role and scholarship on bias, discrimination, microinterventions, and practice-based teacher education, the chapter explores why educators may hesitate to intervene and the consequences of leaving discriminatory language unaddressed. It introduces defensible intervention, a framework that grounds educator responses in professional responsibility, school policy, and student safety. A staged model—Interrupt, Question, Educate, Restore, and Redirect—provides concrete strategies for responding across classroom contexts. Rehearsal scenarios and a reflective debrief protocol demonstrate how teacher preparation programs can help preservice teachers move from awareness of bias to practiced, context-responsive action.</jats:p>

title: Strengthening Workforce Preparedness Through Large-Scale CPR Training at CeSiECQ Jalisco IMSS

bfe341de47a2fc58a6ad1451b5898897c42b7028.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the implementation and educational outcomes of a large-scale simulation-based basic life support training program conducted at the Clinical and Surgical Simulation Excellence Center (CeSiECQ), Jalisco, of the Mexican Social Security Institute (IMSS). Using a mixed-methods approach, the chapter analyzes quantitative changes in theoretical knowledge together with qualitative evidence regarding participants' perceptions of confidence, teamwork, preparedness, and the educational value of simulation. The findings demonstrate significant improvements in knowledge performance and strong acceptance of simulation-based learning among a multidisciplinary workforce that included both clinical and non-clinical personnel. This chapter contributes evidence supporting simulation as a scalable strategy for workforce development, emergency preparedness, and institutional capacity building within public healthcare systems, particularly in low- and middle-income countries.</jats:p>

title: High-frequency enhancement and dual-model ensemble for language-guided COVID-19 pneumonia lesion segmentation
container-title: Biomedical Physics & Engineering Express
1311787a8a76185462f296af25917e6946b79ece.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Accurate segmentation of coronavirus disease 2019 pneumonia lesions in chest x-ray images is critical for disease quantification and clinical decision-making. However, existing methods suffer from blurred lesion boundaries, missed detection of tiny lesions, and limited generalization performance. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a language-guided multimodal medical image segmentation method integrating high-frequency enhancement and a dual-model ensemble. The method is developed along three dimensions: frequency-domain detail enhancement, spatial alignment optimization, and dual-model ensemble. First, a frequency-domain decomposition-based high-frequency enhancement module is designed to mitigate detail attenuation caused by encoder downsampling. Second, a two-dimensional spatial position encoding module is introduced to improve the spatial alignment between text descriptions and visual regions. Third, a dual-model ensemble architecture with differentiated frequency-domain masks is constructed to address the performance ceiling of individual models. Finally, experiments on two public datasets with different imaging modalities and data characteristics demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms existing single-modal and multimodal baseline methods and achieves competitive performance comparable to state-of-the-art approaches, verifying the effectiveness and robustness of the proposed framework. On the QaTa-COV19 dataset, the Dice coefficient reaches 91.85% and the mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) reaches 84.98%. On the multi-institutional MosMedData+ dataset, the Dice coefficient reaches 78.48% and the mIoU reaches 64.66%. The proposed method provides effective technical support for clinical diagnosis and follow-up assessment of pneumonia.</jats:p>

title: Universal machine learning force fields for materials simulation: from model construction to complex-system applications
container-title: Physica Scripta
1207e66cd64abc44be77c0de7adb4e9f1e2c043d.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Machine learning force fields (MLFFs) can reproduce reference electronic-structure energies and forces with high accuracy within validated chemical and configurational domains while substantially reducing the computational cost relative to direct first-principles calculations. Currently, MLFFs are evolving from system-specific models toward universal MLFFs. This review summarizes recent progress in universal MLFFs from data construction, model architecture, fine-tuning strategy, physical priors, and complex-system applications. We focus on three reliability bottlenecks: potential energy surface softening due to biased near-equilibrium pretraining data, catastrophic forgetting during downstream fine-tuning, and insufficient treatment of long-range electrostatics, dispersion, and polarization. Representative datasets and published benchmarks are assessed alongside graph, equivariant, basis-expansion and descriptor-based model families, with attention to model size, inference cost and task-specific validation. We further review forgetting-aware fine-tuning strategies, physics-enhanced frameworks and polarizable long-range models, as well as representative applications in battery electrolytes, solid-state interfaces, ferroelectric phase transitions, phonons, defects and thermal transport. Finally, future directions are discussed toward multifidelity data fusion, task-oriented benchmarks, uncertainty quantification, interpretability and integrated simulation toolchains.</jats:p>

title: Plasma Angiotensin‐Converting Enzyme as a Prioritized Candidate Target for Alzheimer's Disease: Evidence From Proteome‐Wide Mendelian Randomization and a Large Prospective Cohort Study
container-title: Journal of the American Heart Association
43b8b2cdd74b4c8e25e2ff8a1587a4cfd5b2f305.abstract:
<jats:sec xml:lang="en">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p xml:lang="en">We aimed to provide hypothesis‐generating evidence on druggable targets for Alzheimer's disease (AD) by integrating proteome‐wide Mendelian randomization (MR) with evidence from a conventional observational analysis of drug use in a large prospective cohort.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec xml:lang="en">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p xml:lang="en">Proteome‐wide MR analysis was conducted to identify plasma proteins causally related to AD risk using the largest summary‐level data to date, followed by colocalization and multiomic validation analyses (on the gene expression, alternative splicing, and DNA methylation levels in blood and brain, respectively) to prioritize potential druggable targets. We also replicated our MR findings using additional genetic data and performed multivariable MR for the prioritized findings. Conventional observational analysis in UK Biobank, a large prospective cohort, was performed to provide further clinical implications, using active comparator to minimize confounding by indication.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec xml:lang="en">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p xml:lang="en">MR analysis identified 15 plasma proteins with putative causal effects on AD risk. Of them, inhibition of angiotensin‐converting enzyme was found to increase the risk of AD (odds ratio, 1.10 [95% CI, 1.08–1.14]), which was likely independent of blood pressure as suggested by multivariable MR. Observational analysis in UK Biobank showed a higher incidence (hazard ratio, 1.23 [95% CI, 1.00–1.50]) of AD among regular users of angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitors, compared with the active comparator angiotensin receptor blocker users.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec xml:lang="en">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p xml:lang="en">Our genetic analyses prioritized angiotensin‐converting enzyme as a candidate target, and a conventional observational analysis in a large prospective cohort provided supportive evidence that regular angiotensin‐converting enzyme inhibitor use was associated with a higher AD risk, which needs further investigation with high‐quality real‐world evidence and clinical trials before being translated into practice changes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

                      Studies showed that dopamine and opioid systems in the brain have essential role in the modulation of pain perception. The evidence indicated that in the nucleus accumbens (NAc), both dopamine type 2 (D2) receptors and opioid receptors are highly expressed. title: Best Practice International Guidelines on Online Communities of Aphasia Groups
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
75edf257e21cf019bf51d5b7560159b569cf22f8.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We aim to establish best practice guidelines for the design, facilitation, and sustainability of online support groups for people with aphasia (PWA). It explores the benefits, challenges, and psychological considerations of virtual aphasia interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The recommendations presented were developed through a collaborative consensus process by our writing team, which was informed by a comprehensive review of current literature, insights from international experts, and practical experiences across various settings. This process involved meetings held between June 2023 and April 2025, focusing on the “Community of Practice related to online aphasia support.” These discussions examined the types, goals, and key features of online support groups—highlighting person-centered approaches, facilitation skills, and cultural responsiveness—and considered technological, logistical, and funding factors critical for successful implementation. Guided by principles of evidence-based practice and consensus building, the development produced practical recommendations that reflect diverse perspectives and best practices in both face-to-face and online aphasia support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Online aphasia support groups enhance accessibility, foster peer support, and promote social participation, contributing positively to psychological well-being. This tutorial identifies common challenges (e.g., technological barriers, engagement difficulties, and resource constraints), offering evidence-based strategies for mitigation. It underscores the importance of tailored facilitator training and sustainable funding models adapted to diverse contexts.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Online aphasia support groups are valuable tools to improve long-term communication and psychosocial outcomes for PWA. Their success depends on careful planning, skilled facilitation, and inclusive practices. Ongoing research, international collaboration, and adaptable funding strategies are vital to optimize their impact and expand access globally.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Word Retrieval in the Wild: The Feasibility of an Audio-Based Ecological Momentary Naming Protocol Completed by Adults With and Without Poststroke Aphasia
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
591434484a5cf3dbf529ad33afdf190ada784cb5.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) involves collecting data regarding behaviors or states of interest repeatedly in individuals' natural environments, typically from a smart device. The feasibility of EMA protocols with people with aphasia (PWA) remains relatively unexplored, particularly for objective assessments of language ability. We assessed the feasibility of a novel, smartwatch-delivered, audio-based ecological momentary naming protocol.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Fourteen PWA and 13 healthy controls completed a 3-week EMA protocol in which they attempted to name pictured objects delivered via smartwatch prompts while going about daily routines. Participants were pseudorandomly assigned to either a single-item (36 prompts per day, one image each) or nine-item (four prompts per day, nine images each) condition. Feasibility metrics were compliance (number of naming attempts/number of scheduled prompts), completion (number of naming attempts/number of delivered prompts), and perceived ease and burden of completing EMAs (captured via weekly surveys).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Average compliance for both PWA and controls was 77%, with completion at 83% and 84% for controls and PWA, respectively. Participants in the one-item condition trended toward higher compliance (at 83.3%) than individuals in the nine-item condition (at 71.9%). Perceptions of EMA ease and burden did not change over time or vary by group or EMA condition. Higher compliance was associated with temporal variables (day of protocol, time of day, day of week), older age, and better inhibitory control. Higher completion was associated with being unemployed and higher perceived burden. Qualitative analysis of exit interviews indicated that 89% of participants had a generally positive impression of the protocol.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This novel EMA was feasible for adults with and without aphasia. Although EMA research with PWA is still in its infancy, mobile health methodologies provide several promising avenues for improving the accuracy of long-term, in situ surveillance of aphasia symptoms.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Towards theorising the normative agency of Central Europe: iterative identities and norms shaping from a Global East perspective
container-title: Pluriversal International Relations
663673babdbce8296b91e1649af6e3f481f16706.abstract: <jats:p>This article examines under what conditions actors operating through a semi-peripheral regional format can develop an emergent form of normative agency. It treats the Three Seas Initiative as an illustrative Central European case, viewed through the Global East as a relational and epistemic positionality rather than a fixed geography. The article introduces the constructivist model of iterative identities and norms shaping, a heuristic framework tracing how previously articulated norms, identity narratives and regional role claims re-enter later political and institutional contexts and are reinterpreted, contested, amplified or institutionalised. The model identifies identity alignment and norm localisation as the principal conditions of regional normative agency, distinguishing conditional norm co-creation from compliance, locally bounded autonomy and failed agency. Empirically, the article analyses Three Seas Initiative summit declarations from 2016 to 2025, supplemented by institutional documents and selected European Union and North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) materials examining external recognition and convergence. The analysis reconstructs three phases of the initiative’s development: initial identity formation and the search for recognition; institutionalisation and the localisation of connectivity norms; and the post-2021 reinterpretation of infrastructure through resilience, security and eastern-flank vulnerability. The findings suggest that the initiative has generated limited and conditional normative agency through the regionally grounded reinterpretation of broader Euro-Atlantic normative templates. The case does not demonstrate autonomous norm creation but shows how historically norm-receiving actors may contribute to norm transformation when regional institutionalisation combines with wider recognition.</jats:p>

title: Surgery Is Not a Place: Time-to-Scalpel, Surgical Throughput, and Dynamic Load Balancing in Large-Scale Combat Operations
container-title: Military Medicine
823b47d8d2db377169796061bae1e4d3fbb72bf9.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Introduction</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Modern combat casualty care emphasizes rapid evacuation to surgical capability as a proxy for timely operative intervention. In large-scale combat operations (LSCO), however, high casualty density and finite surgical throughput may delay care even after arrival. We evaluated how operative capacity and casualty routing influence time-to-scalpel (TTS) during sustained combat.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This non–human subjects study developed a Division-scale discrete-event simulation representing an 18,000-person force, 9 evacuation origins, three Role 2 facilities each containing a full forward resuscitative and surgical detachment (FRSD) with two operating tables, and one Role 3 facility with four operating tables. The campaign lasted 36 days, with individual 30-day mortality follow-up. Eight casualty densities ranged from 1 to 15 combat casualties per 1,000 personnel per day. Four routing tactics were evaluated: Primary, Alternate, Bypass, and Smart, which prioritized surgical access for the highest-acuity patients. Mean TTS was the primary outcome; mean, median, and 95th-percentile TTS were conditional on operative start. Other outcomes included access among all surgical candidates and combat 30-day case fatality rate (CFR). Routing comparisons used 20 seed-matched replications per scenario with Holm adjustment. Bypass sensitivity analyses at densities 3, 9, and 15 varied delay-related mortality penalties by ±20% and replaced each FRSD with one forward resuscitative and surgical squad (FRSS).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The main experiment included 920 replications across 32 scenarios. At density 15, mean TTS was 136.24 hours with Primary, 19.24 with Bypass, and 82.53 with Smart. Both bypass-capable tactics reduced mean TTS relative to Primary at densities 7-15 (adjusted P &lt; .05). Under Primary, the mean fraction of preoperative delay attributable to surgical queueing exceeded 50% at density 9. Compared with Bypass, Smart shortened urgent-cohort TTS at all tested densities but lengthened TTS among the remaining surgical patients at densities 5-15 (all adjusted P &lt; .05). Smart also had higher CFR at density 9 (+0.307 percentage points; adjusted P = .016) but lower CFR at density 15 (−0.544 percentage points; adjusted P = .010). FRSSs increased TTS and CFR at all 3 sensitivity densities (all adjusted P &lt; .05). Substantial surgical delays persisted under both mortality-penalty assumptions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Under the modeled LSCO conditions, operative congestion increasingly drove delay to surgery. Load balancing casualty routing tactics may preserve operative access more effectively than fixed proximity-based routing alone. However, prioritizing surgical access for the highest-acuity patients does not uniformly improve access or mortality across the casualty population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Geometric calibration of central omnidirectional cameras under the unit-viewing sphere model
container-title: Optics Express
afd0a3cc44ad69a9bce1344ace2009688bf65e63.abstract: <jats:p>This paper presents a full-parameter calibration algorithm for central omnidirectional cameras, including central catadioptric and central fisheye cameras, unified under the unit-viewing sphere model. Existing methods typically require multiple line or chessboard patterns and are sensitive to radial distortion and image noise. In contrast, the proposed algorithm selects line images and views to identify those that provide valid calibration information. Building on this analysis, it requires only a mirror contour and one valid line image from a single view to linearly recover all intrinsic and spherical projection parameters. When at least four planar-point correspondences (or six world-point correspondences) are available, the extrinsic parameters and distortion coefficients can also be estimated. Notably, the effect of radial distortion can be approximately compensated by estimation biases in the effective focal length and the spherical projection parameter. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves robustness and accuracy comparable to classical methods, while enabling the selection of geometrically valid constraints.</jats:p>

title: Violation of parity and flavor symmetries in a Nambu–Jona-Lasinio model
container-title: Reviews in Mathematical Physics
771c3d3b1462a5b47539e478816f3f9c95947e32.abstract: <jats:p>In this paper, we study a lattice Nambu–Jona-Lasinio model with certain continuous chiral and two-flavor symmetries. For the Hamiltonian of the model, we construct a ground state which breaks the parity and flavor symmetries. In our argument, the chiral symmetry plays a crucial role in proving the violation of the parity and flavor symmetries, although the model does not contain the so-called Wilson term.</jats:p>

title: Central limit theorem for the random variables associated with the IDS of the Anderson model on the lattice
container-title: Reviews in Mathematical Physics
180c64892b40e978da4a2e1476207a79c0afd983.abstract: <jats:p>In this paper, we consider the existence of the integrated density of states (IDS) for the Anderson model on the Hilbert space [Formula: see text] as an analog of the law of large numbers (LLN). In this work, we prove an analog of the central limit theorem (CLT) for a collection of random variables associated with the IDS, for the class of test functions [Formula: see text], consisting of all once-differentiable functions on the real line whose derivative is continuous and has at most polynomial growth. Our result extends the work of Grinshpon–White [Spectral fluctuations for the multidimensional Anderson model, J. Spectr. Theory 12 (2022) 591–615], where the CLT was established for polynomial test functions.</jats:p>

title: ChavacanoMNMT: Exploring Language Influences in the Multilingual Neural Machine Translation of a Spanish-Based Creole
container-title: ACM Transactions on Asian and Low-Resource Language Information Processing
a3a1301d07c5732d6b5509990d5ed258faad0bef.abstract:
<jats:p>Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (MNMT) enhances low-resource language translation by leveraging related languages, yet its application to Creole languages like Chavacano, a Spanish-based Creole spoken in the Philippines, remains underexplored. This study investigates the influence of Austronesian (Cebuano, Hiligaynon) and Indo-European (Spanish, English) parent languages on Chavacano MNMT performance.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>We fine-tuned an mT5-base model on the ChavacanoMT dataset, which comprises 1,044,185 samples spanning 20 language pairs involving Chavacano and related languages. Ablation experiments were conducted by excluding individual languages from training to evaluate their impact on model performance. Performance was assessed using BLEU, chrF++, and BERTScore metrics, with Paired Bootstrap Resampling applied to determine statistical significance.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>
                    This study reports that Austronesian languages significantly influence Chavacano translation quality more than Indo-European languages (5 BLEU points,
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                    =0.001). Cebuano and Hiligaynon enhance translation quality (
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                    ⪋0.025), while Spanish contributes less due to structural divergence (VSO vs. SVO) despite Chavacano’s 77% lexical similarity with Spanish. Our model achieves a 17 BLEU point improvement in Chavacano-English translation over prior benchmarks.
                  </jats:p>
                  <jats:p>These findings highlight the role of structural similarity in MNMT and inform auxiliary language selection for low-resource Creole translation, contributing new benchmarks and insights for Chavacano NLP.</jats:p>

title: The Impact of Conversational Turn-Taking on Vocabulary Size in Toddlers With Developmental Delays Using Augmentative and Alternative Communication
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
11abcdea13c2cb5326a4db0dda9480dcd9c3ed9b.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study tracked the growth of conversational turn-taking during augmentative and alternative communication (AAC) intervention and evaluated how conversational turn-taking influenced the effectiveness of a 12-week augmented language intervention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study is a secondary analysis of archival data from Romski et al. (2010) and Romski et al. (2025). In total, 109 parents and their children with a variety of developmental delays (DDs) were randomly assigned to four intervention conditions across the two studies: (1) augmented input, (2) augmented output, (3) augmented input and output, and (4) spoken communication (SC). Language transcripts, including conversational turn count (CTC) and spontaneous augmented/spoken words, were transcribed using the Systematic Analysis of Language Transcripts software for 30-min interaction sessions between the parent and child at baseline, Session 18, and Session 24.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Total CTCs between parent–child dyads were found to have a quadratic growth curve. When separated by speaker, both parents and children had similar quadratic growth in CTCs over the course of the intervention. Additionally, it was found that exposure to AAC moderated the relationship between conversational turns and vocabulary size, such that higher rates of conversational turns were related to larger vocabulary size but only in parent–child dyads exposed to AAC conditions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>AAC creates a unique communicative environment where children with DD can reap the benefits of increased CTC not seen in traditional SC interventions. Parents and practitioners can couple AAC intervention with encouragement of more conversational turns within the population.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Does Portable Voice Amplification Improve Vocal Outcomes in Elementary School Teachers? Evidence From Aerodynamic, Acoustic, and Self-Reported Measures
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
3ab819b4a89b199aaecb7ba9c0986156e0c2bab7.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The present study aimed at evaluating the impact of a voice amplification system plus vocal hygiene on aerodynamic, acoustic, and self-reported outcomes in elementary school teachers with and without voice problems.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 217 elementary school teachers were initially recruited: 108 normal-voiced participants and 109 participants with voice complaints. Participants from both groups were assessed before and after voice intervention, with aerodynamic, acoustic, and self-reported outcomes being observed. Participants were randomly assigned to one of two treatments before starting voice intervention procedures: (a) use of amplification system in their classroom setting plus vocal hygiene program (experimental condition) and (b) vocal hygiene program only (control condition). Thus, four groups were generated for this study. Data were analyzed by implementing mixed-effects models for all dependent variables.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>For dysphonic teachers, significant interactions were observed on Vocal Fatigue Index, Voice Handicap Index, and Vocal Tract Discomfort Scale values, reflecting greater improvement for the experimental group as compared to the control group once the intervention was completed. In contrast, no differential effects were observed for smoothed cepstral peak prominence, airflow rate, subglottal pressure, or phonation threshold pressure. Only one significant interaction was detected in participants with normal voices, suggesting that treatment is more effective for teachers already suffering from dysphonia.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Portable amplification system plus vocal hygiene seems to positively impact dysphonic school teachers' voice, especially in terms of self-reported improvements in functional, physical, and emotional voice-related dimensions; throat discomfort; and vocal fatigue symptoms. No statistically significant changes were observed for aerodynamic or acoustic outcomes. These findings, along with prior evidence, suggest that voice amplification may be most beneficial when implemented as one component of a broader approach to occupational vocal health, combined with other strategies such as voice training and classroom acoustic interventions.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Swallowing Symptoms in Female FMR1 Premutation Carriers: Eating Assessment Tool-10 Findings and Associations With Genetic and FXTAS–Related Features
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
2115aa21b8294b8efb9b9a7a93f64262b37de1d1.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      The
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">fragile X messenger ribonucleoprotein 1</jats:italic>
                      (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">FMR1</jats:italic>
                      ) premutation (FXpm) is a prevalent genetic variant that confers risk for neurodegenerative motor impairments associated with fragile X–associated tremor/ataxia syndrome (FXTAS). Swallowing difficulties may be more common in FXpm carriers but remain understudied. This study investigates swallowing symptoms in FXpm women and their associations with FXTAS-related motor symptoms and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">FMR1</jats:italic>
                      -related genetic variation.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Participants (85 FXpm women, 73 controls) completed the Eating Assessment Tool–10 and the FXTAS Rating Scale–Revised. Genetic measures included cytosine-guanine-guanine repeat length, activation ratio, and repeat size mosaicism. Hurdle models assessed group differences in symptom endorsement and severity. Item-level differences were examined, along with associations between swallowing symptom endorsement, motor scores, and genetic measures using logistic regression and exploratory correlations.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      FXpm women were more likely to endorse swallowing symptoms than controls, particularly at lower education levels (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">OR</jats:italic>
                      = 0.68, 95% confidence interval [CI; 0.49, 0.93],
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      = .017).
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Effort swallowing solids</jats:italic>
                      and
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">food sticking in the throat</jats:italic>
                      were the strongest item-level differentiators of the groups. Parkinsonian motor features (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">OR</jats:italic>
                      = 1.29, 95% CI [1.04, 1.59],
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      = .022) and premutation/full mutation (PM/FM) mosaicism (
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">OR</jats:italic>
                      = 7.72, 95% CI [1.12, 53.30],
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">p</jats:italic>
                      = .038) were associated with higher likelihood of symptom endorsement.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings suggest that some FXpm women, particularly those with lower educational attainment and PM/FM mosaicism, experience elevated swallowing symptom burden, which may reflect early manifestations of motor system involvement. Swallowing symptoms warrant greater clinical attention in this population, with further research integrating comprehensive swallowing assessments needed to clarify the nature, progression, and clinical significance of swallowing symptoms in FXpm women.</jats:p>

title: Global dynamics of a delayed viral infection model mediated by pattern recognition receptors with CTL immune response
container-title: Physica Scripta
1442413dadf8eca52c25333e865024f996c15213.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this paper, we develop a viral dynamics model incorporating three distinct time delays to characterize the complex interplay between viral infection and host immune responses. In the modeling process, we integrate the innate immune signaling pathway mediated by pattern recognition receptors and couple it with the specific adaptive immune response involving cytotoxic T lymphocytes (CTLs). Three physiologically meaningful delays—namely, the intracellular delay, the virus replication delay, and the CTL immune response delay—are introduced to account for the temporal lags in viral production, de novo cell infection, and adaptive immune recruitment, respectively. By constructing appropriate Lyapunov functionals and applying LaSalle’s invariance principle, we rigorously establish the global asymptotic stability conditions for both the infection-free equilibrium and the infected equilibrium, thereby elucidating the influence of delays on the long-term system dynamics. Furthermore, taking the CTL immune response delay as the bifurcation parameter, we analyze the distribution of the characteristic roots and derive sufficient conditions for the existence of Hopf bifurcations. Our results demonstrate that an increase in this delay can induce periodic oscillations, providing a theoretical explanation for the fluctuations in viral load and the dynamic imbalance of immune responses observed in clinical settings. Numerical simulations are performed to corroborate the theoretical findings.</jats:p>

title: Charge collection efficiency in air-vented plane-parallel ionisation chambers at ultra-high dose rates: a self-consistent Garfield++ Monte Carlo model including space-charge effects and ion recombination
container-title: Physics in Medicine & Biology
8b0485c0becde59a07ad65e83c7a3bfba45ce913.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    <jats:italic>Objective.</jats:italic>
                    Ultra-high dose rate (UHDR) irradiation used in FLASH radiotherapy can lead to significant reductions in charge collection efficiency (CCE) in plane-parallel ionisation chambers due to enhanced ion recombination, while the high charge densities involved can also induce strong space-charge-induced electric-field distortions. This work aims to develop a Monte Carlo framework for investigating these coupled effects.
                    <jats:italic>Approach.</jats:italic>
                    We extended the Garfield++ Monte Carlo particle-transport framework by implementing ion–ion recombination and self-consistent space-charge electric field calculations. The resulting model couples particle transport, electron attachment, recombination processes, and dynamic electric-field distortions. The implementation was validated against analytical and numerical models from the literature.
                    <jats:italic>Main results.</jats:italic>
                    Excellent agreement was obtained for the free electron fraction (FEF), CCE, induced current, and electric field evolution under UHDR conditions. The simulations show that space charge can locally increase the electric field by more than a factor of four or reduce it to nearly zero in some regions of the chamber. The results further suggest that the decrease in the FEF caused by electric-field-dependent electron attachment plays a major role in the reduction of the CCE under UHDR conditions.
                    <jats:italic>Significance.</jats:italic>
                    These findings highlight the importance of accurately describing the evolution of the FEF for modelling recombination under UHDR conditions, opening up prospects for improved analytical models and real-time correction methods for ionisation chamber dosimetry. More broadly, this work provides a flexible and self-consistent Monte Carlo framework for investigating recombination phenomena and improving dosimetry models for FLASH radiotherapy.
                  </jats:p>

title: Parental scaffolding and cognitive development in early childhood: Insights from a dynamic systems perspective

<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Grounded in dynamic systems theory, which conceptualizes parent–child interactions as evolving systems of reciprocal influence over time, the main objective of this study was to examine which patterns of parent–child scaffolding in a problem-solving situation were associated with children's early cognitive development and to explore whether these patterns were influenced by prior child characteristics. A total of 193 mother–child dyads (109 girls) were observed during a number–image association task at 48 months. Children were predominantly White (95%) and of Canadian or European ethnic background. Three scaffolding phases were examined using the State Space Grid (SSG): modeling (problem-solving strategies are demonstrated by parents), guidance (characterized by shared participation in task execution), and fading (support is gradually withdrawn and greater initiative is shown by children). Only the fading phase was found to be associated with higher complex executive functioning (β = 0.30) and number knowledge (β = 0.42) 1 year later, at 60 months, controlling for prior child cognitive abilities. Furthermore, higher socioeconomic status, receptive vocabulary, and cognitive flexibility at 42 months were positively associated with fading. These findings highlight the importance of interactional processes that promote children's active participation in problem- solving for subsequent cognitive development.</jats:p>

title: A statistical framework for evaluating the repeatability and reproducibility of large language models
container-title: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
310fa37d6ca2b27293a68cf4da2808fc8bbb1d89.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Systematic evaluation of variability in large language model (LLM)-generated outputs is critical for assessing their reliability. We developed a general statistical framework and Python package (llmReproScore) for quantifying the repeatability and reproducibility of LLM outputs.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following US Food and Drug Administration terminology, our framework establishes four metrics for quantifying LLM repeatability and reproducibility along two dimensions: semantic and internal. Semantic metrics quantify variability in the meaning of LLM-generated outputs, whereas internal metrics quantify variability in token-generation certainty. We validated these metrics, and as an illustrative use case, applied them to diagnostic reasoning outputs generated across LLMs and prompting strategies using US Medical Licensing Examination questions and 90 real-world rare disease cases from the Undiagnosed Diseases Network.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Validation results showed that semantic scores aligned with human ratings (Spearman ρ = 0.88 for repeatability and 0.66 for reproducibility) and confirmed that internal metrics capture variability in token-generation certainty. In the illustrative use case, LLM repeatability was generally not associated with accuracy, suggesting that LLM output variability and accuracy capture distinct dimensions of model performance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed metrics can be used to characterize LLM output variability and systematically compare models, prompts, and generation settings. These comparisons can inform more rigorous selection of LLM configurations based on repeatability and reproducibility.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We developed and validated generalizable metrics for quantifying LLM output variability. The proposed metrics can complement accuracy-based evaluation to inform experimental design and support more rigorous comparison and selection of models, prompts, and generation settings.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A JUNGFRAU-based electron diffractometer with large-scale capacity
container-title: Journal of Applied Crystallography
1ff12d1b500f9d0931f547c042b18d6ab397f639.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    An integrated hardware–software platform for three-dimensional electron diffraction has been developed using the JUNGFRAU 1M charge-integrating hybrid pixel detector. The system combines the field-programmable gate array based Jungfraujoch backend with the
                    <jats:italic>JFGui</jats:italic>
                    graphical interface, providing centralized control of the detector, electron microscope and data-processing software. This workflow enables synchronized data acquisition, live visualization and instantaneous post-processing with established crystallographic programs, including
                    <jats:italic>XDS</jats:italic>
                    ,
                    <jats:italic>DIALS</jats:italic>
                    and
                    <jats:italic>SHELX</jats:italic>
                    . Applications to L-histidine and dioctyl perylene tetracarboxylic diimide crystals are presented, including charge-density evaluation employing the recently developed iSFAC (ionic scattering factors) model. The workflow supports continuous-rotation measurements at speeds up to 10° s
                    <jats:sup>−1</jats:sup>
                    , allowing acquisition of a ∼130° rotation in approximately 15 s and enabling higher-throughput measurements. Comparative measurement at 100 and 200 keV beam energies revealed the trade-off between real-space contrast and diffraction resolution. These developments establish a complete and efficient practical workflow of 3D ED coupled with instrumental evaluation, providing a robust route toward quantitative electron crystallography.
                  </jats:p>

title: Development and validation of hypoxic chambers combined with an oxygen diffusion model for controlled radiobiological experiments
container-title: Biomedical Physics & Engineering Express
f51f2409913d7c2eaa46088824c79d569b915829.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Tumor hypoxia is a hallmark of cancer that drives radioresistance, metastasis and poor clinical outcomes.
                    <jats:italic>In vitro</jats:italic>
                    modeling of hypoxic conditions is therefore critical for understanding tumor biology and testing therapeutic strategies. Commercially available hypoxic chambers, while very efficient at maintaining atmospheric conditions of samples, are often not portable, unsuitable for irradiation experiments and have a significant cost. In this study, we developed and tested two in-house hypoxic chambers (a portable chamber and a glove chamber), combined with a 1-D oxygen diffusion model for performing and validating biological experiments under controlled hypoxic environment. The systems were validated under physiologically relevant oxygen conditions (0%–4% O
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ) through continuous monitoring using PICO-O
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    and LuminOX sensors integrated via Arduino/Bluetooth. A 1-D diffusion model based on Fick’s law was developed, predicting the exposure time required to achieve a target oxygen concentration as a function of the medium height. For a full end-to-end test of the system, we conducted immunofluorescence analysis to verify the hypoxic status of the cells and we irradiated triple negative breast cancer cells (MDA-MB-231) with photons and protons at doses ranging from 2.5–12.5 Gy under normoxic (21% O
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    concentration) and hypoxic (4% O
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    concentration) conditions, followed by clonogenic survival assay to test the cytotoxicity and radioresistance. Our results showed the ability of both chambers to properly maintain the target oxygen levels and the 1D-diffusion model reproduced hypoxia establishment times with <5% deviation from direct measurements in the medium (PICO-O
                    <jats:sub>2</jats:sub>
                    ). Immunofluorescence analysis confirmed effective induction of cellular hypoxia, evidenced by increased hypoxia-associated fluorescence and elevated hypoxia-inducible factors-1
                    <jats:italic>α</jats:italic>
                    expression under hypoxic conditions compared with normoxia. Additional biological results confirmed hypoxia-induced morphological changes and increased radioresistance, with consistent survival outcomes across both chambers. Together, the two chamber designs and the diffusion model provide a low-cost system for studying hypoxia-induced radioresistance
                    <jats:italic>in vitro</jats:italic>
                    .
                  </jats:p>

title: Large language models are unstable as autonomous medical evaluators across clinical tasks
container-title: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association
e0d8ad611804b7e0244a31b57460bc60db4be35f.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as automated evaluators of medical text (“LLM-as-judge”). We tested whether LLM-evaluator performance validated on one medical task against a human reference standard remains stable on a structurally different task.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Materials and methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We evaluated 10 LLMs (3 locally served open-source and 7 API models: Claude, GPT, DeepSeek) as autonomous judges on 3 tasks with human reference labels: LiveQA-Med answer quality (n = 300), PubMedQA research appraisal (n = 300), and Emergency Severity Index (ESI) triage on MIMIC-IV-Ext (n = 256). Each case was scored 3 times per model at temperature zero (25 680 judgments). Analyses used cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals, quadratic-weighted Cohen’s κ, and false-discovery-rate correction.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Evaluator performance was unstable across tasks: no model ranked in the top 3 on all 3 tasks, and every model shifted by 3 or more rank positions between at least one pair of tasks. In the highest-stakes task, ESI level 1 (Resuscitation) cases were under-triaged in 89.1% of evaluations, in all 10 models (range 70.2%-96.9%). Best triage agreement only reached the human inter-rater range (Claude Opus quadratic-weighted κ = 0.60 [0.54, 0.66]). Locally served 7-27B models (no per-query charge) occupied the Pareto frontier on the text tasks but only its low-concordance end on triage.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>LLM-evaluator performance is unstable between medical tasks that differ in cognitive structure; performance validated on one task should not be assumed to transfer to another.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Task-specific validation against human reference labels is required before deployment, and emergency triage demands human oversight at the highest-acuity tier.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The dynamics of a stochastic Leslie-Gower predator-prey model influenced by Lévy noise
container-title: IMA Journal of Applied Mathematics
437b853e7b70697f317bb9fb5dc12ca78136400b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>In this paper, a two-dimensional Leslie-Gower stochastic predator-prey system with jumps is investigated. Path-wise estimation, stochastic ultimate boundedness, existence and uniqueness of the global positive solution, and other properties of the solution are analyzed. Next, the conditions required for the system in question to become extinct are given. Numerical simulations are elaborated based on the Euler scheme and the Fokker-Planck approach. Systems’ parameters analysis is investigated and the obtained results demonstrate that population systems attributes can be altered via Lévy noise.</jats:p>

title: “The Why, the What Now, and the Future”: Lived Experiences From Parents of Former Late-Talking Toddlers
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
9da0d63f58e0a4eecdec27b2d1de00fc6cc75b01.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The aim of this study was to better understand the functional implications of late talking by documenting the lived experiences of parenting a late-talking toddler.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>All parents had previously enrolled their children in a vocabulary intervention study with the authors when their children were toddlers. We created interview questions collaboratively with a focus group of these parents. We then individually interviewed 10 parents of late talkers. Two coders engaged in consensus coding, using an inductive, qualitative content analysis process to develop categories. During the coding process, codes were organized under three major topic areas: (a) support for the child and family, (b) parents' perceptions of their child's communication, and (c) how having a late talker influenced relationship dynamics within the family.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We developed six primary categories to summarize the parents' responses: (a) barriers to support, (b) facilitators to support, (c) parents' suggestions for support systems, (d) child-specific characteristics, (e) child–parent experiences, and (f) within-family roles and relationships.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings are contextualized in terms of action items to better support families of children with late talkers, including improving support for families, attending to family relationship dynamics, academic applications and considerations, and encouragement for families.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A Bispecific Antibody Targeting Dickkopf-1 and Sclerostin Enhances Bone Formation in the Brtl/+ Mouse Model of Osteogenesis Imperfecta
container-title: JBMR Plus
ed571f2830330515c05de5bfab590769c825f6f9.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Osteogenesis imperfecta (OI) is a collagen-related disorder characterized by frequent fractures. Sclerostin neutralizing antibodies (Scl-Ab) have been shown to increase bone mass in mouse models and adults with OI. However, serum concentrations of the WNT antagonist dickkopf-1 (DKK1) are elevated in people with OI and expression of both Sost and Dkk-1 are elevated in mice after Scl-Ab treatment, potentially dampening the therapeutic response. We aimed to evaluate the effect of rodent bispecific antibody (rbsAb) against DKK1 and sclerostin in a mouse model of dominant OI with a Col1a1 structural defect. Ten-week-old male and female Brtl/+ and WT mice received twice weekly injections of rbsAb or vehicle for 8 weeks. Assessment of femoral bone microstructure and density using in vivo microCT showed rbsAb treatment led to greater percent change from baseline in all cortical and trabecular bone mass and microstructural parameters compared to vehicle in all groups (eg. Ct.Th in Brtl/+ males rbsAB: 52%, vehicle: 2%; females rbsAB: 55%, vehicle: 10%). MicroCT-based timelapse morphometry revealed that rbsAb led to greater bone formation and lower bone resorption on endocortical, periosteal, and trabecular surfaces. Fluorochrome-based histomorphometry primarily showed greater mineralizing surfaces with rbsAb treatment. rbsAb treated mice had greater bone strength and stiffness and there was no treatment-related difference in post-yield displacement. MicroCT analysis of L4 vertebrae revealed greater bone mass in all groups with rbsAb treatment compared to vehicle. The percent change from baseline in serum bone formation marker P1NP was greater after 4 weeks of treatment compared to vehicle in all groups, but only in females at 8 weeks; no treatment-related difference was measured in resorption marker TRAcP5b. rbsAb treatment led to greater Dkk-1 and Sost gene expression compared to vehicle in all groups. This data demonstrates rbsAb treatment elicited a potent anabolic response in both WT and Brtl/+ mice.</jats:p>

title: Cascaded design for microstructured optical diffusers using a Gaussian scattering-kernel model

<jats:p>
                    A cascaded design method for surface-relief diffusers composed of concave ellipsoidal microstructures is presented. In this method, area-weighted Gaussian scattering kernels for broad parameter screening are combined with ray tracing for local refinement. In Stage I, a continuous surface is generated for each candidate parameter set. Local surface normals within the effective region of each microstructure are used to calculate output ray angles according to Snell’s law. Their mean and covariance define a two-dimensional Gaussian scattering kernel, while the effective-region area determines its weight. The superposition of all kernels is used for broad parameter search. In Stage II, the selected parameter region is refined by ray tracing. For a nearly circular 30
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    target, a final horizontal FWHM of 29.92
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    is obtained. For an anisotropic 30
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    /20
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    target, the final principal FWHMs are 30.01
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    and 20.05
                    <jats:sup>∘</jats:sup>
                    . The same optimized surfaces are further evaluated for spatial coherence and polarization, with DoLP values of 0.9980 and 0.9991, respectively.
