title: Leading with Inclusion
container-title: Social Justice in Education
15d0c377a0cd037cd3ab9dc7c16f11209a7bbeda.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter views neurodiversity as a social justice issue in English language education from the leadership perspective. Despite a growing emphasis on diversity, equity, and inclusion, neurodivergent learners continue to encounter institutional practices restricting their meaningful participation and access. Drawing on narrative accounts from four English language educators in K-12 and higher education contexts, the chapter explores how leadership practices shape inclusivity. The educators' reflections reveal tensions between institutional policies and teachers' efforts to support neurodivergent learners in the face of curriculum and assessment-related restrictions. These narratives highlight the importance of teachers' role as informal leaders and advocates. From a social justice lens, the chapter argues for an inclusive leadership beyond policy statements to foster flexible, collaborative, and dignity-affirming practices. It displays the pivotal role of neurodiversity in equitable educational leadership and underscores lived experiences for inclusive institutional change.</jats:p>

title: Mapping Inclusive Practices in English Language Teacher Education
container-title: Social Justice in Education
d8b2355d87e6e94e10de161bb61e42611dd69215.abstract: <jats:p>Teachers are not only facilitators of learning but also agents of change, capable of shaping educational systems to become more equitable and responsive to learner diversity. Their preparation within teacher education programs is therefore critical in ensuring that inclusivity moves from being a stated value to a lived reality. This study examines how inclusive education is represented in an English Language Teacher Education Program (ELTEP) and ELT department's artifacts. Data were collected through systematic document analysis of the program framework, mission, vision and goal statements, and program competency framework of the department. Analysis revealed that inclusivity is acknowledged but unevenly embedded, primarily through a single compulsory course and several electives of limited reach. These findings suggest that while inclusivity has some fragmented curricular presence, there is a need for structural revisions to embed it as a systematic, ELT-specific competency.</jats:p>

title: Characterizing Narrative Discourse in Posttraumatic Amnesia and Early Recovery After Severe Traumatic Brain Injury
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
9375137b12e3e015ae4baad68955e02a5cbea3ce.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Following severe traumatic brain injury (TBI), individuals experience a transient period of confusion known as posttraumatic amnesia (PTA). Few empirical speech-language pathology studies have described language and cognitive-communication features during PTA or examined their early recovery. International guidelines recommend routine monitoring of communication during PTA; however, standardized speech-language pathology assessments are generally unsuitable for use during PTA. Narrative tasks offer a structured and repeatable approach to capture clinically meaningful changes. The purpose of this research was to describe narrative discourse characteristics in adults with severe TBI during PTA and examine how performance changed following PTA resolution.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Nine adults with severe TBI admitted to an inpatient rehabilitation setting completed a narrative task during PTA and again after resolution of PTA. Language samples were analyzed across multiple levels, with descriptive analyses used to characterize performance and patterns of change. Discourse performance during PTA was compared descriptively to published data, providing reference data for microlinguistic measures and story grammar in adults without brain injury and adults with TBI who were not in PTA, where data were available.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>All participants demonstrated confused, disorganized narratives during PTA, although the degree and profile of impairment varied markedly across individuals. Macrostructural analyses provided the most meaningful and sensitive indicators of change, with several participants showing clearer narrative structure and increased production of relevant content post-PTA.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A narrative task has the potential to provide insight into the communication ability of patients in PTA, particularly in relation to change over time. This may help to guide decisions about the most appropriate timing for formal speech-language pathology assessment and intervention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Speech-Language Therapists' Lived Experiences of Family-Centered Practice in Early Childhood Stuttering
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
d261a4914c4dd3106a992a23dad846dfa7959bbe.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Family-centered practice (FCP) is widely endorsed in early childhood stuttering (ECS) intervention. Yet how it is experienced and enacted by speech-language therapists (SLTs) in clinical work remains largely unexamined, particularly in contexts where structured institutional support is absent.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A descriptive phenomenological design was used. Data were collected through semistructured interviews with eight SLTs in Türkiye and analyzed to identify shared structures of meaning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Two themes were identified: (a) “Adaptation Through Experience” and (b) “Being With the Family.” FCP was enacted as an individual ethical orientation rather than a shared service model. Despite identifying FCP as a family-centered model, SLTs operated within an expert-driven mode, that is, equating family involvement with family-centeredness with therapeutic decision making remaining firmly with the clinician.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings suggest that FCP in ECS functions as an individual ethical orientation rather than a shared professional practice, sustained by the notion of family-centeredness while decision making remains expert-driven. This configuration reflects a structural absence, not weak professional commitment. ECS research and practice have endorsed family-centered values without developing the conceptual and institutional conditions required to enact them. The conceptual scaffold presented here represents an initial articulation of what those conditions demand.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

f958e0c181d2aee612560a9ff71d0d40b95363cc.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Laser scanning microscopy (LSM) has become an indispensable tool in biomedical research; yet its imaging performance—particularly field-of-view (FOV), resolution, and spectral versatility—is governed by the scanning system. Conventional scanning systems rely on reflective or refractive relay optics to couple the scanning beam into the objective, which inevitably introduces off-axis aberrations or chromatic dispersion, thereby limiting both the accessible FOV and the usable wavelength range. Here, we present a four-scanner virtual-conjugation (4-SVC) system that achieves virtual conjugation on both scanning axes using an all-reflective design. The system exhibits negligible off-axis aberrations at scan angles up to ±11.70° (experiments were performed at ±6.38°) for a 20-mm-diameter beam and delivers >80% transmittance from the visible to the near-infrared region, with minimal chromatic aberration and dispersion. Using the 4-SVC, we demonstrate, for the first time to the best of our knowledge, a one-, two-, and three-photon LSM that achieves a 4-mm FOV with near-submicron resolution over an excitation range of 405–1550 nm. This system enables
                    <jats:italic>in vivo</jats:italic>
                    imaging of neuronal structures and microglial dynamics across both hemispheres, and discrimination of multiple tissue components in mouse kidney slices via broadband excitation. The 4-SVC eliminates the need for refractive relay optics, offering a versatile scanning solution for applications that simultaneously demand large FOV, high resolution, and broadband spectral compatibility.
                  </jats:p>

title: Machine-Learned Particle Flow as a Foundation Model for Collider Physics
container-title: PRX Intelligence
a7c1b0fda6c698ac6ecf5fb9195fb389dd37f5d8.abstract: <jats:p>The workflow from particle collision to physics analysis passes through a series of reconstruction steps that are traditionally modular and disconnected, with no shared representation linking low-level detector data to high-level analysis tasks. We show that casting event reconstruction as a machine learning problem naturally produces such a shared representation. We repurpose a machine learning model trained for particle-flow reconstruction (MLPF) to perform three distinct analysis tasks: jet flavor identification, jet energy regression, and missing momentum regression. By appending the per-particle latent representations learned during reconstruction as additional input features, we substantially improve over baselines that use conventional particle-level features alone. We further demonstrate that a single linear layer trained using only the latent representations achieves competitive performance against state-of-the-art baseline architectures, and outperforms the baseline for missing momentum regression with approximately 35 times fewer parameters. These results demonstrate that the latent representations learned during reconstruction encode essential physics information needed for downstream analysis, establishing MLPF as a foundation model and offering a concrete step toward an end-to-end pipeline from detector data to physics analysis.</jats:p>

title: Health and social care data and the Hippocrates model: Gaps and recommendations
0fa3d7036d963f70b3e275f31539a80131addcd4.abstract:
<jats:p>Health information has an essential role to play in health and social care planning decisions. Traditionally, Ireland lagged behind its European peers in prioritising health data, with several instances of health and social care data either not being recorded, or being recorded and stored but in a manner that prevents their use for planning purposes, or not being easily accessible to those who require it. While investment in this area has increased rapidly in recent years, data and health information deficits continue to impact a range of stakeholders across the health system. This report identifies and discusses data gaps in the Irish health and social care sector, with particular reference to the data required to project future demands for health and social services within the ESRI Hippocrates model. The report focuses on the availability of data – along with notable gaps – in 2024/2025, when the Hippocrates model was most recently updated. Within this context, it is important to acknowledge that several significant data developments are currently underway, which have the potential to transform health data availability in the Irish context; these include the Digital Health Strategic Implementation Roadmap, the Health Information Act 2026 and the European Health Data Space.
Several major data issues in the Irish context limit the amount and type of analysis that can be undertaken to inform health system planning and reform in Ireland. These include:
(i)	incomplete and inconsistent use of an Individual Health Identifier (IHI);
(ii)	incomplete and inconsistent use of electronic health records (EHRs);
(iii)	incomplete data on privately provided/financed services;
(iv)	incomplete data on primary care and community-based services; and
(v)	incomplete data at the Health Region level.
A number of ongoing initiatives seek to address these limitations, which when implemented will significantly improve data infrastructure and availability. In this context, consideration is required from the outset regarding how data collected through ongoing initiatives can and should be used for purposes beyond immediate patient care, including research and service planning. Drawing on recommendations from the World Health Organization (WHO), it is recommended that the sharing of data for research purposes should be done in a manner that is equitable, ethical and efficient, including initiatives such as the Trusted Research Environment.
In 2025, the ESRI published six reports, which included projections of demand and associated capacity requirements, at both the national and HSE region level for public acute hospitals, general practice and older people’s services. While these analyses included the most up-to-date, available data at the time of completion, the extent of the analysis that could be undertaken for each service area was significantly curtailed by data availability.
•	Public acute hospitals: The best available data among the services examined are for the public acute hospital system and, in particular, for day patients and in-patients using the Hospital In-Patient Enquiry (HIPE) scheme. However, there are limitations to these data. For example, the incomplete and inconsistent use of the IHI means that the analysis is at the discharge level rather than the patient level. Consequently, a key recommendation is the enhancement of HIPE as a patient level dataset; further, there are more limited data available on other hospital based services, including emergency departments (EDs) and outpatients; these services would benefit from a patient-level HIPE-type dataset.
•	General practice: There are limited administrative data available on general practice in Ireland. Consequently, the projection analysis relied on survey data, which have inherent limitations, including recall bias and the exclusion of consultations for certain population groups, including those living in communal establishments and who are homeless. This report recommends the development of a regularly updated, centrally held administrative dataset on general practice with a core set of variables. Such a dataset could include information on the general practice workforce and working hours, as well as appropriately anonymised individual level data capturing variables such as age group, sex, medical card status and number of consultations of those registered with a practice.
•	Older people’s services: While there are some administrative data available on older people’s services (in particular long-term residential care (LTRC) and home support), it is limited in nature and needs to be supplemented with survey data for the Hippocrates projection analysis. As with general practice, this report recommends the development of a minimum dataset of LTRC residents and home support recipients in Ireland, which would include details for example on age, sex and dependency levels. Further, there is a need for data on other services used by older people, including Meals on Wheels and respite care.
Arising from the Digital Health Strategic Implementation Roadmap, the Health Information Act and the European Health Data Space, a wide range of initiatives aimed at strengthening the health data infrastructure and availability are currently underway. While some developments are at a more advanced stage than others, full implementation will take time. It is now essential to consider how these initiatives will operate in practice, particularly in relation to how data can be shared beyond immediate clinical care settings. In the meantime, other initiatives could significantly enhance data availability for planning, policy and research purposes. It is vital that improvements to the health data focus not just on publicly provided care, but also on the extensive care provided by voluntary and private providers, much of which is publicly funded.</jats:p>

title: Data Sovereignty and Algorithmic Governance in Developing Economies
container-title: Enabling Human Transformation Through Socio-Technical Systems in Industry 4.0
6fdbeb58e96e829a460768ed1eba7412a41afc2e.abstract: <jats:p>Data is among the most contested resources of the twenty-first century. Citizens in developing and middle-income economies generate it constantly through mobile transactions, health services, and social platforms. Yet, the infrastructure that processes it and the governance frameworks that regulate it have largely been designed elsewhere. This chapter examines data sovereignty and algorithmic governance as twin pillars of an equitable digital transformation agenda, using South Africa as its primary lens. It argues that three connected interventions are essential: sovereign infrastructure architecture, algorithmic transparency and accountability, and genuine community participation in governance design. Drawing on socio-technical systems theory and institutional economics, the chapter demonstrates that data sovereignty cannot be achieved through any single instrument but requires deliberate alignment between technical architecture, governance institutions, and participatory process to produce inclusive Fourth Industrial Revolution outcomes in structurally unequal economies.</jats:p>

title: Rehabilitation of Swallowing and Language Ability in Patients With Severe Acquired Brain Injury: An Online International Survey
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
6e791c8302a8469a630ee675a3bc3743a162be94.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Patients with severe acquired brain injury and disorders of consciousness (DoC) are noncommunicative and present with severe dysphagia. To characterize current practices, identify gaps, and explore emerging approaches in postcomatose rehabilitation, the DoC Special Interest Group of the International Brain Injury Association conducted an international survey on speech-language therapy (SLT) practices.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An online questionnaire, available in seven languages, was disseminated to clinicians involved in swallowing and/or language and communication rehabilitation of patients with DoC. The survey captured (a) sociodemographic and practice setting information, (b) general postcomatose SLT practices, (c) swallowing assessment and management, and (d) language and communication assessment and management.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Responses were obtained from 166 clinicians, predominantly speech-language pathologists (74%), working in acute/subacute care (38%) or in longer-term rehabilitation (71%). Most assessed (74%) and managed (74%) swallowing disorders, and 25% created or adapted their own assessment tools. For language and communication, most respondents reported assessing (82%) and managing (76%) these abilities, with frequent use of augmentative and alternative communication (71%). Family input was considered central, for identifying motivating stimuli (96%) and involving relatives in therapy (87%). While 29% developed their own language assessment tools, 51% did so for intervention tools, reflecting limited validated resources.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Clinicians worldwide assess and manage swallowing and communication in patients with DoC but report a lack of validated tools. Practice often relies on individualized approaches and clinician-developed materials, with family involvement. These findings highlight the need for enhanced training and standardized, evidence-based instruments to strengthen SLT practices across the continuum of care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Supervisor need-thwarting behaviour and followers' turnover intentions: a conditional moderated mediation model
container-title: Leadership & Organization Development Journal
6cfafde08378f78d4d55173dbd93ad05ef48f790.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study examines how supervisor need-thwarting behaviour relates to employee turnover intentions through needs frustration, and how interactional justice and job insecurity conditionally moderate this relationship.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Data were collected through a two-wave survey of Australian workers (n = 359). The proposed conditional moderated mediation model was tested using Hayes' PROCESS Macro Model 11 in IBM SPSS v28.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Supervisor need-thwarting behaviour was positively associated with turnover intentions, both directly and indirectly through needs frustration. The indirect relationship was conditionally moderated by interactional justice and job insecurity. Interactional justice buffered the positive association between need-thwarting behaviour and needs frustration when job insecurity was low. This buffer was nonsignificant at average insecurity, and reversed in slope when insecurity was high, producing a significant index of conditional moderated mediation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study frames supervisor need-thwarting behaviour as an aspect of harmful leadership, and positions needs frustration as the psychological mechanism that connects supervisor behaviour with turnover intentions. Our arguments advance distinct explanatory roles for self-determination theory and conservation of resources theory, and conceptualise interactional justice as a contingent relational resource that provides a buffering capacity which is undermined by job insecurity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Large language models in geospatial science
container-title: Global Knowledge, Memory and Communication
e20d6a7d2d4c9dba958b9f01bf132d87fe48b90a.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Large language models are opening new ways to work with geospatial data, from asking questions about places to building analytical workflows. This study aims to examine how these applications fit together and what they suggest about the developing role of LLMs in geospatial science.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A systematic review of 55 studies was conducted, covering GIScience and related spatial applications. Dictionary-based coding, supported by manual review, was combined with term frequency–inverse document frequency analysis and non-negative matrix factorisation to examine research roles, tasks and themes. Comparisons between core GIScience and adjacent fields helped place the overall patterns in context.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Benchmarking was the most common research role (41.8%), followed by multimodal interpretation (20.0%). Across the literature, two complementary directions emerge: using language models to organise geospatial operations and using vision-language models to interpret spatial observations. The abstracts place particular emphasis on methods, while the thematic analysis connects general GIS evaluation with code generation, remote sensing and applied spatial reasoning.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The synthesis points to the value of combining flexible language interfaces with established GIS computation. Practical evaluation should consider how a system turns a request into a verified spatial result, including the time and expert involvement needed to complete that process.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By bringing GIScience and adjacent spatial research into one analytical framework, the review shows how model capabilities, data representations and external tools contribute to geospatial workflows. This perspective offers a basis for comparing systems and identifying productive connections between research communities.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Stochastic nonlinear dynamics of the FitzHugh–Nagumo model: traveling waves, bifurcations and chaotic neuronal insight
container-title: Engineering Computations
3919d6d53c123946717a9f09d1dfa72ea663f7e1.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This research investigates the nonlinear stochastic FitzHugh–Nagumo equation, with a focus on traveling wave solutions, bifurcation theory, chaotic behavior and emphasizing how noise, such as ion channel oscillations and conductivity changes, affects neuronal pulse behavior.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>By utilizing the extended modified tanh expansion method, diverse analytical solutions, including hyperbolic, trigonometric and periodic forms, are achieved. The impacts of parameter changes on these solutions are visualized in 2D and 3D, and the effects of stochastic excitation are investigated for real-world neuroscience relevance.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study explores the influence of noise on chaotic behavior and wave patterns, with visualizations revealing complex dynamics between parameters and their effects on neuronal activity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While the model provides valuable insights, it doesn't fully account for spatial heterogeneity or higher-dimensional systems, which could be explored in future research.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This work presents novel insights into the role of stochastic noise in neuronal dynamics, providing analytical solutions and deepening our understanding of nerve impulse communication in computational neuroscience.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Institutional pressure and innovative behavior of knowledge workers: a moderated mediation model of leadership style and public service motivation
container-title: Chinese Management Studies
e3853927f51e7997f6cc18d8bca3a3345092e2c3.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to investigate the impact of three types of organizational institutional pressures – coercive, normative and mimetic – on the innovative behavior of knowledge workers. It examines the distinct moderating roles of transformational and transactional leadership, with public service motivation (PSM) serving as the mediating mechanism.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on two independent studies (Study 1:36 teams, 380 responses on transformational leadership; Study 2:41 teams, 407 responses on transactional leadership), the authors used a cross-level moderated mediation model. Confirmatory factor analysis validated the measurement structure, and the use of cross-level data ensured methodological rigor.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Transformational leadership amplifies the positive impact of normative and mimetic pressures on PSM, thereby enhancing innovation. Conversely, transactional leadership undermines the motivational link of coercive pressure to PSM, suppressing innovation. These results highlight the situational dependency of leadership: transformational leadership can unlock the innovative potential inherent in norms and imitation pressures, whereas transactional leadership tends to exacerbate execution rigidity in compliance-emphasizing environments, weakening the translation of coercive pressure into innovative behavior.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>While this study uses cross-level data, it relies on self-reported measures. Although steps were taken to ensure validity in the data analysis, future research could directly measure performance using objective scales to achieve greater scientific rigor.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Organizations should strategically align leadership styles with types of institutional pressure. Transformational leadership is critical for leveraging the motivational and innovative potential of normative and mimetic pressures. In contrast, transactional leadership should be minimized in coercive contexts to avoid suppressing creativity. Cultivating PSM through clear communication of institutional goals and fostering autonomy in rule-driven environments can help convert external pressures into sustainable drivers of innovation.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study categorizes institutional pressures into coercive, normative and mimetic types, exploring their unique interplay with leadership styles. The research reveals an asymmetrical leadership effect: transformational leaders enhance innovation in value-driven contexts, whereas transactional leaders impede it in environments tightly regulated by policies and rules. By integrating institutional theory with leadership studies, this research offers a framework for understanding the innovation processes of knowledge workers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Optimising sleep regularity during shiftwork is important for cognitive performance, sleepiness and mood
container-title: SLEEP Advances
1feb0e7d2cb9f318c1cf9eac264b69994eea234b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Sleep regularity is important for performance and wellbeing. Sleep regularity is underexplored in shiftworkers, a population that may struggle to maintain regular sleep timing due to unstable work hours. It is important to understand how sleep regularity relates to wellbeing and performance outcomes for shiftworkers. Using the sleep regularity index (SRI), we assessed the relationship of sleep regularity to performance and wellbeing in maritime watchstanding shiftworkers who worked two different schedules (known as “watchbills”). Active-duty sailors (N = 23, aged 25.96 ± 3.13 years, [mean ± standard deviation]) wore an actiwatch for ~14 days while underway on the 5-hrs on/10-hrs off watchbill, and four months later for ~10 days while on the 3-hrs on/9-hrs off watchbill. The psychomotor vigilance task (PVT) was administered 2 to 4 times daily during both underway periods; the Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS), Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index (PSQI), and Profile of Mood States (POMS) were administered at the end of both data collection periods. High variability in SRI score was observed for shiftworkers on the same shift of the same schedule. Higher SRI scores were associated with faster reaction times (Spearman’s rho [ρ] = -0.73, p = .019) and better cognitive performance on seven other PVT metrics (all p &lt; .05), and reduced daytime sleepiness (ρ = -0.512, p = .013) and total mood disturbance (ρ = -0.634, p = .005). The study found that sleep regularity is an important dimension of sleep to optimise during shiftwork to improve cognitive performance and reduce daytime sleepiness and mood disturbance.</jats:p>

title: Economic evaluation of the annual and daily costs of the adult foster care model for older dependent adults: Insights from the Karukera Study of Aging in Foster Families
container-title: Innovation in Aging
cf7f5ff12aba6877c7b8c3717df342108493a070.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background and Objectives</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adult foster care may represent a viable alternative to nursing homes for dependent older adults. This study aimed to estimate the annual and daily cost of adult foster care for older adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research Design and Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The Karukera Study of Aging in Foster Families is a prospective, one-year observational study including adults aged 60+ living in adult foster care in the French Caribbean Islands. We measured healthcare resource utilization using the RUD (Resource Utilization in Dementia)-Lite instrument. Costs related to healthcare consumption, foster caregiver remuneration, and training were estimated and expressed per patient-year.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A total of 106 older adults (mean age: 82.2±11.2 years; 61.3% women) were followed for one year (mean follow-up duration: 306.1±90.8 days). The daily cost of outpatient care was estimated at €33.3, of which €29.9 corresponded to community nursing visits. Caregiver remuneration and training represented a daily expenditure of €62.8 per older adult. The total annual cost of adult foster care was estimated at €35,076, or €96.1 per resident per day. Hospitalization costs were estimated at €224.0 per patient-year, while emergency department visits accounted for €42.0 per patient-year.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Discussion and Implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Compared with a daily cost of €121 per resident in metropolitan nursing homes and €150 per resident in nursing homes in the French Caribbean Islands, adult foster care reduced costs by 20.6% and 35.9%, respectively. In the context of constrained healthcare budgets and increasing demand for long-term care related to dependency, adult foster care may represent a scalable and economically sustainable alternative.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Clinical Trial Registration</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>NCT04545775</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Exploring the impact of corporate volunteering characteristics on work engagement, work meaningfulness and job satisfaction
container-title: Journal of Organizational Change Management
45912bc932cbfc128ff18daaf58f7b063f134f1f.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study investigates how work engagement, work meaningfulness and job satisfaction differ within company volunteers depending on four corporate volunteering (CV) program characteristics – namely type of employee competencies involved in volunteering, type of beneficiary, type of employee contact with beneficiaries and role in volunteering program.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We collected data using an online, self-administered questionnaire targeting employees at companies in Poland that implement CV programs. A total of 983 completed questionnaires were collected.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The t-test results indicate that certain CV characteristics significantly influence work engagement, work meaningfulness and job satisfaction. Among these, the type of employee competencies used in volunteering consistently influenced all three outcomes. Beneficiary type had a significant effect only on work meaningfulness, while type of contact with beneficiaries and role played in CV program showed no significant effects on any outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study contributes to the broader organizational behaviour literature by providing empirical evidence of how specific CV program characteristics relate to important work-related outcomes. The results are valuable for managers seeking to create more satisfying, engaging and meaningful workplaces for their employees and, at the same time, to respond to the growing demand for companies to contribute to sustainable development by addressing social and environmental issues. The paper demonstrates the potential of CV programs to drive such workplace transformation, yielding positive effects inside and outside the company. It shows how organizations can transform their CV programs from traditional charity-based activities into strategic tools for developing employees, driving organizational change and achieving broader, positive social impact.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A corrected and extended model of sulfolane thaw release
container-title: Transport Phenomena
60342f559341e71d5ed0998b3f5d01e3696f01f8.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Freeze-induced segregation can generate concentrated early discharge while leaving much of a contaminant inventory unreleased. We correct an inconsistency between activation-dependent release and source depletion in a previously published sulfolane model, then extend the corrected formulation to distinguish solute mobilization from outlet export. With the published parameters and concentration filter retained, correcting the source fluxes increases the illustrative peak from 12.03 to 29.97 wt%, while preferential early enrichment persists. Coupling the corrected sources to a well-mixed receiving pool provides an explicit balance for solute retained in the source, stored in connected liquid, and exported through the outlet. For an illustrative 1.5 h release window, an initial bulk concentration of 10 wt% produces a peak of 31.9 wt%, although only 24.1 % of the initial solute is mobilized and 14.5 % exported by closure. During a source-release pause, continued pool flushing increases export without further source depletion. Restart behavior depends on the prescribed activation history. The earlier experiments supply the physical context; no new experimental measurements are reported. The correction restores consistent source depletion, and the extension quantifies how finite release and liquid storage separate concentration enrichment from contaminant removal.</jats:p>

title: The relationship between AI awareness and thriving at work: exploring the moderated mediation model
container-title: European Journal of Training and Development
2197f659428e01b99695470828484314d3e05f60.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Drawing on the socially embedded model of thriving and the conservation of resources model, this study aims to investigate the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) awareness, seen as a hindrance stressor, and thriving at work. In particular, it explores how AI anxiety mediates this relationship and how self-efficacy moderates the mediating effect.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To securitize the study hypotheses, data were obtained from banking employees via an electronic questionnaire, yielding 320 valid responses. The proposed model relationships were assessed through partial least squares structural equation modeling and process analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The results uncover that while AI awareness is not significantly linked to vitality, it is negatively correlated with learning. Furthermore, AI anxiety mediates the direct influence that AI awareness has on dimensions of thriving at work. In addition, self-efficacy acts as a buffer, mitigating the adverse indirect influence of AI awareness on thriving at work through AI anxiety.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study highlights the need for organizations adopting AI-driven systems to execute‎ initiatives that mitigate AI-induced stress, thereby fostering employee thriving. It is recommended that organizations offer targeted training and digital literacy programs, alongside interventions designed to enhance self-efficacy, to bolster employee well-being amid rapid technological change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study highlights the need for organizations adopting AI-driven systems to execute‎ initiatives that mitigate AI-induced stress, thereby fostering employee thriving. It is recommended that organizations offer targeted training and revise their role descriptions, alongside interventions designed to enhance self-efficacy, to bolster employee well-being amid rapid technological change.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A New Model of Trend Inflation Using Disaggregates, Survey Expectations, and Uncertainty
container-title: Working paper (Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland)
2b03f55f7686ac517c5812c539adda9c47dcbc13.abstract: <jats:p>This paper develops a new empirical model that estimates trend inflation by combining modeling features that have advanced the literature on trend inflation over the past two decades. These features include incorporating information about long-term inflation expectations from surveys in a flexible way, modeling aggregate inflation via sectoral data (goods and services), allowing for stochastic volatility (SV) in the shocks to the trend and transitory components of inflation, allowing for a time-varying price Phillips curve, and allowing for time-varying uncertainty effects on the level of inflation. We estimate the model using Bayesian methods. We assess the relative importance of each feature for trend estimation and document the new model's competitive properties. The new model provides a more interpretable historical decomposition of inflation data than the models it extends. The decomposition suggests that uncertainty effects play a greater role than business cycle effects in explaining inflation fluctuations.</jats:p>

title: PhD researchers’ engagement-burnout profiles and their relationship with research, developmental, and instrumental interest
container-title: Studies in Graduate and Postdoctoral Education
6f7fa33bf5ef9403d06438c37634e450b949a3dd.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aims to explore individual variation in PhD researchers’ well-being and interest integrating academic engagement, burnout and three dimensions of interest (research, developmental and instrumental).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The data were collected from 1,138 PhD researchers at a Finnish research-intensive university in 2025. Adapting a person-oriented approach and using latent profile analysis (LPA), five distinct engagement-burnout profiles were detected.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Five distinct engagement-burnout profiles were detected: Engaged (46%), Moderately engaged (25%), Engaged-exhausted (12%), Cynical (11%) and Burned-out (6%). The results revealed significant differences in interest across these profiles. The engaged-exhausted profile reported the highest levels of all forms of interest. Conversely, researchers in the cynical and burned-out profiles reported the lowest levels of any form of interest. Furthermore, study status (full-time vs. part-time) was explored, and it was found out that it was not significantly related to profile membership.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Research limitations/implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The cross-sectional design prevents causal conclusions, requiring future longitudinal research. Methodologically, latent profile analysis involves subjective interpretation, and the 24% response rate risks bias and unrepresentativeness. In addition, self-reported data is prone to bias. Finally, the sample is restricted to one institution, limiting generalisability. Future studies should implement longitudinal designs, incorporate other indicators alongside self-reports, and explore diverse sociocultural environments to improve generalisability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Practical implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The findings highlight that institutions and supervisors must foster environments offering robust social and supervisory support. Programs should raise awareness of personal interest, helping doctoral researchers design more meaningful paths. In addition, supervisor training must emphasise that high engagement can coexist with exhaustion. Supervisors need to monitor hidden burnout symptoms and implement tailored support strategies. Finally, institutions should use regular well-being assessments, such as surveys, to systematically track mental health and engagement levels among PhD researchers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Social implications</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Doctoral discontinuation carries significant societal consequences, representing a loss of educational investment and threatening the long-term sustainability of the academic workforce and research output. On an individual level, it causes highly unwanted personal circumstances. Conversely, robust community support systematically boosts research engagement, demonstrating that fostering cooperative, supportive academic communities is essential for collective academic success.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>To the best of the authors’ knowledge, no prior person-oriented research on PhD researcher well-being has integrated engagement, burnout and multiple forms of personal interest. Addressing this gap is essential, as these dimensions are likely to jointly shape doctoral researchers’ well-being, outcomes, and long-term trajectories.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Beyond Accuracy: Inner Speech and Error Patterns Reveal Treatment-Based Learning in a Single-Subject Design Study
container-title: American Journal of Speech-Language Pathology
ae2483b6213330ee2e1b7be9a59ef1699c06cef2.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In our recent single-subject design study, we showed that a sense of “successful inner speech (IS)” at baseline (i.e., “I can say it in my head”) predicted treatment-related improvements in naming accuracy in four of five individuals with aphasia. Here, we analyze error patterns from those data to determine whether error patterns also changed after treatment and whether self-reported IS predicted such changes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Five adults with chronic poststroke aphasia completed 2 weeks of a cueing-based naming treatment targeting 40 personalized stimuli: 20 items reported prior to treatment as successful IS (sIS) and 20 items reported as unsuccessful IS (uIS). Before and after treatment, naming attempts were coded ordinally as follows: (0) no response, (1) neologism, (2) unrelated, (3) description, (4) semantic, (5) mixed, (6) phonological, and (7) correct. We used ordinal cumulative logit m
                      <jats:sans-serif>ixed-effect</jats:sans-serif>
                      s models to assess longitudinal changes in error types across all treatment items and in sIS versus uIS items. We evaluated individual-level changes by examining raw error type proportions across time.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Naming performance improved from baseline testing to immediate posttreatment, when accounting for error types alongside naming accuracy. Participants' posttreatment naming attempts had higher odds of being closer to the target for sIS items versus uIS items, after controlling for baseline scores. Finally, most individual participants' error patterns changed across time, including one participant who was a “nonresponder” in our prior accuracy-based analysis.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion:</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>These preliminary findings suggest that error patterns are an important source of information about treatment-based learning in aphasia and converge with recent evidence that IS impacts naming treatment outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: A Comparative Experimental Study on the Influence of Porosity Grades on Tensile and Bending Functions Using the Fuzzy VIKOR Decision Model
container-title: Diffusion Foundations and Materials Applications
5134072529eb79f4ccec9ffbe1a7e59284740afe.abstract: <jats:p>The porosity gradient in the Fusion Deposition Modeling (FDM) technique is a significant mechanism adopted in the functional materials to reduce the model's weight as an economical procedure. However, restricting the enhancement of the tensile and bending functions represents another aspect of the porosity in this technique. Besides, the variance of these functions in the 3D printing's filaments also contributes to employing the suitable type of filament. Therefore, studies that exposed Polylactic Acid (PLA) and Acrylonitrile Butadiene Styrene (ABS) filament, specifically, boosted the modeling process depending on orientation angle, layer thickness, and filling ratio. From here, this study focuses on employing a variety of porosity grades to experimentally investigate the influence of these grades on the tensile and bending functions, utilizing Fuzzy-Vikor as a multi-criteria hybrid decision to select the optimal decision. Besides, the porosity grades used in this work were 0%, 20%, 0%-20%, 0%-20%-0%, 40%, 0%-40%, and 0%-40%-0% with PLA and ABS filaments. In addition, 45˚, 0.25 mm, and 35 mm/s are constant parameters for raster angle, layer thickness, and printing speed consecutively. Hence, the final decision outcomes based on this multi-criteria hybrid decision were 0% for PLA and 40% for ABS, representing the optimal and worst-case successively. In addition, the micrograph investigation of the fracture zone produced by the tensile test for the optimal case revealed homogeneity in this zone, with only slight micro-voids and gas pores compared to the worst-case.</jats:p>

title: Neuro-symbolic AI for proactive risk forecasting: bridging large language models and dynamic Bayesian networks
container-title: Smart and Sustainable Built Environment
0bb98e6ca3b6e4203d765fe27185ba4340bcd31d.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Purpose</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Periodic risk reports constitute a substantial repository of operational data for project management. Despite the inherent informational value, archived records remain largely unstructured and highly fragmented. This study proposes a fully local neuro-symbolic approach for dynamic risk forecasting by translating qualitative project narratives into a quantifiable predictive engine to support decision-making.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Design/methodology/approach</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The proposed methodology adopts a mixed-methods architecture including four layers: (1) spatial morphology reconstruction using a Y-axis density clustering algorithm; (2) a hybrid pseudonymization filter; (3) a local large language model (LLM) with chain-of-thought reasoning; and (4) a symbolic causal engine powered by a dynamic Bayesian network (DBN) to quantify causal propagation into a dynamic risk index.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Findings</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>An empirical evaluation across 28 reporting cycles spanning a 33-month large-scale infrastructure project indicates that the symbolic layer provides a temporally coherent aggregation of the output of a zero-shot perception layer operating at a macro F1-score of 53.62%. By quantifying causal risk propagation, the DBN captured a 93.59% risk-saturation state, for which the retrieved evidence identifies chronic site-clearance bottlenecks. Notably, using an alert threshold selected by sensitivity analysis together with an analytic constraint on the posterior mass attributable to the critical state (talert = 70.0%), the model outputs Bayesian probabilities alongside LLM-extracted textual evidence, yielding an anticipation interval of 1.33 reporting cycles relative to the documented administrative response.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Originality/value</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The neuro-symbolic framework bridges the gap between deep learning perception and causal inference in construction management. By coupling LLM-driven zero-shot ordinal extraction with DBN causal reasoning, the research establishes an auditable framework for risk documentation. The integrated framework transitions AI from an opaque prediction model into an accountable decision-support tool, providing stakeholders with transparent explainable AI diagnostics and supporting a shift from reactive mitigation to proactive, evidence-based risk prevention.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Climate anxiety, agency and systemic educational transformation in early childhood
container-title: Constellations of hope
5c38998b63a8f64ac12f6a93b6d495040bab675c.abstract: <jats:p>As climate change intensifies, its psychological and existential impacts on young children are only beginning to be recognised, particularly in climate-vulnerable small island states. Drawing on research conducted in Malta with children under eight, this article reveals a growing prevalence of climate anxiety in early childhood, driven by fragmented and fear-based understandings of environmental change. Without structured educational support, children risk developing a diminished sense of agency. This article advocates for embedding climate literacy into national curricula using developmentally appropriate, solution-oriented methods such as storytelling and nature-based learning. It calls for systemic reform in teacher education, family engagement and public discourse, arguing that climate education can enhance resilience and cultivate climate agency as well as eco-agency in young children. The implications of the findings for educational policy are substantial. First, early childhood climate education must be embedded in national curricula, ensuring that climate literacy is introduced in an age-appropriate, solution-focused manner. Second, many teacher training programmes still do not include climate change education as a core component. Third, parental education initiatives must equip parents and caregivers with strategies to discuss climate change in constructive, solution-oriented ways. The challenge therefore is not simply to replace fear-based narratives with hopeful ones but to cultivate pedagogical conditions in which children can metabolise uncertainty through relational support, ethical dialogue and opportunities for meaningful participation. In this sense, hope emerges not as reassurance but as a lived educational practice grounded in connection, care and shared responsibility. Addressing this gap is critical for developing accurate, empowering climate literacy. By integrating early childhood climate education into policies, policymakers can cultivate a generation that approaches environmental challenges with confidence, resilience and the knowledge to drive meaningful change.</jats:p>
