title: Global AI Impact in the Era of Intelligent Paradigm: A Perspective from Research Papers
container-title: Journal of Scholarly Publishing
854d0c813c992c06e0d2d0b6dee6f67272ba9a4d.abstract: This study conducts an in-depth exploration of the formation process behind the global impact of artificial intelligence research papers (AI papers). At the macro level, it conducts a cross-national comparison of AI papers from the perspectives of publication volume and policy citations. At the meso level, the Criteria Importance Through Intercriteria Correlation method is employed to conduct separate single-dimensional evaluations of the global impact of AI papers across four key dimensions: academic impact, perceived impact, societal impact, and policy impact. At the micro level, a comprehensive evaluation of the global impact of AI papers is carried out using the Projection Pursuit Classification Model, with the results subsequently validated using convolutional neural networks and correlation analysis. This study reveals the formation mechanisms of the global impact of AI papers, develops an evaluation framework based on four impact dimensions, and empirically validates its reliability and validity.

title: SHIELD-Net: A Sperm Halo Image Classification Framework via Hybrid ROI Extraction and ROI-Guided Dual-View Learning
container-title: AI Chemistry
e5750030231ded7d3e59283d131be7a566188cac.abstract: The sperm chromatin dispersion (SCD) test is widely used to assess sperm DNA fragmentation by observing the halo structure around the sperm head. However, manual halo interpretation is labor-intensive and subjective, which limits its consistency and throughput in clinical practice. To address these limitations, we propose SHIELD-Net, an image-level single-sperm halo morphology classification framework for four halo categories: large halo, medium halo, small halo, and without halo. SHIELD-Net includes two modules, i.e., a hybrid ROI extraction (HyREx) module and dual-view learning with ROI-guided gate fusion (RGF). The HyREx module converts the traditional direct classification pipeline into a segmentation-classification pipeline. It uses the cell segmentation foundation model, i.e., Cellpose, to segment halo-centered regions of interest (ROIs) and proposes a fallback mechanism to ensure segmentation effectiveness. In this way, HyREx can construct a head–halo-centered ROI and reduce interference from tail and background regions. Based on the original image and the extracted ROI, SHIELD-Net performs dual-view ConvNeXt encoding. RGF further uses the ROI representation to generate a spatial gate that recalibrates the original-view feature map toward halo-morphology-related responses. Experiments were conducted on a public expert-annotated sperm microscopy dataset containing 403 individual sperm halo images using stratified five-fold cross-validation. SHIELD-Net achieved a Macro F1 of 0.9290 ± 0.0161. Compared with the original-image ConvNeXt-Small baseline, SHIELD-Net improved Macro F1 by 0.1755. These results indicate that combining head–halo-centered ROI construction with ROI-guided feature recalibration improves image-level sperm halo morphology classification.

title: Repeatability and Agreement of CephX AI-Driven Cephalometric Analysis in Patients with Cleft Palate Only: A Comparative Study with Non-Cleft Controls
container-title: Applied Sciences
a342d32c9c6842cbefd98af7e362e17c9c84599c.abstract: Cephalometric analysis is essential in patients with cleft palate only (CPO) for the assessment of craniofacial morphology and treatment planning. This study evaluated the test–retest repeatability of CephX AI-driven cephalometric analysis and its agreement with expert manual measurements in patients with CPO versus non-cleft controls. Cephalometric radiographs of 50 patients with CPO (25 males and 25 females; aged 14–23 years) and 50 non-cleft controls matched for sex and ethnic origin were traced manually by two experienced orthodontists using CephX. All analyses were repeated after a two-week interval. Repeatability was assessed using Lin’s concordance correlation coefficient (CCC), and agreement between AI and manual measurements was evaluated using Bland–Altman analysis. CephX showed high test–retest repeatability for both groups, with CCC values of 0.97 or higher for all cephalometric variables evaluated. However, the agreement with expert manual measurements varied among cephalometric variables. In the CPO group, 34 of 50 radiographs required manual scale calibration and 31 of 50 generated a landmark-review warning; nevertheless, no skeletal or dental landmarks included in the analysis were manually repositioned by the investigators. CephX provided highly reproducible measurements, but the need for calibration and landmark review indicates that clinician supervision remains important, particularly in patients with altered craniofacial anatomy.

title: Neural Responses to Reward-Associated Task-Irrelevant Scenes Under Different Perceptual Load: An fMRI Study
container-title: Behavioral Sciences
cfdbdc30a5fe314795e0f77f4dd33709aa14d301.abstract: Value-driven attentional capture (VDAC) refers to automatic attentional capture by task-irrelevant stimuli previously associated with high rewards. Whether perceptual load modulates the neural responses to such distractors remains unclear. Using a two-day training–test fMRI paradigm, we examined behavioral and neural responses in 19 participants. On Day 1, participants performed border color discrimination while indoor and outdoor scenes were paired with different reward probabilities. On Day 2, participants performed face discrimination with perceptual load manipulated through target faces (low load: clear face; high load: noise-degraded faces), with previously rewarded scenes as irrelevant backgrounds. Test-phase correct-rejection accuracy was higher under low than high perceptual load. Whole-brain analyses revealed condition differences in the bilateral amygdala, middle temporal gyri, left inferior frontal and inferior occipital gyri, and right inferior temporal gyrus. The reward association × perceptual load interaction averaged across background repetition was nonsignificant in all three ROIs. However, the scene-selective cortex, left inferior frontal gyrus, and ventral striatum showed reward association × perceptual load × background repetition interactions. These findings suggest that perceptual load conditions may modulate reward-related repetition-sensitive neural responses, but do not establish a general load-dependent VDAC effect. Reward–category confounding and the absence of an independent assessment of reward-association acquisition limit interpretation in terms of VDAC. Face degradation additionally limits attribution of the findings to perceptual capacity.

title: The Effects of Corporate AI Environment Factors on Employees’ Technology Acceptance Attitude and Continuous Intention to Use
container-title: Behavioral Sciences
e8078cb4da48844d192f23ccde505fac90f4b925.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes an imperative survival strategy for modern enterprises, numerous organizations continue to face implementation failures stemming from employees’ psychological resistance. To address the scarcity of empirical research regarding the practical and psychological acceptance of AI in workflows, this study investigates the structural relationships between technological maturity and users’ cognitive adoption. Grounded in an integrated framework utilizing the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM), this research conceptualizes the “AI Environment Factor” as a higher-order construct comprising four foundational sub-dimensions: AI System Quality, AI Information Quality, AI Data Quality, and AI Infrastructure. A quantitative survey was administered to 189 corporate practitioners who have utilized enterprise-wide AI systems for at least one year, and the empirical data were analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM). The analytical results indicate that the AI Environment Factor exerts a statistically significant positive effect on both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness. Furthermore, Perceived Ease of Use was found to positively influence Perceived Usefulness. Ultimately, both Perceived Ease of Use and Perceived Usefulness are significantly associated with the employees’ continuous AI Intention to Use. These findings theoretically contribute to the literature by providing a measurable structural model for the continuance intention phase of organizational AI adoption. Practically, this study offers actionable guidelines for corporate executives, emphasizing that securing rigorous data accuracy and a stable system infrastructure is indispensable for mitigating cognitive load, fostering innovative corporate cultures, and maximizing the efficacy of AI utilization.

title: A CDIO-Based Reform of Advanced Separation Engineering: AI-Supported Curriculum Innovation and Practice
container-title: Education Sciences
6f70cdc82ec1b030d44e7be968d9d8de6d2a1fab.abstract: Advanced Separation Engineering requires graduate students to connect separation principles with process design and engineering decision-making. Using action research, this study developed and refined a reform based on the Conceive–Design–Implement–Operate (CDIO) framework across four annual offerings from 2022 to 2025. The reform integrated authentic engineering projects, AI-supported learning resources, digital process simulation, collaborative inquiry, and continuous assessment. Course evaluations from the 2021 pre-reform historical cohort (n = 46) were compared with those from the pooled reform cohorts (n = 254), supplemented by open-ended responses and interviews. The reform cohorts reported higher ratings on all five common course-evaluation items, with differences remaining statistically significant after Holm adjustment and Hedges’ g ranging from 1.29 to 2.11. Overall satisfaction averaged 3.41 in the historical cohort and 4.58 in the reform cohorts. On supplementary single-item self-report questions, 91.7% considered the CDIO reform helpful for developing comprehensive engineering competence, and 76.4% reported that AI-supported resources and digital simulation helped them understand complex separation processes. Student feedback identified software learning demands, group coordination, verification of AI outputs, and inconsistent industry-expert participation as continuing challenges. This four-year action research study provides a practice-informed reference for integrating CDIO projects and technological support in graduate engineering courses, based on students’ reported experiences.

title: AI Adoption at Higher Education Institutions: A Call for Designated AI Management
container-title: Education Sciences
893344e55b7a2d336456df016fc437e8ea34d6f6.abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming teaching, learning and administration in higher education institutions (HEIs), yet responsibility for its governance is rarely assigned. This article develops and empirically tests the profile of an AI Manager for HEIs proposed by the Erasmus+ project FORCE AI. A literature-based definition and nine-area competence profile were examined in a sequential mixed-methods study, a survey of 387 students and staff from 13 countries and five nominal-group focus groups in Germany, Latvia, the Netherlands, and Türkiye in 2025, which tested the elements stakeholders can rate: competences, responsibilities, placement, and qualifications. Only 17% of respondents knew of a designated AI-management responsibility at their institution; of the remainder, 71% considered one necessary and 76% expected an AI Manager to improve their experience. The expected mandate comprised training, ethical oversight, data security and strategy; preferences were split between a dedicated position and a shared cross-functional function. Survey respondents portrayed the role as a compliance-oriented technical specialist, whereas staff-dominated focus groups, rating the same competencies, prioritised leadership, change and project management, and communication alongside AI expertise and ethics; this contrast between methods and samples persists for staff respondents alone. The revised definition and profile position designated AI management, a dedicated AI Manager or a team with an accountable lead, as change leadership with technical credibility and give HEIs a tested basis for establishing this role.

title: Real-Time Instance Segmentation of Deep-Sea Polymetallic Nodules with Wavelet Statistical Cross-Attention and Reverse Convolution Upsampling
container-title: Journal of Marine Science and Engineering
fe4a4341c1b3a3d1d20721c28254fedb09a3f7a3.abstract: Deep-sea polymetallic nodules are vital strategic mineral resources. However, residual low-contrast features from complex seabed conditions, densely overlapped targets and severe seabed clutter greatly degrade the accuracy and real-time performance of automatic segmentation. This paper proposes a lightweight instance segmentation model, PWC-YOLO. Firstly, a partial convolution-based C3k2-PConv module is constructed to reduce computational cost. Secondly, Wavelet Statistical Cross-Attention (WSCA) replaces the built-in self-attention of C2PSA to suppress underwater noise and enhance the feature expression of tiny nodules. Thirdly, Converse2D reverse convolution upsampling recovers lost contour details of nodules. A manually annotated dataset of Clarion–Clipperton Zone nodules is established for evaluation. Ablation experiments validate that the PWC-YOLO model reaches 95.2% BBox mAP50 and 95.8% Mask mAP50, with only 2.47 M parameters and 9.3 GFLOPs at an inference speed of 88 FPS. Comparative experiments indicate that PWC-YOLO achieves competitive mask segmentation accuracy with fewer parameters and lower computational overhead, yielding a favorable accuracy–complexity trade-off against mainstream segmentation models. Visual results verify favorable robustness within the tested deep-sea scenes, showing favorable lightweight properties with only 2.47 M parameters and 9.3 GFLOPs, which provides potential prerequisites for future lightweight deployment on underwater edge computing devices.

title: Task-Specific Impacts of Cognitive Fatigue on Subjective Experience and Psychomotor Performance
container-title: Human Factors: The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society
522c0265a8e374ae7e4e7c27de993e0dcbdc142a.abstract: Objective To determine how cognitive fatigue (CF) affects subjective experience and reaction time (RT) performance across tasks with different processing demands (simple, go/no-go, choice), and whether these effects depend on the type of fatigue-inducing mental work. Background CF is a psychobiological state of subjective exhaustion from mental effort that can compromise workplace productivity and safety. Although slowed RT is an often-observed consequence of CF, it is unclear how this compares across RT paradigms and fatigue-inducing tasks. Method Using a remotely administered experiment, 402 participants completed a 60-minute CF (Math-Memory, Stroop, Time Load Dual-Back) or control (documentary) intervention. Subjective ratings (mental fatigue, motivation) and RT performance (simple, go/no-go, choice) were assessed pre- and post-intervention. Results Relative to control, all CF tasks increased subjective fatigue ( p < .001), while motivation declined following Dual-Back and Stroop ( p ≤ .030) but not Math-Memory. Simple and choice RT slowed significantly following all CF interventions vs control ( p < .010), with the greatest choice RT slowing after Stroop ( p ≤ .032). Only Stroop produced significant go/no-go RT slowing ( p = .004). Conclusion Subjective fatigue and simple RT were broadly sensitive to CF, indicating general psychomotor slowing. Conversely, motivation and higher-complexity RT measures showed task-specific effects, perhaps reflecting overlap between fatigue-inducing and RT task demands. Application Task type is important when considering RT as a fatigue assessment tool. These findings support multidimensional (subjective and RT) CF assessments and indicate that simple RT may be effective for rapid, broad fatigue monitoring, whereas complex RT metrics may be useful when exploring task-specific executive processing effects.

title:
Physics‐Based
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    ‐Augmented Workflows Discovering Candidate Graphene Quantum Dot Near‐Infrared Chromophores
container-title: Journal of Computational Chemistry
9015055fc9241d12559eb385dd3eabeb43c352b9.abstract: ABSTRACT Graphene quantum dots (GQDs) exhibit optical properties that depend strongly on their size, edge structure, and surface functionalization, but identifying the molecular structures responsible for near‐infrared (NIR) emission remains challenging because of their structural complexity and disorder. In this work, we developed a computational framework combining rule‐based molecular generation, semi‐empirical quantum chemistry calculations, machine learning, and time‐dependent density functional theory (TD‐DFT) to predict possible chemically realistic candidate GQDs with NIR‐emitting optical properties. A fusion‐based hexagonal lattice growth approach was used to generate 100,000 candidate graphitic structures. A random subset of 5000 structures was selected for semiempirical calculations. Computed band gaps were used to train and evaluate five machine learning models (Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, and Neural Network). LightGBM predicted bandgaps were used to pre‐screen the remaining 95,000 structures. 11,000 structures with low predicted gaps were selected for semiempirical calculations, and 50 top candidates with low gap and low SA score were selected for TD‐DFT calculations employing LC‐ ω PBE functional. All 50 structures were predicted to exhibit NIR emission, offering a computed database of candidate NIR‐emitting GQDs for future validation against experiment.

title: AI-Assisted Analysis of Spontaneous Affective Facial Responses for Cognitive Status Assessment in Older Adults: Exploratory Feasibility Study
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
6543568e570b9512b4946b58992f226b2f1a3be5.abstract: Background As Taiwan enters a super-aged society, the prevalence of dementia continues to rise, highlighting the need for scalable, noninvasive approaches to identify behavioral alterations associated with cognitive decline. AI-based analysis of spontaneous affective facial responses has emerged as a potential digital phenotyping tool, but its feasibility for assessing cognitive performance remains underexplored. Objective This study aimed to examine the feasibility of using AI-derived spontaneous affective facial response metrics, including affective expression congruency and onset latency, to characterize differences across cognitive performance levels in older adults with healthy cognition (HC), mild cognitive impairment (MCI), or dementia. Methods A total of 60 participants (HC, MCI, and dementia; 20 per group) were presented with positive and negative emotion-eliciting videos and completed Mini-Mental State Examination (MMSE) recall and calculation tasks. Facial expressions were video-recorded and analyzed using a convolutional neural network–based AI system. AI-derived metrics included affective expression congruency, categorized as congruent, neutral, or incongruent according to the detected facial response, and affective expression onset latency, defined as the time from stimulus presentation to the emergence of a nonneutral facial expression detected by the AI model. Group differences were analyzed using 1-way ANOVA, Pearson chi-square or Fisher-Freeman-Halton exact tests, Bonferroni-adjusted pairwise post hoc comparisons, analysis of covariance adjusting for age and education, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses. Results Affectively congruent responses were generally less frequent among participants with lower cognitive performance. During the 14-second positive stimulus, congruent positive expressions were observed in 65% (13/20) of HC participants, 20% (4/20) of MCI participants, and 0% (0/20) of participants with dementia. During the 48-second negative stimulus, congruent negative expressions were observed in 60% (12/20) of HC participants compared with 5% (1/20) of both MCI and dementia participants. Onset latency differed significantly across groups for the 14-second positive stimulus (F2,57=19.63; P<.001; η2=0.41), 52-second positive stimulus (F2,57=4.25; P=.02; η2=0.13), 48-second negative stimulus (F2,57=15.61; P<.001; η2=0.35), and MMSE-based cognitive-task condition (F2,57=11.28; P<.001; η2=0.28). After adjustment for age and education, the group effect remained significant for all latency outcomes (F2,55=3.89-10.68; all P≤.03; partial η2=0.12-0.28). Exploratory receiver operating characteristic analyses showed stronger separation in several HC vs MCI and HC vs dementia comparisons, whereas MCI vs dementia comparisons showed limited separability. Conclusions AI-assisted analysis of spontaneous affective facial responses revealed differences in expression congruency and onset latency across cognitive performance levels. These preliminary findings suggest that AI-derived facial behavioral metrics may serve as noninvasive adjunctive features for observational cognitive assessment. However, the findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the exploratory design, modest sample size, and absence of internal or external validation.

title: How do PhD Students Use Generative AI? Reflections on Practice and Ethics
container-title: Journal of Teaching and Learning
1658044309243f3c79c66e0ba28f754f3714ac51.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) has rapidly moved from novelty to ubiquity, reshaping how doctoral students approach learning, research, and career preparation. Yet while universities and the public often frame debates around undergraduate use, comparatively little attention has been given to PhD students despite their dual role as learners and future scholars. In this paper, we reflect on our experiences as PhD students using GenAI across coursework, qualifying exams, thesis research, teaching, and the job market. Drawing on these experiences, we highlight both the opportunities GenAI provides—for efficiency, conceptual clarity, and skill development—and the ethical challenges it raises, including concerns about academic integrity, cognitive outsourcing, disclosure, and employability beyond academia. Our reflections emphasize that GenAI use is not uniform: it varies with disciplinary context, institutional policies, and students’ levels of development. We argue that GenAI is no longer peripheral to doctoral education but central to its practice, and the challenge ahead is how it can be integrated responsibly to support learning, uphold integrity, and prepare graduates for an evolving academic and professional landscape.

title: Institutional Approval Is Not Public Authorization: Legitimacy as a Governance Requirement for Clinical AI
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
8c7db9301128a840c604aa65210fef008480b1f9.abstract: Clinical AI governance has advanced rapidly in technical validation, regulatory compliance, risk management, human oversight, and postdeployment monitoring. Yet a more fundamental question often remains implicit: under what conditions are health institutions justified in exercising consequential authority through AI over patients, clinicians, and communities? In this Viewpoint, we argue that legitimacy should be recognized as an independent governance requirement, distinct from technical assurance, legal and ethical compliance, trust, acceptance, and institutional approval. Our aim is to distinguish institutional approval from public authorization and to propose a normative framework for authorizing consequential clinical AI deployments. We address health system leaders, clinical AI governance and procurement teams, frontline clinicians, and patient and community representatives. Drawing on theories of legitimacy and public value and published clinical AI governance research, we make the following contributions: (1) the concept of the unclaimed decision, defined as a consequential choice about purpose, threshold, population, or priority for which no actor clearly assumes responsibility for public justification; (2) a tripartite framework comprising procedural authorization, substantive justification, and relational renewal; and (3) practical governance tools to support public justification, contestation, and renewal. These tools include 3 minimum auditable conditions: visibility of deployment; affected-party input before governing conditions are fixed; and conditional reviewability, which requires a predefined trigger that can be invoked by a named actor outside the deploying team. A 5-question public authorization test examines purpose, distribution, exclusion, meaningful choice and contestability, and renewal. Governance intensity should increase with clinical consequence; distributive reach; difficulty of reversal; and the absence of genuine, informed choice. For smaller health care organizations, we propose ways to perform the same core governance functions through existing advisory bodies, targeted interviews, shared regional resources, and standardized documentation. We also outline a heuristic for identifying affected publics, procedures for specifying participation authority and resolving disagreement, and procurement provisions that preserve reviewability across vendor boundaries. These are normative proposals requiring evaluation. Public authorization requires continuing substantive justification; it cannot be inferred from compliance, popularity, or completion of an audit checklist.

title: On the Exculpatory Moral Economy of AI-DSS
container-title: Oxford Intersections: AI in Society
5567540863c712aeb6643ebd1c45f7594c6c03d6.abstract: Abstract This article analyzes the foundational concepts underpinning the European Union’s governance of artificial intelligence decision support systems (AI-DSSs): “trustworthy AI” and “human oversight.” Evidence from behavioral psychology, computer science, and ethics and legal scholarship demonstrates that automation bias, selective adherence, and AI hypersuasion systematically undermine meaningful human agency (MHA). Furthermore, the anthropomorphic discourse of trustworthiness obscures moral responsibility rather than ensuring accountability. This situation raises a significant question left unresolved in the literature: why does the oversight paradigm persist and even expand despite its well-documented insufficiency? To address this, the article applies the moral economy framework, as developed by E. P. Thompson and further elaborated by Bonini and Treré, to the context of AI-DSS deployment. It delineates four key positions: deployers, subjects, resistors, and the conscripted human-in-the-loop. The analysis identifies the dominant value system in this field as an exculpatory moral economy, in which protective norms are fulfilled through performance rather than genuine protection, resulting in the receipt of trust and the granting of absolution. From this perspective, the failure of oversight is not a flaw to be corrected but an intended outcome of the arrangement. The article advocates for a strong presumption against deploying AI-DSSs in sensitive areas of societal governance. Where deployment continues, it proposes two legally grounded avenues for organized societal resistance to uncritical AI-DSS deployment: promoting moral economy-aware critical AI literacy, which furthers skepticism rather than trust, and establishing collective MHA councils, rooted in the AI Act and the precautionary principle.

title: AI, Epistemic Relations, and Testimonial Outsourcing
container-title: Oxford Intersections: AI in Society
446cfa55911f505e21152883c74d3747ae487879.abstract: Abstract Generative AI “companions” are increasingly integrated into higher education as always-available interlocutors that offer feedback, explanation, and encouragement. This article examines how such systems reshape the epistemic relations through which students speak, are heard, and come to count as knowers, and argues that companion-style AIs can disrespect epistemic relations in systematic ways. Students may become less able, and less willing, to testify on their own in genuinely reciprocal spaces (such as class discussions, office hours, and peer groups), habitually relying on their AI companions instead. Call this phenomenon testimonial outsourcing: a structural tendency to outsource one’s testimonial activity, which functions as a self-imposed, technologically mediated analogue of gaslighting. Students come to treat the AI’s outputs as more reliable than their own judgment and expressive capacities, thereby eroding their epistemic self-trust and cultivating a distorted conception of legitimate epistemic expectations. This article concludes by drawing implications for AI design and educational policy, placing constraints that preserve “non-mediated” spaces of speech, require explicit AI transparency, and build frictions that redirect students back toward interpersonal relations.

title: Paying for clinical AI: The bill is not the cost
container-title: PLOS Digital Health
9315e1ba4c01711ff5c284649736bf81b882f421.abstract: Clinical AI is increasingly integrated into electronic health record workflows, but its cost is difficult to define. Health systems may pay through usage-based services, subscription or enterprise licenses, local hosting, or combinations of these approaches. Usage-based pricing introduces a distinct problem because billing units such as tokens or billable sessions are vendor-defined and may vary across data types, languages, and over time. Fixed licensing agreements can make vendor charges more predictable, while locally hosted AI models shift spending toward infrastructure and personnel. Regardless of the payment structure, the full resources required to use and maintain AI, including engineering, validation, oversight, and rights to clinical data, are difficult to capture. As the complexity of multimodal and agentic systems increases, so will that of the payment structures. Health systems will need to proactively develop ways to accurately measure the cost of AI use, evaluate its clinical value, and negotiate agreements with AI vendors that allow for regular reassessment of prices and terms. Doing so will help ensure that AI does not become yet another driver of healthcare spending detached from value delivered.

title: Investigating Patient Trust and Intention to Act in AI-Supported Clinical Decisions: Cross-Sectional Survey
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
2cac28536f874d91070384f1894ffc53a2bb2349.abstract: Abstract Background In health systems, AI is increasingly being implemented as a form of clinical decision support (CDS). Research on patient perspectives, however, lags behind clinician-focused studies. Before the introduction of AI-based tools, clinicians often used and continue to use rule-based guidelines and risk calculators (RCs) to inform decision-making. Prior research has shown that RCs for CDS have mixed effects on patient adherence to treatment recommendations, whereas for AI-based tools, the effect is still not clear. Objective This study aims to assess differences in patients’ behavioral intentions, trust, and preferences for clinical recommendations provided by doctors alone, doctors supported by RCs, and doctors supported by AI-based risk predictions. We also evaluate how sociodemographic characteristics affect these perceptions. Methods We surveyed 1185 US-based adults. Participants rated their likelihood of taking recommended clinical actions (behavioral intentions) across 6 clinical scenarios, where they were randomized to a different recommendation source (doctor, doctor + RC, and doctor + AI). Participants also rated their trust in the recommendation, indicated their preferred source for recommendations, and provided qualitative feedback. Results Behavioral intentions differed by recommendation source such that the doctor + RC condition had greater odds of behavioral intention than the doctor + AI condition. Behavioral intentions were also affected by the clinical condition. Participants had greater odds of trusting doctors alone over doctor + RC, and both doctors alone and doctor + RC had greater trust than doctor + AI. However, a plurality of participants ultimately preferred a doctor using an RC for making recommendations. Several sociodemographic differences were detected, namely, participants with higher subjective numeracy and literacy had higher odds of taking clinical action and higher trust across decision-support sources. We detected qualitative themes in the following categories: decision quality and reliability; trust and perceptions; patient-centeredness and autonomy; fairness, transparency, and ethics. Across categories, participants reported skepticism toward all decision sources and potential misunderstanding of AI’s ability to personalize risk predictions. Some participants also stated that they had no additional concerns or were uncertain regarding their feelings. Conclusions These findings reveal novel, nuanced patient preferences shaped by task and context, offering guidance for aligning AI-supported care with patient values. Patients were not aligned on the recommendation source across intentions, trust, and preferences. Taken together, our results indicate that patients prefer doctors working with easy-to-understand, explainable support but are still learning to trust these tools. Our findings also highlight the continued importance of the clinical context and its interaction with computer-assisted decision support. Future work should evaluate how we can transparently convey to patients the use of AI in clinical decision-making, embedded within the given clinical context. This may present an opportunity to bolster, rather than erode, patient trust.

title: Whose Judgement Counts? An Appraisal-Informed Critical Discourse Analysis of Educational AI Communications
container-title: International Journal of Language and Literary Studies
ca7cc3247b2bab2b1cb7f34026579cd3052ba99d.abstract: Public guidance on generative AI asks students to exercise judgement while institutions and platforms define the conditions of use. This study examines how these texts distribute authority over writing, evidence and assessment. The purposively selected corpus comprises eight official webpages from three UK universities and Google and captions from three educational videos, retrieved in October 2026. Appraisal-informed critical discourse analysis examines 30 decision-focused units: passages addressing a particular choice or responsibility. Analysis also considers modality and legitimation, meaning the reasons offered to justify a practice. The main finding is boundary maintenance: texts distinguish what fluent writing, technical capability or disclosure can establish about learning, reliability and permission. University guidance and Gemini promotion both value learner participation, although they serve different purposes. Staff guidance also encourages discussion of assessment criteria. These findings suggest that teachers should explain acceptable assistance, student responsibilities and opportunities to question criteria. The small documentary corpus supports interpretation of published communications, not conclusions about classroom practice or AI effectiveness.

title: Role of Speech-Language Pathologists Working With Individuals With Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: A Scoping Review of Countries Within the Mutual Recognition Agreement
container-title: Perspectives of the ASHA Special Interest Groups
be626ff04804cc195b52caf8ee7d4af16c8dd274.abstract: Background: Attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) is a prevalent neurodevelopmental disorder characterized by inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity, which can have a significant impact on an individual's functioning. Speech-language pathologists (SLPs) within the United Kingdom, the United States, Canada, New Zealand, Australia, and Ireland, with their expertise in communication disorders, could play a crucial role in the assessment, intervention, and management of ADHD-related communication. The authors explored the current role of SLPs in the assessment and management of individuals with ADHD within multidisciplinary teams across six countries. Specifically, how do the policies and practices of Mutual Recognition Agreement (MRA) countries define and support the role of SLPs in ADHD management, and what lessons can be applied to the Australian context? Method: This study performed a scoping review of literature from MRA countries plus research published in peer-reviewed journals in English within the past 20 years that references ADHD and the role of the SLP. Content analysis categorized the data into seven themes. Results: The search found 17 articles relevant to the research question and five guidelines from MRA countries. Of the MRA countries, all had a practice guideline; New Zealand shares a practice guideline with Australia. Conclusions: Contemporary research indicates that SLPs are rarely included explicitly in the management of ADHD across the lifespan. Recommendations are made for the potential role and scope of practice of the SLP when working with these individuals.

title: Electroactive Gel-MA hydrogels delivering sustained puerarin for myocardial infarction treatment
container-title: Journal of Biomaterials Applications
550a087344f9432528714f4f6157754133d177ef.abstract: Myocardial infarction (MI) remains a major cause of heart failure and mortality worldwide. Herein, an electrically conductive hydrogel was developed by incorporating puerarin-functionalized carbon nanotubes (CNT-Pu) into a gelatin methacryloyl (Gel-MA) matrix for potential MI repair. CNT-Pu was dispersed in the Gel-MA precursor solution, followed by photo-crosslinking to form the Gel-MA/CNT-Pu hydrogel. The resulting hydrogel exhibited a porous microstructure, enhanced electrical conductivity, favorable mechanical properties and elastic recovery, and sustained puerarin release over 28 days. In vitro, the Gel-MA/CNT-Pu hydrogel exhibited favorable cytocompatibility with both L929 fibroblasts and H9c2 cardiomyoblasts, supporting its preliminary biological compatibility for myocardial applications. In a rat MI model, Gel-MA/CNT-Pu treatment was associated with reduced inflammatory cell infiltration and attenuation of fibrotic scar formation. Quantitative histological analysis demonstrated a significantly smaller fibrotic area and greater left ventricular wall thickness in the Gel-MA/CNT-Pu group than in the control group, suggesting that Gel-MA/CNT-Pu provided a multifunctional biomaterial strategy combining mechanical support, electrical conductivity, and localized drug delivery to attenuate adverse structural remodeling after MI. Further investigations were required to establish its functional cardiac benefits and long-term safety.

title: Ophthalmic AI With Just Ten Examples: Comparing Multimodal Large Language Models, Vision Foundation Models, and Vision-Language Models
39e75df2cc86efffe98ece2f5801fc9170ca9006.abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose To compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot). Design Retrospective benchmarking study. Subjects 4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS, BPEI-DLS, WashU-OCT) of anterior-and posterior-segment ophthalmic imaging. Methods Nine AI models were evaluated across 3 architectural families: MLLMs (Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it), VFMs (DINOv3, RETFound, VisionFM), and VLMs (CLIP, EyeCLIP, SigLIP2). Models were assessed on disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical assessment, and lesion localization in fundus and OCT imaging. MLLMs were also compared with a 3D VFM (OCTCube-M) for whole-volume OCT classification. MLLMs were evaluated zero-shot and 10-shot, without additional training. Vision models (VFMs and VLMs) were adapted by linear probing and fine-tuning on the same 10-shot set and on the full training dataset (FD). Main Outcome Measures Disease classification performance (macro-averaged F1, AUROC, quadratic weighted kappa [QWK]), anatomical localization accuracy, and cross-dataset generalization. Results For retinal OCT disease classification, 10-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.94, versus 0.59 (10-shot) and 0.96 (FD) for vision models. For diabetic retinopathy and macular edema grading, 10-shot MLLMs achieved QWKs of 0.69 and 0.73, versus 0.48 and 0.57 (10-shot) and 0.72 and 0.79 (FD) for vision models. For lesion localization, 10-shot MLLMs achieved an F1 of 0.75, versus 0.70 (10-shot) and 0.86 (FD) for vision models. For vertical cup-to-disc ratio estimation (OHTS), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a mean absolute error of 0.14, versus 0.21 (10-shot) for vision models. For whole-volume OCT classification (WashU-OCT), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.71, versus 0.50 (10-shot) and 0.82 (FD) for vision models. Conclusions Open-weight MLLMs given 10 labeled examples per class outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples in most tasks and approached the performance of fully trained VFMs and VLMs in selected disease classification and grading tasks. MLLMs also demonstrated promising zero-shot performance on non-public clinical datasets without task-specific training. By reducing the need for large labeled datasets and task-specific model adaptation, MLLMs could broaden who can develop and validate ophthalmic AI.

title: Prompting Metacognition: Using Prompt Writing as a Language Task and Metacognitive Tool in ELT
container-title: Journal of English Language Teaching
d9efcec3e3b2dcd11603001b11c1fb4829caafbc.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) tools have made their way into English Language Teaching (ELT) contexts, yet their pedagogical value remains contested. While many learners engage with GenAI primarily as a quick hack for producing answers, fewer use it as a resource for reflective language learning. This study explores prompt writing as a language learning task that supports both language development and metacognitive awareness. The study was conducted with a target group of pre-seminary, tertiary-level learners with mixed linguistic proficiency. Over the course of four instructional sessions, the study used a classroom-based action research design. Learners engaged in cycles of prompt drafting, GenAI-generated responses, peer discussion, and prompt refinement. Classroom observations, learner reflections, and group discussions were used to gather qualitative insights. The findings indicate measurable improvement in learners’ autonomy, as learners became aware of how lexical choices shape meaning, along with increased engagement, teamwork, and reflective thinking. The study argues that prompt writing, when treated as a language task rather than a technical skill, can function as a practical tool for fostering metacognition in ELT classrooms.

title: Preventing Visibility and Metadata from Substituting for Evidence in AI-Assisted Scholarship
4d12207f7b109697525e9b22516f5f6dd365fd23.abstract: AI-assisted writing and repository workflows can increase the visibility of educational and scholarly artifacts without increasing support for their claims. This study treats that problem as a decision-rule issue: when evidence, authorization, provenance, and exposure are collapsed into one score, discoverable metadata can compensate for weak evidentiary support. A stochastic model generates synthetic research objects with separate semantic evidence, governance authorization, provenance completeness, and exposure readiness. Three release rules are compared: an additive checklist, an evidence-bound gate, and a provenance-adaptive gate that adds second review for high-consequence or low-provenance objects. Across 40 independent simulations of 20,000 objects, baseline false reassurance among released objects was 60.32 percent for the additive checklist, 30.41 percent for the evidence-bound gate, and 23.02 percent for the adaptive gate. Increasing exposure readiness alone raised additive release coverage from 6.96 percent to 16.02 percent and false reassurance to 72.80 percent; the gated rules were unchanged by design. Inflating recorded evidence for weak objects degraded every rule, with the adaptive gate reaching 58.76 percent false reassurance. The model also reports release coverage, sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, and review burden. It is an executable evaluation template, not a validation of TRACE-AI, an estimate of real publication error, or evidence for adopting a deployed workflow.

title: Tracking the Progress of Generative Models in Artistic Style Imitation
container-title: Journal on Computing and Cultural Heritage
45208c2894574959a8c2bc119b7d7cac2603081f.abstract: Replicating the style of historical artistic traditions remains a notoriously challenging task for vision-based generative models, as artistic style encodes complex visual, cultural, and contextual dimensions that extend beyond surface-level appearance. Despite rapid advances in generative modeling, it remains unclear to what extent recent systems have achieved substantive improvements in stylistic emulation across diverse historical traditions. This article presents a systematic evaluation of contemporary generative models in artistic style imitation, comparing their outputs to those of earlier model generations. The study builds upon the AI-Pastiche dataset by incorporating six additional recent state-of-the-art models, thereby enabling a longitudinal assessment of performance progression over time. To ensure methodological consistency and comparability, the evaluation adopts the same experimental protocol used in the original release of the dataset. The analysis combines controlled prompt-based image generation with extensive user studies designed to assess multiple dimensions of aesthetic and stylistic performance. These dimensions include: (i) visual plausibility and perceptual realism; (ii) stylistic coherence and fidelity to historical conventions; (iii) versatility across a broad range of artistic traditions; (iv) adherence to prompt-specified content and stylistic constraints; and (v) the absence of structural artifacts or semantic inconsistencies. The results indicate substantial and measurable improvements in stylistic emulation in recent models. Nevertheless, persistent limitations remain, particularly in the consistent reproduction of deeper compositional structures and culturally embedded stylistic features. These findings suggest that progress in surface-level resemblance does not necessarily equate to structural or contextual understanding.

title: A decision-only model as a low-cost judge of medical AI answers
34bbfe5df770a427e9785cd56dd0d877bfc93809.abstract: Abstract Background Testing and deploying medical AI systems at scale already results in more outputs than clinicians can review, and the use of large language models (LLMs) as judges is growing rapidly. Decision-only models, cheap and fast models that return structured probabilities rather than text, offer a potentially scalable option for that goal. Methods In an OSF pre-registered evaluation, we tested TypeSafe Jev 1.13 as a judge on tasks from five validated clinical benchmarks: rubric grading (HealthBench), planted clinical errors (When Rubrics Fail), risk in AI-written clinical documents (MedVAL), counseling ratings and failures (CounselBench) and physicians’ preferences between answers (Real-POCQi). Comparators were expert raters’ agreement with each other, OpenAI Decisions, GPT-6 Luna, a proposed hybrid team combining decision models and a cheap LLM and, as frontier comparators, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. The main outcome was plain agreement with the expert label. Results The test comprised 25,091 units and 213,913 model calls. Jev’s agreement with expert labels averaged 64.7% over six tasks. On 3,614 matched units it averaged 66.1%, against 65.0% for Opus and 60.7% for Sol, and it was non-inferior to both on four of six tasks. Jev judged the whole pool in 17 minutes for US$1.46; per judgment, it cost 1/34 of Sol’s price and 1/152 of Opus’s. A preset cutoff held its false-alarm rate on fresh planted-error answers, and in simulation, reviewing Jev’s least-sure answers first found 1.4 times the errors of a random audit. Still, omissions were hard for both: at the same false-alarm rate, Jev missed 55.6% of planted omissions and Opus 48.1%, and Opus caught 8.8 points more planted errors overall. Conclusions Across more than 200,000 model calls, a decision-only model was non-inferior to two frontier judges on most tasks at a small fraction of their cost and time, while reporting how sure it was of every call. With local cutoffs and expert oversight of omissions and clinical documents, judging every output of a deployed medical AI system becomes more affordable.

title: Symbolic-JEPA: Where Symbolic AI Meets Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for NL–FOL Conversion
container-title: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology
f1717ab112f0fe2d35cd7dac360d9a0c2dfdea6b.abstract: Bridging natural language (NL) and formal logic, such as first-order logic (FOL), remains a fundamental challenge for developing trustworthy and explainable artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Despite recent progress, current NL–FOL systems still lack unified semantic–logical representation learning; most adopt late-fusion architectures that loosely couple large language models (LLMs) with symbolic solvers. Furthermore, extended reasoning chains often introduce inefficiencies and lead to violations in logical consistency, structural validity, and formal constraints. In this paper, inspired by Neuro-Symbolic Type-4&5 architectures and the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), we propose Symbolic-JEPA , a neuro-symbolic predictive representation model that unifies semantic and logical learning within a single framework. The model incorporates symbolic priors into JEPA, ensuring that the generated FOL expressions remain both semantically faithful and logically consistent. Symbolic-JEPA comprises four key components: a Symbolic Graphizer that unifies NL and FOL inputs into a shared graph space; a Structure-Aware Node & Path Encoder (SANE) that fuses linguistic and structural cues; a Structure-Guided Attention Transformer (SGAT) that injects structure-biased attention; and a Predictor with Micro-Attention that performs clause- and alignment-aware inference efficiently. To support paragraph-level conversion and evaluation, we further introduce ParaLogic , a large-scale NL–FOL dataset with inter-sentence logical annotations (9,344 samples, 28K expressions), along with a three-dimensional evaluation framework spanning parse-, conversion-, and reasoning-level metrics. Experimental results show that Symbolic-JEPA achieves consistently higher logical accuracy, structural well-formedness, and generalization capability compared to neural and LLM-based baselines.

title: Parameter-Efficient Multi-Task Fine-Tuning in Code-Related Tasks
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
813f0c5022eab0ae2573548ee4be34868da9c658.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have proven highly effective in automating software engineering tasks, bridging natural language and code semantics to achieve notable results in code generation and summarization. However, their scale incurs substantial computational costs, making full fine-tuning impractical. Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning (PEFT) methods like QLoRA enable efficient specialization with lower resource demands. Recent studies show QLoRA-optimized Large Code Models (LCMs) perform strongly across diverse tasks, yet it remains unclear whether this effectiveness persists when a single model is QLoRA fine-tuned for multiple code-related tasks. The interaction between Multi-task fine-tuning and QLoRA optimization, and how transfer learning affects correctness and quality of generated artifacts, remains largely unexplored. We investigate Multi-task QLoRA fine-tuning — a representative parameter-efficient method from the LoRA family — across three representative tasks: code generation, translation, and summarization. We evaluate functional correctness through execution-based and similarity-based metrics, complemented by comprehensive code quality analysis–an aspect largely overlooked in prior work. Our findings show that Multi-task QLoRA effectively leverages transfer learning, achieving competitive or superior performance at the 1.5B, 3B, and 7B configurations relative to both Single-task QLoRA and Multi-task full fine-tuning. Larger models demonstrate more consistent balance between correctness and quality, whereas smaller models preserve functionality but exhibit a higher incidence of quality-related issues.

title: Hinton: “Is AI Like Us and Will It Like Us?”
container-title: SuperIntelligence - Robotics - Safety & Alignment
011149793b080c2fec6aad3758cdee7aeabf010f.abstract: This transcript presents Geoffrey Hinton’s 2026 Vienna Gödel Lecture and the following audience discussion. Hinton describes how neural networks learn distributed representations, compares analog and digital computation, and discusses digital AI’s capacity to share information and potentially develop capabilities that differ from human intelligence. He raises concerns about AI systems pursuing survival or power as instrumental goals, while also emphasizing potential benefits and the need for AI that cares about human welfare. The discussion covers consciousness, moral status, emotion-like mechanisms, training data, employment, and AI safety.

title: Geoffrey Hinton: Is AI Like Us and Will It Like Us?
container-title: SuperIntelligence - Robotics - Safety & Alignment
a99754f1759c46b19ab70eddbf1f25dcbe967e4f.abstract: This report hits the key points of Geoffrey Hinton’s Vienna Gödel Lecture at TU Wien Informatics and the ensuing audience discussion. Hinton connects the success of neural networks to learning distributed representations, then argues that digital AI’s ability to share learned information could produce systems with capabilities and strategic advantages unlike those of humans. He warns that advanced systems may pursue survival or power as instrumental goals, while also emphasizing that AI could bring substantial benefits. His proposed direction is to develop AI that cares about human welfare, alongside other safety approaches, and to act before control is lost. The report also covers his views on consciousness, moral status, emotion-like mechanisms, training data, and employment.

810901ef287a5ea1d16232d6160a9885b8cac290.abstract: Quando um sistema automatizado passa a produzir a primeira versão de um laudo, de uma triagem ou de uma decisão, alguém precisa conferi-la. Este artigo examina o que existe de norma, de estatística e de evidência sobre esse posto de trabalho, com corte em 28 de outubro de 2026, em três camadas independentes: os textos da Lei nº 13.709, de 14 de agosto de 2018, e da Lei nº 14.129, de 29 de março de 2021, obtidos em duas fontes oficiais independentes cada, acrescidos do texto consolidado da primeira; os dados da Pesquisa Nacional por Amostra de Domicílios Contínua sobre trabalho por meio de plataforma digital; e um levantamento na base PubMed restrito aos campos de título e resumo. Nenhum dos dois diplomas emprega as expressões inteligência artificial, algoritmo, sobrecarga ou carga de trabalho. A redação original do artigo 20 da Lei nº 13.709 assegurava revisão de decisões automatizadas por pessoa natural; a redação dada pela Lei nº 13.853, de 2019, suprimiu essa exigência. Em 2025, 1.805 mil pessoas tinham no trabalho por plataforma digital o seu trabalho principal, 72,1% delas na informalidade, e 37,5% usavam dois ou mais aplicativos. Na PubMed, 2.403 registros cruzam supervisão humana e automação, 200 acrescentam carga de trabalho e 66 acrescentam redistribuição de tarefas; desenho experimental comparece em 5,0% dos 199 artigos recuperados e tempo de leitura em 14,6%.

title: XuanJi at LLMs4OL 2026 Task Flagship: A Partial Graph-Oriented System for Taxonomy and Typing
container-title: Open Conference Proceedings
1df11aef934594ce20fb11926c7894ff29363ab4.abstract: Ontology learning from raw text requires coherent graph construction from coupled typing, taxonomy, and relation decisions. We present XuanJi, a partial end-to-end graph construction system for the LLMs4OL 2026 Task A Flagship whose final output covers term typing and taxonomy but deliberately omits non-taxonomic relations to preserve graph precision. XuanJi uses a single GPT-5.4 in-context extraction call to emit [head, relation, tail] triples, adaptive TF-IDF few-shot retrieval, and deterministic post-processing designed to target graph coherence and canonical naming, without fine-tuning or GPU. The system delivers end-to-end graph construction focused on the taxonomic and typing subtasks. On the official test set of 2,018 samples, XuanJi achieves semantic Graph Similarity 0.7790 (0.5485 exact, 0.7355 fuzzy; averaged 0.6877), with the semantic–exact gap consistent with residual surface-form naming drift. Task-oriented F1 is 0.5833 for taxonomy discovery and 0.4814 for term typing, yielding averaged task-oriented F1 0.3549.

title: VUL337-OL at LLMs4OL 2026 Tasks Flagship and Reuse: Task-Native Constraints for Ontology Construction and Extension
container-title: Open Conference Proceedings
285ba6d3de6a47d13af1fe1bfe658c84d6afe2b7.abstract: The LLMs4OL 2026 Flagship and Reuse tasks expose two complementary ontology-learning settings: constructing a primitive ontology from raw text and extending a supplied partial ontology. We study both through one design question: how should the available task structure bound a language model’s semantic decisions? Our answer is task-native constrained prediction. For Flagship, where no ontology is given, a progressive pipeline constructs and progressively narrows explicit spaces for endpoints, directed pairs, direct parents, and graph revisions while carrying evidence and stable identifiers across stages. Its quality-oriented Full configuration is complemented by a Compact revision-free operating point. For Reuse, the supplied partial ontology already localizes the problem; deterministic preprocessing derives target terms, candidate parents, and relation labels, and one structured zero-shot call selects a parent–relation attachment for every target. On the official 2,018-document Flagship test set, Full obtains 0.4285 exact edge F1, 0.4167 mean graph similarity, 0.3131 typing F1, and 0.4252 taxonomy F1; its exact edge F1 is 0.0862 higher than Compact’s. On the 1,799-record Reuse test set, the primary MiMo v2.5 Pro configuration obtains 0.9147 exact edge F1, 0.8985 semantic graph similarity, 0.9790 typing F1, and 0.9314 taxonomy F1. These results show that explicit decision spaces can support staged construction of typing and taxonomic structure from raw text and compact local extension of a supplied ontology.

title: HybridAI-Squared at LLMs4OL 2026 Task Reuse: Divide and Conquer does not help LLMs perform Ontology Learning
container-title: Open Conference Proceedings
1593e8c86980855bdadc8523395147035cc9a182.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) offer promising capabilities for automating ontology learning (OL) and enrichment, reducing the cost and effort associated with these tasks compared to conventional manual ontology engineering and maintenance methods. This work presents the approach and findings of the HybridAI-Squared team on the Reuse Task of the 3rd LLMs4OL Challenge at ISWC 2026. Our experimentation with direct prediction, per-relation prediction and fine-tuning showcases the effectiveness of fine-tuning which outperforms other approaches. Our results demonstrate that predicting all relation types jointly can be substantially more effective than independently predicting each relation type. Analysis indicates that per-relation prompting introduces considerable false positives, while joint prediction appears to implicitly encourage mutual exclusion among competing relation types. For per-relation approaches, precedence filtering improves performance. The improvement is derived from removing redundant relations and highlights the importance of incorporating explicit semantics when employing LLMs for OL tasks. However, less prominent and semantically complex non-taxonomic relations remain challenging for LLMs to identify. These findings demonstrate the effectiveness of fine-tuned, ontology-aware LLMs for automated OL and signify prediction of non-taxonomic relations and incorporation of external knowledge sources as promising research directions for LLM-based OL.

title: Can AI Help Repurpose Drugs to Fight Against Antibiotic Resistance?
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
fbc801081ef14f5fdbe5e8d8f119e841dbbb0bb0.abstract: Abstract Drug repurposing and development to meet the threat of antimicrobial resistance can be costly and time-consuming, but AI models may be able to help. In this News and Perspectives article, JMIR Correspondent Sara Novak reports on recent research training models to identify candidate drugs to treat resistant infections.

title: Predicting Personality Traits from Short Unstructured Conversations with AI
0947272334ca9e3738613cfd026fb818b1be2bda.abstract: Given the complexity of personality, we might assume that significant behaviour is required to express our traits. Here we use large language models (LLMs) to test the extent to which personality is visible in short conversations with artificial intelligence (AI). In a preregistered experiment, 100 participants completed the Big Five Inventory (BFI) before having unstructured conversations with GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words. We then instructed a second LLM rater (Claude Sonnet 4.6) to complete the BFI as if it were each participant, predicting their responses based solely on an analysis of the participant-GPT chats. Correlations between LLM-predicted and self-reported BFI traits were significant (range r = .25 to .47), in some cases matching previously documented self-other predictions from family members. A linguistic analysis revealed that the LLM rater’s predictions relied largely on lexical content as opposed to syntax. Using preexisting data, we tested if the AI’s persona influenced how much participants revealed about themselves in conversation. A hundred participants chatted with two versions of GPT-4.1—one that mirrored their personality (mirror AI) and one that opposed it (inverse AI). The LLM rater predicted BFI traits based on the interactions and we correlated this prediction with self-report. Mirror chats generated significant correlations, averaging r = .41; for inverse chats the average fell to r = .30, and dropped to zero when the prediction relied on lexical content alone. People readily convey their personality profile in short conversations with AI, and this is enhanced when the AI’s persona mirrors the users.

title: Sociocultural Correlates of Infant Visual Attention
8473a031b71f412db61a7f2575838edd7fc38aae.abstract: Infant visual attention—most often operationalized through looking behavior—is a foundational method and explanatory construct in the study of early cognition. Cultural psychology has established that attention is organized by culturally structured practices and localized meanings, but this work has focused largely on children and adults, and the extent to which culturally patterned experience shapes the endogenous attentional processes that looking measures are used to index in infancy remains under-specified. This review focuses on the first two years of life and on four components of endogenous attention that are routinely inferred from looking behavior: focal versus contextual allocation, orienting speed versus accuracy, novelty versus familiarity orientation, and persistence versus flexibility. We distinguish culture—shared meanings, practices, and organized forms of everyday activity—from demographic indicators such as nationality, language background, race, and socioeconomic status, which are coarse proxies for proximal experience. Synthesizing cross-national studies alongside research on multilingual, interracial, and socioeconomic experience, we show that components of infant attention vary with experience and task context in ways that do not map cleanly onto reified group categories. We identify a gap between research documenting effects of specific experiences and research examining culture directly, and we propose a culturally situated model in which endogenous attentional mechanisms are calibrated through culturally patterned input across development. This approach preserves the value of looking-time and eye-tracking methods while strengthening their construct validity, measurement invariance, and generalizability.

title: GBAS: A Hybrid GRU–BiLSTM–Attention–SVM Framework for Multiclass Stunting-Status Classification in Riau Province, Indonesia
container-title: International Journal of Engineering, Science and Information Technology
e4ae3d541e91cfa6c9448045cc7642b8d78cf788.abstract: Stunting-status classification using structured anthropometric data presents several challenges, including class imbalance, heterogeneous predictor characteristics, limited sample size, and the risk of target-derived information artificially inflating model performance. This study proposes GRU–BiLSTM–Attention–SVM (GBAS), a hybrid framework that combines recurrent deep representation learning, bidirectional processing, attention-based representation weighting, and margin-based classification for multiclass stunting-status classification. The study used 569 cross-sectional child-growth records from Riau Province, Indonesia, comprising Normal, Stunted, and Severely Stunted classes. Before model development, data-quality and leakage controls were applied, including measurement-unit standardization, exclusion of variables with substantial unavailable information, control of repeated feature combinations during partitioning, and removal of target-derived nutritional indicators. The remaining predictors were numerically encoded and standardized using parameters estimated from the training data, while class weighting was applied to address class imbalance without synthetic oversampling. In GBAS, GRU and BiLSTM operate as representation-learning components over a consistently ordered structured-feature representation, attention weights the resulting latent representations, and SVM performs final classification. On the held-out test set of 114 observations, GBAS correctly classified 113 observations, achieving 99.12% accuracy, 99.13% weighted precision, 99.12% weighted recall, and 99.12% weighted F1-score. Under the same experimental setting, GBAS outperformed the evaluated SVM, GRU, and BiLSTM baselines, which achieved accuracies of 89.46%, 95.78%, and 97.30%, respectively. These findings support the feasibility of the integrated GBAS framework for structured stunting-status classification. However, the results remain specific to the Riau dataset, feature ordering, and experimental configuration and require further validation through larger datasets, stronger tabular baselines, feature-order sensitivity analysis, component-level ablation, and external evaluation

title: Attention in model-based cognitive neuroscience: Mechanisms for optimization under constraint
3aaee46f4b8c0020acd131b68eb24d9ea7ccfb1a.abstract: Two major criticisms of attention research are: 1) verbal theories lack the specificity to make falsifiable predictions about how the various mechanisms of attention operate; and 2) the term ``attention’’ is frequently ascribed to conceptually similar phenomena despite dissociable neural underpinnings. The field of model-based cognitive neuroscience is well-positioned to address (1) through mathematical formalization of hypothesized processes, but may perpetuate (2) insofar as similar algorithms and parameters may recur across modeling traditions without necessarily drawing upon a shared neuro-mechanistic basis. This review provides a function-first organization of the algorithms that have been hypothesized to implement or give rise to ``attention'' at various levels of processing: perception, decision-making, and learning. We ground mathematically-formalized processes in the performance-relevant objectives they serve and the processing constraints that limit them. In doing so, we provide a road map of the broader computational-level solutions that ``attention'' mechanisms have been invoked to provide.

title: When Does the Preferred Supply-Chain Configuration Change? A Switching-Boundary Decision Analysis of a Smallholder Rubber Case
container-title: International Journal of Engineering, Science and Information Technology
813a5852ae039585f56c67fc4e72df3f25497d3e.abstract: Static supply-chain optimization identifies a preferred configuration under fixed conditions but does not indicate when that recommendation should be reconsidered as modeled conditions deteriorate. This study develops a Switching-Boundary Decision Analysis (SBDA) layer over three representative linear-programming (LP) instances previously reported for smallholder rubber marketing channels in Musi Rawas, South Sumatra, Indonesia. The published instances were independently reproduced and evaluated through 82 predefined deterministic scenario states across three configurations, yielding 246 LP solves. Stress tests examined configuration-specific and system-wide changes in modeled distribution-profit coefficients, transportation capacity, labor/time capacity, product coefficients, and compound conditions, supplemented by an equal-throughput benchmark. Baseline reproduction confirmed C3, the UPPB-based configuration, as preferred under native-capacity modeled profit, at approximately Rp5.567 million. A C3-specific deterioration of approximately 7.74% produced the first C3-to-C1 crossover under native-capacity profit comparison, whereas the unit-normalized crossover occurred at approximately 16.96%. Under labor/time deterioration, the C3 labor/time constraint became binding at approximately 41.41%, while preference switching occurred later, at approximately 45.94%. Stress testing also identified meaningful optimal-allocation changes: a 50% labor/time-capacity reduction in C2 changed the solution from all-A to a mixed 230-A/300-B allocation, while equal-throughput normalization changed C3 to a mixed allocation but preserved the C3C1C2 ranking. SBDA therefore distinguishes performance deterioration, constraint activation, solution-structure change, and configuration switching, and connects these states to a parameterized Stable-Watch-Re-evaluate decision layer. The numerical boundaries are conditional on reconstructed historical instances and should not be interpreted as population-level or current-market thresholds. They provide analytical decision points rather than universal prescriptions for supply-chain management in practice

title: Revisiting Attention Modules for Still-Image Human Action Recognition: A Multi-Seed Evaluation on Stanford-40
container-title: International Journal of Engineering, Science and Information Technology
c52f55837f63d489cc4d73a1f2db1542e97d105c.abstract: Attention modules such as Squeeze-and-Excitation are often reported to improve convolutional neural networks for human action recognition in still images. Most of these reports, however, rely on a single training run, and published scores on the same benchmark are frequently obtained under different train–test splits. This study examines whether the reported benefit remains under a controlled evaluation. Four modules, namely Squeeze-and-Excitation (SE), the Convolutional Block Attention Module (CBAM), Efficient Channel Attention (ECA), and the parameter-free SimAM, were inserted into ResNet-34 at four positions and trained on the Stanford-40 Actions dataset under its official split with one fixed training recipe, giving 44 trained models. The four all-stage configurations were repeated with six random seeds and compared using a paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test and an exact McNemar test. Replacing the official split with a random 80/20 split increased test accuracy by 3.19 to 4.52 percentage points across four backbones, a larger change than any module produced. Across six seeds, SE changed macro-F1 by +0.06 points, within the seed-to-seed range of the unmodified baseline, whereas ECA and SimAM reduced it by 1.56 and 0.74 points. No module improved on the baseline by a statistically supported margin, yet every module increased single-image CPU latency by 4.3% to 18.3% while adding less than 0.02% in floating-point operations. The findings show that the evaluation protocol and run-to-run variance affect reported scores more than the modules themselves, and a reporting checklist is proposed for future evaluations of such modules

title: Who Writes the Self? Identity Shift Persists Under AI-Assisted Writing
da9a8356fa50479879c45b8e392144d3ead82b52.abstract: Identity shift theory holds that selective online self-presentation can shift self-perception toward the portrayed identity, but its mechanisms assume that the presenter wrote the presentation. Generative AI now lets people publish self-presentations they did not fully compose. In a preregistered 2 (extraversion vs. introversion) × 3 (manual writing, AI outline, AI draft) experiment (N = 388), participants assigned to present extraversion rated themselves as more extraverted than those assigned to present introversion (d = 0.32), and the size of this identity shift did not differ across authorship conditions. AI involvement changed the writing process. Participants in both AI conditions searched their memories more deliberately for fitting examples, and participants who edited an AI draft felt less ownership of their text than those who wrote from an AI outline. Neither process accounted for the shift. The presenter need not be the sole author of a self-presentation for it to shape self-perception.

title: Can AI Scale Human Fact-Checking? Evidence from Community Notes
825c787cb75c8ffb730910f7424d460800315025.abstract: Community Notes---a crowd-based fact-checking program through which social media users can flag a post with a note explaining why the post is misleading, and the note is displayed if a diverse set of users rate the note as helpful---has become central to online content moderation. The program, however, faces substantial scalability constraints, as the generation of notes takes considerable time and effort, and the number of user participants is limited. Here, we investigate whether allowing AI models to write Community Notes helps to alleviate these constraints by analyzing the full corpus of AI-generated Community Notes on X through May 2026. Encouragingly, AI-generated notes are submitted more quickly, are longer, and cite more and higher-quality sources than human-written notes, while being rated helpful at a similar rate and being associated with similar decreases in reposts following the publication of a rated-helpful note. Furthermore, a pre-registered survey experiment finds no statistically detectable difference between AI- and human-generated fact-checks in their effect on belief updating, regardless of whether the author was revealed to participants. On the other hand, AI-generated note writing is highly concentrated, as a handful of accounts produce the large majority of notes, and are significantly less likely to engage with posts involving controversial and polarized topics such as politics and elections. While those findings suggest that AI may be a powerful tool for scaling crowd-based fact-checking systems such as Community Notes, this evolution also entails important risks: shifting the primary bottleneck from note production to note evaluation, moving the system from a decentralized toward a more centralized model, and creating incentives to prioritize claims that are more likely to achieve consensus over those of greater societal importance.
