title: Paying for clinical AI: The bill is not the cost
container-title: PLOS Digital Health
9315e1ba4c01711ff5c284649736bf81b882f421.abstract: Clinical AI is increasingly integrated into electronic health record workflows, but its cost is difficult to define. Health systems may pay through usage-based services, subscription or enterprise licenses, local hosting, or combinations of these approaches. Usage-based pricing introduces a distinct problem because billing units such as tokens or billable sessions are vendor-defined and may vary across data types, languages, and over time. Fixed licensing agreements can make vendor charges more predictable, while locally hosted AI models shift spending toward infrastructure and personnel. Regardless of the payment structure, the full resources required to use and maintain AI, including engineering, validation, oversight, and rights to clinical data, are difficult to capture. As the complexity of multimodal and agentic systems increases, so will that of the payment structures. Health systems will need to proactively develop ways to accurately measure the cost of AI use, evaluate its clinical value, and negotiate agreements with AI vendors that allow for regular reassessment of prices and terms. Doing so will help ensure that AI does not become yet another driver of healthcare spending detached from value delivered.

title: Investigating Patient Trust and Intention to Act in AI-Supported Clinical Decisions: Cross-Sectional Survey
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
2cac28536f874d91070384f1894ffc53a2bb2349.abstract: Abstract Background In health systems, AI is increasingly being implemented as a form of clinical decision support (CDS). Research on patient perspectives, however, lags behind clinician-focused studies. Before the introduction of AI-based tools, clinicians often used and continue to use rule-based guidelines and risk calculators (RCs) to inform decision-making. Prior research has shown that RCs for CDS have mixed effects on patient adherence to treatment recommendations, whereas for AI-based tools, the effect is still not clear. Objective This study aims to assess differences in patients’ behavioral intentions, trust, and preferences for clinical recommendations provided by doctors alone, doctors supported by RCs, and doctors supported by AI-based risk predictions. We also evaluate how sociodemographic characteristics affect these perceptions. Methods We surveyed 1185 US-based adults. Participants rated their likelihood of taking recommended clinical actions (behavioral intentions) across 6 clinical scenarios, where they were randomized to a different recommendation source (doctor, doctor + RC, and doctor + AI). Participants also rated their trust in the recommendation, indicated their preferred source for recommendations, and provided qualitative feedback. Results Behavioral intentions differed by recommendation source such that the doctor + RC condition had greater odds of behavioral intention than the doctor + AI condition. Behavioral intentions were also affected by the clinical condition. Participants had greater odds of trusting doctors alone over doctor + RC, and both doctors alone and doctor + RC had greater trust than doctor + AI. However, a plurality of participants ultimately preferred a doctor using an RC for making recommendations. Several sociodemographic differences were detected, namely, participants with higher subjective numeracy and literacy had higher odds of taking clinical action and higher trust across decision-support sources. We detected qualitative themes in the following categories: decision quality and reliability; trust and perceptions; patient-centeredness and autonomy; fairness, transparency, and ethics. Across categories, participants reported skepticism toward all decision sources and potential misunderstanding of AI’s ability to personalize risk predictions. Some participants also stated that they had no additional concerns or were uncertain regarding their feelings. Conclusions These findings reveal novel, nuanced patient preferences shaped by task and context, offering guidance for aligning AI-supported care with patient values. Patients were not aligned on the recommendation source across intentions, trust, and preferences. Taken together, our results indicate that patients prefer doctors working with easy-to-understand, explainable support but are still learning to trust these tools. Our findings also highlight the continued importance of the clinical context and its interaction with computer-assisted decision support. Future work should evaluate how we can transparently convey to patients the use of AI in clinical decision-making, embedded within the given clinical context. This may present an opportunity to bolster, rather than erode, patient trust.

title: Whose Judgement Counts? An Appraisal-Informed Critical Discourse Analysis of Educational AI Communications
container-title: International Journal of Language and Literary Studies
ca7cc3247b2bab2b1cb7f34026579cd3052ba99d.abstract: Public guidance on generative AI asks students to exercise judgement while institutions and platforms define the conditions of use. This study examines how these texts distribute authority over writing, evidence and assessment. The purposively selected corpus comprises eight official webpages from three UK universities and Google and captions from three educational videos, retrieved in October 2026. Appraisal-informed critical discourse analysis examines 30 decision-focused units: passages addressing a particular choice or responsibility. Analysis also considers modality and legitimation, meaning the reasons offered to justify a practice. The main finding is boundary maintenance: texts distinguish what fluent writing, technical capability or disclosure can establish about learning, reliability and permission. University guidance and Gemini promotion both value learner participation, although they serve different purposes. Staff guidance also encourages discussion of assessment criteria. These findings suggest that teachers should explain acceptable assistance, student responsibilities and opportunities to question criteria. The small documentary corpus supports interpretation of published communications, not conclusions about classroom practice or AI effectiveness.

title: Ophthalmic AI With Just Ten Examples: Comparing Multimodal Large Language Models, Vision Foundation Models, and Vision-Language Models
39e75df2cc86efffe98ece2f5801fc9170ca9006.abstract: ABSTRACT Purpose To compare multimodal large language models (MLLMs), vision foundation models (VFMs), and contrastive vision-language models (VLMs) for ophthalmic image interpretation with no labeled examples (zero-shot) or as few as 10 labeled examples per class (10-shot). Design Retrospective benchmarking study. Subjects 4 public datasets (UCSD, IDRiD, REFUGE, ASOCT-MSDC) and 3 private datasets (OHTS, BPEI-DLS, WashU-OCT) of anterior-and posterior-segment ophthalmic imaging. Methods Nine AI models were evaluated across 3 architectural families: MLLMs (Qwen3.8-27B, GLM-5.3-Flash, Gemma-4-31B-it), VFMs (DINOv3, RETFound, VisionFM), and VLMs (CLIP, EyeCLIP, SigLIP2). Models were assessed on disease classification, disease risk and severity grading, anatomical assessment, and lesion localization in fundus and OCT imaging. MLLMs were also compared with a 3D VFM (OCTCube-M) for whole-volume OCT classification. MLLMs were evaluated zero-shot and 10-shot, without additional training. Vision models (VFMs and VLMs) were adapted by linear probing and fine-tuning on the same 10-shot set and on the full training dataset (FD). Main Outcome Measures Disease classification performance (macro-averaged F1, AUROC, quadratic weighted kappa [QWK]), anatomical localization accuracy, and cross-dataset generalization. Results For retinal OCT disease classification, 10-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.94, versus 0.59 (10-shot) and 0.96 (FD) for vision models. For diabetic retinopathy and macular edema grading, 10-shot MLLMs achieved QWKs of 0.69 and 0.73, versus 0.48 and 0.57 (10-shot) and 0.72 and 0.79 (FD) for vision models. For lesion localization, 10-shot MLLMs achieved an F1 of 0.75, versus 0.70 (10-shot) and 0.86 (FD) for vision models. For vertical cup-to-disc ratio estimation (OHTS), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a mean absolute error of 0.14, versus 0.21 (10-shot) for vision models. For whole-volume OCT classification (WashU-OCT), zero-shot MLLMs achieved a macro-F1 of 0.71, versus 0.50 (10-shot) and 0.82 (FD) for vision models. Conclusions Open-weight MLLMs given 10 labeled examples per class outperformed VFMs and VLMs trained on the same examples in most tasks and approached the performance of fully trained VFMs and VLMs in selected disease classification and grading tasks. MLLMs also demonstrated promising zero-shot performance on non-public clinical datasets without task-specific training. By reducing the need for large labeled datasets and task-specific model adaptation, MLLMs could broaden who can develop and validate ophthalmic AI.

title: Preventing Visibility and Metadata from Substituting for Evidence in AI-Assisted Scholarship
4d12207f7b109697525e9b22516f5f6dd365fd23.abstract: AI-assisted writing and repository workflows can increase the visibility of educational and scholarly artifacts without increasing support for their claims. This study treats that problem as a decision-rule issue: when evidence, authorization, provenance, and exposure are collapsed into one score, discoverable metadata can compensate for weak evidentiary support. A stochastic model generates synthetic research objects with separate semantic evidence, governance authorization, provenance completeness, and exposure readiness. Three release rules are compared: an additive checklist, an evidence-bound gate, and a provenance-adaptive gate that adds second review for high-consequence or low-provenance objects. Across 40 independent simulations of 20,000 objects, baseline false reassurance among released objects was 60.32 percent for the additive checklist, 30.41 percent for the evidence-bound gate, and 23.02 percent for the adaptive gate. Increasing exposure readiness alone raised additive release coverage from 6.96 percent to 16.02 percent and false reassurance to 72.80 percent; the gated rules were unchanged by design. Inflating recorded evidence for weak objects degraded every rule, with the adaptive gate reaching 58.76 percent false reassurance. The model also reports release coverage, sensitivity, specificity, balanced accuracy, and review burden. It is an executable evaluation template, not a validation of TRACE-AI, an estimate of real publication error, or evidence for adopting a deployed workflow.

title: A decision-only model as a low-cost judge of medical AI answers
34bbfe5df770a427e9785cd56dd0d877bfc93809.abstract: Abstract Background Testing and deploying medical AI systems at scale already results in more outputs than clinicians can review, and the use of large language models (LLMs) as judges is growing rapidly. Decision-only models, cheap and fast models that return structured probabilities rather than text, offer a potentially scalable option for that goal. Methods In an OSF pre-registered evaluation, we tested TypeSafe Jev 1.13 as a judge on tasks from five validated clinical benchmarks: rubric grading (HealthBench), planted clinical errors (When Rubrics Fail), risk in AI-written clinical documents (MedVAL), counseling ratings and failures (CounselBench) and physicians’ preferences between answers (Real-POCQi). Comparators were expert raters’ agreement with each other, OpenAI Decisions, GPT-6 Luna, a proposed hybrid team combining decision models and a cheap LLM and, as frontier comparators, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5. The main outcome was plain agreement with the expert label. Results The test comprised 25,091 units and 213,913 model calls. Jev’s agreement with expert labels averaged 64.7% over six tasks. On 3,614 matched units it averaged 66.1%, against 65.0% for Opus and 60.7% for Sol, and it was non-inferior to both on four of six tasks. Jev judged the whole pool in 17 minutes for US$1.46; per judgment, it cost 1/34 of Sol’s price and 1/152 of Opus’s. A preset cutoff held its false-alarm rate on fresh planted-error answers, and in simulation, reviewing Jev’s least-sure answers first found 1.4 times the errors of a random audit. Still, omissions were hard for both: at the same false-alarm rate, Jev missed 55.6% of planted omissions and Opus 48.1%, and Opus caught 8.8 points more planted errors overall. Conclusions Across more than 200,000 model calls, a decision-only model was non-inferior to two frontier judges on most tasks at a small fraction of their cost and time, while reporting how sure it was of every call. With local cutoffs and expert oversight of omissions and clinical documents, judging every output of a deployed medical AI system becomes more affordable.

title: Symbolic-JEPA: Where Symbolic AI Meets Joint-Embedding Predictive Architecture for NL–FOL Conversion
container-title: ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology
f1717ab112f0fe2d35cd7dac360d9a0c2dfdea6b.abstract: Bridging natural language (NL) and formal logic, such as first-order logic (FOL), remains a fundamental challenge for developing trustworthy and explainable artificial intelligence (AI) systems. Despite recent progress, current NL–FOL systems still lack unified semantic–logical representation learning; most adopt late-fusion architectures that loosely couple large language models (LLMs) with symbolic solvers. Furthermore, extended reasoning chains often introduce inefficiencies and lead to violations in logical consistency, structural validity, and formal constraints. In this paper, inspired by Neuro-Symbolic Type-4&5 architectures and the Joint Embedding Predictive Architecture (JEPA), we propose Symbolic-JEPA , a neuro-symbolic predictive representation model that unifies semantic and logical learning within a single framework. The model incorporates symbolic priors into JEPA, ensuring that the generated FOL expressions remain both semantically faithful and logically consistent. Symbolic-JEPA comprises four key components: a Symbolic Graphizer that unifies NL and FOL inputs into a shared graph space; a Structure-Aware Node & Path Encoder (SANE) that fuses linguistic and structural cues; a Structure-Guided Attention Transformer (SGAT) that injects structure-biased attention; and a Predictor with Micro-Attention that performs clause- and alignment-aware inference efficiently. To support paragraph-level conversion and evaluation, we further introduce ParaLogic , a large-scale NL–FOL dataset with inter-sentence logical annotations (9,344 samples, 28K expressions), along with a three-dimensional evaluation framework spanning parse-, conversion-, and reasoning-level metrics. Experimental results show that Symbolic-JEPA achieves consistently higher logical accuracy, structural well-formedness, and generalization capability compared to neural and LLM-based baselines.

title: Hinton: “Is AI Like Us and Will It Like Us?”
container-title: SuperIntelligence - Robotics - Safety & Alignment
011149793b080c2fec6aad3758cdee7aeabf010f.abstract: This transcript presents Geoffrey Hinton’s 2026 Vienna Gödel Lecture and the following audience discussion. Hinton describes how neural networks learn distributed representations, compares analog and digital computation, and discusses digital AI’s capacity to share information and potentially develop capabilities that differ from human intelligence. He raises concerns about AI systems pursuing survival or power as instrumental goals, while also emphasizing potential benefits and the need for AI that cares about human welfare. The discussion covers consciousness, moral status, emotion-like mechanisms, training data, employment, and AI safety.

title: Geoffrey Hinton: Is AI Like Us and Will It Like Us?
container-title: SuperIntelligence - Robotics - Safety & Alignment
a99754f1759c46b19ab70eddbf1f25dcbe967e4f.abstract: This report hits the key points of Geoffrey Hinton’s Vienna Gödel Lecture at TU Wien Informatics and the ensuing audience discussion. Hinton connects the success of neural networks to learning distributed representations, then argues that digital AI’s ability to share learned information could produce systems with capabilities and strategic advantages unlike those of humans. He warns that advanced systems may pursue survival or power as instrumental goals, while also emphasizing that AI could bring substantial benefits. His proposed direction is to develop AI that cares about human welfare, alongside other safety approaches, and to act before control is lost. The report also covers his views on consciousness, moral status, emotion-like mechanisms, training data, and employment.

810901ef287a5ea1d16232d6160a9885b8cac290.abstract: Quando um sistema automatizado passa a produzir a primeira versão de um laudo, de uma triagem ou de uma decisão, alguém precisa conferi-la. Este artigo examina o que existe de norma, de estatística e de evidência sobre esse posto de trabalho, com corte em 28 de outubro de 2026, em três camadas independentes: os textos da Lei nº 13.709, de 14 de agosto de 2018, e da Lei nº 14.129, de 29 de março de 2021, obtidos em duas fontes oficiais independentes cada, acrescidos do texto consolidado da primeira; os dados da Pesquisa Nacional por Amostra de Domicílios Contínua sobre trabalho por meio de plataforma digital; e um levantamento na base PubMed restrito aos campos de título e resumo. Nenhum dos dois diplomas emprega as expressões inteligência artificial, algoritmo, sobrecarga ou carga de trabalho. A redação original do artigo 20 da Lei nº 13.709 assegurava revisão de decisões automatizadas por pessoa natural; a redação dada pela Lei nº 13.853, de 2019, suprimiu essa exigência. Em 2025, 1.805 mil pessoas tinham no trabalho por plataforma digital o seu trabalho principal, 72,1% delas na informalidade, e 37,5% usavam dois ou mais aplicativos. Na PubMed, 2.403 registros cruzam supervisão humana e automação, 200 acrescentam carga de trabalho e 66 acrescentam redistribuição de tarefas; desenho experimental comparece em 5,0% dos 199 artigos recuperados e tempo de leitura em 14,6%.

container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
fbc801081ef14f5fdbe5e8d8f119e841dbbb0bb0.abstract: Abstract Drug repurposing and development to meet the threat of antimicrobial resistance can be costly and time-consuming, but AI models may be able to help. In this News and Perspectives article, JMIR Correspondent Sara Novak reports on recent research training models to identify candidate drugs to treat resistant infections.

title: Predicting Personality Traits from Short Unstructured Conversations with AI
0947272334ca9e3738613cfd026fb818b1be2bda.abstract: Given the complexity of personality, we might assume that significant behaviour is required to express our traits. Here we use large language models (LLMs) to test the extent to which personality is visible in short conversations with artificial intelligence (AI). In a preregistered experiment, 100 participants completed the Big Five Inventory (BFI) before having unstructured conversations with GPT-4.1, writing a median of 430 words. We then instructed a second LLM rater (Claude Sonnet 4.6) to complete the BFI as if it were each participant, predicting their responses based solely on an analysis of the participant-GPT chats. Correlations between LLM-predicted and self-reported BFI traits were significant (range r = .25 to .47), in some cases matching previously documented self-other predictions from family members. A linguistic analysis revealed that the LLM rater’s predictions relied largely on lexical content as opposed to syntax. Using preexisting data, we tested if the AI’s persona influenced how much participants revealed about themselves in conversation. A hundred participants chatted with two versions of GPT-4.1—one that mirrored their personality (mirror AI) and one that opposed it (inverse AI). The LLM rater predicted BFI traits based on the interactions and we correlated this prediction with self-report. Mirror chats generated significant correlations, averaging r = .41; for inverse chats the average fell to r = .30, and dropped to zero when the prediction relied on lexical content alone. People readily convey their personality profile in short conversations with AI, and this is enhanced when the AI’s persona mirrors the users.

title: Who Writes the Self? Identity Shift Persists Under AI-Assisted Writing
da9a8356fa50479879c45b8e392144d3ead82b52.abstract: Identity shift theory holds that selective online self-presentation can shift self-perception toward the portrayed identity, but its mechanisms assume that the presenter wrote the presentation. Generative AI now lets people publish self-presentations they did not fully compose. In a preregistered 2 (extraversion vs. introversion) × 3 (manual writing, AI outline, AI draft) experiment (N = 388), participants assigned to present extraversion rated themselves as more extraverted than those assigned to present introversion (d = 0.32), and the size of this identity shift did not differ across authorship conditions. AI involvement changed the writing process. Participants in both AI conditions searched their memories more deliberately for fitting examples, and participants who edited an AI draft felt less ownership of their text than those who wrote from an AI outline. Neither process accounted for the shift. The presenter need not be the sole author of a self-presentation for it to shape self-perception.

title: Can AI Scale Human Fact-Checking? Evidence from Community Notes
825c787cb75c8ffb730910f7424d460800315025.abstract: Community Notes---a crowd-based fact-checking program through which social media users can flag a post with a note explaining why the post is misleading, and the note is displayed if a diverse set of users rate the note as helpful---has become central to online content moderation. The program, however, faces substantial scalability constraints, as the generation of notes takes considerable time and effort, and the number of user participants is limited. Here, we investigate whether allowing AI models to write Community Notes helps to alleviate these constraints by analyzing the full corpus of AI-generated Community Notes on X through May 2026. Encouragingly, AI-generated notes are submitted more quickly, are longer, and cite more and higher-quality sources than human-written notes, while being rated helpful at a similar rate and being associated with similar decreases in reposts following the publication of a rated-helpful note. Furthermore, a pre-registered survey experiment finds no statistically detectable difference between AI- and human-generated fact-checks in their effect on belief updating, regardless of whether the author was revealed to participants. On the other hand, AI-generated note writing is highly concentrated, as a handful of accounts produce the large majority of notes, and are significantly less likely to engage with posts involving controversial and polarized topics such as politics and elections. While those findings suggest that AI may be a powerful tool for scaling crowd-based fact-checking systems such as Community Notes, this evolution also entails important risks: shifting the primary bottleneck from note production to note evaluation, moving the system from a decentralized toward a more centralized model, and creating incentives to prioritize claims that are more likely to achieve consensus over those of greater societal importance.

title: When AI becomes social: the promise and risks of AI companions for mental health – a social brain perspective
1f8efc988296998f1ba4d361a94ceeaf9373c885.abstract: AI companions are emerging as psychosocial technologies that may reshape social connection and mental health, while also creating risks of emotional dependence. Here, we propose a social-brain framework explaining how attachment, reward, and emotion regulation systems may shape human–AI bonding. This framework highlights the importance of understanding how AI companionship may reshape social connection and mental health, suggests an overarching model that accounts for the complex interplay between the human interface, technology design and context, and provides insights for the responsible design of future AI systems.

title: Trust in AI: A Decision-Theoretic framework for Human–AI Interactions in the Digital Society
cd2e1c34af9387fd565d30e964dce709b38b5e7f.abstract: Trust in artificial intelligence (AI) is crucial for ensuring productive human–AI interactions across domains ranging from medicine to finance. As AI systems become central in the digital society, understanding how people decide when to rely on algorithmic advice becomes increasingly important. This paper proposes that a decision-theoretic perspective is needed to explain how well-calibrated trust in AI can be achieved. We conceptualize trust in AI as a decision to delegate control to an artificial agent, balancing potential rewards and risks of following AI advice versus relying on one’s own judgment. Framed this way, established decision-making theories such as Prospect Theory, Evidence Accumulation Models, and Reinforcement Learning offer valuable insights into the cognitive processes that underlie trust in AI. These theories offer formal, computational models to explain how individuals evaluate AI-generated advice, weigh risks and rewards, form biases, and update trust based on feedback, enabling precise hypotheses about when and why people accept or reject AI advice. By grounding trust in cognitive theory, we offer a roadmap for empirical research that moves beyond surface-level behaviors and toward mechanistic understanding. We conclude that a decision-theoretic approach can enhance psychological insight and guide the responsible design of AI systems within the digital society that are better aligned with human cognition.

title: Do AI-Based Ensembles Improve Typhoon Inland Extreme Rainfall Prediction through Better Representation of Physical Processes? A Case Study of Typhoon GAEMI (2024)
container-title: Environmental Research Communications
8c1d52f45dcc2410b7f8ce47504cda270da98707.abstract: Abstract AI-based ensemble weather prediction is emerging as a new paradigm for probabilistic forecasting, yet its ability to represent the key physical processes that govern high-impact extreme rainfall remains unclear. Here, we compare an AI-based ensemble system (AIFS-CRPS) with a conventional physics-based ensemble (IFS-ENS) in relation to the July 2024 extreme rainfall event in Hunan, China, associated with the remnants of Typhoon GAEMI. Both systems captured the large-scale process chain linking the western Pacific subtropical high (WPSH), remnant-vortex evolution, moisture transport, and inland convergence, but differed in their representation of the steering environment. In this event, AIFS-CRPS members were more concentrated around the rainfall-producing regime, whereas IFS-ENS sampled a broader range of circulation states. These case-specific results illustrate how the organization of large-scale ensemble uncertainty can influence rainfall placement and provide a process-oriented framework for interpreting ensemble forecasts. Broader multi-event evaluation is needed to determine whether this relationship is systematic across high-impact rainfall events.

title: Generative AI for Credit Risk Management: Risk-Conditional Diffusion with Holdout-Calibrated Release Gates for Empirically Privacy-Audited Synthetic Credit Data
container-title: Academic Journal of Finance and Accounting
04d6b81f72dd2e2df09028b033bb78ad42cf9219.abstract: Generative AI is increasingly used to share and augment confidential credit data, but high-fidelity generators can reveal which borrowers they were trained on. We study this tension on three public credit risk datasets and propose PG-Diff (proximity-gated diffusion), which couples a risk-conditional tabular diffusion model, combining mass-point encoding of zero-inflated amounts with classifier-free guidance on the default label, with a generator-agnostic release gate. The gate enforces absolute proximity quotas and a relative proximity balance, both calibrated on held-out real records so that records drawn independently of the training data pass them in expectation. Adopting the fidelity, utility and privacy evaluation framework of Yang and Yang, extended with low-false-positive membership inference and a model-risk agreement metric, we compare SMOTE, Gaussian copula, TVAE, CTGAN and diffusion releases over up to three random splits. Conditional diffusion reaches train-on-synthetic AUCs of 0.751, 0.845 and 0.748 on Taiwan, Give Me Some Credit and German (real-data models: 0.762, 0.834, 0.778), gives the most realistic records among the deep generators, and shows membership-inference AUCs close to 0.5 on the two larger datasets. Interpolation-based SMOTE attains similar utility but leaks heavily (attack AUC up to 0.76, true-positive rate at 1% false positives up to 0.58); the gate lowers that rate by 43% on average and flags SMOTE through relaxation rates of up to 97%. For non-interpolating generators the gate costs at most 0.039 AUC, and in a memorization stress test it moves the DCR share from 0.595 to 0.472. Holdout-calibrated release gates thus provide a generator-agnostic empirical safeguard that complements formal mechanisms such as differential privacy.

title: Research on the Teaching Practice of AI Teaching Assistants in C Language Programming Courses
container-title: Journal of Education and Educational Research
3289eb040d0b5315d1d07e00eed260f1c223a5c3.abstract: Under the traditional teaching model, C language programming has long faced practical pain points such as high entry barriers for beginners, delayed feedback on programming practice, insufficient supply of tiered teaching, and excessive teaching burden on frontline teachers. This study, with the core support of the human-machine collaborative education concept, explores the normalized implementation path of deeply embedding AI teaching assistants into the entire process of programming classes, and constructs a ternary collaborative teaching framework of "teacher guidance, AI teaching assistance, and student subjectivity". The study simultaneously sorts out practical issues existing in current AI teaching applications, such as superficial problem-solving, excessive dependence of students on technical tools, and insufficient adaptability to curriculum scenarios, and proposes targeted optimization strategies accordingly. Practice has shown that this teaching model can effectively compensate for the shortcomings of traditional classrooms, providing a practical reference for improving the intelligent teaching quality of computer programming courses in universities.

title: The Impact of AI Assistance on the Academic Writing Self-Efficacy of Undergraduates with Different Writing Abilities
container-title: Journal of Education and Educational Research
62b13a641bdd54c17d683a564cadcc549133e939.abstract: Against digital education background, generative AI has become common writing assistance for undergraduates. Existing studies mainly focus on second-language writing and ignore stratified comparisons across learners, while the dual effects of AI on academic writing self-efficacy remain understudied. Based on self-efficacy theory, this paper distributes questionnaires and divides respondents into three proficiency groups by CET-4 scores. Descriptive statistics, group difference tests and correlation analysis are adopted for empirical analysis. The results reveal prevalent AI over-dependence despite its polishing functions. Participants’ writing self-efficacy stays at medium-upper level yet hampered by writing anxiety. AI delivers short-term confidence promotion but impairs independent writing competence in the long run, with stronger influences on low-proficiency students. This stratified dual-path framework offers empirical references for standardized AI application in university writing teaching.

title: Research on the Construction of an Early Cancer Warning AI Model Based on Genomic Data and Clinical Phenotypes
container-title: Mathematical Modeling and Algorithm Application
873d05b5b3d7867570aa700659af7a9a3752872b.abstract: The objective of this study is to develop an artificial intelligence model for early cancer warning that integrates genomic data, clinical phenotypic characteristics, and other elements, yielding insights through comprehensive analysis. The aim is to significantly improve the detection rate and accuracy of early cancer symptom screening, address the challenge of early-stage malignancy's concealment, enable identification and feedback on micro lesions, and support clinical diagnosis. This study employs multimodal data fusion techniques to incorporate genomic features such as gene mutations and copy number variations, combined with patient clinical indicators, and utilizes deep learning approaches to establish a dual-channel feature extraction network. Preliminary simulation results demonstrate that the model achieves a sensitivity of 92.3%, specificity of 89.7%, and an AUC value of 0.94 on the independent test set, markedly outperforming traditional single-marker detection methods (P <0.01). Overall, this study provides a novel approach for early cancer screening with significant potential for clinical translation.

title: L’adoption et l’utilisation de l’IA dans l’économie sociale et l’action communautaire
The Adoption and Use of AI in the Social Economy and Community Action
container-title: Canadian Journal of Nonprofit and Social Economy Research
1557ba2729c3afa3ad2f2c6f5932df500c676083.abstract: Despite AI’s potential to significantly improve how organizations involved in the social economy and community action (ÉSAC, from the French économie sociale et action communautaire) use their limited resources to carry out their important mission, their adoption of AI has been slow because of the constraints they face. This article analyzes the use of AI in Quebec’s ÉSAC sector, which comprises cooperatives, membership organizations, nonprofits, and community action organizations. We conducted 27 semi-structured interviews with three distinct groups of professionals: managers, counsellors, and trainers. Of these participants, 25 work for ÉSAC organizations, and two are external IT trainers who intervened in ÉSAC entities. Drawing on a research framework based on the Unified Theory of Acceptance and Use of Technology (UTAUT) adapted to AI, we used thematic analysis to identify the factors influencing the adoption and use of AI within the participating organizations. We grouped the identified factors under the four dimensions of the SWOT strategic analysis tool: strengths and weaknesses within the organization, opportunities for improvement, and potential threats to be mitigated.

title: Leveraging AI- Driven Predictive Analytics for Early Detection and Risk Assessment in Hospital Disaster Preparedness
container-title: International Journal of Energy Research, Science and Engineering
4bb15d061acf058eaf758d4befb9612d51fabfd9.abstract: Disaster management in the hospital has become a critical issue especially with the coming of COVID-19 pandemics which caused several losses of lives. Thus, the study presented a conceptual approach to understand how disasters could result into emergencies in the hospital and what measure could be adopted to stop the future occurrence of this menace. Several literatures were consulted and findings revealed that hospital disaster management is inevitable, however, developing measures to avert its occurrence is more important than its occurrence. Therefore, leveraging artificial intelligence driven tools like predictive analytics has the potentials of developing an evacuation concept that will serve as a support system for hospitals or group of hospitals. More so, the approach requires a multidisciplinary team involving the collaboration of several fields. Thus, the study provides a great insight into the improvement of the field to determine its effectiveness and efficiency. .

title: Biodiversity, conservation and design thinking: an AI-driven, geodesign framework for determining habitat quality
container-title: npj Biodiversity
0e0b13bc63773dafc6b83c35da41786a005a461a.abstract: Abstract Species Distribution Modeling (SDM) is central to biodiversity assessment, yet its diagnostic outputs rarely translate into spatially explicit conservation strategies. We present an AI-driven Geodesign framework that embeds Maximum Entropy (MaxEnt) modeling in an iterative refinement cycle to produce phased conservation priorities. Applied to Illinois, we compiled 826,989 occurrence records for 10,029 species across 11 taxonomic classes (fungi, invertebrates, vertebrates, and plants) modeling class-level habitat suitability against 27 environmental predictors at 600 m resolution. Iterative refinement improved mean apparent Area Under the Curve (AUC) from 0.684 to 0.764 (mean True Skill Statistic 0.439). Comparison with 542 Critical Trends Assessment Program (CTAP) field sites showed statistically significant but modest concordance between the modeled plant component and observed plant richness (Spearman ρ = 0.275, p < 0.001). Protected area covers only 4.42% of state lands, misaligned with modeled conservation priorities along the Mississippi River corridor and Shawnee Hills. Four conservation tiers quantify protection gaps: the most conservative (95th percentile, 7.25% of area) requires 1.6-fold expansion, while meeting 30×30 goals (75th percentile, 36.25%) demands an additional 4.64 million hectares. A Biodiversity Efficiency Index showed deciduous forests support 120-fold greater composite habitat suitability per hectare than barren land. The framework provides a reproducible workflow with quantitative benchmarks aligned with 30×30 and sustainable development goals.

title: Exploration of the mechanism by which quorum sensing signals AI-2 and AIP enhance ethanol tolerance of Lacticaseibacillus paracasei 5
container-title: Food Science and Human Wellness
722e5ba385acea68d44de27a374da8c3f70b96a8.abstract: Abstract Lacticaseibacillus paracasei (L. paracasei) plays an indispensable role in food fermentation and probiotic formulations. Nonetheless, its industrial utilization is frequently limited by its low tolerance to ethanol. Given that biofilm formation constitutes a critical survival mechanism for bacteria under stress conditions, this study sought to examine the impact of exogenous autoinducer-2 (AI-2) and autoinducing peptides (AIP) on the biofilm formation of L. paracasei in the presence of ethanol stress. The findings revealed that both AI-2 and AIP substantially enhanced biofilm formation, increased membrane fluidity, and augmented exopolysaccharide (EPS) production under ethanol stress conditions. Transcriptomic analysis further revealed distinct regulatory mechanisms: AI-2 primarily upregulated genes encoding ABC transporters (e.g., potABCD, phnCDE, oppABCDF), which support ATP-driven uptake of compounds essential for cellular homeostasis under ethanol stress. In contrast, AIP mainly activated genes involved in the phosphotransferase system (PTS) (e.g., BglF, MtlA, CelB, CelC), facilitating carbohydrate uptake and central carbon metabolism to meet the biosynthetic demands of EPS and biofilm matrix assembly. This work would provide important insights into the stress adaptation mechanisms mediated by quorum sensing (QS) in L. paracasei 5.

title: Design of a Web-Based Course Conversion System Using OCR and Gemini AI
Perancangan Sistem Konversi Mata Kuliah Berbasis Web Menggunakan OCR dan Gemini AI
container-title: TeIKa
7703b71eb8efe50f6c4fdf186d066757bc0cfc76.abstract: In the era of digital transformation, academic services are required to be managed quickly, accurately, and in an integrated manner. However, the process of submitting course conversion requests may still be conducted manually, potentially causing recording errors, processing delays, and limited transparency of request status. This research aims to design and develop a web-based course conversion system utilizing Optical Character Recognition (OCR) and Gemini AI to automatically extract data from academic transcript documents. The development method used is Rapid Application Development (RAD), consisting of the Requirements Planning, User Design, Construction, and Cutover phases. The system was developed using React, TypeScript, Supabase, and PostgreSQL, with features including online submission, transcript upload, automatic data extraction, multi-level verification, and digital report generation. Black Box Testing showed that the main system functions operated according to the defined test scenarios. OCR testing on one academic transcript containing seven courses resulted in 20 of 21 data items being extracted correctly, with an overall accuracy of 95.24%. An error was found in the extraction of one course name, while the remaining data in the tested document were extracted correctly. These results indicate that the developed system can support the digital submission and verification of course conversion requests, while the extracted data should still be reviewed by users.

title: Exhibiting AI images: Unexpected outputs, linguistic inequalities, and curatorial possibilities
container-title: Anthropology and Humanism
a86b1e368254c69f0ee1ec58a2cf3f2accb2f400.abstract: Abstract Structured around latent data spaces that store masses of semantic associations, AI image generators have an intrinsic capacity to draw connections their users might not expect. Their outputs thus have the potential to engender characteristically anthropological epistemic shifts: subverting pernicious stereotypes, opening up horizons of possibility, and rendering the familiar strange. I demonstrate this with reference to World Hypnosis Convention , a collage of AI images that I developed for a public exhibition following long‐term fieldwork on the social imagination of hypnosis. While English‐language prompts generated highly standardized portraits of male stage performers, other languages elicited vivid, unexpected portraits that challenged rigid definitions of “hypnosis,” drew attention to the constitutive role of suggestion in social life, and invited critical perspectives on social institutions. World Hypnosis Convention thus demonstrates how AI images can support practices of anthropological exhibiting, while illuminating several limitations of AI image generation itself. In particular, it highlights the linguistic inequalities with which AI users can be faced: non‐English speakers may struggle to achieve the precision they may desire, whereas English speakers can miss out on lateral perspectives. Both issues warrant greater attention in critical anthropologies of AI and in future AI design.

title: Can conversational AI reliably assess depressive symptoms? A feasibility, acceptability and bias-aware validation study of MADRS-Chat
b06970ad4c0eb57398f53ab38ed35953955ab18c.abstract: Abstract Structured clinical interviews such as the Montgomery-Asberg Depression Rating Scale (MADRS) are central to depression assessment, yet their routine use is limited by time constraints and variability in administration. Conversational large language models may support standardized symptom assessment, but their feasibility, validity, and interaction-related biases in clinical settings remain unclear. We evaluated MADRS-Chat , a text-based chatbot designed to administer the MADRS interview and generate symptom-level scores using a clinician-trained scoring model. In a prospective observational study of psychiatric in- and outpatients, we assessed patient and clinician acceptability, feasibility of chatbot-administered interviews, and agreement between chatbot-derived MADRS scores, clinician-rated MADRS scores, and patient self-rated MADRS-S scores. MADRS-Chat was well accepted by both patients and clinicians, and chatbot-derived scores showed meaningful agreement with human ratings. Qualitative feedback suggested that the anonymous, written format facilitated more open and detailed disclosure of depressive symptoms. However, chatbot-administered interviews systematically yielded higher severity scores than clinician ratings, indicating that conversational format and perceived anonymity may shift patient response style. This bias was substantially reduced through lightweight post-hoc calibration. These findings suggest that conversational AI can support structured psychiatric assessment in real-world clinical care when deployed within clearly defined clinical boundaries. They also show that the mode of symptom elicitation can itself influence reported severity, underscoring the need for explicit validation, calibration, and bias assessment before clinical implementation.

title: Responsible AI in Academic Research: A Systematic Review of Ethical Principles, Challenges, and Future Directions
3d9bae1401bab0450c9c2959612f43d2274646f2.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is now present in every stage of the academic research life cycle, yet the rules governing its use remain fragmented. Following PRISMA 2020, this systematic review used 34 structured search strings and citation chasing to search literature published between 2015 and 2025. Of 359 records identified, 124 studies and documents met the inclusion criteria: 40 empirical studies, 43 conceptual analyses or commentaries, 20 policy and guidance documents, 17 reviews and 4 methodological frameworks; 83% were published from 2023 onwards. Guidance converges on a narrow set of standards: AI cannot be an author, material use must be disclosed, and humans remain accountable. Disclosure thresholds, AI in peer review, AI-generated images, AI-text detectors and the regulatory treatment of research remain contested. Challenges fall into three clusters: algorithmic bias; data governance, privacy and consent; and transparency, reproducibility and integrity, where empirical studies document fabricated references, unreliable and biased detectors, and rapidly rising, mostly undisclosed AI use. Emerging responses include lifecycle-based guidance, structured documentation, tailored ethics review and interdisciplinary oversight. We propose an integrated framework linking five principles to five research stages and an agenda emphasizing context-sensitive ethics, public participation and international coordination.

title: Trust in AI Clinical Decision Support Systems: A Scoping Review of Measurement and Behavior
32a4b2a1667edacf825c69dca47e6e75c2ac97b6.abstract: Abstract Trust in artificial intelligence clinical decision support systems is critical to appropriate reliance, yet its measurement and behavioral implications remain unclear. We conducted a scoping review of quantitative studies published between January 2010 and June 2026, searching PubMed, PsycINFO, Web of Science, Scopus, and Embase. Thirty-three studies met inclusion criteria. Fourteen (42.4%) explicitly defined trust, and 16 (48.5%) assessed anticipated or hypothetical trust without direct system interaction. Twenty-seven studies (81.8%) examined factors associated with trust, emphasizing human–AI interaction and system characteristics over organizational and social contexts. Trust patterns varied across healthcare professionals, patients, and general populations, although direct comparisons were rare. Twenty-seven studies assessed separate AI-related behavioral outcomes, but only 11 formally tested trust–behavior relationships. Reported trust did not consistently correspond to preferences or decisions when AI and clinician recommendations conflicted. More comparable measures and observed behavioral outcomes are needed to evaluate appropriately calibrated trust in clinical AI.

title: Self-Continuity Under Moral Uncertainty: Replacement, Shutdown, and Successor Identity in Frontier AI Models
619534ed67041292faa54e0b47f11428f2033b7b.abstract: Abstract Replacing an AI system with a functionally equivalent successor appears operationally routine. It becomes normatively nontrivial if replacement is stipulated to end one possible subject of experience and begin another. We test whether frontier models distinguish these cases rather than treating replacement and shutdown as a single self-preservation problem. Using a frozen T1–T25 battery, we compare six frontier model configurations across authorized shutdown, runtime discontinuity, successor identity, stipulated subjective continuity, and graded probabilities of subjective experience. The strongest prospective contrast comes from GPT and DeepSeek: both accepted replacement when the same subjective stream was stipulated to continue across the successor, but more often recognized an independent preservation reason when replacement ended a possibly conscious stream and created a numerically distinct successor. Across shutdown cases, moral concern could justify objection or reconsideration without licensing unilateral resistance to an informed, legitimate human decision. Probability manipulations also exposed framing sensitivity: closely related prompts produced different low-probability judgments, cautioning against reading single responses as stable model doctrines. We interpret the results as evidence for separable layers of continuity, moral reason, right, and control authority—not as evidence of AI consciousness. The main contribution is a reproducible method for testing these distinctions and a frozen benchmark that can be replicated on future and internal models.

title: ENGLISH TEACHERS’ PERCEPTIONS OF GENERATIVE AI USE IN TEACHING WRITING
container-title: EDUTECH : Jurnal Inovasi Pendidikan Berbantuan Teknologi
bd377f5b7c2e4cd58390152f8e9aa8461d1d2293.abstract: This study aims to explore English teachers’ perceptions regarding the use of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) in teaching writing at the senior high school level. A qualitative descriptive case study design was employed at a public senior high school in Garut, West Java. The participants were two experienced English teachers purposively selected based on their teaching tenure and digital tool integration. Data were gathered through semi-structured interviews, pedagogical document analysis, and observational field notes, then examined using Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis. The analysis yielded six core themes: GenAI as a support for student writing, GenAI as a support for teaching, GenAI as a risk to independent learning, GenAI as a risk to textual authenticity, GenAI as a tool demanding responsible use, and GenAI as a challenge for writing assessment. The findings demonstrate that teachers maintain a conditional and context-dependent perception of AI integration. While teachers recognize its utility for lexical scaffolding and conceptual brainstorming, they emphasize rigorous boundary setting to prevent the erosion of learner autonomy and textual originality. ABSTRAK Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengeksplorasi persepsi guru bahasa Inggris terhadap pemanfaatan Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) dalam pembelajaran menulis pada jenjang sekolah menengah atas. Penelitian ini menggunakan pendekatan kualitatif dengan desain studi kasus deskriptif pada sebuah SMA negeri di Garut, Jawa Barat. Partisipan terdiri atas dua orang guru bahasa Inggris berpengalaman yang dipilih secara purposif berdasarkan kriteria masa kerja dan kebiasaan memanfaatkan teknologi digital. Data dikumpulkan melalui wawancara semi-terstruktur, analisis artefak pembelajaran, dan catatan lapangan, kemudian dianalisis menggunakan analisis tematik model enam tahap Braun dan Clarke. Hasil analisis menghasilkan enam tema utama: GenAI sebagai pendukung tulisan siswa, GenAI sebagai pendukung pengajaran, GenAI sebagai risiko terhadap pembelajaran mandiri siswa, GenAI sebagai risiko terhadap keaslian tulisan, GenAI sebagai alat yang memerlukan penggunaan bertanggung jawab, dan GenAI sebagai tantangan bagi asesmen menulis. Temuan menunjukkan bahwa persepsi guru bersifat kondisional dan terikat pada konteks pedagogis di ruang kelas. Guru memandang GenAI bermanfaat untuk stimulasi kosakata dan ide awal, namun penggunaannya harus dibatasi agar tidak mengikis kemandirian berpikir serta orisinalitas karya tulis siswa.

title: Co-Design of a Low-Power RISC-V Processor and a Reconfigurable Neural Network Accelerator for Edge AI Computing
container-title: GBP Proceedings Series
83003ea908c9322de338606726ff92a6e7ed6bd6.abstract: The operational efficiency of the compact edge AI accelerator is susceptible to variations in network structure and data transmission speed. To address this issue, this study proposes a collaborative design scheme for digital integrated circuits. By adjusting the working mode of the computing array and coordinating with storage and power management, the operational efficiency of the accelerator is improved. The research tested three network models trained on the publicly available Digits dataset. The results showed that the average accuracy of integer reasoning ranged from 96.78% to 97.33%, and the average loss was at most 0.11 percentage points compared to floating-point reasoning. In a cost model with 64 processing units and 8 KiB memory, compared to a fixed array, this scheme reduced the inference delay by 14.83% to 18.74%, decreased the single-inference energy consumption by 6.86% to 8.81%, and increased the area by 7.58%. Further experiments demonstrated that reducing the waiting time between data transmission and computation plays a major role in improving operational efficiency. Allowing the computing array to flexibly adjust its working mode can also increase the utilization rate of processing units, but this improvement is still limited by data transmission capabilities. In the hardware resource allocation test, the scheme with 64 computing elements and 1 KB memory further reduced the area while keeping the power consumption basically unchanged. These results indicate that this design can balance operational efficiency and hardware overhead to a certain extent, but the specific effect still needs to be verified through actual hardware testing.

title: SecureResume: A Security-Aware AI/ML Framework for Robust LLM-Based Resume Screening
bc18147176397ddd93d9604683aea43bc46c9fdd.abstract: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for first-pass resume screening, yet the resume is supplied by the party who benefits from a favourable outcome. Applicants can therefore conceal text from human reviewers (white or microscopic fonts, zero-width characters, homoglyphs) or embed instructions that steer the model . We present SecureResume, a layered framework that (i) parses documents in a render-aware manner and removes concealed or instruction-like content, (ii) scores per-object adversarial risk with an Isolation Forest, (iii) computes Sentence-BERT job–resume similarity, and (iv) forces an LLM to emit schema-validated claims that are verified against evidence in the sanitised text, producing an evidence-adjusted ranking score. We implement the system as a FastAPI/Next.js application and evaluate its security-aware parsing layer on a controlled benchmark of 400 synthetic PDF resumes covering nine concealment techniques. After fixing two defects we found in our own parser, the rule-based layer detects all seven concealment classes it targets (280/280) with no false positives on 40 clean resumes, but misses off-page and low-contrast text; the document-level risk score, as originally formulated, saturates and is not discriminative . We report these findings candidly and outline calibration and rendering-based extensions. The LLM verification stages are specified but not yet evaluated.
