title: Pengembangan pembelajaran di perguruan tinggi melalui pemanfaatan artificial intelligence (AI)
container-title: Prosiding Seminar Nasional Sanata Dharma Berbagi
41e60987f1aca9ee8c5b60224b34aeb80d11d79b.abstract: Perkembangan teknologi digital mendorong penggunaan artificial intelligence (AI) dalam pembelajaran di perguruan tinggi. AI dapat digunakan untuk membantu mahasiswa dan dosen dalam berbagai kegiatan pembelajaran. Kajian ini bertujuan untuk mengetahui pemanfaatan AI dalam mendukung pengembangan pembelajaran di perguruan tinggi. Penelitian ini menggunakan metode Systematic Literature Review (SLR) dengan mengumpulkan dan mengkaji artikel ilmiah yang relevan mengenai penggunaan AI dalam pembelajaran perguruan tinggi. Artikel yang dikaji merupakan publikasi tahun 2022–2026 yang membahas penggunaan AI dalam proses pembelajaran, pengalaman belajar mahasiswa, pembelajaran adaptif, pemberian umpan balik, pengembangan bahan ajar, evaluasi pembelajaran, serta kemandirian dan interaksi belajar. Data yang diperoleh kemudian dianalisis dan disusun untuk melihat berbagai bentuk pemanfaatan AI dalam pembelajaran. Hasil kajian menunjukkan bahwa AI dapat membantu mahasiswa dalam memahami materi, mencari informasi, mengembangkan ide, memperoleh penjelasan, dan mendapatkan umpan balik selama proses belajar. Bagi dosen, AI dapat membantu dalam menyusun bahan ajar, mengembangkan materi, merancang kegiatan pembelajaran, dan memberikan umpan balik kepada mahasiswa. Penggunaan AI juga dapat mendukung pembelajaran yang lebih personal, fleksibel, interaktif, dan efisien. Dengan demikian, AI dapat menjadi teknologi pendukung yang membantu mahasiswa dan dosen dalam mengembangkan proses pembelajaran di perguruan tinggi dan mencapai tujuan.

title: ENGLISH EDUCATION STUDENTS’ PERCEPTIONS OF USING AI TOOLS IN ACADEMIC WRITING: A CASE STUDY
container-title: LANGUAGE : Jurnal Inovasi Pendidikan Bahasa dan Sastra
66501361a21ff5492925ee06745c7f557a58b96a.abstract: The integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) has significantly altered academic writing practices in higher education, yet its pedagogical implications for pre-service English teachers remain underexplored. This qualitative case study aimed to investigate English Education students' perceptions of utilizing AI tools in academic writing, specifically examining perceived benefits, operational challenges, and academic integrity negotiations. Ten undergraduate students, comprising eight eighth-semester and two sixth-semester students at Institut Pendidikan Indonesia, were purposively recruited. Data were gathered through an asynchronous online open-ended questionnaire and analyzed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis framework. The findings revealed that students utilized AI tools primarily for brainstorming, outlining, and grammatical refinement, while contending with fabricated citations, stylistic rigidity, and anxieties regarding the erosion of independent critical thinking. In negotiating academic integrity, participants practiced selective verification and established a collective ethical boundary that endorsed linguistic scaffolding while strictly proscribing unreflective wholesale text generation. ABSTRAK Integrasi kecerdasan buatan generatif (generative artificial intelligence) telah merevolusi praktik penulisan akademik di perguruan tinggi, namun pemaknaan pedagogis oleh mahasiswa calon guru bahasa Inggris masih jarang diteliti secara mendalam. Penelitian studi kasus kualitatif ini bertujuan untuk mengeksplorasi persepsi mahasiswa Pendidikan Bahasa Inggris terhadap penggunaan perangkat kecerdasan buatan (AI tools) dalam penulisan akademik, yang berfokus pada persepsi manfaat, tantangan, dan negosiasi integritas akademik. Sebanyak sepuluh mahasiswa sarjana yang terdiri atas delapan mahasiswa Semester 8 dan dua mahasiswa Semester 6 di Institut Pendidikan Indonesia dipilih melalui teknik purposive sampling. Data dihimpun melalui kuesioner terbuka daring asinkron (asynchronous open-ended questionnaire) dan dianalisis menggunakan analisis tematik enam tahap. Hasil penelitian mengungkapkan bahwa mahasiswa memanfaatkan perangkat kecerdasan buatan terutama untuk pencarian ide awal, penyusunan kerangka karangan, serta perbaikan tata bahasa, meskipun mereka menghadapi kendala berupa sitasi halusinasi, kekakuan gaya bahasa, dan kecemasan akan erosi keterampilan berpikir kritis mandiri. Dalam menegosiasikan integritas akademik, mahasiswa menerapkan adopsi selektif dengan memverifikasi rujukan ilmiah serta menyepakati batasan etis bahwa bantuan penyuntingan bahasa dapat dibenarkan, sedangkan penyalinan teks secara utuh merupakan bentuk pelanggaran.

title: AI-based Efficient Hallway Attendance Monitoring using Confidence-driven Face Recognition
container-title: Journal of ICT Research and Applications
b406aea3f3889523d7645dbdb6e71791cb67b823.abstract: Attendance monitoring deployed at entrance areas offers reliable tracking for institutional environments. We propose an efficient face-recognition-based framework combining YOLOv11-based face detection, motion-based tracking, and FaceNet-based recognition. Our key contribution is a confidence-driven face selection method that collects multiple face images per track and selects the highest-quality image for recognition. Experiments on real-world 60-second hallway footage (1,800 frames at 30 FPS) demonstrated up to 77.7% improvement in processing speed (79.36 FPS vs. 44.66 FPS baseline) while maintaining equivalent recognition accuracy. Collection windows of 5 to 7 images provide optimal balance between latency and throughput (73.67–75.86 FPS), demonstrating that strategic recognition frequency reduction enables real-time attendance monitoring suitable for resource-constrained environments

title: Multi Objective Optimization of Distribution in Supply Chains using Green AI via an Enhanced Hippopotamus Algorithm
container-title: Journal of ICT Research and Applications
0c402031b848ca935e138369899a6f7a3f7c0e54.abstract: Modern supply chains require innovative, sustainable, and computationally efficient solutions for physical distribution. This paper proposes the Enhanced Hippo Optimization (EHO) algorithm, a novel, nature-inspired metaheuristic designed to solve the Multi-Objective Vehicle Routing Problem (MO-CVRP). The (EHO) algorithm mathematically models three key hippo herd behaviors: exploration (herd positioning), defensive coordination, and strategic withdrawal, to achieve a dynamic balance between global exploration and local exploitation. By integrating real-world geospatial data from the Google Maps Directions API and customer demand modeling via a Zipf distribution (α = 0.9), (EHO) simultaneously reduces total distance, delivery time, operating costs, and CO2 emissions. The algorithm was evaluated under twenty scenarios across a network of nineteen cities in Egypt, outperforming six advanced algorithms Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO), Genetic Algorithm (GA), Ant Colony Optimization (ACO), RUN, Artemisinin Optimizer (AO), and Fata Morgana in eighteen cases. The framework achieved an average reduction of 26.9% in distance and emissions, with total computational runtime ranging from 12.77 to 25.1 seconds depending on the scenario. Visual analyses, including optimized route maps and radar performance charts, confirmed the robustness, scalability, and practical effectiveness of the EHO system in transforming logistics into a driver of economic and environmental sustainability.

title: When financial expertise shapes AI narratives in China: CEO financial background and symbolic AI disclosure
container-title: International Journal of Emerging Markets
5d3d714cc13ccb15dfd64f7f70c16740da2de5b1.abstract: Purpose This study examines whether CEO financial background shapes corporate artificial intelligence (AI) overclaiming in an emerging-market context. Drawing on upper echelons theory (UET), we argue that financially experienced CEOs may frame AI as a market-oriented strategic narrative while underinvesting in the long-term technological capabilities needed to substantiate such claims. Design/methodology/approach Using Chinese A-share listed firms from 2010 to 2023, we measure AI overclaiming as the gap between AI disclosure and invention-based AI capability. We estimate models with firm and year fixed effects and validate the findings through robustness tests, including AI investment- and residual-based measures, as well as endogeneity, placebo and channel analyses. Findings CEO financial background is positively associated with corporate AI overclaiming. Channel analyses suggest that financially experienced CEOs widen the disclosure–capability gap by increasing short-term financial asset allocation and reducing R&D investment. This effect is stronger when external verification is weak, market pressure is high and policy-driven AI narratives are more salient. Originality/value This study identifies CEO financial background as a managerial antecedent of AI overclaiming. It extends UET by showing how financial career imprints shape emerging-technology narratives and resource allocation. It also advances AI overclaiming research in emerging markets by showing that weak verification, state-guided capital allocation and policy-driven AI narratives intensify symbolic–substantive decoupling.

title: Reimagining adolescent education with ephegogy: generative AI and active learning in practice
container-title: Artificial Intelligence in Education
1d36e8829077dcd2cac6018973035fc5acb85d04.abstract: Purpose This paper introduces ephegogy, a theory addressing the gap between traditional educational models and adolescents' developmental needs in artificial intelligence (AI)-augmented societies. Blending constructivism, connectivism and generativism, it explores how integrating generative AI (GenAI) and active learning can scaffold motivation, autonomy, and relevance for adolescent learners. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-methods case study conducted in a single secondary-school geography course during 2024–2025. Quantitative data came from matched pre- and post-intervention surveys measuring motivation and self-efficacy (N = 17; N = 11 for the self-efficacy composite) and locus of control (N = 12), using instruments adapted for an under-14, predominantly English-as-an-additional-language cohort. A separate matched engagement survey (N = 24) and an end-of-course co-creation survey (N = 33) provided further data. Qualitative data comprised 74 individual student reflections analysed thematically using the cultural-historical activity theory (CHAT) framework, alongside open-text survey responses from 74 students. The study was designed using three frameworks (self-determination theory, ephegogy and CHAT). Findings Findings are associational and exploratory, specific to this pilot. Composite motivation increased significantly (p = 0.043, d = 0.53), led by a significant rise in school enjoyment (p = 0.028). On a separate instrument, confidence in using AI tools showed the largest single increase (p = 0.016) and motivation relative to traditional courses also rose (p = 0.040); as several items were examined, these are treated as exploratory. Self-efficacy and locus of control showed no reliable change. Qualitatively, choice, the learning contract, and resource autonomy were dominant themes; most students disclosed and reflected on their AI use, and the modal student experience was ambivalent, valuing autonomy while finding it demanding. Research limitations/implications As a single pilot case study with small, matched samples, no control group and a single teacher-researcher as sole coder, findings are context-specific and cannot support causal claims. Future research should evaluate the framework with larger samples, control conditions, and across diverse cultural contexts and disciplines. Practical implications Ephegogy provides actionable strategies for scaffolding student autonomy and ethical AI use within project-based learning. Tools such as the Student-Author Voice (SAV) rubric support metacognitive reflection and responsible co-creation, assessing authored voice rather than relying on AI detection. Social implications Ephegogy provides actionable strategies for scaffolding student autonomy and ethical AI use within project-based learning. Tools such as the SAV rubric support metacognitive reflection and responsible co-creation, assessing authored voice rather than relying on AI detection. Originality/value Ephegogy reconceptualises adolescent education for the AI era as a distinct developmental stage requiring its own framework, operationalised through gradual immersion and the assessment of authored voice. This paper reports an initial classroom pilot offering preliminary, transferable insights rather than confirmatory evidence.

title: ВЛИЯНИЕ ПРЕДПОСЕВНОЙ ОБРАБОТКИ СЕМЯН SUAEDA SALSA УЛЬТРАФИОЛЕТОВЫМ ИЗЛУЧЕНИЕМ НА ИХ ПРОРАСТАНИЕ И РОСТ РАСТЕНИЙ
container-title: Agro ilm
8b13aa9c7a54fe2739dfe30c46ffdef1fdd47d61.abstract: This study presents the results of investigating the effects of pre-sowing ultraviolet (UV) irradiation of Suaeda salsa seeds on laboratory germination, germination energy, seedling emergence time, plant growth, and stand density under field conditions. The research was conducted in two stages. In the first stage, the effects of different UV irradiation treatments on laboratory germination and germination energy were evaluated. In the second stage, the treated seeds were sown in open-field conditions to assess plant growth, development, and stand establishment.The results demonstrated that pre-sowing UV treatment increased laboratory germination to 100%, accelerated seed germination, reduced field seedling emergence time by 8–9 days, increased the average plant height to 40–55 cm, and improved stand density to 90–96 plants m². These findings indicate that pre-sowing ultraviolet irradiation is an effective and environmentally friendly method for improving the sowing quality of Suaeda salsa seeds and enhancing plant productivity under saline soil conditions.

title: The contingent effects of AI transparency in service recovery: a moderated mediation model of perceived warmth and competence
container-title: Online Information Review
666bf8d7c855d2f2635e1471c96f1fa7c08d3211.abstract: Purpose This research investigates how artificial intelligence (AI) transparency shapes consumer responses in service recovery. By revealing the reasoning process behind AI decisions, transparency functions as an anthropomorphic cue that humanizes the system's communication. Drawing on social cognitive theory, the research develops and tests a generalizable mechanism framework linking AI transparency, consumer cognition and recovery satisfaction, while identifying boundary conditions. Design/methodology/approach Three scenario-based experiments were conducted. Study 1 (N = 98) tested the direct effect of AI transparency on recovery satisfaction. Study 2 (N = 230) examined the parallel mediating roles of perceived warmth and competence. Study 3 (N = 284) tested the moderating role of service failure severity and the corresponding conditional indirect effects. Findings AI transparency significantly improves recovery satisfaction, indirectly through perceived warmth and competence. Service failure severity moderated the effects of transparency on both mediators. The indirect effects through warmth and competence were significant under low service failure severity but not under high severity, identifying severity as a boundary condition for the effectiveness of AI transparency in service recovery. Originality/value This research conceptualizes AI transparency as a form of anthropomorphism that reveals AI's thought process, thereby extending the application of social cognitive theory to AI-mediated service recovery. It explains how transparency enhances consumer satisfaction through warmth and competence and clarifies how these effects vary with service failure severity.

title: Ethnic AI instructor: when a minority professor uses AI voice-over tools
container-title: Quarterly Review of Distance Education
93e36abd087a5ebe529fdf6878b4263b9811319e.abstract: Purpose Student evaluations of teaching influence faculty promotion and tenure decisions, yet research demonstrates these evaluations systematically reflect instructor demographic characteristics independent of teaching quality. As online education expands and instructors increasingly adopt AI technologies like text-to-speech voice narration, questions arise about whether racial bias and AI skepticism interact to create compounded disadvantages for minority instructors. Design/methodology/approach Using a 2×2 experimental design (Instructor race: White vs. Asian × Voice type: Human vs AI-generated), 172 undergraduate students evaluated identical online lecture content. Instructors were identified through photographs and names. Findings Results showed significant racial bias with the White instructor rated higher than the Asian instructor across evaluation dimensions. Students also rated the AI-voiced lecture significantly worse than the human-voiced lecture across all evaluation dimensions. While voice type did not moderate the race effect statistically, simple effects analyses revealed that racial bias was manifested within the AI voice condition. Perceived social presence mediated voice type effects on evaluations. Students' comfort with AI technology moderated voice type effects, with the AI discount effect weakening among high-comfort students. Research limitations/implications Racial bias in student evaluations persists regardless of voice types, while AI-generated voices substantially reduce evaluations through decreased social presence. These findings have practical implications for equitable faculty assessment as institutions adopt AI technologies and for instructors from racial minority groups who face evaluation penalties independent of teaching quality. Originality/value This study is among the first to examine how racial bias and AI voice technology intersect in student evaluations.

title: The Effect of Problem-Based Learning Integrated with YouTube and AI on Students’ Activities and Mathematical Concept Understanding
container-title: Jurnal Pendidikan MIPA
513b6d069b00cd666907f2484a9e0e7f661bf977.abstract: This study aims to analyze the influence of Problem-Based Learning (PBL) integrated with YouTube media and Artificial Intelligence (AI) on students' activeness and understanding of mathematical concepts. Despite the potential of digital technology, research comprehensively integrating these three components in high school mathematics remains limited. This study employed a quantitative approach with a quasi-experimental nonequivalent control group design involving 60 grade X students at Maarif Pandaan High School, Pasuruan, selected through purposive sampling. The experimental group received PBL instruction enhanced by curated YouTube videos for visual scaffolding and AI tools for adaptive feedback, while the control group received conventional instruction. Data were collected using structured activity observation sheets, mathematical concept comprehension tests, and student perception questionnaires. The instruments demonstrated adequate validity and reliability for the research context. Descriptive analysis revealed substantial improvement in the experimental class, with student activity scores ranging from 74 to 97 and concept understanding scores from 76 to 88, exceeding those of the control class. Independent-samples t-tests yielded t-calculated values of 2.430 for activeness and 2.332 for concept comprehension, both exceeding the t-table value of 1.9876 (p < .05). Furthermore, the coefficient of determination () indicated that the intervention explained 65% of the variance in student activeness and 60.1% in concept comprehension, demonstrating a large and practically meaningful effect size. The study concludes that integrating PBL, YouTube, and AI synergistically significantly enhances both behavioral engagement and deep conceptual mastery. These findings suggest that educators should strategically combine constructivist models with multimodal digital resources to foster a more interactive and personalized learning environment, particularly for complex topics like trigonometry. Keywords: problem-based learning, youtube, artificial intelligence, student activity, understanding of mathematical concepts.

title: Why AI Is Not a Solution to the Healthcare and Climate Crisis
container-title: The Oxford Handbook of Environmental Bioethics
5b08b93f84bc8e635168da6a4b7b7d090621fb0a.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly promoted as a solution to the healthcare crisis and as a driver of the green transition. Within biomedical research, clinical practice, and public health, AI is expected to optimize diagnosis, tailor treatments, and improve system efficiency, while also reducing health care’s carbon footprint. These promises fit within the broader vision of a “twin transition,” in which digitalization and sustainability are seen as mutually reinforcing. However, this techno-optimism overlooks the significant environmental costs of AI systems, including the extraction of minerals, energy and water use in data centres, and electronic waste disposal. Current responses to these concerns are predominantly technical—focused on efficiency gains, carbon accounting, and greener hardware. Yet, such measures rest on three problematic assumptions: that quantification is the most urgent gap; that efficiency solves all harms; and that greater efficiency reduces overall energy consumption. In practice, these framings obscure systemic issues, ignore rebound effects, and exclude unquantifiable harms. This chapter argues that bioethics must move beyond AI solutionism by systematically examining the environmental costs of AI in health care. An empirical bioethics approach can help re-frame debates, interrogate when AI is truly needed, and support decision-making that balances health, justice, and planetary well-being.

title: Same answer, different reasons: AI-moderated interviews uncover topics and reasoning that surveys miss
44d6a2c84e2993cc3090e212ba05d8e7d0499cf4.abstract: Abstract Surveys can reach large samples but capture only pre-defined answers, with identical responses often concealing very different reasoning. We tested whether AI-moderated interviews capture this reasoning at scale. In a pre-registered, randomized, counterbalanced design, 1,953 US adults from a probability-based panel and an opt-in panel completed three AI-moderated interviews as well as a section with closed-ended and open-text survey items. Topics were extracted from transcripts inductively, without a predefined codebook, and validated by a confirmatory follow-up. Participants endorsed 94% of topics as fair descriptions of what they said. 21–51% of topics from the AI interview had no counterpart in the closed-ended battery, and 17–37 percentage points net coverage over open text answers. Among respondents who gave identical closed-ended responses, their reasoning diverged widely in valence and content. AI-moderated interviews surface reasons that closed-ended and open-text items miss, and show how reasoning differs among people who answer alike.

title:
Designing Teaching Agents for Human‐
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Collaborative Classrooms: A Design‐Based Study of Students' Sense of Presence and Learning Engagement
container-title: Journal of Computer Assisted Learning
e4882205b7d0fa92a1cd4f5f8677cdbcc557ed78.abstract: ABSTRACT Background Generative artificial intelligence has expanded the possibilities for teaching agents to provide instructional explanations and feedback. However, limited research has examined how such support can be integrated into teacher‐guided classroom instruction and how students experience and engage with this form of teaching. Objectives This study aimed to iteratively design and refine teaching agents within a teacher‐guided undergraduate classroom and to examine changes in students' sense of presence and learning engagement across three design iterations. Methods A single‐group design‐based research study was conducted in a 10‐week Introduction to Educational Technology course. 36 first‐year undergraduate students majoring in educational technology participated in three design iterations: gesture‐supported presentation, teacher‐mediated real‐time Q&A, and individualized text‐based Q&A. Data were collected through questionnaires, classroom observations, student feedback, question records, and discussion texts. Repeated‐measures analyses were used to examine changes in students' sense of presence and learning engagement, and epistemic network analysis was used to examine changes in co‐occurrence patterns among presence‐related codes in students' post‐class reflections. Results and Conclusions The findings show that students' sense of presence significantly increased across the three iterations, whereas learning engagement did not show a statistically significant change, although the descriptive means showed a small upward pattern. Epistemic network analysis identified changes in co‐occurrence patterns among presence‐related codes in students' post‐class reflections. The strongest connections involved direct instruction, affective expression, and resolution in the first iteration, and affective expression with direct instruction, exploration, and integration in the third iteration. Given the single‐group sequential design, these findings should be interpreted as observed changes during the iterative implementation process rather than causal evidence for the independent effects of specific design strategies. The study contributes process‐oriented evidence and design considerations for integrating teaching agents into teacher‐orchestrated human‐AI collaborative classrooms.

title: Governing artificial intelligence in public services: accountability, transparency and democratic AI governance
container-title: Transforming Government: People, Process and Policy
251e48e292435e1d95249329194f0b7c4eb313d0.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how democratic governments can regulate artificial intelligence (AI) in public services through accountable, transparent and institutionally governable frameworks. It addresses the governance gap between rapid AI adoption and limited democratic regulatory oversight by proposing the Transparent-Accountable-Governable (TAG) Framework. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a qualitative conceptual research design using comparative policy analysis. It critically synthesises interdisciplinary literature in public administration, digital governance and AI ethics alongside the OECD AI Principles (2025), UNESCO Recommendation on the Ethics of Artificial Intelligence (2021), the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) AI Risk Management Framework (2023) and the European Union Artificial Intelligence Act (2024) to develop the TAG Framework. Findings The analysis argues that trustworthy AI depends upon the interaction of transparency, accountability and governability rather than ethical principles alone. The proposed TAG Framework provides an institutional governance model applicable across welfare administration, healthcare, taxation, policing and disaster management. Research limitations/implications This is a conceptual study and therefore does not empirically validate the TAG Framework. Future research should evaluate its applicability through comparative cross-country case studies and institutional assessments of AI implementation within public administration. Practical implications The framework offers policymakers practical guidance by recommending public AI registers, algorithmic impact assessments, meaningful human oversight, independent auditing and adaptive regulatory coordination to strengthen democratic governance and institutional accountability. Social implications By emphasising explainability, citizen participation and procedural justice, the TAG Framework provides a conceptual basis for examining how AI governance can contribute to inclusive and equitable public services. It also highlights the risks of algorithmic bias and opaque decision-making, both of which may undermine public trust. Originality/value This paper proposes the TAG Framework to examine AI governance in democratic public administration. It brings transparency and accountability together with governability, understood as the capacity of public institutions to coordinate their activities, monitor AI systems, learn from experience and adapt governance arrangements over time.

title: Feedback and Reconstruction in Learning with Generative AI: An Integrative Review and Proposed Framework for Unaided Performance
aff814c460f763552bece3fa2680d23d52308248.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) may help students produce higher-quality work; however, its effects on their future ability to work independently remain unclear. This integrative review examines this distinction by analysing research on feedback, metacognitive monitoring, cognitive offloading, and reconstructive learning activities. Targeted web searches and primary-source tracing informed a focused synthesis of adult learning studies and relevant foundational research. Three features may help explain variation in findings across studies: the information feedback conveys, the reasoning learners are expected to undertake and demonstrate, and the conditions under which learning is assessed. The proposed framework distinguishes between a regulatory pathway, in which feedback informs judgments and learning choices, and a practice pathway, in which reconstruction prompts relevant reasoning. This distinction helps explain why learners may become better calibrated without learning more, or learn more without becoming better calibrated. Feedback is expected to enhance the benefits of reconstruction when it improves engagement or reasoning quality, although its incremental benefit may be limited when the activity already provides comparable practice. Four conditional propositions describe these relationships and suggest comparisons that could help distinguish them from the effects of additional instruction, exposure, time, and motivation. The framework provides a foundation for testing when feedback and reconstruction support performance in the absence of assistance. The available evidence is not yet sufficient to establish the full causal pathways or lasting changes in capability, underscoring the value of delayed assessments, transfer tasks, and longitudinal research.

title: IA generativa y bienestar laboral: efectos en el desempeño percibido y la carga laboral en el sector público
Generative AI and workplace well-being: Effects on perceived performance and workload in the public sector
container-title: Multidisciplinary Latin American Journal (MLAJ)
ca7b5575a6d468f13f161d7479c79477886a9c46.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence is expanding across the public sector, yet how it affects the well-being of those who use it remains unknown. This study examined which antecedents of its adoption strengthen the emotional and psychological well-being of public servants and how well-being, in turn, shapes perceived performance and workload. Using PLS-SEM with bootstrap resampling, 433 public servants from El Oro, Ecuador, were analyzed. Three factors explained 79.5% of the variance in well-being: trust and security in AI was the strongest predictor (β = .338; p < .001), followed by perceived usefulness (β = .322; p < .001) and ethics and responsibility in use (β = .196; p < .001), whereas ease of use, institutional training, and fear of replacement were not significant. Well-being proved decisive, accounting for 76.0% of perceived performance (β = .872) and, jointly with it, 73.4% of workload reduction, operating mainly through performance (indirect effect β = .554). The importance-performance map analysis confirmed trust as the priority management lever. Adopting generative AI responsibly thus requires ethical governance, technological trust, and systematic well-being monitoring, redefining the priorities of public human resource management.

title:
When
                    <scp>AI</scp>
                    Anxiety Coexists With Capability:
                    <scp>ICT</scp>
                    Self‐Efficacy and Institutional Support in Preservice Teacher Education
container-title: European Journal of Education
7f511f19173faa4f15b65a9798b97b9b0dc1dcad.abstract: ABSTRACT Preparing preservice teachers for AI‐enabled teaching requires understanding anxiety alongside perceived capability and self‐regulated learning (SRL). Drawing on data from 12,147 third‐year preservice teachers across 17 Chinese institutions, this study combined structural equation modelling, observed‐score moderation, and latent profile analysis. Four profiles emerged: the Moderate Profile, the Lower‐Efficacy, Lower‐SRL Profile, the Low‐Anxiety, Higher‐SRL Profile, and the High‐Anxiety, Higher‐SRL Profile. The two higher‐SRL profiles shared high ICT self‐efficacy despite contrasting anxiety levels. AI anxiety was positively associated with ICT self‐efficacy, which was strongly associated with SRL. Perceived institutional ICT support strengthened the anxiety–efficacy association. These complementary findings identify perceived capability as a key differentiator of regulated learning across anxiety levels. Teacher‐education programmes can assess anxiety, efficacy, and SRL together and provide practice opportunities and institutional resources that support learning.

title: It is a temptation to get it to do the work… Student experiences of navigating the generative AI landscape in UK higher education: A cross-institutional survey with international comparison.
8e1e2a628359c0e60d11e3ff0b2e5f75fc196d8f.abstract: Even in an increasingly digitally mediated higher education, the release of ChatGPT in late 2022 seemed different. This paradigm shift was due to the ability of this technology to potentially complete student and staff work. It questions not only academic practice but the purpose of the university. Incorporating GenAI into universities policies and practice, therefore, requires an evidence-based approach and a strong student voice. Between September and December 2025, the StudentXGenAI Project ran a large-scale, multi-institution (&gt;7000 responses at 7 UK institutions), cross-sectional survey that sought to understand how students used GenAI in their studies, the perceived usefulness, and the factors that influenced their use. In this paper we present the findings from the UK survey using 5 key themes identified by Chung et al (2026) who administered the same survey in Australia in the previous year. We compare the UK and Australian findings, presenting a strikingly similar yet nuanced picture. From our findings, it is clear that despite the discourse that everyone is using it, there are a significant minority of students conscientiously objecting to GenAI use. For those that are using it, the majority of students are honest the majority of the time and are trying to avoid submitting direct GenAI outputs. Yet the data shows that students use GenAI for a range of tasks throughout the entire learning and assessment process. In doing so there is a significant tension between the key motivating factor of efficiency and the discouraging factors relating to ethics. The majority of students are looking for an ethical fast lane rather than a bypass of learning. Therefore, it raises serious questions about how students are able to ethically judge whether their usage is helping or hindering their actual learning, particularly under the pressure of assessment conditions when the temptation to use GenAI is greatest.

title: The dark side of digital distraction: supervisor phubbing and employee performance – the indirect roles of cyberloafing and social distance
container-title: Leadership & Organization Development Journal
cb3a0421c9f2f76f5b73dd0ceb8a9475f5953d1d.abstract: Purpose Supervisor phubbing occurs when supervisors use their mobile devices during face-to-face interactions with subordinates. Despite the increasing prevalence of smartphones in the workplace and the importance of supervisor–employee interactions, limited research has examined how supervisor phubbing is associated with key employee outcomes. This study examines the relationship between supervisor phubbing and employee performance and estimates two theoretically specified indirect associations, one through employee cyberloafing and the other through perceived social distance. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 965 employees working in Egyptian travel agencies and tour operators. The hypothesized associations were estimated using structural equation modeling. Findings The estimated coefficients linked higher supervisor phubbing with lower employee performance, greater employee cyberloafing and wider perceived social distance. Both proposed mediators yielded statistically significant negative indirect associations; the supervisor phubbing–employee performance coefficient remained significant after their simultaneous inclusion, a pattern consistent with complementary partial mediation in statistical terms. Originality/value This study is among the few to employ social exchange theory to interpret the relationships among supervisor phubbing, employee performance, employee cyberloafing and social distance. It extends the literature by bringing a behavioral response and a relational perception into a single empirical model while providing evidence from the Egyptian tourism industry. The resulting pattern offers theoretical and practical insight into the relationship between supervisory digital distraction and employee performance while underscoring the managerial relevance of attentive communication in service-oriented organizations.

title: Digital borders, algorithmic governance and civic digital literacy: examining the educational implications of AI-driven immigration management in post-apartheid South Africa
container-title: Frontiers in Education
59b10eecd73e3fe9d4e78423b54be93163ff24c2.abstract: Introduction South Africa is moving towards AI-based digital border management, including biometric screening, drone-supported aerial surveillance and the Electronic Travel Authorisation (ETA) system. This paper explores the educational consequences of that shift, with a special focus on the civic digital literacy that algorithmic immigration governance requires of citizens, policymakers and educators. Methods The study takes a qualitative, interpretive approach, drawing on critical digital pedagogy, algorithmic accountability theory and postcolonial education studies. It synthesises peer-reviewed scholarly works, policy documents and grey literature on the Border Management Authority's use of biometric surveillance, drone technology and the ETA system. A corpus of 53 sources was screened through an adapted PRISMA-style procedure and analysed through a three-phase thematic synthesis that produced five descriptive and three analytical themes. Results AI-based border governance exposes a pressing and largely ignored digital literacy gap. The communities most affected by algorithmic immigration decisions are those without the conceptual tools to engage with, debate or take part in the governance of the AI systems that regulate their lives and rights. Standard digital literacy programmes are not sufficient to equip learners with the knowledge to participate in the governance of algorithmically driven systems. Discussion Geography and social sciences education has a special role in equipping learners with the skills needed for critical AI citizenship. The study proposes that algorithmic governance be incorporated into the school curriculum, that community-facing digital civic education programmes be developed, and that participatory AI accountability structures be established in border management. The study advances digital learning innovation by theorising civic AI literacy as a new educational priority in the Global South and by showing that algorithmic governance necessitates a fundamental redefinition of digital citizenship education.

title: AI-assisted design exploration for post-disaster housing: reassessing Bam reconstruction
container-title: International Journal of Disaster Resilience in the Built Environment
5db57c6942ed67d73dcc9a215c80babcf294d0ad.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is reassessing Bam reconstruction after earthquake using Artificial Intelligence. Post-disaster permanent housing plays a critical role in ensuring the long-term recovery and well-being of affected communities. However, architectural design processes in disaster responses are often rushed, leading to solutions that may overlook cultural, environmental and functional needs. Design/methodology/approach This study examines the potential role of artificial intelligence (AI) in improving post-disaster housing design by reassessing the reconstruction that followed the 2003 Bam earthquake in Iran. Using a process-oriented perspective, existing post-disaster permanent houses were evaluated against AI-generated architectural alternatives produced through Midjourney. Findings Key indicators and evaluation criteria were identified through a literature review and supported by field surveys conducted in Bam. An evaluation flowchart was then developed to systematically assess design performance in terms of safety, sustainability, cultural compatibility, functionality, accessibility and affordability. Practical implications The findings suggest that generative AI can support architects and planners by rapidly generating diverse design alternatives and expanding the range of solutions considered during the early stages of post-disaster reconstruction. However, the results also demonstrate that expert judgment remains essential for evaluating and adapting AI-generated proposals to local conditions, reconstruction constraints and long-term resilience objectives. Originality/value This study not only demonstrates the application of generative AI in post-disaster housing design using the 2003 Bam earthquake as a case study, but also proposes a rapid evaluation framework for assessing AI-generated architectural alternatives as a complementary decision-support tool in post-disaster reconstruction.

title: The role of AI adoption in the relationship between digital self-efficacy and sustainable entrepreneurship intentions among university students in Jordan
container-title: Management & Sustainability: An Arab Review
31b71467d2d907fa638bb67cb3940cd9d9d934a0.abstract: Purpose This study investigates associations among digital self-efficacy (DSE), artificial intelligence (AI) adoption intention and sustainable entrepreneurship intentions (SEIs) among university students at a private university in Amman, Jordan – a context with high unemployment and national digital agendas. Design/methodology/approach A sequential exploratory mixed-methods design was employed. Phase 1 involved semi-structured interviews with seven entrepreneurship faculty and an incubator director at a private university in Amman. Phase 2 comprised a survey of 150 students from the same institution. The technology acceptance model (TAM) and social cognitive theory (SCT) were integrated in a mediated model tested using partial least squares structural equation modelling. Findings DSE was positively associated with perceived usefulness (PU) (β = 0.570, p &lt; 0.001) and perceived ease of use (PEOU) (β = 0.584, p &lt; 0.001) of AI tools. AI adoption intention (AIAI) mediated the relationship between DSE and SEI. The total indirect effect of DSE on SEI through both serial mediation paths was 0.247 (p &lt; 0.001). The specific serial indirect effects were 0.078 (DSE → PU → AIAI → SEI, p = 0.012) and 0.093 (DSE → PEOU → AIAI → SEI, p = 0.006). The model accounted for 42.8% and 25.3% of the variance in AIAI and SEI, respectively. These findings are limited to university students at one institution; replication with representative samples and longitudinal designs is needed before drawing broader conclusions. Practical implications Within university settings, educators might consider building DSE through experiential training that links AI to sustainability challenges. Universities could explore integrating AI literacy into entrepreneurship curricula. Originality/value This study positions AIAI as a potential mediating mechanism between DSE and SEIs, providing empirical evidence from a Middle Eastern university context. The contribution is incremental and context-specific, providing preliminary evidence consistent with the proposed theoretical mechanism.

title: Teacher competence and institutional governance for learner data privacy in AI mediated education
container-title: Frontiers in Education
e48b93edf9c4e45133c5e116ce9f79fa6304a7d8.abstract: Teachers can recognise a privacy problem yet lack the authority or resources needed to act on that judgement. Conversely, institutions can provide technically safeguarded services while teachers disclose unnecessary information or accept unsupported inferences. This Hypothesis and Theory article develops the Learner Data Protection Competence and Governance Framework to explain these two failures. A purposive conceptual synthesis connects contextual integrity with distinctions between demonstrated competence, confidence, perceived control and actual institutional provision. The framework relates risk recognition, defensible decisions, institutional enablement and accountable review. Its central prediction distinguishes support that complements professional judgement in discretionary tasks from safeguards that substitute for particular skills in constrained tasks. A second central prediction separates access to reporting, implementation of corrective action and subsequent recurrence. Three supporting propositions address recognition, confidence calibration and purpose-specific authorisation. Each proposition specifies separate measures, rival explanations and conditions for disconfirmation. Two hypothetical cases illustrate competing educational and privacy considerations and show why institutional approval is insufficient to establish ethical justification. A bounded application to teacher education and school placements in Zambia identifies context-informed predictions concerning divided authority, advice latency, language and connectivity. The framework offers an explanatory model with normative criteria and assessment implications. Neither the reviewed evidence nor the worked cases validate its causal relationships or demonstrate reduced privacy harm; the contribution is a more discriminating and testable account of how professional judgement interacts with institutional arrangements.

title: DETEKSI GAMBAR AI MULTIKELAS MENGGUNAKAN MODEL HYBRID CNN-ViT DAN BROAD LEARNING SYSTEM (BLS) BERBASIS WEB
container-title: INTECOMS: Journal of Information Technology and Computer Science
d616795e7d38f9b17b28632b3a1466d78701d359.abstract: Perkembangan teknologi kecerdasan buatan memungkinkan pembuatan gambar sintetis yang sangat realistis sehingga menyulitkan proses verifikasi keaslian citra digital. Penelitian ini bertujuan untuk mengembangkan sistem deteksi gambar AI multikelas berbasis web menggunakan model hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) dan Vision Transformer (ViT) yang dikombinasikan dengan Broad Learning System (BLS). Sistem ini dirancang untuk mengklasifikasikan enam kategori citra yaitu hewan asli, hewan AI, manusia asli, manusia AI, benda asli, dan benda AI. Model hybrid memanfaatkan EfficientNet-B0 sebagai ekstraktor fitur lokal dan Vision Transformer sebagai ekstraktor fitur global. Fitur yang diperoleh kemudian digabungkan melalui mekanisme feature fusion dan diklasifikasikan menggunakan Broad Learning System untuk menghasilkan prediksi multikelas secara efisien. Sistem diimplementasikan dalam bentuk aplikasi web menggunakan Streamlit sebagai antarmuka pengguna dan FastAPI sebagai backend. Hasil pengujian menunjukkan bahwa model hybrid CNN–ViT–BLS mampu mencapai akurasi klasifikasi yang tinggi dengan tingkat kesalahan yang minimal. Selain itu, sistem berbasis web dapat berjalan dengan stabil dan responsif sehingga berpotensi digunakan sebagai alat bantu verifikasi keaslian citra digital. Kata Kunci: AI Image Detection, CNN-ViT, Broad Learning, Multiclass Classification.

title: An AI-assisted genomic census of 193,342  assemblies finds a GFP-barrel family in unreported  lineages, carrying pseudogenes in both fungi and  cnidarians
0124b074e37ec881b1c13eb13f468ec2a83f640f.abstract: Abstract Green fluorescent protein and its homologues share an eleven-stranded beta-barrel enclosing a central helix, on which three consecutive residues cyclise to form the chromophore. A family of these barrels carrying a buried network of two arginines, two glutamates and a tyrosine, with a hydrophobic residue in place of the chromophore tyrosine, was recently assembled from protein records by Schneider and Zimmer. Here 193,342 genome assemblies were searched in all six reading frames, returning 396 loci, of which 140 read the complete buried network and collapse to 77 distinct carrying organisms. The charge network family reaches two sponge genera, a coronate jellyfish, three dinoflagellate transcriptome records and an archaeal genome, none of them represented in any proteome. In fungi and in cnidarians a substantial minority of loci carry an in-frame stop or a frameshift: 36 of 144 fungal loci, and 18 of 66 cnidarian loci across eleven genera. A Dollo reconstruction over a 28-genome Aspergillus clade requires two to six independent losses at the species level. The copies that survive are under purifying selection, at a median ratio of non-synonymous to synonymous substitution of 0.146 per species pair over 39 such pairs, and in one anthozoan lineage the gene is instead tandemly amplified to eleven copies. Two novel bacterial copies sit in mobile DNA, one inside a phiE-type prophage in Burkholderia pseudomallei and one beside an IS4 family transposase within a toxin-antitoxin array in a Myxococcota genome. A family that protein records show as intact is, in genomic sequence, intact in some lineages and breaking down in others.

title: Strategic AI Underuse: Effort Incentives, Displacement Risk, and Organizational Responses
container-title: Metroeconomica
5eeee8f3f87116405f1400b7b31ebdb0a75f7804.abstract: ABSTRACT This paper studies how workers' employment concerns can affect the effective use of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools after adoption. When productive use of these tools raises workers' perceived risk of displacement, employees may optimally reduce productive effort, trading current earnings against employment security. The baseline represents the first implementation period, when neither side has yet observed behaviour and production under the new technology. The firm evaluates adoption using the observed pre‐AI effort level, while workers forecast the production scale from the most recently observed aggregate output. Strategic underuse can therefore partly or fully offset the productivity gains expected from AI tools and make an initially attractive technology unprofitable after implementation. After implementation, the firm observes the effective effort response, while its organizational options depend on whether it can diagnose the incentive mechanism behind that response and on the cost or feasibility of workforce adjustment. The firm may choose technological reversion, labour hoarding, workforce restructuring through voluntary separations, or employment‐preserving contracts based on negotiated working‐time reductions. Robustness benchmarks show that the displacement‐induced incentive for underuse can persist when firms and workers form more forward‐looking expectations. A Monte Carlo calibration illustrates that all four organizational responses can arise as profit‐maximizing outcomes.

title: Generative AI Use and Critical Thinking among University Students
container-title: Lecture Notes in Education Psychology and Public Media
d73867f4348e722de2601c95253ea770eb36d831.abstract: How students use artificial intelligence and what they learn from it cannot be ignored. According to how often people use AI tools, the groups were divided, and then descriptive statistics, Welch's ANOVA test and independent-sample t-tests were carried out to compare the critical-thinking scores of these groups. Based on the above description, the mean critical-thinking scores of the four groups using AI are relatively high. However, Welch's ANOVA showed that there were no significant differences among the four groups (F(3, 24.71) = 1.586, p = .218). The two groups were divided into regular and non-regular AI users; the mean critical-thinking scores of the regular-use group (50.06) and the non-regular-use group (45.42) were significantly higher for the regular-use group; t(100) = 2.948, p = .004, and Cohen's d = .750. Based on the above results, the impact of AI on students' critical thinking ability is not straightforward; it may vary according to how they use AI. AI can help students learn better by learning to think independently; however, if they rely on AI too much, they may not develop their own thinking skills. Given the small sample size, uneven distribution of groups, self-reported data, cross-sectional design, etc., only associations can be concluded from the results and not cause-and-effect relationships.

title: The dark side of nurse–generative AI collaboration in the workplace: unveiling work alienation and nurse expediency
container-title: BMC Nursing
db169448caeb6f938256e57f25fc8b7ea6278b91.abstract: Abstract Background The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into nursing practice is expected to enhance efficiency and decision-making. However, this paradigm shift towards “nurse–GenAI collaboration” also introduces underexplored psychological and behavioral risks. While existing literature often celebrates AI’s productivity gains, the potential “dark side”—including work alienation and counterproductive behaviors—remains a critical gap, particularly regarding the specific mediating mechanisms and individual boundary conditions involved. Objective This study aims to examine the potential dark side of nurse–GenAI collaboration by investigating its associations with work alienation and subsequent nurse expediency. Drawing on the Job Demands-Resources (JD-R) model, we propose a moderated mediation model to examine the dual mediating roles of work meaningfulness (cognitive pathway) and emotional exhaustion (affective pathway), and the moderating effect of GenAI anxiety. Methods A cross-sectional survey design was employed, collecting data from 306 registered nurses across various Chinese hospitals who had used GenAI tools in their work. Participants completed validated measures assessing, nurse-GenAI collaboration, work meaningfulness, emotional exhaustion, work alienation, nurse expediency, and GenAI anxiety. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) was used to analyze the hypothesized relationships. Results The findings supported all proposed hypotheses. Nurse–GenAI collaboration was negatively associated with work meaningfulness (β = -0.299, p < 0.001) and positively associated with emotional exhaustion (β = 0.231, p = 0.008). The indirect associations between collaboration and work alienation were positive and significant through both work meaningfulness (β = 0.120, p < 0.01) and emotional exhaustion (β = 0.071, p < 0.05), and the direct association was non-significant when both mediators were included. Work alienation, in turn, was strongly associated with nurse expediency (β = 0.668, p < 0 0.001). Finally, GenAI anxiety significantly moderated both first-stage associations (interaction terms: β = -0.262, p < 0.001 for meaningfulness; β = 0.166, p = 0 0.035 for emotional exhaustion): the associations of collaboration with meaningfulness and with emotional exhaustion were stronger at higher levels of GenAI anxiety. Conclusions In this cross-sectional sample of Chinese nurses, higher nurse–GenAI collaboration intensity was associated with lower work meaningfulness and higher emotional exhaustion, which in turn were associated with work alienation and expedient behaviors, particularly among nurses with high GenAI anxiety. They suggest that the psychological and behavioral costs of GenAI integration deserve attention alongside its efficiency benefits, and they offer a nuanced extension of the JD-R model to human–AI collaboration in nursing.

title: Innovation Direction of Intelligent Products - Research on Personalized Product Design System Based on Generative AI
container-title: Applied and Computational Engineering
098b576c687a5111a167d4c10412dbe79795724a.abstract: In the context of consumption upgrade and intelligent manufacturing, personalized customization has become a core trend in product innovation. Generative AI (AIGC) is gradually a new tool, for the automation product design. This paper puts forward an AI-driven personalized product design system, that integrates engineering constraints and business dimensions. This is built on a diffusion generation model combined with a dual-cycle generative-evaluation architecture, and we use the smart lunch box as an empirical case to verify its feasibility. Through our research, workflow reengineering and quantitative evaluation, our study implecates that the system achieves an engineering feasibility for generated solutions, compared to unconstrained AIGC generation. The design cycle is reduced greatly, representing an efficiency gain. This research not only provides new tools and for product design but also offers a feasible path to achieve mass customization.

title: A Review of the Accuracy and Computational Cost of AI Regression Models for Short-Term Wind Power Forecasting
container-title: Applied and Computational Engineering
97c967a51d07e3af5170a640f8018ef55f4b1a0c.abstract: Short-term wind power forecasting models must meet both accuracy requirements and computational limits. Published comparisons use different datasets, forecast horizons, and timing boundaries. In this focused narrative review, twelve publications on artificial intelligence (AI) regression models and their evaluation are examined. Support vector regression, random forests, XGBoost, and long short-term memory networks are the main model families discussed. Prediction errors and computational costs are compared within studies, and changes in input information are examined. Under the reported experimental conditions, lower prediction errors do not always require higher computational costs. Runtime rankings can also differ between training and inference. Meteorological inputs and data enrichment affect accuracy and the performance gaps between models. However, cost reporting remains incomplete. The evidence cannot establish whether these accuracy gains require longer computation times or more resources. A conditional screening procedure is therefore suggested. The forecasting task and input availability should be checked first. Parameter search, training, and inference costs should then be compared separately. Results should also be tested across several time windows. These recommendations can support model screening under operational constraints. Their applicability still requires validation at the target wind farm.

title: Future Faculty Development in the Age of AI: University Teachers’ Roles, Needs, and Institutional Support
container-title: Frontiers of Digital Education
505d8830ac9df419c1922aa596a0e1b98d3c9b8a.abstract: Abstract AI is reshaping higher education in ways that extend beyond the adoption of new tools, challenging established assumptions about assessment, curriculum, ethics, graduate preparation, and the work of university teachers. Drawing on insights from the Teacher Panel at the International Conference on GenAI and Pedagogical Innovations held in Hong Kong in May 2026, this commentary argues that faculty development in the AI era must move beyond generic technology training towards a more role-based, discipline-sensitive, future-oriented, and ecosystemic approach. The commentary identifies four key insights from the panel discussion: AI use is already widespread and assessment has become an immediate pressure point; AI literacy is necessary but insufficient without disciplinary, professional, ethical, and human-centred dimensions; universities must connect learning more explicitly with the authentic world beyond campus while renewing the role of the campus as a site of experimentation and futures literacy; and institutions need stronger capacity for evidence-informed, forward-looking AI governance. Building on these insights, the commentary proposes seven emerging roles for university teachers: human-centred educator; disciplinary and professional expert; learning architect and intellectual guide; assessment (re)designer; technically competent and critically informed professional; ethical steward; and educational experimenter and evidence-based practitioner. Corresponding faculty development needs are then discussed, including support for human-centred education, curriculum renewal, world-connected learning, assessment redesign, technical-pedagogical AI capability, ethical stewardship, AI policy literacy, and scholarship-informed educational improvement. The commentary concludes with a preliminary role-based framework for faculty development. It emphasises that these roles need not be performed by a single individual teacher. Rather, as educational design and delivery become more complex in the age of AI, university education should increasingly be understood as a collective endeavour involving academic staff, educational developers, technology specialists, professional staff, students, external partners, employers, and community organisations.

title: Comparative Analysis of Text Classification Techniques for Phishing and Smishing Detection Using Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency and Gemini Sentence Embeddings
container-title: AI, Computer Science and Robotics Technology
a1ada76d095ff1aa7ca00b91763987dae7ccc078.abstract: This study presents an approach to phishing and smishing detection using text classification algorithms and two feature extraction techniques: term frequency–inverse document frequency (TF-IDF) and Gemini sentence embeddings. The research uses a curated, self-collected dataset of 27,000 messages, including 2,000 synthetic records to increase linguistic diversity. With TF-IDF, the support vector classifier (SVC) achieved a training accuracy of 97.85% and a test accuracy of 89.37%, indicating a generalization gap. Multilayer perceptron (MLP) and stochastic gradient descent classifiers achieved test accuracies of 88.28% and 86.06%, respectively. Sentence embeddings showed stronger performance, with SVC achieving 94.69% test accuracy, followed by MLP at 92.70% and K-nearest neighbors (KNN) at 92.35%. The decision tree classifier showed comparatively lower performance, with test accuracies of 78.04% using TF-IDF and 64.04% using sentence embeddings. Overall, sentence embeddings outperformed TF-IDF in the evaluated experimental setting. Unlike studies evaluating traditional features or semantic embeddings separately, this work provides a controlled comparison across feature representations, classifiers, and communication channels (email and SMS). The study examines generalization behavior, model stability, and feature representation effects beyond peak accuracy, contributing a structured evaluation framework for natural language processing-based cybersecurity research.
