e4fafb83db6fec734950eb52ea540115de8d42f4.abstract: This study investigated the effect of salinity degree on bacterial abundance in irrigated meadow-takyr soils of the Ziyorat massiv, Karakul district, Bukhara region. Non-saline, slightly saline, moderately saline, and strongly saline soils were examined at depths of 0–25, 25–50, and 50–80 cm during spring, summer, and autumn. The results showed a consistent decline in bacterial abundance with increasing soil salinity and depth.

title: ПУШТА ТЕПАСИГА МИНИМАЛ ИШЛОВ БЕРАДИГАН РОТАЦИОН ЮМШАТКИЧ ПАРАМЕТРЛАРИНИ МАҚБУЛЛАШТИРИШ
container-title: Agro ilm
c509063f35d9011ed66639c6c18d0a92b4359972.abstract: The article presents research on optimizing the design and operating parameters of a rotary ripper for minimum tillage of the ridge top using mathematical planning methods. The effects of the number of ripper discs, vertical load, and travel speed on the degree of soil crumbling and draft resistance were studied. Based on the obtained regression equations, the optimal values for the working organs were determined, ensuring high-quality tillage of the ridge top in accordance with agrotechnical requirements.

title: LEGUME CROP PRODUCTION IN UZBEKISTAN: AN EMPIRICAL ANALYSIS OF DETERMINANTS
container-title: Agro ilm
03504e16fb7ff633b3ad6671704c4e70d6e34612.abstract: This paper examines factors affecting legume production in Uzbekistan using cross-sectional data from 1,225 farmers across 12 districts in the UzFarmBarometer 2024 database. A probit model identifies factors associated with the probability of legume adoption. Results show that older farmers are less likely to cultivate legumes, while larger households and more experienced farmers are more likely to adopt them. Earlier-established farms also show lower adoption. Distance to input markets is positively associated with adoption, whereas distance to output markets is negatively associated with it, reflecting differences in input dependence and transaction costs. We suggest that improving rural market infrastructure, extension services, and stable labor arrangements could support legume cultivation.

title: Is your university prepared for extreme events? Using serious gaming to dialog about organizational capacities
container-title: Disaster Prevention and Management: An International Journal
1198d86e52e41a001d520d49709178e0b997d7bd.abstract: Purpose The rise of disaster risk scenarios poses new challenges for higher education institutions (HEIs), requiring them to develop organizational capacities to prepare for extreme events and disasters. This paper proposes and applies a serious game approach to promote collective reflection on whether (and to what extent) a university is prepared for extreme event scenarios, examining how organizational capacities emerge when the academic community must make decisions under pressure and uncertainty. Design/methodology/approach The serious game draws on an organizational capacity framework combining two dimensions: technical-administrative and political–relational capacities. A serious game-based methodology was adopted for its potential to create a simulated environment where participants engage in structured dialog about disaster preparedness in HEIs. Throughout the game, participants negotiate priorities, allocate limited resources and confront mutually exclusive choices, making visible how organizational preparedness capacities are constructed through decision-making. Findings Most groups prioritized wildfires, reflecting local risk history. Surprise cards reinforced the need for adaptation under polycrisis conditions. While infrastructure, related to technical-administrative capacities, was widely prioritized, the game revealed limits in addressing non-structural measures, especially through outreach/extension activities, which are associated with political–relational capacities. Departmental fragmentation and weak cross-area dialog were identified as barriers to integrated responses and organizational capacity. Originality/value Research on how HEIs prepare for extreme events remains scarce, with Disaster Risk Reduction (DRR) education often fragmented across departments. The main scientific contribution of this study is to open a research agenda on institutional preparedness within HEIs by creating and applying a serious game that promotes collective reflection on their organizational capacities for extreme events.

title: Interesting and impactful research avenues emerge from teaching operations management
container-title: International Journal of Operations & Production Management
6a4bb9dd425ee66138b07ffe432124e0ac403f74.abstract: Purpose This article reflects on how teaching operations management (OM) to graduate students and executives provides a rich source of interesting and impactful OM research avenues. Design/methodology/approach While it is common to hear that the latest research should keep teaching fresh and relevant, this article flips this advice to discuss interesting and impactful OM research topics emerging from the challenges of teaching an MBA core course. Findings This article suggests six avenues for future research that emerged from teaching – how company operations pertain to its strategy, the role of chief operating officer (COO), enterprise processes, process improvement, performance measurement, and automation/artificial intelligence (AI) – and specific research questions within each avenue. Research limitations/implications The proposed research questions are exemplary and not comprehensive. Practical implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to interesting, practically relevant and impactful results. Social implications Addressing the proposed research questions will lead to socially relevant and impactful results. Originality/value This article reverses the typical admonition to let research inform teaching, showing how considering the counter-relationship illuminates interesting and impactful research avenues.

title: The influence pathway of internal audit attributes on credit risk management in emerging economies: evidence from Tanzania
container-title: Journal of Accounting in Emerging Economies
d2903aa2a07b979e6c93a0cb7df1b065dcbc0662.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how internal audit function (IAF) attributes, namely competence, independence, and leadership, influence credit risk management (CRM) in Tanzanian commercial banks, focussing on the mediating role of the IAF's sphere of influence. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 131 relevant employees across all 34 licenced commercial banks in Tanzania. A cross-sectional survey design was applied, and partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) was used to test direct and mediated relationships. Findings Results show that IAF competence and independence significantly enhance CRM both directly and indirectly through the sphere of influence, while the relationship between leadership and CRM is fully mediated by the sphere of influence. Moreover, the sphere of influence exerts a significant positive effect on CRM, underscoring the importance of organisational influence in translating audit insights into effective risk governance. Practical implications The findings suggest that banks in emerging economies should reinforce auditor independence and competence while fostering organisational cultures that empower internal audit functions. Regulators are also encouraged to refine their supervisory frameworks to emphasise the institutional role of internal audits in risk oversight. Originality/value This study extends internal auditing research by conceptualising and validating the sphere of influence as the mechanism through which IAF attributes affect CRM. By integrating Agency Theory and Role Theory into a unified capacity–conversion framework, in which audit attributes create monitoring capacity and organisational influence converts it into governance outcomes, it offers new evidence from an emerging economy and advances understanding of how internal audit creates governance value through risk oversight in developing banking systems.

title: Trust, legitimacy and oversight: drivers of Shariah-compliant robo-advisory adoption in Oman
container-title: Management & Sustainability: An Arab Review
ef40ce715b2651e93a55687811897e1cedb21da2.abstract: Purpose As financial technologies evolve, Muslim investors face unique challenges in aligning automated investment tools with Islamic principles. This study explores the adoption of Shariah-compliant robo-advisory (SCRA) services among retail investors in Oman. Design/methodology/approach The study surveyed 337 retail investors in Muscat, Oman, and tested the proposed model using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The theoretical framework draws primarily on the theory of planned behavior (TPB), with legitimacy theory used to explain the role of perceived legitimacy in the model. Findings The findings reveal that digital financial literacy significantly enhances trust in technology, which positively influences perceived legitimacy and adoption intentions. However, strong religious commitment increases the perceived need for human oversight, reducing acceptance of fully automated tools. Similarly, perceived risk of misguidance negatively affects adoption, though legitimacy mitigates this effect. The results underscore that trust, credibility and religious assurance are essential to foster SCRA adoption. Practical implications Financial institutions can use these findings to pair automated portfolio management with accessible Shariah scholar review, invest in digital and financial literacy programmes and pursue certification from national Shariah boards; regulators such as Oman's Capital Market Authority and Central Bank of Oman can draw on the results to set governance standards for AI-based advisory platforms. Originality/value The study highlights the importance of Shariah governance frameworks, inclusion of religious scholars in system design and investor education, thereby enriching the Islamic fintech adoption literature in the Gulf.

title: Managing commitments for reliable planning: evidence from action research
container-title: Engineering, Construction and Architectural Management
e60dc5cfa35450e9b0dfc5c156558870c44df76a.abstract: Purpose Low planning reliability in construction projects has been linked to weaknesses in commitment management within the Last Planner System (LPS). While the Linguistic Action Perspective (LAP) provides a strong theoretical explanation of commitments as conversations for action, empirical evidence of operational systems that translate these principles into practice remains limited. This paper evaluates a Commitment Management System (CMS) designed to improve commitment reliability and planning performance in construction projects. Design/methodology/approach An action research approach was adopted through a longitudinal, multi-project intervention in four construction projects, two in Chile and two in Colombia, with different levels of LPS maturity. The CMS was implemented through structured interventions embedded in weekly planning meetings. Quantitative and qualitative data were collected to assess commitment-related indicators, LPS maturity, Percent Plan Complete (PPC), PPC variability, engagement behaviours, and schedule deviation. Findings The results indicate that CMS implementation increased LPS maturity levels across all projects and improved commitment performance. Projects exhibiting higher CMS assimilation and engagement showed lower PPC variability and more stable planning outcomes. Schedule deviation was reduced in all cases, with an average improvement of 5.39%, demonstrating the positive impact of structured commitment management on planning reliability. Originality/value This study provides empirical validation of an operational CMS grounded in the LAP and tested through Action Research in real construction projects, strengthening the connection between communication theory and lean construction practice.

title: Fear and egoism, sadness and altruism: how negative textual emotions affect project outcomes in medical crowdfunding
container-title: Industrial Management & Data Systems
97f12437390163bdd274fd434224886c81b32a9b.abstract: Purpose Prior studies on negative textual emotions in medical crowdfunding have yielded inconsistent findings and have largely neglected two critical dimensions of the total funding amount: the number of donors (i.e. donation likelihood) and the amount per donor (i.e. donation amount), as well as relevant boundary conditions. This study investigates the impact of fear and sadness conveyed in the project text on these two dimensions, examines their mediating roles on in determining the total funding amount and explores the moderating effect of the project monetary goal. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on theories of fear and sadness expression and donation motivation, we developed a research model and tested it using text analysis and econometric methods on data from a leading medical crowdfunding platform in China. Findings Our findings indicate that fear increases the number of donors while decreasing the average donation amount, whereas sadness reduces the number of donors but increases the donation amount per donor. These dimensions mediate the effects of fear and sadness on the total funds raised. Moreover, a high project monetary goal diminishes both the positive influence of fear on donor count and its negative impact on the average donation amount. Originality/value This study demonstrates that the negative emotions of fear and sadness exert opposing effects on donor numbers and the amount per donor in medical crowdfunding. Furthermore, it elucidates the mechanisms by which these emotions influence the total funding amount raised and reveals the contingent role of the project's monetary goal. These findings provide practical insights for optimizing emotional communication strategies in medical crowdfunding.

title: AI adoption in purchasing and supply management: how institutional voids rewire the UTAUT framework
container-title: Modern Supply Chain Research and Applications
0bcd714cb04d0b263189b430cff3e961768ff573.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how institutional voids and behavioral factors jointly drive artificial intelligence (AI) adoption in purchasing and supply management (PSM) within emerging economies. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 200 PSM professionals in Morocco were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test an integrated UTAUT–institutional theory framework. Findings Performance expectancy (PE) (ß = 0.530) and social influence (ß = 0.453) primarily drive behavioral intention (BI), while coercive pressure is non-significant (ß = 0.050, p = 0.260). Facilitating conditions (FC) (ß = 0.472) and (BI) (ß = 0.497) exert near-equal direct effects on actual use, confirming an “infrastructure imperative”. Post-hoc multi-group analysis reveals that PE dominates predictive AI adoption, whereas effort expectancy dominates Generative AI. Practical implications Organizations in emerging economies must pair AI software procurement with dedicated infrastructure, data governance and peer-led change management rather than relying on unsupported mandates. Originality/value This study demonstrates that institutional voids modify the UTAUT nomological network by elevating FC to a primary co-determinant of technology use, proving infrastructure readiness equals user intention in driving adoption.

title: Future of work in the era of AI: how technology strategy shapes daily job roles
container-title: International Journal of Organizational Analysis
31a1acb996d897d7876f2aa832ce5ad1572c2f0e.abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore the impact of organizational technology strategies, particularly in the context of artificial intelligence (AI), on employees’ daily job activities. It also looks at the extent of the transformation and the role of leadership, supportive of innovation and cultural change, in reinforcing the transformation. Design/methodology/approach The researcher adopted a quantitative research design based on the survey data collected from employees in various industries in Pakistan. The researcher used structural equation modeling to analyze the relationships among technology strategies, organizational facilitators and the transformation of job roles. Findings The research shows that organizations that implement AI and automation alongside digitized processes and advanced data analysis capabilities will experience fundamental changes in their employees’ work functions, skills and job duties. The implementation of digital strategies enhances operational efficiency, but their impact extends beyond this benefit, as they completely transform how work is executed. The presence of an innovation-supportive culture together with strong leadership commitment creates an enhanced effect. The combination of encouragement of organizational experimentation and active leadership support for technological change results in more visible and positive changes in job responsibilities. Practical implications The research findings demonstrate that organizations need to combine technology investments with operational changes to achieve successful digital transformation outcomes. Organizations must establish supportive cultures together with proactive leadership to assist employees throughout the process of organizational change. Organizations need to develop their employees’ skills and build adaptable workforces while maintaining open communication to implement meaningful job role changes that last over time. Originality/value The research contributes to the future of work literature by examining how workers change their job functions at the individual-employee level rather than observing outcomes at the organizational level. The research describes how organizations use technology strategies and organizational enablers to create distinct work environments for the AI age by integrating Job Demands–Resources and Socio-Technical Systems perspectives.

title: The copilot paradox: configurational pathways to human-AI symbiosis in knowledge work
container-title: International Journal of Organizational Analysis
10429646653846e10fef0781eea8935c49efcda2.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the “Copilot Paradox” in safety-critical operations, offering insights into how the chronic tension between the algorithm’s increased efficiency and operational vulnerability is subdued through socio-cognitive configurations across time. Design/methodology/approach With the use of a two-wave longitudinal fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA), the paper explores the changing dynamics of human–artificial intelligence (AI) symbiosis in the oil and gas industry. Findings Analysis of necessity shows that there is no single condition required in all cases. Sufficiency analysis reveals three distinct, equifinal pathways: buffering, synergy and substitution. At early adoption, institutional re-skilling coupled with psychological safety acts as a buffering mechanism against job insecurity induced by AI. As integration progresses, synergy (fuelled by empowering leadership) and substitution (where team resources fill the gaps in leadership) come to dominate. Practical implications Team psychological safety and capability building are structural safeguards for managers in high-reliability sectors, not optional cultural flourishes. These lessons point to pathways for realising AI copilots while preserving human agency and operational resiliency. Originality/value This paper contributes to paradox theory by developing a socio-cognitive infrastructure that highlights its dynamic, temporal configuration and causal asymmetries. Methodologically, it showcases the new promise of longitudinal fsQCA to model dynamics in algorithms’ infusion by capturing their embeddedness through time.

title: From risk management to AI-enabled governance: five intellectual orientations in EPC and infrastructure project risk governance
container-title: Journal of Engineering, Design and Technology
262b73632bb16a2f06249b0dfe727ae37edc8674.abstract: Purpose This study aims to synthesise the intellectual development of engineering–procurement–construction and infrastructure project risk governance and examine whether bibliometric evidence supports five overlapping intellectual orientations. Design/methodology/approach The study combined bibliometric analysis with Bibliometrix/Biblioshiny, VOSviewer and a scripted workflow to examine 173 Scopus-indexed publications (1999–2026). The analytical corpus was derived through relevance validation of 678 candidate records, with provenance checked against an 801-row master ledger. Fifteen provisional 2026 records were excluded from temporal comparisons. Findings The analysis identified five orientations: risk analysis and control (53 documents), performance and overrun (80), governance and relational mechanisms (52), digital information integration (7) and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled decision support (18). The share of period publications addressing performance and overrun increased from 34.7 % in 1999–2018 to 59.7 % in 2023–2025, whereas the digital and AI orientations remained comparatively limited. These patterns concern the published literature and do not establish organizational maturity or realised capability. Research limitations/implications Scopus coverage, title/abstract-based relevance validation, citation lag, analytical thresholds and interpretive coding delimit the findings. Project-level research is required to test the proposed relationships. Practical implications The orientations provide structured review prompts for risk processes, outcome linkage, decision rights, information integration and human oversight of predictive systems; they are not intended as a diagnostic maturity instrument. Originality/value The study connects construction risk, megaproject governance and construction AI through an auditable corpus and an evidence-bounded conceptual framework.

title: Digital and AI tools in informal care: understanding caregivers’ experiences in rural Nigeria
container-title: Working with Older People
3d95ea5e81a5dd3ac98c9f9e80e04a8c952edbad.abstract: Purpose Although informal caregiving for older adults is well-researched, a significant gap exists in understanding how informal caregivers navigate their caregiving roles with the help of digital technologies, especially in rural Nigeria, where internet connectivity is poor and access to digital devices is limited. This study aims to explore how informal caregivers in rural Nigeria use digital technology to support care for older adults. Design/methodology/approach The study adopted a qualitative descriptive approach, data were collected from 10 informal caregivers, using semi-structured interviews. The data were further analysed thematically using NVivo 14. Findings Results identified that caregivers use digital technology for communication and care coordination, learning and self-empowerment, responding to emergency situations, improving efficiency, reducing stress and maintaining contact between older adults and their diaspora family members. The study also found poor access and limited internet infrastructure as barriers to the use of digital technology to improve caregiving. Research limitations/implications Only caregivers in rural areas were interviewed. This excluded the experiences of caregivers in urban areas, who may face urban economic stressors that shape their overall caregiving experience and their use of digital technology for caregiving. Practical implications The findings highlight the potential of digital technology to support informal caregiving in rural Nigeria. Improving access to affordable digital devices, reliable internet connectivity and digital literacy can enhance care coordination, caregiver support, emergency response and communication with older adults and their families. Originality/value This study is important because it provides new insight into how informal caregivers in rural Nigeria use digital technology to support older adults despite limited connectivity and access to digital devices. It highlights both the potential of digital tools to strengthen caregiving and the infrastructural barriers that must be addressed.

title: Librarians' perspectives on AI for environmental sustainability in Ghanaian academic libraries
container-title: Library Hi Tech
931d99d9c196e1b88e58ba8390c4eca27c050aac.abstract: Purpose This study examined academic librarians' perspectives on the potential of artificial intelligence to advance environmental sustainability through sustainable library practices and efficient service delivery. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative approach was adopted, drawing on semi-structured interviews with 21 academic librarians and guided by the Technology Acceptance Model. Thematic analysis was used to identify key patterns and perspectives on AI adoption for environmental sustainability in academic libraries. Findings The study found that academic librarians recognize AI's potential to advance environmental sustainability through intelligent energy management, predictive maintenance, environmental monitoring, and sustainability planning, yet its practical implementation remains limited. Research limitations/implications The qualitative design and small sample limit generalizability; however, the findings provide contextual insights and a basis for broader research across diverse library settings. Practical implications The findings recommend that universities and library management integrate AI into sustainability planning through effective governance, improved digital infrastructure, and continuous AI literacy training, supported by national policies and investment in responsible AI innovation. Social implications The study highlights the value of AI in advancing environmental sustainability in libraries, emphasizing the need for educational initiatives, institutional policies, and responsible technology adoption. Originality/value This study provides timely empirical insight into AI-enabled environmental sustainability in Ghanaian academic libraries, highlighting the critical gap between librarians' awareness and perceived potential of AI and its limited practical implementation.

title: Institutional pressure and innovative behavior of knowledge workers: a moderated mediation model of leadership style and public service motivation
container-title: Chinese Management Studies
0172ec226c0dce6dd8321322daaf2a9abc193bd6.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the impact of three types of organizational institutional pressures – coercive, normative and mimetic – on the innovative behavior of knowledge workers. It examines the distinct moderating roles of transformational and transactional leadership, with public service motivation (PSM) serving as the mediating mechanism. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on two independent studies (Study 1:36 teams, 380 responses on transformational leadership; Study 2:41 teams, 407 responses on transactional leadership), the authors used a cross-level moderated mediation model. Confirmatory factor analysis validated the measurement structure, and the use of cross-level data ensured methodological rigor. Findings Transformational leadership amplifies the positive impact of normative and mimetic pressures on PSM, thereby enhancing innovation. Conversely, transactional leadership undermines the motivational link of coercive pressure to PSM, suppressing innovation. These results highlight the situational dependency of leadership: transformational leadership can unlock the innovative potential inherent in norms and imitation pressures, whereas transactional leadership tends to exacerbate execution rigidity in compliance-emphasizing environments, weakening the translation of coercive pressure into innovative behavior. Research limitations/implications While this study uses cross-level data, it relies on self-reported measures. Although steps were taken to ensure validity in the data analysis, future research could directly measure performance using objective scales to achieve greater scientific rigor. Practical implications Organizations should strategically align leadership styles with types of institutional pressure. Transformational leadership is critical for leveraging the motivational and innovative potential of normative and mimetic pressures. In contrast, transactional leadership should be minimized in coercive contexts to avoid suppressing creativity. Cultivating PSM through clear communication of institutional goals and fostering autonomy in rule-driven environments can help convert external pressures into sustainable drivers of innovation. Originality/value This study categorizes institutional pressures into coercive, normative and mimetic types, exploring their unique interplay with leadership styles. The research reveals an asymmetrical leadership effect: transformational leaders enhance innovation in value-driven contexts, whereas transactional leaders impede it in environments tightly regulated by policies and rules. By integrating institutional theory with leadership studies, this research offers a framework for understanding the innovation processes of knowledge workers.

title: Artificial Intelligence‐Assisted Automated Optical Coherence Tomography Analysis for Percutaneous Coronary Intervention Planning: From Plaque Analysis to Precision Lesion Preparation and Stent Optimization
container-title: Journal of the American Heart Association
37fa8e0c0c0df64a599f541436286f8f8471bd64.abstract: Percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) remains the cornerstone of revascularization in coronary artery disease. However, despite advances in stent technology, adverse outcomes related to suboptimal stent placement including under‐expansion, malapposition, incomplete coverage, edge dissection, and neoatherosclerosis persist. Optical coherence tomography (OCT) is the highest resolution widely available intravascular imaging modality, allowing unparalleled visualization of stent‐vessel interactions and plaque morphology. However, there are significant barriers to large‐scale OCT adoption, including time‐consuming manual interpretation and dependence on the operator, resulting in significant variability between analysts. Artificial intelligence (AI)‐based automated OCT analysis promises to assist PCI by delivering rapid, reproducible, and standardized stent optimization, but current analysis systems lack important features to optimize stent placement. This review summarizes the principles of OCT in PCI, the evidence for OCT‐guided optimization, and recent advances in AI‐driven automated OCT analysis. We discuss plaque analysis and classification, highlighting how AI‐driven automated OCT analysis can identify fibrous, lipid‐rich, and calcified lesions and guide tailored lesion preparation using balloons, specialty balloons, drug‐coated balloons, intravascular lithotripsy, and atherectomy. We outline emerging AI‐enabled workflows for fully automated PCI optimization, evaluate clinical outcomes, interpretability, and workflow integration. Finally, we explore future directions including AI imaging‐physiology fusion, multiomics integration, and robotics. If successful, automated AI‐empowered OCT analysis could become a central imaging platform for precision PCI, enabling tailored lesion preparation, optimal stent deployment, and improved clinical outcomes in coronary artery disease management.

title: Efficacy of Stellate Ganglion Block for Preventing Postoperative Atrial Fibrillation After Cardiac Surgery: A Randomized, Double‐Blind, Placebo‐Controlled Trial
container-title: Journal of the American Heart Association
47d160a0277168adf9351a8df9bee14429b106b7.abstract: Background Stellate ganglion block (SGB) may reduce postoperative atrial fibrillation (POAF) by modulating the autonomic nervous system. This study evaluated the efficacy of preoperative SGB in preventing POAF following cardiac surgery. Methods In this single‐center, randomized, double‐blind, placebo‐controlled trial, 140 patients undergoing valve surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass were assigned (1:1) to ultrasound‐guided right SGB with 7 mL of 0.5% ropivacaine or 7 mL of normal saline. The primary outcome was the incidence of POAF from postoperative day 0 to day 7 or until discharge. Results A total of 132 patients completed the study and were included in the modified intention‐to‐treat population (SGB group: n=65; saline group: n=67). POAF occurred in 43% of the SGB group and 40% of the saline group (odds ratio [OR], 0.99 [95% CI, 0.46–2.15], adjusted P =0.989). The SGB group demonstrated a lower incidence of intraoperative ventricular fibrillation/ventricular tachycardia requiring defibrillation after aortic cross‐clamp release (6% versus 19%; OR, 0.21 [95% CI, 0.06–0.80]; adjusted P =0.022), lower postoperative high‐sensitivity troponin I levels (median difference: −2562 ng/L [95% CI, −4301 to −45]; P =0.045), and a reduced risk of postoperative acute kidney injury (5% versus 18%; OR, 0.24 [95% CI, 0.06–0.98]; adjusted P =0.046). Conclusions While preoperative SGB did not reduce the incidence of POAF, it was associated with potential benefits, including a lower requirement for intraoperative defibrillation attributable to ventricular arrhythmias, attenuated myocardial injury (as indicated by lower high‐sensitivity troponin I levels), and a decreased risk of postoperative acute kidney injury. Registration URL: https://www.chictr.org.cn ; URL Identifier: ChiCTR2300068572.

title: Rationale and Design of a Parallel Randomized Trial of a DASH‐Enhanced Portfolio Diet With or Without Ultra‐Processed Plant Proteins for Blood Pressure and Other Cardiometabolic Risk Factors in Adults With Hypertension and Obesity: The Substitution of High With Low Ultra‐Processed Soy Protein Foods in a Guideline‐Based Diet Intervention on Cardiometabolic Health Trial
container-title: Journal of the American Heart Association
fd258eb1ea1753217d582be613645556cd841546.abstract: Background Cardiovascular disease remains the leading cause of death and hospitalization globally. Clinical practice guidelines recommend various plant‐based dietary patterns that target specific cardiometabolic risk factors, including the Dietary Approach to Stop Hypertension (DASH) diet for blood pressure and the Portfolio diet for low‐density lipoprotein cholesterol. Combining key elements of these patterns may enhance cardiovascular disease risk reduction. However, many soy‐based products, a key Portfolio component, are classified as ultra‐processed foods (UPFs). This trial will answer 2 questions: (1) Does a DASH‐enhanced Portfolio diet result in clinically meaningful reductions in blood pressure compared with standard of care and (2) Is a high‐UPF noninferior to a low‐UPF soy protein‐containing DASH‐enhanced Portfolio diet for blood pressure reduction? Methods The SWITCH (Substitution of High With Low Ultra‐Processed Soy Protein Foods in a Guideline‐Based Diet Intervention for Cardiometabolic Health) trial is a parallel, randomized, 3‐arm, open‐label, superiority–noninferiority trial. Three hundred adults with hypertension and obesity, including 50% with type 2 diabetes, will be randomized to a high‐UPF or low‐UPF soy protein‐containing DASH‐enhanced Portfolio diet or standard of care for 12 weeks. The primary outcome is systolic blood pressure. Key secondary outcomes are non–high‐density lipoprotein cholesterol and body weight. Other outcomes include cardiometabolic risk factors. Conclusions Findings will provide high‐quality evidence on the use of a DASH‐enhanced Portfolio diet and the role of nutrient‐dense soy foods classified as UPFs within the combination of the 2 guideline‐based dietary patterns to support dietary strategies for cardiometabolic risk reduction. REGISTRATION URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/ ; Unique identifier: NCT06907862.

title: Apartment to business hotel conversion: opportunity or threat to unit ownership rights
container-title: International Journal of Law and Management
ca49013311c69ab29a0bc5a10647949f4dbd5d37.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the legality of apartment-to-hotel conversion in Indonesia by integrating property law, consumer protection, tourism regulation, taxation and spatial planning into a single legal governance framework. Design/methodology/approach The method used is a qualitative approach with normative juridical analysis and case studies on several apartments that have undergone functional changes. Findings The findings indicate that the legality of converting residential apartment units into serviced apartments depends on compliance with apartment licensing, consumer protection and commercial regulations. Such conversion requires conformity with the designated building function, approval through the PPPSRS governance mechanism where applicable and fulfillment of the legal requirements governing commercial accommodation. Failure to comply may create legal uncertainty concerning ownership rights, consumer protection, licensing and taxation obligations. This study recommends harmonizing apartment, tourism, consumer protection and taxation regulations, strengthening government supervision, ensuring transparency in the legal status of serviced apartments and clarifying the legal responsibilities of unit owners, managers and accommodation operators to provide greater legal certainty for all stakeholders. Practical implications This study provides practical guidance for policymakers, local governments, developers, apartment unit owners and hospitality operators in regulating the conversion of residential apartments into serviced apartments. Its integrated legal framework can be used to improve licensing procedures, clarify ownership and operational rights, strengthen consumer protection and harmonize property, tourism, taxation and spatial planning regulations. Originality/value This study offers a novel legal perspective by examining the conversion of residential apartments into serviced apartments as a cross-sector issue involving property law, consumer protection, tourism regulation, taxation and spatial planning. Unlike previous studies that primarily focus on apartment ownership or consumer protection separately, this study develops an integrated legal governance model for regulating apartment conversion.

title: A viewpoint on knowledge sabotage: structured literature review, new survey instrument and recommendations by the concept’s developer
container-title: Journal of Knowledge Management
5d3dbd9418b3afb07a5f538804e9da06002507e0.abstract: Purpose This viewpoint aims to analyze the current state of research on knowledge sabotage from the concept developer’s perspective and introduces a new measurement instrument. Design/methodology/approach In addition to the author’s personal reflections, the methods include a structured literature review of 24 empirical studies and a survey of 204 full-time employees recruited from the CloudResearch Connect crowdsourcing platform. Findings Research on knowledge sabotage has been steadily expanding. The construct is well suited to serve as a mediator but should not be used as an antecedent of personality traits or as a moderator. Future studies should focus more on the outcomes of knowledge sabotage, measure it on a seven- or, preferably, nine-point Likert-type scale and employ qualitative methods. Researchers seeking a general measure of knowledge sabotage may use either the previous or the new scale, but those aiming to examine its dimensions should rely on the new instrument. Practical implications Knowledge sabotage is a widespread phenomenon with severe consequences at multiple levels. It arises from individual-specific factors such as psychological states, personality traits and personal motivations, as well as workplace dynamics involving coworkers, supervisors and subordinates. For victims, it leads to psychological distress, relational breakdowns, performance setbacks, career harm and financial loss. Perpetrators may also face career repercussions. At the organizational level, knowledge sabotage produces both direct and indirect financial losses. In addition, knowledge sabotage negatively affects third parties and society as a whole. Originality/value This viewpoint offers a novel framework and is recommended reading for scholars interested in advancing the study of knowledge sabotage.

title: Pleasure or annoyance? The opposing effects of food-service rituals
container-title: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
b8df6af8935d15255c6c8e5ea65dea54301f6c53.abstract: Purpose Food-service rituals are increasingly prevalent in hospitality practice, yet their effects in real-world settings remain underexplored. Drawing on Interaction Ritual Chain theory, this research aims to investigate when and why food-service rituals enhance versus undermine encounter satisfaction. Design/methodology/approach Three video-based experiments were conducted in a restaurant setting. Findings Study 1 shows a positive main effect of food-service rituals on encounter satisfaction. Study 2 demonstrates that food-service rituals enhance satisfaction by evoking pleasure among customers with hedonic consumption goals but elicit annoyance among customers with utilitarian goals. Study 3 further reveals that food-service rituals exert a positive effect under communal customer-brand relationship norms, but backfire under exchange relationship norms. Practical implications This study offers valuable guidance for restaurant operators. Businesses should consider customers’ consumption goals and customer-brand relationship norms when implementing food-service rituals. Originality/value This study enriches the hospitality management literature by developing a more balanced understanding of food-service rituals and highlighting the conditions and emotional mechanisms that shape customer reactions.

title: Capabilities shaping institutional adoption: modeling generative AI adoption in higher education
container-title: Journal of Knowledge Management
08a009fe077bc5af12d714b4d60c2ab8c6973296.abstract: Purpose Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming higher education, yet its successful institutional adoption extends beyond technological capability to require effective knowledge governance, organizational readiness and coordinated decision-making. This study aims to structurally model the CSFs for GenAI adoption in education using an integrated interpretive structural modeling (ISM)–DEMATEL approach. The authors frame GenAI adoption explicitly as a knowledge management problem, analyzing how governance, infrastructure and privacy conditions enable or inhibit institutional capabilities for creating, sharing and governing GenAI-empowered knowledge. Design/methodology/approach The authors identified ten CSFs through a structured literature review and classified them as enablers, capabilities or outcomes across governance, infrastructure, data privacy, analytics, user experience and academic integrity. To analyze the causal and hierarchical relationships among CSFs, an expert validation was conducted through DEMATEL analysis by 20 experts, followed by ISM modeling, which involved 16 experts. Findings DEMATEL identifies technical infrastructure and scalability (CSF-V), data privacy and security (CSF-VII) and integration with LMS/SSO/enterprise systems (CSF-IX) as prominent causal factors. ISM further positions CSF-V at the deepest foundational level, followed by AI governance, policy and ethics (CSF-III), while assessment integrity and academic honesty (CSF-X) occupies the terminal dependent level. The findings identify assessment integrity (CSF-X), prompt literacy (CSF-IV) and user experience (CSF-VI) as dependent factors, confirming that they emerge from structural readiness rather than acting as independent adoption determinants. Research limitations/implications Results are restricted to expert judgment and defined CSFs, which can reduce generalizability across diverse educational settings. Future research must involve larger samples, validate empirically and use longitudinal designs to study changing relations while also testing the knowledge governance mechanisms revealed in this research. Practical implications The model enables phased prioritization of CSFs for optimal implementation of GenAI. Foundational readiness requires infrastructure, system integration and data governance, followed by governance policies and faculty capacity development, before addressing user experience and academic integrity as dependent outcomes. Originality/value The research provides a systems approach to GenAI adoption in education by presenting an integrated ISM–DEMATEL framework based on TOE and DOI, grounded in knowledge governance theory. It aids authors’ understanding of how technological, organizational and knowledge governance dimensions must be sequentially aligned to enable better implementation of GenAI.

title: Exploring the impact of corporate volunteering characteristics on work engagement, work meaningfulness and job satisfaction
container-title: Journal of Organizational Change Management
6c814f164dcdf0f6998266ef3804b4a560229105.abstract: Purpose This study investigates how work engagement, work meaningfulness and job satisfaction differ within company volunteers depending on four corporate volunteering (CV) program characteristics – namely type of employee competencies involved in volunteering, type of beneficiary, type of employee contact with beneficiaries and role in volunteering program. Design/methodology/approach We collected data using an online, self-administered questionnaire targeting employees at companies in Poland that implement CV programs. A total of 983 completed questionnaires were collected. Findings The t-test results indicate that certain CV characteristics significantly influence work engagement, work meaningfulness and job satisfaction. Among these, the type of employee competencies used in volunteering consistently influenced all three outcomes. Beneficiary type had a significant effect only on work meaningfulness, while type of contact with beneficiaries and role played in CV program showed no significant effects on any outcome. Originality/value This study contributes to the broader organizational behaviour literature by providing empirical evidence of how specific CV program characteristics relate to important work-related outcomes. The results are valuable for managers seeking to create more satisfying, engaging and meaningful workplaces for their employees and, at the same time, to respond to the growing demand for companies to contribute to sustainable development by addressing social and environmental issues. The paper demonstrates the potential of CV programs to drive such workplace transformation, yielding positive effects inside and outside the company. It shows how organizations can transform their CV programs from traditional charity-based activities into strategic tools for developing employees, driving organizational change and achieving broader, positive social impact.

title: How corporate social irresponsibility erodes consumer trust and shapes consumer responses: a mediation analysis
container-title: Management Research Review
77e768a3acdad491327adcc0fb79e0b93c4465f1.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this study is to contribute to the emerging corpus of research on corporate social irresponsibility (CSI) and consumer behavior. To this end, this study explores a structural model on the impact of CSI on consumer trust erosion and the subsequent behaviors. It specifically investigates the extent to which CSI impairs consumer trust and addresses the mediating influence of this loss of trust on adverse behaviors, such as boycotting and complaining. Design/methodology/approach This study uses a sample of 204 consumers who have experienced a CSI incident with a brand (in the fashion industry) and uses structural equation modeling to explore relationship pathways and assess significant mediation effects. Findings The results reveal a significant effect between CSI and declining brand trust, increasing consumer complaints. However, this study did not support the expected direct links between CSI and boycotts, as well as between erosion of brand trust and complaints, suggesting that trust erosion facilitates boycott intentions. In contrast, CSI perception fosters complaints. Erosion of brand trust fully mediates the relationship between CSI and boycotts. Research limitations/implications Although this study tackles unexplored areas of consumer behavior, its limitations could offer valuable direction for further research. This study is limited to examining CSI and its impact on trust erosion, complaints and boycotts in the French context. This conceptual framework used can be examined in other contexts to strengthen the findings’ generalizability. Moreover, the model is based on individual responses to CSI by assuming that the dynamics of groups – anti-consumption or resistant communities – have not been included in the comprehensive model (e.g. Dessart et al., 2020; Valor et al., 2022). In addition, it excludes the cultural impact on the mediating construct, namely, trust erosion. Practical implications This study provides actionable guidance for brands to prevent or repair trust erosion following a CSI incident. This guidance comprises prompt public acknowledgment, transparent corrective action and monitoring trust independently of complaint volume, because low complaint levels do not necessarily indicate contained damage. Social implications This study applies psychological contract violation theory to the field of corporate social responsibility (CSR), viewing CSR as an underlying psychological contract between brands, consumers and society, and shows that perceived breaches of this contract as perceived through companies’ wrongdoing can lead to downward spiral in the relationship and result in brand boycott. Originality/value Even though extensive research on brand responsibility is available, the psychological mechanisms underlying consumer responses to CSI remain constrained. This study demonstrates the importance of trust erosion in post-crisis consumer relationships and the need for proactive strategies to attenuate its adverse impacts on consumer behavior.

title: The role of crowding and decision comfort during sales periods
container-title: Management Decision
dc28929f0b3bca52882c7528cdb17929a221486b.abstract: Purpose Sales periods simultaneously attract consumers through price reductions and trigger avoidance behaviors: a paradox this study addresses by examining decision comfort as a potential mediator of the effects of human and spatial crowding on visit postponement and store-switching. Gender is also examined as a moderator of these relationships. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative approach was adopted, with data collected from 378 consumers in France during official sales periods across several retail locations. The conceptual model was tested using structural equation modeling (SEM) to examine relationships among perceived crowding, decision comfort, visit postponement, and store-switching. Multi-group analysis assessed gender differences. Findings Both human and spatial crowding were negatively associated with decision comfort. Lower decision comfort was associated with higher levels of visit postponement and, less robustly, with store-switching. The indirect effect of spatial crowding on visit postponement through decision comfort was supported; the indirect effects of human crowding on both avoidance behaviors were also supported but modest in magnitude, whereas the indirect effect of spatial crowding on store-switching was not supported. Gender differences were detected in the crowding–decision comfort relationships, whereas no gender differences were detected in the decision comfort–avoidance paths. Originality/value This research contributes to the marketing literature by showing that the mediating role of decision comfort depends on the form of crowding and the avoidance response considered. It extends the application of decision comfort as an emerging construct in the retail context, offering new insights into how crowding shapes consumer decision-making. The study also identifies gender differences in the crowding–decision comfort relationships and provides managerial implications for improving retail experiences during sales.

title: The relationship between AI awareness and thriving at work: exploring the moderated mediation model
container-title: European Journal of Training and Development
cfd18b7156538271965b458c0a8e74dbffca959e.abstract: Purpose Drawing on the socially embedded model of thriving and the conservation of resources model, this study aims to investigate the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) awareness, seen as a hindrance stressor, and thriving at work. In particular, it explores how AI anxiety mediates this relationship and how self-efficacy moderates the mediating effect. Design/methodology/approach To securitize the study hypotheses, data were obtained from banking employees via an electronic questionnaire, yielding 320 valid responses. The proposed model relationships were assessed through partial least squares structural equation modeling and process analysis. Findings The results uncover that while AI awareness is not significantly linked to vitality, it is negatively correlated with learning. Furthermore, AI anxiety mediates the direct influence that AI awareness has on dimensions of thriving at work. In addition, self-efficacy acts as a buffer, mitigating the adverse indirect influence of AI awareness on thriving at work through AI anxiety. Practical implications This study highlights the need for organizations adopting AI-driven systems to execute‎ initiatives that mitigate AI-induced stress, thereby fostering employee thriving. It is recommended that organizations offer targeted training and digital literacy programs, alongside interventions designed to enhance self-efficacy, to bolster employee well-being amid rapid technological change. Originality/value This study highlights the need for organizations adopting AI-driven systems to execute‎ initiatives that mitigate AI-induced stress, thereby fostering employee thriving. It is recommended that organizations offer targeted training and revise their role descriptions, alongside interventions designed to enhance self-efficacy, to bolster employee well-being amid rapid technological change.

title: Unlocking creativity with artificial intelligence: field and experimental evidence on human resource management in the ready-made garments industry
container-title: International Journal of Manpower
5cd33850f1176a0a60ce31b07d460f0b68745e2f.abstract: Purpose This study examines how human–AI collaboration influences human resource management (HRM) creativity in Bangladesh’s readymade garments (RMG) industry, a labor-intensive sector facing persistent manpower challenges related to skills mismatch, absenteeism, turnover, worker voice, compliance, women’s advancement and production continuity. The study develops a human-centered “Goldilocks” perspective, arguing that AI contributes most effectively to HRM innovation when collaboration is neither too limited nor excessive. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on human-centered AI theory, creativity research and sector-specific HRM scholarship, the study adopts a three-study design. Study 1 examines AI collaboration in an RMG-focused HRM innovation task among business professionals. Study 2 extends the analysis to a larger working-adult sample with crowdsourced creativity ratings. Study 3 develops a field-oriented HRM model incorporating collaboration intensity, AI self-efficacy, knowledge diversity, problem restructuring, HR innovation climate, age and tenure. Findings Across the studies, moderate human–AI collaboration produces stronger creative HRM outcomes than low or high collaboration. Knowledge diversity emerges as the strongest explanatory mechanism, suggesting that AI enhances HRM creativity mainly by broadening the range of ideas, comparisons and workforce-related solutions available to managers. Excessive AI reliance, however, risks generic recommendations, anchoring effects, reduced contextual judgement and surveillance-oriented HRM practices. Originality/value The study contributes to manpower and HRM research by explaining how responsible AI collaboration can support creative workforce management in a labor-intensive emerging-economy industry. It advances a calibrated model of AI-enabled HRM in which technology strengthens, rather than replaces, human judgement, ethical interpretation and context-sensitive decision-making.

title: Managing critical raw materials supply chains: aligning capabilities and strategic levers for effective strategy formation under uncertainty
container-title: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management
3b79bec66e149196eeab7e3db690a1396d564c66.abstract: Purpose This study examines how firms should design supply chain strategies to secure Critical Raw Materials (CRM), which are scarce, geographically concentrated, and exposed to geopolitical and institutional interference. These features generate structural uncertainty that amplifies normative and mimetic pressures on strategic decision-making, exposing firms to strategic isomorphic bias and leading organizations to replicate legitimized sourcing templates rather than formulate strategies calibrated to their specific dependence structure. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Resource Dependence Theory, the study links key strategic levers (Supplier Substitutability, Discretion over the Resource, and Importance of the Resource) to underlying supply chain capabilities (resilience, agility, flexibility, sustainability, efficiency). A rank-ordered logit choice experiment with supply chain managers elicits preferred capability configurations in CRM supply scenarios, allowing the inference of the associated strategic levers while reducing strategic isomorphic bias in self-reported strategies. Findings Results show that Supplier Substitutability emerges as the dominant strategic lever for CRM-intensive supply chains. Resilience and sustainability are identified as the core capabilities underpinning this lever, supporting rapid reconfiguration of the supply base and the maintenance of legitimacy and stakeholder support under uncertainty. Originality/value The study theorizes an inside-out, bottom-up capability-driven strategy formation process, in which supply chain capabilities serve to infer effective strategic postures. It also demonstrates the value of experimental choice designs to reduce strategic and institutional bias in supply chain management research, particularly in politically sensitive domains such as the energy transition.

title: Unpacking top management team judgment in ethical cybersecurity disclosure: navigating transparency and confidentiality in corporate reporting across an emerging economy
container-title: International Journal of Ethics and Systems
a70eec4aea11433fd1efe83b74d38a0527150831.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how Saudi executives make cybersecurity disclosure decisions in a rapidly changing digital environment. Ethical principles guide these decisions. Modern ethical frameworks combine with contextual values, including Islamic notions of responsibility and harm prevention, which support balanced judgment when leaders navigate transparency, protection and regulatory expectations. Design/methodology/approach The research draws on 50 semistructured interviews with senior executives from finance, energy, industry, services, health care and technology. A thematic analysis supports the interpretation of ethical reasoning. Double coding, reflexive notes and sectoral comparison matrices strengthen analytical rigor. Findings Executives view cybersecurity disclosure as an ethical act. Transparency matters. Nonmaleficence dominates when disclosure may expose vulnerabilities. Leaders rely on responsibility, fairness and harm prevention. Islamic ethical principles reinforce these choices across all sectors. The Chief Digital Officer plays a central mediating role between technical, regulatory and stakeholder demands. Research limitations/implications The study focuses on one national context and one category of actors. Broader multistakeholder research is needed to deepen understanding. Practical implications Organizations benefit from ethical disclosure frameworks, stronger governance structures and training on ethical risk communication. Integrating Islamic ethics enhances legitimacy, coherence and trust. Originality/value The study provides one of the first empirical analyses showing how ethical and Islamic principles jointly guide cybersecurity disclosure in an emerging market undergoing rapid digital transformation.

title: Leadership agility in UAE public health care: enabling an agile mindset during digital transformation
container-title: International Journal of Islamic and Middle Eastern Finance and Management
aa7fd259ca360eac69c3beae576bb15d78edb321.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine how leadership agility shapes the development of an agile mindset within public health care organizations in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) during periods of digital and organizational transformation. It investigates how leaders at different levels of agility influence adaptability, collaboration and learning in highly regulated, hierarchical health-care environments. Design/methodology/approach A qualitative, multiple case study design was used. Data were collected through semistructured interviews with senior and middle managers, clinical leaders and document analysis across three UAE public health-care organizations. Thematic analysis was conducted using leadership agility theory to guide coding, interpretation and cross-case comparison. Findings Leadership agility operates along a developmental continuum. Expert- and achiever-level behaviors ensured operational stability, regulatory compliance and strategic alignment with national agendas, while catalyst, cocreator and synergist practices fostered adaptability, collaboration, innovation and learning. Organizational culture, learning orientation and strategies for managing resistance to change were identified as critical enablers or constraints in cultivating an agile mindset. Practical implications The study provides actionable insights for leaders and policymakers, emphasizing the need for context-sensitive, culturally informed leadership. Developing higher-level agile capabilities, fostering learning-oriented cultures and reframing resistance as feedback can enhance organizational responsiveness and sustainable transformation. Originality/value This research extends leadership agility theory by offering empirical evidence from a non-Western, public-sector health-care context, demonstrating how leadership agility interacts with culture and learning to enable agile mindsets in complex, regulated organizations.

title: From corporate digital responsibility to responsible cybersecurity: unpacking the role of substantive digital transformation
container-title: Journal of Science and Technology Policy Management
2f26e973df0a52aa4cea1b6fac696f6c6584c7aa.abstract: Purpose As digital-related threats affect organizations and stakeholders, understanding how firms develop responsible cybersecurity has become essential. This study aims to examine the role of corporate digital responsibility dimensions in promoting responsible cybersecurity through substantive digital transformation, addressing the limited empirical evidence on the pathways linking digital responsibility to cybersecurity practices. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey of 382 firms in Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam, was conducted using snowball sampling. The proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling and necessary condition analysis. Findings Ethical digital responsibility is positively associated with the economic, legal and philanthropic dimensions of corporate digital responsibility. Digital responsibilities are positively associated with substantive digital transformation, which statistically mediates the relationship between corporate digital responsibility and responsible cybersecurity. The results also show that legal and ethical dimensions of corporate digital responsibility are necessary conditions for achieving higher levels of substantive digital transformation. Originality/value Drawing on institutional theory, resource-based view and dynamic capabilities theory, this study contributes to the corporate digital responsibility literature by providing empirical evidence on the links between its dimensions, substantive digital transformation and responsible cybersecurity. By combining partial least squares structural equation modeling with necessary condition analysis, the study provides complementary evidence on both sufficiency and necessity relationships, offering an integrated empirical perspective on the conditions associated with responsible cybersecurity.

title: Challenging assumptions in supply chain management accounting and reporting: a metamodern sustainability transformation
container-title: Supply Chain Management: An International Journal
eb264fc9157650030cf6a172ee3c240bee7a499d.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to use a metamodern approach and a problematization lens to challenge the assumption that transparency driven accounting of historical social and environmental harms is sufficient to achieve the scale of sustainability transformation of supply chains required by scientific evidence. It argues that sustainability measurement, accounting and reporting must also encompass future orientated, positive and absolute sustainability contributions enabled by transformative product, business model and supply chain redesign. Design/methodology/approach A metamodern approach is introduced and used in the paper. Drawing on metamodernism, the paper develops a framework for oscillating between incremental, transparency-based measurement and more fundamental assessments of business development. Through problematization of existing literature, it identifies limiting assumptions and advances accounting and reporting for sustainable supply chain transformations. Findings The analysis reveals four dominant assumptions in sustainability accounting and reporting that constrain sufficiently far-reaching sustainability transformations of supply chains: backward looking transparency, supplier assessment logics, harm reduction framing and incremental improvements. The proposed metamodern framework broadens the role of accounting by integrating multiple intelligence sources to support monitoring of existing supply chains and identification of redesign opportunities aligned with planetary boundaries and the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals. Research limitations/implications The paper provides a metamodern foundation for future empirical development and testing of transformative sustainability measurement and accounting that embraces different intelligence sources. Practical implications Measurement and accounting informed by metamodern theory oscillates between different intelligence sources, comprising data, information and knowledge, to support both monitoring of existing supply chain relationships and identification of transformative redesign opportunities. Social implications The argument supports development of supply chain strategies and designs capable of addressing the easing of social and environmental harms as well as development of transformative sustainability opportunities. Originality/value To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this is the first paper to apply a metamodern lens to sustainability accounting and reporting for supply chain management. It shows how oscillation between modernist and postmodern logics opens new pathways for theorizing transformative measurement and positions accounting information as a catalyst for strategic redesign rather than incremental optimization.

title: A new lease on life? A survival analysis approach to the study of professional sport stadiums and arenas
container-title: Sport, Business and Management: An International Journal
25a7ca0d85d39911d705e259afe24572ed68bec9.abstract: Purpose The length of time that a sport facility remains in use is a critical piece of information for sport organizations and the municipalities that allocate hundreds of millions in taxpayer dollars to fund them, rather than contributing funding to societal issues. Despite this fact, prior approaches have either truncated their durations at present day or arbitrarily analyzed subsets of data. Design/methodology/approach As a solution, we analyze a dataset of more than 200 professional sport facilities using survival analysis, and discuss differences based on type of facility, tenants, and whether it is a single or multi-tenant facility. Findings Results indicate that lifetimes vary based on whether measures of central tendency or survival methods are applied. Specifically, results reveal that facility lifetimes are considerably longer than previously calculated. Research limitations/implications This study makes a unique and novel contribution to the stadium literature in its utilization of an advanced data analysis technique to quantify the lifetime of sport facilities. Practical implications These results provide empirical evidence that municipalities negotiating with sport franchises may have a substantiation for significantly longer lease agreements, a novel managerial implication. Originality/value These data may be used by financiers to better assess and plan for the impending death of a facility based on a variety of factors.
