title: AI-Powered Global Expansion: The Impact of Artificial Intelligence Adoption on Firms’ Outward Foreign Direct Investment
container-title: Journal of Academic Research and Advances
637d8e42c2f43232a8a9f9a4df0bdbd08128534a.abstract: Against the backdrop of profound shifts in the global economic landscape and rapid advances in digital technologies, artificial intelligence (AI) offers firms new opportunities to expand into international markets and improve the allocation of resources across borders. Drawing on a sample of Chinese A-share listed firms from 2009 to 2024, this study empirically examines the relationship between AI adoption and outward foreign direct investment (OFDI), with particular attention to the mechanisms underlying this relationship. The findings indicate that AI adoption is positively and significantly associated with firms’ OFDI activities. This result remains robust across a range of alternative specifications, including different measures of AI adoption, adjustments to fixed effects and standard-error clustering, and the exclusion of selected observations. Heterogeneity analyses suggest that the positive relationship is more pronounced among technology-intensive firms and larger enterprises. Further analysis identifies two potential channels through which AI adoption may facilitate OFDI: technological innovation and the alleviation of financial constraints. Together, these mechanisms may strengthen firms’ technological capabilities and improve their access to the financial resources required for international expansion. By examining OFDI through the lens of firm-level AI adoption, this study extends the literature on the determinants of international investment and provides further insight into how AI may shape firms’ internationalization strategies. The findings also offer empirical evidence relevant to the integration of AI into the real economy, the enhancement of firms’ international competitiveness, and China’s efforts to pursue higher-standard economic opening-up.

title: Emphatic Negation as Focus: A Case Study in Italian
La negació emfàtica com a focus: el cas de l’italià
container-title: Catalan Journal of Linguistics
af15f167db99b7321a01e4b5924db8f8d670a51d.abstract: This paper proposes a syntactic approach to ‘emphatic’ negative structures based on three components, namely a) the regular semantics of negation, b) the distinction between Corrective and Contrastive Focus (Bianchi & Bocci 2012), c) the size of the constituent targeted by Focus. We analyze the distribution of Italian ‘emphatic’ negative structures featuring two different lexical items, namely the adverb mica and the response particle NO. On this basis, we argue that their emphatic import corresponds to different functions, which we dub Correction and Confirmation, and that the specific function and pragmatic distribution of each structure is structurally determined.

title: Paying for Quality or Buying Compliance? Rethinking Performance-Based Executive Compensation in Ontario Hospitals
container-title: Healthcare Management Forum
305fb489904c648f3bc48069057bb98412252a4e.abstract: Ontario’s Excellent Care for All Act requires hospitals to link executive compensation to quality improvement plan targets. More than 15 years later, this article asks whether the evidence supports that design. A narrative review of Ontario policy documents, Canadian and international research on executive pay and pay-for-performance was conducted, and behavioural science on incentives was analyzed. Pay-at-risk in Ontario is small, largely penalty-only under compensation restraint, and was associated with conservative target-setting. International evidence shows short-lived process gains, little effect on patient outcomes, and predictable gaming. No published evaluation was identified linking the Act’s pay-at-risk requirement to patient outcomes. Boards can remain compliant while redesigning the link as a small, shared, multi-year, independently verified component weighted towards patient safety and workforce outcomes. The Healthcare Executive Incentive Framework 2030 sets out domains, weights, governance safeguards, and an evaluation agenda.

title: Predicting East Africa’s rainfall extremes with calibrated AI post-processing systems
container-title: npj Natural Hazards
ec9141399a544d08ca24ab587ea2340b91490af5.abstract: Abstract Accurate and reliable rainfall forecasts are crucial for Early Warning Systems (EWS). Artificial Intelligence approaches, which post-process global physical forecasts, enable low-cost ensemble generation, extending skill to medium-range lead times and offering scalable systems to inform EWS, particularly under resource-constrained settings. However, assessing their practical value in representing user-relevant rainfall extremes and guiding decisions for EWS remains critical. We present a low-cost, uncertainty quantification method that calibrates ensemble forecasts to probabilities of exceedances for rainfall extremes. Applied to raw and post-processed rainfall forecasts over East Africa, sub-regional analysis shows the threshold-calibrated, post-processed forecasts better reflecting the observed chances of extremes at higher rainfall thresholds. Case-study results show encouraging added value from post-processed forecasts at longer lead times. Forecast skill decomposed across rainfall and probability thresholds highlights the ranges of rainfall and risk tolerances where most actionable improvement arises, whether using satellite or rain-gauge data as reference. This tailored evaluation helps guide forecast adoption for EWS.

title: The Effect of Technology Utilization, Internal Control Systems, and Environmental Costs on Financial Reporting Quality
container-title: MARGINAL JOURNAL OF MANAGEMENT ACCOUNTING GENERAL FINANCE AND INTERNATIONAL ECONOMIC ISSUES
b6b5ca85138dc5f9fd1b5ed477f3e2d4ed326660.abstract: Financial reporting quality is essential for ensuring transparency, accountability, and the reliability of financial information in hospital management. However, the extent to which technology utilization, internal control systems, and environmental cost management contribute to financial reporting quality requires further empirical examination. This study aims to analyze the effects of technology utilization, internal control systems, and environmental costs on financial reporting quality at Rosela Hospital, Karawang, Indonesia. A quantitative approach was employed using a questionnaire-based survey involving employees in finance, accounting, and administration selected through purposive sampling. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS. The findings indicate that technology utilization and internal control systems do not have statistically significant effects on financial reporting quality, whereas environmental costs have a positive and significant effect. These results suggest that the availability of technology and internal control mechanisms alone may not be sufficient to improve financial reporting quality, while appropriate environmental cost management can contribute to more comprehensive and accountable financial information. This study concludes that hospitals should strengthen the identification, classification, recording, and reporting of environmental costs as part of their financial management practices. The practical impact of this research is to provide insights for hospital management into improving financial accountability and developing more transparent reporting practices. The findings should be interpreted in the context of the study’s limited scope, which focuses on a single hospital.

title: Measuring the geometric parameters of woven fabrics with AI chatbots: a benchmark and three paths to higher accuracy
container-title: Research Journal of Textile and Apparel
4d55cae7f658133b1c2ac11d6e85d0ac844e8650.abstract: Purpose Publicly available multimodal chatbots could make fabric geometry measurement accessible in low-resource settings, yet their accuracy for this task has never been systematically evaluated. This study aims to benchmark six such chatbots and investigates whether protocol-level improvements can raise measurement accuracy without model fine-tuning, unavailable to end users. Design/methodology/approach One hundred woven fabrics were scanned and their ground-truth values – weave type, thread count, cover factor, twist direction and twist angle – were measured according to ISO/ASTM. Six chatbots were tested with five runs per fabric, yielding 3,000 tests. Three improvement paths were examined: intra-system averaging, prompt enrichment with known fabric data and inter-system aggregation. Errors were quantified via misclassification rate (MCR) and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). Findings Baseline accuracy was far below metrological requirements (MCR = 15–46%, MAPE = 9–34%). Three repeated runs indicated variability of ± 2–4 percentage points. Intra-system averaging and prompt refinement produced small, heterogeneous changes within this variability. Inter-system aggregation reduced five errors: weave MCR 32% to 21%, thread count MAPE 14% to 7%, cover factor MAPE 12% to 7%, twist direction MCR 32% to 20% and twist angle MAPE 28% to 18%. Paired tests showed significant differences between Path 3 and matched conditions after correction. Originality/value Aggregating heterogeneous, non-specialised chatbot outputs reduced fabric-geometry measurement error without model training. The resulting applicability matrices illustrate the potential operational range of each parameter, providing a parameter-by-parameter framework for interpreting the trade-off between accuracy and accessibility in low-infrastructure textile screening.

title: Causal Integration of Financial and Non–Financial Information in Strategic Accounting
container-title: Problems of Modern Transformations. Series: Economics and Management
e024e2c0a2c0dba71098797d0e9da7075d63a2c4.abstract: Non-financial indicators can influence strategic decisions, but their joint presentation with financial data does not explain the transmission mechanism. Treating an untested causal hypothesis as an established financial effect creates a risk of false precision. This study develops a conceptual procedure for documenting and revising causal routes in strategic accounting. A purposive integrative review of 20 standard-setting, discussion and scholarly sources is combined with comparative decomposition and logical construction. The research gap is restricted to the reviewed corpus; neither exhaustive literature coverage nor empirical validation is claimed. The working proposition is that the same non-financial change can yield different accounting consequences depending on its mechanism, destination and evidential status. The analysis distinguishes inherited concepts from proposed integration rules and groups review questions by the interpretation failures they address. The resulting Causal Accounting Integration Map (CAIM) connects a measured driver, transmission mechanism, specified accounting or forecast parameter and decision. Accounting addressability is defined as an operational property of a route, distinct from materiality and recognition. Four integration states are presented as a logical classification, while eight evidence criteria constitute an open diagnostic checklist rather than necessary and sufficient conditions. The proposed contribution is a rule separating a hypothesis, a conditional financial scenario and an evidence-supported route, with an explicit accounting destination, disconfirmation conditions and revision procedure. A hypothetical illustration shows why improved resource efficiency need not produce a positive net financial effect. The theoretical implication is a more explicit distinction between financial relevance and the evidential status of a decision input. Potential applications include budgeting, investment appraisal and internal review of assumptions; improved practical outcomes remain untested. Future research should compare CAIM with existing indicator governance and assess agreement between independent reviewers. This is a theoretical and methodological article.

title: Governing work delegated to AI through dynamic control fit
b4bcf2ad069df09c25a6ca3a7753fd577733549c.abstract: Abstract When organizations delegate work to artificial intelligence (AI), controls that remain formally in place may no longer achieve their purposes. We combine systematic identification and selection with integrative analysis of 171 papers across five research streams and 26 supplementary sources. The synthesis develops dynamic control fit: an arrangement's ability to achieve a specified control function while sustaining or restoring the conditions on which that function depends. We explain this ability through a framework of three interconnected requirements: Deliver, Renew and Adapt. Deliver concerns whether coverage, information, expertise and opportunities to intervene support effective control in current work. Renew concerns the practice, feedback and maintenance through which these capabilities persist. Adapt concerns recognizing deficiencies, obtaining authorized changes and verifying restored performance. The framework explains how AI may improve immediate enforcement while reducing experiences through which people develop judgment for future oversight, although other activities may compensate. Coverage, reviewer capacity and revision authority impose distinct constraints requiring different responses. Continued reliance must also be assessed separately from performance because beliefs, external expectations and practical constraints can sustain or limit use. By following a specified function across changes in control arrangements, the review develops testable explanations of improvement, erosion, compensation and recovery.

title: Revisiting Corominas et al. (2014)—Recommendations for the Quantitative Analysis of Landslide Risk
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
4e05ed226a295ee6596316bbd427fec5164ccace.abstract: Abstract Corominas et al. (2014) synthesised recommended methodologies for quantitative landslide hazard, vulnerability and risk analysis across spatial scales and for verification/validation of outputs. This chapter revisits the paper as a technical benchmark for quantitative landslide risk analysis, highlighting its structured decomposition of hazard (spatial, temporal and intensity components), exposure characterisation and physical vulnerability assessment. Strengths include the explicit linkage from susceptibility to hazard, the treatment of different landslide types and a comprehensive toolbox for model testing. Remaining challenges concern the scarcity of temporal information, the limited representation of landslide intensity and runout at broader scales and the consistent propagation and communication of uncertainty in risk estimates.

title: Revisiting Wildavsky & Dake (1990)—Theories of Risk Perception: Who Fears What and Why?
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
d584c17adf3518e7be82be9984f1dd226d787c0f.abstract: Abstract Wondering ‘﻿who fears what and why?’ lies at the heart of risk perception research. This question has challenged scholars to uncover the social, cultural and cognitive-affective roots of how dangers are understood and deliberated (Wildavsky and Dake 1990). Empirically tested Cultural Theory against rival explanations—such as risk knowledge, personality traits and economic and political factors. By distinguishing among hierarchists, egalitarians and individualists, they demonstrated that these socio-cultural worldviews significantly shape risk perceptions. Their work also showcased how a comprehensive, interdisciplinary approach—combining socio-cultural, psychological, economic and political factors—could illuminate why distinct groups perceive and discuss risks differently. In later work, Cultural Theory was integrated with psychometric models of affect, cognitive theories of decision-making and institutional analyses of power and trust. These advancements highlight that risk perceptions are shaped not only by culture but also by affect, material conditions and systemic inequalities. The enduring strength of Cultural Theory lies in its ability to reveal how conflicts over danger often reflect deeper disputes about values, power and social order. However, its modest explanatory power and the static nature of hypothesised cultural categories call for more interdisciplinary work. Future research should focus on bridging Cultural Theory with complementary conceptual frameworks. We may thus better address pressing societal risks that often lead to polarised social debates—from climate change to technological disasters. This may help us foster inclusive, evidence-based and ethically grounded risk governance.

title: Revisiting Fischhoff et al. (1978)—How Safe is Safe Enough? A Psychometric Study of Attitudes Towards Technological Risks and Benefits
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
6afa801ef071190d0fbfff4bca0b269b9b8bc87c.abstract: Abstract Fischhoff et al. (1978) developed the psychometric paradigm of risk perception. The researchers asked 76 participants from Eugene, Oregon’s League of Women Voters and their spouses to rate their perceived risks and benefits of thirty activities or technologies. This participant sample is highly focused, as are the methods by prescribing the activities and technologies to be assessed along with the ways of assessing them. The results proffer patterns, and the authors interpret those patterns sensibly, with appropriate caution and without either overstating or understating significance. The data and analysis ultimately distil into the paper’s core thesis, representing a major advance at the time: the proposition that risk perception is broadly determined across two dimensions. First, a known-unknown axis and, second, the level of certainty of death if something goes wrong. Perceived benefit is added as a third dimension for predicting acceptability of activities and technologies.

title: Revisiting Guzzetti et al. (1999)—Landslide Hazard Evaluation: A Review of Current Techniques and Their Application in a Multiscale Study, Central Italy
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
09f5930c09858869f2afc72eb08c2dcf7025ef48.abstract: Abstract This review analyses the article ‘Landslide hazard evaluation: a foundational insight to landslide hazard assessment’ by Guzzetti et al. (1999), who critically examined the concepts, assumptions and methods underpinning the field at the end of the twentieth century. The paper is rooted in the evolution of risk research and highlights its clear distinction between landslide hazard and landslide susceptibility. By exploring mapping units, modelling approaches and scale effects, and applying these to multiscale statistical analyses in Central Italy, the authors clarified both the potential and the limitations of Geographic Information System-based quantitative methods. The paper demonstrates how susceptibility modelling has consolidated as a legitimate planning tool. While it focuses on this specific aspect, the foundation it builds can pave the way for addressing broader questions of disaster risk, vulnerability and governance in subsequent research and applications. The analysis emphasises the paper’s conceptual rigour, methodological transparency and enduring relevance to modern research, situating its contributions within the hazard-centred paradigms that preceded later advances in integrated disaster risk studies.

title: Revisiting Beck (1992)—From Industrial Society to the Risk Society: Questions of Survival, Social Structure and Ecological Enlightenment
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
c451e074fcebf65e4c1952efffe35ad4f4a0f81d.abstract: Abstract This chapter discusses the article ‘From industrial society to the risk society’, in which the German sociologist Ulrich Beck introduces his theory of the risk society. He argues that society today is confronted with qualitatively new, globally dispersed and potentially catastrophic risks that undermine the risk logic of industrial society, in which risks could be delimited, measured, calculated and controlled. Techno-economic development produces risks that are unmanageable, leaving individuals and societies unprotected and generating new socio-spatial lines of conflict.

title: Revisiting Renn & Schweizer (2009)—Inclusive Risk Governance: Concepts and Application to Environmental Policy Making
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
2fd1803f8dd62c97f6ec179f2934f3b951e61aea.abstract: Abstract Ortwin Renn and Pia Schweizer’s 2009 article, “Inclusive risk governance: Concepts and applications to environmental policy making”, expands the theoretical literature regarding the goals of participatory decision making. The primary contribution of Renn and Schweizer’s article is the introduction of six concepts, grounded in philosophical traditions, for engaging interested parties in decision making. Ultimately, Renn and Schweizer advocate an analytic-deliberative decision process, which reflects functionalist and deliberative concepts. Empirical research has shown that these concepts are popular among the public, but instrumental and coercive goals also exist. Given the polarisation that has accompanied the populist movements in western democracies, cynicism about inclusive governance is understandable. However, a well-managed analytic-deliberative process may provide opportunities for participants to find shared facts and values.

title: Revisiting Keeney & Von Winterfeldt (1986)—Improving Risk Communication
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
189bc3c81d988e67c8874a819c965fac53e98983.abstract: Abstract This article reviews Ralph L. Keeney and Detlof von Winterfeldt’s (1986) article ‘Improving risk communication’, a landmark work that established risk communication as a distinct form of decision-making and risk-analysis practice within the field of crisis management. The challenges, objectives and strategies provided to improve risk communication are still considered important aspects in contemporary debates of risk communication. Nevertheless, its assumptions concerning the dichotomy between experts and the public and its expert-driven focus on translating risks towards the public demonstrate the theoretical assumptions of its era regarding risk communication in the 1980s. The field has since then evolved towards an understanding of the social and cultural aspects within risk perception, the importance of local knowledges from various public groups in risk analysis and the relevance of multiway, relational and participatory dialogue in risk communication. Yet, these participatory approaches bring their own challenges and limitations, which is why the framework proposed in the article continues to offer valuable insights for risk communication today.

title: Revisiting DeConto & Pollard (2016)—Contribution of Antarctica to Past and Future Sea-Level Rise
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
18d44517c0f81c20e8684b77c466fde3be8e7d0d.abstract: Abstract This chapter reviews the 2016 study by DeConto and Pollard, which introduced for the first time two new processes into a continental-scale Antarctic Ice Sheet model, producing sea-level rise projections significantly larger than previous estimates. We contextualise the study within sea-level rise risk research and its reliance on the projections of the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, and examine how subsequent assessments struggled to incorporate its findings given the uncertainty surrounding the processes. The study prompted a rapid response from the scientific community and shaped high-end sea-level rise scenarios used in coastal risk assessments, though its most extreme projections have since been tempered by systematic re-analyses and improved physical modelling of the processes. The paper’s legacy lies in highlighting Antarctica as a potentially large and deeply uncertain contributor to future sea-level rise, with profound implications for coastal adaptation planning.

title: Revisiting Weick (1988)—Enacted Sensemaking in Crisis Situations
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
d0aae13373d3c542dcd0a0f0153b379bb571afd1.abstract: Abstract This article revisits Weick’s (1988) influential paper on enacted sensemaking in crisis situations, exploring how organisational actors actively construct and interpret their environments during crises. It outlines Weick’s background, the context of the Journal of Management Studies , and the main contributions of the original work, including the enactment framework and its focus on commitment, capacity and expectations. Furthermore, it assesses the impact of Weick’s ideas on crisis management research, particularly their role in shaping high reliability theory. It critically examines the structure, logic and evidence of the 1988 paper, noting its conceptual strengths, reliance on qualitative analysis and limitations regarding empirical validation and generalisability. The review highlights how Weick’s work redirected crisis analysis away from technical failures toward the processes of enacted sensemaking within organisations.

title: Revisiting Quarantelli & Dynes (1977)—Response to Social Crisis and Disaster
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
dabfe6e37778811a4a863a221cad0a70148c947c.abstract: Abstract This review revisits Quarantelli and Dynes “Response to social crisis and disaster” (1977) and explains why it became an essential work in disaster and risk research. It highlights its key strengths: a consistent definition of disasters as social events and a synthesis of “substantive” and “structural” trends, including the shift from individual behaviour to organisations, coordination and systems. It also identifies weaknesses: a strong demarcation that excludes related literature and limited inclusion of political conflicts, inequality and controversial disaster responses. The conclusion links these points to current debates on pandemics and the German legal framework for “disasters” and makes a brief reference to the findings of the article and current research on emergent groups, e.g. spontaneous and digital volunteers.

title: Revisiting Davoudi (2012)—Resilience: A Bridging Concept or a Dead End?
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
3ade8820557db8558cfc7a034e6136b5a6031f1c.abstract: Abstract Fifteen years later, this contribution revisits Simin Davoudi’s article, “Resilience: A bridging concept or a dead end?”, focusing particularly on its impact and subsequent debates in urban planning, disaster risk reduction and climate adaptation. Beginning with an analysis of the aims and content of Davoudi’s work, it illustrates how papers published between 2012 and 2026, which explicitly refer to her essay, build upon and expand the notion of evolutionary resilience. The gradual spread of this concept within the theoretical sphere is evident, as is the persistent gap between theory and practice. It also notes the difficulty in providing effective answers to the numerous questions posed by Davoudi and taken up by scholars in subsequent years regarding issues, such as social justice and equity, which are often raised by the application of the concept of resilience.

title: Revisiting Tversky & Kahneman (1974)—Judgement Under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
007b6ba382aa25a64996a9d49f79a6e82db4df2a.abstract: Abstract Tversky and Kahneman’s article represents a foundational shift in the understanding of human judgement under uncertainty, demonstrating that systematic deviations from normative rationality are structurally embedded in cognitive processes. Through minimalist but elegant experimental designs, the authors introduced a heuristic-based account of reasoning that reshaped both theory and methodology in psychology and decision science. At the same time, the paper’s reliance on hypothetical scenarios and controlled laboratory tasks raises enduring questions about empirical robustness, ecological validity and generalisability to real-world decision contexts. Notably, the framework offers no practical strategies for debiasing, education or system design and does not guide the translation of its insights into applied interventions. Critics, such as Gigerenzer, further challenge the assumption that deviation from formal logic necessarily constitutes error, arguing that such tasks measure norm conformity rather than adaptive intelligence. Despite these limitations, the article’s conceptual, methodological and disciplinary impact remains profound, influencing behavioural economics, decision theory, medical decision-making and public policy.

title: Management of tibial post fractures in posterior stabilized total knee arthroplasties: Case series and review of literature
container-title: Traumatology and Orthopedics of Russia
b026dbcede1bce5dd303a68a1d01ae43bddcb778.abstract: Background: Highly Crosslinked Polyethylene was introduced to decrease plastic wear and subsequent osteolysis. However, this was at the expense of the mechanical properties of the polyethylene slightly reducing its overall physical strength. Fracture of the polyethylene tibial post is a rare but catastrophic complication in posterior-stabilized (PS) total knee arthroplasty (TKA). Aim of the study: We report 4 cases of fractured tibial post in a posterior stabilized total knee with highly Crosslinked Polyethylene. Clinical presentations, intraoperative findings, and failure mechanisms are evaluated, alongside a systematic literature review. Methods: Between May 2019 and September 2024, four cases with fractured tibial posts were presented and managed at our institution. Clinical records, pre- and postoperative radiographs, failure timeframes, and surgical intervention were retrospectively reviewed. Results: Patients predominantly presented with unexplained acute onset of instability and effusion in a previously well-functioning total knee arthroplasty. Mean time from the primary knee replacement procedure to the onset of symptoms was 11.25 years (range 9–14). Revision surgery was successfully performed in all four cases ranging from isolated liner exchange to full components revision with a constrained non hinged prosthesis. Conclusions: Tibial post fracture should be strongly suspected in patients with late instability following PS TKA. Surgeons should be aware of this rare complication. The regular use of highly crosslinked polyethylene in Posterior stabilized total knee arthroplasty is not advisable, with a better shift to stronger and newer types of plastic. Keywords: Posterior stabilized total knee arthroplasty; Highly cross linked polyethylene; Tibial post fracture; Revision knee surgery

title: Revisiting Cutter et al. (2003)—Social Vulnerability to Environmental Hazards
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
dbb0854ffbac8636c7844dd5f7d72f60398dc210.abstract: Abstract The Social Vulnerability Index (SoVI), initially published and applied by Susan Cutter, Bryan J. Boruff and W. Lynn Shirley in 2003, marked a pivotal moment in contemporary disaster research. It continues to serve as a key instrument for quantifying and visualising vulnerability. SoVI links spatial and social factors that generate vulnerability and enables their comparative assessment across time and space. Vulnerability-related variables are extracted from disaster research, aligned with available datasets such as census data, and operationalised through factor analysis. Despite limitations related to data availability and operationalisability, SoVI remains a seminal approach to comparative vulnerability assessment and has been widely applied across disciplines.

title: Revisiting Slovic (1987)—Perception of Risk
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
87f502ee446c819a5a251edc53691d81120289d5.abstract: Abstract The chapter analyses Paul Slovic’s review paper in Science on risk perception and the psychometric paradigm. His paper is grounded in the social sciences and the role of non-expert judgments in debates about risk and the risk management process during the 1970s to 1980s. Slovic provides a brief history of risk perception and its measurement (psychometric paradigm) and the utility and usage of the findings for decision-makers to forecast the public acceptance of various technologies or activities. Slovic acknowledges that the public may make errors in their judgments and not have complete information about risks but advocates for non-expert conceptualisation of risks as part of the formal risk assessment process otherwise risk management efforts could fail without public support. The present chapter provides other contextual information on the impact of the paper on the field since its publication, the relevance of its findings, the strengths and weaknesses of the collective research effort, and areas of current and future research.

title: Six Decades of Risk Research: Introduction
container-title: Civil Protection, Disaster Management, and Resilience
Six Decades of Risk Research
c7cad2b823d206d6aa22a9a43abccfafe6fca090.abstract: Abstract Risk research has evolved from a predominantly technical discipline into a broad interdisciplinary field integrating perspectives from engineering, psychology, sociology, geography, geology, economics, governance, among others. This introductory chapter traces the intellectual development of risk research from its historical origins to contemporary debates, highlighting the scientific contributions that have fundamentally shaped the field over the past six decades. Organised chronologically, it examines 42 landmark publications that transformed understanding of risk, including advances in quantitative risk assessment, the psychometric paradigm, cultural theory, vulnerability and resilience research, risk communication, governance, and systemic risk. The chapter further explores the influence of major global events—including technological accidents, climate change, the COVID-19 pandemic, and natural hazards that led to disasters—on the evolution of research priorities and conceptual frameworks. By documenting the historical trajectory of influential ideas and identifying emerging challenges, the chapter provides both an intellectual roadmap of risk research and a foundation for future scholarship in disaster risk reduction, climate change adaptation, and risk governance. Finally, the editors argue for the continued importance of engaging with primary scientific literature to strengthen scientific literacy, critical thinking, and evidence-informed decision-making, while providing the intellectual framework for the volume’s subsequent chapters.

title: Gcn5 and mTORC1 mediated regulation of autophagy controls Drosophila blood cell homeostasis
container-title: eLife
700db83f75519837e25d45ca5d0f3b8c17d2c4a4.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Blood progenitors are regulated by a variety of systemic and nutritional cues from their environment. In the
                    <jats:italic>Drosophila</jats:italic>
                    lymph gland (LG), the Posterior Signaling Center acts as a stem cell niche striking a balance between progenitors and differentiated blood cells. Autophagy is a vital cellular process that maintains homeostasis by removing unnecessary or dysfunctional cell components through autophagic degradation and recycling. Here, using genetic perturbation analysis, we show that autophagy plays a critical role in regulating LG blood cell homeostasis. General control non-derepressible 5 (Gcn5), a histone acetyltransferase, is expressed in the primary LG lobe, and modulation of Gcn5 levels perturbs LG homeostasis. Our results show that hemocyte-specific Gcn5 modulation controls autophagic flux in the hemocytes. Furthermore, we show that modulation of mTORC1 activity can perturb hematopoiesis. Our results indicate that organismal Gcn5 levels respond to dietary shifts and are modulated by mTORC1 signaling. Chemical intervention shows that mTORC1 overrides the effect exerted by Gcn5 in regulating LG hematopoiesis. Taken together, our findings demonstrate that Gcn5 and mTORC1 regulate autophagy to maintain blood cell homeostasis in
                    <jats:italic>Drosophila</jats:italic>
                    .
                  </jats:p>

title: Beyond Belief Updating: A Framework for Self-Belief Formation
3796862ab71587287fb46c3bdf9532408a32202a.abstract: From early childhood, we form self-beliefs about where we belong, what we are good at, or who loves us. Despite extensive psychological research on self-beliefs, the fundamental question of how they initially form has received surprisingly little attention. Existing work on self-belief updating overlooks two critical limitations. First, it treats self-related learning as arising from isolated events, ignoring that self-beliefs typically emerge from sequences of meaningfully connected experiences. Second, because updating paradigms operate in familiar domains, participants already hold precise prior beliefs intertwined with established motives and emotional states making it impossible to study belief formation from a genuinely uninformed starting point. We propose that studying novel experiential domains addresses both problems: individuals enter such domains with neutral, imprecise self-beliefs, enabling formation of “artificial” self-beliefs through repeated feedback in a controlled setting. As a concrete implementation, we introduce the Learning Of Own Performance (LOOP) task, in which participants form beliefs about their abilities in a novel performance domain. Extensions of this approach could illuminate broader aspects of self-belief formation, including personality and identity. This Perspective bridges psychology, computational neuroscience, and sociology around a foundational question: how do we come to think about ourselves the way we do?

title: Decentralized Finance and Digital Assets: A New Perspective on Financial Management and Risk
container-title: Lex localis - Journal of Local Self-Government
13b14090a5c64d7c3224b43ae85f72408e707dbf.abstract: <jats:p>Financial services are being transformed, how they are designed, accessed, and managed, by the rise of decentralized finance (DeFi) and digital assets. These innovations via blockchain networks, smart contracts, and tokenization offer alternatives to existing models for payments, lending, investment, and asset exchange. But the economic, institutional and operating risks of financial intermediation are not eroded when transactions are automated. In this conceptual study, the impact of DeFi and digital assets on financial management is explored, including capital allocation, treasury operations, risk management, and the governance of digital assets. It assesses what could be gained from this technology, alongside its potential technological vulnerabilities, market instability, regulatory uncertainty and inability to provide meaningful financial inclusion. An analysis approach is built to present a managerial perspective, which considers digital financial arrangements from an economic function, dependency and accountability standpoint. It points out that sustainable adoption requires coordination of technology with financial management, strong rights, organizational efficiency and appropriate governance. DeFi is therefore a reorganization of financial management and not the automatic replacement of existing financial institutions.</jats:p>

title: Blockchain Technology in Management: Opportunities, Risks and Governance Challenges
container-title: Lex localis - Journal of Local Self-Government
37cc95f3465e4e0fb32f40a5e9c5644d70c42fdc.abstract: <jats:p>The idea of using blockchain seems to be gaining support as a way to facilitate transactions between organizations which don't have a shared database or administration. The importance of its management, however, is subject to debate. This article provides a critical assessment of the opportunities, risks and governance issues of organizations taking up blockchain technology. Research is synthesized into a focused narrative organized by three themes—Organizational Value, Implementation Constraints and Institutional Governance Responsibilities—that are grounded in the foundational research, further developed by management and information-systems scholarship, and then extended by institutional guidance. Several potential benefits are suggested in the literature: record reconciliation, traceability of the supply chain, auditing and rule-based transaction processing. This is only achievable by partner willingness to share, the validity of the source information and the appropriateness of blockchain over traditional databases. Potential gains might be offset by technical risks, privacy issues, organizational challenges, and uncertainties regarding regulations. In arguing this, the article does not suggest that you can forgo identifiable decision responsibilities, human responsibility or good dispute resolution when you decentralize record validation. Strategic fit, network design, accountability, information stewardship and performance review are the elements of an integrated governance framework. The paper provides an action-oriented consideration of blockchain adoption, considering benefits not as inherent properties of blockchain but rather possibilities that are likely to occur when blockchain is adopted.</jats:p>

title: Managing Investment Decisions and Risk in Decentralized Financial Markets: Evidence from Blockchain-Based Platforms
container-title: Lex localis - Journal of Local Self-Government
5970dbe0d163fa1f2d86a6ee377a5277f5d7e7c5.abstract: <jats:p>Decentralized finance (DeFi) has provided alternative investment, lending, trading, asset management and other methods via blockchain on both public and private platforms. Unlike traditional financial institutions, DeFi protocols rely on smart contracts for transactions, collateral, and financial returns and do not depend on the entire reliance of the centralized intermediaries. The innovations provide access, transparency and operational efficiency but also financial, technological, liquidity, and governance risks to the investor. This study adopts a structured literature review approach of academic studies, institutional reports and documented platforms mechanisms and investigates the investment decision making and risk management in decentralized financial markets. The cases of platform Uniswap, Aave, Compound, and MakerDAO are not meant to represent an empirical sample, but instead serve as examples to illustrate the platforms. Thematic synthesis take account of the concepts of portfolio theory and information asymmetry, highlighting the centrality of factors like expected return, collateral management, security of smart contracts, the reliability of oracles, concentration of governance, and regulatory uncertainty. It concludes that transparency of record and liquidation automation can enhance transaction discipline, but will not be enough to prevent losses in stressed markets all on its own. The study suggests an integrated decision-making approach that incorporates elements of financial, technological due diligence, governance appraisal, Exposure limits and ongoing monitoring. The results offer a basis for future transaction level tests of the effectiveness of risk adjusted investment strategies.</jats:p>

title: A Survey of Learning-based Method Name Prediction
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
48b81eddcf90694d4fefcd0a971c62e474bcae45.abstract: <jats:p>The choice of method names significantly influences code comprehension and maintenance, posing a considerable challenge, especially for novice developers. Automating the prediction of appropriate method names based on the method code body has emerged as a promising approach to address this challenge. In recent years, numerous Machine/Deep Learning (ML/DL)-based Method Name Prediction (MNP) techniques have been proposed. However, a systematic review of these techniques is currently lacking, hindering future researchers from understanding the research status, development trends, challenges, and opportunities in this field. To fill this gap, in this article, we conduct a systematic literature review on learning-based MNP studies. Specifically, we first perform a thorough review of the literature concerning publication venue, publication year, and contribution types. This analysis enables us to discern trends in studies related to MNP. Second, we depict the general workflow of learning-based MNP techniques, which involves three consecutive subprocesses: context extraction, context preprocessing, and context-based prediction. Subsequently, we investigate contemporary techniques/solutions applied in the three subprocesses. Third, we scrutinize the widely used experimental databases, evaluation metrics, and replication packages utilized in MNP studies. Moreover, we summarize existing empirical studies on MNP to facilitate a quick understanding of their focus and findings for subsequent researchers. Finally, based on a systematic review and summary of existing work, we outline several open challenges and opportunities in MNP that remain to be addressed in future work.</jats:p>

title: Assessing the Quality of AI Explanations of Atrial Fibrillation: Comparative Analysis of ChatGPT and Google Gemini
container-title: JMIR Formative Research
598e2fa6d5c1d1ee8bb1eebc101a66353744cb13.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Atrial fibrillation (AF) is one of the most common arrhythmias and is associated with multiple risk factors, including stroke and heart failure. Therefore, it is important that accurate and comprehensive educational resources on AF are available. Artificial intelligence (AI) platforms such as Google Gemini and ChatGPT are emerging tools for medical education. To our knowledge, this is the first study to assess the quality of these platforms for AF education.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This pilot study aimed to (1) assess the quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini explanations of AF and its treatment, (2) compare responses from both platforms, and (3) analyze differences in interpretation between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The prompt “Explain atrial fibrillation and how to treat it to a patient” was entered into both ChatGPT and Google Gemini. The responses, along with a survey created in Google Forms, were sent out to potential participants between September and October 2024. The survey questions were derived from the Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool for Printable Materials and DISCERN criteria. Each survey question was multiple choice and rated on a 5-point Likert scale, where 1 indicated strong disagreement and 5 indicated strong agreement. Averages of each answer from the survey were calculated and compared using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The survey was completed by 28 participants, including cardiologists and cardiology fellows and 17 nonmedical professionals (college graduates not employed in the medical field). No significant overall quality differences were observed between ChatGPT and Google Gemini. When comparing participant groups, cardiologists rated AI-generated responses higher than nonmedical professionals for perceived bias (mean 3.82 vs mean 4.33; P=.04) and for explaining consequences of no treatment (mean 2.85 vs mean 1.86; P=.005). In contrast, nonmedical professionals rated structural and organizational features more favorably than cardiologists, including visual cues (mean 3.97 vs mean 2.48; P<.001), informative headers (mean 4.77 vs mean 3.95; P=.001), concise sections (mean 4.71 vs mean 4.29; P=.04), identifiable patient actions (mean 4.21 vs mean 3.19; P=.04), and references to additional resources (mean 2.65 vs mean 1.71; P=.006).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The comparable quality of ChatGPT and Google Gemini suggests that both are viable for AF education. Differences in ratings of organizational features versus perceptions of bias and consequences of no treatment highlight a disconnect between cardiologists and nonmedical professionals. To optimize clinical application, cardiologists should evaluate both comprehensiveness and clarity of AI-generated responses. This serves as a pilot study, and future research should focus on longitudinal studies of AI-generated responses and their effects on clinical outcomes.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The time course of neural activity predictive of self-initiated movement
6bb29c0fa61a9bb6f281a6f43aa6ce014a54e928.abstract: <jats:p>Decades of research have shown that early ramping activity is a very reliable antecedent of self-initiated movement. However, the dominant paradigm has been to only analyze data epochs culminating in movement, which discounts how often slow ramping might occur when no movement follows. To address this, we introduced a matched control condition that did not culminate in movement. We recorded electroencephalography data and compared these two conditions using a variety of powerful machine-learning classifiers. Although early ramping activity was present, it was not useful in predicting movement. Instead, classification accuracy rose abruptly about 100 ms before movement. By contrast, the traditional approach reproduced the spurious impression of early predictability. Our results substantially constrain the interpretation that early EEG antecedents, including the RP, reflect a commitment to act, instead indicating that EEG-detectable evidence consistent with such a commitment emerges closer to movement onset, in line with the timing of conscious intention and the capacity for late movement inhibition. More broadly, our results show that a reliable antecedent is not necessarily a good predictor, underscoring the need for proper control conditions in time series analyses.</jats:p>

title: Feasibility Analysis of Education in Indonesian Provinces: A Machine Learning Clustering Approach for Regional Classification
container-title: Engineering and Technology Journal
1b5bd0dfe6cab0a4e4dc5dc25d573208b2fdac15.abstract: <jats:p>Education system feasibility varies significantly across Indonesian provinces due to geographic, socioeconomic, and infrastructural disparities. This study applies unsupervised machine learning clustering algorithms (K-Means, Hierarchical Clustering, Gaussian Mixture Models, and Self-Organizing Maps) to classify Indonesian provinces into homogeneous groups based on education feasibility indicators. Using 39 provinces and special territories, we evaluated clustering quality through internal validation metrics (Silhouette coefficient and Davies-Bouldin index) and inter-algorithm agreement measures (Adjusted Rand Index and Normalized Mutual Information). Results demonstrate that Hierarchical Clustering achieves the best Davies-Bouldin index (0.782), while K-Means and GMM produce identical partitions (ARI = 1.0, NMI = 1.0). Self-Organizing Maps identified nine distinct regional education feasibility profiles, with provincial distributions revealing significant heterogeneity in education conditions. These findings provide a quantitative framework for targeted policy interventions and resource allocation to improve education feasibility across Indonesia’s diverse regions.</jats:p>

title: Entrepreneurial culture, social-emotional skills, and self-esteem in students participating in sports programmes in Colombia
container-title: Journal of Human Sport and Exercise
7487e0e532b00ca3a9d308c88e1fc9fc09e90f2f.abstract:
<jats:p>This research presents the results of a systematic review that analyses the relationship between entrepreneurial culture, social-emotional skills and self-esteem in students enrolled in sports programmes in Colombia, with the aim of identifying the factors that influence their positive attitude towards entrepreneurial capacity. In the literature review, 100 articles and academic research papers were selected between 2019 and 2025, prioritised from 42,958 results from different resources such as reference databases, multidisciplinary databases, academic repositories and academic journals. The databases with the highest number of results were Scopus, Web of Science, Wiley, Springer Nature, Science Direct, Ebsco Host, among others such as (COnnecting REpositories), Taylor & Francis, and Google Scholar. The results showed an interest in academia to research and reflect on the relationship between entrepreneurial culture, emotional skills, and young people. However, in most studies, entrepreneurial culture is associated with variables such as emotional intelligence and social skills in university contexts, leaving the field of the relationship between these variables and the field of sports somewhat lacking in studies. Studies that explore this relationship in depth conclude that athletes develop socio-emotional skills that make them strong candidates for entrepreneurship. However, there are limitations in the implementation of mechanisms that promote an entrepreneurial culture ( ) in university contexts for young people studying sports programmes.

title: Assessing the Effectiveness, Engagement, and Acceptability of a Smartwatch Healthy Lifestyle Intervention for Cognitive Enhancement in Healthy Adults: Mixed Methods Electroencephalography Protocol
container-title: JMIR Research Protocols
7e6b65fd0eceaed8ad891218da9c81d3f193d863.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Wearable technologies are rapidly transforming the health care landscape by enabling the tracking of real-time physiological and behavioral data used in healthy lifestyle interventions. Despite their widespread adoption in the consumer market, scientific validation of their impact on the brain remains limited, and factors influencing effects on cognition and adherence are not fully understood. This gap is critical, as consumers, health care providers, and researchers depend on these data to unlock the potential of wearables for cognitive support.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We aim to assess the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of a commercially available smartwatch healthy lifestyle intervention on cognitive enhancement in healthy adults, using a convergent parallel mixed methods design. We seek to provide a comprehensive, replicable methodological framework to evaluate wearable technology interventions targeting cognitive enhancement in healthy adults.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Healthy adults aged 18 to 40 years with a sedentary lifestyle (N=72) interested in participating in a healthy lifestyle intervention will be recruited in the Vancouver Metropolitan Area, BC, Canada. Participants will be randomly assigned into an intervention group using an Apple Watch or a control group following standard physical activity guidelines without an Apple Watch for a period of 4 weeks. Effectiveness will be evaluated through (1) cognitive function (primary outcome)—executive function, specifically inhibitory control, via electroencephalogram-based event-related potentials (N2/P3) during a go/no-go task; (2) resting-state brain activity via electroencephalogram spectral power; (3) behavioral performance (reaction time and accuracy); (4) perceived health (36-item Short Form Health Survey); and (5) qualitative analysis of factors affecting the intervention’s effectiveness. Engagement will be assessed through goal completion metrics and qualitative analysis of barriers, facilitators, and usage patterns. Acceptability will be assessed through System Usability Scale scores and qualitative analysis of factors affecting usability, satisfaction, and user preferences. This design integrates assessments before, during, and after intervention. Qualitative assessments will include weekly check-ins and semistructured interviews to obtain a comprehensive understanding of factors influencing the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of the intervention. Exploratory outcomes include descriptions of possible interactions between the 3 constructs and comparison of smartwatch-tracked vs self-reported goal completion.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The study received funding from the AGE-WELL Network Centres of Excellence (April 2020-March 2023) and was approved by the Simon Fraser University Research Ethics Board. Enrollment for the study is ongoing. As of October 2026, data have been collected from 48 participants and are currently being processed and analyzed. The first results are expected to be published in 2027.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study outlines a foundational framework for evaluating the effectiveness, engagement, and acceptability of wearable health interventions targeting cognitive enhancement in healthy adults. Furthermore, our mixed methods approach with randomized controlled comparison is expected to inform the design and development of effective, engaging, and friendly wearable brain health technologies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Multi-omic integration using interpretable machine learning reveals genetic mechanisms of trait variation and phenotypic plasticity in switchgrass
d5ecaf8e9c0ab25f0f77449121b30e109d87be40.abstract: <jats:p>Uncovering the genetic architecture of quantitative traits is challenging because polygenic control yields small individual gene effects and because gene–gene and genotype-by-environment interactions add further complexity. To understand the genetic basis of polygenic traits and their plasticity across environments, we integrated genome-wide SNPs and RNA-seq transcript data with interpretable statistical and machine learning models in a switchgrass (Panicum virgatum) diversity panel grown at contrasting field sites in Michigan and Texas. Notably, in addition to single environments, our trait prediction models were able to predict phenotypic differences, across environments i.e., plasticity. By interpreting trait prediction models with explainable machine learning methods, we identified genes that are the most predictive of flowering time and annual biomass production across environments, based on their associated gene expression levels and nearby SNPs. This approach recovered canonical flowering regulators and revealed novel, environment-specific candidate flowering genes. Further, transcriptome models consistently recovered more switchgrass genes homologous to experimentally validated genes in Arabidopsis and rice than SNP-based models. Feature interaction scores from the models also allow the identification of trait- and environment-dependent gene–gene interactions, where flowering time showed stronger and more abundant interactions than biomass. While some of the interactions identified are consistent with the link between flowering time and yield, most are novel predictors that need to be further evaluated. These findings provide insight into the genetic basis of trait variation and plasticity across environments and help prioritize candidate genes for functional validation and cultivar improvement.</jats:p>

title: Endoscopic ultrasound-based deep learning for predicting chemotherapy response in unresectable pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma
container-title: World Journal of Gastroenterology
1f6a560325fb967b8d7fb19fd1972b99328cdc40.abstract:
<jats:p>BACKGROUND</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) is one of the most lethal malignancies, and chemotherapy remains the main treatment option for patients with unresectable disease. Reliable prediction of chemotherapy response is therefore critical for individualized treatment planning. Endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) provides high-resolution, tumor-specific imaging that may be well suited for deep learning-based prediction of chemotherapy response.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>AIM</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>To develop and validate an EUS-based deep learning model for predicting first-line chemotherapy response in patients with unresectable PDAC, and to evaluate its prognostic value for overall survival (OS) stratification.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>METHODS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>In this retrospective, single-center study, 190 patients with histologically confirmed PDAC diagnosed between February 2016 and March 2025 were included. All patients were deemed ineligible for upfront surgical resection based on formal multidisciplinary team evaluation, including those with locally advanced or metastatic disease and those considered medically or personally unsuitable for surgery. Patients diagnosed in 2023 or earlier were assigned to the training and internal validation cohort (n  = 152) using five-fold cross-validation, whereas patients diagnosed from January 2024 onward at a separate campus of the same institution constituted a temporally independent test cohort with site separation (n  = 38). Tumor regions of interest were manually annotated on pre-treatment EUS images. Four convolutional neural network (CNN) architectures (VGG19, VGG19-BN, ResNet50, and ResNeXt50) were trained to predict progressive disease, as defined by RECIST version 1.1 after first-line chemotherapy. Model performance was evaluated at the patient level using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and accuracy, and model-derived risk stratification was assessed for OS.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>RESULTS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>In the independent test cohort, ResNeXt50 demonstrated the best discriminatory performance (AUC = 0.848; sensitivity, 65.38%; specificity, 84.19%), followed by ResNet50 (AUC = 0.844), whereas VGG19-BN (AUC = 0.775) and VGG19 (AUC = 0.614) showed lower performance. Model-predicted probabilities enabled effective risk stratification, with high-risk patients exhibiting significantly shorter OS compared with low-risk patients (log-rank P  < 0.01; hazard ratio = 1.77). In contrast, baseline carbohydrate antigen 19-9-based stratification did not significantly discriminate survival, and CNN-based models demonstrated higher discriminatory performance compared with the conventional serum biomarker.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>CONCLUSION</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>CNN models based on region-of-interest-level EUS imaging can predict chemotherapy response and provide clinically meaningful prognostic stratification in PDAC. Among the evaluated architectures, ResNeXt50 demonstrated the most consistent and robust performance across independent testing and sensitivity analyses. This noninvasive imaging-based approach shows potential for integration into clinical workflows to support personalized treatment planning.</jats:p>

title: Towards Realistic Project-Level Code Generation via Multi-Agent Collaboration and Semantic Architecture Modeling
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
2e98affb75fe6b1c9fa0a80bf39cb6bb48af6b14.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In recent years, Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved remarkable progress in automated code generation. In real-world software engineering, the growing demand for rapid iteration and continuous delivery underscores the importance of project-level code generation, where LLMs are expected to generate complete software projects directly from complex user requirements. This task, however, presents greater challenges due to larger input scales, multi-modal information, and the need for holistic architectural reasoning. Although existing studies have made initial explorations, they still face key limitations, including unrealistic datasets and unreliable evaluation metrics that fail to reflect real-world complexity, the semantic gap between human-written requirements and machine-interpretable structures, and difficulties in managing hierarchical dependencies and maintaining quality throughout the generation process. To address these limitations, we first introduce
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , a project-level code generation dataset built from 18 real-world repositories with 12.7 files and 2,388.6 lines of code per task on average, supplemented with documentation and executable test cases for automatic evaluation. We further propose
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    , a multi-agent framework that decomposes projects into architecture design, skeleton generation, and code filling stages with iterative refinement and memory-based context management. Within this framework, we introduce the Semantic Software Architecture Tree, a structured and semantically rich representation that effectively bridges user requirements and source code implementation. Experiments show that
                    <jats:sc>ProjectGen</jats:sc>
                    achieves state-of-the-art performance, passing 52/124 test cases on the small-scale project-level code generation dataset DevBench, a 57% improvement over the baseline approaches, and 310 test cases on
                    <jats:sc>CodeProjectEval</jats:sc>
                    , representing an improvement of roughly tenfold compared to the baselines.
                  </jats:p>

title: Wine, Politics, and Markets
a1477911e3f6fe9d8e457d1b117363ace5c1f507.abstract:
<jats:p>Wine has been at the heart of human civilization for thousands of years, and for centuries governments around the world have regulated wine production, consumption, and trade for reasons ranging from consumer protection and quality assurance to tax revenue and the protection of vineyard owners’ rents. The European Union (EU) alone has introduced more than two thousand wine regulations. Some of today’s regulations date back hundreds of years; others are more recent; and there is considerable variation over time.

The rich history of wine regulation offers fascinating insights into the political economy of public policy and the ways in which such policies persist and evolve. This book examines specific historical developments involving wines that are well known today, such as Champagne, Port, Chianti, and Burgundy. Drawing on original historical sources and multilingual archival research, it provides the first comprehensive analysis of global wine regulations from an integrated political, economic, and historical perspective.

It will appeal to a wide range of readers, including academics and students across disciplines, and anyone interested in wine and wine markets around the world.</jats:p>
