title: Agentic AI as a Catalyst for Intelligent Transformation in Higher Education Administration
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
666d4eec1099228678f9ba6af74a13a32a982a4f.abstract: <jats:p>The growing complexity of higher education administration has exposed the limitations of fragmented, rule-based systems that struggle to support timely and data-driven decision-making. This chapter examines agentic artificial intelligence (AI) as a catalyst for transforming administrative ecosystems into adaptive, intelligent, and coordinated systems. Moving beyond traditional automation, agentic AI introduces autonomy, context-awareness, and continuous learning, enabling real-time data integration, predictive–prescriptive analytics, and workflow orchestration across core domains. Drawing on frameworks such as multi-agent systems, decision intelligence, and socio-technical systems, the chapter analyzes how agentic AI reshapes institutional processes and decision structures. It also highlights key challenges, including data silos, governance complexities, and ethical concerns. Ultimately, the chapter argues that effective implementation requires systemic integration, robust governance, and strong human–AI collaboration.</jats:p>

title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence for Decision-Making Augmentation in Higher Education Administration
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
4753ec1853130197948d90a206fa4f559f31bc1c.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid digital transformation of higher education has intensified the need for more adaptive, data-driven administrative decision-making systems. This chapter examines the emergence of agentic artificial intelligence (AI) as a transformative approach that extends beyond traditional analytics and generative models by enabling autonomous, goal-directed, and context-aware decision processes. It outlines the conceptual foundations of agentic AI through intelligent agent theory, decision intelligence, and socio-technical systems, and analyzes its core capabilities, including perception, reasoning, planning, and action. The chapter further explores its applications across key administrative domains and highlights its potential to enhance efficiency, predictive capacity, and institutional responsiveness. Despite these benefits, critical challenges related to governance, ethics, data fragmentation, and human-AI collaboration are emphasized, underscoring the need for balanced and responsible implementation.</jats:p>

title: Decision Intelligence for AI-Enabled University Governance and Data-Driven Administrative Transformation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
1ea21bd12f81b110514bb8aff08dc36ff1204ee4.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming governance and administrative processes in higher education institutions. Traditional systems relying on manual operations and fragmented data are increasingly inadequate. This chapter proposes an AI-driven decision intelligence framework for efficient, data-driven, and policy-aligned governance. The framework integrates data collection, preprocessing, feature selection, and predictive analytics within a unified architecture, where institutional data from student, financial, and human resource systems are analyzed using machine learning models to generate insights. These are refined through policy-based decision mechanisms to ensure transparency and compliance. Results show improved decision accuracy, operational efficiency, and reduced processing time, supported by dashboards for real-time monitoring. Ethical concerns such as data privacy and bias are also addressed. A case study from Tamil Nadu demonstrates the framework's applicability as a scalable model for AI-enabled governance.</jats:p>

title: Agentic AI as a Governance Partner in Higher Education Leadership
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
57435d97d2fd69fae64c511686c94b37c80641ef.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter advances the argument that agentic artificial intelligence should be theorized as a governance partner in higher education leadership rather than as a mere administrative tool. As universities operate within intensifying accountability, datafication, and audit regimes, agentic systems increasingly participate in enrollment, budgeting, accreditation, and research decisions, reshaping institutional decision architectures. To address this shift, this chapter proposes the Strategic Agentic Governance Framework, a feedback-driven model linking data intelligence, normative framing, decision orchestration, accountability, and adaptive institutional learning. Drawing on distributed leadership, institutional agency, algorithmic governance, and socio-technical systems theory, the framework reconceptualizes leadership as meta-governance, the deliberate design of hybrid human and machine decision systems. The chapter also examines accountability diffusion, algorithmic bias, and data sovereignty, and offers testable propositions and a maturity continuum for future research.</jats:p>

title: Digital Catalytic Leadership for Governing Agentic AI
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
a7a2f25db22c009ea70fb3c60ff8c7c5966288e7.abstract: <jats:p>The evolution of agentic AI is transforming higher education administration beyond simple automation. This chapter examines the governance challenges of AI integration in universities and proposes Digital Catalytic Leadership (DCL) as an adaptive governance framework. The study finds that while agentic AI can improve administrative effectiveness, it also creates challenges related to accountability, data security, and human–AI relations. This chapter argues that DCL is important for building adaptive, ethical, and human-centered higher education governance in the AI era.</jats:p>

title: From Paperwork to Predictive Governance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
59ed15c0f7f338ea6f034d707cac8523fbdf31f4.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter presents a Cambodia-specific framework for implementing agentic AI in higher education administration, converting bureaucracy and paperwork into a predictive, evidence-based governance model. Cambodia's higher education faces accountability, accreditation, student expectations, and limited admin capacity. AI adoption is fragmented, causing delays, duplicate reports, and inconsistent services. The chapter suggests agentic AI can act as an orchestration layer for institutions by integrating systems and enhancing decision-making in Admissions, Enrolment, Scheduling, Finance, HR, Research Administration, and Quality Assurance. It highlights key use cases such as coordinating student services, automating accreditation evidence management, forecasting queues, and identifying compliance gaps. The chapter aims to provide a pragmatic policy synthesis based on practice and resource constraints in Cambodia. The chapter's main contribution is a practical model to facilitate the adoption of responsible agentic AI that aims to improve administrative efficiency and transparency.</jats:p>

title: Intelligent Budget Allocation and Predictive Financial Analytics Using AI in Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
811b776505e2e740c926ee67de48c35b2159227e.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter considers the potential use of an agentic AI in changing the face of financial planning and budgeting in higher education organizations characterized by uncertain funding, unpredictable enrollments, and increasing accountability. This chapter criticizes the conventional approach to incremental budgeting and advances a governance-centered model in which AI functions as an agent for enhancing collaboration in financial decision-making rather than taking control from people's hands. Informed by Dynamic Capabilities theory, the contribution illustrates the role of AI in improving the capabilities for sensing, seizing, and reconfiguring at institutions for adaptive management. This chapter further develops the concept of a four-step RACT model for implementing AI in responsible ways. The contribution is enriched through institutional case illustrations with emphasis on the advantages gained through AI adoption. The challenges associated with the application of AI in financial management are discussed, alongside mitigation approaches. Research gaps are clearly stated.</jats:p>

title: A3 Model in Indian Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
c1ad93ee7e0991c260ac643de8c3fa1e55541ddd.abstract: <jats:p>The appearance of Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Indian academic spaces has ushered in a wave of revolutionary changes, bringing new tools like intelligent automation, supporting governance, intelligent data-based decisions, and the like. This subchapter attempts to bring out a framework, A3 Model, where Agentic AI, Administrative Resilience, and Educational Excellence are offered within one overarching design from a more applied framework. The chapter goes on with an empirical inquiry where mixed methods and PLS-SEM are used on data from Indian universities, focusing on how Agentic AI shapes institutional responsiveness and academic performance. The results show that there exists a strong and positive connection among the capabilities of AI, the existence of an agile organization, and the realization of desirable academic outcomes, but most significantly, the interaction of those effects in the context of escalating and fostering the productive and efficient administration within the higher education system.</jats:p>

title: Administrative System Transformation Through Agentic AI in Enrollment and Admissions Management
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
19d4c9a3cbac21418f82ad721e79494df8fa79eb.abstract: <jats:p>Administrative challenges are increasing in higher education establishments in light of the rising enrollment pressures, changing student needs, and heightened demands for accountability. Agentic AI, with its capacity to self-directly perceive, plan, act, and learn, opens up avenues for a novel way to revolutionize enrollment and admissions management. This chapter provides an overview of the ways in which agentic AI is transforming the enrollment cycle, including the engagement of students, admission applications, prediction and planning, decision-making, and yield management. Based on the recent research and practical experience of various educational establishments, the potential, as well as possible difficulties associated with automation, ethical issues, privacy concerns, workforce transformation, among other issues, are discussed.</jats:p>

title: Agentic AI in Enrollment and Admissions Management
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
00d998159a5393674028a10b076cd1fb8a858ea4.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the role of agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) in transforming enrollment and admissions management within higher education institutions. The chapter discusses the evolution of admissions systems from traditional manual structures to intelligent, data-driven administrative ecosystems supported by predictive analytics, workflow automation, applicant screening, and conversational AI. The study highlights how AI-enabled systems improve enrollment forecasting, communication responsiveness, institutional coordination, and operational efficiency while reducing administrative delays and inconsistencies. Empirical findings from multi-institutional analysis demonstrate measurable improvements in applicant engagement, screening accuracy, workflow synchronization, and fairness in admissions processes. The chapter further explores governance, ethical considerations, explainability, and human-AI collaboration frameworks necessary for responsible implementation of intelligent admissions systems in higher education.</jats:p>

title: Agentic AI in Higher Education Administration
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Agentic AI for Transforming Higher Education Administration Systems
cf8cf6f3740adc256c5ee8a80e0a1c1edcb0aaeb.abstract: <jats:p>Higher education institutions are increasingly transitioning from traditional rule-based automation toward autonomous, goal-directed agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) systems within administrative environments. Unlike conventional automation tools, agentic AI systems can interpret context, plan actions, utilize external tools, and adapt dynamically to changing conditions. This chapter examines the opportunities and risks associated with these systems in student support services. It discusses benefits such as improved responsiveness, continuous service availability, and reduced administrative workload, while also evaluating risks including algorithmic bias, data privacy concerns, decision opacity, and the potential reduction of human-centered support. The chapter further proposes a governance framework based on Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) and Human-on-the-Loop (HOTL) oversight models to support responsible and transparent AI deployment in higher education administration</jats:p>

title: A reconfigurable self-biased optoelectronic transistor for integrated high-fidelity sensing and neuromorphic signal recovery
container-title: Nano Research
e018bbe628411ad609344ae5e4ab1588d1363600.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Space-ground optical links enable ultra-high-bandwidth and secure long-distance communication but are severely limited by atmospheric-turbulence-induced signal distortion and fading, requiring both high-fidelity linear optoelectronic conversion and nonlinear signal recovery. Neuromorphic computing provides a promising framework for processing temporally complex signals with reduced training cost and improved efficiency. However, its practical deployment in optical communication systems is hindered by the absence of compact and reconfigurable devices capable of simultaneously supporting sensing and processing within a unified hardware platform. Here, we report a reconfigurable self-biased optoelectronic transistor that enables tightly coupled high-fidelity sensing and nonlinear processing at the device level. By leveraging gate-drain coupling and electrostatic doping, the built-in electric field can be dynamically modulated, resulting in reconfigurable carrier transport with continuously tunable linear and nonlinear responses. For high-fidelity optoelectronic conversion, the device exhibits symmetric, bidirectional responses with exceptional linearity (R2 = 0.99) across various wavelengths and illumination intensities. For accurate signal recovery, we present a novel reservoir computing design that employs expansive neurons in place of compressive ones and is directly hardware-realized via the device’s nonlinear characteristics, substantially reducing the bit error rate from 10−2 (typical of conventional equalizers) to 10−4 while lowering the trainable-parameter count to 45.1% and training time to 1.4%. This work establishes a unified, reconfigurable optoelectronic device platform, enabling the practical deployment of neuromorphic computing for robust space-ground optical links.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The Role of Color Dice Media in Islamic Education Learning as an Educational Tool for Introducing the Pillars of Faith and the Pillars of Islam to Students at Slatri 02 Public Elementary School
container-title: AL GHAZALI: Jurnal Pendidikan dan Pemikiran Islam
fb46a01fa965f97b4df2904d73e29ce355ae2c3c.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to examine the role of color dice media as an educational tool in Islamic Education learning for introducing the Pillars of Faith and the Pillars of Islam to fourth-grade students at Slatri 02 Public Elementary School, Brebes. This study employed a descriptive qualitative approach conducted through direct observation, semi-structured interviews, and documentation involving students, the Islamic Education teacher, and the school principal. The findings show that the use of color dice created a more interactive and enjoyable learning environment, increased students’ learning motivation and active participation, and supported their understanding and retention of fundamental Islamic concepts. The activity also encouraged cooperation, responsibility, social interaction, and positive religious attitudes. The novelty of this study lies in positioning color dice not merely as a game-based learning medium but as a simple, contextual, and multidimensional Islamic Education tool that integrates visual, kinesthetic, cognitive, social, and character-development dimensions in learning the Pillars of Faith and the Pillars of Islam. These findings demonstrate the potential of low-cost educational games to strengthen innovative and meaningful Islamic Education practices at the elementary school level.</jats:p>

title: Collaborative Knowledge Distillation and Reinforcement Learning for Automated Ticket Triage in Large-Scale Production Systems
container-title: ACM Transactions on Software Engineering and Methodology
8b0253b0417c564346ca68d9c57a0a0b2b97123a.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    In large-scale enterprise environments, growing system complexity makes failures inevitable, threatening business continuity and customer satisfaction. To maintain system stability, efficient ticket triage is crucial for timely incident resolution. However, it remains a knowledge-intensive task requiring substantial domain expertise and detailed analysis, revealing the limitations of traditional rule-based and text-based methods. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) offer new possibilities for automating triage through their remarkable reasoning and language capabilities. Yet, in industrial settings, LLMs often struggle to leverage domain-knowledge essential for accurate triage. We present
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">CoTriage</jats:italic>
                    , a practical and scalable end-to-end automated ticket triage system, designed and deployed for real-world industrial scenarios.
                    <jats:italic toggle="yes">CoTriage</jats:italic>
                    leverages novel collaboration between large and small models: a small set of labeled tickets is used to distill high-quality LLM reasoning into a lightweight model, which is further optimized through a self-reinforcement mechanism. The refined triager then acts as a reward model to fine-tune a ticket summarizer using reinforcement learning. Comprehensive experiments conducted in the production environment of ByteDance, a leading global online video service provider, demonstrate the effectiveness of CoTriage, reducing the average triage time to 15.0 seconds and significantly enhancing operational efficiency and accelerating incident resolution in practice.
                  </jats:p>

title: ESL Classrooms in the Age of AI
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
9ec5be19b6f57cc824ddd32998fbae5b92f230e2.abstract: <jats:p>Between 2020 and 2025, EFL and ESL classrooms have undergone rapid platformization, with AI writing tutors, learning management systems, and online proctoring becoming central to instruction and assessment. This chapter examines how these AI-mediated technologies reshape gender dynamics in language education, with attention to learners outside the traditional gender binary. Combining a critical narrative review (2020-2025) with a structured walkthrough of ten platforms evaluated against a three-criterion Gender-Inclusivity Audit, the chapter finds uneven patterns: while flagship generative AI has improved its handling of gender-neutral pronouns, legacy writing-evaluation tools, learning management systems, and biometric proctoring continue to enforce binary, Western-normative baselines. The chapter contributes a comparative theoretical synthesis, empirical evidence on algorithmic bias, and a five-step practitioner framework, arguing that educational equity requires gender-responsive, decolonially-grounded design rather than superficial gender-neutrality.</jats:p>

title: Gendered Dimensions of Emotional Labor in Technology-Mediated English Language Learning
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
afa9c09180f8ae02239c558e1d2aff4bf8c0c337.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence into English as a Foreign Language (EFL) education is widely framed in terms of efficiency and personalization. This chapter argues that such framings obscure a more consequential transformation: the redistribution of emotional labor across teachers, learners, and algorithmic systems along gendered lines. Drawing on Hochschild's emotional labor theory, Butler's gender performativity framework, and self-determination theory, it examines how AI systems simulate empathy, encode gendered service scripts, and restructure the affective architecture of language learning without eliminating the human burden of care. To conceptualize this restructuring, the chapter proposes the Gender-Responsive Affective Redistribution framework, which treats AI integration as affective restructuring rather than technological enhancement, and introduces the concept of autonomy drift to describe the gradual displacement of self-regulated learning by system-initiated prompts.</jats:p>

title: Inclusive English Language Instruction Through Flipped Learning
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
94fc234e27e459b844bcbf8fb29984ce7d27d185.abstract: <jats:p>The influence of socio-cultural variables on the development of the English language is not a new phenomenon, and gender is among the most significant yet complex aspects. Gender is not the only factor that determines learners' linguistic identity. Still, it is also a mediating factor in terms of access, participation, confidence, and achievement in an English language learning environment. Therefore, Flipped Learning (FL) has emerged as a revolutionary learning philosophy that is restoring the aspect of teachers and learners where direct instruction is outside the classroom and classroom time is spent in interaction, collaboration and application. FL can offer an effective approach to addressing gender diversity by creating flexible, learner-oriented, and inclusive English language learning. In the chapter, it will be proposed to investigate how FL can be implemented in a strategic way to facilitate inclusive English language classes that recognize, see, and respond to gender diversity.</jats:p>

title: Language, Identity, and Gender in English Language Learning Spaces
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
10937901dd75497665de1150443afa014940c22d.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores the interplay between language, identity, and gender in English language learning, positioning gender as a dynamic, socially constructed element shaping learner experiences. Moving beyond binary perspectives, it highlights how gender influences motivation, participation, discourse practices, and access to resources across formal and digital contexts. Drawing on sociocultural and critical linguistic frameworks, the chapter examines how institutional structures, pedagogies, and sociocultural norms reinforce or challenge gendered inclusion. It further evaluates the role of technology in both enabling identity expression and reproducing inequalities. The study advocates for gender-responsive pedagogies that promote equity, inclusivity, and learner agency. Ultimately, it contributes to rethinking English language education as an empowering and socially just space for diverse gender identities.</jats:p>

title: Sociotechnical Production of English Proficiency in EFL and ESL Learning Ecologies
container-title: Examining Gender Dynamics in English Language Development
e7191931036f740ec255978fc606e47178657fdb.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter develops a conceptual framework for understanding English proficiency in EFL and ESL contexts as a sociotechnically produced, gender-mediated, and ecologically distributed achievement. Moving beyond binary and deficit logics, it synthesizes gender theory, language acquisition theory, motivation theory, identity theory, assessment theory, and platform governance to show how opportunity structures, participation economies, recognition regimes, affective climates, and institutional architectures shape linguistic development. The chapter theorizes gender as a multiscalar force structuring access to input, output, feedback, legitimacy, and mobility. It advances a framework for gender-responsive pedagogy, fair assessment, and inclusive digital governance, positioning English education as a site of epistemic justice, instructional integrity, and policy design within globally stratified learning ecologies.</jats:p>

title: Energy-efficient FPGA acceleration of reinforcement learning algorithms using high-level synthesis
container-title: International Review of Applied Sciences and Engineering
aec2a1237c1c73116e06ec62bddb3caef28d3bc2.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Low latency and energy-efficient design are important requirements for Reinforcement Learning (RL) algorithms deployed on embedded and edge computing systems. Software based Q-learning shows increased power consumption as well as the overhead of sequential execution. The paper shows an energy-efficient FPGA architecture for the Q-learning update based on High Level Synthesis (HLS). An FPGA accelerator targeting the device platform Xilinx Zynq-7000 (xc7z020clg400-1) has been designed and implemented. Loop pipelining and precision fine-tuning design techniques were applied to optimize the architecture. This improvement was achieved by 50 percent as a baseline architecture got a latency of 14 cycles, which was reduced to 7 cycles when the architecture was pipelined with loops. A relative comparison of fixed point (ap_fixed<16,8>) and floating point implementations has shown that the floating point arithmetic increases the number of LUTs used by 4 times, the number of DSPs used by more than 2 times, and the delay by 29 cycles. Post implementation power analysis for fixed-point architecture shows that its energy consumption is about 4 times less per Q-update operation than a floating-point design. The results show that pipelined fixed-point FPGA architectures are a good solution to speed up the reinforcement learning process in resource-limited embedded systems.</jats:p>

title: Functions of pairs of commuting self-adjoint operators under relatively bounded perturbations
container-title: Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society
b30bb1c47411841e45e3820ca30d3d4d03752d32.abstract: We study the behaviour of functions of pairs of commuting self-adjoint operators under perturbations by relatively bounded operators. We obtain analogs of our earlier results for functions of a single self-adjoint operator under relatively bounded perturbations. The main tool is double operator integrals.

title: Fostering Connections
container-title: Enhancing Classroom Well-Being Through Relational Teaching
a42383536037923b070c4b814d7202924804e25f.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the transformative potential of integrating Social-Emotional Learning (SEL) into relational teaching to create nurturing and dynamic educational environments. Relational teaching focuses on building meaningful, trust-based connections between teachers and students, recognizing that positive relationships are foundational for effective learning. By embedding SEL principles within this framework, educators can enhance students' emotional intelligence, resilience, self-awareness, and interpersonal skills, fostering both academic excellence and personal growth. Drawing from established theoretical models, the chapter provides a comprehensive exploration of SEL as a critical component of relational teaching. It presents evidence-based strategies, including classroom practices and teacher-student interaction techniques, to seamlessly incorporate SEL into daily pedagogical routines. Real-world case studies further illustrate the impact of this integration on classroom dynamics, student engagement, and overall well-being. Through these insights, the chapter offers a practical roadmap for educators to harmonize SEL and relational teaching, ultimately contributing to the development of emotionally intelligent, socially competent, and academically successful learners.</jats:p>

title: Higher Well-Being With Social-Emotional Learning and Relational Teaching in Early Childhood Classrooms
container-title: Enhancing Classroom Well-Being Through Relational Teaching
67d9cf36b839281d826ac5cbb247118262964f93.abstract: <jats:p>Research has shown that many adverse experiences negatively affect children's physical, social, and emotional development and well-being both in childhood and adulthood. Social Emotional Learning (SEL) is one of the many concepts and methods recommended to promote well-being. SEL skills help children understand, express, and regulate their emotions and adapt to adverse childhood experiences. Relational teaching (RT), on the other hand, is an approach that emphasizes that learning occurs as a result of the interaction between teachers and students, and therefore the role and attitude of the teacher in this interaction is important in the child's learning process. It supports the provision of a positive classroom climate and teacher-child interaction by shaping the teacher's classroom behavior. In this context, it can be said that RT can be a method and tool that will support and facilitate the SEL process with the teacher's stance. Developing SEL skills at an early age with the support of RT contributes to children's well-being by enabling them to cope with adverse life events.</jats:p>

title: Conceptualizing, Designing and Implementing Literacy Ecosystems for Sustainable Learning
container-title: Designing and Implementing Literacy Ecosystems
6471ade5e76190e4fceeeaa158568adcd727d116.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter discusses the concept, design and implementation of literacy ecosystems as an innovative approach to promoting sustainable learning in the twenty-first century. It defines literacy beyond the traditional ability to read and write; to include ecological, digital, cultural and systems literacies that prepare persons and communities to engage an increasingly complex world. Literacy ecosystems are contextualized as interconnected networks of learners, families, schools, communities, institutions, technologies and resources that collectively support lifelong learning and development. The chapter determines core principles instrumental in the development of effective literacy ecosystems, including inclusivity, adaptability, sustainability and collaboration among stakeholders. It links formal, non-formal and informal learning environments, generating continuous learning opportunities. Basing on case studies, the chapter establishes how literacy ecosystems encourage educational access, social inclusion, cultural preservation, economic empowerment and community resilience.</jats:p>

title: STEM Learning Through Functional Literacy in Primary Schools
container-title: Designing and Implementing Literacy Ecosystems
dcd4fb1f79905357d0f7a90b953a6814ebcf4355.abstract: <jats:p>Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics (STEM) aspirations have not translated into literacy-rich instruction. This study examined the role of functional literacy in STEM learning in Tanzanian primary schools through teachers' perceptions and practices and students' learning experiences. A convergent parallel mixed-methods design involved 89 teachers and 253 students from 12 schools across six low-performing districts. Data were collected through questionnaires, interviews, focus group discussions, classroom observations, and document analysis. Findings showed that teachers valued functional literacy but demonstrated limited understanding and implementation. Students reported weak classroom support and reliance on self-directed learning. Resource availability emerged as the strongest predictor of STEM learning. The study recommends improving STEM resources, training, and assessment.</jats:p>

title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
Project-Based Learning in Music Education
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
897f56ad810b9538a8cdca2c7451ed319c1a08fd.abstract: <jats:p>Music education is undergoing a global shift toward creativity, collaboration, and real-world relevance. Project-Based Learning (PBL) has emerged as an effective approach that engages students in meaningful, context-based musical experiences. This chapter presents a case study of a community-centered music project implemented in an undergraduate setting. Students assumed diverse roles as composers, performers, cultural curators, and event organizers, collaboratively creating and presenting a live community performance. The project followed a structured PBL framework integrating cultural exploration, original composition, and community engagement. Results show notable improvements in student motivation, creative confidence, ensemble performance, and intercultural awareness. This study contributes to innovative music pedagogy and provides practical insights for integrating PBL into music education.</jats:p>

title: Reviving Traditions Through Project-Based Learning and Innovative Technology in Punjabi Folk Music
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
a4d83da8d5d0e8762371da1d3d301b958fb96366.abstract: <jats:p>The Folk music of Punjab including famous folk forms has been the core of its cultural identity. However, due to modernization and impact of mainstream media, these traditional punjabi folk forms are being forgotten. This chapter provides a summary of previous and existing studies that use project-based learning (PBL) and innovative technologies to preserve Punjabi Folk music. Analyzing current literature and practical strategies, it examines how PBL involves students and communities in recording and performing traditional folk arts. It also investigates how technology such as virtual reality (VR) performances, artificial intelligence (AI)-powered music analysis and digital archives, improve accessibility and preservation of Punjabi Folk traditions. It emphasizes the opportunities of future research, effective practices and ethical awareness resulting into interdisciplinary collaborations between educators, technologists and folk artists in developing the authentic and community rooted experiences.</jats:p>

title: Lessons From China's Music-Led Aesthetic Education
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
1f21b1a7b696591986213a55df0f84a6394a7a9e.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter presents lessons from China on how project-based learning (PBL) can support aesthetic education in primary school music education through a design-oriented approach. The chapter argues that aesthetic learning does not emerge automatically through artistic activities but requires a coherent pedagogical design that connects participation, reflection, embodiment, and meaning-making across lessons. The chapter presents “Dream Theatre,” a music-led PBL in which students transform the traditional Chinese story “The Shepherd Who Mended His Fence After Losing Sheep” into a musical performance. The LivePBL DEEP Method (Direction–Education–Event–Project) is adapted to structure learning across project phases, interactions, and progression. Lessons learned from China indicate that aesthetic learning must be intentionally designed rather than assumed, embodied and collaborative participation is central to artistic PBL; the fragmentation in PBL is fundamentally due to a lack of project design methodology.</jats:p>

title: Effect of Nazrul Sangeet on Academic Achievement of Elementary School Students
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
d6db59cc87cbbbe13f4407fb6ca3e43d18501d92.abstract: <jats:p>This study examined the effect of Nazrul Sangeet on the academic achievement of elementary school students in Purba Bardhaman district, West Bengal, India. Using a quasi-experimental pre-test–post-test design, 50 Class VIII students were purposively selected and divided equally into an experimental group (n = 25), receiving traditional instruction augmented by weekly Nazrul Sangeet sessions, and a control group (n = 25), receiving conventional instruction only. Academic achievement in Bengali, English, and Mathematics was measured using a researcher-developed, expert-validated 30-item multiple-choice test. Results indicated a large negative effect size within the experimental group (Cohen's d = −0.715) and a moderate effect size between groups at post-test (Cohen's d = −0.665). A significant between-group difference emerged in Mathematics but not in Bengali or English. Among demographic variables, study duration and frequency of song listening significantly influenced post-test scores in the experimental group, whereas gender, location, and caste did not.</jats:p>

title: Beyond Musicology and Language, Not Beyond Culture
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
8345a25b5f58e41e2d4d64c1c9e449084f8bda42.abstract: <jats:p>Music allows rituals of emotional connection that transcend language, while dialogue offers an opportunity to interpret and articulate cultural perspectives across different eras. Cultural meaning-making processes through both affective engagement and reflective practice are possible through project-based approaches to musicology. Collaborations across civilizations highlight how effective communication between nations enables critical discussion of historical and social contexts regarding the patterns of cultural expression through emotions in music. This process also encourages students to develop critical thinking as they navigate the complexities of musical symbolism, cultural narratives, and the ways emotions are encoded and expressed. Ultimately, this approach highlights how cross-cultural musical engagement can cultivate empathy, insight, and collaborative understanding in global music education.</jats:p>

title: On Community-Based and Intergenerational Music Projects
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
fcda546019d160917ecddbbc8b8128d7709f97bf.abstract: <jats:p>PPPs and innovation ecosystems can be discussed as important tools in scaling development, accessing governmental assistance and commercial expertise and technology. Such partnership form vibrant worlds in which the stakeholders, firms, institutions, and policymakers push innovation, resources and knowledge exchange. PPP models allow financial freedom, policy facilitation, and risk dispersion whereas innovation systems facilitate innovation and dissemination of ideas. The two are together to help in scalable solutions in the different fields such as energy, health, and education. Proper governance, digitalism, and strategy alignment are needed to provide sustainability and an inclusive growth in these collaborative systems.</jats:p>

title: From Singing to Social Support
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
7b4983ef4de6a769e93cb8bdcb25560ba74645a5.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter discusses elderly singing as a socially embedded learning process. While existing research highlights the wellbeing and social benefits of group singing, it often treats these outcomes as natural results of participation without explaining how they are produced. Drawing on cases from Inner Mongolia, China, this study proposes a LivePBL DEEP (Direction, Education, Event, Project) design framework to structure elderly choirs as project-based learning networks. The framework views participants as active contributors whose roles develop from personal expression to collaboration and community engagement. Through three design cases, the chapter demonstrates that role development is a key mechanism for generating and sustaining social support. The study provides a practical approach for organising community music activities and supporting social networks through participation.</jats:p>

title: Raga to Reality
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
d3da0d818fee2c8236865688c262c44bc07e6ae3.abstract: <jats:p>Project-Based Learning (PBL) is increasingly considered a pedagogical approach that integrates creativity, collaboration, and experiential learning across learning contexts. PBL within Carnatic music classes, which shifts the learning context from a traditional, teacher-centered classroom to a rich, student-centered learning context. Employing constructivist and experiential learning theories, Through lesson observations, student reflections, and the analyses of descriptions of the project work, this study describes how PBL prompted deeper musical meaning, critical thinking, and independence as artists' in learning about raga, kriti, tala, and performance delivery. The chapter makes visible the institutional enablers and barriers, and the findings reveal how PBL scaffolds deeper conceptual engagement and aesthetic engagements in Carnatic music while improving engagement, motivation, cross-disciplinary connections and confidence in performance. PBL approach aiming to reinforce and encourage project based learning experiences in Indian classical music education</jats:p>

title: From Guru to Group
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
34b44ebf48ee6aec9ed0560ded23de783d64606d.abstract: <jats:p>Hindustani Classical Music is an Art form that is transmitted traditionally through the Guru-Shishya Parampara. There is no need to change teaching strategies because students' interests have broadened and collaborative skills are now essential. The Guru-Shishya Parampara preserves the style and depth of music, but it is necessary to combine contemporary teaching with it. Based on youth festival preparations, this study aims to understand how group rehearsal performances benefit students' learning. PBL in this chapter is a medium to bridge the gap between the modern education system and conventional training. According to practice sessions and observation interviews, this method improves students' tala grasp, raga understanding and stage confidence. It develops soft skills like teamwork and a collaborative learning environment, which boosts students' confidence. The study concludes that festival-based PBL is an excellent model for music institutions since it keeps Guru-Shishya Parampara while preparing students for modern-world challenges.</jats:p>

title: A Life-Cycle Social Foundation in Music Learning
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
27ff3cf21e019629c18ec0fcdec0b40d4206de47.abstract: <jats:p>This China-based chapter reconceptualises early years music curriculum as a design methodology for building a social foundation that supports life-cycle learning. Rather than viewing curriculum as content delivery, it argues that learning develops through structured interaction among children, teachers, families, and communities. Project-based learning (PBL) is explored as an approach for organising participation within existing curriculum systems, addressing fragmentation, limited continuity, and weak stakeholder integration. The chapter introduces the LivePBL DEEP (i.e., Direction, Education, Event, and Project) framework as a methodology for structuring developmental missions, relational engagement, shared action, and cumulative learning. Three design cases—rhythm games, chanting, and instrument exploration—demonstrate how everyday activities can function as socially embedded curriculum practices, offering implications for educational practice and research across diverse contexts.</jats:p>

title: Integrating Music, Movement, and PBL
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
f26b46b4f6abf5d9a07c431beeccc1630053e5a3.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the ways in which using music, movement and Project based learning (PBL) can enhance the learning and general development of the students. It offers a real-life example, in which the students collaborated to produce and perform their own music and movement-based projects on the theme of the community. The research indicates that this method enhances creativity, motivation, teamwork, and emotional abilities of students. It also makes students more attached to their culture and community. The chapter addresses issues like scarcity of resources, time management, and assessment problems in addition to the positive aspects. There are practical recommendations that can be given to teachers that desire to employ this method in their classrooms. On the whole, the chapter helps to appreciate the importance of learning based on creative and hands-on experiences to make the educational process more meaningful, inclusive, and enjoyable to students.</jats:p>

title: Orchestrating Children as Young Creators in the Curriculum
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
d3fedd17769b47ed2dac3101b7a9dd998ae68ae3.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores how young children become creators in music education. Here, orchestration means the coordination of social relationships and interactive participation through which creative learning develops. Although Project-Based Learning (PBL) research often discusses creativity and collaboration, less attention has been given to micro-level design structures for organising learning processes. The chapter presents a design-oriented PBL approach by adapting the LivePBL DEEP framework (Direction, Education, Event, Project) for creativity-oriented learning. In the Chinese context, the project case of “Our Sound Concert” is presented as three interconnected micro-projects involving sound exploration, experimentation, and collaborative performance. Based on a small-scale qualitative experiment, the study analyses how creativity develops through sound, peer interaction, and collective performance. The findings suggest that orchestrating learning processes is critical in fostering creativity in early childhood education.</jats:p>

title: Body, Voice, and Story
container-title: Cases on Project-Based Learning in Music Education
373321c91a2334110f0841ec2370f0d21a10546f.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores the incorporation of Theatre and Music through the PBL approach in child-oriented education through the concept of Body, Voice, and Story. In light of the increasing need for multidisciplinary education and experiences, this chapter highlights how movement, voice, music, and storytelling may contribute to the overall growth and development of children socially, emotionally, cognitively, and creatively. In terms of the Body dimension, it promotes movement, rhythm, gesture, and space; the Voice aspect stresses breathing, songs, sound, and speaking. PBL is further described here as having a natural fit for the use in performing arts education since activities related to theatre and music naturally include collaboration, inquiry, rehearsing, reflecting, and performing. Emphasis is also placed on the importance of cultural tradition, folk tales, oral histories, and community theatre to encourage multilingualism and intergenerational learning processes.</jats:p>

title: Coexistence of AI Nurse and AI-Simulated Patient in Nursing Education Using a Bidirectional Fine-Tuning Pipeline: Development and Content Analysis Study
container-title: JMIR Biomedical Engineering
83be49219b02021add3414e1cbea9cacaa7c21ab.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Simulated patient systems are essential in nursing education but face actor scarcity, instructor burden, cost, and disrupted continuity where in-person simulation cannot be sustained. Existing large language model (LLM)–based systems address these issues but treat the dialogic partner—the AI nurse—as a static prompt or unspecialized model, compromising data collection quality and pedagogical applicability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We report (1) the construction of 2 specialized fine-tuned models, NURSE-ONE (AI nurse) and PATIENT-ONE (AI-simulated patient), via a 5-step bidirectional fine-tuning pipeline; (2) their evaluation using Berelson content analysis validated by independent human coders; (3) an exploratory third-party evaluation by nursing faculty; and (4) the design of a coexistence simulation ecosystem supporting 3 operating modes, including offline disaster preparedness applicability.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>On a single consumer-grade graphics processing unit (NVIDIA RTX 4090; 24 GB video random access memory), the multimodal base model gemma4-E4B-it was fine-tuned via low-rank adaptation in five steps: (1) a 251-scenario base from 29 institutionally authored nursing care plans and 20 items from the 115th Japanese National Nursing Examination; (2) a provisional dialogue system (AutoGen v18, maxmsg=25) to collect training dialogues; (3) NURSE-ONE fine-tuning across 3 training volume conditions (245, 735, and 1225 cases); (4) 4-condition Berelson comparison; and (5) PATIENT-ONE fine-tuning on NURSE-ONE–generated dialogues with a 3-condition comparison. Interrater reliability was confirmed by 2 independent nursing experts (196 blinded utterances, κ=0.770) and corroborated by 2 LLM raters (κ=0.742). Ten nursing faculty evaluated 3 coexistence modes in a working web user interface (21-item rubric; item-level content validity index=1.00).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      Four-condition Berelson analysis (
                      <jats:italic>χ</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      <jats:sub>15</jats:sub>
                      =42.0,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001) identified the 735-case nurse-side condition (open question rate=21.5%) as NURSE-ONE; information collection rate reached 15.5% (~4× baseline) at 1225 cases. PATIENT-ONE A/B/C analysis (
                      <jats:italic>χ</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                      <jats:sub>10</jats:sub>
                      =11.8,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      =.30) showed no significant category shift but the lowest response length variability (SD 24.5) and highest information-providing rate (47.9%) at 735 cases, adopted as PATIENT-ONE. The 2 adapters appeared to operate on different axes—qualitative questioning style on the nurse side and quantitative response stability on the patient side—a preliminary observed pattern we term functional asymmetry, pending replication. Third-party evaluation rated the AI-simulated patient, AI nurse, and dyadic interaction at 90.3%, 69.0%, and 84.8%, respectively, with role maintenance at ceiling (mean 5, SD 0). All 3 modes met the prespecified 3-second latency threshold.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>A 5-step bidirectional fine-tuning pipeline produced 2 specialized models whose joint deployment constitutes a design pattern for nursing education simulation. The preliminarily observed functional asymmetry between qualitative nurse-side variation and quantitative patient-side stabilization appears to underwrite the system’s coherence, supporting 3 operating modes on consumer-grade hardware and deployable offline in disaster preparedness contexts. Third-party evaluation confirmed exploratory educational applicability, with all evaluators rating the system as usable, providing a foundation for future learner outcome studies.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status Classification: Hybrid Machine Learning–Large Language Model Ensemble Retrospective Validation Study
container-title: Journal of Medical Internet Research
192e9e9ce872beb2256e134e878d7dd3e9527463.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="background">
                    <jats:title>Background</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The American Society of Anesthesiologists Physical Status (ASA-PS) classification system fundamentally shapes perioperative care delivery but suffers from poor interrater reliability (0.4‐0.6). Machine learning (ML) models and large language models (LLMs) offer complementary remedies: ML processes structured data consistently but cannot interpret the nuance of clinical narratives, while LLMs parse narrative text and generate explanations but adhere inconsistently to diagnostic criteria.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="objective">
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study aimed to develop and evaluate a parallel ML-LLM ensemble that combines the complementary strengths of both approaches for automated ASA-PS classification.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="methods">
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      We retrospectively analyzed 3000 adult surgical encounters from the University of Arkansas for Medical Sciences (UAMS) between August 2024 and May 2025. Cases were randomly allocated to training (n=2000), validation (N=500), and held-out test sets (N=500). The validation set was used exclusively for architecture comparison and hyperparameter tuning, and the held-out test set was reserved for final model performance validation. We developed multiple architectures, including traditional ML models (Extreme Gradient Boosting [XGBoost], Light Gradient Boosting Machine [LightGBM], ExtraTrees), an LLM-only baseline (Generative Pretrained Transformer-4o [GPT-4o]), and hybrid approaches. The parallel ensemble processed structured data through XGBoost and unstructured clinical notes through GPT-4o independently, with outputs combined via weighted averaging. Model performance was evaluated using macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score, exact match accuracy, and ±1-class accuracy.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="results">
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>
                      A theoretical performance ceiling of macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score=0.59 was determined through evaluation by an expert panel of 2 board-certified anesthesiologists (AF and GF) who independently rated 50 patient charts for ASA-PS scores. On the true held-out test set (N=500), the parallel ensemble (
                      <jats:italic>α</jats:italic>
                      =0.30) achieved a macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score of 0.530 (95% CI 0.350‐0.600), exact match accuracy of 0.630 (95% CI 0.580‐0.670), and ±1-class accuracy of 0.980 (95% CI 0.968‐0.992), exceeding the frozen LLM-only baseline evaluated on the same set (macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score 0.493, exact match accuracy 0.621,±1-class accuracy 0.981). On the validation set used for architecture selection, the ensemble outperformed structured-only ML (XGBoost macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score=0.333,
                      <jats:italic>P</jats:italic>
                      <.001), and the LLM-only model reached a macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score of 0.642 (95% CI 0.525‐0.691), nominally exceeding the expert panel ceiling. Per-class analysis attributed this to a perfect score on the 2 validation ASA-PS 5 cases. Excluding that class, the adjusted macro-
                      <jats:italic>F</jats:italic>
                      <jats:sub>1</jats:sub>
                      -score was approximately 0.55, within the range of the parallel ensemble. The LLM component also generated explanations detailing comorbidities, severity descriptors, and functional status indicators.
                    </jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec sec-type="conclusions">
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The parallel ML-LLM ensemble achieved performance approaching the theoretical ceiling established by the expert panel benchmark while providing interpretable clinical explanations. The ±1-class accuracy of 0.980 (95% CI 0.968‐0.992) may enhance operational safety by minimizing extreme misclassifications. This approach demonstrates how complementary AI architectures can enhance perioperative risk assessment, which is particularly valuable given current health care workforce shortages.</jats:p>
