title: The Illusion of Security
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
6dadac891d789dc075b97f149fa34e6239ec0ee6.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter critically examines the assumption that artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cybersecurity inherently strengthens data protection within educational environments. Drawing on a critical review of interdisciplinary literature, it argues that the rapid adoption of AI-driven educational technologies has outpaced the development of effective governance, resulting in significant challenges relating to data privacy, transparency, provenance, informed consent, human-centered design, and cybersecurity. Rather than viewing these issues as isolated concerns, the chapter demonstrates how they interact to create an illusion of security, whereby systems marketed as protective may simultaneously introduce new vulnerabilities and accountability gaps. It concludes that addressing these challenges requires an integrated approach that combines cybersecurity, human-computer interaction, AI governance, and educational policy to develop more transparent, ethical, and user-centered AI-mediated learning environments.</jats:p>

title: Ethical AI and Responsible Data Use in Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
0ca0030d0a293ae102a203b25f3dbc50eda12d8c.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter introduces the concept of personalised learning, learning analytics, automated assessment, and the emergence of generative AI in transforming education, while also highlighting the ethical, privacy, governance and cybersecurity dilemmas that arise with implementation of Artificial Intelligence in the education sector. The chapter gives an overview of ethical and responsible use of AI in education, starting with an examination of the educational AI ecosystem, followed by a discussion of data lifecycle in education, and concluding with an exploration of algorithmic bias, transparency, informed consent, data ownership, surveillance and risks posed by generative AI. It outlines the principles of responsible data governance, privacy-by-design, privacy-preserving methods and other international frameworks like GDPR AI Ethics and OECD Principles. The topics of AI-driven cybersecurity, key practice insights for both educators and institutions, developers and policymakers, and future research areas for AI are also discussed.</jats:p>

title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence and Ethical Data Governance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
761441594d890ca22a4cdde05f036ec2f7ff492d.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is transforming education by supporting personalized learning, intelligent decision-making and data-driven practices. As AI becomes more integrated into teaching, learning, assessment and institutional management, the ethical use of educational data has become increasingly important. This chapter examines responsible AI and ethical data governance in education. It discusses AI applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning and learning analytics together with the opportunities and challenges they present. The chapter explores the educational data ecosystem, including data sources, governance, ownership and ethical principles such as fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy and explainability. It also examines responsible data management, informed consent, data security and approaches to reducing algorithmic bias. Emerging issues including student surveillance, online proctoring, generative AI, academic integrity, learner autonomy and well-being are discussed.</jats:p>

title: Protecting Student Data in AI-Driven Education Privacy, Consent, Ownership, and Ethical Use
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
1adcff266d66b42b3bb260619da2d8a4f2415ffe.abstract: <jats:p>Through technologies like intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, adaptive learning platforms, and generative AI, artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming education by making learning more efficient, personalized, and interactive. Large volumes of student data are necessary for these technologies to comprehend learning trends, deliver prompt feedback, and aid in educational decision making. While AI has many advantages for educators, institutions, and students, it also brings up significant issues regarding the gathering, storing, sharing, and security of student data. As educational institutions implement AI-enabled systems, concerns about privacy, informed consent, data ownership, transparency, fairness, and ethical use have grown in significance. The main obstacles to safeguarding student data in AI-driven education are examined in this chapter, including concerns about surveillance, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity threats, and unauthorized access.</jats:p>

title: Information Governance of Student Data in AI-Powered Educational Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
9ebb5c39ff6576139082e5f69c7ac01d59c0f7b9.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) examining student data cybersecurity and information governance within AI-powered educational systems. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the review systematically screens 237 published documents to ensure a transparent, replicable, and unbiased synthesis of the intersecting legal, technical, and pedagogical challenges in EdTech. The technical analysis is structured around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF 2.0), evaluating the literature across its six core pillars: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. Furthermore, the study anchors its regulatory analysis within FERPA and the GDPR, with a specific focus on how the GDPR's strict lawful-basis and data-minimization principles govern complex, cross-border educational data flows. Ultimately, this review bridges theory and compliance to offer a comprehensive framework for securing student data in the AI era.</jats:p>

title: Secure Design Principles for AI-Driven Learning Platforms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
32bea6d3eaecbb0e62a89d791d1f4072a5b07d66.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into educational tools such as learning management systems, analytics dashboards, adaptive assessment services, and generative AI assistants. These platforms support personalized learning and institutional decision-making, but they create risks linked to digital identity, learner profiling, data misuse, model leakage, prompt injection, and weak governance. This chapter analyzes cybersecurity governance in AI-driven learning platforms from the perspective of identity security and data privacy. It examines AI-specific privacy threats and safeguards such as zero trust, decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, encryption, federated learning, differential privacy, secure aggregation, and accountable oversight. The chapter proposes a layered cybersecurity framework integrating identity assurance, privacy-preserving processing, AI model protection, secure platform operations, institutional governance, and continuous risk monitoring. The contribution supports trustworthy, privacy-aware, and secure AI-enabled education ecosystems.</jats:p>

title: Distributed Artificial Intelligence for Privacy Preservation and Cyber Resilience in Educational Ecosystems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
1113e5c161f937ef659921855138bbf40a571a58.abstract: <jats:p>The digitization of education has concentrated vast volumes of sensitive learner data within centralized platforms that are priority targets for cyber attackers. It is argued that the dominant centralized model of educational artificial intelligence is structurally misaligned with modern privacy and resilience needs, and an alternative grounded in Distributed Artificial Intelligence is proposed. A layered architecture is presented that couples Federated Learning with Belief-Desire-Intention extended (BDIx) agents to deliver privacy-preserving analytics and autonomous cyber resilience without centralizing raw data. Learner records remain on institutional premises; model updates are protected by differential privacy and secure aggregation; and collaborative threat detection and self-healing are performed by distributed BDIx agents. BDIx-FL reached 99.17% accuracy, 98.93% macro-F1 and 99.76% macro AUC in simulation. Controversies are examined, deployment recommendations are offered and open directions are identified for educational ecosystems that are trustworthy by design.</jats:p>

title: Cybersecurity Awareness and Digital Literacy for Students and Educators Strengthening Data Privacy with AI-Powered Cybersecurity
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
30cafb06bf9daabec321a6848bf1479377de9a8e.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to investigate the significance of cybersecurity awareness, digital literacy, and artificial intelligence in fostering data privacy protection for students and teachers in North India. The study was an exploratory descriptive study with a cross-sectional quantitative design, based on primary data gathered from a structured questionnaire with 620 respondents. The methods used were descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. The correlation was positive for all of the variables, and the highest was between the AI-driven cybersecurity and data privacy protection (r = .741, p < .001). The results of the regression showed that artificial intelligence cybersecurity, digital literacy and cyber security awareness had significant predicting power for data privacy protection, accounting for 66.3% of its variance. The results highlight the need for a holistic approach to integrating AI into education, fostering digital literacy, and raising cybersecurity awareness to ensure safer and privacy-conscious learning spaces.</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Financial Phishing and the Digital Literacy Deficit Protecting Student and Young Learner Data
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
65ab6f5f760fd3d653bfc26c66ada7b9512e9487.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence has structurally transformed financial phishing, collapsing the cost of personalised attacks; India recorded 135,173 financial phishing attacks in H1 2024, a 175% rise over 2023. This chapter examines the convergence of AI-enabled phishing, student data vulnerability, and digital literacy deficits in India's skill-based educational institutions (ITIs, polytechnics, skill universities), a population absent from existing cybersecurity literature despite holding data regulated under the DPDP Act, 2023. Drawing on Routine Activity Theory, Protection Motivation Theory, the Digital Literacy Continuum, and Institutional Theory, it develops the Protection Gap construct and a Four-Layer Institutional Defence Model. A primary survey (N = 96, seven states) finds 66.7% encountered suspected phishing, mostly via WhatsApp; only 25.0% identified a genuine message; 59.4% were unaware of the DPDP Act; and 43.8% reported no explicit consent for Aadhaar/bank data. The chapter closes with recommendations for MeitY, AICTE, NSDC, and the Data Protection Board of India.</jats:p>

title: AI-Generated Deepfakes and Trust in Digital Communication in Namibia
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
9ae33c567c1e3c1be30b3c19886f0820b1ea2ad9.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated the development of deepfake technology, enabling the creation of highly realistic fabricated audio, video, and visual content that closely resembles authentic media. A mixed-method approach was employed, combining an online survey of 47 Namibian internet users and a total of 12 key informants were interviewed. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data were subjected to thematic analysis. The findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on deepfake technologies by providing empirical evidence from Namibia and offering practical recommendations for enhancing digital literacy, strengthening regulatory frameworks, and improving institutional preparedness.</jats:p>

title: KUZGI BUG‘DOY NAV VA TIZMALARINI HOSILDORLIK, NDVI VA VEGETATSIYA DAVRI BO‘YICHA KOMPLEKS BAHOLASH

ac7f4d0c42777770e9754fd7c47567f965171a5c.abstract: <jats:p>Forty winter wheat varieties and breeding lines were jointly evaluated under dry agroecological conditions using grain yield, vegetation period, and NDVI. The analysis was based on field data obtained in 2024 at the experimental site of the Southern Agricultural Research Institute in Karshi district. Grain yield reached 89.75 c/ha, while the maximum NDVI value was 0.855. An auxiliary screening index, assigning 60% weight to yield and 40% to NDVI, was applied to integrate the indicators for preliminary selection. title: Quantum-secure and AI-driven UAV-enabled 6G networks: a unified architecture for communication, intelligence, efficiency, and resilience
container-title: The Computer Journal
2706b267c202c5d2b4e0d881162c56dccf975efc.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The sixth generation (6G) of wireless networks is expected to meet stringent requirements such as ultra-low latency, massive connectivity, global coverage, and intrinsic security. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are emerging as key enablers of space–air–ground integrated networks, providing flexible and on-demand communication support for beyond-5G and 6G applications. In parallel, advances in quantum communication introduce new opportunities for achieving information-theoretic security against postquantum threats. This paper proposes a unified framework for quantum-secure and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven UAV-enabled 6G networks, integrating communication, intelligence, energy efficiency, and resilience into a coherent architecture. Beyond the design perspective, the paper evaluates network performance through Quality of Service and Grade of Service metrics, comparing 5G and 6G systems with and without AI and quantum-security capabilities. A ranking-based analysis is developed to assess the impact of these technologies on latency, reliability, scalability, and overall service performance. The results highlight the performance gains enabled by AI-driven optimization and quantum-secure communication, while also revealing trade-offs related to energy consumption, system complexity, and deployment constraints. Key challenges such as interoperability, hardware limitations, and scalability are discussed, along with design directions for realizing efficient, secure, and resilient UAV-enabled 6G networks.</jats:p>

title: scSpAS: an integrated single-cell and spatial atlas of transcript isoform regulation
container-title: Nucleic Acids Research
44626398d0c191c82bec37415038dc95ffe6e20e.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Alternative transcript initiation, splicing, and 3′-end processing jointly shape transcript isoform diversity, but these regulatory layers remain fragmented across separate single-cell and spatial resources. Here, we present scSpAS, an integrated database of alternative transcription start site (ATS), alternative splicing, full-length transcript isoforms, and alternative polyadenylation (APA) in human and mouse. It contains 123 datasets, including over 418 000 cells and 82 000 spatial spots across healthy and disease contexts, covering 13 cancer types, 5 infectious conditions, 8 inflammatory diseases, and 90 healthy samples. Based on uniformly standardized pipelines, we utilized 5′ capture and 3′ capture single-cell RNA-sequencing data to identify ATS and APA sites, and the Smart-seq2 and long-read sequencing data to identify the alternative splicing events and isoforms. In total, scSpAS contains &gt;648 000 alternative splicing events, 432 000 ATS, and 621 000 APA sites, as well as over 551 000 transcript isoforms. The database further integrates regulatory annotations derived from CLIP-seq, ATAC-seq, and CAGE-seq, together with predicted splicing regulatory motifs. scSpAS enables users to retrieve events, isoforms and genes, examine differential usage at cell-type and spatial levels, and in different biological and physiological conditions; furthermore, users can inspect the potential regulatory mechanisms of all events. It is freely available at https://scspas.chenlulab.com/.</jats:p>

title: The Self-Reinforcing Consensus of Money in U.S. Politics
container-title: Political Science Quarterly
80aa7cec5f0dbfb186a46179b720ac762dc45215.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Why does money dominate congressional politics? In The Money Signal: How Fundraising Matters in American Politics, Danielle M. Thomsen argues that money matters because candidates, donors, journalists, and party leaders treat fundraising as a signal of viability and strength. Drawing on four decades of House fundraising reports, elite interviews, a candidate survey, conjoint experiments, and local newspaper coverage, Thomsen reveals how this self-reinforcing consensus shapes who runs, who stays in the race, who wins, and who prospers in office. Thomsen masterfully unites disparate strands of campaign finance scholarship with the burgeoning literature on primary elections. This review situates The Money Signal within the scholarly landscape of money in congressional politics, assesses its evidence chapter by chapter, and considers its implications under a regulatory environment that has only grown more permissive since publication. I argue that future work should extend one of the book's key contributions: shifting attention away from whether money causes electoral and legislative outcomes and toward how money functions as a signal, from political elites to the mass public. Just as Buckley v. Valeo treated the appearance of corruption as a harm in its own right, The Money Signal highlights opportunities for further investigation into the implications of the appearance of money's influence in politics.</jats:p>

title: PlantVirDisConDB: an integrated resource linking plant virus sequence records with hosts, phenotypes, targets, antiviral evidence, and AI-assisted prioritization
container-title: Nucleic Acids Research
94e3d3d5856ce7833815016738df99245ff17364.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Research on plant viruses depends on taxonomy, nucleic acid sequences, host and disease records, molecular targets, and antiviral assays. These data are distributed across separate resources, making integrated retrieval and comparison difficult. PlantVirDisConDB (https://dpai.ccnu.edu.cn/PVDCDB) is freely accessible without login or registration and links these data through curated plant virus records. At the July 2026 reporting date, it comprised, in round numbers, 5000 virus and subviral agent records and 38 000 sequence accessions. It also included approximately1900 hosts, 9000 virus–host associations, 4800 disease names, 5000 structure records, and 25 000 small molecules. Direct assay records for plant viruses are distinguished from general antiviral background data; experimental and predicted structures, and measured activities and model outputs, are also labelled separately. Linked record pages support retrieval across these data types, access to individual sequence records, target searches, and molecular similarity searches. An activity prediction module ranks candidate molecule–virus pairs with applicability warnings and does not imply experimental or field efficacy. PlantVirDisConDB links viral nucleic acid entities to hosts, phenotypes, targets, and antiviral information and is updated through continuing curation and user feedback.</jats:p>

title: YEASTRACT+: the 2026 update with focus on global quantitative transcription regulation data and metabolic engineering applications
container-title: Nucleic Acids Research
a35977bbf57f7794215c1e86ffe7cbb0f62e8829.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>YEASTRACT+ (http://yeastract-plus.org/) is a tool for the analysis, prediction, and modelling of transcription regulatory data at gene and genomic levels in yeasts. It incorporates three integrated databases: YEASTRACT, PathoYeastract, and NCYeastract, focused on Saccharomyces cerevisiae, pathogenic yeasts, and non-conventional yeasts of biotechnological relevance, respectively. In this release, YEASTRACT+ offers upgraded information on transcription regulation for 13 yeast species, extending the database to two additional yeasts of the basidiomycota phylum, the pathogenic yeast Cryptococcus neoformans, and the biotechnologically relevant Rhodotorula toruloides. A dramatic upgrade in the quality of the data provided occurred, as regulatory associations between transcription factors (TFs) and target genes are now associated with quantitative assessment. Quantitative impact of TFs on gene expression levels enabled the construction and release of two additional analytical tools: quantitative rank by TF, for the prediction of the most relevant TFs underlying a given transcriptomics dataset; and metabolic engineering based on integrating the quantitative impact of TF expression into genome-scale metabolic models. Altogether, this release of YEASTRACT+ provides unparalleled access to massive, curated, quantitative data associated with gene expression control in 13 yeast species, and a set of tools to enable its full exploitation towards fundamental, biotechnological, and health-related applications.</jats:p>

title: A Proposed Model for Teachers' AI Competencies Based on UNESCO and DigCompEdu Frameworks: A Qualitative Study
container-title: Arid International Journal of Educational and physcological sciences
7a8fb5e87b709a8a3bc5fe456897cd79f3dc7754.abstract:
<jats:p>Teachers’ competencies in artificial intelligence (AI) constitute a fundamental element for achieving innovative and effective education aligned with the demands of the twenty-first century. This study aims to propose a comprehensive model of teachers’ AI competencies based on the UNESCO AI Competency Framework for Teachers and the European Digital Competence Framework for Educators (DigCompEdu), while adapting them to suit the needs of teacher preparation programs in faculties of education.

The study adopts a qualitative approach using focus groups with experts in curriculum and instruction as well as educational technology. The domains, standards, and indicators of both frameworks were analyzed and discussed in order to derive a practical and contextually relevant model.

The study resulted in a proposed model comprising five main domains, 15 standards, and 48 performance indicators, covering cognitive, pedagogical, ethical, professional, and assessment dimensions. It also provides practical recommendations for developing teacher preparation and continuous professional development programs, with a focus on integrating artificial intelligence in a responsible and effective manner to support interactive and inclusive learning for students.</jats:p>

title: Graphene-enabled microstructured PDMS triboelectric nanogenerator for self-powered human-machine interfaces
container-title: 2D Materials
9d44bfd96415529e6f102ee0bf65536fb5e6ec45.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>
                    Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) provide a promising route toward self-powered wearable sensors by converting low-frequency human motion into electrical signals. However, the practical use of soft polymer TENGs in human-machine interfaces remains limited by inefficient contact formation, low charge density, and restricted power delivery. Here, a graphene-enabled microstructured PDMS TENG is developed for self-powered gesture sensing. The device combines two complementary design strategies. Micropatterning the PDMS surface improves interfacial contact, pressure localisation and contact-separation recovery, while graphene incorporation introduces 2D polymer-filler interfaces that enhance dielectric polarisation, interfacial charge storage and charge induction within the elastomeric matrix. The optimised graphene@PDMS tribolayer delivers an open-circuit voltage of 150 V, transferred charge of 34 nC, and a power density of 1.92 W m
                    <jats:sup>−2</jats:sup>
                    , showing a 16-fold improvement over pristine microstructured PDMS. The enhanced output is attributed to an effective pre-percolation graphene network that strengthens interfacial polarisation while avoiding dominant leakage and electrostatic screening. Integrated into a five-channel wearable glove, the TENG array generates finger-specific voltage patterns for proof-of-concept self-powered sign-language recognition. This work establishes a simple 2D-material-enabled microstructure-composite engineering strategy for high-output flexible TENGs and wearable human-machine interfaces.
                  </jats:p>

945d92687c6d7953d19a14cadf41191d142af600.abstract: <jats:p>Morphometric and reproductive-biological traits of grass carp (Ctenopharyngodon idella Valenciennes, 1844) aged 3-5 years (n=540; 270 females, 270 males) reared in 2023-2025 at three farms (one monoculture, two polyculture) were studied. No significant differences in body size were found among farms (p>0.05), whereas gonadosomatic index (GSI) differed significantly among all three farms (Welch ANOVA, F=838.15; p<0.001; Games-Howell post-hoc). Compliance with the GSI≥12% criterion showed an absolute association with farm (100%, 0% and 100%; χ²=226.0; p<0.001). Most importantly, females selected by the GSI criterion significantly outperformed a traditional unselected control group on every reproductive measure ‒ relative fecundity (141.4 vs 111.8 thousand eggs/kg; p=0.023), fertilization rate (86.6% vs 78.0%; p<0.001), hatching rate (80.5% vs 74.1%; p<0.001), and survival to active feeding (75.7% vs 65.0%; p<0.001). These findings experimentally validate the practical effectiveness of GSI-based selection as a scientifically grounded method for forming a high-productivity broodstock.</jats:p>

title: Construction learning in the second language classroom
container-title: Applied Linguistics
fd5f2979c99fa19585074c0240c5bfcd48bddacd.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>This study investigates the second language (L2) development of wh-questions in English and French under a usage-based linguistic framework. It draws on two longitudinal corpora documenting spoken production data from different groups of classroom-taught learners; the French Progression Corpus, tracking twenty-four learners over three years, and the Barcelona English Language Corpus, tracking nine learners over seven years. Learners’ earliest wh-questions appear as similar prototypical multiword units and lexically specific constructions used in predictable role-play interactions. Progression-level differences across the datasets are found to be dependent on a learner’s ability to interact with lexically specific material and schematize related constructions from this. The paper discusses the implications of these findings for construction-grammar-informed pedagogies and highlights the value of teaching constructions as form-function pairings to accelerate early productive abilities in foreign language classrooms.</jats:p>

title: Wearable sensors and VOC monitoring: data fusion and machine learning for non-invasive disease detection
container-title: Journal of Breath Research
1dc5c19f9908da8810c82868817ccfc712898588.abstract: Abstract Emerging technologies that detect volatile organic compounds (VOCs) emanating from the body enable rapid and non-invasive detection of diseases. Respiratory illnesses, in particular, can be identified through measurement of VOCs in exhaled breath. However, the low specificity of some methods leaves room for improvement. By combining information from multiple data streams, we can potentially improve on the results obtained from using each data stream individually. Here we evaluate a novel data fusion approach combining a wearable vitals monitor and exhaled breath VOCs for the classification of asthma patients. The wearable vitals monitor or ‘e-glove’ measures key information such as skin temperature, trans-epidermal water loss, heart rate, and galvanic skin response, while the breath VOC data (measured by gold standard gas chromatography-mass spectrometry) provide insight into the biochemical and metabolic state of the body. Data fusion is a process used in many applications for combining information from disparate sources. We leverage data fusion in this case to achieve superior classification accuracy using the integrated data streams. The low-level data fusion achieved a higher ROC AUC score (0.88) in asthma classification than the breath VOC-only approach (0.72, p < 0.001). These results are promising for future data analysis workflows for non-invasive diagnostic and health monitoring.

title: Level 2.5 Large Deviations and Uncertainty Relations for Non-Markov Self-Interacting Dynamics
container-title: Physical Review Letters
d2ca60d847e08b3ac2e895f51bb53a4a707262f5.abstract: We address the general problem of formulating the dynamical large deviations of non-Markovian systems in a closed form. Specifically, we consider a broad class of “self-interacting” jump processes whose dynamics depends on the past through a functional of a state-dependent empirical observable. Exploiting a natural separation of timescales, and under the corresponding mixing conditions, we obtain the exact (so-called “level 2.5”) large deviation joint statistics of the empirical measure over configurations and of the empirical flux of transitions. As an application of this general framework, we derive explicit general bounds on the fluctuations of trajectory observables, generalizing to the non-Markovian case both thermodynamic and kinetic uncertainty relations. We illustrate our theory with simple examples, and discuss potential applications of these results.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice: How Should Rheumatologists Evaluate and Monitor Emerging Tools?
container-title: Arthritis Care & Research
9209aa530195c0580ccf0880fd39aad3145531a5.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in rheumatology practice, to assist with tasks such as documentation, record summarization, and clinical decision support. Rheumatologists need a practical approach to determining what evidence and oversight each application requires. This narrative review proposes a framework based on two dimensions: contextual complexity and influence on patient care. Greater contextual complexity can make errors harder to detect, whereas greater influence on care increases the potential consequences of an undetected error. We examine evidence for workflow benefits and clinical effectiveness within this framework and consider safety, equity, privacy, governance, and implementation. Existing evidence on the benefits, accuracy, and reliability of AI applications remains mixed. For example, studies of ambient AI scribes suggest reduced documentation burden, but evidence of improved patient outcomes from applications supporting clinical decisions is more limited. For applications with limited clinical influence, evaluation has initially focused on workflow, usability, and documentation quality. Tools that synthesize longitudinal information require additional assessment of completeness and source traceability. Those influencing diagnosis or treatment require prospective evaluation of clinical benefit and safety. Relevant vendor evidence should be assessed alongside proportionate local testing and ongoing monitoring. Safeguards should address risks such as hallucinations, automation bias, and propagating documentation errors, with attention to performance across patient groups. Changes in functionality or clinical use should prompt reassessment. The framework provides a structured basis for adoption decisions and identifies priorities for research on patient outcomes and feasible oversight in routine rheumatology care. image

title: State-Based Reinforcement Learning Safe Trajectory Tracking for Autonomous Vehicles via Geometric Safety Representation and Lagrangian-PPO
container-title: Unmanned Systems
32fb8fbf3322a42f83876568f2a720ef10453029.abstract: This paper investigates a state-based Safe Trajectory Tracking (STT) control framework for autonomous vehicles in dynamic environments, where the objective is to design a controller that ensures accurate trajectory tracking while guaranteeing nonconservative collision avoidance. Existing learning-based approaches often suffer from inaccurate geometric safety representations and unstable training when incorporating safety constraints. To address these challenges, we propose a geometry-aware framework by integrating an analytical Rotating Supporting Hyperplane (RSH)-based safety representation with a Lagrangian Proximal Policy Optimization (Lagrangian-PPO) reinforcement learning algorithm. By modeling vehicles and obstacles as rigid ellipsoids, an explicitly differentiable signed distance is derived to provide a continuous and nonconservative safety cost. Based on this representation, the trajectory tracking problem is formulated as a constrained Markov decision process, enabling unified optimization of tracking performance and safety via a reward–cost decoupled learning structure. Finally, asymptotic convergence and effectiveness of the proposed approach are validated through simulation and Vehicle-in-the-Loop (ViL) experiments, demonstrating superior tracking accuracy and robust obstacle avoidance compared with existing methods.

title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
ee1a53267db02baf46a3d0edf5461a8422c80e07.abstract: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span delves into the evolving journey of teacher educators, exploring how professional learning and identity develop from initial preparation through to leadership and sustained inquiry. This book brings together diverse perspectives and research to illuminate the complexities and opportunities of professional growth across a teacher educator’s career. Organised around key contexts, including initial teacher preparation, induction, leadership, and ongoing inquiry, the book foregrounds equity-centred teacher education and the vital role of communities of practice and school-university partnerships. Contributors critically examine how teacher educators learn, adapt, and lead within changing sociocultural and policy landscapes, offering fresh insights into the knowledge, skills, and reflective practices that shape the profession. Drawing on a range of methodologies and lived experiences, this collection not only advances scholarship in teacher education but also provides practical guidance and reflective questions for readers. It is an essential resource for anyone committed to fostering meaningful professional learning and advancing equity in teacher education across the professional life span.

title: Embracing the Complex Tapestry of Professional Learning: A Narrative Inquiry Through a Doctoral Foundational Course
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
f9983957b32fef94cc7715dbe9f057025ecde99c.abstract: Abstract We continue to live in a world that is cultivated by the influence of teachers. As such, the field of teacher education is a foundation for fostering change, but we, as teacher educators, must also be willing to examine the complexity and importance of our work by seeking opportunities to affect equitable change. In this chapter, the authors illustrate their journey in a foundational doctoral course, Learning and Instruction throughout the Lifespan, to illustrate how they embrace professional learning as teacher educators. Through narrative inquiry, the authors delve into the dynamic, multifaceted nature of their roles within the course from various perspectives: one as the instructor of record and three as doctoral students. While sharing their reflective processes, grounded in the principles of sustaining inquiry as stance, this chapter is based on the following question: How do our roles and inherent responsibilities throughout a foundational doctoral course serves as a means of professional learning and influence our growth as teacher educators? Throughout the chapter, the authors address how their development as teacher educators was informed by course elements that expanded their breadth and depth of knowledge and skills.

title: More Than Rolling With the Punches: Growing as a Teacher Educator
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
676cce43cfdd3a5638e4dd0bf405dc8b9779efe5.abstract: Abstract In this chapter, the author describes her identity development and professional learning as a teacher educator over the last decade through self-study in teacher education for professional learning. Through personal experience with supervising student teachers, she recognizes that classrooms are ever-changing. Each year in teacher education she desires to have effective and relevant teaching. She reflects to determine if she merely acknowledged change and then taught the same content, methods and dispositions. In this sustained inquiry through self-study she examines how her teaching identity was transformed with a focus on being relevant and effective. First she identifies these changes in three areas: curriculum, pedagogy, and the student demographics of the classroom. Then through self-study she analyzes multiple sets of data to identify the practices that were most useful in her professional learning about these changes. She concludes with key practices that enabled her to grow as a teacher educator amid changes in teaching and classroom demographics.

title: From Teacher to Teacher Educator: A Journey in Friendship and Conversation
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
0773132775fa2c0e14817af424a500850a98ceee.abstract: Abstract Two longtime friends and fellow teacher educators discuss our journey to becoming educational researchers and teacher educators. Using reflective writing and recorded conversations, we employ autoethnographic methods to tell our stories based on distinct periods of our careers. Framing this chapter, we share vignettes from our friendship and work, we weave together our learning as teachers, graduate students and then as faculty. Through an analysis of our writing and conversations, we found both internal and external forces which helped us think critically about the role of community, identity, and intellectual work associated with teacher education and being a teacher educator.

title: Reconciling Teaching and Teacher Education Metaphors: Realizing an Instructional Centering
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
ba1e85edbf74e8a9fd88db24ba4cbfd592d4f5a1.abstract: Abstract In the following chapter, the teaching and teacher education metaphors of one teacher educator embraced across a career are shared and examined for their perceived effectiveness in supporting their respective roles. In this self-case study, five teaching and three teacher education metaphors are identified. The teaching metaphors detailed here were found to be somewhat limiting when applied to teacher education. Additionally, the initial teacher education metaphors which emerged were not felt to be completely contributing to effective teaching. The resulting tension between teaching and teacher education metaphors found release for the author through the creation of a composite metaphor which could efficiently function in both arenas as well as in some areas of life outside of academia. Based on this study’s findings, it is suggested that teacher educators regularly reflect on their own metaphors to determine whether their teaching, teacher education, and potentially the metaphors they embrace from other aspects of their lives, can be combined in some way to function more effectively.

title: Benefits of Autoethnography Across the Teaching Career Span: An Argument for Inclusion
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
3c163e08cdc94daf83437f548e4c63fc0e44abca.abstract: Abstract Developing the capacity for self-reflection is a central component of continual teacher growth. Practices such as journaling help educators rapidly improve by enabling them to identify challenges in lesson planning, assessment, behavior management, and classroom culture. Autoethnography, a research method that integrates reflective journal entries with existing scholarship, offers a structured approach for deepening this self-reflective work. Introducing autoethnographic practices to both future and current educators can therefore cultivate stronger reflective habits across all stages of a teaching career. For preservice teachers, engaging in autoethnography encourages them to connect their emerging classroom observations with established research, promoting evidence-based decision-making early in their professional development. These reflective habits can support long-term success by helping new teachers internalize practices that foster continuous improvement. For teachers in their first years, autoethnography provides a tool for managing the steep learning curve they face as they encounter educational challenges for the first time. Reflective journaling paired with research can offer clarity, reduce overwhelm, and help them make sense of their experiences. Veteran teachers also benefit from autoethnographic practices, as the method can deepen their understanding of complex or evolving issues—such as the growing influence of artificial intelligence in classrooms—by linking ongoing experiences with contemporary scholarship. Finally, teacher educators who use autoethnography themselves gain methodological proficiency, strengthen their own teaching, and develop authentic examples to share with those they mentor. This chapter explores the value of integrating autoethnographic practices into teacher education to support reflective growth at all career stages.

title: Who We Are in the Classroom: Navigating Emotions and Positionality of Two Novice Teacher Educators in a Multicultural Education Course
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
323e864da3ead677fc4842f4cc2bdc6553726498.abstract: Abstract This study examines how our differing positionalities as novice teacher educators (TEs) influence our emotional responses teaching a foundational multicultural education (MCE) course at a predominantly white institution. One of us, Mariah, identifies as a Latina from a working-class family, while the other, Kyle, is a white man from an affluent background. By investigating the interplay between our backgrounds and our emotional responses to teaching an MCE course, we seek to highlight the nuanced role of identity in shaping the experiences of TEs. As both educators and learners in these spaces, we navigate our own identities—race, gender, class, etc.—while supporting students engaging with their own. In teaching students to understand systems of oppression and develop equity literacy, we also recognize that our positionalities are situated within systems of oppression, and this affects how we position ourselves in relation to each other and to the important work of social justice in MCE. Through narrative inquiry we analyze data collected from our reflective journals, recorded conversations with each other, and correspondence with students to illustrate how our different positionalities impacted our emotional responses to self-affirming and challenging moments. Our findings offer insights into the induction process for TEs and the presentation of their positionalities in MCE courses while engaging in communities of practice.

title: Longitudinal Development of Science Teacher Educators’ Sense-Making Skills
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
686a67a8baee52fc28ff34483014a71650d8828f.abstract: Abstract Teachers are the single most important school-based factor that influences students’ learning, and arguably, science teacher educators (STEs) exert a comparable influence on the quality of science teacher education. Very little is known, however, about which STE practices ought to be emulated and how these practices develop. Research, to date, rarely includes real-time analysis of STEs at work. This chapter is a study of three STEs over multiple semesters (four to seven terms) as they worked to learn and effectively practice their sense-making skills with preservice teachers (PSTs) during oral final exams in an elementary science methods course. Findings revealed that the greatest challenge for STEs occurred when attempting to respond to PST thinking. In early semesters, STEs displayed an imitative phase where they copied a mentor’s practices, followed by a digression as they attempted independently to scaffold PSTs toward deeper understanding. Later, in semesters 4 and 5, STEs began to design more sophisticated sense-making episodes using authentic teaching scenarios which exposed PSTs’ contradictory thinking and challenged them to negotiate these contradictions. STE effectiveness in generating useful sense-making experiences for PSTs was positively influenced by consistent support from a more knowledgeable other.

title: Transforming Teacher Educators’ Beliefs in Recruiting and Retaining Future Teachers of Color
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
705ea2f7792a0314e0124aabc8cfbf935bd8ca52.abstract: Abstract The four authors of this chapter are at different stages of their careers as teacher educators ranging from an assistant professor to a full professor who is an Associate Dean, yet we share the same passion of equity-centered teacher education (Jacobs, 2023). Over the last two years, our university has created a Grow Your Own (GYO) program, which we call Teaching Fellows, to fund the education of traditional and nontraditional students from underrepresented school districts in our state. The main purposes of the GYO program are to address the teacher shortage and to increase the number of teachers of Color. This chapter highlights the opportunities and obstacles of recruiting future teachers of Color into the GYO program and what we learned about ourselves as teacher educators along the way. Our findings suggest ways to reform teacher education practices so that programmatic elements are indicative of an ever-changing world.

title: Mentor Teacher Professional Learning: Promising Practices, Activities, and Structures Within Teacher Residency Programs
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
013bf0d03e051c89499fed3eabc161b664a4c077.abstract: Abstract This chapter draws on 15+ years of experience designing and scaling over 175 teacher residency programs across 35 states, including in-depth insights from 14 programs that informed the development of a framework for mentor teacher professional learning. The authors examine the complex and multifaceted role of mentor teachers in residencies who serve as essential links between institutions of higher education and K-12 schools, helping new teachers navigate often unstated and/or misaligned expectations for teacher resident learning resulting from their preparation program. The knowledge and skills required for this work extend well beyond effective K-12 teaching, encompassing relationship-building for adult learning and navigating systems. Despite these mentoring skills being foundational to learning for preservice teachers, they often go unrecognized and undersupported, limiting the full potential of the teacher residency program. This chapter underscores the importance of developing a shared, cross-organizational vision for both new teacher residents and their mentor teachers, and presents four promising practices for the professional learning that mentor teachers need in order to consistently succeed. By prioritizing intentional support for mentor teachers focused on their critical position as “navigators,” teacher residencies can enhance their overall impact, ensuring a more effective and sustainable teacher development ecosystem.

title: Synergy Within Teacher Education: Connecting Theory and Practice Through “Mentoree” Moments
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
d6c145e681bd36ec664496cc1478d458ca66ccd8.abstract: Abstract We are tasked with preparing secondary English language arts teachers to be social justice and multiliteracies oriented, but our students often find themselves struggling with theory-to-practice connections. In this collaborative self-study, adopting a double-helix model of teacher education, we situate our findings around mentoree moments: a recursive relationship between serving as a mentor while also gleaning insight as a mentee. We end with implications and insights from our personal and professional journeys on how our experiences might benefit teacher educators to participate in synergistic mentoree moments across their professional life span.

title: Growing as Equity-Centered Teacher Educators Using Drama-Based Pedagogy: A Community of Practice
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
5e61ae178d1ec9470bd4ee17c535dcc3111a5414.abstract: Abstract In this chapter, we describe the theoretical and practical possibilities of Drama-Based Pedagogy (DBP; Dawson & Lee, 2018) to support ongoing equity-centered learning with the goal of improving preservice teacher preparation. To prepare educators in culturally relevant pedagogy, teacher education programs must intentionally model culturally relevant and sustaining pedagogies and praxis, not just teach about the theories. As university faculty, we formed a Community of Practice to support our collaborative and individual professional learning in DBP to strengthen our ability to prepare educators to teach for social justice. We share our process of learning about and honing how we model culturally relevant and sustaining pedagogies through DBP.

title: Mentoring Beyond the Degree: Equipping the Meaning-Makers
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
18687df2d5a4b9b83dee5f09693b815c4d7ba23b.abstract: Abstract The teacher shortage in the United States has forced Education Preparation Programs (EPPs) to rethink their practices and overall philosophies. A growing area of importance for teacher educator preparation in this volatile time may now be the post-completer phase or the first years of a new teacher’s career. With the dramatic rise of conditional licensure and high teacher turnover rates, the need to support teachers after they leave their EPP and complete their programs of study, and those who prepare them, is paramount. Beyond any specific practice or method, in the widest sense, EPPs may now have an ethical prerogative to continue to support completers after they leave their programs. This chapter focuses on administrators who support teacher educators, and specifically, who support teacher educators who work with completers. This chapter will detail how one department in an SOE in a small private institution created an infrastructure to support their teacher educators who work with completers. The main question here is, how can administrators support and build capacity for teacher educators in this critical phase? And relatedly, how do administrators maximize the talents and knowledge base of those who prepare teachers to deliver this support? And finally, how can administrators help their teacher educators convey that teaching is not simply a technical endeavor, but an act of love, transformation and meaning-making?

title: Moving Through Discomfort: Communities of Practice Supporting Early Career Teacher Educators’ Culturally Responsive Teaching Practice
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
0f12745129da2ac10ba4e316b26c0af21e761f47.abstract: Abstract Early-career teacher educators (TEs) navigate dual roles as learners and facilitators of teacher learning (Stamatis et al., 2019). In this chapter we, a group of pretenure TEs working at an urban university serving mostly white preservice teachers (PSTs), explore how our attempts at using video as a vehicle for PST reflection around culturally responsive teaching (CRT; e.g., Gay, 2000; Ladson Billings, 1995) led interrogation of our own practice. We draw from the work of Boler and Zembylas (2003) on pedagogics of discomfort as we unpack our efforts to help PSTs grapple with their developing understanding of CRT. Engaging in a collaborative inquiry process led us as early-career TEs to identify and move through cycles of discomfort to question and disrupt our current practices and approaches to CRT.

title: Teaching is Learning: Reflections on Teacher Education
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
7fa0450cb01132d4c2d18cae3a6ff84b07c373b3.abstract: Abstract This chapter presents the story of teacher educator learning in a school-based professional development program in which elementary and middle school teachers engaged in disciplined inquiry as reflective practitioners. The authors share what they have learned during the pilot year of this program with an emphasis on how their understanding of the work of professional development and, more specifically, their roles and identities in supporting teacher research have evolved over time. Reflecting on the research literature and their experiences, they conclude that many ideas about the nature of leadership and coaching are best described as processes that require curiosity, adaptation, participation, and an openness to be as much learner as teacher. In a spirit of “utopian thinking,” the authors suggest that there is more learning to be had when a community of practice becomes a true learning community; not merely building on what we already know but building new knowledge and the next generation of practices our developing profession requires.

title: A Three-Pronged Approach to Teacher Educator Learning: Toward Understanding Teacher Leadership
container-title: Teacher Educator Learning Across the Professional Life Span
9ab9a31ee91e72cbade1633a259abf5ff4d8fdd2.abstract: Abstract This chapter presents concrete examples that illustrate our approach to teacher educator learning and its impact on supporting early career teacher leadership development. Our model—rooted in inquiry, professional learning, and dissemination—prioritizes teacher educator learning as an inclusive, collaborative, and adaptive practice, grounded in a commitment to equity and collective growth. Through iterative cycles of inquiry, we align our practices, goals, and programmatic resources to meet diverse teacher needs. Recognizing gaps in our understanding, we engage in ongoing professional learning, by drawing on current and seminal research, book studies, and peer collaboration. Dissemination is central to our work, enabling us to codify our learning within our organization and share our findings more broadly. Through dissemination, we contribute to the broader educational landscape, advocating for teacher voices and collaborative knowledge-building. This model of teacher educator learning emphasizes collective growth, reflective practice, and sustainable development inspiring transformative change across educational communities.

title: Absolute phase recovery from reduced phase-shifted fringe patterns via composite-loss-driven deep learning
container-title: Optics Express
4305666317d0297a3fb28658b6db03cec3d3cb4d.abstract: Conventional multi-frequency heterodyne phase-shifting profilometry enables high-accuracy three-dimensional reconstruction but typically requires the acquisition of 12 fringe patterns, which limits measurement efficiency. This paper proposes a few-step absolute phase recovery method based on a multi-frequency fringe completion network (MFC-Net) and a composite loss function. At each of the three frequencies, two fringe patterns with phase shifts of 0 and π are captured, resulting in a total of six measured images. The network predicts the missing π/2- and 3π/2-shifted fringe patterns, which are combined with the measured patterns to form a complete three-frequency four-step sequence. Absolute phase is subsequently recovered using standard four-step phase demodulation and multi-frequency heterodyne unwrapping. The composite loss function comprises an L1 loss, a hard example mining loss, and a spatial gradient consistency loss, which constrain global intensity fidelity, high-error pixels, and local structures, respectively. Experiments were conducted on multiple test objects using two frequency combinations, 100/90/81 and 64/56/49. For objects with smoothly varying surfaces, the absolute phase RMSE of the proposed method was only 3.2%–8.5% higher than that of the three-frequency four-step method. For an object containing complex edges and occlusions, the proposed method reduced the RMSE by 42.8% compared with the three-frequency three-step method under the 64/56/49 frequency combination. Compared with other deep-learning-based recovery strategies, the proposed method generally achieved better point-cloud completeness and local-profile preservation. These results demonstrate that the proposed method reduces the number of physically captured fringe patterns from 12 to 6 while largely preserving absolute phase accuracy and three-dimensional reconstruction quality.

title: How reliable are self-reports of debt? Misclassification, selection, and measurement bias between survey and administrative data in the UK Household Longitudinal Study
container-title: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A: Statistics in Society
68f4736f1e2e57af25a8458c9f1844f749dbb66e.abstract: Abstract Self-reported and administratively recorded debt measures are susceptible to measurement error, while selection bias may arise if individuals who consent to data linkage differ systematically from those who do not. This study evaluates the quality of self-reported and administrative debt measures by assessing selection into linkage, agreement between data sources, and the implications of measurement differences for associations with mental health. Using Wave 4 of the UK Household Longitudinal Study linked to Credit Reference Agency (CRA) records, we compared 8 debt types across 3 analytical samples: the full analytical sample, nonconsenters sample, and linked consenters sample. Agreement between self-reported and CRA-recorded debt was assessed using misclassification, sensitivity, specificity, positive predictive value, and negative predictive value. Mental health associations were estimated using Bayesian hierarchical regression models. Respondents who consented to linkage were more likely to be older, partnered, employed, homeowners, and UK-born. Misclassification varied across debt types and was lowest for overdrafts, personal loans, and retail finance. Substantial discrepancies were observed between self-reported and CRA-recorded debt prevalence, particularly for credit cards and other running debts. Differences between data sources also influenced estimated debt-mental health associations. These findings underscore the need to account for selection and measurement error in linked debt data.

title: Bias meets Bayes: Bayesian aggregation for peer and self-ranking
container-title: Journal of the Royal Statistical Society Series A: Statistics in Society
f04182ff4fbb6ef31f77f56b3b7577d1c0d58b6e.abstract: Abstract Rank aggregation, which aims to combine multiple ordinal rankings into a single, reliable ranking, is widely studied in diverse fields. In academic and professional settings, peer- and self-evaluations play a pivotal role and offer insights into both individual performance and the competence of rankers. However, subjective biases can lead to unreliable or unfair outcomes, especially in a small sample setting. Despite the broad applications of rank aggregation, existing methods often fail to address nuanced biases and the special structure of such data. This paper introduces BayeSPeer, a novel Bayesian hierarchical model designed to jointly estimate latent performance scores and self-assessment biases in peer- and self-ranking data. Through comprehensive simulation studies, BayeSPeer demonstrates superior performance in rank recovery and top-k identification under various levels of sample size, ranking quality, and bias magnitudes. Real-world applications in classroom peer evaluations also highlight the model’s interpretability and practical utility. Our findings showcase the advantages of incorporating structured bias correction rather than omitting self-evaluation, offering a statistically principled and transparent approach to bias-aware ranking in educational and other evaluation contexts.

title: Simpler is not always better: Phylodynamic misspecification and deep-learning corrections
container-title: Molecular Biology and Evolution
0917c120cf91a3b08664a8659c29ee5fc87e5186.abstract: Abstract Phylodynamics bridges the gap between epidemiology and pathogen genetic data. The birth-death (BD) model and its extensions serve to infer the average number of secondary infections Re and the infection duration d from time-scaled pathogen phylogenies. Moreover, more complex models add extra parameters, such as the average length of the incubation period, the proportion of superspreaders in the infected population, or the speed-up in detection after contact-tracing. However, these additional parameters come at an important computational cost: While the simplest, BD, model, has a closed-form solution, its extensions do not and require numerical methods for their likelihood computation. This leads to increased computational times and potential numerical errors. Therefore, the BD model remains the favorite researchers’choice for real dataset analyses, and is often applied even in cases where more complex epidemiological aspects are present. We investigated, using simulations, how model misspecification influences inference of Re and d in the phylodynamic framework. We showed that the use of models not accounting for various epidemiological aspects leads to bias. In particular the simplest, BD, estimator tends to underestimate Re in the presence of super-spreading, incubation or contact-tracing, which might be dangerous from the public health perspective. In contrast, deep-learning-based estimators for complex models, accounting for multiple epidemiological factors, performed well in our simulations both on the data where those factors were present and where they were absent. This motivates the use of complex epidemiologically realistic estimators, whose design has recently become possible thanks to deep learning.

title: Level-2.5 large deviations and uncertainty relations for self-interacting jump processes: Tilting constructions and the emergence of timescale separation
container-title: Physical Review E
82100f20fc0fe0a19d3a1027430f5cdc929f3a13.abstract: Self-interacting jump processes (SIJPs) describe systems with non-Markovian stochastic dynamics in which transition rates depend on empirical observables of the process, which gives rise to long-range memory and feedback. We derive the “level-2.5” large deviation (LD) principle governing the joint fluctuations of empirical occupation measure and the flux matrix for a broad class of SIJPs with general functional dependence on an empirical observable. The derivation is based on an exponential tilting construction and reveals a separation between a faster timescale of the microscopic dynamics and a slower timescale of the memory-driven evolution of transition rates, which is expressed through an exponentially discounted LD rate functional. Using this variational framework, we derive kinetic and thermodynamic uncertainty relations that extend classical Markovian bounds to non-Markovian systems and illustrate their performance with simple examples.

title: Accelerated formulation screening of multi-component bioinks via a deep learning-integrated high-throughput gradient printing platform
container-title: Biofabrication
0b3bbe6821441d24c9a151a2ea6322699d19ccdd.abstract: Abstract The development of performant multi-component bioinks is severely bottlenecked by the astronomical size of the possible design space and the inefficiency of empirical, trial-and-error experimentation. Existing high-throughput screening methods, such as microarrays and droplet microfluidics, remain limited by discrete sampling, cell-unfriendly environments, and a lack of integrated analytics. Herein, a high-throughput gradient printing (HTGP) platform is employed to overcome these barriers by integrating continuous combinatorial bioprinting with deep learning (DL)-powered phenotyping. The HTGP system rapidly generates bioink libraries with gradients within a native three-dimensional hydrogel environment, preserving cell viability and enabling in situ , direct interrogation of cell-material interactions. Coupled with an automated neural network pipeline, the platform quantitatively deciphers complex relationships between bioink composition and cellular responses from massive images. Under the tested in vitro conditions, it identified a formulation that enhanced human umbilical vein endothelial cell proliferation and spreading, as well as a candidate bioink that exhibited osteo-inductive potential by promoting osteogenic differentiation of bone marrow mesenchymal stem cells. Critically, the formulation identified through DL-assisted screening showed an enhanced early regenerative response in a rat periodontal bone defect model compared with the controls. The HTGP platform shifts from discrete testing to intelligent, continuous exploration, poised to accelerate the discovery of advanced biomaterials for personalized tissue engineering.

title: DQIRMask: dual-quality and instance-relation mask learning for fluorescent neuronal cell instance segmentation
container-title: Physica Scripta
c73195ab07d22c887dc98cbd4fda49e8c421c594.abstract: Abstract Fluorescent neuronal cell instance segmentation detects individual cells and delineates each cell at the pixel level for cell counting, soma morphology measurement, and spatial-organization analysis. Weak contrast, nonuniform fluorescence, substantial shape variation, and frequent contact or overlap can produce incomplete masks, boundary leakage, merged instances, and confidence scores that do not reflect mask quality. We propose Dual-Quality and instance-relation mask (DQIRMask), a CenterMask-based framework that combines Crowded-Instance Relation Reasoning, a Prototype-boundary decoder (PBD), and Dual-quality calibration. On the Yellow subset of Fluorescent Neuronal Cells v2, the full model improves average precision (AP) by 3.2 points over the strongest BlendMask configuration and by 5.1 points over the strongest CondInst configuration; the corresponding AP 75 gains are 6.5 and 10.1 points. Across six backbone ablations, the full configuration improves AP by 0.1–1.5 points and AP 75 by 0.1–3.0 points over the matching CenterMask baselines. The standalone effects are backbone dependent: the PBD reduces AP for four of six backbones. On the Green and Red subsets, AP 75 improves in all ten backbone-subset comparisons, although AP and F 1 do not improve in every case. These results support the full DQIRMask configuration for boundary-sensitive fluorescent-cell segmentation and show that component-level effects vary across backbones.

title: Learning Rényi entropy in neural network quantum states
container-title: Physica Scripta
f470833d71ca2d1983df851ad71e6f40c54cbb8b.abstract: Abstract We study the Rényi entropy in a one-dimensional transverse-field quantum Ising model by virtue of the machine learning methods with neural networks. The Rényi entropy is investigated both in the static ground state and in the dynamical state after a linear quench, by employing a swapping operator acting on the states prepared from the neural networks. In the ground state, the behavior of Rényi entropy can unveil the critical point from paramagnetic to ferromagnetic phase. At the critical point, the relation between the Rényi entropy and the subsystem size from the machine learning method satisfies the predictions from conformal field theory. In the quenching dynamics, coherent oscillations of the Rényi entropy are observed after the end of the quench. These oscillations have universal frequencies stem from the superpositions of the excited states. More importantly, an asymptotic scaling of the reduced Rényi entropy is observed, implying a novel length scale away from the critical point.

title: Learning the geometry of matched-filter mismatch for gravitational-wave template banks with machine learning
container-title: Classical and Quantum Gravity
1516639cf875d537850469e18f294e8c2aa5530f.abstract: Abstract Matched filtering provides the foundation for gravitational-wave detection, with waveform similarity traditionally described through the local geometry of the template-space metric. We investigate whether the exact pairwise matched-filter mismatch (PMM) over a finite waveform bank can instead be used to learn a global coordinate system for gravitational-wave templates. As a controlled proof of concept, we consider finite banks of nonspinning IMRPhenomD binary-black-hole waveforms over a fixed component-mass range. We formulate this as a supervised representation-learning problem in which physically computed PMM provides the supervision signal, and train a neural network so that Euclidean distances between latent coordinates approximate the mismatch between waveform pairs. Across waveform banks containing up to 8192 templates, the learned representation preserves both global pairwise mismatch relationships and local matched-filter neighborhoods while consistently outperforming Euclidean retrieval in the physical coordinate systems considered. Comparison with Classical Multidimensional Scaling shows that the learned encoder provides a competitive low-dimensional approximation of the finite-bank mismatch geometry while simultaneously learning an explicit mapping applicable to previously unseen waveforms. For previously unseen query waveforms drawn from the same waveform family and parameter distribution, the learned representation recovers the exhaustive best-matching template for 99.02% of queries using only 10 candidate templates from an 8192-template bank and for all queries using 20 candidates, reducing the number of exact matched-filter evaluations by factors of 819.2 and 409.6, respectively. Within this controlled setting, these results demonstrate that PMM provides an effective supervision signal for learning global geometric representations of waveform similarity and establish a proof of concept for mismatch-supervised organization and candidate retrieval in finite waveform banks.
