More than a story, this case study offers proof. Meli’s model demonstrates how learning, when it mirrors nature, can transform not just individuals but systems. It is not only about surviving the polycrisis of our time — it is about remembering how to live, together.

title: Commoning as learning
container-title: Constellations of hope
be7453b69692fe2c7b984514d7d4d359fdc1cde2.abstract: In response to today’s interlinked ecological, social and institutional crises — often referred to as the polycrisis — this paper explores the potential of commoning as a practice of place-based learning, governance and transformation. Grounded in a case study from Switzerland, it presents an initiative led by IDEE 21, an eco-social cooperative that combines the co-creation of a commons manual with the development of a transdisciplinary community of practice. This dual intervention bridges the gap between commons theory and implementation by translating key principles — drawn from Elinor Ostrom’s design principles, Indigenous ways of knowing, systems thinking and bio-regioning — into practical, context-sensitive tools for collective stewardship. It offers insights into how commoning can serve as embodied, collective learning and collaborative stewardship, particularly in multistakeholder processes dealing with complex, uncertain problems. Positioned at the intersection of theory and grounded experimentation, the project explores how commons-based learning can reweave relationships between people, place and the living world. It emphasises stewardship over control and learning as a relational and participatory process rooted in specific ecologies and communities. Through participatory methodologies — such as stakeholder workshops, governance prototyping and peer exchange — the project highlights the importance of social process design, ecological thinking and distributed leadership in building resilient commons. The paper argues that commoning, when grounded in place and supported by intentional social learning, holds transformative potential for navigating complexity and cultivating systems resilience. It contributes to emerging scholarship on commons-based governance by documenting applied practices and design insights, positioning the commons as both a framework for action and a site for multigenerational, practice-led learning.

title: Learning in nature’s classroom
container-title: Constellations of hope
e470e4df76defbc71041e4e4dd9699d6f4412c2f.abstract: Our work addresses the concern that not only are we living beyond our limits as a human species but we are also using the resources of other species on which we are dependent. In order to “learn for life,” the community of practice spans projects in Indonesia and South Africa with graduates, their students, colleagues and members of the community. The ancient societies of Ciptagler (West Java, Indonesia) and Bady (Bantam Province, Indonesia) and the resilient communities in South Africa led by Dzomo la Mupo are inspiring intergenerational learning. We have chosen to work in Africa and Indonesia, two emerging economies that share a colonial legacy. The case study areas also share concerns associated with the following: high rates of urbanisation, habitat and species loss and displacement and the risks associated with climate change, such as food, water and energy security. The potential implementation of our research for future learning and educational policies would involve setting up learning communities as multispecies hubs that work together to enable local green circular economies. The common good needs to be supported by democratic engagement using metalogues and structured democratic dialogues. Our area of concern is 1) learning lessons from communities that have food security and are self-reliant; 2) how to protect these communities; 3) applying the lessons to support local green circular economies in other communities.

title: Reclaiming pedagogies rooted in Himalayan ecologies
container-title: Constellations of hope
d25917e11a654a8aa4d662e41cd9e2ecdcfc5e6d.abstract: This paper explores the potential of a living pedagogy, a regenerative, place-based pedagogical framework grounded in intergenerational knowledge, place-based practice and collective responsibility, within the Himalayan context of Sikkim, India. As the region confronts intensifying climate vulnerability and a growing disconnection between young people and agrarian life, we argue that education systems must shift from maintenance learning to transformative learning. Drawing on our conversational and transect walks with farmers, the study identifies pedagogical tools rooted in traditional ecological knowledge, such as seed-saving practices, reciprocal labour systems like Aicho Paicho and farm-based mentorship. These tools exemplify how land-based knowledge transmission from farmer practitioners can cultivate ecological literacy, cultural continuity and community resilience among younger generations. Rather than treating Indigenous and local knowledge systems as supplemental, this paper positions them as foundational to building climate resilience and reimagining education systems. It contributes to global debates on decolonial education and intergenerational learning by proposing mechanisms for reviving and integrating these unconventional pedagogies into contemporary frameworks. While these approaches are envisioned as complementary to formal education and embedded in extracurricular activities, we investigate community-rooted experiences as nonetheless integral to fostering climate consciousness and belonging among learners. By mapping the pedagogical power of intergenerational knowledge, place and seeds, underpinned by local social practices, the paper presents a vision for climate-adaptive pedagogies rooted in relationships between people, land and generations and invites broader reflection on how learning systems might reconnect with life through context-specific, relational and embodied practices.

title: Collective leadership to nurture a new democratic paradigm in remote and rural Scotland
container-title: Constellations of hope
983c2adc855260072567d761ecd43178219d27d3.abstract: Argyll and Bute embraces innovation out of necessity. Despite its natural beauty, including 23 inhabited islands, the region faces significant challenges like an aging and declining population, a finite public sector and a fragile economy. Partners have worked for over 15 years to nurture collective power in local communities to respond to these challenges. Having gained momentum following the pandemic, partnerships were built on a vibrant third social enterprise sector, high social capital, plentiful natural resources, plus engaged citizens. Collaborations and partnerships have been nurtured and invested in over time to empower communities to work together on intersecting issues like health, inequality, poverty, the economy and climate. Objectives include building relationships across sectors, shifting power to local communities to reset a top-down public sector and working together to co-produce local solutions. A cohort of 10 members formed in 2022 and expanded to a community of practice of more than 30 people from a range of sectors and locations by 2025. Financial investment from the public sector has been matched by a significant charitable grant to resource this work. Participants are developing relational working practices and community engagement skills alongside creative storytelling, which is resulting in increased reach and enthusiasm for these transformative approaches. Looking ahead the initiative has clear priorities. Firstly, a smaller public sector with increased demands requires a theory of change involving a brave new social democracy. Secondly, enacting a paradigm shift can empowers and activate communities to be in control of their own destinies. In this case, it has the potential to transform decline on the fringes of Scotland to success and optimism for the future.

title: The power of paradigms
container-title: Constellations of hope
223974eabde9ae8c53916a8cbd002c50aeed86d3.abstract: Humans have developed the concept of sustainability to describe actions that maintain the quality of life for current generations without undermining future generations’ ability to meet their own needs. However, operationalising this vision is challenging given the diversity of values shaping its implementation. As the economy, which is embedded in society, which is embedded in nature continues on a business as usual trajectory, the risk of polycrisis grows. The current global social-ecological system is extractive, polluting and prioritises monetised economic growth within a constrained biophysical system. A circular economy seeks to decouple growth from environmental degradation and non-renewable resource use, but whether it can achieve sustainability without a paradigm shift remains unclear. First Nations communities in Australia are known to hold a different human-nature paradigm to business as usual and have supported health and wellbeing within planetary boundaries for over 65,000 years. This article qualitatively compares these three social-ecological systems to explore how paradigms shape sustainability outcomes and the implications for sustainability learning and education. Using systems modelling, we show that sustainability requires solutions that directly address the human-nature relationship and that reframe the paradigms underpinning education and economic systems. Our theoretical framework and high-level models reveal how a flawed human-nature relationship undermines system sustainability. We then explore learning and knowledge across systems, with particular emphasis on First Nations ways of knowing, doing and being. Grounded in relational responsibility, connectedness and complexity, these approaches offer clear principles for designing social-ecological systems that sustain both people and the planet — but achieving this shift first requires recentering First Nations voices and knowledge, including in education.

title: Human revolution as transformative learning
container-title: Constellations of hope
6c6153751e673b395470b73fb6f0fcd8418963f4.abstract: This paper explores grassroots educational practices inspired by the Soka Gakkai’s concept of “human revolution,” and their alignment with the call for transformative learning outlined in No Limits to Learning (Botkin et al., 1979). Through the framework of “Learn–Reflect–Empower,” Soka Gakkai members in Japan and India have developed community-based educational activities that embody the values of participatory, integrative and anticipatory learning. Three case studies are examined: (1) the awareness-raising campaign on the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) conducted by Bharat Soka Gakkai (India), which empowers youth to take concrete steps towards achieving the SDGs; (2) the Tohoku Future Research initiative in Japan, in which youth engage local communities through surveys and dialogue to address an aging society and revitalise their cultural identity; and (3) the lived practices of community engagement undertaken by Soka Gakkai members serving as leaders in neighbourhood associations and public housing complexes, which serve as informal sites of lifelong learning. These examples demonstrate how inner transformation can generate sustainable social impact at the local level. They also offer insight into how spiritually based empowerment and community learning can help address the “human gap” and build capacity for hope and resilience amid global uncertainty. This paper argues that these practices are not only compatible with global educational discourses but also provide unique contributions to the evolving understanding of transformative learning for better futures.

title: Think globally, change inwardly, act locally
container-title: Constellations of hope
aa7f1f098faf66be77880409ef0a805f97ba88e8.abstract: This qualitative case study is based on a pilot programme implemented in public schools in Italy. It explores participants’ experiences and views, with particular attention to the influence of observation, collaborative learning and dialogue centred on local issues that appear to influence the participants’ relationship with their environment in positive ways. Inspired by Daisaku Ikeda and Aurelio Peccei’s (1984) call for a human revolution and couched in Daisaku Ikeda’s philosophy of human education (2021a), the pilot programme organised participants in multiple circles of mutual learning driven by participatory problem solving. Individuals honed their capacity for anticipation and participation (Botkin et al., 1979) and collaborated to devise solutions to sustainability-related issues in their schools and communities. This critical instrumental case study examines key concepts from Ikeda’s philosophy of education through the participants’ experiences and views, affirming the relevance of value-creating education for educational praxes and policies. Participants’ feedback evidences the transformative potential of value-creating approaches to sustainability education, mobilising participants’ capacity to bridge the existing gap between humans and their environment through collaborative learning and participatory problem solving. The programme was implemented by the project I Change, the World Changes [Cambio io, cambia il mondo]. Rooted in the ethos of “Think globally, change inwardly, act locally,” the project is promoted and coordinated by the Be the Hope Foundation.

title: Climate anxiety, agency and systemic educational transformation in early childhood
container-title: Constellations of hope
779745823c0724de085125693a8f51d1442c9756.abstract: As climate change intensifies, its psychological and existential impacts on young children are only beginning to be recognised, particularly in climate-vulnerable small island states. Drawing on research conducted in Malta with children under eight, this article reveals a growing prevalence of climate anxiety in early childhood, driven by fragmented and fear-based understandings of environmental change. Without structured educational support, children risk developing a diminished sense of agency. This article advocates for embedding climate literacy into national curricula using developmentally appropriate, solution-oriented methods such as storytelling and nature-based learning. It calls for systemic reform in teacher education, family engagement and public discourse, arguing that climate education can enhance resilience and cultivate climate agency as well as eco-agency in young children. The implications of the findings for educational policy are substantial. First, early childhood climate education must be embedded in national curricula, ensuring that climate literacy is introduced in an age-appropriate, solution-focused manner. Second, many teacher training programmes still do not include climate change education as a core component. Third, parental education initiatives must equip parents and caregivers with strategies to discuss climate change in constructive, solution-oriented ways. The challenge therefore is not simply to replace fear-based narratives with hopeful ones but to cultivate pedagogical conditions in which children can metabolise uncertainty through relational support, ethical dialogue and opportunities for meaningful participation. In this sense, hope emerges not as reassurance but as a lived educational practice grounded in connection, care and shared responsibility. Addressing this gap is critical for developing accurate, empowering climate literacy. By integrating early childhood climate education into policies, policymakers can cultivate a generation that approaches environmental challenges with confidence, resilience and the knowledge to drive meaningful change.

title: Bridging the human gap through data-driven, multilingual and holistic student success interventions in engineering education
container-title: Constellations of hope
3a0680adcc29524bfca0a5107d83fd2bd9294802.abstract: In response to global calls to reimagine education, the Faculty of Engineering & the Built Environment at the University of Cape Town pioneered a transformative project. Grounded in systemic, anticipatory and participatory learning principles, the Student Success Project aims to foster inclusive academic environments. Key interventions include an early risk-assessment framework, peer-led study groups and mentorship, and a multilingual digital glossary in isiXhosa, Sesotho, Kiswahili, Afrikaans and accessible English. These are integrated into a data-driven, AI-enabled student success hub for personalised support. By confronting academic exclusion and language marginalisation, the project demonstrates how higher education can bridge the “human gap” and cultivate learner agency, shifting from maintenance to transformative learning. This work offers a replicable model for empowering educators and learners to co-create equitable futures

title: Learning to affirm open futures
container-title: Constellations of hope
a4cd69c2e00ccba7280dcf25fd79f39f899ab1cb.abstract: This article presents three interventions developed by the Crosscultural Research in Architecture Collective (CRAC) with the aim of fostering situated practices. Integrating Eastern relational thinking, decolonial and feminist theories and the radical pedagogies of Paolo Freire and Augusto Boal, these interventions challenge Western architectural discourse's emphasis on static forms and technological fixes, failing to successfully address the ongoing ecological crises. Our interventions open alternatives to these approaches. The first intervention, A Hat for Three at a Picnic (2012–2019), engaged over 800 architecture students at Xi'an Jiaotong–Liverpool University in designing wearable architectural devices that moderate social dynamics through role-play and collaborative material exploration. Students worked with everyday materials to create dynamic wearables for complex character interactions, emphasising architectural design as social technology. The second intervention, TEXTILE-lab (2023–present), establishes a platform at the Norwegian University of Science and Technology that weaves together analogue textile crafts with architectural education. Students engage with traditional techniques, such as wool spinning and weaving, to develop transdisciplinary practices and embodied learning. The third intervention, SKIRTs: Appropriating Public Space (2025), involves wearable soft architectures that activate public spaces through feminist performative methods. Students create participatory architectural events that question spatial ownership and generate alternative possibilities for public engagement. These interventions demonstrate how cross-cultural pedagogies combining material thinking, embodied learning and performative practice can generate transformative educational experiences. By emphasising process over product and relationships over objects, they offer alternatives to conventional education, preparing students to co-create sustainable futures through collaborative sense-making and an active engagement with uncertainty.

title: Building sustainable futures through higher education
container-title: Constellations of hope
5dd2aa49f166f466db31937a9a895299508694f6.abstract: Interdisciplinarity is central to facing the challenges of sustainability transitions. Many faculties in different universities have adopted sustainability in their disciplinary studies as a goal in higher education. At the University of Jyväskylä, Finland, the novel Basic Multidisciplinary Studies in Sustainability Transitions study module addresses the need to integrate these diverse viewpoints to facilitate multidisciplinary development and change. In this paper, we analyse the design process of the module and the sustainability competences that emerged during that process. The Basic Multidisciplinary Studies in Sustainability Transitions module introduces students to the needs, barriers and opportunities of sustainability transitions from a multidisciplinary perspective. The content of the studies is grounded in the three spheres of transformation framework by Karen O’Brien and Linda Sygna, and sustainability transitions are examined from practical and technical, cultural and psychological, and political and structural perspectives. The module involves all faculties of the University of Jyväskylä in its design and implementation. The data for this case study were collected through focus group interviews and project documents. The analysis of the planning process revealed that the crucial factors behind the successful planning process of the study module were the university's decisions, plans and strategies; the cooperation of the planning group; and the engagement of individual planning group members. The multidisciplinary approach has proven to be fruitful. Sustainability competences were analysed according to the structure of the European Competence Framework, GreenComp. The designers viewed sustainability as value‑laden and emphasised the importance of diverse perspectives. They recognised that interdisciplinary cooperation is needed because the sustainability transition is a complex phenomenon. Dialogue on differing disciplinary interpretations was seen as essential for broadening perspectives. The designers hoped that the Basic Multidisciplinary Studies in Sustainability Transitions module would enable students to become agents of change.

title: Reimagining sustainability education
container-title: Constellations of hope
d90c617b7fd9cf98eaf6dae0065d4fcc476c251b.abstract: This paper explores the transformative potential of critical environmental education by integrating decolonial perspectives and intercultural knowledge exchanges between high-income and low-and middle-income countries. Grounded in the framework of No Limits to Hope, this approach seeks to cultivate inclusive, justice-driven sustainability education that challenges dominant paradigms. We present a case study of a master’s-level sustainability course, implemented over two semesters with 23 interdisciplinary, multicultural students. Central to the course is project-based learning, which fosters critical thinking, creativity and educational innovation. Data were drawn from five student-led sustainability projects that addressed themes such as digital equity, green-skills job alignment, cultural resilience, health and wellbeing, and the emotional dimensions of climate communication. Using Fairclough’s critical discourse analysis framework, focusing on intertextuality, interdiscursivity, presuppositions and dialectical pairs, we examined how students’ discursive practices reflected, reproduced or resisted dominant epistemologies. Findings indicate that combining critical environmental education, decolonial pedagogy and project-based learning promotes a more inclusive, justice-centred approach, deepening students’ engagement with complex sustainability challenges. Building on these insights, we propose six pedagogical strategies, from “cartographies of territory” to “collaborative prototyping labs”, designed to move from symbolic inclusion to epistemic centrality, fostering intellectual emancipation and transformative learning in sustainability education.

title: Interrupting the human gap
container-title: Constellations of hope
c002924e8006e3caac6b249dba434eddcea298f3.abstract: Environmental education exposes students to the severity of ecological crises, sometimes triggering feelings of anger, anxiety, grief and hopelessness. This paper explores the transformative potential of a hope-based pedagogical approach to supporting learners to engage with these responses. It focuses on the Hopeful Futures Programme, which invites students to use hope theories to explore an environmental topic of their choice. Using focus groups with current students and graduates, alongside autoethnographic reflections from educators and researchers, this study investigates the immediate and lasting impacts of the Hopeful Futures Programme. The findings reveal that while many students initially experience discomfort when engaging with hope, these emotions can act as catalysts for transformation when supported through reflective, relational and autonomous learning processes. Over time, many students develop more nuanced understandings of hope and report sustained changes personally and professionally. Four themes emerged: emotional complexity, shifting perspectives, impacts on future pathways and pedagogical insights. The importance of student autonomy, critical reflection and emotional engagement in fostering lasting educational transformation is highlighted. The paper underscores the necessity of integrating hope across the curriculum, not as a passive sentiment but as an active, empowering tool for navigating uncertainty and shaping sustainable futures. It thereby creates a role for critical inquiry around hope in interrupting the “human gap.” This research contributes to emerging scholarship on emotional resilience in environmental education. It offers practical insights for educators seeking to support students through existential challenges and affirms the value of emotionally responsive teaching in cultivating empowered, hopeful and future-oriented graduates.

title: Hope in leadership labs
container-title: Constellations of hope
c38c872dd22b950c70b87bdbe0c9e4a08e4f2a5c.abstract: Higher education plays a vital role in shaping ethical, adaptive leaders to confront global challenges and promote sustainable futures. This study investigates how Bowen University, Nigeria, employs transformational leadership and collaborative learning through programmes like the One Day Management Team Initiative, Bowen Baptist Students Fellowship, departmental executives, and Students Representative Council. A quantitative analysis examines how these experiential roles foster skills in ethical decision-making, systems thinking and resilience, echoing the Club of Rome’s vision for systemic, hope-driven solutions. Surveys from students highlight that these structured leadership opportunities boost empathy, collective problem-solving and preparedness for real-world issues. The findings align with Astin and Astin’s (2000) research on extracurricular engagement enhancing collaboration; Dvir et al.’s (2002) work on transformational leadership tying personal values to societal needs; and Kolb’s (1984) experiential learning theory, which underscores reflective practice, linking theory to ethical action. By connecting local efforts, such as sustainability projects, to global objectives like the Sustainable Development Goals. Bowen positions universities as leadership incubators. This approach, rooted in Nigeria’s postcolonial context, challenges hierarchical norms, fostering equity-focused, student-led solutions. Advocating hands-on, collaborative learning, the study supports the Club of Rome’s No Limits to Hope initiative, urging curricular reforms that prioritise agency and interconnectedness. Ultimately, it reveals higher education’s potential to transform classrooms into laboratories of hope, cultivating leaders who redefine possibilities with courage and creativity.

title: Environmental education
container-title: Constellations of hope
a618cacd8028ed424c508a60b1da85a9c8f74944.abstract: According to many environmental activists and educators, environmental education is a fundamental tool for changing behaviours to protect natural resources and contribute to sustainable development. It plays a key role in both formal education, such as schools and universities, and informal education, including activities carried out by civil society organisations, public administrations and other stakeholders. Efforts are also being made to strengthen environmental education through initiatives such as summer schools. In this regard, our contribution highlights the importance of environmental education in general, with particular emphasis on the opportunities offered by summer schools, such as the Nairobi Summer School on Climate Justice (NSSCJ), from which our association has benefited. We have sought to apply this experience in Tunisia while ensuring that it is properly contextualised within the national framework. This contribution addresses the following key points: defining and establishing the foundations of environmental education; presenting the Nairobi Summer School on Climate Justice; and outlining the involvement of our association, Association pour la Protection de l'Environnement et le Développement Durable de Bizerte (APEDDUB), in environmental education and in the Nairobi Summer School.

title: Shapeshifting
container-title: Constellations of hope
62491e8e2535c89ea7c94219c7f8375d07bb6e42.abstract: This article emerges from a space of hope and desperation. Through an autobiographical lens, I explore how life experiences have (re)shaped the way I frame sustainability and my role within it. Drawing from nine shapeshifting incidents over more than a decade, I trace how certain incidents challenged my cognitive frames and set in motion processes of reframing. While the literature around reframing highlights the interplay between external factors and internal sensemaking, this article adds an emotionally embodied perspective. Emotional responses and ongoing reflection emerged as central dynamics that initiated or deepened my reframing shifts. Emotions became signals of inner misalignment. They represented openings through which deeper inquiry began. Reflection then served as the bridge, connecting feeling with sense-making, and at times, action. This article presents a lived inquiry into what it means to navigate shapeshifts from within to external transformation. It invites you, as a reader, educator, facilitator and change-maker, to consider how we might open learning and living spaces that welcome emotional and reflective depth as integral to the reframing processes needed for sustainability transformations.

title: Transformative learning pathways through arts and culture-based approaches
container-title: Constellations of hope
4738ff94a7a00a8e7ed62fbf0b58c70114570411.abstract: Science communication has raised public awareness of climate change but has struggled to catalyse large-scale behavioural change or systemic reform. This paper argues that arts- and culture-based practices offer a transformative pathway towards systemic change by engaging affective, embodied and multispecies forms of learning. Drawing on projects like Planton Móvil, HighWaterLine, Yo Prefiero el Lago and the mourning practices of Marind communities, this article demonstrates how the arts — and culture-based education — activate social imagination, cultivate empathy and critical thinking and foster new relationships with place, land and community. In an era marked by ecological collapse, disinformation and social fragmentation, these creative strategies offer critical tools for rebuilding trust, shifting mindsets and forging sustainable futures.

title: Regenerating education through a living systems approach to place, process and partnership
container-title: Constellations of hope
990bd9bdba31a7903f6cd39865ead2694f4910ad.abstract: In 2024, Kaospilot’s Outpost semester in Lisbon became a living case of pedagogical innovation grounded in living systems thinking and regenerative development. Co-designed with the Portuguese cooperative LÚCIDA, this three-month immersive educational experience explored how learning environments might be intentionally designed to regenerate people, partnerships and places while responding to the systemic crises of our time. Guided by an implicit theory of change, the Outpost was held as a living system rather than a temporary programme. It was designed to operate simultaneously at three interrelated levels: individual inner development, collective self-organisation and reciprocal engagement with Lisbon as a socio-ecological living system. Drawing on regenerative development principles, the Outpost was re-envisioned through three nodal design shifts: from connected parts to nested wholes, from project-focused to place-oriented learning, and from problem-solving to potential activation. This article examines how these design choices shaped learning processes and outcomes. Student reflections and project narratives reveal shifts in leadership understanding, context awareness, intercultural humility and regenerative literacy. Beyond the student cohort, emerging changes in local collaboration patterns point to wider civic and institutional effects, particularly in the Lisbon neighbourhood of Penha de França. The Kaospilot Lisbon Outpost case presents a situated learning process, which can offer guidance and inspiration; it is not presented to be replicated. It illustrates how education aligned with life’s principles can foster anticipatory, participatory and integrative learning, contributing to the kind of transformative learning envisioned in No Limits to Learning and renewed through No Limits to Hope.

title: Rebuilding systems from the ground up
container-title: Constellations of hope
ab9d6619a39fcccc439bfcd2d565cb7f29ee697a.abstract: This paper presents an emerging pedagogy for systemic change called “Systemic Renewal.” It is designed for industry leaders who are rebuilding their systems “from the ground up.” The methodology recognises that to achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) many organisations and sectors are being called on to rebuild and reconstruct their vision and infrastructure and that, in so doing, they are bridging the “human gap” described in the No Limits to Learning report (Peccei, 1979, p. xiii). Systemic Renewal posits that to achieve this, a “ground up” methodology is required, incorporating a range of actors in highly contextualised learning, including representatives from governance, management and operational levels of a system. This is contrasted with the predominantly “top down” approaches that continue to dominate change-leadership practices and that often rely heavily on external consulting. The study presents a six-year action research project in which participants from a range of contexts worked to develop a pedagogy for renewal, drawing from critical and Franciscan pedagogy, pragmatism, systemic action research methodologies, restorative practice and narrative transformation. Three stages of research are presented. First, the researcher undertook a critical historical analysis of the early Franciscan movement as a model for achieving sustainable change within long-established institutions. In the second phase of the research, a working theory for Franciscan pedagogy was piloted across three years of participatory action research, working with thirty-five faith-based leaders in Melbourne. Finally, Systemic Renewal was piloted with a further 27 actors from 11 nations, including leaders of all faiths and leaders without faith.

title: Innovative learning with World Heritage in the early post-Anthropocene
container-title: Constellations of hope
60f014bc2d445af57a09814f17ee94f947ff22c5.abstract: Amidst a planetary polycrisis a new civilisational paradigm is emerging: ecocultures of an early post-Anthropocene are traceable all over the world, challenging the fossil fuel era’s remnants by reconnecting humans and Earth. Our contribution reflects on how Education for Sustainable Development (ESD) can support this mind-shifting cultural transformation in this critical moment. We explore how UNESCO World Heritage Sites can serve as living laboratories for transformative learning, fostering (re-)weaving nets of meanings and values to reconnect to Earth. Such sites are powerful tools for ESD offering tangible connections to deep time, history, culture, the environment and traditional knowledge. They are spaces of past and present anticipations and potentialities for a range of futures. Through interdisciplinary and intercultural encounters, learners explore the associative richness of these sites, developing a critical awareness of current challenges and the cultural patterns shaping them. By understanding the constructed nature of worldviews, learners are empowered to develop pathways towards alternative futures. Heritage-based learning, which foregrounds experiential, place-based education, enables learners to move from cognitive understanding to action — bridging the “human gap” that separates knowledge from systemic transformation. Ultimately, this work contributes to the vision of No Limits to Hope by advocating for education grounded in connection, critical reflection and cultural resonance. Furthermore, emphasising images as elements of learning empowers learners to imagine and co-create sustainable futures.

title: Daring regenerative futures
container-title: Constellations of hope
69ec5a88157c7a3698c363518e164a280796e919.abstract: Regenerative futures are a daring idea — a hopeful and radical concept based on the realisation that doing “less worse” is not good enough. As several planetary boundaries are being reached, calls for new ways of learning and engaging with nature are clear and loud. Yet offering alternatives to learning about social-ecological change is challenging. It is far from obvious what is needed to imagine and design regenerative futures in a learning context. In our work as educators and researchers, we have increasingly seen the importance of creating spaces for exploring hope and imagination. Many educators lack the tools, methods and guidance to go beyond teaching the facts and problems of global challenges and to inspire learners to be creative and actively engage in regenerative and desirable futures. To address this gap, we initiated the collaborative book project Imagining, Designing and Teaching Regenerative Futures: Art-Science Approaches and Inspirations from Around the World,” emerging from a global network of educators, practitioners and changemakers committed to restoring the relationship between humans and nature and inspiring hope. Featuring 65 tools provided by 120 authors from 30 countries, this book offers support for educators in exploring hopeful ways of teaching and learning. Creative approaches are a powerful way to engage in global challenges, opening our minds to more-than-human perspectives and providing spaces for imagination, experimentation and perspective-taking. Notwithstanding the recognised potential of creative approaches to support learning about social-environmental challenges, wide application across disciplines and geographical contexts is still lagging. Our contribution to the No Limits to Hope initiative includes the key findings and guiding principles that emerge from this collaborative effort. It illustrates how education can serve as a vehicle for systemic transformative change. It empowers educators to transcend conventional disciplinary pedagogies and cultivate interdisciplinary learning spaces that nourish commitment to transformation, anchored in community, creativity and care.

title: Unlearning design
container-title: Constellations of hope
f4640809d48d67d2e3916d8b649de35cc5671459.abstract: This case study investigates how to catalyse a mindset transformation through place-based learning, co-creation and more-than-human perspectives to develop agency for design pathways with nature and equity at their core. It documents the learning journey of 58 students situated in both high-income and low- and middle-income countries who were enrolled in a module of the MA Sustainable Fashion (online) course at Falmouth University in the UK. This module is designed with and through the dissemination of values like the ethics of care, feminist viewpoints, regenerative principles and rhizomatic learning to leverage the Anthropocene’s disruption of natural and societal systems. Seven key methods presented in this article aim to provoke questioning about linear design practices and to create situated system interventions instead. They encourage students to engage with local cultures and traditional knowledge and processes in contrast to taking on a siloed designer-first approach. This can require the unlearning of common practices and hierarchies when students have had traditional design education or prior industry experience. Findings highlight that transformative mindset change occurs when students prioritise processes over physical outcomes; others cherished a deep dive into embodied rituals and traditions to overcome their unfamiliarity with other cultures. Redefining the meaning of a fashion product, students engage in curriculum development, community building, or local policymaking through design. They develop local commons, nurture collaboration and facilitate non-linear approaches to systemic change. While the case study is framed by an online learning environment that informs the intercultural educational experience, the discussed methods can be transferred to in situ education and other disciplines too.

title: Addressing planned obsolescence through radical imagination
container-title: Constellations of hope
c76bed8ba61d458afbd342c35a9692818ee7ee02.abstract: This article presents an action research case study that uses planned obsolescence (PO) as a tangible entry point to critically examine the dominant logic of disposability embedded in education. Over 18 months, students at a Dutch University of Applied Sciences engaged in a co-inquiry developing a tabletop role-playing game. Through this process, students interrogated the systemic roots of PO and reimagined their roles as future professionals. The project underscores the necessity of radical imagination in education as a means to resist defeat.

title: Creative methods for biodiversity governance
container-title: Constellations of hope
f348f9a5e11c4869982af5a82c1f2dc11693fe17.abstract: This article examines the design and development of an open-access online training course that aims to support inclusive and critically engaged biodiversity decision-making by enabling the uptake of creative and participatory intervention methods. Designed as part of the PLANET4B project (understanding Plural values, intersectionality, Leverage points, Attitudes, Norms, behaviour and social lEarning in Transformation for Biodiversity decision-making), the course draws directly on grounded insights and practical experiences from 11 place-based and sectoral case studies. The article argues that biodiversity loss is not only a techno-scientific empirical issue but a deeply relational and structural challenge requiring disruption of both exclusionary norms and hierarchical knowledge systems. An adapted version of Donella Meadows’s leverage points offers a framework to trace dynamics of change while accounting for intersectionality and situated power relations. Building on this framework, the article offers a critical appraisal of creative, discursive and experiential methods, emphasising the importance of designing and implementing approaches so that they address structural inequality, support reflexive practice and foster place-based engagement. These conceptual ideas are translated into practice through a bespoke course design targeting four sets of key enabling players: policymakers, business, academic researchers and civil society. The design is informed by a clear rationale, a set of method-selection criteria and a framework for sharing and adapting the selected methods. By way of illustration, the discussion focuses on three methods featured in the online course: the Who Am I? game, participatory theatre and debriefing. The article contributes to broader debates around the democratisation of knowledge, the politics of participation and the role of learning in advancing ecological justice. It aligns closely with the ethos of No Limits to Hope, offering grounded tools and perspectives for understanding and enabling transformations in biodiversity governance.

title: Cultivating seeds of the future
container-title: Constellations of hope
4c261a0872550e2a2bc571fe3381eea3477a592a.abstract: Amid a growing number of interconnected societal crises, many people are experiencing mental distress and an associated sense of powerlessness. Scholars increasingly suggest that our greatest challenge is not climate change, biodiversity loss, geopolitical tensions or polarisation — but the widespread illusion of our own insignificance. Feelings of meaninglessness, hopelessness and apathy are among the underlying causes, fuelling a vicious cycle of deteriorating individual, collective and planetary wellbeing. At the same time, spirituality and religion are gaining attention for their potential to foster meaning, hope and engagement in the face of existential crises. However, their potential role in supporting deeper societal transformation remains under-explored. Our study addresses this gap by investigating the innovative online course “Zen and the Art of Saving the Planet” (ZASP), which has attracted over 6,500 participants globally in the past two years. Based on document analyses, surveys and “spaces for listening and dialogue,” our findings highlight the course’s contribution to the emerging field of inner transformation and associated education, which aims to accelerate change by integrating inner and outer dimensions of sustainability. We show how spirituality can mediate the entangled creation of meaning, hope, agency and engagement across individual, collective and system levels. Together, our findings advance knowledge on the complex intersection between inner development, culture and system change; the role of faith-based groups; and the integration of diverse knowledge systems for transformative education — offering a precedent that other training institutions could follow or learn from.

title: Regenerative practices as a paradigm shift in transformative learning
container-title: Constellations of hope
bc83f3602d9d4ba8aa9e151856f83090f6456817.abstract: Education systems were never designed to handle collapse. As planetary and socio-economic instabilities accelerate, the gap between what we teach and what we need to know becomes impossible to ignore. Conventional learning models, designed for industrial-age efficiency and linear problem solving, fail to equip learners to navigate complexity, uncertainty and systemic change. In contrast, regenerative practices offer more than a set of ecological methodologies: these provide a paradigm that reconfigures education as an adaptive, life-generating system. This paper explores how regenerative design, when integrated with artistic and pedagogical innovation, can catalyse transformative learning. By fostering ecological literacy, complex systems thinking and creative agency, regenerative learning cultivates a mindset attuned to interdependence and long-term resilience. Drawing from case studies in design and speculative pedagogy, this research examines how these principles reshape cognitive, spatial, and institutional approaches to education. Using qualitative inquiry and interdisciplinary analysis, it explores how regenerative principles can decolonise and reorient learning spaces. Education is reframed not as transmission of knowledge, but as an ongoing process of co-evolution between learners, communities and ecological systems. Embedding regenerative design into educational structures enhances adaptability and nurtures an embodied sense of stewardship and pragmatic hope — both critical in times of crisis. Ultimately, this paper calls for an urgent reconfiguration of education as a living system. Learning environments — physical, conceptual or digital — must be designed as symbiotic, decolonised and flourishing-oriented ecosystems that enable the emergence of regenerative worlds.

title: Trustfully moving into the polycrisis of the Anthropocene as another birth in the process of human becoming
container-title: Constellations of hope
a9b36092f1e0fdb37e2e304c38873cba5b3b151b.abstract: In this paper, I reflect on the emergence of the Anthropocene as a hopeful transformational phase in the process of human becoming and in the evolution of life towards greater complexity and consciousness. Drawing on perspectives from Earth system science, complex systems theory and social psychology, I propose an interpretation that understands the Holocene as the systemic “womb” of the current global civilisation, and the transition into the Anthropocene as a civilisational “birth” within the ongoing self-organisation of life on Earth. I argue that cultivating awareness of the impermanence of the current civilisation can serve as a crucial resource for catalysing an emerging mode of (human) life on Earth, grounded in a healed relationship between human and non-human life. For learning and educational systems, these reflections carry profound implications. I discuss a hopeful orientation towards aliveness as a key principle for shifting the underlying logic of educational practices away from a mindset of “responding to challenges” or “solving problems” and towards nourishing processes that are congruent with patterns of healthy aliveness. Specifically, I propose that designers and facilitators of transformational learning processes focus on four aspects: (1) creating space for relationship-building, (2) empathically containing fear-driven reactions to the polycrisis, (3) practising compassionate “hospice work” for decaying elements of the Holocene-based civilisation, and (4) celebrating and leaning into aliveness wherever it emerges.

title: The study of intelligence in nature for an ecocentric perspective in education
container-title: Constellations of hope
6aa7185f0d7acf0d9376809bf72dca706adb0174.abstract: One of the greatest challenges of our time is establishing a new relationship with nature by adopting different knowledge, values, and attitudes. Currently, the anthropocentric worldview dominates social systems — from economics to education — and from this perspective nature and living beings are mere objects valued only for human benefit. To move forward, we must recognise the intrinsic value of all life, from microbes to entire landscapes, by adopting an ecocentric worldview. We can learn from Indigenous cultures that view humans and the natural world as a single community guided by reciprocity, respect and devotion. In these traditions, nature is alive, intelligent and a teacher. Simultaneously, scientific fields such as cognitive ecology, ethology and bioacoustics are providing compelling evidence that intelligence is an inherent characteristic of life. Furthermore, technologies like machine learning are now helping us decode non-human communication, a clear feature of intelligence. These insights offer a transformative opportunity to create educational content that supports an ecocentric perspective, awakening wonder, compassion and critical thinking. This article explores the philosophical foundations of ecocentric education and its relationship with intelligence in nature — examining capacities such as animal culture, communication and memory. Ultimately, it advocates for a paradigm shift: moving away from a mechanistic view of life towards a holistic, ecological perspective where nature is no longer an object, but a subject and a mentor.

title: Past hopes for desirable societies
container-title: Constellations of hope
fa402c0ab4e8d3292d034fbbbd280bcbbd127bdf.abstract: The 1970s were characterised by numerous constructive and hopeful initiatives that did not reach their full potential after the economic shift to neoliberalism in the 1980s. Among many, one from the Global South, Fundación Bariloche (Argentina), challenged the Northern proposal, The Limits to Growth, the first report to the Club of Rome authored by a group of Massachusetts Institute of Technology researchers, with a mathematical computer model. Fundación Bariloche published their book Catastrophe or New Society?: A Latin American world model in 1976. Its normative model was grounded in ethical and political perspectives, emphasising basic needs and citizen participation. The normative proposal of this article involves reencountering a holistic model of nine human needs, developed by Carlos Mallmann, president of the Bariloche Foundation, as a possible frame for the Latin American World Model. Mallmann also participated in the report No Limits to Learning, in which he indirectly addresses how studying unmet human needs can contribute to understanding them. This focus on needs presents a hopeful framework across four dimensions (vital, solidaristic, responsible and conscious hands) that serve as a compass/map at both micro and macro levels for a planet under human stewardship. A proposed formula guides this framework, according to which the “vital hand,” representing human beings on the planet, depends on the effective management of the other three hands. A key element of this formula is “synergy,” a concept that anthropologist Ruth Benedict adapted to the social sciences and Mallmann proposed as a human need. Examples of synergistic efforts provided from each of these four perspectives can help us learn how to build more synergetic societies.

title: Designing for hope
container-title: Constellations of hope
7043b7079770f8f6a5d30083bc69a53d76352421.abstract: How can the synergy between artificial intelligence (AI) and collective intelligence (CI) transform how we learn and collaborate in the Anthropocene? We explore this question through a participatory research process grounded in co-design. Framing AI as a catalyst for “learning transitions” — both understanding systemic change and reimagining how we learn — we position AI not as a replacement for human intelligence, but as an amplifier of collective problem-solving. Through iterative collaboration with diverse stakeholders, we co-designed four AI-enabled research prototypes: (1) AI-enhanced project-based learning, (2) AI for CI and governance via Model UN, (3) AI literacy, and (4) integrating Indigenous knowledge in AI design. Our approach integrates knowledge mapping, concept exploration and mindful deviation to foster creativity and inclusion. This work aligns with the No Limits to Hope vision by advancing learning paradigms that bridge knowledge and action, support local context and prioritise long-term wellbeing over efficiency in navigating planetary challenges.

title: There are no limits to learning
container-title: Constellations of hope
f4286a51a0a029c69e876d3795e2e6d78fd08a52.abstract: What does it mean to claim there are no limits to learning — especially in a moment defined by planetary limits? This contribution takes seriously the proposition that learning, in its fullest sense, is not merely a technical process of information transfer but an ontological unfolding: a transformation in how we relate to ourselves, others and the living world. In dialogue with The Limits to Growth (1972) and the hopeful intervention of No Limits to Learning (1979), this paper argues that the future of education depends on our capacity to learn with the world, not just about it. The dominant image of the learner in contemporary schooling remains tethered to the independent self — a construct shaped by Enlightenment rationalism and liberal modernity. This image distorts the relational nature of being and contributes to ecological harm by disembedding individuals from their communities and ecosystems. In contrast, many non-Western traditions — including Indigenous knowledge systems, animist cosmologies, African philosophies and Asian pedagogies — understand learning as emergent, situated and participatory. Knowledge arises through relationship: with land, kin, ancestors and more-than-human beings. Learning, in these contexts, is not about mastery, but attunement — becoming-with the world. This paper builds a conceptual bridge between these traditions and contemporary relational theories of education, including the distinction between Type I and Type II learning. We propose learning as mutual transformation between learner and world. Learning with the world, in this view, is a mode of being. It invites pedagogies rooted in interdependence and an education without limits.

title: The dynamic relationship between L2 possible selves and learning experience during study abroad: A longitudinal multiple case study of Chinese language learners
container-title: International Review of Applied Linguistics in Language Teaching
5798db4bc7640131240341b982b194a6aeaa8d4d.abstract: Abstract This multiple case study employed the L2 motivational self-system (L2MSS) (Dörnyei, Zoltán. 2005. The psychology of the language learner: Individual differences in second language acquisition . Mahwah, NJ: Lawrence Erlbaum Associates, Inc; Dörnyei, Zoltán. 2009. The L2 motivational self-system. In Zoltán Dörnyei & Ema Ushioda (eds.), Motivation, language identity and the L2 self , 9–42. Clevedon, UK: Multilingual Matters) to understand the motivational dynamics of Chinese (Mandarin) language learners during a study abroad (SA) sojourn. It examined the qualitative changes in learners’ L2 possible selves by adopting the complex dynamic system theory (CDST) (Larsen-Freeman, Diane & Lynne Cameron. 2008. Complex systems and applied linguistics . Oxford: Oxford University Press) and the person-in-context perspective (Ushioda, Ema. 2009. A person-in-context relational view of emergent motivation, self and identity. In Zoltán Dörnyei & Ema Ushioda (eds.), Motivation, language identity and the L2 self , 215–228. Bristol: Multilingual Matters). Participants were three undergraduate Chinese language learners from different countries (Salvador, Myanmar, and Solomon Islands) enrolled at a Chinese university. Data were collected through a motivational questionnaire administered upon arrival, followed by four semi-structured interviews with each participant conducted over a four-month period during the first semester of their SA sojourn. Through thematic analysis, the study illustrates the process of how learners’ L2 possible selves were constantly refined during SA (e.g., developed more capable actual L2 selves, extended perceived ideal L2 selves, strengthened and internalized ought-to L2 selves). An ongoing interplay between L2 possible selves and learning experience was found: while learning experience abroad shaped learners’ L2 possible selves, their enriched possible selves further guided learners’ behaviors and, in turn, created new learning experiences.

title: NO‘XATNI SUG‘ORISHNING ILDIZ TIZIMIDAGI TUGANAK BAKTERIYALARI SHAKLLANISHIGA TA’SIRI
container-title: Agro ilm
328c2811455766f15c52fe23724799c45e0d5bbc.abstract: The article investigates the effect of irrigation on the formation and accumulation of nodule bacteria in the root system of the chickpea varieties “Yulduz” and “Milyutin-6” under meadow sierozem soil conditions in the Samarkand region. Field experiments were conducted using non-irrigated control and irrigated treatments. In the irrigated treatment, three irrigations were applied during the growing season at rates of 700, 1200, and 1200 m³/ha, respectively. The results showed that irrigation had a positive effect on the formation and accumulation of nodule bacteria in the chickpea root system. In the “Yulduz” variety, the mass of nodules on the roots of 10 plants was 3.2 g in the non-irrigated treatment and 10.3 g in the irrigated treatment, while in the “Milyutin-6” variety, the corresponding values were 3.2 and 10.1 g. Irrigation maintained an optimal soil moisture level, contributing to better root system development and increased activity of nodule bacteria. It was also established that a soil temperature of approximately 18 °C is favorable for active nodule development.

title: JANUBIY CHEGARA HUDUDLARINING ATROF-MUHIT OBYEKTLARI VA OZIQ-OVQAT MAHSULOTLARI  TARKIBIDAGI PESTITSIDLAR QOLDIQ MIQDORINI GIGIYENIK TAHLILI
container-title: Agro ilm
8ccb89ea325892c326bce90450f85ae81d2fa37a.abstract: An analysis of samples from 18 types of food products collected in 2020, 2021, and 2022 showed that in 2020, out of 1,859 samples, pesticides were detected in 30 fruit and vegetable samples, with concentrations remaining within permissible limits. In 2021, out of 6,825 samples, pesticides were detected in 5,707 food samples; of these, 56 were fruits and vegetables (with 32—or 57.1%—being potatoes), and 9 (47.3%) were potatoes. In 2022, out of 3,226 samples, pesticides were detected in 18 (47.3%) fruit and vegetable samples, but concentrations did not exceed permissible limits.

title: IPAK QURTI ZOT, LINIYA VA DURAGAYLARIDA BIOLOGIK KO‘RSATKICHLAR HAMDA TUXUM QO‘YMALARINING MIKROSKOPIK TAHLILI
container-title: Agro ilm
905bc87a5e41fa59c09045e84504aa164095a6ca.abstract: The article presents a comprehensive scientific analysis of the viability dynamics and the proportion of defective cocoons across various silkworm breeds, lines, and their inter-family hybrid combinations. The study confirmed the complete absence (0%) of pathogens causing highly dangerous diseases—such as nosemosis and nuclear polyhedrosis—in all samples. Hybrids belonging to the Line 31 group, as well as certain reciprocal combinations (13x57, 30x46, 314x191, 165x74, 5x155), demonstrated an absolute result: 100% healthy silkworm egg batches. The data obtained constitute a valuable practical and theoretical resource for selecting highly resistant genotypes and establishing breeding stock in sericulture.

title: ОСАЖДЕНИЕ НЕОДНОРОДНЫХ ПО КРУПНОСТИ НАНОСОВ ПРИ ДЕЙСТВИИ ВЕТРОВЫХ ВОЛН
container-title: Agro ilm
c962443678f7a1c69c2acae52901d1b4024d9f8e.abstract: A mathematical model of the settling of non-uniform sediment particles in water under wind-wave action is considered. Using the momentum and continuity equations for the solid and liquid phases, relationships are obtained for the variation of particle concentration with depth and time. Accounting for wave action makes it possible to refine the sequential settling behavior of sediment fractions. The resulting relationships can be applied to hydraulic calculations of settling basins and reservoirs by jointly considering flow parameters, wind velocity, and wave characteristics.

title: ЗАРАРЛАНГАН ТУПРОҚДА Pb(II) ИОНЛАРИНИ МОДИФИКАЦИЯЛАНГАН БЕНТОНИТ–САПРОПЕЛ КОМПОЗИТЛАРИ БИЛАН ИММОБИЛИЗАЦИЯЛАШ
container-title: Agro ilm
e8e7fffabfcb5dc5b6a429ba8a7278312e06d35f.abstract: The paper reports the Pb immobilization efficiency of composites prepared from Navbahor bentonite and Tashkent sapropel by mechanical and thermal activation, in a soil spiked with 1500 mg/kg of lead. Two mobile Pb fractions were determined at seven B:S ratios, five doses and three incubation times; the results were compared with three commercial humic sorbents and the advantage of the thermally activated composite is shown quantitatively.

title: TЕХНОЛОГИЯ И МАШИНА ДЛЯ УЛУЧШЕНИЯ АРИДНЫХ ПАСТБИЩ
container-title: Agro ilm
0e7368076f7d3fd009a01fba87bf4951ef28822e.abstract: This article presents information on the development of an environmentally friendly and energy-saving technology for improving arid pastures, as well as the design of a machine for its implementation. Certain specific features of sowing seeds of desert forage plants, which were taken into account during the machine's development, are presented.

title: KARTOSHKA YETISHTIRISHDA URUG‘–TUPROQ–O‘SIMLIK MAJMUIGA ULTRABINAFSHA NURLANISH BILAN ISHLOV BERISHNING SAMARADORLIGI
container-title: Agro ilm
b836279870e98a6986e89e7d12b58dc4a5615095.abstract: The paper examines the effect of combined pre-sowing ultraviolet (UV) irradiation of soil and seed tubers on potato emergence. Five irradiation variants at 10–50 cm from the source (0.42–0.76 mJ/cm²) and an untreated control were tested on cv. Santa in three replications. On day 15 after planting, emergence in all UV variants exceeded the control (56.7 %), reaching 63.3–83.3 %. The best result was obtained at 30 cm and 0.56 mJ/cm² (83.3 %; +26.6 percentage points over control, p = 0.047). Treated plots showed little Colorado potato beetle infestation; the trial used no fertilizers or chemical protection.

title: MONITORING OF SOURCES OF INDUSTRIAL TECHNOGENIC HAZARDS IN THE SAMARKAND REGION, ASSESSMENT OF THEIR TERRITORIAL DISTRIBUTION AND IDENTIFICATION OF HAZARDOUS OBJECTS BASED ON GIS
container-title: Agro ilm
eca09e7672449a9e53a6a065f219da9165f3cb10.abstract: This study is devoted to monitoring the sources of industrial techno genic risks in the Samarkand region, assessing the features of their territorial distribution and identifying dangerous objects based on geographic information technology (GIS). As part of the research, information about industrial enterprises and facilities that pose a potential anthropogenic hazard in the region is being collected, systematized and entered into a geoformation database. A comprehensive analysis of the spatial location of sources of danger, their technical condition, the likelihood of accidents, population density, environmentally sensitive areas and other factors is carried out. GIS technologies are used to map man-made risk zones and identify objects with a high level of potential danger. The results obtained can be used to assess territorial risks, prevent emergencies, ensure environmental safety and improve the management of sources of anthropogenic hazards.

title: O‘ZBEKISTON RESPUBLIKASI IQTISODIYOTI VA AGRAR SEKTORINI KLASTERLI MODERNIZATSIYA QILISH
container-title: Agro ilm
a4389bf32c3ec182fb2c7e4083888340ece3ad94.abstract: This article analyzes the economic content, institutional dynamics, and efficiency of cluster modernization processes in the agrarian sector of the Republic of Uzbekistan. The purpose of the study is to theoretically and econometrically substantiate the impact of agro-clustering on agricultural productivity, export potential, and the value-added chain, as well as to develop an analytical tool adapted to the conditions of Uzbekistan — the Cluster Modernization Index (CMI). The methodological framework includes a comparative-analytical method, index evaluation, and panel data-based econometric modeling (OLS, Fixed Effects, Random Effects, and Dynamic Panel/System GMM where necessary).

title: Academic librarians' perceptions of new skills, competencies and professional development needs in the AI age
container-title: Library Hi Tech
3610c8c0f0d1c535e41c0b71849dce304d1c7a28.abstract: Purpose This study examined academic librarians' perceptions of new skills and competencies, use of AI tools and professional development needs. Design/methodology/approach An online survey was distributed via professional networks, and data were collected and analysed from 155 valid respondents across Australia, European countries and the USA. Findings The findings demonstrate that the highly ranked new skills needed by academic librarians included AI tools and output evaluation, application of data governance and management, AI literacy instruction and integration of AI into curricula. The new competencies consisted of ethical implementation and governance, critical analysis and evaluation of AI tools and AI literacy and conceptual understanding of AI. AI tools could be used to improve information service provisions through responsible and ethical information management and discovery. Key training and knowledge areas included critical evaluation of AI-generated content. Hands-on tutorials with case studies and in-person or hybrid workshops were the most suitable training formats. Practical implications The findings are helpful and practical for academic librarians to develop new skills and competencies and support professional development and curriculum renewal. Originality/value The new contribution of this study lies in the identification of important new skills and competencies that academic librarians need to utilise AI tools in a successful way, mitigate associated potential risks and adapt to changing professional roles.

title: How narrative perspective in luxury brand stories enhances brand preference: the role of self-enhancement motivation and demand-side scarcity
container-title: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing
ea61196415232eb83bfd27d8f349e481a4d0a41d.abstract: Purpose Luxury brands increasingly use first- and third-person stories in digital and interactive marketing, but which perspective increases brand preference, why and when remain unclear. Drawing on communication accommodation theory and self-discrepancy theory, we propose that third-person (vs. first-person) narratives provide contrastive (vs. assimilative) cues, enlarge ideal-self distance and activate self-enhancement motivation. This effect should be stronger for demand-side scarce products, which signal desirability and attainability, than for supply-side scarce products, which signal restricted access. Design/methodology/approach Six experiments, including eye tracking, manipulated narrative perspective, brand type, self-enhancement motivation and scarcity type. Brand preference, self-enhancement motivation, assimilation and contrast were measured and analyzed with ANOVA/ANCOVA, t-tests and bootstrapped mediation models. Findings Third-person narratives increased preference only for luxury brands. Self-enhancement motivation mediated the effect, and assimilation and contrast formed parallel serial pathways. The advantage of third-person narratives appeared under demand-side scarcity but not supply-side scarcity. Practical implications Luxury managers should use third-person narratives for demand-side scarce products and match narrative perspective to interactive channels and consumer characteristics. Narrative perspective alone should not be expected to offset the inaccessibility signaled by supply-side scarcity. Originality/value The research explains narrative perspective as an interactive marketing language cue rather than merely another story feature. It identifies self-enhancement motivation as the mechanism and demand-side scarcity as the attainability-based boundary condition.

title: Beyond the laggard myth: time-series analysis of AI job market dynamics in construction
container-title: Smart and Sustainable Built Environment
4e1908c31127b7c180069c373440c5cd8dc5cf0e.abstract: Purpose This study presents one of the first time-series, cross-industry analyses of the artificial intelligence (AI) job market for the construction sector. It benchmarks construction against both digital and traditional industries to interrogate prevailing assumptions of linear diffusion and temporal catch-up in AI workforce adoption. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on 51 months of Lightcast job postings (January 2021–March 2025), with construction defined as ANZSIC Division E, the study employs an interpretable analytical toolkit comprising Seasonal-Trend decomposition using Loess decomposition (period = 12), month-of-year bootstrap tests on detrended series, cross-correlation analysis with bootstrap confidence bands, Newey–West trend estimation on sectoral share ratios and conservative one-step Exponential Smoothing State-Space (ETS) forecasts. All results are re-estimated excluding the partial final month (March 2025) as a sensitivity check. Findings Construction's AI hiring is very sparse, accounting for under 1% of AI postings and is more volatile than hiring in peer sectors, but it grew fastest: annual construction postings rose more than fourfold between 2021 and 2024, against increases of 13% and 9% in the digital and traditional sectors, whose postings peaked in 2022. Construction's share of AI postings relative to both comparators therefore rises (converges) rather than falls. No delayed-follower pattern is detected: no lag at which the comparator sectors lead construction is statistically reliable, and the short-run associations that are detected are weak, near-contemporaneous and sensitive to the sample end. Unlike the comparator sectors, construction shows no statistically significant within-year seasonality and short-horizon ETS forecasts do not improve on a seasonal-naïve benchmark. These findings are robust to the exclusion of the partial final month of data. Construction thus appears as a low-base, fast-growing entrant with its own hiring dynamics, not a “laggard” following digital-sector cycles with a delay. Practical implications The findings suggest that construction firms should prioritise internal capability building and domain-specific AI skills where external hiring is thin, support flexible, year-round upskilling, and design policy and vendor strategies tailored to the sector's operational realities rather than importing digital-sector playbooks. Originality/value This study provides among the first data-driven, time-series evidence that qualifies the dominant “late adopter” narrative in construction. It shows that construction's low level of AI hiring coexists with the fastest growth and a rising share, without a delayed-follower timing pattern, distinguishing a low starting point from a lagging trajectory and offering an empirically grounded alternative to technologically deterministic accounts of cross-industry AI adoption.

title: Case-based learning for facilities management education in a developing country context: bridging theory, practice and local realities
container-title: Education Innovations: Systems and Future Learning
fb5703d2038e44f130f78f61c971fe0407142d5c.abstract: Purpose Although case-based learning (CBL) has gained considerable attention as an active learning strategy in higher education, empirical evidence regarding its effectiveness in facilities management (FM) education, particularly within developing-country contexts, remains limited. This study examines the students' perceptions of CBL in relation to knowledge application, soft skills, learning preferences, and employability among FM undergraduates at a state university in Sri Lanka. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative survey generated 268 responses, of which 221 complete responses were retained for analysis. Descriptive statistics and Friedman tests were used to examine students' perceptions, learning preferences and differences across academic levels, with effect-size measures used to assess practical significance. Findings Students generally perceived CBL as contributing positively to knowledge application, critical thinking, self-directed learning, teamwork, engagement, and professional preparedness. They also associated CBL with greater confidence in problem-solving, decision-making under uncertainty, and handling industry-related responsibilities. Collaborative and application-oriented approaches, particularly group discussions and action-based activities, were preferred over more complex methods such as role-play and integrated project-based tasks. Overall, these findings are consistent with the principles of Experiential Learning Theory and Work-Integrated Learning, suggesting that CBL may provide a useful means of connecting academic learning with authentic professional contexts. Originality/value The study extends existing case-based learning research by providing discipline-specific empirical evidence from Facilities Management education in Sri Lanka, a developing-country context that remains underrepresented in the CBL literature. By examining students across multiple academic levels and comparing their perceptions of different CBL activities, the study provides context-sensitive insights for the design of practice-oriented FM curricula.

title: The new STEM educator: how school teachers adapt to rapid technological and pedagogical shifts: a qualitative approach
container-title: Education Innovations: Systems and Future Learning
c5534312acfc430f7c1ccefd599d1c6132e8328d.abstract: Purpose This study explores how science, technology, engineering, and mathematics (STEM) educators of secondary schools in Punjab, Pakistan, perceive, experience, and adapt to rapid technological and pedagogical shifts in their teaching practices. It foregrounds teachers' lived experiences, classroom-level challenges, adaptive strategies, and perceptions of institutional and systemic support in a developing-country educational context. Design/methodology/approach The study employed a qualitative interpretive phenomenological design. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 15 STEM educators from 10 public and private secondary schools in Punjab, selected through maximum-variation purposive sampling. Data were analyzed using Braun and Clarke's six-phase thematic analysis, supported by manual coding and NVivo-assisted organization. The study was theoretically informed by the Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge framework and Transformative Learning Theory. Trustworthiness was enhanced through member checking, reflective memoing, systematic coding, audit-trail documentation, and detailed contextual description. Findings Four major themes emerged: perceptions of technological and pedagogical change, experiences of adapting to new instructional demands, individual and collaborative adaptation strategies, and institutional/systemic support structures. Teachers generally viewed technological and pedagogical change as necessary for modern STEM education, but their adaptation was shaped by infrastructure limitations, time constraints, insufficient training, curriculum rigidity, exam-oriented assessment, and uneven leadership support. The findings show that STEM teacher adaptation is not merely a technical or pedagogical process; rather, it is an emotional, professional, disciplinary, and context-dependent experience shaped by the interaction between teacher agency and structural constraints. Originality/value This study contributes to a teacher-centered and context-specific understanding of STEM educators' adaptation in Pakistan. It extends policy- and adoption-focused research by showing how teacher agency, leadership, infrastructure, disciplinary demands, curriculum expectations, and professional identity collectively shape technology-supported pedagogical change in secondary STEM classrooms.
