It supports measurement of gas-lift injection rates, lifting-depth determination, leak identification, produced-gas quantification, liquid-level detection, and valve-performance assessment. Field application demonstrated optimized gas allocation, early integrity issue identification, improved MAASP compliance, and estimated cost avoidance of USD 0.3 to 0.5 million per gas-lift well. This paper presents the technical basis, deployment workflow, diagnostic applications, implementation controls, field observations, limitations, lessons learned, and opportunities for wider digital integration.

title: Advanced Self-Sealing Cement Technology for Complete Zonal Isolation in High-Water Environments
container-title: ADIPEC
6d40ae1fa1e97e888caca3e42698c55f815c9e06.abstract: Abstract Water channelling through the cement annular sheath causes early water breakthrough, increased water handling costs, tubular corrosion, ESP failures, and reduced oil production. Conventional cement cannot self-repair once micro-cracks or micro-channels form, making this a persistent global challenge. The Reactive Self-Sealing cement system was developed to address this gap — providing mechanical resilience and self-sealing capability to preserve annular integrity throughout the well's life, eliminate remedial cement jobs, and protect production rates. Standard cement slurries are rigid and brittle after setting. They cannot accommodate cyclic pressure and temperature changes during production, nor can they heal once micro-channels develop. Reactive Self-Sealing is engineered with specific mechanical properties to resist premature sheath failure and incorporates reactive additives that trigger self-sealing upon water contact — even in fully water-saturated environments. The re-healing process is repeatable, offering continuous protection over the well's lifespan. The system is fully compatible with conventional rig-site batch mixers and pumping units, requiring no specialized equipment. Laboratory testing confirmed that Reactive Self-Sealing specimens, after deliberate fracturing, achieved complete re-healing and full integrity recovery when exposed to water as well as Carbon dioxide environment. Three field trials validated these results. The first and second applications — primary cement jobs in North and West Kuwait Oil Fields — both produced good cement bond logs across the zones of interest. The third application, a workover water shut-off squeeze job, resulted in a substantial reduction in water cut and a corresponding increase in oil production rate. Reactive Self-Sealing proved effective across both primary cementing and remedial scenarios. The key innovation is Reactive Self-Sealing ability to combine strong bonding integrity with active self-sealing in 100% water environments — a capability no conventional cement system offers. Because the cement can re-heal multiple times according to the actual concentrations, it provides lasting annular protection rather than a one-time fix. This prevents early water breakthrough, avoids costly remedial operations, reduces non-productive rig time, and delivers incremental oil production gains over the life of the well.

title: AI-Driven Predictive Optimization of Operational Pigging Frequency in ADNOC Onshore Multiphase Pipelines: A Real-World Application
container-title: ADIPEC
ea53f189a23a8a479e950c7131c7666b897cfeb0.abstract: Abstract Internal corrosion is one of the main threats to pipeline integrity worldwide, and ADNOC Onshore's network is no exception. Globally, operating companies set operational pigging frequency from a Corrosion Risk Element (CRE) weightage matrix that is scored once a year and, in practice, tends to move only after degradation has already shown up on an inspection report. This paper puts forward an AI-based framework, built and piloted in-house, that adjusts pigging schedules for multiphase transfer lines as conditions change rather than on a fixed calendar schedule. The aim was to ensure corrosion risk is maintained within accepted parameters. The model was trained on three years of historical pig run records from fourteen multiphase crude transfer pipelines. The data inputs included mix flow velocity, water cut (BS&W), SRB counts, assessed internal corrosion rate, debris composition and intelligent pigging survey (IPS) findings. The recurrent neural network was used to handle the time-series streams and predicted how quickly corrosion threats would build up between runs. The dynamic prediction outputs formed the basis for the frequency recommendation in place of the traditional static CRE matrix approach. Predictions were validated against actual debris tonnage, iron species concentration (FeS, FeO), and wall-loss measurements recorded post 1LI runs. Ten of the fourteen lines were placed under live AI management for a twelve-month study; with the remaining four held as a control group under unchanged manual scheduling. The total pig runs fell 23.0%, from 243 to 187, across the ten managed crude transfer lines with no measurable change in wall condition or debris accumulation. Within the same period; the total pig runs rose 2.6%; from 76 runs to 78 for the four control lines. More so, in two pipelines where SRB bacterial counts exceeded 10 CFU/mL, the model proactively increased pigging frequency recommendations to monthly intervals which consistent with procedural requirements with an average of nineteen days ahead of laboratory confirmation, enabling earlier biocide batch treatment. Furthermore, the model achieved 91% accuracy in predicting debris weight (categorised as light, moderate, heavy) for the subsequent pig runs based solely on real-time operational parameters. False- negative rates were maintained below 3.8%, ensuring pipeline integrity was never compromised by under-pigging recommendations. Economic analysis estimated savings of approximately USD 1.42 million a year across the study scope, from reduced production deferment, mechanical handling, pig procurement, laboratory sampling and waste disposal. The framework also demonstrated ability to trigger frequency re-assessment flags automatically upon detecting operating condition changes including water cut exceeding above 30% and velocity drops below 1.5 m/s thereby eliminating reliance on manual annual reviews such as annual CRE scoring cycle. These results confirm that Al integration into operational pigging programs represents a viable, high-value advancement for corrosion management governance. This work is among the first documented applications of recurrent neural network-driven pigging frequency optimization in the upstream sector, directly interfaced with an operator's existing risk information management system (RIMS) infrastructure. Unlike conventional risk-matrix approaches, the proposed framework continuously learns from each pig run outcome, improving predictive accuracy over time. The methodology is Pipeline-neutral and scalable across an operator's entire piggable network, offering a replicable model for intelligent corrosion management across the broader company's group portfolio.

title: Enhancing 3D Static Geological Models Using Unsupervised Machine Learning (IPSOM) for Rock Typing: A North Oman Case Study
container-title: ADIPEC
1840d32a670ca7c645a9edbd0d143a70723539c8.abstract: Abstract Reliable rock typing is fundamental to static reservoir modelling, but conventional methods often struggle in thin-bedded, heterogeneous clastic reservoirs where subtle lithological changes cannot be fully captured from core data alone. In the Shammar reservoir of North Oman, this limitation added significant uncertainty to facies distribution, petrophysical modelling, and hydrocarbon volume estimates, with a direct impact on field development planning. Conventional deterministic workflows often grouped intervals with different flow characteristics into the same rock class because the available data could not distinguish subtle differences in reservoir quality. As development progressed, this reduced confidence in the static model and pointed to the need for a more objective way to represent reservoir heterogeneity while staying consistent with geological observations and production behaviour. This study presents a workflow that applies an Iterative Probabilistic Self-Organizing Map (IPSOM), an unsupervised machine learning technique, to classify electrofacies from standardized well-log data. The workflow combines quality-controlled wireline logs, core measurements, and production data to generate data-driven rock types, which were then checked against core observations, Production Logging Tool (PLT) data, and dynamic field performance. Before clustering, the datasets were quality-controlled, environmentally corrected, depth-matched, and normalized to ensure consistency across the field. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) was used to assess how much each logging parameter contributed to the clustering and to identify which variables gave the best discrimination between electrofacies. The resulting electrofacies were built into a three-dimensional static geological model to improve facies distribution, petrophysical modelling, reservoir characterization, and uncertainty assessment, while keeping the model consistent with dynamic production behaviour. The workflow identified three electrofacies: Excellent Rock, Good Rock, and Non-Reservoir. Compared with the previous modelling approach, the IPSOM-derived facies gave a better representation of vertical heterogeneity and reservoir continuity and reduced interpreter bias. Facies-dependent saturation-height functions increased the Base Case STOIIP estimate by 4.3%, improved the match with historical production, and made it easier to identify reservoir flow units and bypassed pay. The updated model also supported ranking of future infill drilling opportunities with greater confidence. Independent checks showed good agreement between the electrofacies classification, core descriptions, PLT observations, and production history, confirming that the electrofacies reflected real geological differences rather than statistical clustering alone. Wells intersecting a larger proportion of the Excellent Rock facies consistently showed higher injectivity and better production performance, adding further confidence in the workflow. The study shows that IPSOM offers a practical, repeatable, and scalable way to classify electrofacies in heterogeneous clastic reservoirs. Combining machine learning with conventional geological interpretation, petrophysics, and production data improves the reliability of static models, reduces uncertainty in reservoir characterization, and supports better-informed development decisions. The method is not intended to replace geological workflows but to give them a more objective, data-driven basis for combining multiple subsurface datasets. It is readily transferable to other mature clastic reservoirs where conventional rock typing cannot capture fine-scale heterogeneity.

title: Centralized AI-Enabled Energy Performance Management Over Enterprise IIoT Platform
container-title: ADIPEC
529107a74162d3fb048ca9162484270ffe256d1a.abstract: Abstract Energy is one of the largest controllable operating costs and a primary source of greenhouse-gas emissions in upstream oil and gas operations. Yet in most large assets, energy information remains fragmented across electrical meters, supervisory control systems, historians, spreadsheets, and monthly reports. This fragmentation delays optimization actions, obscures emissions performance, and prevents systematic energy governance at scale. This paper presents a large-scale, centralized, Artificial-Intelligence (AI) enabled Energy Performance Management and Reporting System built on an enterprise Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) platform for upstream field operations. The system integrates field-to-enterprise energy data, monitors electrical and fuel-gas consumption, computes Energy Performance Indicators (EnPIs), generates AI-assisted targets, detects anomalies, and delivers role-based dashboards and automated reporting, all designed for scalable deployment across assets and major energy users. The architecture contextualizes distributed energy-meter, supervisory-control, historian, operator-round, and control-system data into asset, system, and equipment hierarchies, and converts it into EnPIs, baselines, targets, and alerts. A resilient connectivity backbone, combining a private 5G operational-technology network with a hybrid low-power wide-area network (LPWAN) sensor layer, provides the field-to-enterprise data path, enabling high-bandwidth telemetry from major facilities alongside low-power monitoring of previously unmetered and remote energy users. Machine-learning models support target generation, deviation detection, forecasting, and abnormal-consumption analysis, while configurable dashboards serve management, operations, energy teams, and functional specialists to enable timely corrective action and governance. At asset scale, the approach supports monitoring of major electrical users, fuel-gas consumers, water-injection systems, pumps, compressors, fired heaters, gas turbines, production facilities, and accommodation loads. It enables real-time EnPIs such as energy per barrel of oil, power per barrel, fuel gas per barrel, energy per unit of injected water, equipment and thermal efficiency, greenhouse-gas indicators, and daily operating cost. AI-assisted targets and anomaly detection allow users to compare actual against expected performance, identify inefficient operating patterns, and prioritize corrective actions. The paper concludes that a centralized AI-enabled energy performance management platform can improve energy-efficiency governance, reduce reporting delays, enhance emissions visibility, support cost avoidance, and provide a scalable model for enterprise-wide energy optimization. The contribution is a practical field-to-enterprise architecture that converts fragmented energy and process data into actionable intelligence for efficiency, emissions reduction, and operational excellence.

title: AI-Driven Plunger Lift Optimization: Insights from Multi Field Deployments
container-title: ADIPEC
2841d9da1878a63dc39ef40fc9292dc863105244.abstract: Abstract The paper presents an AI-driven plunger lift optimizer that leverages real-time operating data to recommend optimal controller setpoints (e.g. timers, pressure limits, gas flow rate limit), improving cycle performance, and dynamically maximizing production as operating conditions change. With deployments in both the Eagle Ford and Marcellus, the study highlights cross-field implementation learnings and documents achieved operational gains at scale. The approach combines (1) AI models that simulate plunger lift operation and predict flow rates based on operating conditions and controller setpoints, (2) an optimization algorithm that leverages the AI models to maximize production while maintaining stable operation and considering field-specific operational and physics-based constraints, (3) a pre-execution workflow that analyzes current operating conditions to decide if controller setpoint changes are advisable, and (4) a post-execution workflow that evaluates outcomes of recommendations on production and operation. Models are trained per basin and controller configuration using historical well and operating data (production and sensor streams, controller settings, well attributes, plunger design, and fluid properties). The optimizer was deployed in the Eagle Ford and Marcellus across 200 wells. Recommendations were reviewed by production engineers and once implemented, were evaluated through a 13-day post-execution workflow monitoring plunger lift cycles and production response. When negative responses were detected (e.g., liquid loading indicators, non-arrivals, or sustained production decline), the workflow triggered a reversion recommendation to pre-change settings. In total, more than 80% of recommendations were accepted and executed, and less than 18% of executed recommendations were reverted. Across implemented recommendations, post-execution assessment showed uplift of 2% in Marcellus and 2.8% in Eagle Ford relative to the pre-optimization baseline. The multi-field results confirm the broad applicability of the approach across different reservoir types, from dry-gas Marcellus to gas-condensate Eagle Ford, and across diverse plunger designs and controller configurations. Lessons learned emphasize data validation, basin/hardware-specific constraint tuning, structured change management, and governance to rank recommendations by confidence and operational context. The study concludes that AI-driven optimization provides a scalable mechanism to improve performance and shorten optimization cycle time relative to manual tuning. This work presents AI-driven plunger lift optimization that integrates predictive models, physics- and operations-informed constrained optimization, and post-execution evaluation. Novelty includes multi-basin validation (Eagle Ford and Marcellus) and an operational governance framework (human-in-the-loop review, recommendation confidence ranking, and auditable change tracking) that enables safe scaling beyond a single-asset pilot.

title: Revitalizing Mature Unconventional Plays Through Machine Learning-Driven Reservoir Characterization: A Scalable Sweet Spot Detection Framework with Global Applicability
container-title: ADIPEC
ea46ef2612052e6e620d46273fd8242b744036fc.abstract: Abstract Mature unconventional plays such as the Barnett Shale of the Fort Worth Basin still hold real, untapped potential in thin, heterogeneous intervals that fall beneath the resolution of conventional post-stack seismic inversion and were bypassed by earlier development campaigns as a result. This study presents a scalable, machine-learning (ML)-driven reservoir characterization framework built to resolve these thin-bed sweet spots and to generalize to analogous plays worldwide, including emerging unconventional targets across the Middle East and North Africa. Petrophysical logs from the V2P and E4P wells were quality-controlled with unsupervised anomaly-detection algorithms, then used to derive Total Organic Carbon (TOC, via Schmoker's density relationship) and a Brittleness Index (from normalized Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio). Spectral decomposition of the 3D seismic volume enhanced vertical resolution below conventional seismic bandwidth, and the resulting frequency-dependent attributes were combined with conventional seismic attributes into a multi-attribute feature space. We benchmarked eight supervised regression algorithms and nine classification algorithms across six performance metrics (R2, MSE, MAE, RMSLE, MAPE, and training time) to select the optimal predictive engine. The Extra Tree Regressor gave the strongest performance for elastic-property prediction, and the Extra Tree Classifier exceeded 90 percent accuracy in binary sweet-spot classification, ahead of every other algorithm benchmarked. A multi-criteria qualification standard (P-impedance below 12,000; S-impedance below 6,000; Poisson's ratio between 0.15 and 0.35; Brittleness Index at or above 35 percent; TOC above 2 weight percent), applied volumetrically, identified previously unrecognized reservoir intervals within the Upper Barnett member: an approximately 2-meter interval at V2P below the 19-millisecond window, and an approximately 2.5-meter interval at E4P below the 35-millisecond window both undetectable by conventional deterministic inversion. Geocellular modeling confirmed the lateral continuity of these compartments across the study area. This work is among the first to couple spectral-decomposition-enhanced seismic attributes with ML-driven elastic-property modeling to resolve shale sweet spots as thin as 2.0 to 2.5 meters. Because the classification framework is physics-grounded and needs only limited additional data once calibrated at well control, it is directly transferable to other mature unconventional basins, giving operators a practical route to recovering bypassed reserves and extending field life without the cost of new 3D seismic acquisition.

title: Less Gas, More Oil: Unlocking Production and Gas Efficiency Through Generative AI-Enabled Gas-Lift Optimization
container-title: ADIPEC
90b9b5893d5263892f672a745fe04829f5a37986.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is playing an increasingly pivotal role in transforming production optimization within the oil and gas industry by enabling data-driven and near real time decision-making. In gas-lifted wells, where injection gas is often a constrained and valuable resource, AI provides a robust framework to optimize gas allocation, enhance well performance, and maximize overall asset value. Through the application of advanced analytics and intelligent automation, operators can systematically reduce inefficiencies associated with over-injection, improve well stability, and unlock additional production while preserving gas for export and higher-value use. This paper presents a field-deployed generative AI based application developed to optimize gas lift performance and enhance overall production system efficiency. The approach integrates physics-constrained proxy modeling with engineering constraints to evaluate well performance under varying gas-lift operating conditions. A field-deployed Generative AI-enabled decision-support application was developed to interpret validated optimization outputs and provide engineers with structured recommendations for gas-lift allocation. Optimal gas-injection setpoints are determined by the production proxy and field-wide optimization framework, while the GenAI layer provides engineering rationale, operating context, and implementation guidance. The workflow includes data preprocessing, proxy-model development, continuous validation, optimization, and deployment within daily operations. The system dynamically ranks wells based on responsiveness to gas lift, enabling efficient gas redistribution across the field based on historical trends. Field implementation demonstrated substantial improvements in gas lift efficiency and overall production performance. The AI-driven system effectively reduced total gas lift injection rates while maintaining and in several cases increasing oil production, indicating the elimination of over-injection in multiple wells. Optimized gas allocation enhanced well stability, minimized production cycling, and improved overall operational reliability. In addition, the reduction in gas lift requirements enabled the reallocation of surplus gas volumes to export streams, resulting in increased sales gas and improved asset value. The generative AI-based application facilitated faster, more consistent, and data-driven decision-making compared to conventional manual optimization practices. Notably, gas-lift injection reductions reached approximately 90% in the most significant individual-well case, accompanied by measurable increases in wellhead temperature. This behavior indicates the mitigation of gas circulation effects and more efficient lifting performance, ultimately enhancing oil production with minimal gas lift input and OPEX reduction. Overall, the results confirm that integrating AI-driven analytics with sound engineering judgment can deliver sustainable production gains, improve operational efficiency, and optimize resource utilization across gas lift operations. This paper presents a novel integration of production proxy modeling, field-wide optimization, and Generative AI-assisted engineering decision support, moving beyond standalone predictive or optimization workflows. The field-proven workflow demonstrates scalable deployment, near-real-time usability, and measurable value creation through simultaneous production enhancement and gas conservation, contributing to smarter and more sustainable asset management.

title: Next Generation Autonomous Well Testing: An AI-Powered Platform for Scheduling, Stability Verification, Validation, and Decision Making
container-title: ADIPEC
52499691f0923236ac0bbe76d1f4efb87b49c07f.abstract: Abstract Production well testing in mature conventional carbonate fields poses challenges that extend well beyond those encountered in unconventional shale developments. Multiphase flow behavior, highly variable GOR and water cuts, pronounced reservoir heterogeneity, and ageing surface infrastructure collectively limit the effectiveness of static, rule-based test automation. While earlier work addressed fixed-threshold scheduling and validation for single-phase unconventional wells, a fully adaptive, closed loop context aware data-intelligence-native platform spanning the entire well-test lifecycle in a large, mature conventional field has not previously been reported. This paper presents the field deployment and operational validation of such a platform. The platform is built on an integrated digital architecture that combines data driven machine learning, real-time SCADA ingestion, production-database integration, and physics-informed constraint modelling. It is implemented through five cooperating context aware data intelligent layers. Intelligent Multi-Constraint Scheduling dynamically prioritizes the well-test queue by balancing test-overdue status, production contribution, performance deviation, facility availability, and routing feasibility. Adaptive Stability Determination uses field-trained time-series models to identify valid steady-state windows across multiphase flow regimes, replacing fixed-threshold logic. Multi-Dimensional Data Validation combines dynamic production-envelope modelling, phase-ratio consistency, allocation correlation, data driven anomaly detection, and a Virtual Flow Meter that provides an independent, physics-based verification of measured rates. Contextual Anomaly Classification categorizes detected anomalies into instrumentation drift, testing-facility anomalies, slugging, separator carryover, or genuine production change, thereby reducing false-positive intervention rates. Recommendation-Driven Approval Orchestration presents confidence-scored results recommendations through an integrated dashboard, collapsing the traditional multi-step manual review into a single-screen decision interface. Field deployment delivered measurable operational and production benefits, including a 90% reduction in engineering hours for scheduling and validation, a 20% improvement in first-pass test acceptance, and an 80% reduction in test-to-approval cycle time. The platform enabled an 80% increase in testing volume without additional manpower and was associated with a measured 2% production uplift. Near-real-time approvals and higher-quality validated test data accelerated well-optimization decisions and enabled automated, field-ready production scenarios in place of manual forecasting. This work shifts industry practice from encoding static engineering rules toward AI systems that learn and reason from operational data, enabling improved allocation integrity, reservoir surveillance, and accelerated decision-making at scale.

title: Machine Learning-Based Virtual Flow Meter for Oil Rate Estimation and Production Back-Allocation in a Mature Giant Onshore Carbonate Field
container-title: ADIPEC
f38cbfb8d3df9e5926f2a6af5fb2ccfebe10a711.abstract: Abstract Accurate well-level oil-rate estimates underpin production surveillance, reservoir management, production optimization, and back-allocation. In mature fields with large well stocks, continuous well-level metering is frequently unavailable because of cost, infrastructure, maintenance, and operational constraints, and well rates are instead obtained from periodic production tests. This leaves a visibility gap between tests during which choke changes, pressure fluctuations, and water-cut or gas-oil-ratio evolution are not reflected in reported rates. This paper presents a practical, explainable machine-learning workflow that estimates well-level oil rate for naturally flowing wells using only routinely available production-test and operating data. The study is based on 2,816 approved production-test records acquired over a 24-month period from 280 naturally flowing wells in a mature giant onshore carbonate field (Field A). Model inputs were choke size, wellhead pressure (WHP), flowline pressure (FLP), water cut (WC), gas-oil ratio (GOR), and an engineered pressure-differential feature (ΔP = WHP − FLP). To reflect realistic deployment conditions, WC and GOR were taken from the most recent preceding tests rather than from the test being predicted. Twelve regression algorithms were benchmarked using R2, mean absolute error (MAE), root-mean-squared error (RMSE), and mean absolute percentage error (MAPE). Under a record-level 60/20/20 split, nonlinear ensemble tree models clearly outperformed linear and regularized regressors. Although ExtraTrees achieved marginally higher accuracy, it produced a perfect training fit; Random Forest was therefore selected as the deployment model for its comparable accuracy, smaller generalization gap, and interpretability. The selected model achieved a validation R2 of 0.818 and a hold-out test R2 of 0.811, with hold-out MAE of 240 STB/D and RMSE of 363 STB/D. Model behavior was examined using three independent explainability methods—impurity-based importance, permutation importance, and SHAP—which consistently identified choke size, water cut, and pressure differential as the dominant predictors, in agreement with choke-flow and nodal-analysis principles. Five field cases based on new tests not used in model development showed that the ML estimates were markedly closer to subsequent multiphase-flow-meter (MPFM) measurements than the interim allocation estimates, with case errors between 0.3% and 8.5%. The workflow operates entirely on existing field data without additional sensors, physics simulators, or synthetic training data, and is currently being extended to additional fields. It is intended as a surveillance and allocation-support tool that complements—rather than replaces—validated well testing and fiscal metering. Priority enhancements include well-blind and time-forward validation, prediction-uncertainty estimation, and artificial-lift-specific and physics-guided models.

title: From Passive Video Surveillance to Scalable HSE Intelligence: Field Lessons from AI-CCTV Validation in a Harsh Desert Oil Field
container-title: ADIPEC
1d3a42bec17df281472c9ac2c9a57f24ae75f41d.abstract: Abstract At remote oil and gas facilities, closed-circuit television still relies on a person watching live views and searching stored footage after an event. As camera counts rise, that arrangement misses brief, distant, partly hidden, or visually ambiguous events more easily. This paper examines field validation of an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled closed-circuit television (CCTV) system, referred to here as AI-CCTV, in a large onshore field exposed to intense sunlight, glare, dust, long viewing distances, low-light conditions, sparse infrastructure, and a mix of fixed optical and moving infrared or pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) cameras. The workflow combined secure video ingestion, computer-vision detection, multi-object tracking, context-preserving evidence, structured vision-language assistance, a monitoring interface, and human alarm disposition. Representative scenarios covered personnel presence, personal protective equipment compliance, portable gas-monitor recognition, liquid-like anomalies, falls, selected unsafe behaviors, and restricted-area monitoring. The evidence shows functional feasibility and recurring failure mechanisms, but it does not justify a universal accuracy claim. In many cases, the limiting factor was whether the scene made the target observable, not which model was selected. Small or distant targets required changes to imaging, camera position, tracking, and evidence capture; detector tuning alone rarely solved the problem. Moving cameras required a separate analytical contract for camera state, dwell time, target reacquisition, and return-to-route behavior. Generic models were useful starting points, but field use still required local hard negatives, controlled configuration, shadow-mode testing, and a release process that could be audited. Nuisance alarms were treated as a system cost and managed with temporal persistence, context, semantic checks, risk rules, and human review. These observations are organized into six scale-up gates covering operational value, observability, local evidence, infrastructure, controlled use, and lifecycle ownership. A three-wave rollout and a minimum metric set are also defined. The result is a governed health, safety, and environment (HSE) decision-support service, not an autonomous protection layer.

title: Development of a Moodle LMS-Assisted Blended Learning Model in the Information Systems Study Program at Institut Hasan Sulur
container-title: Journal of Multidisciplinary Science: MIKAILALSYS
24f928721647083b71e879c5a4604a6ad78d711f.abstract: Integrating face-to-face and online learning in higher education requires coherent instructional design and appropriate digital support. This study evaluated the feasibility, practicality, and effectiveness of a Moodle-assisted blended learning model in the Information Systems Study Program. A research and development (R&D) approach was employed, with data collected through expert validation, student responses, classroom activity observations, and pretest and posttest assessments. Evaluation scores were 90% for learning materials, 91% for media presentation, 90% for practicality, 88% for pedagogical aspects, 93% for instructional devices, and 89% for the user guidebook. Individual, small-group, and field trials yielded scores of 84.76%, 89%, and approximately 96%, respectively. The student learning activity assessment yielded 87%. Mean test scores increased from 31.53 before implementation to 45.93 afterward, out of a maximum of 54. These descriptive findings support the model’s feasibility and practicality, while the observed score increase provides preliminary evidence of potential learning benefits. The study contributes a technology-supported instructional model for systematically integrating face-to-face and online activities in higher education, with practical implications for lecturers and institutions implementing blended learning. Further evaluation involving a control group and inferential statistical analysis is recommended to establish the model’s effectiveness more rigorously.

title: Machine Learning-Based Proxy Modeling for Real-Time Prediction of Mud-Filtrate Cleanup While Drilling in Highly Deviated Wells
container-title: ADIPEC
d48bcf32f5bbbaa25fa4f47713e6edeb1af9ee38.abstract: Abstract Downhole fluid sampling using logging-while-drilling (LWD) formation testers represents an unmatched opportunity for early fluid characterization and reservoir evaluation, leading to optimized subsequent completion and development plans. Reliable prediction of cleanup operations is critical to ensure obtaining representative fluid samples with an acceptable level of mud-filtrate contamination (i.e., below 5% v/v). Time to reach this tolerance ranges from minutes to hours, depending on fluid properties, wellbore geometry, flow rate, and pressure limits. Real-time prediction of cleanup time during drilling in deviated wells is especially challenging due to the competing effects of active mud-filtrate invasion and formation-fluid pumpout, as well as the added computational complexity of well deviation. In this paper, we present a novel machine learning (ML) proxy modeling workflow for real-time prediction of contamination cleanup while drilling in highly deviated wells. The interaction between mud filtrate and reservoir fluid (i.e., mud invasion) is modeled using a Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulator with a single-phase, two-component, fully miscible formulation. The simulation design varied mud filtration rate, wellbore diameter and inclination, formation thickness, sampling tool position, probe orientation, filtrate invasion depth, permeability anisotropy, and viscosity ratio. The resulting database of input–output pairs was used to train ML models, where inputs represented cleanup-controlling parameters and outputs were contamination cleanup curves as a function of pumped volume. Traditional ML methods, including Random Forest, ExtraTrees, and K-Nearest Neighbors, were evaluated alongside temporal models, including Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Temporal Convolutional Network, and Transformer architectures. A total of 5,328 CFD simulations were generated for training, with 300 additional cases reserved for evaluation. The developed proxy model demonstrated that temporal ML models can accurately reproduce contamination cleanup behavior while greatly reducing computational cost. Among the tested methods, the LSTM model achieved the best performance. Other temporal models, including TCN and Transformer, also significantly outperformed traditional approaches such as Random Forest and ExtraTrees. In this paper, the impact of active mud filtration on cleanup prediction accuracy was investigated and integrated into the development of the proxy models. The strong agreement between predicted and simulated cleanup curves enables rapid estimation of the pumped volume required to reach target contamination levels and supports more confident decisions when evaluating multiple stations, tool placements, well inclinations, and flow-rate constraints before or during sampling jobs. We developed ML-based proxy models for contamination cleanup planning using high-fidelity simulation data. The proxy model reduced evaluation time, providing predictions within seconds compared to approximately 30 minutes required by 3D numerical simulations. This efficiency enables rapid scenario assessment and improved job planning, particularly in highly deviated wells.

title: Physics-Informed AI-Assisted Well Portfolio Management: Integrated Diagnostics to Field-Proven Production Gains
container-title: ADIPEC
9f730b613dc5a138f3c170ded4c96de5f24031d4.abstract: Abstract Managing mature oil and gas assets requires continuous production optimization across large well inventories characterized by multiple reservoirs, diverse completion intervals, varied artificial lift configurations, and dynamic operating conditions. Identifying underperforming wells and prioritizing high- impact interventions remains challenging in such environments, as engineers allocate significant effort to manual data consolidation and surveillance, which limits scalability and delays operational decisionmaking. This paper presents a field deployed Well Portfolio Management (WPM) framework implemented across the mature Greater Hapjan Field of Oil India Limited for 150 wells of which approximately 115 are producing and distributed across 40 reservoirs. The framework integrates structured and unstructured production, operational, and surveillance data within a unified analytics environment and combines conventional reservoir engineering diagnostics with physics-informed artificial intelligence (PI-AI) methods to enable scalable, engineering consistent production optimization. The workflow applies portfolio scale screening followed by diagnostic modules including water breakthrough analysis, decline curve analysis, productivity index evaluation, type-well comparison, gas-lift performance assessment, and production engineering diagnostics. Outputs are consolidated into a ranked, physics-constrained decision-support framework, with recommendations validated through engineering review and reintegrated through a closed-loop mechanism. Across the producing inventory the framework generated over 50 intervention recommendations. Four interventions were implemented during the study period two bean-size optimizations and two isolation repair with selective perforation workovers delivering a combined production increase of approximately 100 m3/d, with analysis-to-decision cycle times reduced from days to hours. In each case the productionlimiting mechanism identified by the framework was confirmed by independent engineering evaluation. The results demonstrate that combining engineering driven surveillance with physics-informed analytics can improve diagnostic consistency, accelerate intervention decision making, and deliver measurable production uplift across large mature well portfolios.

title: Unlocking Liquefaction Capacity and Reducing Energy Intensity in Multi-Train LNG Facilities Through AI-Driven Supervisory Optimization: A Non-Intrusive, Physics-Informed Reinforcement-Learning Framework for Coordinated Train Balancing, Approach-Temperature Optimization, and Boil-Off Gas Management
container-title: ADIPEC
feedcca6cbb8d636632ce1c97ab9e53478fead52.abstract: Abstract Objectives/Scope Multi-train LNG facilities are routinely operated below true liquefaction capacity due to limited observability of internal heat exchanger thermal states, conservative refrigeration margins, and uncoordinated throughput allocation across parallel trains. This paper presents the application of an AI-driven supervisory optimization system to a multi-train LNG facility, with the objective of unlocking latent liquefaction capacity, reducing refrigeration energy intensity per tonne of LNG produced, and minimizing boil-off gas flaring while maintaining full compliance with safety-instrumented systems. Methods, Procedures, Process The system integrates distributed temperature sensing (DTS) deployed along main cryogenic heat exchangers (MCHEs) and propane pre-coolers with distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) installed on refrigeration and BOG compressor piping. DTS-derived spatial profiles quantify heat-transfer effectiveness and fouling progression; DAS-derived acoustic features detect incipient compressor surge and flow instability. These inputs continuously update a hybrid digital twin combining physics-based liquefaction thermodynamics with data- driven surrogate models. A reinforcement learning supervisory optimizer generates bounded operating targets including refrigeration load redistribution across trains, approach temperature adjustments, compressor bias targets, and BOG compression scheduling validated via forward simulation before dispatch to existing APC layer, without modification to safety-instrumented systems. Results, Observations, Conclusions DTS-enabled inference of MCHE fouling and approach temperature margins consistently identifies operating headroom that conventional point instrumentation cannot resolve, enabling trains to operate closer to true thermal constraints with quantified confidence bounds. Refrigeration load redistribution guided by the reinforcement learning optimizer reduces inter-train imbalance and eliminates the conservative margins that previously capped aggregate throughput. Real-time surge margin estimation for refrigeration compressors allows the system to exploit available mechanical capacity without approaching instability thresholds. Across multi-train configurations, coordinated supervisory targets achieve measurable liquefaction capacity uplift, verifiable through production historian data and the system's built-in performance attribution module. BOG compression scheduling reduces unplanned flaring by proactively managing tank inventory against ambient conditions and production ramp trajectories. The supervisory layer deploys non-intrusively above existing DCS and APC applications, confirming feasibility for brownfield LNG assets. Novel/Additive Information This paper presents the first documented integration of spatially distributed fiberoptic sensing with physics-informed hybrid digital twins and reinforcement learning for multi-train LNG supervisory optimization. Unlike prior approaches that optimize individual unit operations in isolation, this framework coordinates full-facility observability and cross-train load allocation within a single non-intrusive system. The built-in performance verification module provides auditable evidence of throughput uplift and energy reduction, advancing the state of knowledge on quantifiable AI value realization in LNG operations.

title: Legacy to OSDU: A Software Engineering Blueprint for Migrating Siloed Well Intervention Data to Open Standards
container-title: ADIPEC
e0372efb1bca5210eeaca1cb41b71cfe5929552f.abstract: Abstract Well intervention operations — the workovers, coiled-tubing runs, and wireline jobs that maintain, restore, and enhance producing wells — generate a rich but fragmented data trail. Across a mature portfolio of roughly 2,000 wells and two decades of operations, these records accumulate in five to ten legacy repositories, each with its own field vocabulary, structure, and vintage. This fragmentation blocks cross-well benchmarking, portfolio-level analytics, and the deployment of artificial-intelligence workloads that depend on consistent, machine-readable data. This paper presents a software-engineering blueprint for migrating siloed well-intervention data onto the Open Subsurface Data Universe (OSDU) R3 open standard. The blueprint is a five-service, TOGAF 10-aligned pipeline — Source Inventory, Extraction, Ontology Mapping, Transformation, and Load and Governance — designed to be reusable across operators and source systems. We validate the approach with a rule-based proof of concept that maps real Daily Well Intervention and Services Report (WIDR) records onto OSDU R3 schema kinds using a deterministic dictionary. The proof of concept confirms that a substantial share of well-intervention fields — notably well-control pressures (PCP, SCP, FTHP, CITHP) and health, safety, security, and environment (HSSE) observation counts (UA, UC, SA) — have no direct equivalent in the published OSDU R3 standard. We document this gap rigorously as the principal finding and outline its implications for standard evolution and for operators planning migrations of their own.

title: From Raw Downhole Gauge Streams to Optimized Field Production: A Field Pilot of Automated Pressure-Transient Surveillance and Integration with an AI-Assisted Production Optimization Architecture
container-title: ADIPEC
b68313bfb8889147adb4335dd2e5afdf5268a134.abstract: Abstract Pressure-transient analysis (PTA) and rate-transient analysis (RTA) remain high-value but often episodic reservoir-engineering workflows. In a fully instrumented offshore field, continuous permanent downhole gauge (PDHG) streams created an opportunity to move from periodic manual screening toward repeatable, exception-based surveillance. This paper presents a field pilot that automated the processing of high-frequency pressure and associated rate data, detected pressure buildup and falloff candidates, prepared analysis-ready transients, applied engineer-seeded interpretation models, and retained time-stamped results for governed reuse. Three anonymized well examples, comprising two producers and one injector, are used to illustrate data-quality challenges, event-detection settings, engineering validation, and the sensitivity of permeability and skin trends to rate conditioning. For the reviewed examples, the automated workflow identified 14 candidate shut-ins in one producer, with two requiring manual boundary extension; 19 candidates in a second producer, with one rejected after quality review; and four falloffs in an injector, all accepted. These observations demonstrate practical review-by-exception, but they do not establish a field-wide false-positive rate because the source package does not contain a complete event-level acceptance log. An activity-based time model indicates a potential annual saving of 624 engineering hours for 39 wells and two events per well per year, based on a reduction from 8.85 to 0.85 hours per event. This is a modeled benefit, not a before-and-after time study. The workflow is positioned within a broader hybrid production-optimization architecture in which approved interpreted parameters can support model calibration, virtual metering, allocation, reservoir surveillance, and constrained optimization. The paper distinguishes evidence demonstrated by the pilot from forecast benefits that require further field validation.

title: Self-Calibrating Physics-Informed Virtual Flow Metering: A Zero-CAPEX Alternative to MPFMs for Mature Fields
container-title: ADIPEC
fa78b67b966bfcd50ca56b384cec238e3bf430ea.abstract: Abstract The primary objective of this research is to develop a self-calibrating Physics-Informed Virtual Flow Meter (PI-VFM) to provide a high-fidelity, zero-CAPEX alternative to physical multiphase flow meters. The scope focuses on mature assets where declining reservoir pressures cause traditional empirical correlations to suffer a "mathematical collapse." This study aims to bridge the gap between pure data-driven analytics and first-principles multiphase flow mechanics for continuous 24/7 production surveillance. Utilizing the official Volve Field dataset spanning over 2,500 production days, a gradient-boosted decision tree architecture (XGBoost) was developed. The model's predictive core is constrained through monotonic physical relationships, ensuring predicted flow rates vary consistently with pressure drop and choke aperture changes. The process integrates physics-engineered features, including differential pressure, quadratic choke area, and pressure ratio. To bridge the data gap between physical separator tests, a randomized operational training strategy was employed to simulate a calibration loop. Benchmarking results demonstrate that while industry-standard empirical correlations, such as the Gilbert formula, suffer total predictive failure in low-pressure regimes—with R² scores dropping as low as −9.48—the PI-VFM maintains exceptional stability, recovering to an R² of 0.94 in that same well. The proposed framework achieved R² values of 0.93 to 0.96 for oil, 0.86 to 0.95 for gas, and 0.82 to 0.98 for water phases. The integration of physical constraints and the simulated calibration loop resulted in a 78 percent reduction in Mean Absolute Error (MAE), from 1011.6 to 220.5 bbl/d, over the empirical baseline. In conclusion, the PI-VFM establishes a scalable digital twin solution that ensures physically consistent production intelligence and precise hydrocarbon allocation without requiring prohibitive hardware investment. This paper introduces a novel methodology by embedding monotonic physical constraints directly into the ensemble learning split-finding process to eliminate physically inconsistent predictions. Furthermore, it provides additive knowledge to the industry by demonstrating how randomized data-shuffling can be used to simulate realistic operational calibration cycles. This creates a self-evolving digital twin that remains robust throughout the entire lifecycle of a mature petroleum asset.

title: Intelligent Hydraulic Fracturing Design Optimization Using Machine Learning
container-title: ADIPEC
e80cb45aa7afb3ad02346800179e992d1ac4a666.abstract: Abstract This paper presents the development and field application of an AI- and machine-learning-assisted workflow for improving hydraulic fracturing design in unconventional reservoirs. The workflow was developed addressing common challenges such as reservoir heterogeneity, inconsistent stage performance, and operational inefficiencies. Rather than relying only on offset-well analogs or assumption-based time-consuming physics models, the approach combines data-driven optimization with expert-level interpretation to support pre-job design, real time operational decision-making, and post-fracture evaluation. The workflow was applied to multiple gas wells completed in a heterogeneous reservoir. Compared with wells designed using the conventional approach, the AI-ML-assisted designs achieved an average improvement of around 15–20% in initial production rate. The proportion of wells showing sub-optimal flow performance decreased from about 25% to less than 10%. Screen-out incidents were also reduced by around 30%, which was associated with improved prediction of fracture behaviour and better adjustment of pumping schedules. The analysis further identified completion variables that added cost without providing a corresponding production benefit. As a result, excessive proppant usage was reduced by around 12% without negatively affecting well performance. From an operational perspective, the ability to test different scenarios and understand the variables influencing model predictions gave engineers greater confidence when making design decisions. The real field application also highlighted several practical considerations. Continued model retraining was necessary as additional wells were completed and the understanding of different reservoir behaviours. Equally important was the integration of completion and reservoir engineers in selecting meaningful input variables and interpreting model results. The workflow therefore does not replace traditional engineering analysis; rather, it provides an additional quantitative tool for identifying patterns and screening design alternatives, Overall, this work demonstrates a practical and field-tested approach for incorporating AI and machine learning into hydraulic fracturing design. The main contribution is not simply the development of predictive models, but their integration with engineering workflows and optimization methods in a form that can be used during actual completion planning. By combining predictive analytics with prescriptive optimization, the proposed workflow provides a scalable approach for improving production performance, reducing unnecessary completion costs, and lowering operational risk in unconventional reservoir development.

title: Real-Time Hardware-In-The-Loop Data Streaming with Dynamic Fault Injection for Edge AI-Based Prognostics Using Ensemble Machine Learning
container-title: ADIPEC
e168b5a8d2179d3001b1be25669737147f170637.abstract: Abstract This paper proposes an edge AI prognostics system architecture that incorporates real-time sensor signals streaming using hardware-in-the loop. Kalman-filter-based fusion was utilized alongside ensemble machine learning, adaptive drift detection, dynamic fault injection, and explainable AI, all unified in an edge-deployable pipeline. Multiple sensor signals attached to a turbofan engine using the NASA C-MAPSS FD001 dataset were imported, modeled, and normalized in an HIL real-time simulator to be streamed as 0-3.3 V. A customized analog-to-digital conversion board was built and fabricated to ingest fourteen analog sensor signals. The ADC board comprised four 16-bit ADS1115 converters which were interfaced over I2C with the Edge AI device in use. Three fault injection scenarios were imposed on the sensor signals, a drift on the pressure channel Ps30 modelled as a ramp, a bias on the core speed Nc modelled as a step, and precision degradation on the temperature T50 modelled as gaussian noise. The magnitudes of said faults were sized as multiples of the healthy-stream standard deviation. Causal Kalman filtering and principal-component fusion fed a 30-feature causal representation to a weighted Random Forest XGBoost ensemble, which was selected with engine-grouped cross-validation. Online deviation alarms were generated by an adaptive EWMA innovation monitor, and offline attribution was provided by SHAP. A terminal RMSE of 12.15 cycles was achieved by the ensemble, the MAE was 9.01 cycles, the R2 was 0.914, and the NASA score was 180.46 over the 100 test engines, which is a result that qualifies competitive with deep-learning benchmarks with proven lower computational cost. The largest remaining-useful-life displacement of 16.5 cycles was produced by the abrupt Nc step, and was detected at onset, while smaller displacements and delayed alarms resulted from gradual and stochastic faults, which led to the quantification of the trade-off between detection sensitivity and noise rejection. The 16-bit ADC emulation led to an increase in the RMSE by 0.13 cycles and preserved all alarm cycles. The proposed framework enables systematic validation of edge prognostic models against escalating fault conditions without dataset modification, which provides a practical foundation for deployment on live test rigs.

title: Industrializing Drilling Geomatics Using UAV and AI Technologies to Enhance HSE and Operational Excellence
container-title: ADIPEC
ca1debef505ba51ecb1da031407cf124d36081b7.abstract: Abstract Drilling geomatics is a critical enabler of safe and efficient well delivery, supporting location planning, site verification, topographic mapping, safety-buffer mapping, rig positioning and route assessment. This paper presents an integrated UAV- enabled framework developed through two progressive trials in different operating areas. Trial 1 was a feasibility and scouting campaign covering 25 km2 and 45 planned drilling locations. Trial 2 was an operational scale-up covering 56.2 km2 and supporting 9 drilling pads and 20 planned drilling locations. The workflow combined high-resolution photogrammetry, LiDAR, RTK/PPK positioning, terrain modelling, Rig-3D verification, virtual site review and AI-assisted feature extraction. Trial 2 achieved Ortho mosaic horizontal RMSE of 0.038 m and DTM vertical RMSE of 0.034 m. Comparison with 7,311 RTK observations showed that 99.97% of DTM differences were below 1 m. Across 45 planned locations, 250 m survey acquisition decreased by 83.3%, while pad-level acquisition decreased by 87.5%. AI development progressed from U-Net pixel classification to dedicated YOLO segmentation, with the strongest later model achieving 88% precision, 85% recall and 86% F1. Preliminary cut-and-fill outputs remain under verification. A 2026 study forecast 31.36% potential substitution of conventional field tasks; this is not an implemented result. The two-trial progression demonstrates a governed pathway from feasibility to scalable, HSE-led operational deployment.

title: Evaluation of Reinforcement Learning for Autonomous Operation: A Distillation Column Case Study
container-title: ADIPEC
b4a7d27776da76ad107aee6ef27ea09ff545e9a7.abstract: Abstract Industrial process autonomy is limited by nonlinear dynamics and the need for operators to handle abnormal events manually. In current practice, economic optimization is managed through a hierarchy of real-time optimization (RTO) and model predictive control (MPC). However, these systems are typically designed for normal operation and rely on human intervention for safety-critical abnormal events. While recent reinforcement learning (RL) studies suggest an alternative to this hierarchy, most use low-fidelity simulators and address control in isolation. This study addresses these gaps by using a high-fidelity CORYS INDISS Plus simulator to implement a dual-agent RL architecture that unifies economic optimization and abnormal event handling within one framework. The first agent manages normal operation during feed-flow disturbances to maximize butadiene and benzene recovery while meeting product quality specifications. This agent acts as a cascade master, adjusting reflux flow, steam flow, and vent flow setpoints. We used the SmoothRecurrentTD3 algorithm, which employs gated recurrent units (GRU) to handle process time delays and smoothing regularizes to reduce valve oscillation. When benchmarked against RTO-MPC baseline on identical cascade setpoints, the RL agent increased combined profit by 9.8% (5256$/h vs 4788$/h). The second agent handles abnormal operations during complete feed loss or lower feed. It uses a safety-oriented reward function to keep reflux and reboiler levels within safe operating bands to prevent pump cavitation and column flooding. This agent was validated over a five-hour test period, with control switched between the economic and safety agents via a feed-flow threshold. RL inference relies on simple function evaluation, which is significantly faster than the iterative optimization required by RTO-MPC. This allows for quicker responses to dynamic disturbances. Field deployment will require further work on agent trust regions, sensor resilience, and adaptation to process drift. This case study provides an empirical benchmark of RL against industrial supervisory control and offers a practical route to reduce operator dependence.

title: AI-Enabled ROP Optimization for a Middle East Offshore Operator: Field Validation of Drilling Real-Time Advisory Workflow
container-title: ADIPEC
12d436dbc79fa533ea3b2969fd99c8f3d7956f59.abstract: Abstract This paper presents the offshore field validation of a real-time, machine learning (ML)-based rate of penetration (ROP) optimization workflow deployed for offshore drilling operations in the Middle East. The objective was to evaluate whether an operator-trained ML model, constrained by drilling limits and executed through a centralized real-time drilling advisory workflow, can deliver measurable on-bottom performance improvement under live operating conditions. The work represents the offshore field-validation stage of a multi-year predictive drilling development program, building on earlier publications spanning ML-based ROP prediction. Two operator-specific predictive models were trained on high- and low-frequency drilling data from historical offshore wells and hosted in an in-country cloud environment to comply with data residency requirements. Model readiness was validated during a proof-of-concept (PoC) phase against a predefined accuracy criterion, including a blind test, before field deployment. During the pilot, optimization recommendations were constrained by formation-specific and downhole toolspecific operating limits, and were delivered in advisory mode through a centralized remote support workflow, with recommendation adherence tracked stand by stand. Five wells comprising ten hole sections were drilled in advisory mode using three rigs across two offshore fields. The workflow delivered a 19% cumulative on-bottom ROP improvement relative to the operator's top-quartile (P75) benchmark, more than 77 hours of on-bottom drilling time savings, and approximately USD 0.58 million in realized value. Section-level analysis demonstrated a generally positive relationship between adherence to recommended setpoints and achieved ROP uplift, indicating that performance gains were primarily driven by disciplined execution within the valid operating envelope rather than advisory visibility alone. Field execution highlighted several factors that bounded optimization effectiveness, including strict trajectory control, anti-collision management, and torque and vibration constraints, which required the selective acceptance of recommendations. The results demonstrate that when predictive models are integrated with dysfunction filtering and governed by disciplined execution practices, ML-generated setpoints can be safely and effectively implemented in live offshore environments. These findings validate a practical method for converting predictive capability into quantifiable performance gains and underpins a controlled scale-up toward future closed-loop drilling systems.

title: AI-Enabled Competency Development for Rig Technicians – A New Model for Workforce Transformation
container-title: ADIPEC
1a7f0d7937ce8ca74ae48a353d1cf02856d1a432.abstract: Abstract Objectives/Scope Digitalization on both land rigs and offshore jack-ups has introduced new layers of complexity into electrical, control, and mechanical systems. Many technicians still struggle with basic digital tasks—such as accessing PLCs, interpreting controller alarms, or troubleshooting VFD faults—despite prior training. This paper presents an AI-enabled competency development model designed to accelerate technician learning, improve diagnostic consistency, and strengthen structured troubleshooting behavior across mixed-fleet drilling operations. Methods, Procedures, Process The model combines hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) and software-in-the-loop (SIL) simulators, scenario-based simulations, and a rule-based troubleshooting assistant. Competency gaps were identified through technician interactions with simulated rig systems, including real failure modes such as SCR misfiring, VFD overheating, and PLC interlock faults. Adaptive learning concepts were incorporated to outline how future modules may tailor training based on technician behavior. Field observations from actual rig support—such as hesitation to access PLC logic or reliance on intuition instead of diagnostic tools—were integrated to ensure realism and relevance. Results, Observations, Conclusions Technicians trained within the simulator-based environment demonstrated measurable improvements, including a 35% increase in troubleshooting accuracy and a 40% reduction in diagnostic time. Simulation results indicate potential for more consistent diagnostic behavior, improved alarm interpretation, and reduced reliance on senior personnel. These improvements were achieved without live-rig deployment and therefore represent expected performance gains under controlled validation conditions. Novel/Additive Information This work introduces a competency development ecosystem built specifically for rig technicians, integrating HIL/SIL simulators, structured diagnostic workflows, and real failure data into a scalable training model. The approach addresses longstanding gaps in conventional training—particularly the lack of realistic digital scenarios—and provides a practical pathway for modernizing technician development in increasingly digitalized rig environments.

title: Decision-Centric Energy Operations: Integrating Edge Intelligence, Operational Digital Twins, Industrial Work Surfaces, and Agentic AI
container-title: ADIPEC
1af45810d093a029724673a2f2c636ee47c2794e.abstract: Abstract Energy operators are not short of data. Most assets already have sensors, historians, supervisory systems, engineering tools, dashboards, digital twins, and a growing number of AI pilots. The harder problem starts after an event is detected. Engineers still have to bring together operating trends, work history, procedures, constraints, and approval requirements from several systems before they can make a safe decision. This paper proposes a decision-centric operating architecture that connects edge intelligence, an operational digital twin, an industrial work surface, and agentic AI within a human-in-the- loop model. The layers are intentionally separated. Edge intelligence qualifies events near the asset. The digital twin adds asset context, operating state, constraints, and history. The work surface places the case into investigation, approval, and execution workflows. Agentic AI supports the engineer by retrieving evidence, invoking approved tools, checking rules, and preparing an explainable recommendation. The pattern is intended for workflow-level deployment rather than unconstrained automation. A representative implementation pattern shows how a qualified trigger initiates context retrieval from live data, engineering documents, maintenance history, procedures, prior events, and constraint models. The agent prepares a recommendation package that exposes evidence, assumptions, alternatives, constraint checks, confidence levels, and required human approval before action. The contribution is a practical reference pattern for moving from data visibility to decision execution. The paper emphasizes bounded AI use, evidence traceability, workflow ownership, auditability, and human authority. It does not argue for transferring accountability to autonomous systems. Instead, it shows how AI can reduce investigation effort, improve decision consistency, and give engineers and operators a clearer basis for action.

title: An Active Learning Approach to Inflow Control Device Optimization and Production Information Valuation in Heterogeneous Offshore Dual Lateral Wells
container-title: ADIPEC
b495da8a06921e847ee5e72836801f4d73a3e145.abstract: Abstract Completion design with inflow control devices (ICD) and autonomous inflow control devices (AICD) in dual lateral wells requires coordinated choices of device type, placement, flow resistance strength and compartment length under geological uncertainty and water encroachment. When multiple layouts and reservoir scenarios are considered, direct evaluation with a coupled reservoir and wellbore simulator can demand a substantial simulation budget. Using the SPE10 model as the geological basis, this study develops a surrogateassisted optimization workflow to identify completion designs that may improve cumulative oil production in dual lateral wells. It further evaluates how early production measurements may support intervention planning and production constraint adjustment. High fidelity data were generated with an inhouse coupled reservoir and wellbore simulator, incorporating multisegment well modelling, junction hydraulics and nonlinear pressureloss models for ICD and AICD. Simulations spanned six equally weighted SPE10based geological–aquifer scenarios and production constraints. A Gaussian process surrogate was trained on an initial spacefilling sample, then refined through active learning. At each iteration, an acquisition function selected design–scenario combinations with high predictive uncertainty or large expected improvement in cumulative oil production; only these cases were evaluated with the fullphysics simulator, directing effort toward informative, potentially highperforming regions. Evaluated strategies included openhole, passive ICD, lateralspecific AICD and segmented AICD completions. A staged decision framework then assessed the value of future measurements, including lateral rate allocation, watercut evolution and zonal flow distribution. Outcomes were grouped into bins, conditional expected production was computed per bin, and the resulting decision was compared with the unconditional optimum. Value of information (VoI) was quantified for well intervention and production constraint adjustment. The workflow identified designs whose fullsimulator cumulative oil production was confirmed while using fewer coupled simulations than complete evaluation of the design matrix. Device strength and lateral resistance placement emerged as the main controls on interlateral flow competition and water breakthrough timing. The staged analysis showed that information value depends on the decision being supported: watercut evolution and interlateral rate allocation offered greater value for intervention timing. Combining two complementary measurements captured most attainable value, with limited gains from additional measurement types. Under the present action set, monitoring before water breakthrough provided higher relative decision value than later monitoring. This work extends prior ICD and AICD optimization studies by embedding activelearning surrogate modelling in an SPE10based dual lateral design problem under geological uncertainty. It also extends flow control valve (FCV)–oriented VoI frameworks by decomposing information value across intervention timing and measurement levels, providing measurementspecific guidance for offshore multilateral completion design.

title: Beyond Threshold Alarms: A Multimodal On-Premises AI Framework for Intelligent Fault Detection and Guided Maintenance of Industrial Pump Set
container-title: ADIPEC
e389a98b3e9d8022ef3e109255dd5122aa363760.abstract: Abstract Equipment breakdowns in the oil and gas (O&G) industry are costly and disruptive, both financially and operationally. Predictive maintenance powered by artificial intelligence (AI) can help prevent these breakdowns, but most AI solutions rely on the cloud — which is often impractical at O&G sites because of data security requirements and unreliable connectivity. This paper presents an on-premises, multimodal AI framework for predictive maintenance that keeps the field engineer at the center of the process, rather than replacing them. The framework combines three AI capabilities that work together to support the people doing the actual repair work. A lightweight LSTM model continuously watches sensor data — vibration, temperature, pressure, and power — to catch early signs of trouble. A YOLO-based vision model watches live camera feeds to spot visible problems such as seal leakage, misalignment, and wear. When either model flags something unusual, the two models are combined in a fusion layer to produce a more confident diagnosis. That diagnosis is then handed to a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chatbot, running on a small language model hosted entirely on site. Rather than sending a static alert, the chatbot has a conversation with the field engineer — asking clarifying questions to narrow down the likely cause, as an experienced colleague would, and drawing its answers from historical maintenance records and OEM manuals rather than guessing. Once the cause is identified, an augmented reality (AR) interface walks the engineer through the repair step by step, right at the equipment. Because everything runs on-premises, the framework continues to work even when connectivity is unreliable and keeps sensitive operational data on site rather than sending it to the cloud. The human-in-the-loop design is central to this: AI does not make the call on its own — it gives the field engineer earlier warning, a second set of eyes on visible defects, and an expert-like assistant to think through the problem before acting. This paper describes the architecture, presents field observations from an initial deployment, and discusses how the approach reduces unplanned downtime while staying practical for the connectivity and security constraints typical of O&G field sites.

title: Lab-Trained Virtual Flow Metering Using a Physics-Guided Machine Learning Framework for Multiphase Flow Through Field Production Chokes
container-title: ADIPEC
548d4140e59945b27a8bfbd9fd9187277f4a9541.abstract: Abstract The objective of this study is to develop a physics-guided neural network (PGNN) framework that establishes a scalable pipeline for potential deployment of a purely lab-trained PGNN model as a virtual flow meter (VFM) for field production chokes across differing fluid systems, phase compositions, and operating ranges. The framework achieves both laboratory-to-field and laboratory-to-laboratory generalization for multiphase mass-flow-rate prediction through chokes while outperforming data-driven machine learning and several mechanistic industrial choke-flow models. The proposed PGNN methodology incorporates multiphase choke-flow physics into neural network (NN) by embedding mechanistic industrial correlations including Sachdeva, Modified Sachdeva, Safran & Kelkar, Hydro, and Simplified Bernoulli models into input feature space. Sharp-edged orifice gas-water laboratory data (550 measurements) is divided into 90% training and 10% validation subsets. Model training and hyperparameters are optimized using genetic algorithm with 10-fold cross-validation on training subset. Optimized network is tested on validation subset for gas-water laboratory performance. External generalization is evaluated using unseen Ekofisk oil-gas field data (87 measurements) and Porsgrunn oil gas-water laboratory data (64 measurements). Performance is benchmarked against mechanistic correlations and purely data-driven NN. The PGNN model accurately predicted mass flow rate on unseen oil-gas field data (3.4-35.1 kg/s), achieving R2 = 0.919, RMSE = 1.912 kg/s, MAE = 1.526 kg/s, and MAPE = 12.04%, despite being trained entirely on training subset of gas-water laboratory data comprising only 550 measurements over small range of 0.16 to 3.1 kg/s. It outperformed Modified Sachdeva, top mechanistic correlation evaluated on same field dataset, increasing R2 from 0.846 to 0.919 while reducing RMSE from 2.641 to 1.912 kg/s, MAE from 2.315 to 1.526 kg/s, and MAPE from 19.58% to 12.04%. Additionally, on unseen oil-gas-water laboratory data (0.6-3.1 kg/s), PGNN yielded R2 = 0.867, RMSE = 0.215 kg/s, MAE = 0.139 kg/s, and MAPE = 9.35%. Compared with best mechanistic model (Safran & Kelkar) evaluated on this dataset, PGNN matched its R2 (0.853) and RMSE (0.225 kg/s) while reducing MAE from 0.196 to 0.139 kg/s and MAPE from 15.87% to 9.35%. In contrast, data-driven NN trained on gas-water lab data failed to generalize when tested across unseen field and laboratory multiphase conditions. Overall, results suggest PGNN could potentially support scalable lab VFM pathway for transferability to unseen fields and laboratories with different fluid systems, phase compositions, and operating ranges. This study directly demonstrates a laboratory-trained PGNN approach for accurate field- and lab-scale virtual flow metering. It breaks new ground by demonstrating simultaneous cross-phase (gas-water to oil-gas & oil-gas-water), cross-scale (low- to high-flow), and cross-facility (lab-to-field & lab-to-lab) transferability. This architecture supports potentially scalable laboratory VFM deployment for production monitoring, allocation, optimization, and decision-making in challenging environments where physical field measurements from multiphase flow meters are limited, costly, or completely unavailable.

title: Human-Centered AI for Maritime Safety Culture
container-title: ADIPEC
4bcbca2cab61dcf5835afa9e6e57371edbb208c9.abstract: Abstract This paper examines how human-centered artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen maritime safety culture in offshore vessel operations supporting the petroleum industry. The scope is operational and integrates crew-generated health, safety, and environment (HSE) observations, unsafe acts and unsafe conditions, corrective actions, training completion, safety quizzes, vessel activities, inspection findings, and recurring risk themes within a digital safety-intelligence framework. The objective is to convert frontline reporting into timely preventive decision support without increasing reporting burden or replacing professional judgment. The study applies an operations-focused retrospective workflow analysis to anonymized maritime HSE records. Reports originally categorized as unsafe acts or unsafe conditions were reviewed to determine whether the assigned classification accurately reflected the observed behavior, workplace condition, event type, available evidence, and appropriate response pathway. AI-assisted functions were mapped across the workflow, including narrative structuring, category recommendation, identification of similar reports, recurrence analysis, correlation of tasks, behaviors, conditions and potential consequences, corrective-action review, targeted training recommendations, quiz generation, AI-supported safety podcasts, and preventive alerting. All consequential outputs remained subject to competent human review and approval. The analysis showed that original reporting labels do not always represent the underlying safety issue. Some reports classified as unsafe behavior were more appropriately treated as equipment, environmental, housekeeping, or access-related conditions. Other reports combined both behavioral and physical factors, required incident or near-miss investigation, lacked sufficient information, or belonged outside a behavior-based safety workflow. These findings demonstrate that safety interventions should be selected only after the report has been interpreted in its operational context.
