title: Defining Prompt Literacy in Higher Education and Faculty Development for Prompt Literacy
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
02732e64d99fbff87251316f3d9cd6bc3ce2f987.abstract: <jats:p>The current high rate of adoption of generative artificial intelligence in higher education has led to a sense of urgency in the need to come up with immediate faculty-level literacy development. The idea of prompt literacy described in this chapter is a conceptual extension of AI literacy, focusing on the skill of developing effective prompts to achieve meaningful results in teaching, learning and assessment. It explores the current gaps in faculty preparedness and points to the absence of systematic institutional strategies to promote this new competency. The chapter also suggests faculty developmental strategies that are based on experiential learning, ethical awareness and continuous skill improvement. It also gives a detailed institutional framework to inform the systematic incorporation of prompt literacy into the faculty development programs. The chapter, with its focus on pedagogical and organizational aspects, will also help create a sustainable, responsible and context-sensitive implementation of AI in higher education.</jats:p>

title: Typologies and Competencies of Prompt Literacy in Generative Artificial Intelligence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
013ea58d255cd2cb20230cf35206aa2e5da0de6b.abstract: <jats:p>This scoping review summarizes findings on an emergent area, “prompt literacy,” in generative artificial intelligence (GenAI). It specifically maps key types identified in prompt literacy, including the competencies associated with each. Using a systematic approach to analyze recent literature on the types of prompts (e.g., instruction, exploration, iteration, and evaluation) used throughout GenAI's development provides insight into how they have shaped users' experiences and interactions with new AI-based systems. Additionally, this report provides a list of basic competencies to support effective development of prompt literacy skills, including linguistic accuracy/precision, context awareness, ethical reasoning, and iterative problem-solving—all of which help individuals become successful with their digital and information literacy skills but offer new challenges when people work with AI systems. In conclusion, this review revealed that prompt literacy is a technical/cognitive skill set that encompasses (but isn't limited to) flexibility and critical thinking at all levels.</jats:p>

title: Prompt-Based Cognitive Scaffolding
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
bf7bc1447e7ed3caf087f04fb77606d4e98c71c2.abstract: <jats:p>While research on AI literacy, prompt engineering, and prompt literacy has expanded rapidly, an integrated framework explaining prompt-mediated learning remains underdeveloped. We introduce the Prompt-Based Cognitive Scaffolding (PBCS) model, which conceptualizes prompts as regulatory mechanisms that coordinate cognitive, epistemic, and metacognitive processes during human–AI interaction. Building on cognitive scaffolding, distributed cognition, epistemic cognition, and prompt literacy, PBCS explains learning as a recursive coordination process in which human reasoning and AI-generated outputs are continuously refined. The model is operationalized through three interacting scaffolding dimensions and a functional prompt typology. Its explanatory scope is demonstrated across seminar-based learning, academic writing, collaborative learning, and research-oriented inquiry. We provide a theoretical foundation for understanding recursive human–AI knowledge construction.</jats:p>

title: Prompt Engineering as Distributed Cognition and Epistemic Infrastructure in Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
d3ce7c75e5f8d37877d734c90b6dc48c96bd1c5b.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter theorizes prompt literacy as epistemic infrastructure in higher education, conceptualizing prompting as distributed cognition across learners, generative systems, artifacts, and disciplinary genres. It models prompting as a regulated workflow of specification, constraint-synthesis, iterative diagnosis, triangulated verification, uncertainty labelling, and accountable disclosure, reframing authorship as auditable process rather than polished output. Integrating mediated action, activity-system contradictions, pragmatics, genre theory, and epistemic cognition, the chapter translates construct logic into scalable pedagogies, evidence-centred assessment architectures, and integrity-by-design governance. It foregrounds equity as a capability condition, embedding culturally responsive prompting, multilingual burden reduction, accessibility-by-design, and privacy-security postures within institutional quality assurance. The result is a tool-agnostic blueprint for future-ready universities that stabilizes validity, trust, and learning under platform volatility.</jats:p>

title: Prompt Competence in Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
d32288e5236e0a2532c8a3039cde17ecc97a0f14.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid growth of artificial intelligence in higher education has changed how knowledge is accessed, created, and assessed. A key idea in this shift is prompt competence. It refers to the ability to design, refine, and interpret inputs for AI systems. This chapter explains the basic ideas behind prompt competence. It links the concept with digital literacy and critical thinking. It also discusses simple ways to include prompt-based learning in different courses. Teaching methods, assessment approaches, and real-life uses are explained. The chapter also looks at policy issues such as ethical use, academic honesty, data privacy, and institutional rules. It connects theory with practice and policy. It offers clear guidance for educators and institutions to use AI in a responsible way and support future-ready learners.</jats:p>

title: Prompt Literacy as a Pedagogical Resource
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
feb94f033fe2b7abcd2d34ab83cd576746ea93a7.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid integration of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education is reshaping teaching, learning, and assessment practices. Within this evolving landscape, prompt literacy, the ability to design, refine, and critically evaluate prompts for AI systems, has emerged as a crucial yet underexplored competency. This chapter conceptualizes prompt literacy as a pedagogical resource within the Job Demands–Resources (JD-R) framework. It argues that while AI introduces new cognitive, pedagogical, and ethical demands, prompt literacy functions as a key resource that helps mitigate these challenges and enhances engagement, teaching effectiveness, and learning outcomes. Drawing on insights from digital literacy, AI literacy, and educational theory, the chapter develops a multidimensional understanding of prompt literacy. It also highlights implications for curriculum design, faculty development, and institutional policy, positioning prompt literacy as a strategic capability for fostering responsible and sustainable AI-enabled education.</jats:p>

title: Designing Prompt Literacy
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
90eec376cccee410354ee6fd243510dd98fd84c6.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores prompt literacy in three interrelated aspects: theoretical, pedagogical, and institutional policy frameworks. Through a qualitative research design based on thematic analysis and systematic literature review, the study gathers the scholarly contributions from 2020 to 2026. The results show that prompt literacy improves critical thinking, learner agency, and academic achievement, while raising concerns about academic integrity, epistemic trust, and ethical use of AI. The chapter suggests an innovative interactive framework for incorporating prompt literacy in higher education curricula and emphasizes that it is time to be courageous in policy formation. It concludes by outlining future research directions and institutional strategies to ensure equitable and responsible integration of AI technologies in education.</jats:p>

title: Pedagogies of Prompting
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
8f0e6973756f9577bd3eeb5de26592a0529bcd79.abstract: <jats:p>The growing integration of generative AI in higher education has positioned prompt literacy as an essential pedagogical competency across disciplines. No longer confined to technical domains, prompting now shapes inquiry, learning, assessment, and knowledge production. This chapter argues for a shift from informal AI use to structured teaching grounded in constructivist, cognitive, and digital literacy frameworks. It explores how prompt literacy can be effectively taught across humanities, social sciences, sciences, and professional fields, emphasizing its role in problem framing, critical thinking, ethical reasoning, and reflective practice. A cross-disciplinary framework is proposed, integrating scaffolding, disciplinary alignment, and ethical engagement. Viewing prompting as dialogic interaction, the chapter highlights its potential to enhance creativity, inquiry, and responsible AI use while addressing risks of superficial learning and inequity.</jats:p>

title: Generative AI in Fashion Design Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
63247d82c461a4523c3e4a79b2e2ae1f0fd715d7.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter covers the transformative role of artificial intelligence in fashion design education, with particular attention to the creation of a framework for prompt literacy utilizing generative AI technologies, including ChatGPT, Gemini, Midjourney, and Newarc AI. This chapter also examines how second-year students in Amity University Kolkata's fashion design and fashion communication department generate virtual rapid clothing prototypes of their designs and develop print motifs using AI-powered tools, especially generative AI, which ultimately enhances the significance of these tools for the changing fashion landscape. Participants have created artwork in a variety of mediums, including Mahbubani art, terracotta, ceramics, and print motifs inspired by seashells, insect using mandalas art, Persian carpets, and other subjects like “Joy in Simplicity” and “The Harmony of Nature and Feminine Grace”. The AI-Augmented Fashion Design Education Framework (AI-AFDEF) was emphasized in this book chapter's discussion of traditional versus tech-driven approaches.</jats:p>

title: Prompt Literacy in Flipped Pedagogy
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
b2f959206d0e0830e780ed1979a8107c445901f6.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter critically examines scholarly literature on prompt literacy and its relationship with flipped pedagogy in Economics education. It aims to establish conceptual clarity, identify dominant research trends, and highlight gaps in the emerging scholarship. A PRISMA-informed scoping review methodology was adopted to map the evidence, clarify key concepts, and identify research gaps. The findings conceptualize prompt literacy as a multidimensional competence encompassing pedagogical, cognitive, ethical, and disciplinary dimensions. In response, the chapter proposes a Flipped Pedagogical–AI-Mediated Learning Framework that positions prompt literacy as a mediating competence connecting AI-supported flipped pedagogy with students' cognitive, behavioural, ethical, and disciplinary learning outcomes. The framework provides a conceptual foundation for responsible and pedagogically purposeful AI integration in flipped Economics education.</jats:p>

title: Prompting for Academic Writing and Research
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
381b8ae3adf774d45c5ddbe6dc73d8a600b6339a.abstract: <jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is transforming academic writing and research, creating an urgent need for prompt literacy as a core competency in higher education. This chapter develops an integrated framework that positions prompt literacy as a cognitive, pedagogical, and ethical capability supporting responsible human–AI collaboration. Drawing on contemporary scholarship, this chapter synthesises existing literature to examine prompt design, evaluation, research applications, instructional strategies, and ethical governance. It further proposes a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) verification framework to strengthen transparency, academic integrity, and the reliability of AI-assisted scholarship. This chapter contributes a structured conceptual model that informs curriculum design, research training, assessment practices, and institutional policy, enabling higher education institutions to foster responsible, critical, and future-ready AI-enabled scholarship.</jats:p>

title: Prompting for Academic Writing and Research
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
a33a6033f3bf398f73b26ab21bb6cfa211ed34c1.abstract: <jats:p>The chapter examines the role of prompt literacy as a structured academic competence in AI-supported writing and research within higher education. It develops and empirically tests a conceptual framework linking prompt quality to academic writing and research performance through the mediating role of cognitive engagement and the moderating influence of institutional academic integrity orientation. Drawing on cognitive, academic literacy, metacognitive, and socio-technical perspectives, the chapter demonstrates that effective prompting is not merely technical but central to scholarly practice. Findings indicate that high-quality prompts enhance analytical depth, coherence, and methodological clarity, particularly when users actively engage with AI outputs. Furthermore, institutional integrity environments strengthen responsible AI use and amplify performance outcomes. The chapter contributes theoretical, pedagogical, and policy insights by positioning prompt literacy as essential for sustaining academic rigor in AI-mediated scholarship.</jats:p>

title: From Prompts to Publications
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
0591dcbe31cc30e58b9111db20f64b03b4dde500.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid emergence of generative AI systems such as GPT-4, Gemini, and Claude has significantly transformed academic writing and research practices, raising critical questions about authorship, originality and intellectual labor. This chapter introduces the concept of prompt literacy as a foundational academic competency for effectively engaging with large language models. It proposes a four-mode typology of prompting strategies exploratory, analytical, generative and evaluative, mapped across different stages of the research lifecycle. Based on interdisciplinary scholarship, the chapter outlines practical techniques such as context-setting, iterative prompting and constraint specification to enhance AI-assisted research. It also critically examines ethical concerns including bias, academic integrity and over-reliance on AI. The chapter concludes by suggesting guidelines for responsible and pedagogically sound integration of generative AI in higher education, emphasizing the need to preserve human intellectual agency while leveraging AI as a supportive scholarly tool.</jats:p>

title: Assessing Prompt Literacy Without Rewarding AI Dependence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Prompt Literacy in Higher Education
87efe6b64abb52ecb3ebc29c6cb22b3f5ea3063e.abstract: <jats:p>Generative AI has made a visible educational skill, yet many assessments still reward polished final outputs more than genuine understanding. This creates a perverse incentive: students who outsource the most thinking often appear the most competent. This chapter argues that prompt literacy must be assessed in ways that do not reward AI dependence. It reframes prompt literacy as evaluative and disciplinary judgement, demonstrated when students frame tasks, set constraints, iterate purposefully, verify outputs, document tool use, and decide when to limit or refuse AI support. The proposed approach rests on three ideas: rubrics that value judgement over polish, authentic tasks that make process and transfer visible, and academic integrity by design. Supported by seven tables and five figures, the chapter offers practical tools and concludes that the real challenge is designing assessment that promotes accountable thinking, calibrated trust, and durable learning rather than automated text production.</jats:p>

title: Towards robust deep reinforcement learning against environmental state perturbation
container-title: CAAI Artificial Intelligence Research
03c403935ac7cf7d7ce137794c5a47451c782ec3.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Adversarial attacks and robustness in deep reinforcement learning (DRL) have been widely studied in various threat models; however, few consider environmental state perturbations, which are natural in embodied scenarios. To improve the robustness of DRL agents, we formulate the problem of environmental state perturbation, introducing a preliminary non-targeted attack method as a calibration adversary, and then propose a defense framework, named boosted adversarial training (BAT), which first tunes the agents via supervised learning to avoid catastrophic failure and subsequently adversarially trains the agent with reinforcement learning. Extensive experimental results substantiate the vulnerability of mainstream agents under environmental state perturbations and the effectiveness of our proposed attack. The defense results demonstrate that while existing robust reinforcement learning algorithms may not be suitable, our BAT framework can significantly enhance the robustness of agents against environmental state perturbations across various situations.</jats:p>

title: Uncertainty-Aware Multitask Bayesian Federated Learning for Multilingual Edge Translation
container-title: International Journal on Artificial Intelligence Tools
24a47884e41eccebbcdc55835978142ea3741f9a.abstract: <jats:p>Multilingual edge translation must transfer knowledge across uneven language resources while controlling uncertainty and communication. Multitask Bayesian Federated Learning (MT-BayesFL) combines a shared six-layer Transformer encoder, target-specific decoders, lightweight adapters, and matrix-normal posteriors. The refined formulation separates Gaussian pooling from separable covariance approximation, preserves positive-definite sampling factors, and applies error feedback before sparse transmission. An adaptive projected-moment variant adds bounded reliability weights, between-client disagreement, and participation-dependent shrinkage. Reference-system results span eight English-to-target directions and five reported seeds. Low-resource macro BLEU is 26.0 versus 22.6 for FedMTL, with a 3.43-BLEU gain calculated from pairwise means. English–Swahili reaches 28.3 BLEU and expected calibration error 0.082. BLEU retention is 92.1% at 30% dropout; normalized retention over 0–40% dropout is 94.54%. Communication is 1.8[Formula: see text]MB per round, 70.5% below the dense-upload ablation, and personalization improves by 4.5 BLEU on average. The parameter-efficient comparator remains stronger on English–Chinese. Numerical checks verify covariance and residual invariants; translation gains from the refinement remain unmeasured. These results support uncertainty-aware sharing for imbalanced multilingual clients, subject to configuration-matched evaluation.</jats:p>

80e78eebcad6ce7cd583e1cff46a520d7991049e.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid expansion of solar energy has accelerated the adoption of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to improve forecasting accuracy, photovoltaic performance, intelligent control, fault diagnosis, energy storage management, and smart grid operation. Recent advances in machine learning, deep learning, Digital Twins, Physics-Informed Machine Learning, Edge AI, Federated Learning, and Generative AI have transformed solar energy systems into more adaptive and data-driven infrastructures. Despite these advances, challenges related to data quality, model generalization, computational efficiency, cybersecurity, and explainability continue to limit large-scale deployment. An integrated perspective is presented by connecting AI applications across photovoltaic systems, solar thermal technologies, energy storage, and intelligent energy networks within a unified renewable energy ecosystem. Emerging research trends and future directions highlight the evolution toward AI-native energy systems that support efficient, resilient, and sustainable intelligent societies.</jats:p>

title: Standalone PV System for EV Charging Optimization Based on Loss of Power Supply Probability
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

0f779933daa21b2f965772ae79d941e341e497a6.abstract: <jats:p>The electric vehicle (EV) is the future transportation mode. It necessitates great power from the grid to be charged. The energy demand can affect its stability. The main chapter presents a charging system based on a standalone photovoltaic system. The PV production is intermittent. Thus, the integration of a storage system is recommended. The presented configuration consists of a PV array, a lithium-ion battery for the EV with a unidirectional inverter and another battery as a storage system with a bidirectional inverter. Effective charging system, an energy management system was developed. The designed approach aims to feed the EV through the PV array. BSS are used to store excess of energy during peak hours and to ensure a continuous charging in case of deficit power. The optimization is done using the loss of power supply probability. The battery State of Charge (SOC) is predicted using the Extended Kalman Filter. The Root mean Squared Error does not exceed 1%. The simulation results show that the proposed system ensures an effective charging process with an LPSP equal to zero.</jats:p>

title: AI for Wind Energy Systems

d6d8adf202aed253644ed73dead2e3bcff980f7b.abstract: <jats:p>The renewable energy is being transformed by Artificial Intelligence (AI) to create smarter, efficient, and adaptive wind systems. AI forecasts the wind using machine learning and neural networks and optimizes the performance of turbines and minimizes costs related to maintenance using predictive analytics. These inventions assist the operators in predicting the changes, setting the turbines, and reducing downtime. Urban deployment of AI facilitates the seamless synchronization of mass-scaled wind energy with smart grids as well as the systems of IoT. It balances loads dynamically, for instance, it trades energy in real time and improves stability in the grid. Heavy reliance on fossil fuels and extensive reliance on carbon emissions and fossil fuels can be reduced through the implementation of AI-driven systems that enhance energy efficiency, reliability, and sustainability through the integration of renewable sources, storage, and intelligent control.</jats:p>

4f4dc990deb9ecb4d79f7eb21160b4d6a0c8d4aa.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming the wind energy sector, marking a major step toward sustainable and intelligent societies. As global energy demands rise and carbon reduction becomes urgent, AI offers powerful tools to enhance the efficiency, reliability, and scalability of wind power systems. Through technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, digital twins, and predictive analytics, AI optimizes turbine design, predictive maintenance, load forecasting, and smart grid integration. By leveraging big data from sensors, meteorological sources, and operational parameters, AI enables accurate wind prediction, timely fault detection, and real-time performance optimization. Additionally, AI-driven systems play an emerging role in urban wind integration by improving micro-wind utilization, energy storage, and distributed generation within smart cities. The chapter also addresses economic feasibility, environmental sustainability, and ethical implications of AI-enabled wind energy applications.</jats:p>

title: Geothermal Energy and AI Integration

0a94185efa705e533048f8ecb2e7e97f676948cd.abstract: <jats:p>The future of sustainable power generation is being transformed by the application of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to geothermal energy systems that improves the precision of their exploration, efficiency of their operations, and sustainability of their reservoirs. The chapter analyzes the main principles of geothermal energy, considers the latest methods of AI in the energy system, and seeks to emphasize how AI-based models can contribute to real-time monitoring, predictive maintenance, and surface characterization. The chapter illustrates the real usefulness of AI-supported geothermal processes using case studies and worldwide initiatives and covering the current issues regarding data quality, integration of the system, and ethical concerns. New tendencies like digital twins, intelligent geothermal facilities, and powerful predictive analytics are discussed to demonstrate possible research opportunities in the future. On the whole, the integration of geothermal technologies with AI has a high potential to speed up the innovation of renewable energy and add to the global energy.</jats:p>

427d1a26ce798d2133705e4eaa4fe9ba71a1502d.abstract: <jats:p>AI-powered geothermal systems are changing renewable energy by making it easier to find new sources of energy, lowering the cost of drilling, improving reservoir management, and making power plants work better. AI techniques look at data from geology, seismology, and operations to find anomalies, predict reservoir properties, and improve energy extraction. Intelligent drilling systems let you control parameters in real time and do predictive maintenance, which lowers costs and risks. AI-based reservoir simulations help with dynamic control of injection and extraction processes, which makes sure that they last for a long time. On the surface, smart monitoring and forecasting tools make plants more efficient and help them connect to the grid better, which supports stable hybrid renewable networks. AI also makes environmental monitoring better by finding seismic and emission risks early on. AI-enhanced geothermal technologies make things much more reliable, efficient, and sustainable, even though there are problems like not having enough data and models that are hard to understand.</jats:p>

title: AI Optimization of Energy Storage Systems for Enhancing Efficiency, Capacity, and Resilience
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

cea59c00d46249ed8267dc08bd0d2e35d2aa48a6.abstract: <jats:p>The global shift from fossil fuels to renewable energy has increased the need for energy storage systems to ensure reliability, flexibility, and resilience in modern power grids. Although solar and wind reduce emissions, their intermittency challenges grid stability and supply–demand balance. Energy Storage Systems (ESS), such as batteries, supercapacitors, hydrogen, and mechanical storage, play a key role in addressing these issues. However, ESS face limitations like efficiency loss, capacity degradation, uncertainty, and high costs. Artificial Intelligence (AI) offers a transformative solution by improving prediction accuracy, optimizing real-time operation, managing degradation, and enabling smart decision-making. This chapter introduces the global energy transition, importance of ESS, major challenges, and the role of AI in enhancing ESS performance and lifecycle. It presents the mission, motivation, and scope of the work, forming the basis for detailed discussions on technologies, AI-driven control, predictive maintenance, and future smart storage systems.</jats:p>

36115464283b4a94eb1013a154df03e7f1a1e053.abstract: <jats:p>As the earth's energy requires to grow, it is important to make sustainable power sources like sun, wind, and hydropower work as efficiently as possible. As power lines get more complicated and energy sources change, old ways of managing energy are not always up to the task. So, there is a greater need for new energy systems and methods to deal with issues like energy loss and waste. Big data and AI are transforming renewable energy and grid system worldwide. These technologies optimise renewable energy generation as demand for novel energy systems develops. AI-powered Smart Grid Technology improves real-time monitoring and matches energy flows to demand. Additionally, AI-driven energy optimization improves solar and wind resource allocation and operating efficiency. Predictive analytics improves renewable energy management by predicting output and consumption. This article shows how AI and big data are becoming crucial in renewable energy and grid management system. It addresses how improved forecasting and energy efficiency create a more robust and sustainable energy future.</jats:p>

cf23bf1f0405a3031b63f652b560a34ed04f777f.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter addresses the intelligent management of energy resources at the microgrid level, with a strong focus on the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) for smart grid optimization. The study considers a grid-connected building integrating local renewable energy generation and energy storage systems. The microgrid configuration is presented along with the objectives of the proposed energy management approach and the performance indicators used to assess operational costs, environmental impacts, and renewable energy utilization. Particular attention is given to the interaction between the building and the main grid to optimize power exchanges while ensuring grid stability. A case study modeled and simulated using WindPRO software demonstrates the effectiveness of AI-driven solutions and highlights their potential to enable clean, resilient, and economically viable energy systems at the microgrid scale.</jats:p>

f20481898dd366f5395dcbbf2be914d08a780e36.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays a transformative role in enhancing predictive accuracy and operational performance in renewable energy systems. As the global shift toward sustainable energy intensifies, AI enables improved efficiency, reduced costs, and greater reliability across energy infrastructures. This study investigates AI's potential to optimize energy production forecasting, consumption patterns, and smart grid operations. Findings reveal that AI significantly enhances forecasting accuracy, system adaptability, and real-time energy management. By integrating AI, renewable energy systems become more resilient and efficient, supporting long-term sustainability goals. The study offers strategic insights into how AI technologies can be effectively leveraged to advance renewable energy development and intelligent grid performance.</jats:p>

title:
Three-dimensional particle velocimetry in digital in-line holography
				via a channel-attention autofocusing network
container-title: Applied Optics
f645074bdb03734330a8cf37f576379abaf3187a.abstract:
<jats:p>Three-dimensional particle velocimetry using digital in-line holography
					is limited by axial localization errors. This paper proposes a method
					based on a channel-attention autofocusing network (CAF-NET), which
					predicts particle axial distances end-to-end via a channel attention
					mechanism and reconstructs three-dimensional velocity fields combined
					with a two-frame matching algorithm. On a public dataset, CAF-NET
					reduces the average axial localization error by 40.4% compared to
					FocusNET and improves PSNR and SSIM by 16.7% and 6.7%, respectively.
					In simulated velocimetry, the average absolute velocity error is
					reduced by 40.9% relative to FocusNET. Experiments yield a maximum
					relative error of 6.7% for the measured average velocities. The method
					effectively mitigates the impact of axial localization errors on
					velocimetry, offering a high-precision solution for holographic
					three-dimensional flow field measurement.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence in functional gastrointestinal disorders: From symptom recognition to personalised management
container-title: Artificial Intelligence in Gastroenterology
f57453a3c420a7290237c42086b5bc296cd8b07c.abstract: <jats:p>Functional gastrointestinal disorders, now termed disorders of gut-brain interaction, are heterogeneous conditions shaped by psychological, physiological, microbial, and environmental factors. Diagnosis and treatment remain difficult because symptoms overlap, trajectories fluctuate, and no single objective biomarker exists. This minireview synthesises human evidence for artificial intelligence (AI) in symptom classification, digital phenotyping, microbiome and multi-omics prediction, treatment-response estimation, wearable monitoring, and language-based care. Targeted PubMed searches were updated through September 20, 2026. Current studies show feasibility, but most use small, single-centre cohorts, retrospective designs, or internal validation; calibration and prospective impact evaluation are uncommon. The most plausible near-term role of AI is therefore clinical augmentation: Identifying longitudinal patterns, supporting shared decisions, and detecting changes that require reassessment while preserving human oversight and patient autonomy. Large language models may improve education and communication, but disorder-specific evaluations reveal imperfect diagnosis and treatment recommendations with marked overconfidence. Translation requires representative cohorts that include overlapping organic disease, explicit endpoints despite the absence of a diagnostic gold standard, external validation, calibration, equity assessment, and prospective evaluation of patient benefit. AI should be judged by outcomes and care experience, not discrimination alone.</jats:p>

title: Algorithmic Hydrology Governing Transboundary Waters in the Age of Artificial Intelligence and Climate Disruption
container-title: Climate Policy, Spatial Planning, and Resilience in Border Regions
5ef36f0879bf07bd3418d7593afdfc3688ecf8fb.abstract: <jats:p>This study analyzes how climate-induced hydro-climatic non-stationarity undermines existing frameworks for managing shared freshwater resources, increasing demand for adaptive governance. It assesses the role of artificial intelligence (AI) in transboundary water governance, highlighting both its potential to support international water law principles through improved transparency and its risks, including opacity, accountability gaps, and technological asymmetries. Case studies from the Brahmaputra, Indus, and Segura basins show that AI may either enhance cooperation or intensify fragmentation, depending on governance contexts.</jats:p>

title: From Borders to Buffers
container-title: Climate Policy, Spatial Planning, and Resilience in Border Regions
696f635388ee442fbbf0187a9ca742e8a9343a54.abstract: <jats:p>Frontier regions—often defined by political borders, ecological fragility, and socio-economic marginality—are increasingly exposed to compounded climate risks. Traditional climate risk assessments, constrained by administrative boundaries and static indicators, are insufficient to capture the spatial complexity of vulnerability in these regions. This conceptual chapter advances the notion of spatial intelligence as a transformative lens for understanding climate risk, vulnerability, and adaptive capacity in frontier landscapes. By integrating geospatial reasoning, contextual analytics, and governance sensitivity, spatial intelligence enables a shift from border-centric risk framing to buffer-oriented resilience planning. The chapter synthesizes interdisciplinary scholarship to conceptualize how spatial intelligence can support anticipatory governance, equitable adaptation, and climate-informed decision-making in frontier regions, particularly in the Global South, where climate vulnerability intersects with institutional, infrastructural, and socio-political constraints.</jats:p>

title: Understanding the Electric-Taxi Travel Experience Through Identity, Autonomy, and Anxiety
container-title: Transforming Tourism Through Electric Mobility
b41e83d8bb453710cd9b87555c0ca5a4f01b3ba2.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how sustainable travel identity, perceived autonomy, and electric vehicle usage anxiety shape travellers' hedonic experience of electric taxis. Drawing on experiential consumption, self-determination, environmental self-identity, and perceived-risk perspectives, it develops an experiential mobility framework for platform-mediated travel. Survey data were collected online from prospective electric-taxi users in Delhi, India. After screening 250 responses, 227 cases were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. The findings identify perceived autonomy as the principal predictor of hedonic travel experience. Sustainable travel identity did not significantly influence autonomy or enjoyment, and its indirect effect through autonomy was unsupported. EV usage anxiety was positively associated with autonomy but did not directly affect hedonic experience, indicating that anxiety may encourage information seeking and preparedness rather than restrict perceived control.</jats:p>

title: From Common Asset Demand to Intermediary Choice: A Focused Reanalysis of Attention Complementarity across U.S. Spot Bitcoin ETFs
container-title: The Journal of FinTech
1ecd734f11db66af0507144de857e9a9ea778797.abstract: <jats:p>The launch of U.S. spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds created an unusual allocation problem: 10 intermediaries offered nearly the same underlying exposure, yet their flows diverged sharply. This paper is a focused reanalysis of the fund-flow and Reddit panel introduced by [Shi, J., Z. Wang, D. Ding, Y. Wang, C. Xia, Q. Ding, and T. Lim, 2026, Who Gets the Flows? AI-Based Brand Visibility, Social Media Sentiment, and Capital Allocation in the U.S. Spot Bitcoin ETF Market, Mathematics, 14, 1959, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14111959]. It does not present the dataset, text measures, BrandScore or the baseline sentiment-by-visibility association as new. Instead, it asks what the established association reveals about the division between category demand and intermediary choice. The contribution consists of three interpretive emphases applied to estimates already reported by [Shi, J., Z. Wang, D. Ding, Y. Wang, C. Xia, Q. Ding, and T. Lim, 2026, Who Gets the Flows? AI-Based Brand Visibility, Social Media Sentiment, and Capital Allocation in the U.S. Spot Bitcoin ETF Market, Mathematics, 14, 1959, https://doi.org/10.3390/math14111959]: within-date differences across funds as evidence about allocation, asymmetry across the conditional flow distribution and variation across market states. The pairwise flow-sensitivity formulation makes the allocation interpretation explicit. In the previously reported two-way fixed-effects model, common daily shocks are absorbed and the sentiment-by-visibility coefficient is identified from differences in issuer visibility among funds facing the same Bitcoin news. The coefficient is positive, the direct visibility effect changes sign between large-redemption and large-creation states and the interaction appears less consistently during stressed markets. The Driscoll–Kraay and issuer-bootstrap checks apply to the baseline coefficient (2.930), not the two-way fixed-effects coefficient (3.802), for which those checks were not conducted. The evidence is thus an associative allocation regularity, not a causal social-media effect: differences in issuer visibility are consistent with different flows across financial wrappers conditional on common category sentiment.</jats:p>

title: MULTIMODAL SPATIOTEMPORAL BIOMECHANICAL MODELING FOR MUSCULOSKELETAL INJURY RISK SCREENING OF BODY MOVEMENTS BASED ON CROSS-MODAL ATTENTION NETWORK
container-title: Journal of Mechanics in Medicine and Biology
f75d4115ac94c6b86ec43f361db77e566c5bf6af.abstract: <jats:p>Ethnic dance involves large-amplitude and repetitive movements that may impose substantial and uneven mechanical demands on the musculoskeletal system, potentially increasing the risk of joint and soft-tissue injuries. Conventional injury assessment relies largely on manual observation and clinical evaluation, which limits the ability to continuously and quantitatively characterize movement-related risk. To address this limitation, this study proposed a Cross-Modal Attention-based Injury Risk Perception Network (CMA-IRPN) for noncontact movement analysis, movement-pattern risk screening, and injury risk assessment in ethnic dance. The framework jointly modeled Red, Green, and Blue (RGB) video sequences and human skeletal keypoints. A dual-branch encoder combining a three-dimensional convolutional neural network (3D-CNN) and a graph convolutional network (GCN) was used to extract spatiotemporal visual and skeletal features, while spatiotemporal cross-modal attention modules were introduced to model interactions between movement appearance and joint-topological information. The model was evaluated for movement recognition using the publicly available MPII Human Pose and SportsPose datasets and for movement-pattern risk grading using a self-constructed ethnic dance dataset. CMA-IRPN achieved accuracies of 96.03% and 94.86% on the MPII and SportsPose datasets, respectively, with statistically significant improvements over the comparison models ([Formula: see text]). On the ethnic dance dataset, the model achieved a Macro-F1 score of 92.25% for movement-pattern risk grading and a sensitivity of 93.75% for the high-risk category. These results suggest that CMA-IRPN can identify risk-related movement patterns from noncontact multimodal data and provide quantitative support for movement screening and injury risk assessment in ethnic dance training. The predicted risk levels represent visual–kinematic movement patterns rather than direct measurements of joint torque, tissue stress, or other mechanical loads and therefore should not be interpreted as operational real-time injury early warnings or as substitutes for clinical biomechanical assessment or medical diagnosis.</jats:p>

title: Economía popular y solidaria en Pastaza: cooperativas y asociatividad agrícola ante el marco legal
Social and solidarity economy in Pastaza: agricultural cooperatives and associativity under Ecuadorian law
container-title: Verdad y Derecho. Revista Arbitrada de Ciencias Jurídicas y Sociales
5cf9e0c60611ce9232233ba2d292fca207128c51.abstract: <jats:p>La asociatividad agrícola es una vía para que los pequeños productores accedan a mercados, insumos y crédito, y la Constitución ecuatoriana la respalda mediante la economía popular y solidaria. El artículo analizó el alcance y los límites de las cooperativas y de la asociatividad agrícola en Pastaza frente al marco legal ecuatoriano. Se realizó una revisión documental de normas y literatura arbitrada sobre cooperativismo, desarrollo rural y cadenas de valor, con análisis en tres ejes: beneficios, limitaciones y marco legal. La literatura asocia la membresía cooperativa con mejoras de ingreso y de acceso a mercados, aunque con resultados desiguales según el contexto y el tipo de productor, y señala la gobernanza y la escala como retos. Se concluye que el marco legal reconoce las formas asociativas, pero su eficacia en Pastaza requiere evidencia local. No se recogieron datos primarios.</jats:p>

61cd609948b423358f2c2ce5a39c4654a50e376f.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter explores the intersection of artificial intelligence and inclusive education across the educational continuum from early childhood development to post-secondary levels. It examines foundational AI principles, including machine learning and natural language processing, within the framework of inclusive education that prioritises equitable access for all learners. The chapter critically analyses how AI applications such as adaptive learning platforms and assistive technologies can personalise instruction and support diverse learners. It also addresses significant ethical considerations, including data privacy, algorithmic bias, and the risk of exacerbating digital divides. Drawing on contemporary research, the chapter offers strategic frameworks for implementing AI to promote inclusion, emphasising educator professional development, equitable infrastructure, and participatory governance.</jats:p>

title: AI and the Digital Divide in Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
6f35cbc8c37837db42e9888922aa3f76c437d688.abstract: <jats:p>The introduction of artificial intelligence (AI) into the educational field promises a revolution of greater individualization, automation, and access however, unequal access poses a risk of amplifying already extant socio-economic and gender, as well as geographic, digital inequality, favouring some and disadvantaging others. In the chapter, the researcher conducts a meta-analysis of policy frameworks in various nations and regions globally to explore how structural obstacles, including poor infrastructure, teacher ill-equipment, and forms of governance vacuums, could limit the equitable use of AI, further fuelling algorithmic bias, exclusion and ethical hazard. It offers a threefold equity-based argument connecting computer infrastructure, educator maturity improving, and answerable information mechanisms, intended to carry out decentralized, responsible, and sustainable AI practices.</jats:p>

title: Preparing Educators and Institutions for the AI-Powered Inclusive Future
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
1e4d81b51f90e4a34f575296a9def630bceefa9a.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in advancing inclusive education and preparing educators and institutions for an evolving digital future. As AI technologies shape teaching, learning, and institutional operations, there is a need to align innovation with equity, accessibility, and ethical responsibility. Drawing on theoretical perspectives such as Constructivism, Universal Design for Learning (UDL), and Education 5.0, the chapter explores how AI can support individualized learning, enhance participation, and reduce systemic barriers for diverse learners. It further identifies key competencies required for educators and an analysis of institutional readiness. It concludes with policy implications that emphasize inclusive, human-centered, and context-sensitive AI integration.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Personalised Disability Support Systems in Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
b7123b4039cd08aad8d731df8428ac6da5ff3c51.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the role of artificial intelligence in advancing personalised disability support within higher education. It analyses key applications, including adaptive learning systems, predictive analytics, and assistive technologies, highlighting their capacity to improve access, engagement, and student success. Attention is given to opportunities for enhancing institutional performance through data-informed decision-making and scalable support systems. Ethical considerations, including transparency, fairness, privacy, and user autonomy, are critically explored, alongside the importance of human-centred and participatory design approaches. The chapter further discusses governance, policy alignment, and capacity building as essential conditions for responsible AI integration. It argues that the transformative potential of AI depends on sustained institutional commitment to inclusive, equitable, and ethically grounded practices.</jats:p>

title: Exploring How AI Can Support and Drive Inclusivity, Belonging, and Social Justice Strategies
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
8be354f1c57c30c5f39b2c28700b5e7031ffd115.abstract: <jats:p>This book chapter examines the strategic use of Artificial Intelligence to promote inclusivity, belonging, and social justice in social and educational settings. Following a systematic conceptual review and policy-focused analytical method, the chapter integrates interdisciplinary literature, theoretical framework on ethics, and selected practice based examples in order to evaluate the benefits and threats of AI-based inclusion systems. It suggests guidelines that is based on fairness, transparency, accountability, and human-centered design to facilitate equitable AI implementation. The analysis studies problem of algorithmic bias, the exclusion of data, and limitations on the governance, and provides a set of action-oriented measures that can be implemented to incorporate social justice principles into the design and implementation of AI. The chapter presents practical and policy-related implications to researchers, practitioners, and decision-makers, to utilize AI in a responsible manner to achieve inclusive and fair outcomes by providing a frame of AI as a socio-technical system.</jats:p>

title: AI-Powered Monitoring and Evaluation of Disability Support Programs
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
77a4dec30768552cbcfc53914d4e2ef5cdb910c2.abstract: <jats:p>Millions of people all over the world are assisted by disability support programs, but their M&E systems are still manual, resource-consuming, and inconsistent, with fragile data fragmentation and slow reporting. This chapter introduces an AI-based system that combines XGBoost, deep neural networks, and transformer encoders in a system that is aware of fairness. The design is based on publicly available data: ACS PUMS, UK FRS, and WHO GHO indicators. Projected accuracy, F1-score and AUC-ROC of a simulated validation are 0.89, 0.87 and 0.93 respectively. The fairness-conscious ensemble achieves demographic parity difference that is below 0.06 across all gender, race, age and regional subgroups, which is 47 percent lower than that of standalone models. Findings indicate that AI-based M&E has the potential to improve timeliness, accuracy and equity and keep interpretability. The future direction is still imperative in terms of empirical validation.</jats:p>

title: Assistive Monitoring and Support Quality in Cognitive Disability Care
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
db5a35fb0006e94c20dd6e10396daf586441ad4d.abstract: <jats:p>Disability support organisations must maintain safety while supporting independence for people with cognitive disabilities. Traditional supervision relies on routine observation, manual documentation, and reactive intervention, which often creates workload pressure and inconsistent outcomes. Intelligent monitoring systems provide continuous behavioural observation and automated alerts. Many organisations fail to achieve measurable improvement because monitoring data is not integrated into staff workflows, response responsibility, and performance evaluation. This chapter examines monitoring as an organisational decision integration challenge using implementation science, socio-technical theory, and technology adoption theory, explains how monitoring signals influence staff decisions, workflow coordination, and service performance. Introduces the Institutional Integration Framework, which translates monitoring signals into structured workforce response and measurable performance outcomes</jats:p>

title: Ethical and Regulatory Dimensions of Artificial Intelligence in Disability Support Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
f73767fb12d904e94360afda9b122ae34110a549.abstract: <jats:p>The gradual integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into disability support systems offers significant potential to enhance accessibility, autonomy, and the quality of service delivery across healthcare, education, and social welfare domains. Simultaneously, these developments raise complex ethical and regulatory challenges that test existing frameworks of human rights, governance, and technological accountability. Adopting a critical and interdisciplinary perspective grounded in legal theory, sociotechnical analysis, and rights-based policy, this paper examines the normative and institutional dimensions of AI deployment in disability contexts. It explores how algorithmic decision-making, data-driven personalization, and platform-based service provision interact with principles of dignity, non-discrimination, transparency, and informed consent, while assessing the capacity of emerging risk-based AI regulation and data protection regimes to address structural vulnerabilities and inequalities faced by persons with disabilities in an increasingly digitised welfare environment.</jats:p>

title: Ethical AI and Financial Inclusion
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
b0a013beb14c35675ffb52135d960aea3b6a70e3.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the role of ethical artificial intelligence in advancing inclusive financial education for persons with disabilities within contemporary digital financial systems. It aims to analyse how AI-driven technologies can enhance access to financial knowledge, improve decision making, and support participation in formal financial services. The chapter also explores the risks associated with algorithmic bias, data inequality, and limited representation, which may reproduce existing patterns of exclusion. It further discusses the importance of inclusive design, accessibility, and ethical governance in the development and deployment of AI systems. The chapter argues that financial literacy, when supported by responsible and context-sensitive AI, can contribute to economic empowerment and social inclusion. It concludes by outlining institutional and policy strategies required to ensure equitable and sustainable financial participation.</jats:p>

title: From Financial Stewardship to Inclusive Excellence
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
a372f8886dd5284b3139e7b0aace529b7c5c299b.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming accounting by strengthening financial stewardship, improving decision-making, and supporting more inclusive resource management. This chapter examines how AI applications can reposition accounting from traditional financial control toward inclusive excellence in institutions that support people with disabilities. It discusses conceptual foundations of AI-driven financial stewardship, AI applications in budgeting, reporting, auditing, performance analytics, and disability-responsive financial management. The chapter also explores governance, ethics, explainable AI, data integrity, implementation strategies, and emerging technologies that shape future accounting practice. It argues that responsible AI adoption enhances transparency, accountability, and evidence-based decision-making while promoting equitable allocation of resources for accessibility and disability support. Integrating intelligent accounting with inclusive governance enables institutions to achieve sustainable financial performance alongside meaningful social value creation.</jats:p>

title: Visual-Auditory Assistive Systems for People With Visual Impairment
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
0f243d3bed6fd13cf514ca1c736e49a820b62b59.abstract: <jats:p>Visual impairment makes the same state of visual information that is available to others inaccessible for people with vision impairment, creating a major difficulty to their independence. In this paper, an integrated deep Learning system is evaluated to assist persons with vision impairment in automatically understanding scenes. The system generates descriptive image captions and sends them to the speakers. VGG-16 is used as a feature extractor, but LSTM networks and attention mechanisms are often used in the encoder-decoder pipeline. Combined models translate visual information effectively into auditory feedback. However, some difficulties still remain. The system must work in real time, maintain high accuracy in various practical scenes, and meet users' daily needs for testing. To advance from research into practical assistive technology, future work should focus on adding modern architectures, such as Visual Transformers; exploring multimodal learning; bringing accessibility even closer with edge devices; and setting up rigorous, human-centered benchmarks for evaluation.</jats:p>

title: Agentic AI Framework for Multimodal Document Understanding, Structured Info Extraction, Voice QA
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Advancing Disability Inclusion Through AI
f1bba628f93446aa4fb5985115c5a0c46172fdf8.abstract: <jats:p>Accessing digital documents remains a major challenge for visually impaired users, particularly when documents contain complex layouts such as multi-column text, tables, and embedded visual elements. To address this, DocuMind is proposed as a full-stack, accessibility-focused document intelligence system that transforms unstructured visual documents into structured and voice-interactive representations. The system combines computer vision-based preprocessing, OCR with positional data extraction, and a custom hierarchical document tree to preserve logical reading order and layout semantics. It further integrates an agent-based AI pipeline to generate audio navigation guides and summaries, along with a keyword-driven. Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) mechanism using synonym expansion to retrieve precise document context and reduce incorrect outputs. Furthermore, the system features a cross-lingual interaction model, dynamically translating spoken queries and audio responses to enable users to interact with foreign language documents natively.</jats:p>

title: Empathetic Digital Leadership
container-title: Governance for Sustainability, Resilience, and Innovation
6e36dbcf27fd9077eea7376620ff324efa90bc72.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how compassionate leadership might enhance resilience in public administration and strengthen digital governance. This chapter aims to investigate how emotional intelligence enhances the legitimacy of governance, builds institutional trust, and supports leadership effectiveness in digitally evolving public sectors. The conversation focuses on important issues in governance transition, such as organizational resistance, legitimacy threats, and gaps in leadership competencies. Additionally, the chapter offers public sector organizations implementation tools and a framework for empathic leadership. To promote theoretical advancement and innovative governance, future research avenues are suggested. This chapter advances knowledge of human-centered leadership strategies that facilitate sustainable public management and adaptive governance in quickly changing digital contexts.</jats:p>

title: Emotional and Relational Dimensions of Public Leadership
container-title: Governance for Sustainability, Resilience, and Innovation
c71e6e0f252a85baff667c4a9252da40cd63a981.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the emotional and relational dimensions of public leadership, emphasizing the critical role of empathy and emotional intelligence in enhancing governance effectiveness and leadership legitimacy. In increasingly complex and interconnected governance environments, leaders must move beyond technical expertise to develop emotional awareness, relational capabilities, and stakeholder sensitivity. The chapter integrates key theoretical perspectives, including emotional intelligence theory, relational leadership, and legitimacy frameworks, to explain how leaders build trust, manage conflicts, and foster collaboration. It highlights the importance of citizen-centered governance, participatory engagement, and ethical leadership in strengthening institutional credibility. Furthermore, the chapter explores the role of emotional leadership during crises and proposes frameworks for developing emotionally intelligent leaders capable of sustaining trust and achieving effective governance outcomes.</jats:p>

title: Artificial genetic augmentation of T6SS activity affects effector repertoire and host toxicity
container-title: Microbiology Spectrum
4469b66658797fded6f480d89d1b2fd24c1bcfdf.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title/>
                    <jats:p>
                      Type VI secretion system (T6SS), a toxic effector-delivery apparatus primarily studied for its antibacterial properties, has recently emerged as a widespread anti-eukaryotic determinant, particularly in members of the genus
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Vibrio</jats:italic>
                      . Although various anti-eukaryotic effectors have been described, it remains unknown whether effectors target distinct hosts in a similar manner. Moreover, it is unclear whether the entire effector arsenal encoded in a single genome is co-regulated across different conditions and by the same regulators. Here, we employ the anti-eukaryotic T6SS3 of
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">Vibrio proteolyticus</jats:italic>
                      to address these knowledge gaps. By monitoring toxicity during infection of oyster hemocytes and comparing the results with previous infections of murine macrophages, we find that the effector Tie1 plays a role only in intoxicating murine cells, whereas Tie2 intoxicates both cell models. Furthermore, we show that artificial augmentation of T6SS3 activity by deleting the negative regulator
                      <jats:italic toggle="yes">hns1</jats:italic>
                      fails to induce the orphan effector Tie3, whereas overexpression of the T6SS3-specific activator, Ats3, induces all three known effectors. Using Ats3 overexpression to activate all three effectors, we show that both Tie2 and Tie3 participate in hemocyte intoxication. Collectively, these findings indicate that analyses of T6SS-mediated infections must factor in the possibility of partial activation of the effector repertoire even when the main gene cluster is fully induced, and that the contribution of anti-eukaryotic T6SS effectors to intoxication may be host-dependent.
                    </jats:p>
                    <jats:sec>
                      <jats:title>IMPORTANCE</jats:title>
                      <jats:p>
                        The type VI secretion system (T6SS), a bacterial toxin-delivery apparatus, has recently been shown to mediate virulence in various marine
                        <jats:italic toggle="yes">Vibrio</jats:italic>
                        species. Each T6SS delivers a cocktail of toxins into a host cell, yet it is unknown whether toxins intoxicate different hosts in the same manner. Moreover, many investigations of T6SSs artificially activate the system by manipulating a transcription factor, yet it remains unknown whether different regulators induce the same toxin repertoire. Here, we show that a T6SS toxin that intoxicates one organism can be inert during the infection of another host. Furthermore, we demonstrate that T6SS-inducing regulators can activate distinct toxin repertoires. These findings suggest that conclusions about the role of T6SS toxins during infection should be drawn with caution, given the specific host model used, especially when the T6SS is artificially activated.
                      </jats:p>
                    </jats:sec>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Geometry-driven magnetization reversal and spin-wave dynamics in permalloy artificial anti–spin ice lattices
container-title: Physical Review Applied
cd385619ab03216c2cd13670bc1d5cc58b1d3f54.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Antiartificial spin ice (AASI), realized through spin-ice-derived antidot lattices of stadium-shaped holes in continuous Permalloy (
                    <a:math xmlns:a="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" display="inline">
                      <a:msub>
                        <a:mtext>Ni</a:mtext>
                        <a:mn>81</a:mn>
                      </a:msub>
                      <a:msub>
                        <a:mtext>Fe</a:mtext>
                        <a:mn>19</a:mn>
                      </a:msub>
                    </a:math>
                    ) films, provides a powerful route for embedding geometry-induced magnetic anisotropy within a connected magnonic medium. Here, homogeneous and bicomponent AASI lattices are investigated through a combined experimental and micromagnetic approach, establishing a direct link between lattice geometry, magnetization reversal, and spin-wave (SW) dynamics. Magneto-optical Kerr effect measurements, Brillouin light scattering spectroscopy, and simulations reveal that antidot size, lattice heterogeneity, and magnetic field orientation collectively govern both equilibrium states and dynamic excitations. The static response exhibits pronounced angular anisotropy in coercivity and remanence, with bicomponent lattices showing distinct reversal pathways and shifted anisotropy extrema relative to homogeneous systems. These variations are directly reflected in the SW spectra, where edge-, node-, and domain-wall-localized modes, as well as mode splitting and frequency flattening, emerge as signatures of geometry-induced magnetization textures. The excellent agreement between experiment and simulation establishes a microscopic connection between equilibrium magnetic configurations and SW excitations. These findings demonstrate a direct transfer of configurational anisotropy into tunable magnonic functionality, highlighting AASI as a versatile platform for geometry-encoded SW architectures.
                  </jats:p>
