title: AI as a Tool for Inclusive Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
2008fbfe45df9c72649fb888472056d12c0aa3be.abstract: <jats:p>There is an increasing presence of artificial intelligence (AI) in the classroom, but our conversation on how it can serve inclusive education (in both face-to-face and online settings) is inconsistent and often underdeveloped. Much of the discourse around AI celebrates that it can finally address large, structural inequalities in education, but this is not truly the case. When put into practice, AI tools tend to widen or narrow the gap based on how they are integrated into institutional practice. This chapter introduces AI as a practical, and sometimes suboptimal, means to serve diverse needs of learners in both online and offline contexts. The focus is on learners who have frequently been marginalized in instructional design, including those with disabilities, non-native learners, students who are first generation, and those in low-resource settings. AI-powered applications such as speech-to-text systems, intelligent reading platforms, automatic translation, and personalized feedback engines will be explored in realistic classroom scenarios.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Assessment Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
3b1af0102e45438b02902d5aaef2200558af7377.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence rapid integration into educational assessments is reshaping monitoring, measurement and support of learning across diverse educational contexts worldwide. Artificial Intelligence powered tools present unprecedented opportunities for efficiency, personalization and scalability while simultaneously raising complex ethical, equity-related and pedagogical challenges. This book chapter therefore critically examines transformative potential of Artificial Intelligence driven assessments, situating it at the intersection of inclusivity, innovation and integrity. Drawing from multiple theories, the chapter develops a model balancing automation and human oversight for transparency, fairness, and well-being. It examines applications and explores policy, governance, bias, privacy, and readiness, guiding responsible adoption. This chapter concludes with implications for practice, policy, and research, emphasizing AI as a human-centered tool for learning, innovation, and equity, and presents a framework for ethical, adaptive AI assessment.</jats:p>

title: AI-Driven Educational Innovation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
0304897651337a7bb39664e76309ee3a7ff3c822.abstract: <jats:p>The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) has revolutionized modern education, changing the way teaching and learning are designed, delivered, and experienced. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping the landscape of modern education by reimagining the instructional design and development, personalization of learning, and engagement in learning through adaptive and data-driven systems of education. This chapter explores how AI can be applied to curriculum innovation, interactive learning environments, intelligent tutoring systems, and pedagogies that focus on the learner. It also examines the ways in which AI-powered tools enhance accessibility, motivation, and immediate feedback and aid teachers in planning and assessing instruction. The chapter also assesses critically ethical, social, and pedagogical issues such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, and digital inequality. Last but not least, it identifies future directions and strategic implications for the sustainable integration of AI in the education sector.</jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence in Teacher Professional Development for Instructional Leadership Capacity
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
7d41db2f250c4a9b81480c5166a73d3c12b6229e.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the transformative role of artificial intelligence (AI) in teacher professional development (PD) within a rapidly evolving global education landscape. It begins by situating AI as a catalyst for shifting from traditional, episodic training models to continuous, data-driven learning ecosystems. Drawing on key theoretical perspectives—including automation to augmentation, socio-technical systems, and diffusion of innovation—the chapter explains how AI supports systemic educational transformation. It further explores intelligent models such as adaptive learning systems, predictive analytics, and AI-enabled coaching that personalize teacher growth. The discussion highlights how AI strengthens instructional leadership and curriculum fidelity through real-time data insights while addressing critical issues of ethics, governance, and digital equity. Finally, it proposes a strategic framework and policy directions to support sustainable, inclusive, and context-responsive AI adoption in education systems.</jats:p>

title: Behavioural Laboratories and Smart Games for AI-Driven Educational Innovation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
2388769aa5f39ba722184caad912298e0d1014b5.abstract: <jats:p>This Chapter examines the integration of behavioral laboratories and Artificial Intelligence enabled smart games as complementary infrastructures for advancing educational innovation. It establishes the purpose of grounding AI-driven systems in robust empirical evidence, theoretical frameworks, and ethical considerations to enhance instructional design and decision making. Behavioral laboratories are presented as controlled environments for generating high quality data on learner cognition, motivation, and behavior while smart games operationalize these insights though adaptive learning, real time feedback and learning analytics. Drawing on Self Determination Theory, Constructive Learning Theory and Behavioral Learning Theory, this Chapter proposes a multi-layered framework linking experimental research, computational modelling and institutional implementation. Applications across teacher professional development, early childhood education, vocational training, and resource constrained contexts are examined.</jats:p>

title: Comparison of ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot Performance in Answering Questions About the Structure of Atoms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
f648170227a2dcf14c457db8406cc2d4610f0113.abstract: <jats:p>In fields with a high concentration of abstract concepts, such as science education, large language models (LLMs) are attracting attention for their potential to provide explanatory and personalized content. This study aims to compare the performance of LLMs ChatGPT, Gemini, and Copilot in explaining the topic of “The Structure of the Atom” in the context of science education, based on criteria such as scientific accuracy, clarity, pedagogical appropriateness, and misconception risk. Ten questions appropriate for the middle school level were prepared with expert opinion to evaluate the models' response generation capacity and analyzed using rubric-based scoring. The study utilized descriptive statistics, the Friedman test, and the technique for order preference by similarity to ideal solution to determine the models' overall performance levels. The findings indicate that ChatGPT demonstrated consistent and superior performance. The findings guide in terms of science concept teaching, misconception prevention strategies, and scientific accuracy.</jats:p>

title: Designing Meaningful Learning in the AI Era
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
3c25d7c0f40619104554425c39194f433f48c95f.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into education is prompting teacher education programs to reconsider their pedagogical foundations. Many current approaches, however, equate technological adoption with meaningful learning, overlooking deeper epistemological and instructional challenges. This chapter presents the Meaningful AI-Integrated Learning Framework (MAILF), a theoretically grounded model designed for teacher education. Drawing on constructivism, Meaningful Learning Theory, and the TPACK model, MAILF defines four interconnected dimensions: conceptual grounding, critical AI literacy, reflective pedagogical design, and ethical agency. It argues that effective AI integration depends less on technical skills and more on developing educators' critical, reflective, and ethical capacities. The framework positions AI as a cognitive partner that enhances learning. Implications for curriculum design, faculty development, and institutional policy are also discussed.</jats:p>

title: Enhancing Writer Identity Through Generative AI
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
020e0600325ece480d5771e7e3d50a13da2cbdfb.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid integration of generative AI tools has transformed writing instruction, raising questions about authorship, agency, and academic integrity in teacher education. Unlike search engines, generative AI produces synthesized text that supports brainstorming, drafting, revising, and feedback. While these tools can reduce cognitive load and enhance higher-order thinking, they may also weaken productive struggle, writer identity, and promote overreliance without intentional instructional design. These issues are especially relevant for preservice teachers who must learn to use AI both ethically and instructionally. Grounded in self-regulation, self-efficacy, metacognitive theory, and the cognitive process model of writing, this study frames AI as metacognitive scaffolding for writing development. The framework highlights a gap between preservice teachers' frequent use of AI and their limited readiness to teach with it. The article argues that intentional, theory-driven integration can support planning, monitoring, and reflection while preserving student voice and autonomy. I</jats:p>

title: Epistemological Collapse
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
a6b55c3a24ec0d856449c909b12e776e61262374.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how generative AI disrupts the epistemic foundations of take-home academic assignments. It argues that written products can no longer be reliably interpreted as evidence of student thinking, as AI enables the production of fluent, academically credible work without corresponding cognitive effort. Drawing on teaching practice, the chapter shows how student submissions have shifted in form, tone, and ownership. It then reframes the problem as one of construct validity, where the link between performance and learning becomes unstable. In response, the chapter proposes presence-based assessment as a partial solution and argues that meaningful change requires institutional redesign of assessment architecture.</jats:p>

title: Ethical Integration of Artificial Intelligence in Education Through Human Agency, Equity, and Sustainable Innovation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
a9d3e453c30184c487d1b8cef1ee54e51d76277d.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines the ethical integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in education, emphasizing the need to align technological advancement with human agency, equity and sustainable innovation. It explores how AI is reshaping instructional practices, assessment systems, and educational governance across global and African contexts. Drawing on framework s such as UNESCO's recommendations on AI ethics and the OECD principles, this chapter per the authors analyses critical issues including algorithmic bias, overdependence, and the erosion of creativity. It further highlights the central role of teachers as ethical stewards, mediators, and facilitators of responsible AI use. The discussion underscores the importance of inclusive and assistive AI technologies in expanding access for marginalised learners while cautioning against reinforcing existing inequalities. Additionally, the chapter addresses policy, governance and accountability mechanisms necessary for ethical AI development advocating a human-centered approach that ensures AI supports educational goals.</jats:p>

title: Examining K-2 Educators' Perceptions of Project Read AI in Developing Instructional Materials
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
29c4149b0dd803e30bf4a61cd3842b2b95796a1a.abstract: <jats:p>This qualitative study examined K-2 early childhood educators' perceptions of Project Read AI, an artificial intelligence platform designed specifically to support phonics-based instruction aligned with the Science of Reading. Grounded in the Technology Acceptance Model, the study investigated both the perceived ease of use and perceived usefulness of the platform among six kindergarten through second-grade teachers at a suburban New York elementary school. Findings indicated that educators perceived the platform as generally user-friendly and expressed strong intentions to integrate it into their practice. Evaluations of instructional materials yielded mixed results: the Decodable Game was viewed as a highly effective engagement tool, the Lola Science of Reading chatbot produced lesson frameworks valued as supplemental resources, and the Decodable Text Generator showed instructional promise but required improvements. Implications are given for educator practice, professional development, and future research on AI-powered literacy tools in early childhood education.</jats:p>

title: From Tool to Pedagogy
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
a94b07b1610a5e77588995f323e5c721a15a3357.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping education across sectors, yet its adoption often remains tool-focused rather than pedagogically grounded. This chapter argues for reframing AI as a pedagogical innovation informed by established learning theories and frameworks. Drawing on constructivism, sociocultural theory, connectivism, cognitive load theory, self-determination theory, Universal Design for Learning, TPACK, SAMR, Activity Theory, and human-centered AI, it presents a synthesis for meaningful and ethical integration. The discussion highlights AI's implications for instructional design, learner agency, equity, and assessment, while critically examining tensions around personalization, surveillance, automation, and professional autonomy. By advancing a theory-driven perspective, the chapter provides educators, researchers, and policymakers with a structured lens to evaluate AI's transformative potential beyond technical functionality.</jats:p>

title: Future Directions and Policy Implications of Artificial Intelligence in Higher Educational Institutions
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
4e99f03a9173294c5fd7f7a0bd3e096b4ee8910f.abstract: <jats:p>With the advent of artificial intelligence, technology has advanced significantly in recent years. In this regard, artificial intelligence has the potential to play a role in higher education institutions in accelerating sustainable development. This chapter discusses global artificial intelligence policies and current debates in formulating them. As artificial intelligence tools become more accessible, educational institutions increasingly need to develop artificial intelligence education policies that equip students with the necessary knowledge and skills. Several countries have policies around using artificial intelligence in higher education institutions. Regarding this, the present chapter mainly aims to understand the future directions of artificial intelligence in higher education institutions in developed, developing, and underdeveloped countries and the main policy issues surrounding artificial intelligence and ethical codes that can ensure artificial intelligence and that support human rights</jats:p>

title: Institutionalizing AI Literacy in Teacher Preparation
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
64c8459cd7f2dfb824514d9f0d3651ac28aff692.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is reshaping teaching, learning, assessment, and professional judgment across P–16 education. This chapter presents a competency-based microcredential framework designed to prepare teacher candidates for responsible AI use before clinical practice. The framework positions AI literacy as a professional competency grounded in instructional design, ethical stewardship, data privacy, equitable access, human–AI collaboration, and reflective judgment. It moves from foundational understanding to applied classroom implementation through modules focused on responsible AI adoption, AI fluency, prompt literacy, AI limitations and risks, instructional design in AI-rich environments, classroom guardrails, and a culminating AI Integrity Statement. Drawing on literature synthesis, stakeholder feedback, policy analysis, and professional standards, including TPACK and UDL-informed approaches, the chapter offers an adaptable framework for guiding responsible implementation across educator preparation contexts.</jats:p>

title: Integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence in Flipped Classrooms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
1e4670d3841466f96a03163cc6c1855c53c8ffb3.abstract: <jats:p>This study explores the impact of integrating Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into a flipped classroom in higher education. Using a quantitative approach with complementary qualitative data, the research involved 136 management students, yielding 77 valid responses. Data were analysed via IBM SPSS 29.0, employing descriptive, inferential, and Exploratory Factorial Analysis. Findings indicate that GenAI integration enhances student engagement and promotes a deeper understanding of AI tools. Students reported increased awareness of GenAI's capabilities and limitations, and improved critical evaluation skills. Class size emerged as a significant factor influencing participation and organizational effectiveness. Overall, results provide empirical evidence of the educational benefits of GenAI in flipped settings, supporting teaching and learning. The study contributes to discussions on fostering critical GenAI use and offers practical implications for AI-driven pedagogical strategies.</jats:p>

title: Leading Artificial Intelligence for School Improvement
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
64e65d55c8556d4b2a167f31947f3fc9b06d4164.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter examines how K-12 school leadership can convert artificial intelligence (AI) from a collection of tools into a governed programme of school improvement. It adopts an evidence-informed conceptual approach that integrates leadership theory, selected empirical research, and authoritative policy guidance on instructional use, administration, professional learning, decision-making, and ethical governance. No single leadership style is sufficient. Effective implementation depends on a configuration of transformational, digital instructional, distributed, adaptive, servant, ethical, and managerial functions, mediated by organisational AI readiness. The chapter differentiates low-, moderate-, high-risk, and normally prohibited applications; clarifies the human-AI division of labour; and connects leadership responsibilities with teaching, learning, assessment, operations, procurement, and stakeholder accountability.</jats:p>

title: Positioning AI as a Tool to Revitalise Kenya's Higher Education Sector
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
ef7bb52bc1b22a095002589d4c1959c4788e780a.abstract: <jats:p>The Kenyan education system is undergoing reform through the Competency-Based Education (CBE) and through the integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI). In the higher education sector, both educators and students are embracing AI as a powerful tool in the learning process. Students, many of whom are more techno-savvy than their teachers, have embraced AI excitedly. This chapter employed a qualitative methodology to analyse selected AI policies applied in Kenya to interrogate how the adoption of the technology is harnessed in the higher education sector. Findings indicate that some of the selected AI policies do not adequately address Kenya's higher education issues. The study further established that a huge segment of the higher education sector has not yet institutionalised AI adoption into policy. The chapter argues that Kenya's higher education sector must actively participate in the AI policy and regulation discussion to ensure that the innovation is embraced in the ongoing education reforms.</jats:p>

title: Strategic AI Integration in Higher Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Harnessing AI for Education Reforms
da3558bb98cb0ef90363674494624fdfcfde03c2.abstract: <jats:p>The integration of artificial intelligence in higher education is occurring at a rapid pace and institutions are still playing catch-up with piecemeal strategies. This chapter presents a governance model that integrates artificial intelligence into curricula, teaching practices, ethical considerations and student learning outcomes. The work is informed by recent research on adaptive learning systems, algorithmic accountability, and outcome-based education (OBE). The model places emphasis on four key elements: curriculum design, faculty training, student data management and institutional governance, outlining roles and decision-making processes. The argument is clear. The incorporation of AI is not a technical issue The framework presented here is grounded in current literature from 2020 to 2024 and incorporates evidence from global pilot programmes in the US, United Kingdom, Australia and India. The chapter concludes that sustainable AI integration depends not on the sophistication of the tools deployed but on the quality of the human decisions made around them.</jats:p>

title: An Artificial Intelligence Framework to Predict Box Office Performance through Multimodal Analysis of Movie Trailers and Online Audience Responses
container-title: International Journal on Artificial Intelligence Tools
4dce9fcc50a8e08deb086128b3b510918718f9cd.abstract: <jats:p>In the film industry, box office predictions are crucial for making investment decisions, marketing plans, and distribution choices. Current prediction approaches mainly use movie metadata or single-modal information, ignoring trailer video content and audience responses, resulting in low prediction accuracy and robustness. The proposed framework is novel in that it uses a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN)–Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BiLSTM)–Attention (CNN–BiLSTM–Attention) regression and Artificial Rabbits Optimization (ARO)-based feature selection to integrate trailer visual features, trailer audio features, movie metadata, and audience responses into a single multimodal architecture. The proposed framework used the Movies YouTube Trailers and Sentiment dataset, which was preprocessed using mean value imputation, followed by Min–Max normalization and one-hot encoding. Vision Transformer (ViT) was used to extract visual characteristics from the trailer, and Mel-Frequency Cepstral Coefficients (MFCC), chroma, spectral centroid, zero-crossing rate, and Root Mean Square (RMS) energy were used to extract audio features. Audience response features were derived from sentiment scores, favorability, and vote counts. Visual, audio, metadata, and audience response features were fused into a unified multimodal representation. In order to forecast box office revenue, ARO chose the CNN–BiLSTM–Attention network’s most informative feature subset. Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.0246, Mean Squared Error (MSE) of 0.0009, Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 0.0304, Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 0.0586, and Coefficient of Determination [Formula: see text] of 0.9549 were all attained by the suggested model. The results showed that the proposed model improved prediction accuracy and provided an effective decision-support tool for movie producers and distributors.</jats:p>

title: Predicting pathological complete response to neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy in rectal cancer via artificial intelligence: A systematic review and meta-analysis
container-title: Artificial Intelligence in Gastroenterology
33ed4ac8c0119b7799da9d05fa3d511835f28fdb.abstract:
<jats:p>BACKGROUND</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>For patients with locally advanced rectal cancer (LARC), achieving a pathological complete response (pCR) after neoadjuvant chemoradiotherapy (nCRT) creates an opportunity for organ preservation through a “watch-and-wait” strategy, thereby avoiding radical surgery. Artificial intelligence (AI) models applied to medical imaging offer a non-invasive way to predict this response, yet the landscape of available predictive tools remains fragmented. Importantly, pCR is a histopathological endpoint that can only be confirmed after surgical resection, whereas clinical complete response is assessed clinically and used to guide watch-and-wait decisions.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>AIM</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>To evaluate the diagnostic performance of image-based AI models in predicting pCR (ypT0N0) for patients with LARC following nCRT.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>METHODS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>We searched PubMed, EMBASE, Web of Science, and Cochrane CENTRAL up to May 17, 2026. Studies developing image-based AI or radiomics models predicting pCR were included. Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool, Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-AI, and Radiomics Quality Score were used to evaluate methodological quality, while Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation-Diagnostic Test Accuracy assessed certainty of evidence. A bivariate random-effects model was used to pool sensitivity and specificity, and a hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) curve was used to estimate the pooled area under the curve (AUC). Between-study heterogeneity was quantified using the Zhou and Dendukuri approach. For the primary meta-analysis, we used only data from validation cohorts, as these estimates better reflect generalizable performance. Training-only estimates were excluded to minimize the risk of overestimating model performance. Pooled predictive values were calculated from the pooled sensitivity and specificity at specified prevalence levels and are reported as illustrative, prevalence-dependent estimates rather than directly pooled measures.</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>RESULTS</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>We included 13 studies with a total cohort of 2062 patients. The primary meta-analysis used validation cohorts from these studies, comprising 1393 patients. The pooled HSROC AUC was 0.889 (95%CI: 0.85-0.93), with sensitivity of 79.6% (95%CI: 70.6%-86.4%) and specificity of 84.2% (95%CI: 78.6%-88.5%). Between-study heterogeneity was low (I ² = 11.3% by the Zhou and Dendukuri approach). Among radiomics-based machine learning (ML) studies (n  = 9), the pooled AUC was 0.851 (95%CI: 0.81-0.88). Deep learning (n  = 2) and hybrid approaches (n  = 2) showed individual AUCs ranging from 0.72 to 0.92; however, the limited number of studies precluded reliable inference. External validation studies (n  = 7) achieved a pooled AUC of 0.84 (95%CI: 0.80-0.88), compared with 0.91 (95%CI: 0.87-0.94) for internal/temporal validation studies (n  = 6; ΔAUC = 0.07, P  = 0.003), indicating significantly higher reported performance among internally validated models. Restricting the analysis to low-risk-of-bias studies (n  = 5) yielded a comparable pooled AUC of 0.886 (95%CI: 0.85-0.92), indicating that high-risk studies did not materially inflate the primary estimate. The Egger-type regression test for publication bias was non-significant (P  = 0.65).</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>CONCLUSION</jats:p>
                  <jats:p>ML and radiomics show moderate diagnostic accuracy for predicting pCR (pooled HSROC AUC = 0.889), with low between-study heterogeneity and comparable performance across validation types and risk-of-bias strata. However, the pooled positive predictive value (54.4%) remains insufficient for AI to confirm pCR independently. Because AI models predict a pathological endpoint rather than clinical complete response, their outputs cannot be directly equated with eligibility for watch-and-wait management. Prospective, multicentre, externally validated studies with standardized reporting are required before any clinical translation.</jats:p>

title: Nursing leadership and performance metrics in artificial intelligence integrated gastrointestinal surgical care: A narrative review
container-title: Artificial Intelligence in Gastroenterology
cada5b0c6d7967d393747f2731fe158a7596b7a4.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being integrated into gastrointestinal and complex surgical care, yet its practical impact on nursing work remains insufficiently defined. This narrative review examines how nursing leadership can support the safe use of AI across perioperative pathways and how its effects can be evaluated through measurable nursing-sensitive outcomes. Literature was identified through PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science, with emphasis on peer-reviewed studies, systematic reviews, guidelines, consensus statements, and implementation frameworks relevant to gastrointestinal surgery, perioperative nursing, clinical decision support, and AI. The review focuses on preoperative assessment, intraoperative coordination, postoperative surveillance, and discharge planning in high-acuity surgical settings. Particular attention is given to workflow efficiency, response times, early recognition of complications, risk-stratified care, documentation quality, interdisciplinary communication, cognitive workload, and patient safety. The proposed framework is intended as a practical, non-validated structure for future evaluation rather than as an established measurement instrument. Its use will require prospective validation and adaptation to local staffing, digital infrastructure, resources, and clinical workflows. AI should therefore be judged not only by predictive performance, but by whether it helps nurses recognize risk earlier, communicate concerns clearly, and deliver safer perioperative care.</jats:p>

title: The Illusion of Security
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
6dadac891d789dc075b97f149fa34e6239ec0ee6.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter critically examines the assumption that artificial intelligence (AI)-powered cybersecurity inherently strengthens data protection within educational environments. Drawing on a critical review of interdisciplinary literature, it argues that the rapid adoption of AI-driven educational technologies has outpaced the development of effective governance, resulting in significant challenges relating to data privacy, transparency, provenance, informed consent, human-centered design, and cybersecurity. Rather than viewing these issues as isolated concerns, the chapter demonstrates how they interact to create an illusion of security, whereby systems marketed as protective may simultaneously introduce new vulnerabilities and accountability gaps. It concludes that addressing these challenges requires an integrated approach that combines cybersecurity, human-computer interaction, AI governance, and educational policy to develop more transparent, ethical, and user-centered AI-mediated learning environments.</jats:p>

title: Ethical AI and Responsible Data Use in Education
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
0ca0030d0a293ae102a203b25f3dbc50eda12d8c.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter introduces the concept of personalised learning, learning analytics, automated assessment, and the emergence of generative AI in transforming education, while also highlighting the ethical, privacy, governance and cybersecurity dilemmas that arise with implementation of Artificial Intelligence in the education sector. The chapter gives an overview of ethical and responsible use of AI in education, starting with an examination of the educational AI ecosystem, followed by a discussion of data lifecycle in education, and concluding with an exploration of algorithmic bias, transparency, informed consent, data ownership, surveillance and risks posed by generative AI. It outlines the principles of responsible data governance, privacy-by-design, privacy-preserving methods and other international frameworks like GDPR AI Ethics and OECD Principles. The topics of AI-driven cybersecurity, key practice insights for both educators and institutions, developers and policymakers, and future research areas for AI are also discussed.</jats:p>

title: Responsible Artificial Intelligence and Ethical Data Governance
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
761441594d890ca22a4cdde05f036ec2f7ff492d.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is transforming education by supporting personalized learning, intelligent decision-making and data-driven practices. As AI becomes more integrated into teaching, learning, assessment and institutional management, the ethical use of educational data has become increasingly important. This chapter examines responsible AI and ethical data governance in education. It discusses AI applications such as intelligent tutoring systems, adaptive learning and learning analytics together with the opportunities and challenges they present. The chapter explores the educational data ecosystem, including data sources, governance, ownership and ethical principles such as fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy and explainability. It also examines responsible data management, informed consent, data security and approaches to reducing algorithmic bias. Emerging issues including student surveillance, online proctoring, generative AI, academic integrity, learner autonomy and well-being are discussed.</jats:p>

title: Protecting Student Data in AI-Driven Education Privacy, Consent, Ownership, and Ethical Use
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
1adcff266d66b42b3bb260619da2d8a4f2415ffe.abstract: <jats:p>Through technologies like intelligent tutoring systems, learning analytics, adaptive learning platforms, and generative AI, artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming education by making learning more efficient, personalized, and interactive. Large volumes of student data are necessary for these technologies to comprehend learning trends, deliver prompt feedback, and aid in educational decision making. While AI has many advantages for educators, institutions, and students, it also brings up significant issues regarding the gathering, storing, sharing, and security of student data. As educational institutions implement AI-enabled systems, concerns about privacy, informed consent, data ownership, transparency, fairness, and ethical use have grown in significance. The main obstacles to safeguarding student data in AI-driven education are examined in this chapter, including concerns about surveillance, algorithmic bias, cybersecurity threats, and unauthorized access.</jats:p>

title: Information Governance of Student Data in AI-Powered Educational Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
9ebb5c39ff6576139082e5f69c7ac01d59c0f7b9.abstract: <jats:p>This chapter presents a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) examining student data cybersecurity and information governance within AI-powered educational systems. Adhering to PRISMA 2020 guidelines, the review systematically screens 237 published documents to ensure a transparent, replicable, and unbiased synthesis of the intersecting legal, technical, and pedagogical challenges in EdTech. The technical analysis is structured around the NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 (CSF 2.0), evaluating the literature across its six core pillars: Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. Furthermore, the study anchors its regulatory analysis within FERPA and the GDPR, with a specific focus on how the GDPR's strict lawful-basis and data-minimization principles govern complex, cross-border educational data flows. Ultimately, this review bridges theory and compliance to offer a comprehensive framework for securing student data in the AI era.</jats:p>

title: Secure Design Principles for AI-Driven Learning Platforms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
32bea6d3eaecbb0e62a89d791d1f4072a5b07d66.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence is increasingly integrated into educational tools such as learning management systems, analytics dashboards, adaptive assessment services, and generative AI assistants. These platforms support personalized learning and institutional decision-making, but they create risks linked to digital identity, learner profiling, data misuse, model leakage, prompt injection, and weak governance. This chapter analyzes cybersecurity governance in AI-driven learning platforms from the perspective of identity security and data privacy. It examines AI-specific privacy threats and safeguards such as zero trust, decentralized identifiers, verifiable credentials, encryption, federated learning, differential privacy, secure aggregation, and accountable oversight. The chapter proposes a layered cybersecurity framework integrating identity assurance, privacy-preserving processing, AI model protection, secure platform operations, institutional governance, and continuous risk monitoring. The contribution supports trustworthy, privacy-aware, and secure AI-enabled education ecosystems.</jats:p>

title: Distributed Artificial Intelligence for Privacy Preservation and Cyber Resilience in Educational Ecosystems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
1113e5c161f937ef659921855138bbf40a571a58.abstract: <jats:p>The digitization of education has concentrated vast volumes of sensitive learner data within centralized platforms that are priority targets for cyber attackers. It is argued that the dominant centralized model of educational artificial intelligence is structurally misaligned with modern privacy and resilience needs, and an alternative grounded in Distributed Artificial Intelligence is proposed. A layered architecture is presented that couples Federated Learning with Belief-Desire-Intention extended (BDIx) agents to deliver privacy-preserving analytics and autonomous cyber resilience without centralizing raw data. Learner records remain on institutional premises; model updates are protected by differential privacy and secure aggregation; and collaborative threat detection and self-healing are performed by distributed BDIx agents. BDIx-FL reached 99.17% accuracy, 98.93% macro-F1 and 99.76% macro AUC in simulation. Controversies are examined, deployment recommendations are offered and open directions are identified for educational ecosystems that are trustworthy by design.</jats:p>

title: Cybersecurity Awareness and Digital Literacy for Students and Educators Strengthening Data Privacy with AI-Powered Cybersecurity
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
30cafb06bf9daabec321a6848bf1479377de9a8e.abstract: <jats:p>This study aims to investigate the significance of cybersecurity awareness, digital literacy, and artificial intelligence in fostering data privacy protection for students and teachers in North India. The study was an exploratory descriptive study with a cross-sectional quantitative design, based on primary data gathered from a structured questionnaire with 620 respondents. The methods used were descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation and multiple regression. The correlation was positive for all of the variables, and the highest was between the AI-driven cybersecurity and data privacy protection (r = .741, p < .001). The results of the regression showed that artificial intelligence cybersecurity, digital literacy and cyber security awareness had significant predicting power for data privacy protection, accounting for 66.3% of its variance. The results highlight the need for a holistic approach to integrating AI into education, fostering digital literacy, and raising cybersecurity awareness to ensure safer and privacy-conscious learning spaces.</jats:p>

title: AI-Enabled Financial Phishing and the Digital Literacy Deficit Protecting Student and Young Learner Data
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Securing Data Privacy in Education With AI-Powered Cybersecurity
65ab6f5f760fd3d653bfc26c66ada7b9512e9487.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence has structurally transformed financial phishing, collapsing the cost of personalised attacks; India recorded 135,173 financial phishing attacks in H1 2024, a 175% rise over 2023. This chapter examines the convergence of AI-enabled phishing, student data vulnerability, and digital literacy deficits in India's skill-based educational institutions (ITIs, polytechnics, skill universities), a population absent from existing cybersecurity literature despite holding data regulated under the DPDP Act, 2023. Drawing on Routine Activity Theory, Protection Motivation Theory, the Digital Literacy Continuum, and Institutional Theory, it develops the Protection Gap construct and a Four-Layer Institutional Defence Model. A primary survey (N = 96, seven states) finds 66.7% encountered suspected phishing, mostly via WhatsApp; only 25.0% identified a genuine message; 59.4% were unaware of the DPDP Act; and 43.8% reported no explicit consent for Aadhaar/bank data. The chapter closes with recommendations for MeitY, AICTE, NSDC, and the Data Protection Board of India.</jats:p>

title: AI-Generated Deepfakes and Trust in Digital Communication in Namibia
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

9ae33c567c1e3c1be30b3c19886f0820b1ea2ad9.abstract: <jats:p>The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence (AI) has accelerated the development of deepfake technology, enabling the creation of highly realistic fabricated audio, video, and visual content that closely resembles authentic media. A mixed-method approach was employed, combining an online survey of 47 Namibian internet users and a total of 12 key informants were interviewed. Quantitative data were analysed using descriptive and inferential statistics, while qualitative data were subjected to thematic analysis. The findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on deepfake technologies by providing empirical evidence from Namibia and offering practical recommendations for enhancing digital literacy, strengthening regulatory frameworks, and improving institutional preparedness.</jats:p>

title: Quantum-secure and AI-driven UAV-enabled 6G networks: a unified architecture for communication, intelligence, efficiency, and resilience
container-title: The Computer Journal
2706b267c202c5d2b4e0d881162c56dccf975efc.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>The sixth generation (6G) of wireless networks is expected to meet stringent requirements such as ultra-low latency, massive connectivity, global coverage, and intrinsic security. Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) are emerging as key enablers of space–air–ground integrated networks, providing flexible and on-demand communication support for beyond-5G and 6G applications. In parallel, advances in quantum communication introduce new opportunities for achieving information-theoretic security against postquantum threats. This paper proposes a unified framework for quantum-secure and artificial intelligence (AI)-driven UAV-enabled 6G networks, integrating communication, intelligence, energy efficiency, and resilience into a coherent architecture. Beyond the design perspective, the paper evaluates network performance through Quality of Service and Grade of Service metrics, comparing 5G and 6G systems with and without AI and quantum-security capabilities. A ranking-based analysis is developed to assess the impact of these technologies on latency, reliability, scalability, and overall service performance. The results highlight the performance gains enabled by AI-driven optimization and quantum-secure communication, while also revealing trade-offs related to energy consumption, system complexity, and deployment constraints. Key challenges such as interoperability, hardware limitations, and scalability are discussed, along with design directions for realizing efficient, secure, and resilient UAV-enabled 6G networks.</jats:p>

title: Virtual metrology for process perturbation prediction in lithographic alignment marks using a physics-guided directed attention network
container-title: Applied Optics
8265acd6d2b87f6713dd6ef322c348c2ccd4b056.abstract:
<jats:p>
                    Process perturbations in lithographic alignment marks deform multilayer profiles, break mark symmetry, and introduce alignment position uncertainty. Although alignment position deviation (APD) and wafer quality (WQ) responses contain process-dependent information, retrieving the underlying perturbations remains challenging because the inverse relationship is nonlinear and strongly coupled. We formulate this task as alignment mark virtual metrology, in which process perturbation values are estimated from paired APD/WQ response matrices. To solve this inverse problem, we propose a physics-guided directed attention network (PG-DAN). PG-DAN uses diffraction limit masked attention (DLMA) to inject wavelength, diffraction order, propagation, locality, and identity priors into APD/WQ attention logits, enabling the model to use physically meaningful token relations rather than unconstrained data correlations. A directed decoder further follows multilayer coupling during prediction. Evaluated on a rigorous coupled wave analysis (RCWA) dataset, PG-DAN achieves a mean
                    <jats:italic>R</jats:italic>
                    <jats:sup>2</jats:sup>
                    of 0.999875, a mean range-normalized RMSE of 0.34%, and a mean range-normalized MAE of 0.23%, with lower estimation errors than conventional neural inverse models. These results support physics-guided inverse modeling for alignment mark process perturbation estimation.
                  </jats:p>

title: PMDA-Net: a polarization-conditioned multi-scale dynamic attention network for polarimetric hyperspectral camouflage target classification
container-title: Applied Optics
e3741308864e6d0ff381ac36b7b4229b1f39913f.abstract: <jats:p>To effectively fuse heterogeneous polarimetric hyperspectral data and improve the classification performance of camouflage targets in complex backgrounds, this paper proposes a polarization-conditioned multi-scale dynamic attention network (PMDA-Net). PMDA-Net adopts a dual-stream framework for modality-specific feature extraction, where spectral and polarimetric information are separately modeled. A multi-scale dynamic AoLP attention module is designed to transform geometric information encoded in the angle of linear polarization into dynamic weights. A polarization-conditioned spatial-channel attention module is designed to adaptively calibrate spectral features using polarimetric information, facilitating cross-modal interaction and complementary feature fusion. Experimental results on three self-collected datasets and one public dataset show that PMDA-Net outperforms mainstream hyperspectral deep learning models, traditional polarization-feature-based methods, and recent multimodal fusion methods on all four datasets. Compared with the model using only hyperspectral information, PMDA-Net improves the average accuracy by 5.87, 5.38, 25.71, and 5.01 percentage points on the four datasets, respectively. These results indicate that polarization information can effectively complement spectral representations and help suppress aliasing responses caused by spectral similarity in complex scenes. This work provides a promising approach for polarimetric hyperspectral image classification and camouflage target recognition.</jats:p>

title: Artificial intelligence in gastroenterology practice: Current perspectives and emerging prospects
container-title: Artificial Intelligence in Gastroenterology
c88d70948c68fbb0d9352f97f8df1cd015826f78.abstract: <jats:p>Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly changing the landscape of gastroenterology by improving disease detection, diagnosis, risk stratification, prognostication, and clinical decision-making. Machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, large language models, and multimodal data integration have facilitated the development of accurate diagnostic and predictive algorithms for a wide spectrum of gastrointestinal and hepatopancreatobiliary diseases. In upper gastrointestinal diseases, AI has enhanced the detection and characterization of gastroesophageal reflux disease, Barrett’s esophagus, esophageal cancer, gastric neoplasia, and gastroesophageal varices. The use of AI in capsule endoscopy has facilitated small intestinal mucosal lesion detection and reduced reading time. Computer-aided detection and diagnosis systems have improved adenoma detection and polyp characterization in colorectal diseases, while AI is increasingly being applied to molecular profiling and prognostic modeling in colorectal cancer. In inflammatory bowel disease, AI facilitates more objective endoscopic and histologic assessment, as well as prediction of disease outcome and treatment response. Promising AI-based radiomics, digital pathology, biomarker discovery, and risk prediction models have been emerging in pancreatic, biliary, and liver diseases. Large language models and multimodal AI may further enable integration of heterogeneous information and support personalized decision-making. Computer-aided quality assessment represents an emerging application for standardizing procedural quality in endoscopy. Several AI-assisted platforms have received regulatory approval with ongoing integration into clinical practice. However, limited external validation, population and device-related heterogeneity, dataset bias, interpretability, workflow integration, and uncertain cost-effectiveness remain important barriers to generalizability and clinical adoption. Robust multicenter prospective validation and responsible implementation will be essential to optimize its clinical impact.</jats:p>

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Clinical Practice: How Should Rheumatologists Evaluate and Monitor Emerging Tools?
container-title: Arthritis Care & Research
3f160ed41d422ffb9dd3b8b7e40c689996ef000c.abstract:
<jats:p>Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being used in rheumatology practice, to assist with tasks such as documentation, record summarization, and clinical decision support. Rheumatologists need a practical approach to determining what evidence and oversight each application requires. This narrative review proposes a framework based on two dimensions: contextual complexity and influence on patient care. Greater contextual complexity can make errors harder to detect, whereas greater influence on care increases the potential consequences of an undetected error. We examine evidence for workflow benefits and clinical effectiveness within this framework and consider safety, equity, privacy, governance, and implementation. Existing evidence on the benefits, accuracy, and reliability of AI applications remains mixed. For example, studies of ambient AI scribes suggest reduced documentation burden, but evidence of improved patient outcomes from applications supporting clinical decisions is more limited. For applications with limited clinical influence, evaluation has initially focused on workflow, usability, and documentation quality. Tools that synthesize longitudinal information require additional assessment of completeness and source traceability. Those influencing diagnosis or treatment require prospective evaluation of clinical benefit and safety. Relevant vendor evidence should be assessed alongside proportionate local testing and ongoing monitoring. Safeguards should address risks such as hallucinations, automation bias, and propagating documentation errors, with attention to performance across patient groups. Changes in functionality or clinical use should prompt reassessment. The framework provides a structured basis for adoption decisions and identifies priorities for research on patient outcomes and feasible oversight in routine rheumatology care.</jats:p>

title: Using Artificial Intelligence in Qualitative Lupus Pregnancy Research: The Potential of Large Language Models and Prompting Strategies

49af6cbea7d0a1475e89a3eeb0df446c8b67b9b6.abstract:
<jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Our objective was to evaluate the ability of different large language models (LLMs) to translate and analyze qualitative interviews describing pregnancy experiences among women with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE). An additional objective was to compare themes identified by LLMs with those identified by human researchers.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>We analyzed 26 semistructured interviews originally conducted in Portuguese by Rodrigues et al among women with SLE exploring their perinatal care experiences. Three prompting strategies (zero‐shot, few‐shot, and chain‐of‐thought) were used on the transcripts across four state‐of‐the‐art LLMs (GPT‐4o, OpenAI; Claude Sonnet 4.5, Anthropic; Gemini 2.5 Flash, Google; and DeepSeek R, DeepSeek) to generate key themes. Model outputs were evaluated using an LLM‐as‐a‐judge framework assessing thematic coverage, thematic unity, and semantic similarity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Across models and prompting strategies, LLMs generated similar themes that closely aligned with those identified by human researchers. LLM‐as‐a‐judge evaluations demonstrated high thematic unity and semantic similarity. Claude Sonnet 4.5 showed the most consistent performance. Few‐shot prompting consistently outperformed zero‐shot and chain‐of‐thought approaches.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusion</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>LLMs show promise as supportive tools for analyzing qualitative research by preserving thematic coherence and capturing the complexity of pregnancy experiences in women with SLE. Although zero‐shot prompting is widely used, it produced lower thematic results in our study, whereas few‐shot prompting achieved the most comprehensive and coherent theme extraction. LLM‐assisted qualitative analysis may complement human interpretation and has the potential to support the inclusion of non–English language data and diverse patient perspectives in lupus research.</jats:p>

title: Cognitive correlates of diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space index in amnestic mild cognitive impairment: a preliminary study
container-title: Archives of Clinical Neuropsychology
1e1bf996cda945b0527e40176b2aa62fdc1d4c7d.abstract:
<jats:title>ABSTRACT</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The diffusion tensor imaging analysis along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS) index is an imaging-derived metric related to perivascular water diffusion and has been reported to correlate with global cognitive performance in dementia. However, its associations with specific cognitive functions in mild cognitive impairment (MCI) remain underexplored. This study aimed to characterize the cognitive correlates of the DTI-ALPS index in individuals with amnestic MCI.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Method</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>In this cross-sectional study, 57 participants with amnestic MCI underwent brain magnetic resonance imaging and a neuropsychological assessment battery. Correlations between the DTI-ALPS index and performance across the assessed cognitive measures were examined before and after adjustment for age, sex, education, and Fazekas score.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Prior to adjustment, the DTI-ALPS index showed significant positive correlations with global cognitive measures, episodic memory retrieval, and semantic verbal fluency. After controlling for potential confounders, only the correlations with episodic memory and semantic verbal fluency remained significant.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>The DTI-ALPS index remained significantly associated with episodic memory retrieval and semantic verbal fluency in amnestic MCI after adjustment, suggesting a possible link with frontotemporal network-related cognitive functions. Further studies incorporating multimodal imaging and disease-specific biomarkers are warranted to clarify the biological significance of the DTI-ALPS index and its potential clinical relevance in early cognitive impairment.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: The development and validation of artificial intelligence model to assess the degree of mucosal cleanliness of the upper gastrointestinal tract
container-title: Diseases of the Esophagus
2a8b8c9699d4c9e51424b8b357b53f32e0c286f4.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Mucosal cleanliness of the upper gastrointestinal (UGI) tract is one of the important quality indicators of esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD). The aim of the current study was to create and validate an artificial intelligence (AI)-based system to assess cleanliness during EGD. A total of 520 EGD video samples of the esophagus, stomach, and duodenum were collected between August 2021 and February 2025 at five endoscopic centers and annotated by two endoscopists using the previously validated PEACE scale (from 0—completely obscured, to 3—perfect cleanliness). The dataset was divided into training (332 videos), validation (84 videos), and test (104 videos) datasets. The RegNetY-3.2GF deep learning model architecture was used. The accuracy of videos testing for 12 classes ranges between 90.38% and 100%. The macro recall, precision, F1 score, and Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC) were 0.669, 0.697, 0.668, and 0.684 respectively. The precision, recall, and F1 score ranged between 0.341 and 0.880, 0.303 and 0.885, and 0.321 and 0.883, respectively. For distinguishing between inadequate (scores 0–1) and adequate (scores 2–3) cleanliness, the algorithm achieved a recall of 0.927, precision of 0.864, and a F1 score of 0.895, with a MCC of 0.77. All reported metrics were computed exclusively on the held-out test set. The current AI model demonstrated a high accuracy for both frames and video assessment of mucosal cleanliness along with appropriate identification of the UGI segments. This model allows for real-time use studies to assess this important EGD quality measure.</jats:p>

title: THE REGIONAL SOCIAL ECONOMY SUPPORT SYSTEM AS AN ORGANIZATIONAL FIELD: THE ROLE OF REGIONAL CENTRES FOR SOCIAL POLICY IN COORDINATING ACTORS AND RESOURCES
container-title: Polityka Społeczna
a76299fd84f4bd19b054a3ff384dff66c41f3fd1.abstract: <ns3:p><p class="Abstrakt" style="text-align:justify"><span style="font-size:11pt"><span style="line-height:normal"><span style="font-family:&quot;Arial&quot;,sans-serif"><span lang="EN-AU" style="font-family:&quot;Arial Narrow&quot;,sans-serif">This article examines the regional social economy support system as an organizational field, focusing on the role of Regional Centres for Social Policy (ROPS) in coordinating its actors. The analytical framework combines organizational field theory with a governance perspective, which explains non-hierarchical mechanisms of cooperation and interest alignment, and a systems approach, which captures flows of information and resources between the support system and its environment. The analysis draws on legislation, policy documents, materials concerning the social economy support system in Małopolska, the activities of the Małopolska Social Economy Development Committee, and findings from regional research and evaluations. </span></span></span></span><span style="font-size:11pt"><span style="line-height:normal"><span style="font-family:&quot;Arial&quot;,sans-serif"><span lang="EN-AU" style="font-family:&quot;Arial Narrow&quot;,sans-serif">The findings show that the regional social economy field comprises actors with complementary but unevenly distributed resources, whose interdependence persists despite the formal allocation of responsibilities. ROPS performs a coordinating role without hierarchical authority over other actors, relying primarily on legitimacy, expertise, relationships, and its capacity to facilitate cooperation. Regional social economy development committees can serve as institutionalized arenas of governance, translating actors’ knowledge and interests into regional policy solutions. From a systems perspective, diagnosis, planning, implementation, and feedback are essential to organizational learning and adaptation. </span></span></span></span><span style="font-size:11pt"><span style="line-height:normal"><span style="font-family:&quot;Arial&quot;,sans-serif"><span lang="EN-AU" style="font-family:&quot;Arial Narrow&quot;,sans-serif">The analysis also identifies the dual role of EU funding: while providing essential resources for developing the regional support system, its project-based logic, eligibility rules, and standardized instruments shape actors’ practices and constrain regional adaptive autonomy. Key tensions arise between project-based funding and long-term sustainability, supraregional standardization and regional adaptation, and the social and economic functions of social enterprises, particularly the uneven support provided for their economic activities.</span></span></span></span></p></ns3:p>

title: THE INVOLVEMENT OF SOCIAL ECONOMY ENTITIES IN FAMILY SUPPORT AND FOSTER CARE SERVICES: AN ANALYSIS OF EXISTING DATA AND THREE SELECTED PRACTICES
container-title: Polityka Społeczna
664de8deb3b37d6115820743132767d0d44e71dd.abstract: <ns3:p><p><span style="font-size:12.0pt"><span style="line-height:115%"><span style="font-family:&quot;Arial Narrow&quot;,sans-serif">The article presents available data on the involvement of social economy entities in the provision of family support and foster care services and analyses three purposively selected organisational practices. The study is review-based and analytical in nature and draws on a secondary analysis of data from Statistics Poland (GUS) and the Ministry of Family, Labour and Social Policy (MRPiPS), legal acts, academic literature, institutional reports, and materials concerning the activities of the organisations analysed. The analysis identifies solutions that may potentially contribute to the development of local social services; however, it does not provide sufficient grounds for concluding that social economy entities are more effective than public-sector providers. The main limitations include the purposive and non-representative selection of practices, the substantial reliance on data produced by the organisations implementing these practices, and the lack of comparable data on costs and long-term outcomes.</span></span></span></p></ns3:p>

title: SOCIAL SERVICES IN SOCIAL WELFARE AND THE ROLE OF SOCIAL ECONOMY ORGANISATIONS IN THEIR PROVISION. PRELIMINARY CONCLUSIONS FROM THE AVAILABLE RESEARCH
container-title: Polityka Społeczna
9a5ea8d38a1dfd7a695cb8dd48cd2e188c811931.abstract: <ns3:p><p style="text-indent:0cm; text-align:justify"><span style="font-size:12pt"><span style="line-height:normal"><span style="font-family:&quot;Times New Roman&quot;,serif"><span lang="EN-GB" style="font-family:&quot;Arial Narrow&quot;,sans-serif">The aim of this article is to analyze the forms of community-based social services within the sphere of social assistance, considering the role of Social Economy Entities (PES) and the NGO sector as their potential providers.</span></span></span></span></p><p style="text-align:justify; text-indent:19.85pt"><span style="font-size:12pt"><span style="line-height:normal"><span style="font-family:&quot;Times New Roman&quot;,serif"><span lang="EN-GB" style="font-family:&quot;Arial Narrow&quot;,sans-serif">The first part of the article outlines the possible forms of these social services. The second part is devoted to an analysis of the available data (ministerial reports and statistical data from the Central Statistical Office (GUS) relating to these services. The third part presents the results of a new survey of local authorities on the social services they provide. This survey appears to be one of the first studies on the provision of various types of social services in Polish local authorities.The survey results indicate that in 2025, the most commonly provided services were care services, respite care and personal assistance for people with disabilities (over 84 per cent of the municipalities surveyed). The relatively new neighbourhood support service is provided in 44 per cent of municipalities. Meanwhile, services in the form of training flats and supported housing had a low coverage rate (23 per cent). Social services were more frequently provided in towns with county rights, although in rural municipalities the three most popular forms of support mentioned above had a high coverage rate (80 per cent).</span></span></span></span><span style="font-size:12pt"><span style="line-height:normal"><span style="font-family:&quot;Times New Roman&quot;,serif"><span lang="EN-GB" style="font-family:&quot;Arial Narrow&quot;,sans-serif">The involvement of PES and NGOs depends on both the type of service and the type of municipality: it is particularly evident in addiction treatment, transitional housing and activities for older people, and is weakest in neighbourhood support services. In county-status towns, PES and NGOs are more likely to provide specialist services, whilst in rural areas their involvement focuses primarily on integration activities for older people. Municipalities with a Social Services Programme or an equivalent document were significantly more likely to report providing less common social services and to delegate these more extensively to PES and non-governmental organisations.</span></span></span></span></p></ns3:p>

title: SOCIAL PUBLIC PROCUREMENT AS A STATE POLICY INSTRUMENT STIMULATING THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE SOCIAL ECONOMY IN POLAND
container-title: Polityka Społeczna
eced07cd608ecb274acae3d575d83a4a0082fe05.abstract: <ns3:p><p><span lang="EN" style="font-size:11.0pt"><span style="line-height:115%"><span style="font-family:&quot;Arial Narrow&quot;,sans-serif">Social public procurement (socially responsible public procurement) is an approach that involves taking social considerations into account when awarding public contracts. The European Union has been promoting this approach for over 20 years to support the achievement of various social policy objectives. Social public procurement employs solutions that allow for the consideration of social aspects provided for in EU public procurement law. Such mechanisms have been present in Polish law for nearly 17 years, and the state promotes their use in public procurement. Supporting the development of the social economy is one of the various objectives served by social public procurement. From the perspective of the Polish state, this is the most important goal. Examples of social public procurement in Poland to date have demonstrated its effectiveness in achieving this objective; however, the limited scale of its application remains a challenge. In addition to explaining the concept of social public procurement and the legal mechanisms that allow for the inclusion of social considerations, this article presents information on the current state of its implementation and offers recommendations for promoting its wider use as a tool to support the development of the social economy in Poland.</span></span></span></p></ns3:p>

title: Cognitive-affective functions, neighborhood opportunity, and social functioning in youth with neurofibromatosis type 1
container-title: Journal of Pediatric Psychology
2cb14b067c0eae9b7de70db16716ce2cc29c074b.abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Objective</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>This study evaluated associations between social functioning and cognitive-affective functions (CAF), including executive function, face processing, and theory of mind, and neighborhood opportunity, in youth with neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Methods</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Youth with NF1 (n = 37), ages 8–14 (M = 11.8 years), with no prior autism diagnosis, completed assessments of CAF and peer relationships. Parents completed questionnaires on executive function skills, social impairments, and peer relationships. The Childhood Opportunity Index national composite score quantified neighborhood opportunity. Correlation and hierarchical linear regression analyses evaluated associations between social functioning, CAF, and neighborhood opportunity.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Results</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Executive functioning and neighborhood opportunity were significantly associated with parent reports of social impairments and peer relationships. Executive functioning and facial expression recognition were correlated with self-reported peer relationships, but were not significant in regression models. Facial identity recognition was significantly correlated with social impairments and parent-rated peer relationships. Theory of mind was not associated with any outcome.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>
                  <jats:sec>
                    <jats:title>Conclusions</jats:title>
                    <jats:p>Findings underscore the interplay between CAF, neighborhood opportunity, and social functioning in children with NF1. Case conceptualizations should integrate social determinants of health with measures of cognition and behavior. Longitudinal research is needed to understand mechanisms driving variability in social outcomes and inform equitable care.</jats:p>
                  </jats:sec>

title: Use of Digital Transformation to Create an Inclusive Learning Environment in Tourism by Mediation of Artificial Intelligence in Africa
container-title: Inclusion and Diversity in Business and Tourism Education
17dc2e9d71a5c2404fd74c20991d5e29adb15fed.abstract: <jats:p>Inspecting the connection among digital transformation, artificial intelligence (AI), as well as the synthesis of inclusive environment of learning in the awareness among tourists sector is the article's primary goal. It tackles the issue of how this technological synthesis can augment educational accessibility and participation for a range of scholar demographics. The investigation employs a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative surveys and qualitative interviews to gather data from educators and scholars. Key outcomes demonstrate that digital transformation considerably promotes inclusivity in learning experiences, while AI plays a critical mediating function in personalizing education and catering to expert scholar requirements. In order to incubate more equitable environment of learning s, educational institutions should strategically incorporate digital tools along with artificial intelligence (AI) into their curricula, as per to the outcomes. Future initiatives assimilate comparative investigations across various educational contexts.</jats:p>

title: Accuracy and Efficiency of Articicial Intelligence Tools for Transcription in Qualitative Research
container-title: American Journal of Qualitative Research
3fb554ca1ea2ca5b9deafdc6db775bf91436427f.abstract: <jats:p xml:lang="en"><i>Verbatim transcription in qualitative research is hugely time consuming, yet critical for data validity. The rise in artificial intelligence tools for transcription provides new opportunities for researchers. We assessed the accuracy and efficiency of two widely accessible AI tools and human transcription to provide empirical guidance for researchers.&nbsp; We compared 10 verbatim transcripts generated via three transcription modes: human, Otter.ai and MAXQDA. We compared transcription time, cost, errors (volume and type), and correction time. Results show that the AI tools were highly time/cost efficient but had 2-3 times more errors than human transcription. Accounting for average correction time, AI tools generated a transcript in 1.25 - 2.5 hours for USD31-38 per transcript; thus 3–6 times faster and 3 times cheaper than human transcription. However, human review of AI transcription remains critical for data validity; thus, AI tools can assist in the transcription process versus generating the final product. We develop recommendations for each phase of the research process to maximize the benefits of using AI transcription tools.</i></jats:p>

title: Artificial Intelligence and Digital Health Policy for Reducing Global Health Inequalities
container-title: Innovation, Governance, and Resilience in Global Health Systems
a214df633cac73fcb7c72dbe04bdbf9a60400dd6.abstract: <jats:p>There are still high levels of inequality in healthcare access, quality of services and health outcomes between regions and populations in global health systems. Digital health technologies and Artificial Intelligence have already become the potential solution to close such disparities through better disease surveillance, increasing telemedicine service access, and assist in making health policy decisions based on the data. This chapter explores how AI-powered healthcare applications and digital health platforms can help to enhance healthcare access and health surveillance of populations as well as identify critical issues related to governance, ethical issues, data privacy, and the digital divide. The chapter, based on the conceptual analysis and the recent case studies, outlines the policy strategies that should be in place to ensure the responsible, inclusive, and equitable implementation of AI technologies in the healthcare systems across the world.</jats:p>

title: Digital Health and Artificial Intelligence in Global Health Policy
container-title: Innovation, Governance, and Resilience in Global Health Systems
9d2e274995dd8f32b7735b3232f10a964121b207.abstract: <jats:p>Digital health and artificial intelligence are becoming influential in shaping global health policy due to the opportunities they will offer in improving access, efficiency and health outcomes globally. At the same time, such technologies spark critical issues regarding inequality, ethics, and governance-especially in developing countries in low-income and middle-income countries. This chapter focuses on how digital health and AI are changing the global health systems and just how both these can have a positive effect or a threat towards those who might not have access to usable technology or AI. It examines policy issues concerning governance, regulation, and human rights and the role of international collaboration when working towards equitable and responsible adoption of health technologies using artificial intelligence.</jats:p>

title: Legal Challenges of Artificial Intelligence in Global Health Policy
container-title: Innovation, Governance, and Resilience in Global Health Systems
8e6a4d0442251e27ef2f25a2b827f4e9de5407b2.abstract: <jats:p>This article focuses on the legal challenges arising from the use of artificial intelligence in healthcare from the perspective of global health policy. While the active application of AI at various stages of healthcare demonstrates increasing efficiency, it also increases legal risks and highlights the necessity of an adapted legal framework. The article argues that the integration of artificial intelligence in healthcare is more challenging from a legal perspective than from a technological or ethical point of view, as it actively raises issues such as patient rights, the principle of informed consent, liability, and other related concerns, requiring coherent regulatory standards and coordinated policy responses. The authors propose a human-centered governance model that ensures the best possible balance, protects human rights and minimizes legal challenges arising from AI-related outcomes.</jats:p>
