The approach combines (1) AI models that simulate plunger lift operation and predict flow rates based on operating conditions and controller setpoints, (2) an optimization algorithm that leverages the AI models to maximize production while maintaining stable operation and considering field-specific operational and physics-based constraints, (3) a pre-execution workflow that analyzes current operating conditions to decide if controller setpoint changes are advisable, and (4) a post-execution workflow that evaluates outcomes of recommendations on production and operation. Models are trained per basin and controller configuration using historical well and operating data (production and sensor streams, controller settings, well attributes, plunger design, and fluid properties). The optimizer was deployed in the Eagle Ford and Marcellus across 200 wells. Recommendations were reviewed by production engineers and once implemented, were evaluated through a 13-day post-execution workflow monitoring plunger lift cycles and production response. When negative responses were detected (e.g., liquid loading indicators, non-arrivals, or sustained production decline), the workflow triggered a reversion recommendation to pre-change settings. In total, more than 80% of recommendations were accepted and executed, and less than 18% of executed recommendations were reverted. Across implemented recommendations, post-execution assessment showed uplift of 2% in Marcellus and 2.8% in Eagle Ford relative to the pre-optimization baseline. The multi-field results confirm the broad applicability of the approach across different reservoir types, from dry-gas Marcellus to gas-condensate Eagle Ford, and across diverse plunger designs and controller configurations. Lessons learned emphasize data validation, basin/hardware-specific constraint tuning, structured change management, and governance to rank recommendations by confidence and operational context. The study concludes that AI-driven optimization provides a scalable mechanism to improve performance and shorten optimization cycle time relative to manual tuning. This work presents AI-driven plunger lift optimization that integrates predictive models, physics- and operations-informed constrained optimization, and post-execution evaluation. Novelty includes multi-basin validation (Eagle Ford and Marcellus) and an operational governance framework (human-in-the-loop review, recommendation confidence ranking, and auditable change tracking) that enables safe scaling beyond a single-asset pilot.

title: Less Gas, More Oil: Unlocking Production and Gas Efficiency Through Generative AI-Enabled Gas-Lift Optimization
container-title: ADIPEC
90b9b5893d5263892f672a745fe04829f5a37986.abstract: Abstract Artificial Intelligence (AI) is playing an increasingly pivotal role in transforming production optimization within the oil and gas industry by enabling data-driven and near real time decision-making. In gas-lifted wells, where injection gas is often a constrained and valuable resource, AI provides a robust framework to optimize gas allocation, enhance well performance, and maximize overall asset value. Through the application of advanced analytics and intelligent automation, operators can systematically reduce inefficiencies associated with over-injection, improve well stability, and unlock additional production while preserving gas for export and higher-value use. This paper presents a field-deployed generative AI based application developed to optimize gas lift performance and enhance overall production system efficiency. The approach integrates physics-constrained proxy modeling with engineering constraints to evaluate well performance under varying gas-lift operating conditions. A field-deployed Generative AI-enabled decision-support application was developed to interpret validated optimization outputs and provide engineers with structured recommendations for gas-lift allocation. Optimal gas-injection setpoints are determined by the production proxy and field-wide optimization framework, while the GenAI layer provides engineering rationale, operating context, and implementation guidance. The workflow includes data preprocessing, proxy-model development, continuous validation, optimization, and deployment within daily operations. The system dynamically ranks wells based on responsiveness to gas lift, enabling efficient gas redistribution across the field based on historical trends. Field implementation demonstrated substantial improvements in gas lift efficiency and overall production performance. The AI-driven system effectively reduced total gas lift injection rates while maintaining and in several cases increasing oil production, indicating the elimination of over-injection in multiple wells. Optimized gas allocation enhanced well stability, minimized production cycling, and improved overall operational reliability. In addition, the reduction in gas lift requirements enabled the reallocation of surplus gas volumes to export streams, resulting in increased sales gas and improved asset value. The generative AI-based application facilitated faster, more consistent, and data-driven decision-making compared to conventional manual optimization practices. Notably, gas-lift injection reductions reached approximately 90% in the most significant individual-well case, accompanied by measurable increases in wellhead temperature. This behavior indicates the mitigation of gas circulation effects and more efficient lifting performance, ultimately enhancing oil production with minimal gas lift input and OPEX reduction. Overall, the results confirm that integrating AI-driven analytics with sound engineering judgment can deliver sustainable production gains, improve operational efficiency, and optimize resource utilization across gas lift operations. This paper presents a novel integration of production proxy modeling, field-wide optimization, and Generative AI-assisted engineering decision support, moving beyond standalone predictive or optimization workflows. The field-proven workflow demonstrates scalable deployment, near-real-time usability, and measurable value creation through simultaneous production enhancement and gas conservation, contributing to smarter and more sustainable asset management.

title: Next Generation Autonomous Well Testing: An AI-Powered Platform for Scheduling, Stability Verification, Validation, and Decision Making
container-title: ADIPEC
52499691f0923236ac0bbe76d1f4efb87b49c07f.abstract: Abstract Production well testing in mature conventional carbonate fields poses challenges that extend well beyond those encountered in unconventional shale developments. Multiphase flow behavior, highly variable GOR and water cuts, pronounced reservoir heterogeneity, and ageing surface infrastructure collectively limit the effectiveness of static, rule-based test automation. While earlier work addressed fixed-threshold scheduling and validation for single-phase unconventional wells, a fully adaptive, closed loop context aware data-intelligence-native platform spanning the entire well-test lifecycle in a large, mature conventional field has not previously been reported. This paper presents the field deployment and operational validation of such a platform. The platform is built on an integrated digital architecture that combines data driven machine learning, real-time SCADA ingestion, production-database integration, and physics-informed constraint modelling. It is implemented through five cooperating context aware data intelligent layers. Intelligent Multi-Constraint Scheduling dynamically prioritizes the well-test queue by balancing test-overdue status, production contribution, performance deviation, facility availability, and routing feasibility. Adaptive Stability Determination uses field-trained time-series models to identify valid steady-state windows across multiphase flow regimes, replacing fixed-threshold logic. Multi-Dimensional Data Validation combines dynamic production-envelope modelling, phase-ratio consistency, allocation correlation, data driven anomaly detection, and a Virtual Flow Meter that provides an independent, physics-based verification of measured rates. Contextual Anomaly Classification categorizes detected anomalies into instrumentation drift, testing-facility anomalies, slugging, separator carryover, or genuine production change, thereby reducing false-positive intervention rates. Recommendation-Driven Approval Orchestration presents confidence-scored results recommendations through an integrated dashboard, collapsing the traditional multi-step manual review into a single-screen decision interface. Field deployment delivered measurable operational and production benefits, including a 90% reduction in engineering hours for scheduling and validation, a 20% improvement in first-pass test acceptance, and an 80% reduction in test-to-approval cycle time. The platform enabled an 80% increase in testing volume without additional manpower and was associated with a measured 2% production uplift. Near-real-time approvals and higher-quality validated test data accelerated well-optimization decisions and enabled automated, field-ready production scenarios in place of manual forecasting. This work shifts industry practice from encoding static engineering rules toward AI systems that learn and reason from operational data, enabling improved allocation integrity, reservoir surveillance, and accelerated decision-making at scale.

title: Objective Pre-Shift Cognitive Readiness as a Human Factors Barrier: Field Evidence from Offshore Operations
container-title: ADIPEC
f6494d7a443b791d77efca4dd5e7e864812b1ae9.abstract: Offshore operations depend on reliable performance in safety-critical functions, and the industry's human performance framework treats that performance as shaped by the conditions under which work is done, among them workload, sleep opportunity, rotation design, and supervision (IOGP 2026). When these conditions degrade, the effect reaches the operation as well as the safety record: in the deployments described in this paper, events whose investigations recorded reduced human performance among the contributing factors also carried production cost, in interrupted operations and deferred output. The controls that address these conditions, from fatigue risk management to competence assurance, primarily operate at the level of the schedule and the job category, and do not ordinarily provide a standardized, individual-referenced signal before the shift. In current practice, that space is covered by the supervisor's judgment and the pre-shift conversation. A standardized signal would give that judgment an instrument: an indication of when to offer support, and when to review the day's risk controls before critical work begins. The barrier literature offers a test for what a daily process built around such a signal would need to do. Sklet (2006) describes active safety barriers as realizing a sequence of functions: detect a deviation, decide on a response, and carry the response out. In the barrier models the industry applies across many domains, bowtie analysis among them, degraded human performance appears as one of several escalation factors that can erode the performance of other barriers, together with technical and organizational degradation. The controls that address the contributing conditions are set in advance and calibrated for groups: rosters, hours-of-service limits, training cycles. The growing use of leading indicators in operational safety follows a logic that applies here as well: monitor conditions relevant to barrier performance before the barrier is called on, instead of counting the events it failed to stop (IOGP 2023). A daily, individual-referenced readiness signal has not been routinely integrated with this set of controls, a gap discussed at greater length in the field study that precedes this paper. That field study showed the signal can be produced under routine offshore conditions. Before the shift, each operator in a safety-critical function completes a short cognitive task of under three minutes, delivered as a standardized digital application with the format of a game and the function of an instrument: the result is derived from measured performance on the task, not from a questionnaire. The task is calibrated to each function through an onboard neuroergonomic assessment, the application of neuroscience methods to the study of work (Parasuraman and Wilson 2008), which characterizes the cognitive demands the activity places on whoever performs it. The result is read against the operator's own accumulated baseline together with the cognitive demands of the function, so a deviation records a change in test performance relative to that combined reference, and it enters the day's risk assessment as an individual-referenced input, read much as a wind limit is read before work at height: the value is compared with a reference range, and an out-of-range reading changes how the task is conducted and which controls apply. A green result, within the operator's normal range, requires no further step. A yellow result opens a support conversation between operator and supervisor and activates predefined, graded, non-punitive risk controls, co-designed with the asset team, before critical work begins; the result is not a diagnosis and is not used for appraisal or discipline, and activation is used in this sense throughout the paper. Over a 22-month evaluation at one asset, the program was associated with a sustained reduction in events whose investigations recorded reduced human performance among the contributing factors, and in the production downtime attributed to those events (Baldassim et al. 2026, in press).

title: Numerical Model for Calculating Human-Factor Risk in Well Integrity for HSE Performance Enhancement Using a 5×6 Lifecycle Maturity Matrix
container-title: ADIPEC
fd3e3022d6beea46f3658de6bd70e8cb20a1614b.abstract: Abstract Effective HSE performance requires measurable control of human and organizational risk. Human and organizational weaknesses can progressively erode well barrier reliability, yet they are rarely measured in a structured or auditable manner within well integrity assurance. This paper presents a quantitative human‑reliability framework that converts human‑factor controls into measurable, risk‑informed maturity indices directly applicable to lifecycle well integrity management. The framework integrates five human‑factor control layers—governance, competence, execution, assurance, and learning—across six ISO‑aligned well lifecycle phases: basis of design, design, construction, operations, intervention, and abandonment. The resulting 5×6 lifecycle matrix defines 30 phase–layer control cells, each assessed using a five‑level maturity scale ranging from reactive to resilient, enabling qualitative organizational behaviors to be translated into auditable maturity evidence. To quantify system performance, three indices are introduced: Phase Maturity Index (PMI), Layer Maturity Index (LMI), and Well Integrity System Maturity (WISM). These indices transform ordinal maturity levels into percentage‑based scores using an exponential maturity function with configurable phase and layer weightings. The exponential form increases sensitivity to low‑maturity conditions, where human‑factor weaknesses pose the greatest risk to barrier reliability, while a safety factor (S) represents residual risk consistent with ALARP principles. Across 30 assessment cells and five maturity states, the framework represents approximately 9.3×1020 possible maturity configurations, providing high diagnostic resolution to distinguish localized control weaknesses from system‑level governance and assurance gaps. The configurable weighting structure allows adaptation to different asset types, risk profiles, and regulatory environments while preserving a consistent calculation basis for transparent benchmarking and improvement planning. The proposed model delivers a scalable numerical method for embedding human and organizational controls into lifecycle well integrity governance, assurance prioritization, and continuous improvement. By quantifying human‑factor maturity and linking it directly to assurance focus and decision‑making, the framework supports stronger barrier reliability, risk‑based assurance prioritization, and measurable progression toward resilient well integrity performance.

title: From Passive Video Surveillance to Scalable HSE Intelligence: Field Lessons from AI-CCTV Validation in a Harsh Desert Oil Field
container-title: ADIPEC
1d3a42bec17df281472c9ac2c9a57f24ae75f41d.abstract: Abstract At remote oil and gas facilities, closed-circuit television still relies on a person watching live views and searching stored footage after an event. As camera counts rise, that arrangement misses brief, distant, partly hidden, or visually ambiguous events more easily. This paper examines field validation of an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled closed-circuit television (CCTV) system, referred to here as AI-CCTV, in a large onshore field exposed to intense sunlight, glare, dust, long viewing distances, low-light conditions, sparse infrastructure, and a mix of fixed optical and moving infrared or pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) cameras. The workflow combined secure video ingestion, computer-vision detection, multi-object tracking, context-preserving evidence, structured vision-language assistance, a monitoring interface, and human alarm disposition. Representative scenarios covered personnel presence, personal protective equipment compliance, portable gas-monitor recognition, liquid-like anomalies, falls, selected unsafe behaviors, and restricted-area monitoring. The evidence shows functional feasibility and recurring failure mechanisms, but it does not justify a universal accuracy claim. In many cases, the limiting factor was whether the scene made the target observable, not which model was selected. Small or distant targets required changes to imaging, camera position, tracking, and evidence capture; detector tuning alone rarely solved the problem. Moving cameras required a separate analytical contract for camera state, dwell time, target reacquisition, and return-to-route behavior. Generic models were useful starting points, but field use still required local hard negatives, controlled configuration, shadow-mode testing, and a release process that could be audited. Nuisance alarms were treated as a system cost and managed with temporal persistence, context, semantic checks, risk rules, and human review. These observations are organized into six scale-up gates covering operational value, observability, local evidence, infrastructure, controlled use, and lifecycle ownership. A three-wave rollout and a minimum metric set are also defined. The result is a governed health, safety, and environment (HSE) decision-support service, not an autonomous protection layer.

title: Dispersed Particle Gel (DPG) Application for Conformance Control in High-Temperature, High-Salinity Carbonate Reservoir: Laboratory Validation and Pilot Design
container-title: ADIPEC
de42e23d3f12272b884469e21b7ad6e88b708d71.abstract: Abstract Mature waterflooded carbonate reservoirs commonly exhibit conformance deterioration as injected water preferentially flows through high-permeability streaks, thief zones, natural fractures, vuggy intervals, or strongly connected injector-producer pathways. This flow imbalance accelerates water breakthrough, reduces contacted pore volume, increases produced-water handling requirements, and limits recovery from lower-permeability oil-bearing intervals. Dispersed Particle Gel (DPG), composed of deformable gel particles in the nano- to micro-size range, is evaluated in this study as a profile-modification and mobility-control technology to increase flow resistance selectively in dominant water-conductive paths while maintaining acceptable injectivity. The paper presents an integrated workflow for laboratory qualification, reservoir-simulation assessment, and pilot design of DPG application in a high-temperature, high-salinity carbonate reservoir in the UAE. Candidate selection integrated production and injection performance, high-water-cut behavior, tracer-confirmed injector-producer communication, and remaining-oil potential. The laboratory program included brine and crude-oil compatibility testing, rheological characterization, particle-size-distribution measurement, thermal and salinity stability evaluation, and dynamic core flood experiments performed under representative reservoir pressure, temperature, salinity, and carbonate-rock conditions. Core flood tests were used to quantify injectivity response, resistance factor, residual resistance factor, permeability modification, and treatment selectivity between high- and lower-permeability flow paths. The results showed that the DPG system retained structural integrity under harsh high-temperature/high-salinity conditions, remained compatible with reservoir fluids, and could be injected without unacceptable near-wellbore or formation impairment. Dynamic displacement tests demonstrated preferential water-mobility reduction in high-permeability media and indicated recovery-factor improvement potential of up to 15% because of improved volumetric sweep. Laboratory-derived mobility-control behavior was incorporated into reservoir simulation to evaluate slug placement, injection strategy, pattern-level production response, and sensitivity to permeability contrast and reservoir heterogeneity. Simulation forecasts indicated sustained oil-rate uplift and water-cut reduction after DPG placement, driven primarily by improved areal and vertical sweep efficiency and mitigation of channelized water flow. The proposed pilot consists of two sequential DPG slugs injected through selected injectors, with performance evaluated using injection-rate and pressure trends, producer water-cut response, oil-rate behavior, production logging tool/reservoir saturation tool surveillance, and post-treatment conformance diagnostics. The integrated technical and preliminary economic screening indicates positive project value and supports DPG as a candidate conformance-control option for field validation and potential scale-up in analogous high-temperature, high-salinity waterflooded carbonate reservoirs. The main contribution of this work is a confidentiality-safe, integrated qualification-to-pilot workflow that connects material validation, dynamic displacement behavior, simulation forecasting, and surveillance design for DPG deployment in harsh carbonate waterflood conditions.

title: Integrated Screening and Pilot Design Workflow for Surfactant EOR in an Ultra-Mature Carbonate Reservoir, Sultanate of Oman
container-title: ADIPEC
b28a017b521f0ed01cd5786e67117f757bfa45c7.abstract: Abstract Musallim (MLM) is an ultra-mature Lower Shuaiba (LS) carbonate reservoir in the Sultanate of Oman, developed by long-term waterflood (WF) and now producing at water cut (WC) above 95% with a recovery factor (RF) in the range of 20-25%. Laboratory qualification completed in earlier work established the technical basis for surfactant EOR under representative high-salinity, elevated-temperature carbonate conditions, confirming wettability alteration and interfacial-tension reduction as the active mechanisms. The outstanding challenge was therefore not chemical selection but translation: how to convert a laboratory-proven mechanism into a first field pilot that is technically justified, operationally executable, and interpretable. This paper presents the integrated opportunity-screening and pilot-design workflow developed to make that translation. Screening proceeded hierarchically, from five field areas to reservoir polygons and finally to individual wells, with each stage applying criteria appropriate to its scale. Area 1 and Area 3 were carried forward, and nine of the nineteen polygons evaluated within them were shortlisted on remaining oil potential, reservoir quality, oil-column position, productivity, and dynamic waterflood maturity (DWFM). The distinguishing element of the workflow is the use of hydrocarbon pore volume (PV) injected together with RF at 2PV and 3PV to identify compartments that are sufficiently swept yet underperforming, so that the pilot targets post-WF microscopic displacement inefficiency rather than immature sweep. Well-level screening then combined subsurface potential with operational readiness, reducing 22 operational wells to 12 ranked candidates: four primary Huff & Puff (H&P) wells and eight backups. A four-well H&P configuration was selected as the proof-of-concept mode, not as a full-field (FF) development scheme, because it delivers direct surfactant exposure to the target rock, a controlled soak for wettability alteration and imbibition, execution within existing well and facility constraints, and well-level before-and-after response evaluation. A phased surveillance plan (SP) and a pre-committed response classification are defined in advance so that the pilot outcome is interpretable regardless of direction. The contribution is a repeatable, decision-oriented framework that carries a surfactant EOR opportunity from laboratory evidence through polygon-scale waterflood maturity (WFM) and operational well screening to a defensible pilot design, transferable to other ultra-mature carbonate reservoirs facing the same translation problem.

title: Field-Validated Integrated Cementing Strategy for Multizone Depleted HP/HT Yamama Carbonates: Dual-Plug Liner Sequence, Expandable Liner Hanger Deployment, and Engineered Slurry Design for Reliable Zonal Isolation
container-title: ADIPEC
f7941a6abf28d1242c04349d7d71b9678921b597.abstract: Abstract The Yamama carbonate reservoir in Southeast Iraq, characterized by high-pressure/high-temperature (HP/HT) conditions, multiple productive zones, interzonal depletion, and narrow equivalent circulating density (ECD) windows, presents critical cementing challenges, such as poor cement bond in depleted intervals, fluid migration, and microannulus formation. An integrated cementing strategy is presented, which employed thermally stable engineered slurry systems, a dual-plug liner sequence, and an expandable liner hanger to deliver robust zonal isolation and long-term well integrity throughout heterogeneous pressure regimes. The methodology involved combined laboratory validation, advanced hydraulic models, and precise field execution to help ensure effective cement placement under HP/HT conditions. A specialized fluid-loss control system and engineered spacer minimized filtrate invasion in high-permeability zones, while a tailored slurry design optimized rheology for superior mud displacement. A dual-plug liner sequence helped prevent slurry intermixing. Operational refinements included improved casing centralization, controlled reciprocation, and high-rev/min rotation of the expandable liner hanger system within torque limits, with support from optimized pumping schedules. Post-operation evaluation using cement bond logs (CBLs), variable density logs (VDLs), and top-of-cement (TOC) verification confirmed improved isolation and provided insight for further improvement in depleted carbonate formations. Field implementation in multiple Yamama wells demonstrated measurable and repeatable improvements in cement sheath integrity under combined HP/HT and depletion-driven narrow-margin conditions. The engineered lead slurry effectively bridged the depleted zone, where previous campaigns had recorded poor cement bond, and CBLs/VDLs confirmed improved bond quality in previously problematic intervals. The dual-plug liner system successfully helped prevent slurry intermixing throughout all operations, with consistent bump confirmation that validated plug integrity and displacement efficiency. Expandable liner hanger rotation and reciprocation improved mud removal at the liner top and delivered a reliable metal-to-metal seal, which substantially reduced liner-top leak risk in high-differential-pressure environments. Engineered spacer formulations effectively cleaned the annulus in high-permeability intervals and minimized filtrate invasion and microdebonding. Collectively, these integrated chemical, mechanical, and procedural refinements produced superior zonal isolation compared with legacy well campaigns and established a replicable, field-validated framework applicable to analogous depleted HP/HT carbonate reservoirs. The first field-validated, fully integrated cementing framework purpose-built for HP/HT multizone carbonate reservoirs with interzonal depletion and narrow ECD margins is presented in this work. The novelty lies in the synergistic combination of a zonal-specific dual-slurry design, a dual-plug liner system for contamination prevention, and expandable liner hanger deployment with controlled rotation. This combination delivered consistent improvements in cement bond quality in both depleted and competent zones.

title: Human Thinking Potential: Integrating Western Epistemology and Islamic Perspectives on Reason, Science, and Education
container-title: Journal of Multidisciplinary Science: MIKAILALSYS
0a5605967df8311f6f60d4a47e0157b6b68f2ef1.abstract: This study examines the epistemological foundations of human intellectual potential through the philosophy of science and the Islamic conception of reason. It explores the roles of reason and sensory experience in knowledge construction, the relationship between Western epistemology and the Islamic understanding of ‘aql, and the development of intellectual potential through science and education. A qualitative library research approach was employed to identify, screen, analyze, and synthesize relevant scholarly articles, academic books, and supporting documents. The findings emphasize the complementary roles of rational reflection and empirical observation: reason enables logical analysis and conceptual understanding, while sensory experience provides information about observable phenomena. Rationalism and empiricism are thus presented as distinct but complementary approaches to knowledge. Within the Islamic perspective, ‘aql is understood as a divine gift that enables knowledge acquisition, reflection on nature, and moral discernment. Al-Kindi’s account further frames intellectual development as the actualization of potential reason through learning and knowledge acquisition. The analysis identifies critical inquiry, systematic reasoning, empirical examination, and ethical awareness as integral to scientific development. Education supports these capacities through questioning, argument analysis, independent reasoning, and reflective learning, while connecting intellectual development with moral and spiritual responsibility. The study concludes that human intellectual potential integrates reason, experience, and ethical orientation. It offers a philosophical basis for educational practices that combine critical inquiry with Islamic values to cultivate intellectually independent, reflective, and morally responsible individuals.

title: Physics-Informed AI-Assisted Well Portfolio Management: Integrated Diagnostics to Field-Proven Production Gains
container-title: ADIPEC
9f730b613dc5a138f3c170ded4c96de5f24031d4.abstract: Abstract Managing mature oil and gas assets requires continuous production optimization across large well inventories characterized by multiple reservoirs, diverse completion intervals, varied artificial lift configurations, and dynamic operating conditions. Identifying underperforming wells and prioritizing high- impact interventions remains challenging in such environments, as engineers allocate significant effort to manual data consolidation and surveillance, which limits scalability and delays operational decisionmaking. This paper presents a field deployed Well Portfolio Management (WPM) framework implemented across the mature Greater Hapjan Field of Oil India Limited for 150 wells of which approximately 115 are producing and distributed across 40 reservoirs. The framework integrates structured and unstructured production, operational, and surveillance data within a unified analytics environment and combines conventional reservoir engineering diagnostics with physics-informed artificial intelligence (PI-AI) methods to enable scalable, engineering consistent production optimization. The workflow applies portfolio scale screening followed by diagnostic modules including water breakthrough analysis, decline curve analysis, productivity index evaluation, type-well comparison, gas-lift performance assessment, and production engineering diagnostics. Outputs are consolidated into a ranked, physics-constrained decision-support framework, with recommendations validated through engineering review and reintegrated through a closed-loop mechanism. Across the producing inventory the framework generated over 50 intervention recommendations. Four interventions were implemented during the study period two bean-size optimizations and two isolation repair with selective perforation workovers delivering a combined production increase of approximately 100 m3/d, with analysis-to-decision cycle times reduced from days to hours. In each case the productionlimiting mechanism identified by the framework was confirmed by independent engineering evaluation. The results demonstrate that combining engineering driven surveillance with physics-informed analytics can improve diagnostic consistency, accelerate intervention decision making, and deliver measurable production uplift across large mature well portfolios.

title: Unlocking Liquefaction Capacity and Reducing Energy Intensity in Multi-Train LNG Facilities Through AI-Driven Supervisory Optimization: A Non-Intrusive, Physics-Informed Reinforcement-Learning Framework for Coordinated Train Balancing, Approach-Temperature Optimization, and Boil-Off Gas Management
container-title: ADIPEC
feedcca6cbb8d636632ce1c97ab9e53478fead52.abstract: Abstract Objectives/Scope Multi-train LNG facilities are routinely operated below true liquefaction capacity due to limited observability of internal heat exchanger thermal states, conservative refrigeration margins, and uncoordinated throughput allocation across parallel trains. This paper presents the application of an AI-driven supervisory optimization system to a multi-train LNG facility, with the objective of unlocking latent liquefaction capacity, reducing refrigeration energy intensity per tonne of LNG produced, and minimizing boil-off gas flaring while maintaining full compliance with safety-instrumented systems. Methods, Procedures, Process The system integrates distributed temperature sensing (DTS) deployed along main cryogenic heat exchangers (MCHEs) and propane pre-coolers with distributed acoustic sensing (DAS) installed on refrigeration and BOG compressor piping. DTS-derived spatial profiles quantify heat-transfer effectiveness and fouling progression; DAS-derived acoustic features detect incipient compressor surge and flow instability. These inputs continuously update a hybrid digital twin combining physics-based liquefaction thermodynamics with data- driven surrogate models. A reinforcement learning supervisory optimizer generates bounded operating targets including refrigeration load redistribution across trains, approach temperature adjustments, compressor bias targets, and BOG compression scheduling validated via forward simulation before dispatch to existing APC layer, without modification to safety-instrumented systems. Results, Observations, Conclusions DTS-enabled inference of MCHE fouling and approach temperature margins consistently identifies operating headroom that conventional point instrumentation cannot resolve, enabling trains to operate closer to true thermal constraints with quantified confidence bounds. Refrigeration load redistribution guided by the reinforcement learning optimizer reduces inter-train imbalance and eliminates the conservative margins that previously capped aggregate throughput. Real-time surge margin estimation for refrigeration compressors allows the system to exploit available mechanical capacity without approaching instability thresholds. Across multi-train configurations, coordinated supervisory targets achieve measurable liquefaction capacity uplift, verifiable through production historian data and the system's built-in performance attribution module. BOG compression scheduling reduces unplanned flaring by proactively managing tank inventory against ambient conditions and production ramp trajectories. The supervisory layer deploys non-intrusively above existing DCS and APC applications, confirming feasibility for brownfield LNG assets. Novel/Additive Information This paper presents the first documented integration of spatially distributed fiberoptic sensing with physics-informed hybrid digital twins and reinforcement learning for multi-train LNG supervisory optimization. Unlike prior approaches that optimize individual unit operations in isolation, this framework coordinates full-facility observability and cross-train load allocation within a single non-intrusive system. The built-in performance verification module provides auditable evidence of throughput uplift and energy reduction, advancing the state of knowledge on quantifiable AI value realization in LNG operations.

title: Optimizing Post-Fracturing Milling Operations in Unconventional Wells Through Integrated BHA and Fluid Design
container-title: ADIPEC
68cfec770ff6b225e5db6711c189af15b01e95bf.abstract: Abstract Post-fracturing plug milling is a critical intervention phase in unconventional well completions. As horizontal well lengths increase and the number of fracturing stages and isolation plugs grows, the milling operation can become a significant contributor to completion time and operational exposure. Conventional milling practices, which are often developed from field experience and individual equipment capabilities, may not provide sufficient efficiency when applied to increasingly complex well geometries and higher plug counts. This paper presents a field-based optimization methodology for post-fracturing plug milling operations in unconventional wells. The methodology integrates bottomhole assembly (BHA) torque capacity, motor and mill selection, coiled tubing (CT) string design, fluid-system optimization, and revised operating practices into a single engineering workflow. Performance was benchmarked using six wells executed with the conventional milling methodology and compared with fourteen wells in which the optimized approach was implemented. To provide a consistent comparison across wells with different plug counts and depths, time per plug was selected as the primary performance indicator, supported by milling throughput and depth-normalized performance metrics. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in milling efficiency. Average milling time per plug decreased from approximately 45 minutes under the conventional methodology to approximately 10 minutes using the optimized approach. The improvement was achieved despite an approximately 70% increase in average plug count and approximately 24% increase in well depth. After excluding a well affected by severe nonproductive time, total milling operation time decreased, and depth-normalized analysis further confirmed the improvement.

title: From Raw Downhole Gauge Streams to Optimized Field Production: A Field Pilot of Automated Pressure-Transient Surveillance and Integration with an AI-Assisted Production Optimization Architecture
container-title: ADIPEC
b68313bfb8889147adb4335dd2e5afdf5268a134.abstract: Abstract Pressure-transient analysis (PTA) and rate-transient analysis (RTA) remain high-value but often episodic reservoir-engineering workflows. In a fully instrumented offshore field, continuous permanent downhole gauge (PDHG) streams created an opportunity to move from periodic manual screening toward repeatable, exception-based surveillance. This paper presents a field pilot that automated the processing of high-frequency pressure and associated rate data, detected pressure buildup and falloff candidates, prepared analysis-ready transients, applied engineer-seeded interpretation models, and retained time-stamped results for governed reuse. Three anonymized well examples, comprising two producers and one injector, are used to illustrate data-quality challenges, event-detection settings, engineering validation, and the sensitivity of permeability and skin trends to rate conditioning. For the reviewed examples, the automated workflow identified 14 candidate shut-ins in one producer, with two requiring manual boundary extension; 19 candidates in a second producer, with one rejected after quality review; and four falloffs in an injector, all accepted. These observations demonstrate practical review-by-exception, but they do not establish a field-wide false-positive rate because the source package does not contain a complete event-level acceptance log. An activity-based time model indicates a potential annual saving of 624 engineering hours for 39 wells and two events per well per year, based on a reduction from 8.85 to 0.85 hours per event. This is a modeled benefit, not a before-and-after time study. The workflow is positioned within a broader hybrid production-optimization architecture in which approved interpreted parameters can support model calibration, virtual metering, allocation, reservoir surveillance, and constrained optimization. The paper distinguishes evidence demonstrated by the pilot from forecast benefits that require further field validation.

title: Intelligent Hydraulic Fracturing Design Optimization Using Machine Learning
container-title: ADIPEC
e80cb45aa7afb3ad02346800179e992d1ac4a666.abstract: Abstract This paper presents the development and field application of an AI- and machine-learning-assisted workflow for improving hydraulic fracturing design in unconventional reservoirs. The workflow was developed addressing common challenges such as reservoir heterogeneity, inconsistent stage performance, and operational inefficiencies. Rather than relying only on offset-well analogs or assumption-based time-consuming physics models, the approach combines data-driven optimization with expert-level interpretation to support pre-job design, real time operational decision-making, and post-fracture evaluation. The workflow was applied to multiple gas wells completed in a heterogeneous reservoir. Compared with wells designed using the conventional approach, the AI-ML-assisted designs achieved an average improvement of around 15–20% in initial production rate. The proportion of wells showing sub-optimal flow performance decreased from about 25% to less than 10%. Screen-out incidents were also reduced by around 30%, which was associated with improved prediction of fracture behaviour and better adjustment of pumping schedules. The analysis further identified completion variables that added cost without providing a corresponding production benefit. As a result, excessive proppant usage was reduced by around 12% without negatively affecting well performance. From an operational perspective, the ability to test different scenarios and understand the variables influencing model predictions gave engineers greater confidence when making design decisions. The real field application also highlighted several practical considerations. Continued model retraining was necessary as additional wells were completed and the understanding of different reservoir behaviours. Equally important was the integration of completion and reservoir engineers in selecting meaningful input variables and interpreting model results. The workflow therefore does not replace traditional engineering analysis; rather, it provides an additional quantitative tool for identifying patterns and screening design alternatives, Overall, this work demonstrates a practical and field-tested approach for incorporating AI and machine learning into hydraulic fracturing design. The main contribution is not simply the development of predictive models, but their integration with engineering workflows and optimization methods in a form that can be used during actual completion planning. By combining predictive analytics with prescriptive optimization, the proposed workflow provides a scalable approach for improving production performance, reducing unnecessary completion costs, and lowering operational risk in unconventional reservoir development.

title: Real-Time Hardware-In-The-Loop Data Streaming with Dynamic Fault Injection for Edge AI-Based Prognostics Using Ensemble Machine Learning
container-title: ADIPEC
e168b5a8d2179d3001b1be25669737147f170637.abstract: Abstract This paper proposes an edge AI prognostics system architecture that incorporates real-time sensor signals streaming using hardware-in-the loop. Kalman-filter-based fusion was utilized alongside ensemble machine learning, adaptive drift detection, dynamic fault injection, and explainable AI, all unified in an edge-deployable pipeline. Multiple sensor signals attached to a turbofan engine using the NASA C-MAPSS FD001 dataset were imported, modeled, and normalized in an HIL real-time simulator to be streamed as 0-3.3 V. A customized analog-to-digital conversion board was built and fabricated to ingest fourteen analog sensor signals. The ADC board comprised four 16-bit ADS1115 converters which were interfaced over I2C with the Edge AI device in use. Three fault injection scenarios were imposed on the sensor signals, a drift on the pressure channel Ps30 modelled as a ramp, a bias on the core speed Nc modelled as a step, and precision degradation on the temperature T50 modelled as gaussian noise. The magnitudes of said faults were sized as multiples of the healthy-stream standard deviation. Causal Kalman filtering and principal-component fusion fed a 30-feature causal representation to a weighted Random Forest XGBoost ensemble, which was selected with engine-grouped cross-validation. Online deviation alarms were generated by an adaptive EWMA innovation monitor, and offline attribution was provided by SHAP. A terminal RMSE of 12.15 cycles was achieved by the ensemble, the MAE was 9.01 cycles, the R2 was 0.914, and the NASA score was 180.46 over the 100 test engines, which is a result that qualifies competitive with deep-learning benchmarks with proven lower computational cost. The largest remaining-useful-life displacement of 16.5 cycles was produced by the abrupt Nc step, and was detected at onset, while smaller displacements and delayed alarms resulted from gradual and stochastic faults, which led to the quantification of the trade-off between detection sensitivity and noise rejection. The 16-bit ADC emulation led to an increase in the RMSE by 0.13 cycles and preserved all alarm cycles. The proposed framework enables systematic validation of edge prognostic models against escalating fault conditions without dataset modification, which provides a practical foundation for deployment on live test rigs.

title: Industrializing Drilling Geomatics Using UAV and AI Technologies to Enhance HSE and Operational Excellence
container-title: ADIPEC
ca1debef505ba51ecb1da031407cf124d36081b7.abstract: Abstract Drilling geomatics is a critical enabler of safe and efficient well delivery, supporting location planning, site verification, topographic mapping, safety-buffer mapping, rig positioning and route assessment. This paper presents an integrated UAV- enabled framework developed through two progressive trials in different operating areas. Trial 1 was a feasibility and scouting campaign covering 25 km2 and 45 planned drilling locations. Trial 2 was an operational scale-up covering 56.2 km2 and supporting 9 drilling pads and 20 planned drilling locations. The workflow combined high-resolution photogrammetry, LiDAR, RTK/PPK positioning, terrain modelling, Rig-3D verification, virtual site review and AI-assisted feature extraction. Trial 2 achieved Ortho mosaic horizontal RMSE of 0.038 m and DTM vertical RMSE of 0.034 m. Comparison with 7,311 RTK observations showed that 99.97% of DTM differences were below 1 m. Across 45 planned locations, 250 m survey acquisition decreased by 83.3%, while pad-level acquisition decreased by 87.5%. AI development progressed from U-Net pixel classification to dedicated YOLO segmentation, with the strongest later model achieving 88% precision, 85% recall and 86% F1. Preliminary cut-and-fill outputs remain under verification. A 2026 study forecast 31.36% potential substitution of conventional field tasks; this is not an implemented result. The two-trial progression demonstrates a governed pathway from feasibility to scalable, HSE-led operational deployment.

title: AI-Enabled ROP Optimization for a Middle East Offshore Operator: Field Validation of Drilling Real-Time Advisory Workflow
container-title: ADIPEC
12d436dbc79fa533ea3b2969fd99c8f3d7956f59.abstract: Abstract This paper presents the offshore field validation of a real-time, machine learning (ML)-based rate of penetration (ROP) optimization workflow deployed for offshore drilling operations in the Middle East. The objective was to evaluate whether an operator-trained ML model, constrained by drilling limits and executed through a centralized real-time drilling advisory workflow, can deliver measurable on-bottom performance improvement under live operating conditions. The work represents the offshore field-validation stage of a multi-year predictive drilling development program, building on earlier publications spanning ML-based ROP prediction. Two operator-specific predictive models were trained on high- and low-frequency drilling data from historical offshore wells and hosted in an in-country cloud environment to comply with data residency requirements. Model readiness was validated during a proof-of-concept (PoC) phase against a predefined accuracy criterion, including a blind test, before field deployment. During the pilot, optimization recommendations were constrained by formation-specific and downhole toolspecific operating limits, and were delivered in advisory mode through a centralized remote support workflow, with recommendation adherence tracked stand by stand. Five wells comprising ten hole sections were drilled in advisory mode using three rigs across two offshore fields. The workflow delivered a 19% cumulative on-bottom ROP improvement relative to the operator's top-quartile (P75) benchmark, more than 77 hours of on-bottom drilling time savings, and approximately USD 0.58 million in realized value. Section-level analysis demonstrated a generally positive relationship between adherence to recommended setpoints and achieved ROP uplift, indicating that performance gains were primarily driven by disciplined execution within the valid operating envelope rather than advisory visibility alone. Field execution highlighted several factors that bounded optimization effectiveness, including strict trajectory control, anti-collision management, and torque and vibration constraints, which required the selective acceptance of recommendations. The results demonstrate that when predictive models are integrated with dysfunction filtering and governed by disciplined execution practices, ML-generated setpoints can be safely and effectively implemented in live offshore environments. These findings validate a practical method for converting predictive capability into quantifiable performance gains and underpins a controlled scale-up toward future closed-loop drilling systems.

title: AI-Enabled Competency Development for Rig Technicians – A New Model for Workforce Transformation
container-title: ADIPEC
1a7f0d7937ce8ca74ae48a353d1cf02856d1a432.abstract: Abstract Objectives/Scope Digitalization on both land rigs and offshore jack-ups has introduced new layers of complexity into electrical, control, and mechanical systems. Many technicians still struggle with basic digital tasks—such as accessing PLCs, interpreting controller alarms, or troubleshooting VFD faults—despite prior training. This paper presents an AI-enabled competency development model designed to accelerate technician learning, improve diagnostic consistency, and strengthen structured troubleshooting behavior across mixed-fleet drilling operations. Methods, Procedures, Process The model combines hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) and software-in-the-loop (SIL) simulators, scenario-based simulations, and a rule-based troubleshooting assistant. Competency gaps were identified through technician interactions with simulated rig systems, including real failure modes such as SCR misfiring, VFD overheating, and PLC interlock faults. Adaptive learning concepts were incorporated to outline how future modules may tailor training based on technician behavior. Field observations from actual rig support—such as hesitation to access PLC logic or reliance on intuition instead of diagnostic tools—were integrated to ensure realism and relevance. Results, Observations, Conclusions Technicians trained within the simulator-based environment demonstrated measurable improvements, including a 35% increase in troubleshooting accuracy and a 40% reduction in diagnostic time. Simulation results indicate potential for more consistent diagnostic behavior, improved alarm interpretation, and reduced reliance on senior personnel. These improvements were achieved without live-rig deployment and therefore represent expected performance gains under controlled validation conditions. Novel/Additive Information This work introduces a competency development ecosystem built specifically for rig technicians, integrating HIL/SIL simulators, structured diagnostic workflows, and real failure data into a scalable training model. The approach addresses longstanding gaps in conventional training—particularly the lack of realistic digital scenarios—and provides a practical pathway for modernizing technician development in increasingly digitalized rig environments.

title: Decision-Centric Energy Operations: Integrating Edge Intelligence, Operational Digital Twins, Industrial Work Surfaces, and Agentic AI
container-title: ADIPEC
1af45810d093a029724673a2f2c636ee47c2794e.abstract: Abstract Energy operators are not short of data. Most assets already have sensors, historians, supervisory systems, engineering tools, dashboards, digital twins, and a growing number of AI pilots. The harder problem starts after an event is detected. Engineers still have to bring together operating trends, work history, procedures, constraints, and approval requirements from several systems before they can make a safe decision. This paper proposes a decision-centric operating architecture that connects edge intelligence, an operational digital twin, an industrial work surface, and agentic AI within a human-in-the- loop model. The layers are intentionally separated. Edge intelligence qualifies events near the asset. The digital twin adds asset context, operating state, constraints, and history. The work surface places the case into investigation, approval, and execution workflows. Agentic AI supports the engineer by retrieving evidence, invoking approved tools, checking rules, and preparing an explainable recommendation. The pattern is intended for workflow-level deployment rather than unconstrained automation. A representative implementation pattern shows how a qualified trigger initiates context retrieval from live data, engineering documents, maintenance history, procedures, prior events, and constraint models. The agent prepares a recommendation package that exposes evidence, assumptions, alternatives, constraint checks, confidence levels, and required human approval before action. The contribution is a practical reference pattern for moving from data visibility to decision execution. The paper emphasizes bounded AI use, evidence traceability, workflow ownership, auditability, and human authority. It does not argue for transferring accountability to autonomous systems. Instead, it shows how AI can reduce investigation effort, improve decision consistency, and give engineers and operators a clearer basis for action.

title: Transforming Incident Investigations Through Causal Reasoning and Human Factor Implementation
container-title: ADIPEC
76d30454ec674552167007f54005302adbedb60e.abstract: Abstract This paper presents Petroleum Development Oman's (PDO) innovative transformation of its incident investigation process, shifting from a compliance driven, reactive model to a systems-thinking, learning-oriented framework. The scope includes redesigning investigation workflows to adopt causal reasoning, embedding reflective learnings, standardizing human error classification, and deploying AI-enabled tools to enhance accountability, reduce manhours, and increase the strategic value of investigations. The initiative aligns with PDO's internal HSE policies and SPE's emphasis on safety culture and operational excellence The redesign followed a structured, evidence-based approach: literature review, benchmarking against global best practices, and one to one stakeholder interviews across PDO's operations (further details in section 2.1). A twotiered investigation model (Standard vs. Detailed) was developed with clear classification criteria, RASCI (Responsible, Accountable, Supportive, Consulted, and Informed) accountability matrices, and escalation paths to for high impact events. The process was piloted across 54 operational units, refined through iterative feedback, and integrated with a corporate dashboard and AI tool for real-time tracking, classification, and action logging. Code 10 (uncontrolled release from subsurface equipment) integrity investigation framework was introduced for the first time, and embedding Human Factor specialist into the investigation workflow to deepen root cause analysis The redesigned process delivered measurable improvements: 63% reduction in investigation manhours, 30% detailed vs. 70% standard investigations to optimize resource allocation, and stronger line ownership through clear accountability structures. The AI tool enabled faster classification (reducing delays more than 63%) and improved compliance via the corporate dashboard. Repeat incidents dropped significantly, and the first-ever Code 10 integrity investigations were successfully implemented. Human error classification was standardized across PDO, enhancing consistency and learning. The process also drove a cultural shift investigations are now viewed as strategic learning opportunities rather than administrative tasks. Key outcomes include improved prevention of recurrence, higher quality corrective actions, and stronger integration of HSE into operational decision making. This paper introduces a scalable, systems-thinking framework for incident investigations in upstream oil and gas, combining behavioral science, process redesign, and AI, that moves beyond traditional root cause analysis. It offers a replicable model for other operators seeking to transform investigations from administrative tasks into strategic learning engines. The integration of Human factor specialists, Code 10 investigations, and AI-enabled classification represents a novel approach not widely documented. The paper contributes to the state of knowledge by demonstrating how cultural, procedural, and technological levers can be aligned to drive sustainable safety improvement in complex operational environments

title: Beyond Threshold Alarms: A Multimodal On-Premises AI Framework for Intelligent Fault Detection and Guided Maintenance of Industrial Pump Set
container-title: ADIPEC
e389a98b3e9d8022ef3e109255dd5122aa363760.abstract: Abstract Equipment breakdowns in the oil and gas (O&G) industry are costly and disruptive, both financially and operationally. Predictive maintenance powered by artificial intelligence (AI) can help prevent these breakdowns, but most AI solutions rely on the cloud — which is often impractical at O&G sites because of data security requirements and unreliable connectivity. This paper presents an on-premises, multimodal AI framework for predictive maintenance that keeps the field engineer at the center of the process, rather than replacing them. The framework combines three AI capabilities that work together to support the people doing the actual repair work. A lightweight LSTM model continuously watches sensor data — vibration, temperature, pressure, and power — to catch early signs of trouble. A YOLO-based vision model watches live camera feeds to spot visible problems such as seal leakage, misalignment, and wear. When either model flags something unusual, the two models are combined in a fusion layer to produce a more confident diagnosis. That diagnosis is then handed to a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) chatbot, running on a small language model hosted entirely on site. Rather than sending a static alert, the chatbot has a conversation with the field engineer — asking clarifying questions to narrow down the likely cause, as an experienced colleague would, and drawing its answers from historical maintenance records and OEM manuals rather than guessing. Once the cause is identified, an augmented reality (AR) interface walks the engineer through the repair step by step, right at the equipment. Because everything runs on-premises, the framework continues to work even when connectivity is unreliable and keeps sensitive operational data on site rather than sending it to the cloud. The human-in-the-loop design is central to this: AI does not make the call on its own — it gives the field engineer earlier warning, a second set of eyes on visible defects, and an expert-like assistant to think through the problem before acting. This paper describes the architecture, presents field observations from an initial deployment, and discusses how the approach reduces unplanned downtime while staying practical for the connectivity and security constraints typical of O&G field sites.

title: Overcoming Microfracture Testing Limitations in High-Strength Carbonate Reservoirs Using Enhanced Design Microfracture Tool. A Mature Offshore Oilfield
container-title: ADIPEC
fd8684c136b6c1ccd5a035071b8aaf9d1ee201d3.abstract: Abstract This paper presents a field application of a high-strength straddle packer for microfracture testing in ultra-high-strength carbonate reservoirs within a mature offshore field. The study demonstrates how enhanced pressure-capability microfracture technology can overcome historical limitations associated with high rock strength, large borehole diameters, elevated mud weights, and high well inclinations, which have traditionally restricted reliable in-situ stress measurement and reduced confidence in geomechanical models used for field development planning. An integrated well planning approach was developed to incorporate a pilot hole within a long-reach horizontal development well located in a crestal area affected by severe losses and free-gas migration. This strategy eliminated the need for a dedicated appraisal well but introduced additional operational complexity. Key challenges included the limited pressure capacity of conventional microfracture tools in large-diameter boreholes, differential sticking risks during prolonged stationary periods, and an expanded data-acquisition program involving reservoir sampling and extended testing across multiple pressure regimes. To address these challenges, a high-strength straddle packer specifically engineered for high-pressure microfracture applications was deployed. The operation was executed successfully with zero non-productive time despite the challenging well architecture and reservoir conditions. All planned test intervals were fractured as designed, demonstrating reliable fracture initiation in formations previously considered unsuitable for microfracture testing. Measured breakdown pressures closely matched pre-job geomechanical model predictions, providing validation of the modelling workflow. Injection pressures reached approximately 7,400 psi above hydrostatic pressure, confirming the enhanced pressure capability and mechanical integrity of the high-strength straddle packer under extreme operating conditions. The results demonstrate that conventional microfracture systems may be constrained in ultra-high-strength carbonate reservoirs where large borehole diameters, high mud weights, and elevated well inclinations are required. The successful deployment of high-strength microfracture technology enabled accurate and repeatable in-situ stress measurements, improving confidence in geomechanical model calibration, wellbore stability assessments, and fracture design. These outcomes support more informed field development decisions in complex offshore reservoirs. This study provides one of the first documented offshore applications of high-pressure microfracture testing enabled by a next-generation high-strength straddle packer. It introduces a practical and repeatable workflow that integrates complex well architecture, elevated pressure requirements, and advanced microfracture technology to achieve reliable in-situ stress characterization in reservoirs previously considered unsuitable for microfracture testing, contributing valuable insights to both geomechanics and offshore well planning practices.

title: Innovative Design and Application Research of Gas-Tight Threads for Large-Diameter, Thick-Wall Casing in 10,000-Meter-Deep Wells
container-title: ADIPEC
a386fc24db1d2c51b91c1730ffa4e0fd942d0cab.abstract: Abstract With the continuous deepening of oil and gas exploration, 10,000-meter-deep wells are becoming increasingly common. To facilitate downhole operations in such ultra-deep wells, both intermediate and production casings now employ large-diameter, high-grade, thick-wall casings. However, these casings introduce new challenges for thread connections, including misalignment during make-up, severe galling leading to downhole casing string disconnection, and high-temperature (260°C) thread sealing failures that result in annular pressure buildup. These issues critically threaten the safe operation of 10,000-meter-deep wells. This study focuses on the development of a high-performance, regular coupling-type gas-tight thread for 125TS-grade technical casings (OD 365.12 mm, wall thickness 13.88mm) deployed in two 10,000-meter-deep wells drilled by China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC). Field investigations of gas-tight thread failures in large-diameter casings revealed that the significant weight and length of the casings cause tilting and oscillation during wellhead make-up, hindering vertical alignment between the external and coupling internal threads. This misalignment induces severe compressive deformation of thread guiding surfaces. Logging data indicated a 5–8 mm gap between the casing external thread end and the coupling shoulder, confirming inadequate make-up as the root cause of disconnection and sealing failure. Structural analysis of failed threads, characterized by a 1:16 taper and crest/root parallelism to the pitch diameter, demonstrated that the API Spec 5B buttress thread form is unsuitable for thick-wall casings with a 365.12 mm OD. Building on failure mechanism analysis, this research proposes an innovative gas-tight thread design methodology: (1) A thread profile integrating alignment guidance, anti-impact protection, and self-correcting make-up capabilities to prevent misalignment; (2) Load-bearing surfaces, guiding surfaces, and sealing surfaces optimized for anti-galling under over-torque conditions. Finite element analysis (FEA) was employed to optimize thread height, full thread count, and sealing interference based on structural and sealing integrity requirements under a 260°C combined load envelope (VME90%). Full-scale physical testing under extreme tolerances verified that the new design doubles galling torque resistance compared to field-used threads while maintaining VME90% structural and sealing integrity at 260°C. Field applications achieved a 100% first-attempt make-up success rate, with shoulder torque stabilized within 23–64% of the total make-up torque, resulting in zero disconnections or sealing leaks in the one 10,000-meter wells. The novel thread profile significantly enhances alignment accuracy and galling resistance. During deployment in ultra-deep wells, wellhead make-up torque curves for large-diameter casing threads exhibited clarity and consistency, with stable shoulder torque. Optimized sealing structures improved galling resistance, damage tolerance, and high-temperature sealing integrity. Successful field applications validated the superior performance of the new gas-tight threads for large-diameter, thick-wall casings in 10,000-meter environments. This study establishes an innovative design methodology for large-diameter, thick-wall casings, yielding a high-performance gas-tight thread tailored for ultra-deep wells. The design demonstrates exceptional wellhead operability and adaptability to downhole ultra-high-temperature conditions.

title: Human-Centered AI for Maritime Safety Culture
container-title: ADIPEC
4bcbca2cab61dcf5835afa9e6e57371edbb208c9.abstract: Abstract This paper examines how human-centered artificial intelligence (AI) can strengthen maritime safety culture in offshore vessel operations supporting the petroleum industry. The scope is operational and integrates crew-generated health, safety, and environment (HSE) observations, unsafe acts and unsafe conditions, corrective actions, training completion, safety quizzes, vessel activities, inspection findings, and recurring risk themes within a digital safety-intelligence framework. The objective is to convert frontline reporting into timely preventive decision support without increasing reporting burden or replacing professional judgment. The study applies an operations-focused retrospective workflow analysis to anonymized maritime HSE records. Reports originally categorized as unsafe acts or unsafe conditions were reviewed to determine whether the assigned classification accurately reflected the observed behavior, workplace condition, event type, available evidence, and appropriate response pathway. AI-assisted functions were mapped across the workflow, including narrative structuring, category recommendation, identification of similar reports, recurrence analysis, correlation of tasks, behaviors, conditions and potential consequences, corrective-action review, targeted training recommendations, quiz generation, AI-supported safety podcasts, and preventive alerting. All consequential outputs remained subject to competent human review and approval. The analysis showed that original reporting labels do not always represent the underlying safety issue. Some reports classified as unsafe behavior were more appropriately treated as equipment, environmental, housekeeping, or access-related conditions. Other reports combined both behavioral and physical factors, required incident or near-miss investigation, lacked sufficient information, or belonged outside a behavior-based safety workflow. These findings demonstrate that safety interventions should be selected only after the report has been interpreted in its operational context. The framework also demonstrates how validated reports and recurring risk themes can be converted into task-specific learning content, including microlearning, toolbox-talk material, scenario-based quizzes, and AI-generated safety podcasts. Connecting reporting, classification, corrective action, learning, feedback, and recurrence monitoring creates a closed safety-learning loop and helps reduce the likelihood that repeated unsafe acts or conditions develop into more serious incidents. The paper concludes that human-centered AI can help offshore marine operators move from isolated and reactive record handling toward earlier recognition of recurring risks and more focused preventive action. The technology can support seafarers, vessel managers, and shore-based HSE teams by making frontline information easier to interpret and connect with corrective actions, inspections, operational exposure, and targeted learning. It should not assign blame, determine disciplinary outcomes, establish root cause autonomously, or replace the authority of competent maritime professionals.

title: Redefining CBM Hydraulic Fracturing: Innovative Evolution of Fracturing Treatment Design Delivering Transformative Production Uplift in the Raniganj Block, India
container-title: ADIPEC
382c5948a522b88e0ef058908f88fa866b613f20.abstract: Abstract This paper presents progressive hydraulic fracturing treatment designs implemented in the Raniganj CBM block to enhance sustainable production. The study traces the development of fracturing strategies in CBM with respect to advanced fluid formulations and tailored proppant placement techniques, highlighting how real-time diagnostics revolutionize traditional CBM stimulation approaches. By challenging thumb-rule based placement methodologies, these designs demonstrate significant improvements in fracture conductivity, sand placement efficiency, and long-term production performance by achieving effective reservoir drainage. The study employed a systematic methodology beginning with the forensic classification of historical fracturing data of prolific seams vulnerable to premature screen-outs based on characteristic signatures and formation response patterns. In pursuit to optimise fluid-reservoir compatibility and improving fluid placement and recovery, we implemented fluid systems specifically engineered for target coal seam properties – including combination fluid systems incorporating HVFRs to achieve desired viscosity while preventing residue damage, complemented by real-time analytics to optimize pumping rates and proppant type and concentration on a per-stage basis. Each treatment was preceded by DFIT, SRT, and multi-rate shutdown analyses to calibrate treatment design. Simulator inputs derived from these diagnostics informed conductivity optimization, while post-treatment analysis combined with quantified performance improvements and production data - progressively enabled increased proppant placements in subsequent stages, from 4,000 lb/ft to 20,000 lb/ft. The improved treatment designs yielded significant results, challenging long-established CBM fracturing conventions. Key performance indicators demonstrated marked improvements: proppant placement efficiency increased by 100% for deeper wells; screen-out incidents were less than 1% while maintaining operational efficiency. Post-job simulation modelling confirmed longer effective fracture half-lengths and improved conductivity compared to traditional treatment designs. The modified fluid rheology profiles, customized proppant selection criteria, and optimized pumping schedules demonstrated exceptional correlation between predicted and observed production enhancements. Wells completed with these advanced designs exhibited significantly higher initial production rates and substantially flatter decline curves, with a significant production increase compared to offset wells using traditional methods in deeper well categories. Economic analysis confirmed that the initial 15-20% higher completion costs were fully recovered within 4-6 months through accelerated production and enhanced sustainability. This work improves upon the existing methodologies of CBM fracturing by broadening the scope of innovation potential within the industry. By demonstrating that sophisticated fluid systems and strategic distribution of proppant placement yield exceptional economic returns, we establish a new framework for CBM stimulation design. These results validate that CBM fracturing design paradigms can be meaningfully improved through rigorous engineering approaches that integrate diagnostics, simulation, and field implementation within an iterative optimization process.

title: Integrated Hydraulic Fracturing and Reservoir Simulation to Optimize Multi-Stage Stimulation Design in a Layered Tight Gas Reservoir
container-title: ADIPEC
068138d401daed960271a1ab91175515a396b17d.abstract: Abstract Layered low-permeability gas reservoirs, particularly those comprising thin, vertically heterogeneous limestone stringers separated by interbedded shale layers, can suffer from poor fracture connectivity and low recovery under natural depletion. This study evaluates the optimization of hydraulic fracture design parameters, including stage count, perforation intervals, and stage positioning to maximize fracture effectiveness and recovery from the reservoir in Well B. The objective was to identify the optimal stimulation strategy using fully coupled fracture‑reservoir modeling that explicitly captures vertical heterogeneity and the resulting impact on stage‑wise productivity. Post-stimulation evaluation of the first stage of Well B was reasonably consistent with model predictions. Insights from this stage were used to refine the design of subsequent stages. A fully coupled hydraulic fracture and reservoir simulation workflow was applied using a model calibrated to Well A, which had previously been hydraulically fractured. Calibration incorporated fracture treating pressure, instantaneous shut-in pressure (ISIP), fracture height estimates from temperature logging, well test production data, and fracture conductivity inferred from well test analysis. Reservoir heterogeneity was captured using a detailed layer‑cake model, with limestone lobes and ultra‑tight stringers discretized separately and assigned representative porosity, net-to-gross, saturation, and permeability ranges. Using this calibrated framework, multiple stimulation scenarios for Well B were evaluated, including stage count, perforation placement, permeability contrast, and the impact of fracture interaction between closely spaced stages. The calibrated model and offset field data indicate that without hydraulic fracturing or other stimulation methods such as matrix acidization, the wells exhibit limited deliverability, which is expected to result in low recovery across the completed intervals. Simulation results indicate that the optimized four-stage design could increase cumulative production to 3.5 times that of the unstimulated case. The simulations identified hydraulic fracture stage count and placement as important design parameters, followed by injection rates. For instance, the model predicts that increasing the stage count from three to four would increase cumulative gas production by 30%, reflecting improved modeled reservoir coverage and fracture connectivity. Sector-scale simulations predicted that a four-stage fracture design could increase the average recovery factor from ~4% in the no-fracture base case to ~15% with fracturing over a five-year production period. The production allocation model demonstrates that a limited number of limestone lobes dominate flow, contributing 75–80% of total gas in both fractured and unfractured cases, with substantially higher absolute recovery predicted following stimulation. In terms of subsurface uncertainty, sensitivity results showed that permeability variation has the largest effect on well performance. Proppant embedment and fracture conductivity reduction with time have secondary but measurable impacts. Stage-1 stimulation in Well B demonstrated improved productivity relative to pre-stimulation flow tests and provided valuable calibration data for subsequent stages. However, validation of the overall four-stage stimulation design remains ongoing.
