title: Generative AI Misuse and Rule Compliance Among University Students in Bhutan: Implications for Assessment and Institutional AI Policy
container-title: Journal of Education and Learning Reviews
803b74b5cc2e0e79e1abc6b3b1070e03ff677b5b.abstract: Background and Aim: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) use is expanding in Bhutanese universities while institutional policies remain under development. Guided by an extended Theory of Planned Behavior, this study examined factors associated with unauthorized AI use and intention to comply with institutional AI policies. Materials and Methods: An anonymous, cross-sectional survey was conducted in June 2026 among a convenience sample of 713 Bhutanese university students. Seven-point Likert-type responses were analyzed using factor analyses, reliability assessments, correlations with false discovery rate correction, multiple and moderated regression, and bootstrapped indirect association tests. Robustness checks included robust standard errors and demographic controls. Results: The models explained 24.5% of variance in AI misuse and 19.6% in compliance intention. Approximately 29% of respondents endorsed at least one misuse item. Misuse was associated with misuse acceptability, AI familiarity, academic pressure, moral rationalization, rule clarity, subjective norms, and learning impact. Compliance intention was associated with subjective norms, rule clarity, behavioral control, productive AI use, institutional enforcement, and moral rationalization. Institutional enforcement showed a small independent association with compliance intention (β = .086). Compliance intention was inversely associated with misuse (B = −0.10, p = .004). All six indirect associations were small, with bootstrap confidence intervals excluding zero. Demographic adjustment preserved findings; academic level showed no significant moderation. Conclusion: Findings support evaluating assignment-specific AI guidance, coordinated workloads, classroom discussion of misuse rationalizations, and communicated institutional policies. Cross-sectional data preclude causal inference, and convenience sampling limits generalizability. These associations provide a basis for evaluating approaches to responsible AI governance.

title: Operating regimes of quarter-turn-aware frontier-based coverage path planning
container-title: Frontiers in Robotics and AI
7840491ba039ccd1b052fae108ae8047dcb4116c.abstract: Introduction The practical question in turn-aware coverage planning is when reduced angular travel compensates for extra distance and overlap. Methods We study that question with TURN-F, a deliberately simple deterministic frontier planner that searches cell–heading states and charges angular travel in 90 ° units. Its normalized motion-cost index is J β = L + β Q , where L is path length, Q is the number of quarter turns, and β exposes grid pitch, platform speed, and a rotation-to-translation power ratio; it is not measured battery energy. The main evaluation combines 178 public layouts, 4 distance-only baselines, and 2 heuristic turn-aware comparators re-planned at every β . Results At β = 1 , TURN-F reduces quarter turns by 21.2% relative to GREEDY but travels 6.1% farther and increases overlap from 0.154 to 0.192, yielding a small 1.25% mean advantage (108 wins in 178 grids) that the rank-based post hoc test does not separate. A β = 0 same-code control provides no detectable evidence that state representation or tie-breaking explains that advantage ( + 0.18 % in J 1 , 95% CI [ − 0.22 , 0.56 ] % , p = 0.20 ). The corpus-mean crossing is β * = 0.82 (grid-bootstrap 95% interval 0.74–0.89). For β > 0 , an exploratory geometry-conditioned model improves grouped-CV prediction over a β -only model, but leave-one-family-out validation fails on HouseExpo, and calibration varies by family. On 20 seeded-random non-overlapping windows from five real-robot laser logs, TURN-F is 3.21% lower at β = 1 (17 wins); the five-source test is statistically inconclusive ( p = 0.0625 ) . The result remains TURN-F-favoring for boundary-rich, low-boundary, all-candidate, and 2,000 repeated random selections. Under a rest-to-rest acceleration model, predicted completion time is 4.5%–9.7% lower, but no controller execution or energy measurement was performed. Discussion The contribution is therefore a reproducible analysis of a turn–travel trade-off and its limitations, not a universal planner ranking or a hardware-validated energy claim.

title: Comparative evaluation of ResNet-Based AI models for breast cancer detection in digital mammography and digital breast tomosynthesis
container-title: Frontiers in Systems Biology
b5cd32e8397df1843cd74bcffa6248924139b1ea.abstract: Introduction Early detection of breast cancer is crucial for better treatment options; however, physicians usually encounter challenges when reading breast mammograms because some tissues can overlap or look similar. New computer technologies can help by highlighting areas that may contain cancer. In this study, we assessed computer systems to identify whether a breast image is normal, benign or malignant and compared their performance on standard digital mammography (DM) and digital breast tomosynthesis (DBT) images. Methods This retrospective study included 31 (100 after augmentation) images with malignant breast lesions, 175 with benign findings, and 475 normal images. We developed a deep learning convolutional neural network (CNN) model to classify images using ResNet-18 and ResNet-50. We trained the model via 10-fold cross-validation and Holdout validation. Performance was measured for each model. We computed performance metrics on original (non-augmented) images from 10-fold cross-validated predictions, with 95% confidence intervals from a stratified patient-level bootstrap (2,000 replicates), precision–recall analysis with average precision (AP), and paired DeLong and exact McNemar tests with Holm correction. We increased the malignant class from 31 to 100 images in the training set via data augmentation for the stage-2 classifier. Validation used non-augmented images. Results In normal versus abnormal classification (679 original images per view; ResNet-18, 10-fold cross-validation), DM CC, DM MLO and DBT MLO achieved an AUC-ROC of 0.995 (95% CI 0.991–0.998), 0.984 (0.975–0.992) and 0.994 (0.989–0.998), sensitivity of 95.1%, 95.6% and 95.1%, and specificity of 96.6%, 94.1% and 98.5%, respectively. DBT had significantly higher specificity than DM in selected comparisons (ResNet-18 vs. DM MLO and ResNet-50 vs. DM CC; Holm-adjusted p ≤ 0.002), with no significant AUC-ROC differences between modalities or architectures (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.13). In benign versus malignant classification (131 original images, 31 malignant), AUC-ROC ranged from 0.977 to 0.999 and AP from 0.946 to 0.996, with no significant differences between DM and DBT or between ResNet-18 and ResNet-50 (all Holm-adjusted p ≥ 0.50). The detection and classification of malignant, benign, and normal images in DBT and DM using an artificial intelligence (AI) training model achieved comparable performance to the medical field. Conclusion Computer systems can detect and classify breast findings with high accuracy, helping to reduce errors and support physicians’ decisions. The original number of malignant images was relatively small (n = 31), which may affect the model’s generalizability and highlights the need for validation on larger, multi-institutional datasets. These findings may encourage more use of computer-assisted detection in breast imaging and contribute to developing better tools for early breast cancer diagnosis.

title: Investigating the impact of generative AI on academic integrity in universities student attitudes, ethical challenges, AI-assisted plagiarism, and institutional responses
container-title: Perspectives in Social Sciences
855e32a3120a9cd40b45cb459b808616e4102978.abstract: This study aimed to explore the influence of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) on academic integrity within Pakistani universities, examining students' perceptions, ethical dilemmas, the role of AI in plagiarism, and institutional measures. A mixed-methods research approach was employed to draw out students' experiences and institutional views of academic use of generative AI. The targeted population consisted of students of undergraduate and post graduate level in public and private universities of Pakistan. The sample size for quantitative analysis was 350 students while for qualitative analysis, the students, lecturers and academic administrators were sampled. A structured questionnaire and interview questions were used to discuss the use of AI, ethical awareness, academic dishonesty, and institutional policies. Overall, the findings indicated that students were positive about the use of generative AI as an educational tool, particularly for writing assistance, research, and information retrieval. However, issues arose about AI-assisted plagiarism, dependence, originality, and the trustworthiness of AI-generated information. The findings also revealed that the policies in universities were not consistent, and students' awareness of AI was not high, which made it hard to implement responsible AI. The study highlighted the importance of establishing institutional policies, promoting AI literacy, transparency in disclosure, and adjusting assessment systems to maintain academic integrity and stimulate technological innovation in higher education in Pakistan.

title: Fail-Closed Authorization for Tool-Using AI Agents: A Capability Contract and Case Study
732fc9ee0d24c7cb1bcb0899e1e4272b04f11159.abstract: Abstract For tool-using LLM agents the decisive question is whether a concrete tool call is authorized before it executes. We describe the Agent Security Contract (ASC), a deny-by-default, pre-execution gate for agent and MCP tool calls. An ASC policy pins a SHA-256 digest of the approved tool catalog, declares per-agent tool allowlists with argument constraints, marks high-impact tools that require out-of-band approval, and bounds call rates; each decision (ALLOW, BLOCK, REQUIRE_APPROVAL) is emitted as an integrity-checked (unkeyed) JSON evidence envelope, and every error path we enumerate and test resolves to BLOCK. We evaluate the open-source implementation on static, recorded tool-call traces only; no live agent is run. Bypasses of the v0.1.0 demo policy found in review were fixed in v0.2.0; on a 60-case adversarial probe, allowed attacks fall from 32 to 1 (a policy gap), at the cost of 3 new benign over-blocks. On the author-constructed 66-scenario v0.2.1 corpus, designed around these checks, ASC returns the expected verdict in 66/66 cases; tool-name RBAC (Python and OPA/Rego) admits 30 of its 33 attacks by construction, and mutation testing shows the corpus exercises few policy constraints (8 of 62 single-constraint mutants killed). As a held-out check we replay 132 AgentDojo v1.2 ground-truth traces under policies frozen beforehand. With tool-level approval policies, 25 of 26 non-empty attack traces but also 60 of 97 benign tasks are held for approval. v0.2.0's strict-argument rule makes these unadapted policies block 94 of 97 benign tasks. Policies derived mechanically from AgentDojo's tool signatures first hit v0.2.0's lack of optional arguments (31 benign blocks); with v0.2.1 they reproduce the tool-level verdicts on all 132 traces, with no blocks and no newly admitted attack, so type-only declarations add no protection here. Median in-process latency is about 38 us per trace.

title: Superpower Competitiveness in the 4IR: AI, FinTech
container-title: Frontiers of Finance
3251c76328c511578625b2ebd589e40943676381.abstract: This study compares the competitiveness of the USA, EU, China and India over 2017–2025, using verified international indices (GII, GTCI, NRI) and descriptive indicators of AI, FinTech, human capital and innovation. Three exploratory propositions, motivated by endogenous growth in 4th Industrial Revolution, dynamic comparative advantage, and institutional theory, are examined. Innovation scores converge modestly relative to incomes per head. Talent competitiveness (GTCI) and Global innovation (GII) move together in levels, but initial talent does not predict later gains. Risk-based regulation is not associated with higher FinTech adoption: the EU records the lowest adoption, China the highest, the USA leads in capitalization. A Network Readiness Index (NRI) integrating talent, infrastructure, capital, regulatory complexity is partly computable. Three qualitative 2030 scenarios, with multipolar specialization most plausible, are exploratory, not forecasts. Policy implications (prioritizing human-capital investment, adaptive governance, infrastructure complementarity, open knowledge flows against costly technological decoupling) are hypotheses for testing on larger samples.

title: Perceived Usefulness and Willingness to Consider AI Legal Assistants for Preliminary Guidance in Bangladesh
966f4c0ed2ba0d2d8ed062df52cf7b13a947ac4d.abstract: Abstract AI legal assistants may expand preliminary information access, but perceived usefulness and willingness to consider a service should not be equated with improved access to justice. This study examines their alignment using 385 adult, consenting, AI-aware responses from Bangladesh, collected through a mixed online and in-person questionnaire approach. The legally oriented sample includes 227 law students. Low internal consistency across four questionnaire blocks motivates item-level analysis rather than composite mediation. Methods combine full response distributions, paired endorsement contrasts, joint response patterns, rank correlations and adjusted binary and ordinal models. Basic access, time saving and convenience have identical means of 3.85, yet 44.9% of respondents differ in endorsement between time saving and basic access. Willingness to consider preliminary AI guidance is endorsed by 63.9%; 30.4% jointly endorse time saving, convenience and willingness. The conditional statement that transparent explanations increase willingness receives 87.5% endorsement, exceeding general willingness by 23.6 percentage points. No focal coefficient survives multiplicity correction in the primary adjusted binary model; the nominal barrier-reduction association also does not persist in ordinal sensitivity analysis. The findings reveal broadly favourable marginal evaluations without a reliably established individual pathway from perceived benefits to willingness. The contribution is to distinguish informational convenience, prospective consideration and justice outcomes, while showing how similar averages conceal different respondent configurations. Implications favour task-specific information support, verifiable sources and human referral, evaluated through comprehension and completed service pathways. The results concern perceptions within a legally oriented sample, not demonstrated improvements in legal assistance, procedural fairness or dispute resolution.

title: CardioTwin-AI: development and internal validation of a digital twin-based adaptive risk-aware learning framework for heart disease prediction
container-title: Frontiers in Digital Health
ad124e367bd9776c8ecde4d8d57bbe7082beaa2f.abstract: Heart disease is one of the most common causes of death in the world and early identification of individuals at elevated cardiovascular risk requires reliable risk-assessment methods that can support clinical decision-making. Many conventional machine-learning models focus primarily on disease classification or risk prediction and do not explicitly provide patient-specific virtual representations. This study introduces CardioTwin-AI, a Digital Twin-based Adaptive Risk-Aware Learning Framework (ARLF) to predict the presence or absence of heart disease. We propose a data-driven, patient-specific Digital Twin representation based on clinical attributes, in which the patient state is mapped to a corresponding virtual state and evaluated using state-level synchronization measures, including Twin Simulation Error (TSE) and Twin Fidelity Score (TFS) to quantify representation consistency. The deep feature representations are generated by feature engineering process based on autoencoder, and then analysed by the ARLF prediction model to estimate the probability of the presence of heart disease. It achieved high patient-state representation consistency between the source clinical state and its virtual representation, with a Twin Fidelity Score of 99.76% and a Twin Simulation Error of 0.002402. The proposed ARLF model achieved accuracy of 90.21%, precision of 90.32%, recall of 94.11%, F1-score of 92.18%, and ROC-AUC of 95.13% in the fixed held-out evaluation. The results indicate the potential of CardioTwin-AI for predicting the presence or absence of heart disease and assessing patient-state representation consistency, subject to further external validation and prospective clinical evaluation.

title: Gender-differentiated effects of motion-enhanced AI-generated images in instructional videos: a mixed-process study using TAM-related perceptions and cognitive load theory
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
6c320926fe075b32b1922147c5b572f0252164bf.abstract: With the widespread adoption of online educational technologies, instructional videos have become a pivotal tool for flexible and efficient learning. The integration of visual aids, such as animations and dynamic elements, aims to enhance the learning experience; however, their effectiveness remains debated. This study examined learning performance and subjective experience when instructional videos presented static AI-generated images or manually animated versions of those images. A 2 × 2 between-subjects experiment was conducted with 40 undergraduate participants ( n = 10 per cell), comparing static versus motion-enhanced presentation conditions across male and female participant groups. Stable Diffusion XL generated the base images, and CapCut was used to add motion; the motion itself was not AI-generated. Participants viewed a 140-s mobile video on mortise-and-tenon structures, completed a 10-item accuracy test, and rated willingness to continue learning, preference, acceptability, ease of understanding, and mental effort. The ANOVA results provided no statistically significant evidence of a main effect of motion on learning accuracy. Differences across gender groups were observed for several subjective outcomes. For acceptability, the gender × motion interaction was statistically significant, but Bonferroni-adjusted simple-effect tests supported a gender-group difference only in the static condition. For mental effort, the interaction was also statistically significant; adjusted simple-effect tests indicated higher mental effort among female than male participants in the dynamic condition and higher mental effort in the static than dynamic condition among male participants. Given the small sample and multiple outcomes, these findings should be interpreted as exploratory.

title: SynForge-Cardio: a unified multimodal synthetic dataset generation framework for privacy-preserving cardiovascular AI
container-title: Frontiers in Digital Health
53d7a1f04e63b97105e6928eb46809e02c7207b9.abstract: Multimodal cardiovascular AI systems benefit from jointly available chest radiographs, 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs), and structured electronic health record (EHR) variables. In practice, multi-institutional model development is constrained by privacy regulations, institutional data silos, and class imbalance for less common findings. Existing open-source synthetic data tools are largely modality-specific: tabular libraries such as Synthetic Data Vault (SDV)/Conditional Tabular Generative Adversarial Network (CTGAN), image generators based on latent diffusion, and time-series methods such as Time-series Generative Adversarial Network (TimeGAN) each require its own setup, configuration, and validation. This study presents SynForge-Cardio, a multimodality orchestration framework for prompt-driven synthetic dataset generation across chest X-ray (CXR), 12-lead ECG, and EHR modalities. Rather than introducing a new generative backbone, SynForge-Cardio coordinates established components—latent diffusion with optional low-rank adaptation for CXR; parametric and bounded morphology-preserving augmentation (with an optional TimeGAN path) for ECG; and size-aware routing among jitter augmentation, Gaussian copula, and CTGAN/Tabular Variational Autoencoder for EHR—behind a shared clinical prompt interface, a rule-based router, and a postgeneration quality/privacy reporting layer. The three modalities were generated independently from separate datasets; the framework does not perform patient-level joint synthesis and makes no claim of anatomical or physiological consistency across modalities. This system is implemented as a FastAPI backend with a React frontend and can run on a single workstation GPU. Herein, we formalize the orchestration objective, specify modality-wise models and metrics [Fréchet Inception Distance (FID), dynamic time warping (DTW), power spectral density similarity, Kolmogorov–Smirnov statistics, correlation preservation, and distance-to-closest-record privacy screening], and describe an evaluation protocol on public corpora (NIH Chest X-ray14, PTB-XL, and the UCI Cleveland Heart Disease dataset), including a four-regime train-on-synthetic/test-on-real (TSTR) utility analysis with five random seeds. On the framework alone, we measured 94.6% modality-routing accuracy, 100% direct-vs.-routed generation equivalence on the evaluated cases, 59 unnecessary generator calls avoided, and 100% validation/reporting completeness (1,105/1,108 tests pass, 3 skipped). Downstream-utility results were mixed: augmenting a 25%-real training set with synthetic data changed the held-out AUROC by −0.041 to +0.050 across three CXR tasks (none significant at five seeds); by +0.019 for ECG MI-vs.-NORM [produced by mode B (bounded real-waveform augmentation, whose synthetic samples can be matched to their true source recording at top-1 ≈ 42.7–43.4%, and hence, mode B is not an independently learned generative model)]; and by +0.017 for EHR heart disease classification, which is not evidence of benefit given the 61-record hold-out set (the test-set bootstrap 95% CI for the difference includes zero). Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV acquisition was not completed because credentialed access was unavailable; all reported EHR results were UCI-based. SynForge-Cardio is intended as a practical, reproducible research framework for privacy-conscious cardiovascular data augmentation and prototype development.

title: From cognitive relief to motivational enhancement: associations between perceived Agentic AI Capability and student engagement in systems development courses
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
27aafbc2fd89ad8063440234ea6febf14a27bb85.abstract: Generative AI agents are increasingly emerging as important learning partners for supporting complex problem-solving in higher education; however, the psychological processes associated with student engagement remain insufficiently understood. Grounded in Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory, this study examines how perceived Agentic AI Capability is associated with students' extraneous cognitive load, academic self-efficacy, and overall student engagement in systems development courses. An empirical study was conducted among undergraduate students majoring in e-commerce who participated in systems development-related courses. The results indicate that perceived Agentic AI Capability is negatively associated with extraneous cognitive load and positively associated with academic self-efficacy. Extraneous cognitive load is negatively associated with academic self-efficacy and student engagement, whereas academic self-efficacy is positively associated with student engagement. The indirect associations through academic self-efficacy and the sequential pathway are statistically significant. The findings provide evidence on cognitive and motivational correlates of AI-supported learning while, given the cross-sectional design, not establishing causal or temporal relationships. This study extends the application of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Cognitive Theory to human–AI collaborative learning environments and provides theoretical insights and practical implications for integrating generative AI into systems development education.

title: PhageLysData: an evidence-aware and AI-ready dataset of phage lytic enzymes and depolymerases
container-title: Frontiers in Bioinformatics
8b0c08ff820626b15401ffaa2d0fca3d450f7f1f.abstract: Bacteriophage lytic enzymes and depolymerases are relevant to phage biology, antimicrobial development, and protein engineering, but their sequence and annotation data remain dispersed across general databases, specialized resources, genome-centred collections, and prediction-oriented datasets. We present PhageLysData, an evidence-aware and AI-ready resource constructed through reproducible multisource integration, provenance tracking, and exact-sequence consolidation. The release integrates 807,366 source observations from seven primary resources into 759,105 unique exact-sequence entities, comprising an evidence-supported Core of 11,867 entities, a Prediction Extension of 745,092 prediction-only candidates, and 2,146 Context entities retained for provenance and reference. This architecture preserves broad sequence-space coverage while maintaining a clear distinction between non-predictive and prediction-derived support. Core entities are enriched with harmonized biological annotations, physicochemical properties, independent InterProScan-derived functional annotations, mapped PDB and AlphaFold DB structural assets, and reusable numerical representations. For 11,259 eligible Core sequences, PhageLysData provides embeddings from 11 protein language models together with one-hot encoding under a common representation contract. Release-facing examples demonstrate latent-space exploration, unsupervised clustering, supervised classification, and evidence-aware candidate retrieval without defining a universal predictive benchmark. PhageLysData provides a traceable, versioned, and computationally accessible foundation for protein retrieval, comparative analysis, task-specific dataset construction, and machine-learning applications involving phage lytic enzymes and depolymerases.

title:
Beyond AI Productivity: Enterprise AI Systems,
Human–AI Responsibility, and the Future of Work
0de0d9ca1f0ef63e0d4a49798cbf60ef60b57dd8.abstract: Abstract A prior U.S. review, Enterprise AI at the Decision Point, established that enterprise artificial intelligence (AI) as-sistants have task-dependent productivity effects and that public evidence does not identify an independent financial return or a complete chain from AI cost to verified workforce replacement. The human side of that productivity record, and any organiza-tional consequences of workforce change, were left open. This study examines responsibilities, training, job insecurity and well-being, human oversight, and performance after U.S. enterprise AI adoption from November 2022 through September 2026. The design is a critical integrative review. Firms that report a task effect most often report exclusive augmentation. Frequent AI use is associated with greater fear of job loss. In one worker panel, displacement concern, rather than use frequency itself, is associated with lower engagement and higher burnout. The contribution is a responsibility-transfer framework with five constructs and four testable propositions. A proposed computa-tional specification of that framework, Human–AI Responsibility-Aware Workflow Optimization (HARWO), places verification and accountability on the workflow graph. Gross task-time savings are separated from net employee time. HARWO is not solved or estimated in this paper. The evidence gap reflects a measurement disconnect: existing studies separately examine task productivity, workforce changes, and employee well-being, but the evidence examined here does not adequately link these outcomes within the same organizations over time. Consequently, whether AI-driven efficiency gains reduce human workload or redistribute responsibilities remains unresolved. The U.S. record is consistent with the separation of task change from employment change, and with anticipatory strain. The performance of organizations that combine AI with workforce reduction remains unmeasured, and the propositions are not empirically validated.

title: Why is Nvidia so powerful in the AI world, and what could Jensen Huang’s scandal really cost?
Toward Resilient Explainable AI–Digital Twin Frameworks for Cyber-Secure Renewable Energy Systems: An Uncertainty-Aware Lifecycle-Integrated Architecture
7c34f1d12274c306fbba6780b03395ce165e8322.abstract: Abstract The accelerating penetration of variable renewable energy sources into modern power systems demands digital infrastructures capable of supporting predictive, autonomous, and trustworthy grid operation. While digital twins (DT) and artificial intelligence (AI)—particularly multi-agent and agentic architectures—are key enablers, their integration remains fragmented across three critical dimensions: explainability, cybersecurity, and uncertainty management. This paper proposes a conceptual, uncertainty-aware, lifecycle-integrated architecture that couples explainable AI (XAI) with digital twin modeling to support resilient, cyber-secure renewable energy operations. Based on a structured review spanning component-, building-, and urban-scale DT infrastructure, XAI-driven forecasting and fault diagnosis, distributed energy resource (DER) multi-agent control, and DER cybersecurity vulnerabilities, we identify a persistent scholarly disjunction. Few studies treat interpretability, adversarial resilience, and stochastic uncertainty as co-design requirements across the entire asset lifecycle. Using a design-science methodology and thematic synthesis, we develop a five-layer architecture: sensing and data acquisition, digital twin simulation, XAI-mediated agentic decision-making, cybersecurity and resilience, and lifecycle governance. The core contribution lies in defining the structural logic through which these layers interoperate to achieve transparency, security, and adaptability. This framework provides a foundation for future simulation-based validation and advances debates on digitalized energy infrastructure governance.

title: From disclosure to epistemic accountability: preserving meaningful human control across the AI-assisted research lifecycle
container-title: Frontiers in Research Metrics and Analytics
39f274b19f134ead91b0eb8a2ec61f55c6302bc2.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming embedded across the scientific research lifecycle, while prevailing governance remains centered on disclosure of tool use and the assignment of responsibility to human authors. We argue that disclosure is necessary but insufficient because it does not establish that researchers understood, verified, challenged, and authorized the AI-assisted processes that shaped scientific claims. We define this disconnect as the epistemic accountability gap and develop the Lifecycle Epistemic Accountability Framework (LEAF) as a testable theory of how meaningful human control can be preserved across AI-assisted knowledge production. Drawing on a structured integrative review and critical interpretive synthesis, LEAF links four human-control capacities—competence, contestability, intervention authority, and traceable ownership—supported by evaluability by design, to five lifecycle checkpoints spanning evidence identification, study design and ethics, data processing and analysis, interpretation, and reporting or knowledge translation. The framework proposes that accountability improves when oversight is exercised prospectively at epistemically consequential decision points, documented through an audit trail, and calibrated to epistemic materiality: the extent to which AI assistance can alter the validity, interpretation, or consequences of a scientific claim. Six propositions specify testable relationships among disclosure, epistemic materiality, meaningful human control, lifecycle checkpoints, auditability, and defensibility of scientific claims. LEAF therefore shifts AI research governance from retrospective visibility to prospective, risk-proportionate control. We identify boundary conditions, implementation pathways, and an empirical research agenda for testing the framework across disciplines and resource settings. LEAF's distinctive explanatory mechanism is conditional: epistemic materiality escalates oversight, evaluability enables four human capacities, lifecycle checkpoints interrupt error propagation, and retained audit evidence makes consequential decisions answerable.

title: Rare Earths, AI, and Digital Finance: Supply-Chain Risk and Managerial Implications
container-title: WSEAS Transactions on Business and Economics
91a499c077615109d6520c7c70518a9b6015101e.abstract: Rare earth elements (REEs) are an underexamined asset class at the intersection of digital finance, artificial intelligence (AI) and strategic resource management. AI infrastructure sustains demand for neodymium, dysprosium and terbium, whose supply chains remain highly concentrated in China. This paper analyses how REE supply-chain risk propagates into the equity markets of AI-intensive firms. Using open-source data from the International Energy Agency, the VanEck Rare Earth and Strategic Metals ETF (REMX) and the USGS Mineral Commodity Summaries, we characterise REE-sensitive instruments over 2020-2026 and propose a Shapley-value decomposition of REMX return predictions into concentration, geopolitical, technology-demand and macro-financial channels. The evidence suggests that REE concentration risk is a financially material and insufficiently priced systemic factor. We derive recommendations for portfolio construction, corporate disclosure and the regulation of digital finance infrastructure.

title: What respondents recruited through European patient organisation networks think about AI in healthcare: reflections from an exploratory survey
container-title: Frontiers in Digital Health
683bf579509d7fa18fc1e21435d65fb310cbb659.abstract: Background The use of artificial intelligence (AI) in healthcare is rapidly increasing. Patients represent an important group of stakeholders whose perspectives on AI implementation are essential to explore. Objective This exploratory survey aims to investigate patient perspectives across different European countries on various aspects related to the use of AI in healthcare. Methods An online survey was disseminated through the European Patients’ Forum (EPF) member organisations from April until August 2025. Results A total of 874 respondents completed the survey. Almost all respondents report that there are benefits (93.48%) as well as concerns (97.71%) to the use of AI in healthcare. The top three indicated benefits included: support healthcare professionals (HCPs) in delivering more personalised care (64.65%), faster/more accurate diagnosis (62.59%), and support patients’ self-management and treatment adherence (61.78%). For concerns the top three comprised: lack of human empathy and personal touch (69.79%), biased AI-driven decisions (68.08%), and AI making incorrect diagnoses (59.27%). Most respondents indicated that, to their knowledge, they had not yet experienced AI use in their own healthcare (61.44%). Their information preferences show that respondents want to be informed about AI being used in their care: mostly at the very beginning (93.36%), through their HCP (81.69%), and with patient-friendly information (67.73%). Conclusions The findings suggest that respondents recognise the possible benefits AI could bring to healthcare, while also expressing concerns about its integration into clinical practice, possibly resulting in conditional acceptance. This highlights the importance of involving patients throughout the implementation process trying to promote trust and facilitate acceptance of AI in healthcare.

title: From Role-Play to AI Interaction: Speaking Confidence Development among EFL Nursing Students at AKPER YPTK Solok
container-title: IJELTAL (Indonesian Journal of English Language Teaching and Applied Linguistics)
9bad9be3de9cc0043d5c9290557e506d07dceaff.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence is now a common sight in classrooms for foreign languages, but evidence of it improving speaking confidence compared to established techniques like role-play is still not available. With a sample of 60 EFL nursing students who were part of the program AKPER YPTK Solok, in West Sumatra, Indonesia, the explanatory sequential mixed-methods study looked into how combining classroom role-play with structured ChatGPT-assisted rehearsal performed against a control group role-playing only. Speaking confidence, willingness to communicate, speaking anxiety, and oral performance were the four factors assessed using modified scales and an analytic speaking rubric, together with interviews of eight students to elaborate upon the quantitative results. A significant increase in spoken confidence was detected in the group with AI assistance by a very small margin. The gains in willingness to communicate and oral performance were relatively small, and as for speaking anxiety, no significant difference was found. The interview data suggest that the learners experienced greater confidence and readiness in class after repeatedly practicing dialogue that was free of any judgment, and they found that a conversation with a person and with AI resulted in significantly different reactions. Based on these findings, it seems that a good use of conversational AI is as a rehearsal tool that develops learners' confidence in speaking and prepares them for authentic human interaction it has not replaced.

title: Do Machine Learning Security Detectors Survive New Attacks? A Leakage Free Evaluation of Hidden Prompt Injection Detection in AI Coding Agents, Malicious npm and PyPI Package Detection, and Network Intrusion Detection
917fb821d55341e2557e46a52cf1b17828f0c15f.abstract: Abstract Machine learning detectors for cybersecurity are usually tested by splitting one dataset at random, so the attacks in the test set closely resemble the attacks seen in training. Real attackers change technique. This paper asks whether three kinds of machine learning security detectors still work when they meet an attack technique they have never seen, using one shared, leakage free evaluation protocol. Study A builds a corpus of 4,955 real AI agent instruction files and Model Context Protocol tool descriptions from GitHub, plants harmless hidden instructions with nine hiding techniques used in 2026 prompt injection campaigns, and tests five detectors. Study B tests malicious npm and PyPI package detection on 13,317 packages, training on samples published before 2026 and testing on the 2026 attack waves. Study C revisits network intrusion detection on CICIDS2017, CICIDS2018 and UNSW NB15 with duplicate removal, time ordered splits, unseen attack families and cross dataset transfer. On standard random splits, almost every detector scores a ROC AUC between 0.95 and 1.00. Against hiding techniques never seen in training, a feature based detector of hidden instructions falls from 0.87 to 0.04 recall at a one percent false alarm rate, while a canonicalising character model keeps 0.89 and a fine tuned DistilRoBERTa keeps 0.98. A malicious package model built on static features falls from 0.90 to 0.41 recall on 2026 packages once its size shortcut is removed. An intrusion detector trained on earlier days of CICIDS2018 scores a ROC AUC of 0.49 on later days and finds 10 percent of unseen attack families. Small open language models (Qwen2.5 Instruct, 1.5B to 7B parameters) obeyed hidden instructions in up to 67 percent of poisoned files, larger models obeyed more often, and removing invisible characters made zero width attacks more effective. Our Study A detector, trained only on synthetic poisoning, found 80 percent of 202 real malicious AI agent skills. We release the scripts and give a short checklist for testing security detectors against new attacks.

title: The Care Plan Compiler as an Agentic AI Framework for Translating Clinical Recommendations into Feasible Patient-Centered Care
container-title: Universal Library of Innovative Research and Studies
ff02636293254b9f3bb85078086cf9eae80101ec.abstract: A clinical recommendation becomes care after someone confirms coverage, finds a facility that provides the service, arranges language support and transportation, books an appointment, and verifies that the visit took place. When no organization owns this work, it falls to the patient, and a missed service is recorded as nonadherence, even when the failure occurred within the health system. The review examines five adjacent fields, each addressing part of this problem, and develops the Care Plan Compiler, an agentic AI framework that treats the clinician-approved recommendation as a protected source specification and compiles it into a graph of tasks with named owners. A deterministic readiness checker releases a task once all prerequisites hold and classifies any unknown coverage, capacity, or accessibility as unresolved. Feasible plans are compared across a multidimensional burden vector, and a change in context triggers recompilation of the dependent tasks. A synthetic case of diabetic retinal screening illustrates the compilation, and a four-stage evaluation program sets a screening completed within the approved window and verified within 90 days of referral approval as its primary endpoint. The framework moves responsibility for missed care to the system layer where the failure occurs.

title: Neural Mechanisms of Willed Attention Control
6c47127d70f109a58cb6025488b9cb7e3e64f432.abstract: Cueing paradigms are commonly used to study the neural mechanisms of visual spatial attention control. In these paradigms, each trial starts with an external cue, which instructs the subject to pay covert attention to a spatial location in anticipation of an impending stimulus (instructed attention). Recent work has introduced a new type of cue which prompts the subject to spontaneously decide which spatial location to attend (willed attention). We studied the neural mechanisms of willed attention control by analyzing fMRI and EEG data recorded at two institutions (UF and UC Davis) using the same willed attention paradigm. The findings include: (1) both instructional cues and the choice cue activated the DAN, (2) the choice cue additionally activated a frontoparietal decision network consisting of dorsal anterior cingulate cortex (dACC), anterior insula (AI), anterior prefrontal cortex (APFC), dorsal lateral prefrontal cortex (DLPFC), and inferior parietal lobule (IPL), (3) the decision about where to attend can be decoded in frontoparietal decision network in choice trials but not in instructional trials, and (4) EEG alpha oscillation patterns immediately preceding the choice cue, but not the instructional cues, predicted the postcue direction of attention and the frontoparietal decision network activity. Based on these findings we proposed a model of willed attention control suggesting how the direction of visual spatial attention was decided upon in the absence of external instructions.
