title: Beyond TAM: a mediated-moderated analysis of perceived anthropomorphism and technology trust as catalysts for AI adoption
container-title: Global Knowledge, Memory and Communication
f42fc18f511ad00f2591df2314c14dd596c3b3e4.abstract: Purpose This study examines customers’ adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in the Jordanian telecommunications sector by extending the technology acceptance model (TAM). Specifically, it aims to investigate the effects of perceived usefulness, perceived ease of use and perceived anthropomorphism on actual use of AI, while testing customer intention as a mediator and technology trust as a moderator. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative approach was employed. Data were collected through self-administered questionnaires from customers of telecommunications companies in Jordan. Using stratified random sampling, 482 questionnaires were distributed, and 438 valid responses were analyzed. Partial least squares structural equation modeling using SmartPLS 4 was applied to assess the measurement model, structural relationships, mediation effects and moderation effect. Findings The results show that perceived ease of use and perceived anthropomorphism significantly and positively influence customers’ intention to adopt AI, whereas perceived usefulness has no significant effect. Customer intention significantly predicts actual AI use and mediates the relationships between perceived ease of use, perceived anthropomorphism and actual AI use. However, intention does not mediate the relationship between perceived usefulness and actual AI use. Technology trust significantly moderates the relationship between customer intention and actual AI use. Practical implications Telecom providers should design AI-enabled services that are simple, intuitive, human-like and trustworthy. Managers should also communicate the tangible benefits of AI more clearly to strengthen customers’ usefulness perceptions and encourage sustained usage. Originality/value This study extends TAM by integrating perceived anthropomorphism and technology trust into a mediated-moderated model of AI adoption in an underexplored Middle Eastern telecommunications context.

title: Differentiated Motor Cognition Process in Self-initiated and visual-guided Movements Revealed by Effective Connectivity Network
container-title: Psychoradiology
7530770676c12c4f5eaf293e2ef04df387ff6829.abstract: Abstract Background Self-initiated (SI) and visual-guided (VG) movements engage distinct motor cognitive processes, yet the distinctive hierarchical organization and directional information flow that underpin these two cognition modes remain unclear. Objective This study aimed to delineate how the brain dynamically reorganizes its directional information flow to support two distinct modes of motor cognition: SI and VG movements using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. Methods We analyzed fMRI data of 39 healthy adults who participated in SI and VG finger-tapping tasks. Time series were extracted from task-related brain regions identified by conjunction analysis. Individual-level directed connectivity matrices were constructed using CGC, and permutation testing was employed to identify group-level significant connections and compare connectivity differences between tasks. Results The VG task exhibited a sensory-driven feedforward architecture, with information flow originating from visual cortices and propagating to motor areas and the basal ganglia. In contrast, the SI task engaged a cognitive motor control circuit characterized by the supplementary motor area (SMA) as a hub, exerting descending drive to the putamen (PUT) while receiving feedback from visual cortices. Between-task comparisons revealed that, relative to SI, VG showed stronger connectivity from visual cortices to motor areas and the basal ganglia. Conversely, SI exhibited enhanced effective connectivity from the SMA to the basal ganglia, along with strengthened feedback interactions within visual cortices and from visual cortices to the SMA. Conclusion Our study found the differentiated directional information transfer underlying the SI and VG movements, which provided neuroimaging evidence that advances our understanding of neural mechanisms in motor cognitive, and might help explain selective vulnerabilities of internal movement generation in PD and related disorders.

title: SeekRBP: Leveraging Sequence-Structure Integration with Reinforcement Learning for Receptor-Binding Protein Identification
container-title: Bioinformatics
a3ebcc3f1668084d57829873f1b2737987d82eee.abstract: Abstract Motivation Receptor-binding proteins (RBPs) initiate viral infection and determine host specificity, serving as key targets for phage engineering and therapy. However, the identification of RBPs is complicated by their extreme sequence divergence, which often renders traditional homology-based alignment methods ineffective. While machine learning offers a promising alternative, such approaches struggle with severe class imbalance and the difficulty of selecting informative negative samples from heterogeneous tail proteins. Existing methods often fail to balance learning from these “hard negatives” while maintaining generalization. Results We present SeekRBP, a sequence–structure framework that models negative sampling as a sequential decision-making problem. By employing a multi-armed bandit strategy, SeekRBP dynamically prioritizes informative non-RBP sequences based on real-time training feedback, complemented by a multimodal fusion of protein language and structural embeddings. Benchmarking demonstrates that SeekRBP consistently outperforms static sampling strategies. Furthermore, a case study on Vibrio phages validates that SeekRBP effectively identifies RBPs to improve host prediction, highlighting its potential for large-scale annotation and synthetic biology applications. Availability The source code of SeekRBP is available via: https://github.com/Saillxl/SeekRBP.

title: When AI takes control, who takes responsibility? Structural analysis of agentic AI risks in supply chains
container-title: Industrial Management & Data Systems
856fe8a0aa1ef33e7ac05c1632f3b6d6a499b839.abstract: Purpose Agentic AI systems execute procurement decisions, reroute shipments and renegotiate supplier contracts at speeds that preclude real-time human review. The existing literature offers limited analytical attention to the risks that arise when decision authority is delegated to agents. This paper develops a risk taxonomy for agentic AI in supply chains and traces the hierarchical dependencies and influence magnitudes among the identified risks. Design/methodology/approach A systematic review of literature, analyzed through theories–characteristics–contexts–methods framework, produces the risk taxonomy. A hybrid modified total interpretive structural modeling and fuzzy decision-making trial and evaluation laboratory methodology is then applied to structured expert judgments to establish the causal hierarchy and quantify inter-risk influence. Findings Three risks, namely workforce skill gap, data quality and reliability and ethical misalignment occupy the deepest level of the causal hierarchy. Lack of accountability and governance and data privacy emerge as terminal outcomes. All three analytical methods converge on a conclusion: agentic AI risks originate at the institutional layer, with technical risks acting as transmission mechanisms. Practical implications The findings indicate that effective governance requires that workforce capability, data integrity and objective-function alignment are addressed before deployment. The stratified agentic AI governance framework is proposed that translates hierarchical structure into a sequenced intervention architecture, providing practitioners with governance priorities organized by risk-propagation logic. Originality/value This paper contributes a systematically derived risk taxonomy and a causally weighted governance map for agentic AI risks in supply chains. Five propositions are derived from the causal structure and are advanced as a testable research agenda.

title: An SIDM-hydro hybrid method for simulating self-interacting dark matter
container-title: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society
9611b86948841f0c531e115d57416ae0286469ed.abstract: Abstract We present a new scheme to couple existing numerical methods for elastic self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) to the hydrodynamic equations via a continuous function of the local Knudsen number. The method, an SIDM-hydro hybrid (SHH), allows more efficient simulation of the evolution of inhomogeneous halos deep into the regime of gravothermal collapse. With the improved efficiency gained by moving to a hydrodynamical description in high-density regions, the SHH method allows central densities of two orders of magnitude higher to be reached in considerably less simulation time than traditional methods. Our implementation should be considered as the first step toward a robust SHH method, as we interpolate the first and second moments of the Boltzmann equation in the ideal-fluid limit only. The simulation results are qualitatively similar to those found with other methods, although there are differences in the implementation of the primary physics driving the dynamics, and in the details of the resulting halo profiles. However, our results indicate that the SHH technique shows promise to investigate gravothermal collapse in diverse, dynamical environments. The method can be extended to incorporate non-ideal fluid terms and dissipation, as needed for dark-matter scenarios where interactions beyond the elastic regime may be important in the dense interiors of some halos.

title: Conformational inversion mediated organic crystal actuator with extended stroke, self-healing, and optical switching
container-title: National Science Review
344d0e4225829fa4831c8fee11f24a44c5a4e48d.abstract: Abstract Dynamic molecular crystals with the capability to effectively convert thermal energy into mechanical work offer a compelling platform for microactuators. However, developing crystalline actuation materials that simultaneously achieve large and reversible deformation, rapid response, robust cyclability, and integrated optoelectronic functionality remains a formidable challenge. Herein, we take advantage of the conformational inversion of cyclohexyl groups and have rationally developed a dynamic organic crystal based on a dibenzothiophene sulfone derivative, BcDT, which exhibits exceptionally large, rapid, and reversible elongation. The thermally induced chair-to-boat conformational inversion of the introduced cyclohexyl moieties drives a cooperative phase transition that yields a linear elongation of ~14.3% along the crystal long axis, which delivers a work density of ~6.8 × 102 J m−3 and an efficiency of ~0.014%. Notably, the crystal features an uncommon self-healing capability, autonomously repairing macroscopic cracks during heating/cooling stages, ensuring its structural integrity and reliable actuation over multiple thermal cycles. The phase transition also enables reversible switching of linear and nonlinear optical properties, including a 4.2-fold modulation of two-photon excited fluorescence and tunable polarization anisotropy. Leveraging these properties, we demonstrate that BcDT crystals can function as microactuator devices to propel a heavy object and cooperatively lift a platform. This work establishes a molecular design strategy that integrates rapid, high-stroke actuation, self-healing, and optical switching within a single crystalline system, overcoming key functional limitations of current microactuators based on dynamic molecular crystals.

title: The probability of self-related stimuli modulates heartbeat-evoked potentials
container-title: Social Cognitive and Affective Neuroscience
40fb148d130530a4fd2710df576006c0bfff443a.abstract: Abstract Interoception, the cortical processing of visceral signals, has been proposed as a foundation of self-processing. Heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEPs) provide a measure of interoceptive processing and have been linked to self-processing, but whether HEP modulations reflect self-specificity rather than familiarity and depend on probabilistic context remains unclear. We recorded EEG and ECG during passive listening to subject’s own names (SON), familiar names (FN), and unfamiliar name (UN) under equal- and biased-probability conditions. In the equal-probability condition, HEP amplitudes were more positive for SON than for FN and UN over centro-parietal-occipital sites at 164–242 and 258–296 ms after the R peak, whereas FN and UN did not differ. This self-specific pattern was not detected under biased probabilities. Within-name comparisons revealed probability-related HEP effects for SON and UN with distinct spatiotemporal characteristics, indicating that stimulus probability did not produce a uniform effect across name types. The late positive potential showed a comparable probability-dependent self-specific pattern, and SON-evoked LPP amplitudes positively covaried with HEP amplitudes during SON perception across conditions. These findings indicate that self-specific HEP modulations depend on probabilistic context and is associated with relatively late external self-related processing, highlighting a context-sensitive relationship between interoceptive and external self-related processing.

title: Up-regulation of CXCR3 on tonsillar T-cells in patients with IgA nephropathy
container-title: Clinical and Experimental Immunology
a760f967a44d34d0268360b2ca8a35dce8d45b6f.abstract: Abstract IgA nephropathy (IgAN), the most common type of primary glomerulonephritis, is a tonsillar focal disease. Although tonsillectomy is performed in patients with IgAN to prevent renal failure, evidence that the tonsils are the disease focus remains insufficient. Circulating CXCR3-positive T cells have recently been implicated in IgAN pathogenesis. In this study, we examined CXCR3 expression in tonsillar T cells from patients with IgAN. Immunohistological analysis revealed greater accumulation of CXCR3-positive cells in the interfollicular areas of IgAN tonsils than in non-IgAN tonsils. CXCR3-positive cells and IP-10 were also detected in renal tissue, and multiplex immunofluorescence demonstrated co-localization of CXCR3 and CD3 predominantly in the tubulointerstitium. The chemotactic response of tonsillar mononuclear cells to IP-10 was significantly higher in IgAN. Flow cytometric analysis showed a higher proportion of CXCR3+CD3+ cells in IgAN tonsils and a Th1/Tc1-associated phenotype of CXCR3-positive T-cell subsets. Furthermore, co-culture experiments showed that CXCR3-positive T cells enhanced Gd-IgA1 production by tonsillar B cells. Tonsillar CXCR3+CD3+ cell proportions were higher in patients who achieved clinical remission after tonsillectomy, whereas circulating CXCR3+CD3+ cells decreased after tonsillectomy in IgAN but not in non-IgAN patients. These findings suggest that tonsillar CXCR3-positive T cells may contribute to IgAN pathogenesis through enhanced Gd-IgA1 production and recruitment to renal lesions via the CXCR3–IP-10 axis, where they may promote local inflammation.

title: The AI augmentation gap: data richness, automation and business value
container-title: EuroMed Journal of Business
a9d4693b4aede355f90e6e8d3722e0aafd2cb720.abstract: Purpose Grounded in the resource-based view (RBV), this study examines how data richness, as an organisational resource, is associated with business value through two deployment processes, automation and artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled augmentation, and whether they differ in their capacity to generate value. Design/methodology/approach Survey data from 366 Greek firms across four sectors were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM) with bootstrapped mediation analysis and coefficient-difference tests; business value is measured as perceived value from digital technology. Findings Data richness is positively associated with both deployment processes. Automation is positively associated with business value and channels part of the association between data richness and value, whereas AI-enabled augmentation, the less developed process, shows no significant direct association; the difference is statistically significant, revealing an AI augmentation gap. Data richness also retains a significant direct association with value, and additional analyses suggest that the capability associations with value run through enacted digital transformation. Practical implications Firms should build a strategically governed data foundation, expand automation for near-term returns and develop augmentation as a longer-term capability built on skills, role redesign, validation and trust in AI-supported decisions; EuroMed policy instruments can be aligned with this sequencing. Originality/value Drawing on the RBV, the study shows that deployment processes of the same digital resource differ significantly in their association with value, a heterogeneity interpreted as reflecting the maturity of the complementary capabilities each requires, and provides evidence from a resource-constrained Mediterranean economy.

title: Modelling leadership capital and expenditures from a cybernetic perspective – monitoring, intervention, and contradiction under conditions of complexity
container-title: Strategy & Leadership
bdbcc442e5e775df92d94d4f8d49098221169974.abstract: Purpose From a cybernetic perspective, leadership can be approached as informed practices of status monitoring and intervention. This paper aims to use this approach to describe leadership capital and expenditures in complex-adaptive systems, addressing the efforts to keep an organization in the state of boundary stability between order and chaos. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on recent works on complexity leadership, the authors capture two different monitoring and intervention activities. One is directed at the creation of order, the other at its disturbance. A combination of both is needed to avoid both stagnation and complete disintegration. In consequence, it also becomes necessary to spend effort on handling contradictions resulting from this combination. To illustrate the validity and relevance of their approach, the authors discuss its application to (1) identify leadership capital and expenditures (2) understand implications of different leadership styles. Findings The model distinguishes three types of issues that leadership must address to enable successful management, which can be further broken down to monitoring, intervention and processing contradiction. This leads to a radically different account of leadership capital and expenditures than elsewhere in organizational studies. Requisite variety in the organization emerges as a critical factor regarding the frequency of interventions and confrontation with contradictions and tensions. Originality/value The model shows how leadership in complex-adaptive systems can be formalized to identify intangible assets for leadership in organizations, identify necessary expenditures and discuss strengths and weaknesses of different leadership practices. It departs from earlier work in cybernetics focusing exclusively on floating equilibria, shifting the focus on boundary stability between order and chaos as the goal of monitoring and intervention.

title: Architectural hedging capacity: preserving strategic optionality in AI provider relationships
container-title: Strategy & Leadership
1f10cf4b1b679b2084257feedf9f44642c6acab3.abstract: Purpose Firms increasingly depend on a small number of external providers for artificial intelligence (AI) models, yet that dependence is not only imposed by supplier concentration; it can also be reproduced by a firm’s own technology-integration decisions. This paper aims to examine how provider-specific integration progressively erodes a firm’s ability to switch providers, and what company leadership can do about it. Design/methodology/approach This paper is conceptual. Using resource dependence theory as its base, it draws on transaction cost economics, modularity and real options reasoning, organisational routines theory, and the attention-based view to develop a mechanism and an organisational capability, formalised in four core propositions, a typology matrix and a remedy audit. Findings The paper develops integration drift, a reinforcing process in which locally rational integration decisions cumulatively raise the cost of switching providers. It also introduces architectural hedging capacity (AHC), an organisational capability enacted through three recurring routines: governance-enforced modularity, rehearsed recalibration and sustained managerial attention. And lastly, the argument also identifies a boundary condition in resource dependence theory: where dependence is continuously reproduced through organisational integration, maintaining autonomy requires continuously reproduced exit capacity rather than a one-time remedy. Originality/value The paper extends resource dependence theory to settings where dependence is reproduced inside the firm through its own architecture, not only imposed externally. A typology and a remedy audit checklist give boards and managers a diagnostic for assessing and managing AI-provider dependence.

title: The relationship of parental acceptance-rejection and perceived social support with depressive symptoms and self-confidence in LGBT+ individuals
container-title: Mental Health and Social Inclusion
1ae868c662743f933cc46a94c31db0bacf83ec0a.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine the relationships between parental acceptance and rejection and perceived social support variables and depressive symptoms and self-confidence in LGBT+ young adults living in Turkey. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional correlational online survey was conducted with 126 LGBT+ young adults aged 18–35 living in Turkey. Participants completed scales measuring maternal and paternal acceptance and rejection, perceived social support, depressive symptoms and self-confidence. Pearson correlations and four two-step hierarchical regression analyses were applied to examine the relationships between the variables. Using reverse-order hierarchical regressions, the additional variance explained by the parental rejection variable was evaluated after controlling for perceived social support. Maternal and paternal rejection coefficients were directly compared using linear contrasts. Finally, age and employment status were controlled for in sensitivity analyses, and HC3 robust standard errors were applied. Findings A total of 51.6% of participants scored at or above the Beck Depression Inventory cutoff. Perceived social support was significantly associated with lower depressive symptoms and higher self-confidence (all p = 0.001). Maternal rejection maintained a significant association with depressive symptoms (ß = 0.275, p = 0.002) and self-confidence (ß = −0.182, p = 0.044) after controlling for social support. Paternal rejection was significant in the initial models but was no longer statistically significant when social support was added. In reverse-order hierarchical regression analyses, maternal rejection explained significant additional variance in both outcome variables after controlling for social support. Paternal rejection did not contribute significantly. In the direct comparison, maternal and paternal rejection coefficients differed significantly for self-confidence, but not for depressive symptoms. Sensitivity analyses generally supported the main findings. However, when we used robust HC3 standard errors, the association between maternal rejection and self-confidence lost statistical significance. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional design prevents causal interpretation of the observed associations. The relatively young, predominantly university–student sample and convenience-based online recruitment may also limit generalisability. Because all core variables were assessed using self-report measures, common method variance and social desirability bias should be considered. In addition, multiple regression analyses increased the risk of Type I error. Future research should replicate these findings using larger and more diverse samples, longitudinal designs and confirmatory analyses to clarify the temporal relationships among parental rejection, social support, depressive symptoms and self-confidence. Practical implications The findings highlight the importance of considering parental rejection and perceived social support variables in the psychological assessment of LGBT+ young adults. However, because the design is cross-sectional, causal inferences cannot be made. Social implications The findings highlight the importance of supportive family and social environments for the psychological well-being of LGBT+ young adults. Greater perceived social support was consistently associated with fewer depressive symptoms and higher self-confidence, suggesting that strengthening access to supportive relationships may be particularly relevant for this population. The persistent associations of maternal rejection with both outcomes also underscore the potential value of family-focused psychoeducation, counselling and social support initiatives aimed at reducing rejecting responses and promoting more affirming family relationships. Originality/value This study extends previous LGBT+ mental health research by distinguishing maternal from paternal acceptance-rejection rather than combining parental experiences into a single construct. It also examines self-confidence as a distinct outcome, an area less frequently studied than self-esteem. In addition, the study tests the incremental contribution of perceived social support beyond parental acceptance-rejection across depressive symptoms and self-confidence. The results show that maternal rejection retained unique associations with both outcomes, whereas paternal rejection did not after social support was entered, highlighting potentially different parental patterns.

title: The social self in sustainable luxury services: psychological ownership, identification and willingness to use
container-title: Journal of Services Marketing
30e81d2a0066b03779e9131409ad165890382b3f.abstract: Purpose Drawing on symbolic interactionism, this study aims to examine how social expressiveness influences consumers’ willingness to use sustainable luxury services (SLS). It further investigates the mediating roles of identification with SLS and utilitarian well-being, and the moderating role of psychological ownership. Design/methodology/approach The research uses a two-study design. Study 1 uses survey data from Prolific to test the hypothesized direct, mediation and moderation relationships and to assess the measurement model. Study 2 provides field-based evidence using two Facebook advertisements for a sustainable luxury hotel and click-through rate (CTR) as the behavioral outcome. Study 1 was analyzed using structural equation modeling and moderation analysis. Findings Social expressiveness is positively associated with willingness to use SLS, and this relationship is sequentially mediated by identification with SLS and utilitarian well-being. Psychological ownership significantly moderates the relationships among social expressiveness, identification, utilitarian well-being and willingness to use SLS; however, the negative interaction terms indicate attenuation rather than the hypothesized strengthening. In Study 2, the social-expressiveness advertisement generated a CTR more than 40% higher than the non-social-expressiveness advertisement. Originality/value This research extends luxury service research by showing how a socially expressive motive is translated into willingness to use SLS through identification and well-being. It also positions psychological ownership as a boundary condition in a non-ownership service context, while showing that high psychological ownership can reduce the marginal importance of other drivers of willingness. The study thereby offers an extension and refinement of existing luxury service theory rather than treating SLS as an entirely separate theoretical domain.

title: When AI signalling backfires: a threshold model of perceived firm innovativeness
container-title: Journal of Services Marketing
e7ff3a52b723ffba9e1d77084570515269cb1034.abstract: Purpose This study aims to interrogate the implicit monotonicity assumption in service-dominant logic by examining whether AI signalling intensity uniformly enhances perceived firm innovativeness (PFI) or exhibits threshold-dependent fragility. The study empirically validates relational coherence as a perception-level mediating state, thereby confirming its role as the integrator of AI-enabled capability inference, and specifies structural and demographic boundary conditions. Design/methodology/approach A two-study archival design tests the proposed threshold model. Study 1 exploits discrete AI capability announcements among 1,012 Asian service firms (2012–2024) using event-study difference-in-differences to identify dynamic shifts in customer text-based PFI. Study 2 estimates a dynamic panel system generalised method of moments model incorporating lagged PFI, non-linear AI intensity and relational coherence, addressing reverse causality and omitted capability shocks while computing turning points and moderated curvature. Findings AI signalling exhibits an inverted-U relationship with PFI: moderate intensity strengthens capability perception, whereas high intensity attenuates and reverses effects. Relational coherence mediates this relationship, with the indirect pathway weakening and becoming negative beyond a calculable threshold. The curvature steepens and the threshold occurs earlier in high-contact services and firms serving older customer segments. Originality/value The study advances service-dominant logic by introducing threshold-fragility into its resource-integration premise, repositioning technological operant resources as legitimacy-constrained rather than uniformly accretive. It conceptualises relational coherence as the perception-level integrator governing AI-enabled capability inference and embeds demographic and structural heterogeneity within a formally identified non-linear, dynamic analytical model structure.

title: The impact of explorative generative AI usage on construction project professionals' innovative work behavior: a technology affordance actualization perspective
container-title: Engineering, Construction and Architectural Management
d4b9feb8355cb976dddf7887f9e4fb88383051a9.abstract: Purpose This study attempts to investigate the influence of generative AI (GenAI) on construction project professionals' innovation, specifically by exploring how and under what contextual conditions the use of GenAI fosters innovative work behavior. Design/methodology/approach Grounded in the technology affordance actualization perspective, we identified explorative GenAI usage as the critical trigger of innovative work behavior, specifically by boosting knowledge acquisition, and organizational support as a buffer of the translating process. The theoretical model was empirically tested using the structural equation modeling approach with 239 valid responses from the Chinese construction industry. Findings The findings reveal that explorative GenAI usage acts as a critical actualization behavior that significantly enhances construction project professionals' knowledge acquisition, which subsequently empowers their innovative work behavior. Crucially, this study highlights that the positive effects of explorative GenAI usage are valid when organizational support is high, instead of low. Originality/value This study contributes to construction project management literature by deepening the understanding of the impact of emerging GenAI on micro-level individual behavioral patterns and provides valuable implications for construction managers in today's GenAI era.

title: Racial identity and Chinese language learning among Asian American students
container-title: Journal for Multicultural Education
c03fd7851ac1375eb6160879515e242222ff6751.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine Asian American students’ racial identity and Chinese learning at two Midwestern suburban high schools. Design/methodology/approach Qualitative methodology is used in this study. Through in-depth interviews with student participants, this study explores how Asian American students interpret their racial identity and Chinese language learning experience. Findings This study finds that students’ racial/ethnic identity is shaped by dominant ideologies and power relations. Racism and stereotypical images toward Asian American students are visible and have negatively affected their schooling. Students validate their learning in Chinese and perform their racial/ethnic identity as capital to be invested. However, they barely experience and reflect on racial and cultural diversity at schools. Practical implications The findings of this study have implications for both research and practice at suburban schools. This study suggests school leaders and teachers work with students toward antiracism and create inclusive and equitable learning spaces. Originality/value This study will contribute to an in-depth understanding of Asian American students’ racial/ethnic identity, knowledge and experience in Chinese language classrooms. It will enrich the current literature on Asian American education and identity in second language learning.

title: Beyond grades to learning enhancement: development, implementation and evaluation of a conversational AI agent in medical education
container-title: Education + Training
084b6523ad822ed6a663bd21d0cf5dfd788d527b.abstract: Purpose The integration of conversational artificial intelligence (AI) in medical education shows promise but lacks empirical evidence of effectiveness. This study evaluated a customized generative pre-trained transformer (GPT)-4-based conversational agent designed explicitly for a pharmacology block in undergraduate medical education. Design/methodology/approach A mixed-methods sequential explanatory design was employed in a four-week elective pharmacology block at the College of Medicine, Sulaiman Al-Rajhi University. Phase 1 involved a cross-sectional survey of enrolled students (n = 58) who used the AI tool, with a comparative analysis of their academic performance against historical cohorts without access to AI (2022–2023: n = 33; 2023–2024: n = 37). Academic performance was measured through mid-block quizzes, end-of-block examinations, and total block score. Phase 2 comprised semi-structured interviews (n = 9), transcribed and analyzed thematically. Findings The survey response rate was 89.6% (52/58), and 98.1% (51/52) reported using the tool. Among users, 74.5% engaged with the GPT tool daily. Students reported exceptionally high satisfaction: 92.2% found it more effective than traditional methods, 94.1% felt it made learning more engaging, and the likelihood of recommending it averaged 4.65 ± 0.73 (on a 5-point scale). Frequency of use was significantly associated with perceived improvement in learning (χ2 = 15.84, p &lt; 0.05). Academic performance showed marginal, non-significant improvements: total scores increased by 2.5% (75.52 vs. 77.40, p &gt; 0.05), with pass rates improving from 92.9% to 98.3% (p &gt; 0.05). Qualitative analysis revealed six themes: learning support and academic enhancement; efficiency and accessibility; GPT's supplementary role in learning; perceived strengths and unique features; limitations and challenges; and suggestions for improvement. Originality/value The disconnect between exceptional user engagement and minimal performance improvements challenges traditional evaluation paradigms. While conversational AI may not directly enhance examination scores, students' accounts suggest it may support metacognitive development, reduce cognitive load, and foster critical-thinking skills essential for modern medical practice, thereby necessitating multidimensional assessment frameworks.

title: Design, Implementation, and Empirical Evaluation of a Human–AI Collaborative Adaptive Assessment Model in Higher Education
container-title: Journal of General Education and Humanities
c4fc7c2df67e25e958c78f59c8dc7e87340a3c13.abstract: AI-supported assessment increasingly enables adaptive tasks, automated analysis, and personalized feedback, yet their integration into coherent, human-supervised formative assessment remains insufficiently established. This study developed and evaluated the Human–AI Collaborative Adaptive Assessment Model (HA-CAAM) using Design and Development Research structured through the ADDIE framework. Implemented in a higher-education Media Education course, the model employed performance-responsive task adaptation using predefined thresholds, rubric-guided AI-assisted scoring, formative feedback, and instructor verification. Five experts validated the model, 148 students provided quantitative and qualitative implementation feedback, and 50 student responses were independently assessed by two human raters and AI. Expert validation provided initial evidence of content validity (mean Aiken's V = 0.818). Students reported generally favorable experiences, particularly regarding clarity and feedback usefulness, although Learning Support and Overall User Experience received comparatively lower ratings. AI-generated scores demonstrated strong agreement with human-reference scores (ICC = 0.898), despite individual discrepancies. These findings provide initial evidence of content validity, positive implementation experiences, and scoring agreement, rather than demonstrated improvements in learning outcomes or equivalence between AI and human assessment decisions. HA-CAAM contributes an empirically refined, seven-stage assessment framework that coordinates performance-responsive adaptation, AI-assisted analysis, formative feedback, and instructor-led quality assurance within a human-supervised assessment process.

title: Please Forward this Postdigital Feminist Chain-Letter on Living with AI in Higher Education
container-title: Postdigital Science and Education
97107e75549a7b1d23b73a701cdc9f4ca9237854.abstract: Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) enters higher education within established hierarchies of knowledge and expertise, becoming entangled with judgments about who sounds authoritative and which forms of writing carry weight. Those judgments were gendered, long before GenAI arrived. Drawing on feminist postdigital inquiry and collaborative, experimental approaches to knowledge production, this article reports a chain-letter experiment. Thirteen academics who identify as women or gender-diverse, from nine countries, write in relation to the letters preceding their own. The chain letter produces knowledge through response, so that each letter is partial and the argument accumulates between them. Read together, the letters describe a persistent need to defend expertise within a field shaped by masculine norms of authority, and the frustration and exhaustion this produces. Authors variously report work intensifying rather than easing, critique of GenAI tools being reframed as failures of individual users, and a sense that AI-assisted writing diminishes what makes teaching and research pleasurable. Their positions differ, with some refusing these tools while others work closely with them. At the same time, the exchange brings solidarity, hope and relief, and the discovery that these difficulties are structural as well as personal. The letters suggest that GenAI makes long-standing, gendered questions about expertise and working conditions more pressing, and that these remain shared and unfinished. The article closes with an open invitation to join a feminist and postdigital conversation about GenAI in research and education.

title: A study on the synergistic effects of teacher–student interaction patterns and an AI-based emotional feedback system in secondary school chemistry laboratory classes: an intervention experiment grounded in inquiry-based instruction
container-title: Frontiers in Education
96b6b86b3b878503d2576ece5930fa96e5fb585b.abstract: While prior research has examined how teacher-student interaction influences student learning in conventional chemistry laboratory instruction, few studies have systematically disentangled the synergistic mechanisms that connect dynamic patterns of teacher-student interaction with AI-driven emotional feedback systems-and, critically, how these interactions jointly shape educational outcomes in AI-integrated chemistry laboratory classrooms. This gap constrains the evidence-informed design of emotion-responsive, intelligent chemistry pedagogy. This study employed a mixed-methods design integrating a quasi-experimental intervention with qualitative thematic analysis. A semester-long intervention was implemented with two cohorts of ninth-grade students: an experimental group ( n = 40) receiving inquiry-based chemistry laboratory instruction augmented by an AI-powered emotional feedback system, and a control group ( n = 38) receiving equivalent inquiry-based instruction supported solely by conventional teacher-student interaction. The study comparatively analyzed students' emotional experiences across the two instructional conditions. Distinct emotional trajectories emerged between the groups. The AI-supported experimental group exhibited a statistically significant increase in chemistry laboratory anxiety over the semester, with no meaningful improvement in subjective achievement. In contrast, the control group maintained stable anxiety levels and demonstrated consistent growth in perceived achievement. Moreover, the control group outperformed the experimental group in procedural compliance and the rigor of hands-on laboratory operations. No statistically significant intergroup differences were observed for other affective indicators-including sense of accomplishment and willingness to collaborate. These findings advance the theoretical understanding of human-machine collaborative pedagogy within intelligent learning environments. Empirically grounded, they yield actionable insights for the design of chemistry laboratory instruction in AI-integrated settings-particularly in developing learner-centered, emotion-aware frameworks for human-AI co-teaching.

title: Designing the Future: Leadership and AI
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
48d1a912943fae642bf3d6ccadf6945742236023.abstract: This chapter explores the evolving, reciprocal relationship between leadership and augmented/artificial intelligence (AI) across individual, team, organizational, and societal levels. While we use the term AI throughout in recognition of its widespread usage, we acknowledge the growing preference for augmented intelligence – a framing advanced by leaders in human–machine teaming, such as Paul G. Kaminski (2020), which emphasizes cognitive extension and human–AI partnership. Just as leadership helped shape – and was reshaped by – the Agricultural, Industrial, and Information Ages, the emerging Age of AI demands a renewed focus on human values and moral courage. Far from a neutral tool, AI reflects the intentions of its designers and the integrity of its leaders, and in turn, transforms how we work, relate, and lead. Grounded in authentic and moral leadership theory, systems thinking, and sociotechnical design, we examine how leaders can engage AI in ways that safeguard human dignity, foster trust, and advance ethical innovation. Through a multilevel lens, we explore how AI influences self-awareness, interpersonal responsibility, team dynamics, and global leadership strategies. We extend prior work on efficacy-performance spirals to the AI context, showing how trust, learning, and adaptation can reinforce or erode across levels over time. Drawing on work published in Organizational Dynamics, this chapter also applies the TRUST, COACH, and CARES frameworks to AI leadership. As AI reshapes decision-making and connection, the defining force will not be technology itself, but the authenticity, trustworthiness, and moral imagination of those who lead it.

title: Digital Transformation 2.0: Integrating AI and Empowering People for Sustainable Growth in the Future of Work
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
cd295fcbb5cd4820a5d40948a004a94d7d35cbec.abstract: The digital era has reached a new inflection point, accelerated by artificial intelligence (AI) and organizations’ need to adapt to dynamic, technology-driven conditions. This chapter examines the legacy of Digital Transformation 1.0—highlighting failures and their causes—and defines the imperatives of AI-infused Digital Transformation 2.0. Drawing from relevant case studies, research, and executive interviews, it emphasizes the critical shift from episodic digitization to sustained AI-embedded digitalization. Leaders must enable systems-level transformation across people, process, and technology while aligning cultural, ethical, and operational domains. Digital Transformation 2.0 demands coordinated iterative design over monolithic strategy, requiring organizations to reimagine work as a fluid mix of tasks rather than fixed roles. Human–AI collaboration is a new reality that depends on psychological safety, AI literacy, and digital dexterity across the blended human-AI workforce. Successful transformation hinges on new leadership behaviors that elevate trust, agency, and adaptability while modeling and encouraging the use of new tools. The piece explores decentralized workforce models, the urgency of building AI-ready cultures, and a new social contract. It examines how agile frameworks, value mapping, and upskilling efforts create coherence amid complexity, making change tangible and participatory. The Future of Work is framed not as a fixed destination, but as a dynamic system requiring deliberate, ongoing leadership to combine machine capabilities with uniquely human capabilities. Ultimately, this work calls for defining or reframing organizational purpose and progress: AI can multiply what we value, but it is up to us to define what we value—and how we lead with it.

title: A Cautionary Tale: When AI Outpaces Character in Leadership Development
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
0b2e9c41561f67c0653a2cb28c371eb88152dc74.abstract: This chapter, A Cautionary Tale, explores the risks and unintended consequences of pursuing leadership development and organizational transformation without grounding efforts in ethical discernment, evidence-based practice, and human-centered design. Drawing from decades of experience in the military, higher education, and executive coaching, the chapter highlights how well-intentioned initiatives often falter when leaders prioritize efficiency, image, or short-term outcomes over trust, character, and sustainable growth. Through illustrative narratives and applied research, it examines how misplaced reliance on tools, trends, or unchecked authority can erode organizational culture, diminish performance, and compromise individual well-being. The cautionary perspective emphasizes that leadership is not merely the accumulation of skills or the exercise of influence but a continual process of reflection, humility, and responsibility. Practical insights are offered for leaders navigating high-pressure contexts, including the importance of aligning purpose with practice, cultivating resilience, and embedding feedback loops that elevate both performance and values. Ultimately, the chapter argues that the true cost of neglecting character in leadership is not only organizational inefficiency but also the erosion of human dignity and trust – resources far more difficult to restore than financial capital. By reframing leadership as a moral as well as strategic endeavor, A Cautionary Tale serves as both a warning and a guide for leaders committed to building organizations that endure and uplift.

title: Agents of Change: Teamwork and Collaboration with AI at the Table
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
dcfd8d7ff89f9b704d69b63c67897d2290b5f515.abstract: This chapter explores the transformative implications of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) technologies as a “teammate” in leading virtual and hybrid teams. The growing prevalence of GenAI tools and the shift toward remote and hybrid work create a critical need to reexamine how leaders demonstrate essential leadership competencies in these environments. Framed by discussions on GenAI as both a collaborator and a tool, this chapter considers the ethical dilemmas, pedagogical innovations, and practical strategies for integrating GenAI into team leadership. Building on the authors’ previous work in exploring leadership competencies for leading at the virtual table, it investigates how GenAI reshapes trust, collaboration, and productivity in diverse teams while balancing human agency and technological capabilities. Through critical questions, a case study reflection, and practical takeaways, the chapter offers a roadmap for fostering GenAI literacy (LeaderAIcy), managing ethical and technical considerations, and leveraging GenAI for meaningful leadership and teamwork in global, hybrid contexts.

title: Using AI Tools for Leader Development and Assessing Competencies
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
6670b996a20df16f557191ac8831733fc9abb418.abstract: This chapter explores how the United States Air Force (USAF) leader development course (LDC) used artificial intelligence (AI)/sentiment analysis (SA) for leader development and assessing leader development competencies that support learning objectives and course outcomes. A narrative format is first used to describe the engaged practice with key stakeholders and the staged approach process that underlaid the development of how innovation is driving change for leaders, assessing performance specific to selected competencies in mixed reality scenarios, and offering ways of strengthening leader development. A five-phased qualitative structure is used along with content analysis, design thinking, and a grounded theory approach. After coding data using thematic analysis from phases 1 to 4, a grounded theory approach is used to better understand the findings and discoveries with literature related to innovation development, AI technology associated with immersive learning environments, design thinking and change, performance and competency assessment, and leader development. A new theory (AI-augmented leader development theory) and a new model, emotionally tuned competency assessment model (ECAM), emerged as well as emphasis on the power of using dialogic development in virtual contexts to train, assess, and develop leaders. Theoretical and practical implications, as well as recommendations are provided for improving how AI tools can be used for leader development.

title: AI as a Catalyst for Change: Transforming Human Resources in Educational Institutions
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
93d2ee78452d2d36780fedbbf08d870e031b50d3.abstract: This chapter delves into the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and the human resources (HR) function within a public school district, offering a detailed case study of its implementation. It examines how AI tools were leveraged to streamline recruitment, enhance employee engagement, and support data-driven decision-making. The chapter highlights key challenges and opportunities, focusing on trust building and change management strategies essential for the successful adoption of AI tools. Ethical considerations are explored, including the need to mitigate algorithmic bias, ensure fairness in automated processes, and uphold data privacy and security standards. Recommendations emphasize the importance of transparent communication, reengaging employees through inclusive practices, and building trust in AI systems while reskilling and upskilling employees. By combining practical insights with emerging trends in digital transformation, this chapter provides a roadmap for educational leaders and HR professionals seeking to responsibly leverage AI in their organizations.

title: Leading Inclusively: Universal Design Principles in the Age of AI
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
ce20000e654b8aeff35b1155111a8b38d1312b8b.abstract: Modern organizational leaders increasingly encounter artificial intelligence (AI) technologies in their workplaces, creating both opportunities and challenges for inclusive leadership. This chapter introduces Universal Design for Learning (UDL) as a framework for navigating these technological changes while maintaining human-centered approaches to inclusion. UDL’s three core principles – multiple means of representation, engagement, and action/expression – provide leaders with practical strategies for creating flexible workplace systems that benefit all employees. When thoughtfully implemented, AI technologies can support these principles through personalized learning experiences, enhanced accessibility features, and improved communication tools. However, the chapter cautions leaders to ensure that technology is amplifying rather than replacing human judgment and cultural competence. The chapter addresses critical considerations for leaders, including the risks of algorithmic bias, the limitations of automated solutions in complex interpersonal situations, and the importance of maintaining employee agency and choice. It examines common implementation barriers – from cost concerns to misconceptions about technology as a cure-all for inclusion challenges – while demonstrating that UDL principles require minimal investment and generate significant returns. Through examination of both opportunities and pitfalls, leaders learn to distinguish between technological applications that enhance inclusion and those that may inadvertently create barriers. The chapter provides actionable guidance for implementing UDL principles in technology-enhanced environments, positioning inclusive leadership capabilities as essential competencies for organizational success regardless of technological context.

title: Generative AI Powered by Large Language Models for Leadership Development: Between Epistemic Responsibility and the Future of Innovation
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
2befe576d22df3abb8f03a51478516f11ce0d40c.abstract: This chapter examines language-based generative AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), as active epistemic agents in leadership development. Moving beyond their perceived neutrality, the authors argue that LLMs serve as mirrors of dominant assumptions, co-constructors of leadership meaning, and framing devices of legitimate knowledge. The sources highlight how these systems reinforce prevailing Euro-American managerial ideals, often marginalizing diverse leadership paradigms such as Indigenous, collectivist, or spiritual frameworks, thereby amplifying structural and cultural biases. Through epistemic feedback loops and personalization, LLMs can subtly shape leadership identity and constrain developmental horizons, leading to adaptive standardization or performative conformity. The chapter emphasizes the critical need for epistemic responsibility in innovation leadership, advocating for leaders to interrogate system framings, reflect on their influence, and cultivate design awareness. This involves fostering inclusive data practices, participatory design methodologies, and culturally responsive AI governance to ensure AI-mediated innovation ecosystems are just, inclusive, and reflect pluralistic worldviews. Ultimately, the chapter calls for leaders to reclaim framing power and engage AI dialogically to foster an innovation leadership that is reflexive, ethically grounded, and attuned to human complexities.

title: The Influence of Generative Artificial Intelligence on K–12 Educational Leadership
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
2e16eaf81aea3695e6f9f9b263f8c5764ccfa4cb.abstract: This chapter examines the transformative influence of generative artificial intelligence (AI) on K–12 educational leadership after the wake of the COVID-19 pandemic. The rapid adoption of remote learning technologies created a tech-dependent educational environment, accelerating AI integration in both classroom instruction and school administration. As generative AI tools, such as large language models (LLMs) and chatbots, become increasingly accessible, school leaders face new opportunities and challenges in leveraging these tools to support instructional design, data-driven decision-making, and school governance. This chapter explores how AI is reshaping educators’ roles, enabling real-time feedback, streamlining administrative tasks, and personalizing learning experiences, while also requiring ethical oversight, digital literacy, and sustained professional development. Attention is given to the complexities of equity, access, and teacher readiness, emphasizing the need for thoughtful implementation and culturally responsive AI use.

title: Inverse design of terahertz metasurface polarization converters based on generative adversarial networks
container-title: Optics Continuum
739abe95c331ed3ee886745c2727c1c6332ce894.abstract: A reflection-type broadband terahertz metasurface polarization converter with a three-layer structure—comprising a patterned metal layer, a dielectric layer, and a metallic ground plane—is inversely designed based on a Wasserstein generative adversarial network with gradient penalty (WGAN-GP). By incorporating the Wasserstein distance and a gradient penalty term, the WGAN-GP effectively overcomes the training instability inherent in conventional generative adversarial networks, thereby enabling the construction of an end-to-end mapping model from target spectra to metasurface structural parameters. The results demonstrate that the WGAN-GP achieves efficient and high-accuracy inverse design, with a single inference time of only 30 ms and a mean absolute error of structural parameter prediction as low as 0.1263. The optimized metasurface polarization converter exhibits a consistently high polarization conversion ratio exceeding 0.8 over the 3–7.5 THz frequency range, corresponding to a relative bandwidth of up to 86%, and maintains excellent angular stability within an incidence angle range of 0° to 50°. This work not only verifies the efficiency and reliability of WGAN-GP in the inverse design of complex electromagnetic devices, but also provides an effective solution for the development of high-performance terahertz metasurfaces, with the potential to accelerate device innovation and applications of terahertz technologies in key fields such as communications, sensing, imaging, and spectrum security.

title: Generative structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model for MR to CT image synthesis in radiotherapy planning
container-title: Physics in Medicine & Biology
cfa98f94b57aed8a928c9fb300f2a97663467510.abstract: Abstract Objective . Radiotherapy (RT) planning uses magnetic resonance (MR) imaging for soft tissue information, while computerized tomography (CT) imaging is necessary for dose calculation. Synthetic CTs generated from MR images (MRI) streamline the clinical workflow by reducing the need for an actual CT acquisition while minimizing radiation exposure, enabling adaptive RT workflows. The objective of this study is to propose a new RT planning model combining stable structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) with MRI conditioning, for generating synthetic CT (sCT) images. Approach . The model combines a hybrid network architecture with a dynamic guidance mechanism, conditioned on MR images, to direct the reverse diffusion process and preserve structural details. The model integrates both a denoising and a refinement network: the denoising network predicts and progressively removes the noise added during the forward diffusion process, while the guidance strength adapts at each timestep based on the noise level. This adaptive guidance mechanism uses a non-linear formulation that satisfies noise constraints, optimizing the denoising process while preserving structural integrity. The training process includes a weighted structure-guided loss function that combines the DDPM noise loss with a dynamic guidance regularizer term for sCT image generation via noise prediction, along with a reconstruction loss for refinement. Main results . Evaluated on three paired MR/CT datasets (head and neck (HaN), as well as brain), our model outperforms recent MR to CT synthesis models, showing the best performance in image quality based on the mean absolute error in Hounsfield units, as well as improved peak signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity index and gradient magnitude similarity deviation compared to other DDPM and generative adversarial network approaches. When comparing tumor segmentation quality, it achieves the best results in Dice score (0.76 ± 0.04), Hausdorff distance (7.9 ± 2.0), intersection over union (0.69 ± 0.04), geometric consistency index (0.84 ± 0.04) and precision-recall index (PRI) (0.88 ± 0.03) for segmented tumor regions in the generated sCT images. Finally, it achieves the best mean square error of 10.1 ± 2.6 Gray (Gy) in the head-and-neck cohort, when evaluating dose planning on sCT, with a conformity index of 0.61 ± 0.02 and a homogeneity index of 0.10 ± 0.02. Significance . Performance shows promise in integration for RT in HaN, as well as in brain cancers.

title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
93efb8d8a2efd6ac00960e2f7910f482c84055f4.abstract: Abstract Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

title: Distributed Neural Dynamics Underlie the Shift from Movement Preparation to Execution
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
7a79083e41e8564c05cef0c9e6a1179e83f26049.abstract: Abstract Understanding how neural population activity supports the transition from movement preparation to execution remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience. Invasive recordings in nonhuman primates indicate that motor preparation and execution occupy orthogonal subspaces within the primary motor cortex (M1), yet how these neural dynamics evolve across broader networks and support skilled, memory-guided action remains poorly understood. We used source-resolved magnetoencephalography during a memory-guided finger-sequence task to track population dynamics across a cortico-hippocampal network. Manifold trajectories and decoding revealed that preparation and execution of movement sequences occupy distinct, yet not fully orthogonal, neural subspaces—a separation that generalized across all regions but was most pronounced in motor regions. Crucially, we identified a hierarchical spatio-temporal transition across the brain: The state shift originated in the hippocampus via theta-band modulations and rippled through the pre-SMA, SMA, and lateral premotor areas before culminating in M1 via broadband activity. This progression follows the functional hierarchy of descending motor pathways, with M1 shifting last, 160 msec before the first button press. Although sequence identity could be decoded from all areas during execution, only the hippocampus and M1 maintained predictive representations of upcoming sequences during preparation. These findings demonstrate that the initiation of complex motor sequences relies on a well-timed integration of hippocampal memory systems with primary motor output, rather than being a process localized to the motor cortices alone.

title: Sequential Sampling from Memory Underlies Perceptual Decisions Unyoked from Actions
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
a917d6aa52f462098a3786e8e5c48f2839ba057f.abstract: Abstract Perceptual decision-making refers to the class of decisions in which sensory evidence is used to categorize percepts and guide actions. Conventionally, categorical decisions are thought to precede motor actions. However, recent studies in nonhuman primates challenge this assumption—when perceptual decisions were uncoupled from the actions they bear upon, animals postponed the decisions until relevant response options were revealed. To determine whether this postponement stems from cognitive limitations unique to nonhuman primates, we conducted a similar experiment with human participants. Naive participants viewed a random dot motion (RDM) stimulus that was difficult to categorize. After a delay period following the RDM, two choice targets were presented and participants decided which target lay closer to the perceived motion direction. Decision accuracy varied across participants, reflecting individual differences in ability to integrate motion evidence. Notably, participants with higher decision accuracy showed prolonged deliberation after choice-target presentation. Furthermore, the time they took to report their decisions depended on the strength of the motion evidence. This pattern of accuracy and decision reporting time could be accounted for by a bounded diffusion model in which participants sequentially sample stored sensory information from memory during the target selection phase. When the RDM was challenging to categorize, the subsequent appearance of the targets provided a framework to interrogate stored evidence and render a decision. Our results reveal a strategic feature of working memory of retaining information based on its future utility. This observation opens new avenues for investigating how memory and decision-making interact.

title: Confounds in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging—Part III: Auxiliary Data
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
7ebbf91cc1104ca6a325a8fc4b3255a08d3c579e.abstract: Abstract In the first part of this series, we reviewed the pathways that bring about confounding nuisance signals in fMRI. Then, in the second part, we considered how human factors can modify these pathways. In this, the third and final part, we review auxiliary data that may allow researchers to identify and perhaps correct for nuisance signals and their modifiers. We consider three broad categories of data: (1) measures that can be collected synchronously with the fMRI, (2) other MRI scans that either capture trait information or attempt to define the state that exists during an fMRI scan in the same session, and (3) non-MRI measures that can be collected before or after the scan and that also capture trait or relevant state factors influencing the fMRI. We conclude with some recommendations on ways to improve fMRI experiments going forward.
