title: Cognitive Metaphors as a Means of Persuasive Influence in Texts of Various Genres
container-title: Journal of Management Practices, Humanities and Social Sciences
82422fddc0741ef8edb2c1df403a0499c983b067.abstract: The present research is dedicated to the effectiveness of cognitive metaphors as a means of persuasion in political, media, and artistic discourses. Even though numerous studies have already been conducted on metaphorical conceptualization in particular discourse types, comparisons of metaphor structure, function, and audience reactions are rare. In the present study, 30 English texts (published between 2020 and 2024) belonging to the genre of political speech, media, and art (10 texts in each genre) were selected among materials from political databases, English-language magazines and literary journals. 90 people aged 20-35 (M = 26.2) evaluated metaphorical messages using C. Osgood’s semantic differential, questionnaire about the effectiveness of persuasive message and free answers. Content analysis and contextual-semantic analysis, along with descriptive statistics and one-way ANOVA were used to identify some patterns. The major source domains in political discourse include: WAR, PATH, MECHANISM, BODY and GAME, in media discourse: ELEMENT, DISEASE, THEATER, ORGANISM, and WEAPON, in artistic discourse: NATURE, LIGHT/DARKNESS, JOURNEY, BODY, and EVERYDAY LIFE. The research revealed the following: political metaphors have a tendency to be normative and rationalizing; media metaphors are critical-evaluative and disturbing; artistic metaphors show better emotional appeal and symbolism. The distinctive feature of the research is a combination of conceptual, pragmatic, and recipient-based analysis of cognitive metaphors. The findings of the research contribute to the development of cognitive metaphor theory by providing evidence concerning the persuasive and emotive effects of metaphor usage.

title: Prospective associations between diet quality, frailty and incident cognitive impairment in the health and retirement study
container-title: BMC Global and Public Health
80417bcdac85d08136be021ebebfe83d3bb6e56b.abstract: Abstract Background Diet quality is a modifiable determinant of healthy aging, potentially influencing physical and cognitive functioning through inflammatory and metabolic pathways. Although healthier dietary patterns have been linked to reduced frailty and cognitive decline, findings remain inconsistent. The interrelationships among diet quality, physical frailty, and incident cognitive impairment, including potential modification by specific dietary components, remain poorly understood. Methods We analyzed 1,636 cognitively normal participants in 2016 from the Health and Retirement Study, a longitudinal study of adults in the United States (U.S.), with diet assessed in 2013, frailty in 2016, and cognitive follow-up through 2022. Cognitive impairment was assessed with cognitive tests and used the Langa–Weir classification; diet quality was measured using the Healthy Eating Index–2015 (HEI-2015); and physical frailty used a modified Fried phenotype. Survey-weighted regression, Cox models, four-way decomposition, competing-risk and multistate models, and additive Bayesian network (ABN)–informed generalized structural equation models (GSEM) were applied. Results Higher HEI-2015 scores were associated with lower frailty (β = −0.13, P < 0.001), but not with incident cognitive impairment. Frailty was associated with higher cognitive risk in minimally adjusted models (Hazard Ratio (HR) = 2.27, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.56–3.32), with attenuation after full adjustment. Exploratory analyses identified 13 nominally significant food-item associations with composite cognitive impairment, including higher risks associated with selected dairy products, processed meats, and beverages, and an inverse association with red wine (HR = 0.77, 95% CI: 0.66–0.89). None survived FDR correction. Five dietary associations with probable dementia alone survived FDR correction but remained exploratory. Four-way decomposition provided limited evidence of dietary mediation or interaction, while sensitivity analyses supported attenuation of frailty–cognition associations. Conclusions Higher diet quality was associated with lower physical frailty but not independently with incident cognitive impairment. Food-specific associations were heterogeneous and largely did not survive multiple-testing correction. Findings warrant replication before drawing dietary recommendations for cognitive health.

title: A Teacher's Concerns about AI in Primary School: Critical Thinking, Personal Data and the Fear of Cognitive Dependence
container-title: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
48daf9f5949effd20204e7775dffc33ae168a630.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. Written from the perspective of a primary school teacher and principal, this perspective paper examines three interrelated concerns of the author herself. These concerns arose from a wish to protect her pupils and led her to study the topic for her own professional development and to help her colleagues make teaching safer and better. They concern developing critical thinking towards AI-generated answers, protecting the personal data of minors, and the fear that excessive assistance from AI will weaken pupils' thinking. Drawing on a narrative, non-systematic review of recent research on cognitive offloading, the European and Greek regulatory framework, and illustrative examples from the author's own teaching practice and lesson scenarios for primary school, it argues that the fear of cognitive dependence is a plausible concern rather than an established finding for primary school pupils. The available evidence, which comes mainly from adolescents and adults, suggests that the form of AI support (whether it replaces the learner's effort or scaffolds it) may be an important factor. AI is regarded throughout as a valuable tool; the risk lies mainly in the way it is used. The classroom examples come from ordinary lessons whose only purpose was to teach pupils to question AI answers and to protect themselves when using AI. They were not planned as research, no research data were collected, and they are offered as the author's practitioner reflections, not as findings. The author's classroom experience illustrates that such activities can be implemented in ordinary primary school lessons, but their effects on pupils' critical thinking have not yet been evaluated. The paper relates the three concerns to long-standing educational principles, in particular Socratic questioning, Dewey's reflective thought and Vygotskian scaffolding. On this basis, it proposes a simple, as yet untested three-step classroom protocol (``think -- ask -- check''), age-appropriate data protection rules, and a role for school leadership, and outlines questions for future research.

title: The personal side of cognitive effort
container-title: Translation, Cognition & Behavior
Translation, Cognition and Behavior
ae01894e5cbb76871e2d262fad88c10d8b1365d0.abstract: Abstract This study investigates whether the Need for Cognition (NFC), an individual’s inclination to engage in mentally challenging tasks, predicts cognitive effort in translation and moderates how effort scales with text readability. Twenty-one native Arabic-speaking translators completed the 18-item NFC scale and translated six English texts of varying readability; eight eye-tracking and keylogging indicators captured their effort. Robust linear mixed-effects models showed limited direct effects of NFC, with marginal positive associations with character insertions and source-text reading time. NFC played a clearer role as a moderator. On the second-hardest-to-read text, high-NFC translators made more deletions and insertions and had longer production times than low-NFC peers. On the hardest-to-read text, high-NFC translators spent longer reading the source text. These findings suggest that translation process research accounts of effort should incorporate stable motivational dispositions alongside source-text demands. Given the modest sample, the findings are exploratory and require replication.

title: Learning mathematics in rural and urban schools
container-title: Australian and International Journal of Rural Education
24079e646f3a74e57ec036c3c45114583c0fa9da.abstract: Students’ mathematical problem solving is influenced not only by curriculum and instruction but also by the territorial contexts in which schools operate. This study examines how school typology—Rural, Urban, and High-Diversity Urban—relates to primary students’ performance and cognitive processing in arithmetic word problems. A total of 2,306 students from Grades 1–6 in Castellón (Spain) completed problem-solving tasks for this study using AWPSolver, a digital environment that captures detailed indicators of reading behaviour, problem-solving actions, and efficiency. We analysed success rates, reading and solving times, and efficiency indices using generalized linear models for performance, non-parametric tests for processing times, and correlations between speed and accuracy. Results revealed clear developmental improvements across grades, with older students showing higher success rates and shorter reading and solving times. Rural students tended to show favourable patterns of success and efficiency in several comparisons, particularly in the upper grades, whereas High-Diversity Urban students showed lower estimated success probabilities in some grades and stronger associations between processing time and performance in the upper grades. By integrating outcome and process-based measures, this study provides new insight into how territorial educational contexts are associated with the cognitive dynamics of mathematical problem solving. The findings suggest that school typology relates not only to achievement outcomes, but also to students’ reading and problem-solving processes. These results contribute to research on rural–urban educational differences and offer implications for designing context-sensitive instructional strategies that account for students’ social, territorial, and linguistic environments.

title: Associations of white matter microstructural damage with both cross-sectional and longitudinal cognitive decline in cerebral amyloid angiopathy and non-CAA mild cognitive impairment
container-title: Frontiers in Aging Neuroscience
33bb561edbd24eebc6e8ee0e2d3d40cb2d0139e4.abstract: Background Peak width of skeletonized mean diffusivity (PSMD) is an automated diffusion marker that captures white matter microstructural damage more sensitively than conventional small vessel disease markers. We investigated the cross sectional and longitudinal associations of PSMD and amyloid β (A β ) burden with cognition, and whether concomitant cerebral amyloid angiopathy (CAA) modifies these relationships in mild cognitive impairment (MCI). Methods A total of 124 MCI patients were included from the Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, classified as CAA-MCI or non-CAA MCI by Boston criteria version 2.0. Cross-sectional and longitudinal associations between baseline PSMD, amyloid burden, and cognitive outcomes were assessed using linear regression, linear mixed-effects models, and Cox proportional hazards models. Results PSMD showed strong cross-sectional associations with processing speed and executive function, however this association was not modified by CAA status. No significant difference for longitudinal cognition changes between CAA and non-CAA groups. Within CAA-MCI, higher PSMD correlated with lower A β burden but not with cognition. Over 4 years, PSMD did not predict decline after correction for multiple comparisons in both CAA and non-CAA groups. Greater A β burden predicted multi- domain decline and dementia conversion in both groups, and the A β -associated decline in global cognition was steeper in CAA-MCI. Conclusion PSMD indexed current processing speed and executive function rather than subsequent change, independently of conventional small vessel disease markers and of CAA, whereas A β burden drove longitudinal decline and dementia conversion. The two biomarkers therefore appear to capture processes unfolding on different time scales. Whether concomitant CAA modifies amyloid-related decline requires confirmation in larger cohorts.

title: T-cell memory, tumor microenvironment, and alloreactivity in intracellular neoantigen–targeted immunotherapy
container-title: Frontiers in Immunology
95b4f2cd4bddbeff1d3fcf4bf97c70a4d7bc78ff.abstract: Advances in genetic engineering have transformed cancer immunotherapy, enabling the development of T-cell–based and antibody-based strategies that target intracellular neoantigens. In particular, TCR-engineered T cells and TCR-mimic antibodies recognizing peptide–MHC complexes have expanded the range of targetable tumor antigens beyond surface proteins. This Perspective outlines a conceptual framework in which three interacting but context-dependent biological axes–T-cell memory differentiation, tumor microenvironment (TME) regulation, and control of alloreactivity–collectively determine therapeutic efficacy and safety. While T-cell memory and TME-mediated suppression broadly influence the persistence and function of engineered T-cells, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD) represents a distinct challenge restricted to allogeneic settings. Emerging evidence highlights the importance of memory T-cell subsets, particularly stem-like and central memory populations, in sustaining long-term antitumor immunity. However, their function is frequently constrained by immunosuppressive cellular networks and metabolic barriers within the TME, including regulatory T cells, tumor-associated macrophages, and myeloid-derived suppressor cells. In parallel, advances in graft engineering and T-cell receptor editing provide strategies to mitigate alloreactivity while preserving graft-versus-tumor effects. By integrating these dimensions, this Perspective emphasizes the need for coordinated therapeutic strategies that balance durability, immune tolerance, and microenvironmental adaptation. A deeper mechanistic understanding of these interactions will be critical for the rational design of next-generation immunotherapies targeting intracellular tumor antigens.

title: The role of the right temporal lobe in neural network mechanisms during working memory encoding
container-title: Frontiers in Human Neuroscience
faa6905dfb61b7120ab6c9bc8594c020571e8766.abstract: Background Visual working memory (vWM) impairment is common in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and is more severe in those with right TLE (RTLE), suggesting the significant role of right temporal lobe in WM processes. Methods We recruited patients with left TLE (LTLE group, n = 20), RTLE (RTLE group, n = 20) and 35 healthy controls (Control), and examined their vWM performance while simultaneously recording task-based EEG. The alterations in the neural oscillations and neural network were analyzed during the WM encoding phase. In addition, we examined the relationship between the neural oscillations and WM performance, as well as the relationship between the neural network and WM performance, to further explore the role of the right temporal lobe in WM encoding. Results Remarkably lower accuracy (both p &lt; 0.001) and significantly longer response times (LTLE vs. Control: p = 0.026; RTLE vs. Control: p &lt; 0.001) were found in both LTLE and RTLE groups compared with controls. The RTLE group experienced notably delayed response time in comparison to the LTLE group ( p = 0.026). In comparison to the LTLE group, the RTLE group displayed reduced theta power spectral density for the frontal ( p = 0.024) and occipital ( p = 0.011) regions, along with the Fz channel ( p = 0.047). DTF F_outflow and DTF Fz_outflow values in the RTLE group displayed reduction relative to the LTLE group (DTF F_outflow : p = 0.026; DTF Fz_outflow : p = 0.037). The LTLE group showed weakened information flow from Fz to P3 (IF Fz → P3 , ANOVA, F = 3.45, p = 0.037; LSD, LTLE vs. Control: p = 0.013), whereas the RTLE group exhibited weakened information flow from Fz to P4 (IF Fz → P4 ; ANOVA, F = 3.78, p = 0.028; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.029), Fz to T4 (IF Fz → T4 ; ANOVA, F = 4.67, p = 0.012; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.009), and Fz to TP8 (IF Fz → TP8 ; ANOVA, F = 3.11, p = 0.050 ; LSD, RTLE vs. Control: p = 0.017), which were positively associated with accuracy and inversely associated with response time. Conclusion Abnormal information transfer from the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex to the superior parietal lobe during the encoding phase may causes WM deficits; damage to information transfer from the dorsomedial prefrontal cortex to the right middle temporal and right inferior temporal gyri exacerbates WM impairments.

title: Generative AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement in university EFL writing: a mixed-methods study of autonomy, self-regulated learning, and AI literacy
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
afb75769dc989373555c79649418b5d149ca608a.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to obtain feedback in English as a foreign language (EFL) writing, but its educational significance depends on how learners interpret and regulate that feedback. Grounded in Self-Determination Theory and self-regulated learning theory, this explanatory sequential mixed-methods study examined an AI-supported motivated self-regulated learning framework using a cross-sectional survey of 486 university EFL students and follow-up interviews with 20 students. Structural equation modeling identified a positive direct association between reported AI feedback use and deep cognitive engagement, together with a positive indirect statistical association through learning autonomy and self-regulated learning. The AI feedback use–autonomy association was stronger at higher modeled levels of AI literacy. Interview accounts described feedback-related control, critical evaluation, and awareness of AI limitations, alongside contrasting experiences of rapid polishing and careful evaluation despite limited familiarity with AI. Integration of the two strands highlighted variation in how learners evaluated and incorporated feedback. These self-report findings do not establish temporal ordering or causal effects. They identify learner agency, strategic regulation, and critical evaluation as relevant considerations for future investigations of AI-supported writing.

title: Information overload, cognitive fatigue, and postgraduates’ intention to use generative artificial intelligence for English academic writing: the role of lower-order cognitive offloading
container-title: Frontiers in Psychology
44519a3982b4f3a7618933a7c685ba32b093e792.abstract: Background Generative artificial intelligence (AI) returns large amounts of information that postgraduates must judge and integrate when they write in English. The stressor-strain-outcome framework suggests that such overload strains cognitive resources and weakens plans for further use. This study tested whether cognitive fatigue links perceived information overload with later behavioral intention to use AI for English academic writing. It also tested whether lower-order cognitive offloading, such as having AI summarize papers, conditions the overload-fatigue association. Methods In total, 475 Chinese master’s and doctoral students who used AI for English academic writing completed three surveys at two-week intervals. Overload and offloading were measured at Time 1, fatigue at Time 2, and intention at Time 3. A moderated mediation model adjusted for baseline fatigue, baseline intention, and AI-use frequency. Results Higher perceived information overload accompanied higher cognitive fatigue 2 weeks later and weaker behavioral intention 4 weeks later, net of baseline levels. Cognitive fatigue was associated with weaker later intention and carried part of the overload-intention association. The overload-fatigue association was weaker at higher levels of lower-order cognitive offloading. Among the most frequent offloaders it was not statistically significant, which does not indicate its absence. The indirect association through fatigue was likewise weaker at higher offloading. These patterns held with additional covariates, a competing interaction with AI-use frequency, and shortened scales. Conclusion In this sample, cognitive fatigue accompanied the prospective association between overload and weaker plans to use AI. This pathway was weaker among postgraduates who delegated foundational tasks more often. Writing programs can teach students which foundational tasks to delegate, and tool developers can limit output overload.

title: Atherogenic index of plasma and cognitive recovery trajectories after ischemic stroke: a retrospective longitudinal cohort study
container-title: Frontiers in Behavioral Neuroscience
d6dc75817dcb14a78d909c9e414016fb939ed79e.abstract: Background Early cognitive recovery after ischemic stroke is heterogeneous. We examined global cognitive recovery trajectories and their associations with the atherogenic index of plasma (AIP) during and after inpatient rehabilitation. Methods This retrospective longitudinal cohort included 210 patients with imaging-confirmed ischemic stroke and available cognitive assessments at rehabilitation admission, discharge, and approximately 3 months after discharge. AIP was calculated from triglyceride and high-density lipoprotein cholesterol concentrations in the same first fasting blood sample collected within 24 h after rehabilitation admission. Latent class mixed models characterized Chinese Mini-Mental State Examination (CMMS) trajectories. Secondary, exploratory analyses examined AIP associations with trajectory membership and longitudinal CMMS and Modified Barthel Index (MBI) scores. Trajectory-membership analyses accounted for classification uncertainty using two-stage joint likelihood estimation with 1,000 parametric bootstrap draws. Results Three trajectories were identified: moderate-baseline marked-improvement (94 patients [44.8%]), higher-baseline modest-improvement (69 [32.9%]), and low-baseline persistently low (47 [22.4%]). In the fully adjusted model, each 1-SD higher AIP was associated with greater odds of the low-baseline persistently low trajectory versus the moderate-baseline marked-improvement trajectory (odds ratio, 1.85; 95% CI, 1.16–2.96; nominal p = 0.0095), but not versus the higher-baseline modest-improvement trajectory. Each 1-SD higher AIP was associated with 0.77 points less CMMS improvement from admission to follow-up (95% CI, −1.09 to −0.44; nominal p &lt; 0.001). There was no clear association with longitudinal MBI recovery. Conclusion Early global cognitive recovery followed heterogeneous patterns. Higher rehabilitation-phase AIP was associated with less CMMS improvement and with the persistently low rather than the marked-improvement trajectory. These exploratory findings require independent replication; their clinical importance and prognostic utility remain uncertain.

title: Association between any informal helping and cognitive function among older adults: a propensity score study
container-title: Frontiers in Public Health
712173a9caa4ceb9a02f08a748588bf6e858bce8.abstract: Objectives Whether everyday informal helping is associated with cognitive function in later life, particularly among older adults recruited from healthcare and residential care institutions, remains insufficiently characterized. This study examined the association between any informal helping and cognitive function and explored the cross-sectional statistical indirect association through depressive symptoms. Methods Using a multicenter cross-sectional design and non-probability convenience sampling, we recruited adults aged 60 years or older from seven healthcare and residential care institutions in Hubei Province, China, between June 2025 and June 2026. To reduce baseline differences between participants who did and did not provide any informal helping, seven propensity score (PS) approaches were applied, including inverse probability of treatment weighting (IPTW) and overlap weighting (OW). Depressive symptoms were assessed using the 10-item Center for Epidemiologic Studies Depression Scale (CES-D-10), and an exploratory cross-sectional mediation analysis was conducted to estimate the statistical indirect association through depressive symptoms. Finally, sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the consistency of the observed associations across alternative estimators and outcome definitions. Results Among 864 participants, the median age was 69.00 (64.00–74.00) years; 474 (54.86%) were men, and 214 (24.77%) reported any informal helping. Although several baseline covariates were imbalanced before PS adjustment, adequate balance was achieved afterward. The estimated mean differences from PS matching, stratification, and IPTW were 2.214 (95% CI, 0.987–3.440), 3.519 (95% CI, 2.614–4.424), and 3.588 (95% CI, 2.742–4.433), respectively. The direction of the association was consistent across alternative analytical approaches. An exploratory cross-sectional mediation analysis identified a statistical indirect effect through depressive symptoms (estimate = 2.122, 95% CI, 1.638–2.691; p &lt; 0.001). Conclusion Any informal helping was associated with higher cognitive function scores among older adults. An exploratory analysis also identified a cross-sectional statistical indirect association involving depressive symptoms. These observational findings require further investigation in longitudinal studies.

title: The role of iNOS expression in cognitive impairment caused by lead exposure
container-title: Frontiers in Molecular Neuroscience
0aa9459375b97d934e6a569e2cfb17e834eca959.abstract: Introduction The effect of lead on spatial memory has been widely confirmed. Inducible nitric oxide synthase (iNOS) is a key enzyme in inflammatory responses that is significantly upregulated upon microglia activation. However, prior to this study, there has been no direct evidence that iNOS mediates excitatory toxicity. Methods Sprague-Dawley rats (SD rats) were given ad libitum access to drinking water containing lead (Pb, 100 mg/L) from postnatal day (PND) 24 to 45, and each treatment group was paired with a supplement group that received either minocycline or S-methylisothiourea (SMT) via the corresponding administration route. Results The results showed a significant difference in spatial memory and induction of hippocampal long-term potentiation (LTP) in the Pb exposure group when compared with controls. Simultaneously, Pb exposure also caused hippocampal microglia activation, iNOS expression, and neuronal apoptosis. Furthermore, the expression levels of syntaphilin (SNPH) and synaptophysin (Syp) were significantly decreased after lead exposure, along with glutamate accumulation in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF). Further studies revealed that minocycline administration significantly inhibited microglia activation and subsequent iNOS expression, which was accompanied by a decrease in neuronal apoptosis, reversal of the expression of SNPH and Syp, reduction in glutamate accumulation, and significant improvement in the induction of synaptic plasticity and learning and memory ability. Furthermore, after SMT specifically inhibited the expression of iNOS, the observed effects were significantly reversed. Discussion This study presents new evidence suggesting that the upregulated expression of microglial iNOS upon lead exposure may lead to lower expression levels of synaptic-associated proteins syntaphilin and synaptophysin. Subsequently, this may result in the accumulation of glutamate, neuronal damage, and synaptic plasticity impairment, ultimately leading to cognitive dysfunction.

title: Multimodal Czech online handwriting and cognitive data from children with and without handwriting disabilities
container-title: Scientific Data
77bcb3a1f1ab9e2369b1b9c67acc98a8cfa7c4d0.abstract: Abstract Handwriting is a fundamental skill that significantly influences academic achievement and cognitive development. Despite its importance, open-access datasets combining online handwriting data with comprehensive cognitive profiles are scarce, particularly for children with handwriting disabilities. We present a multimodal dataset consisting of online handwriting and cognitive assessment data from 276 Czech children (ages 8–12), including 161 individuals with handwriting disabilities. The data acquisition utilized a Wacom Cintiq 16 tablet and a digital pen to record 16 graphomotor and writing tasks, capturing high-resolution x-y coordinates, pressure, azimuth, and pen tilt at an average frequency of 167 Hz. Alongside these raw data, the dataset includes scores from standardized assessments of cognitive abilities, visuospatial skills, phonological awareness, and self-reported handwriting proficiency. We provide raw data in SVC format and integrated, preprocessed records in JSON and RDS formats, supported by specialized Python and R processing scripts. This resource is intended to facilitate research in graphonomics, machine learning, and educational psychology, providing a benchmark for the development and comparison of computational methods for analyzing children’s handwriting.

title: AI Literacy and Science Self-Efficacy as Predictors of Senior High School Students’ Perceived Scientific Research Skills
container-title: Davao Research Journal
18124df4420feb678361cb8ce7575b017450836f.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in education underscores the need to understand how AI literacy and science self-efficacy relate to students' research capabilities. This study examined senior high school students' perceived levels of AI literacy, science self-efficacy, and scientific research skills in Lupon West District, Davao Oriental, Philippines. It aimed to assess whether AI literacy and science self-efficacy uniquely predict scientific research skills. The study employed a cross-sectional predictive-correlational design, involving 261 Grade 12 students selected through proportionate stratified random sampling, with simple random selection within each school. Data were collected using paper-and-pencil questionnaires comprising three adapted instruments. Students reported moderate AI literacy (M = 3.22, SD = 0.65) and science self-efficacy (M = 3.39, SD = 0.71), but high perceived scientific research skills (M = 3.53, SD = 0.70). AI literacy was positively correlated with perceived scientific research skills, r(259) = .623, p < .001, as was science self-efficacy, r(259) = .79, p < .001. The regression model was significant, F(2, 258) = 224.66, p < .001, explaining 63.5% of the variance in perceived scientific research skills. AI literacy (B = 0.19, β = .17, p < .001) and science self-efficacy (B = 0.67, β = .67, p < .001) each made significant unique statistical contributions, with science self-efficacy having the larger standardized coefficient. These findings may inform research instruction by integrating responsible AI use and creating opportunities to enhance students’ confidence in science.

title: Teachers’ Assessment of the Effectiveness of AI and Digital Tools Among Middle School Students in an International School: A Tool for Deeper Learning
container-title: QualiSearch Journal of Educational Research and Practice
3d23d8d784c06aa981f8246e271db5c47577db1b.abstract: This study examined teachers’ assessments of middle school students’ dependency on artificial intelligence (AI) and digital tools and the effectiveness of these technologies in supporting deeper learning at an international school in Phnom Penh, Cambodia. The quantitative correlational study included 82 Grades 6–8 teachers through total enumeration. Data from a researcher-developed questionnaire were analyzed using frequencies, percentages, weighted means, standard deviations, independent-samples t tests, one-way analyses of variance, and Spearman’s rank correlation. Teachers rated student dependency as high across critical thinking, independent study habits, problem-solving, and reliance on technology for outputs. They rated the tools effective for content delivery, student engagement, and academic performance, but less effective for skill development and for deeper learning overall. Selected dependency ratings differed by sex, educational attainment, and frequency of tool use. Effectiveness ratings differed by frequency of use. Perceived dependency and effectiveness were moderately and positively associated (ρ = .537, p < .001). These findings informed the Deeper Learning Pathway, a proposed school-based program that pairs guided use of AI and digital tools with opportunities for independent reasoning and problem-solving.

title: A Teacher's Concerns about AI in Primary School: Critical Thinking, Personal Data and the Fear of Cognitive Dependence
container-title: Advances in Mobile Learning Educational Research
48daf9f5949effd20204e7775dffc33ae168a630.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is already part of pupils' everyday lives and of school life. Written from the perspective of a primary school teacher and principal, this perspective paper examines three interrelated concerns of the author herself. These concerns arose from a wish to protect her pupils and led her to study the topic for her own professional development and to help her colleagues make teaching safer and better. They concern developing critical thinking towards AI-generated answers, protecting the personal data of minors, and the fear that excessive assistance from AI will weaken pupils' thinking. Drawing on a narrative, non-systematic review of recent research on cognitive offloading, the European and Greek regulatory framework, and illustrative examples from the author's own teaching practice and lesson scenarios for primary school, it argues that the fear of cognitive dependence is a plausible concern rather than an established finding for primary school pupils. The available evidence, which comes mainly from adolescents and adults, suggests that the form of AI support (whether it replaces the learner's effort or scaffolds it) may be an important factor. AI is regarded throughout as a valuable tool; the risk lies mainly in the way it is used. The classroom examples come from ordinary lessons whose only purpose was to teach pupils to question AI answers and to protect themselves when using AI. They were not planned as research, no research data were collected, and they are offered as the author's practitioner reflections, not as findings. The author's classroom experience illustrates that such activities can be implemented in ordinary primary school lessons, but their effects on pupils' critical thinking have not yet been evaluated. The paper relates the three concerns to long-standing educational principles, in particular Socratic questioning, Dewey's reflective thought and Vygotskian scaffolding. On this basis, it proposes a simple, as yet untested three-step classroom protocol (``think -- ask -- check''), age-appropriate data protection rules, and a role for school leadership, and outlines questions for future research.

title: Survival of the fittest tool: choosing between open and closed artificial intelligence in pharmaceutical science
container-title: Journal of Pharmacy & Pharmaceutical Sciences
f138d8c0351cbed7334e74838f358d06c9cf5c0f.abstract: Three years ago, this journal published the editorial Technological Darwinism , urging pharmaceutical scientists to adapt to artificial intelligence (AI) rather than resist it. Since then, the question has shifted from whether to use AI to which AI to use, under what circumstances, and with what evidence. This review addresses that question by mapping current AI tools across the five canonical stages of drug development, from discovery to post-market pharmacovigilance. It is a narrative review, not a systematic one, and it treats openness as a spectrum rather than a binary. It compares two broad categories: open systems free, often open source or open weight, inspectable, and locally deployable and closed systems, which are proprietary, commercial, and delivered as a service. The central conclusion is pragmatic. For routine laboratory, educational, and research tasks, capable open tools now exist for almost every application, including manuscript drafting, literature review, reference management, statistical analysis, pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamic modelling, calibration and standard-curve fitting, chemical structure drawing and SMILES handling, image and figure generation, and prediction of physicochemical, ADMET (absorption, distribution, metabolism, excretion, and toxicity), formulation, and excipient compatibility properties. Free web services, however, may require confidential structures to be uploaded to a third party, so openness is distinguished here from private deployment, and independent head to head evidence against commercial tools is uneven. In contrast, integrated end to end drug discovery and validated regulatory workflows remain dominated by proprietary platforms. During the period covered by this review, the first generative AI-designed molecule targeting a generative AI-derived protein reported positive Phase IIa results and entered Phase III in July 2026; protein structure prediction was recognized with the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, shared by Hassabis, Jumper and Baker and became partly open; an autonomous frontier language model improved a longstanding medicinal chemistry reaction through thousands of wet-laboratory experiments; and regulatory agencies issued their first guidance on AI credibility. The review argues that the most enduring competency is not mastery of any single AI platform but the ability to select appropriate tools, critically validate their outputs, and document their credibility in proportion to the decisions they inform. Accordingly, open AI systems should be the default for routine, low-risk, and educational applications, whereas proprietary platforms currently retain advantages for integrated discovery and regulated development. Credibility is defined operationally, human oversight is treated as a condition of use, and the review states where comparative evidence is lacking.

title: Chaos control and bifurcations of a discrete Hepatitis B virus model
container-title: International Journal of Biomathematics
693f4861faf920a5e4eaa755e8feaed12fa162d7.abstract: In this paper, we examine the local dynamics, bifurcation sets, basic reproduction number (BRN), chaos, convergence rate and bifurcation analysis at equilibrium states of a four-dimensional discrete HBV model. More specifically, we first give the mathematical formulation of a four-dimensional discrete HBV model, and then local behavior is explored by the linear stability theory. Moreover, at equilibrium states, we have identified the bifurcation sets, and then we have studied the bifurcations at equilibrium states of the discrete HBV model by the bifurcation theory. We have studied chaos and convergence rate for the understudied HBV model. Finally, our theoretical outcomes are confirmed numerically.

title: Influence of out-of-plane electric fields in an ex vivo model of transcranial electrical stimulation
container-title: Journal of Neural Engineering
ed96c9f78e61db7a73c7682410cb7c282b73512b.abstract: Abstract Objective. Electrical stimulation is the most commonly used modality for neuromodulation, with a number of clinical and scientific applications. Although the basic mechanisms of neural activation by electrical stimulation are well understood, important questions remain regarding neural responses to diffuse electric fields such as those generated by transcranial electrical stimulation. For such diffuse fields, the orientation of the electric field with respect to the neurons being stimulated matters, but previous ex vivo brain slice studies–commonly used to study how neurons respond to external electric fields-have only considered electric fields applied in the plane of the slice. Approach. We used two electrode arrays–one oriented parallel and the other perpendicular to coronal brain slices–to generate electric fields oriented orthogonally to the slice as well as along the cortical column. We measured responses in Layer 5 of the somatosensory cortex using several 2-electrode stimulation configurations, while also varying the distance between the electrodes and the slice. Main results. Electrode patterns generating a large electric field component orthogonal to the slice evoked the largest neural responses at every electrode-slice distance. Moreover, neural thresholds were >5× lower for electric fields orthogonal to the slice compared to electric fields along the cortical column. Significance. These results provide a better understanding of the brain slice as a model for noninvasive stimulation and could lead to new electrode configurations for efficient transcranial neural stimulation.

title: Periodic–kink, lump, and rogue waves with parameter discovery in an integrable model: Bilinear and physics-informed neural-network approaches
container-title: Modern Physics Letters B
4659833ff83635dce064831a88f744089cf0f548.abstract: This research investigates nonlinear wave dynamics of the integrable [Formula: see text]-dimensional extended Bogoyavlensky–Konopelchenko equation, which models the interaction of a Riemann wave and a long wave in fluid dynamics. The equation has important applications in the modeling of shallow water waves, ion acoustic waves, and the propagation of fluids. Initially, we employ Hirota’s bilinear framework with symbolic single-hidden-layer neural-network architectures, referred to as bilinear neural networks (BNNs), and prescribed analytical activation functions to construct complex wave structures, including periodic–kink waves, M-lumps, lump–kink interactions, and modulated lump solutions. A Jacobi-elliptic activation function is employed within the symbolic BNN ansatz to construct and investigate rogue-wave solutions. In the second phase, an enhanced Physics-Informed Neural Network (PINN), equipped with a global adaptive activation function and residual-based attention, is introduced for physics-informed solution approximation and inverse parameter identification. The proposed PINN accurately reproduces the periodic–kink, M-lump, and lump–kink dynamics, showing good agreement with the analytical solutions and low error metrics, while the comparative analysis highlights the complementary strengths and limitations of the analytical and physics-informed numerical approaches. The framework also exhibits good stability in recovering nonlinear coefficients from noisy data, demonstrating its potential for parameter discovery. The results demonstrate that combining BNN-based exact solution construction with enhanced PINN-based numerical forward and inverse modeling provides a versatile framework for nonlinear wave analysis and the investigation of complex wave phenomena in applied mathematics and nonlinear physics.

title: Geomorphic Approach for Beach Downdrift of Fishing Ports and Marinas: Parabolic Model and Software MeePaSoL
container-title: International Journal of Ocean and Coastal Engineering
aa1bf29ba82f25bdcdce97f4f84fd36663d545e8.abstract: Coastal erosion problems associated with a fishing port or marina on a sandy coast are caused by an imbalance of longshore sediment transport and bay shape formation on downdrift. Regardless of the availability of littoral transport, the tip of its outer breakwater would behave as an updrift control point for an embayed beach to form, by combined wave diffraction-refraction aided by nearshore current circulation. Conventional approaches to mitigate downdrift erosion have applied laboratory tests and numerical modelling, together with hard structures (seawalls, groins and detached breakwaters). On the contrary, an efficient geomorphic model with software MeePaSoL is now available, which can readily sketch the curved shoreline planform in static equilibrium or verify the stability of an existing planform, without laborious laboratory tests and complicated numerical programming. Not only is this geomorphic approach a reliable method, but it also serves a purpose as a useful tool for planning an initial breakwater layout and examining the effects of relocating an existing breakwater for port expansion projects. By combining the parabolic model with the software MeePaSoL, an appropriate shore protection scheme can also be devised to achieve a resilient coastal environment. Examples applying this geomorphic approach for mitigating downdrift beach erosion are explained, together with four case studies for the benefits to coastal professionals.

title: Leveraging Technology for Group Effectiveness: An Educational Model to Facilitate Group Development and Leadership Learning
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
a94abde8fdbc9c69c3725929b6b8dedfcf12d2bd.abstract: As individuals increasingly engage in group work across in-person, hybrid, and virtual settings, it is essential for educators to intentionally design and facilitate group experiences that support both effective teamwork and meaningful leadership learning for students. In this chapter, we present a model to guide educators in leveraging the group experience as a space for learning through engaging – and a learning space that values process just as much as outcomes. Grounded in group development and leadership frameworks – including Tuckman’s stages of group development, Lencioni’s Five Dysfunctions of a Team, the emotionally intelligent leadership (EIL) model, and the relational leadership model (RLM) – we introduce a three-phase model: plan for process, probe the process, and process the process. Across each phase, we offer strategies and tools that can be applied in a variety of learning environments and adapted to different group contexts. Rather than allowing technology to overshadow the human dynamics of collaboration, we encourage purposeful integration of tools that enhance core elements of group work. Through thoughtful design and facilitation, educators can create group experiences that foster learning, reflection, and leadership growth.

title: Scaling Innovation Through Centers of Excellence: A Strategic Model for Enterprise-wide Learning and Leadership Development
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
13e25602335779cf6c76f0e0b6a54b3097f99799.abstract: This chapter presents a case study of Carnegie Mellon University’s pioneering development of a cross-functional, enterprise-level “Centers of Excellence” (CoE) program, designed to foster leadership development, skill advancement, and innovation across the institution. Grounded in applied practice and strategic alignment with institutional goals, the CoE model functions as a hub for skill-building, policy evolution, and enterprise learning – leveraging diverse instructional modalities such as coaching cohorts, just-in-time training, and real-world simulation scenarios to drive cultural transformation and workforce agility. Drawing from over 15 years of experience in IT strategy, digital transformation, and organizational leadership, the author outlines the phased implementation approach, stakeholder engagement strategies, and sustainability mechanisms that have made the CoEs a replicable blueprint for other institutions seeking to embed innovation into their operational DNA. The chapter also explores how the model is anchored in service excellence and inclusive design. Through this lens, the chapter offers both a conceptual foundation and a practitioner’s guide for readers in higher education, nonprofit, and enterprise sectors aiming to scale leadership and skill building in dynamic environments.

title: Generative AI Powered by Large Language Models for Leadership Development: Between Epistemic Responsibility and the Future of Innovation
container-title: Technology and Leadership Connections
2befe576d22df3abb8f03a51478516f11ce0d40c.abstract: This chapter examines language-based generative AI, particularly large language models (LLMs), as active epistemic agents in leadership development. Moving beyond their perceived neutrality, the authors argue that LLMs serve as mirrors of dominant assumptions, co-constructors of leadership meaning, and framing devices of legitimate knowledge. The sources highlight how these systems reinforce prevailing Euro-American managerial ideals, often marginalizing diverse leadership paradigms such as Indigenous, collectivist, or spiritual frameworks, thereby amplifying structural and cultural biases. Through epistemic feedback loops and personalization, LLMs can subtly shape leadership identity and constrain developmental horizons, leading to adaptive standardization or performative conformity. The chapter emphasizes the critical need for epistemic responsibility in innovation leadership, advocating for leaders to interrogate system framings, reflect on their influence, and cultivate design awareness. This involves fostering inclusive data practices, participatory design methodologies, and culturally responsive AI governance to ensure AI-mediated innovation ecosystems are just, inclusive, and reflect pluralistic worldviews. Ultimately, the chapter calls for leaders to reclaim framing power and engage AI dialogically to foster an innovation leadership that is reflexive, ethically grounded, and attuned to human complexities.

title: Generative structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model for MR to CT image synthesis in radiotherapy planning
container-title: Physics in Medicine & Biology
cfa98f94b57aed8a928c9fb300f2a97663467510.abstract: Abstract Objective . Radiotherapy (RT) planning uses magnetic resonance (MR) imaging for soft tissue information, while computerized tomography (CT) imaging is necessary for dose calculation. Synthetic CTs generated from MR images (MRI) streamline the clinical workflow by reducing the need for an actual CT acquisition while minimizing radiation exposure, enabling adaptive RT workflows. The objective of this study is to propose a new RT planning model combining stable structure-guided denoising diffusion probabilistic model (DDPM) with MRI conditioning, for generating synthetic CT (sCT) images. Approach . The model combines a hybrid network architecture with a dynamic guidance mechanism, conditioned on MR images, to direct the reverse diffusion process and preserve structural details. The model integrates both a denoising and a refinement network: the denoising network predicts and progressively removes the noise added during the forward diffusion process, while the guidance strength adapts at each timestep based on the noise level. This adaptive guidance mechanism uses a non-linear formulation that satisfies noise constraints, optimizing the denoising process while preserving structural integrity. The training process includes a weighted structure-guided loss function that combines the DDPM noise loss with a dynamic guidance regularizer term for sCT image generation via noise prediction, along with a reconstruction loss for refinement. Main results . Evaluated on three paired MR/CT datasets (head and neck (HaN), as well as brain), our model outperforms recent MR to CT synthesis models, showing the best performance in image quality based on the mean absolute error in Hounsfield units, as well as improved peak signal-to-noise ratio, structural similarity index and gradient magnitude similarity deviation compared to other DDPM and generative adversarial network approaches. When comparing tumor segmentation quality, it achieves the best results in Dice score (0.76 ± 0.04), Hausdorff distance (7.9 ± 2.0), intersection over union (0.69 ± 0.04), geometric consistency index (0.84 ± 0.04) and precision-recall index (PRI) (0.88 ± 0.03) for segmented tumor regions in the generated sCT images. Finally, it achieves the best mean square error of 10.1 ± 2.6 Gray (Gy) in the head-and-neck cohort, when evaluating dose planning on sCT, with a conformity index of 0.61 ± 0.02 and a homogeneity index of 0.10 ± 0.02. Significance . Performance shows promise in integration for RT in HaN, as well as in brain cancers.

title: Trust Modulates Speech Entrainment: Enhanced Cortical Tracking for Low-trust Speakers
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
93efb8d8a2efd6ac00960e2f7910f482c84055f4.abstract: Abstract Trust is a critical component of human communication, providing a foundation for understanding, information exchange, and social coordination. Much of the research on trust in speech communication has focused on how vocal characteristics impact perceived trustworthiness. However, little is known about how trust in a speaker affects the neural processing of speech. Here, we demonstrate a two-stage experimental framework to study that question using noninvasive EEG. First, participants engage in a trust-building stage, where they play an investment game with fictional characters, each paired with a distinctive voice and trustworthiness level (i.e., frequency and magnitude of lies). Next, participants engage in a story-listening stage, in which they are presented with stories from the same characters. Data acquired from 20 young adults confirm a statistically significant correlation between the perceived and actual trustworthiness of the fictional characters. Cortical speech tracking was quantified using a temporal response function analysis on the EEG data. We found that the trustworthiness established during the trust-building stage influenced the cortical tracking of speech in the subsequent story-listening stage, with lower trustworthiness corresponding to a stronger cortical tracking of speech. Interestingly, trustworthiness selectively modulated tracking strength, with no statistically significant changes in the spatial and temporal temporal response function dynamics.

title: Distributed Neural Dynamics Underlie the Shift from Movement Preparation to Execution
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
7a79083e41e8564c05cef0c9e6a1179e83f26049.abstract: Abstract Understanding how neural population activity supports the transition from movement preparation to execution remains a central challenge in systems neuroscience. Invasive recordings in nonhuman primates indicate that motor preparation and execution occupy orthogonal subspaces within the primary motor cortex (M1), yet how these neural dynamics evolve across broader networks and support skilled, memory-guided action remains poorly understood. We used source-resolved magnetoencephalography during a memory-guided finger-sequence task to track population dynamics across a cortico-hippocampal network. Manifold trajectories and decoding revealed that preparation and execution of movement sequences occupy distinct, yet not fully orthogonal, neural subspaces—a separation that generalized across all regions but was most pronounced in motor regions. Crucially, we identified a hierarchical spatio-temporal transition across the brain: The state shift originated in the hippocampus via theta-band modulations and rippled through the pre-SMA, SMA, and lateral premotor areas before culminating in M1 via broadband activity. This progression follows the functional hierarchy of descending motor pathways, with M1 shifting last, 160 msec before the first button press. Although sequence identity could be decoded from all areas during execution, only the hippocampus and M1 maintained predictive representations of upcoming sequences during preparation. These findings demonstrate that the initiation of complex motor sequences relies on a well-timed integration of hippocampal memory systems with primary motor output, rather than being a process localized to the motor cortices alone.

title: Sequential Sampling from Memory Underlies Perceptual Decisions Unyoked from Actions
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
a917d6aa52f462098a3786e8e5c48f2839ba057f.abstract: Abstract Perceptual decision-making refers to the class of decisions in which sensory evidence is used to categorize percepts and guide actions. Conventionally, categorical decisions are thought to precede motor actions. However, recent studies in nonhuman primates challenge this assumption—when perceptual decisions were uncoupled from the actions they bear upon, animals postponed the decisions until relevant response options were revealed. To determine whether this postponement stems from cognitive limitations unique to nonhuman primates, we conducted a similar experiment with human participants. Naive participants viewed a random dot motion (RDM) stimulus that was difficult to categorize. After a delay period following the RDM, two choice targets were presented and participants decided which target lay closer to the perceived motion direction. Decision accuracy varied across participants, reflecting individual differences in ability to integrate motion evidence. Notably, participants with higher decision accuracy showed prolonged deliberation after choice-target presentation. Furthermore, the time they took to report their decisions depended on the strength of the motion evidence. This pattern of accuracy and decision reporting time could be accounted for by a bounded diffusion model in which participants sequentially sample stored sensory information from memory during the target selection phase. When the RDM was challenging to categorize, the subsequent appearance of the targets provided a framework to interrogate stored evidence and render a decision. Our results reveal a strategic feature of working memory of retaining information based on its future utility. This observation opens new avenues for investigating how memory and decision-making interact.

title: Confounds in Functional Magnetic Resonance Imaging—Part III: Auxiliary Data
container-title: Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience
7ebbf91cc1104ca6a325a8fc4b3255a08d3c579e.abstract: Abstract In the first part of this series, we reviewed the pathways that bring about confounding nuisance signals in fMRI. Then, in the second part, we considered how human factors can modify these pathways. In this, the third and final part, we review auxiliary data that may allow researchers to identify and perhaps correct for nuisance signals and their modifiers. We consider three broad categories of data: (1) measures that can be collected synchronously with the fMRI, (2) other MRI scans that either capture trait information or attempt to define the state that exists during an fMRI scan in the same session, and (3) non-MRI measures that can be collected before or after the scan and that also capture trait or relevant state factors influencing the fMRI. We conclude with some recommendations on ways to improve fMRI experiments going forward.

title: Lost in translation: Language and implementation gaps in South African patient-held records
container-title: South African Family Practice
e523a1307961eca71a702c952449dbfce9c568ac.abstract: Patient-held records like South Africa’s Road-to-Health Booklet (RtHB) and Maternity Case Record (MCR) support continuity of care by serving both clinical documentation and patient education functions. However, patient-directed educational content is predominantly available in English. To explore how language accessibility influences patient engagement with patient-held records and to identify implementation gaps in multilingual patient education across maternal and child health services, public sector primary healthcare clinics and district hospitals in South Africa. Reflective analysis combines clinical experience and a review of national patient-held records. Patient-directed educational content within patient-held records is predominantly in English, limiting accessibility for many patients and caregivers in South Africa’s multilingual context. Child health services include a multilingual educational companion alongside the RtHB although its implementation appears inconsistent. In contrast, no routinely implemented multilingual educational companion exists for the MCR despite expectations that patients understand danger signs and management plans. Contribution: The principal gap lies not in the absence of multilingual educational models but in their inconsistent implementation. Strengthening multilingual patient education within patient-held records could improve patient engagement, support health literacy and promote more equitable healthcare communication.

c5c341b7f3c1b71300183f3b53ae913a428c8afe.abstract: В статье оценены факторы туристских потоков в Узбекистан и влияние реформы либерализации визового режима 2018–2019 годов. Для этого предложена «Модель факторов туристской привлекательности», объединяющая гравитационную модель, анализ событий и алгоритмы машинного обучения. Гравитационная модель оценена методом псевдомаксимального правдоподобия Пуассона по официальным данным в разрезе стран за 2014–2025 годы. Согласно результатам, туристский поток определяется численностью населения страны (эластичность 0,83), доходом (0,89) и расстоянием (−1,59); поток из сопредельных стран выше в 7,5 раза, из стран СНГ – в 11,4 раза. Эффект визового режима формировался в течение нескольких лет и в 2022–2024 годах соответствовал росту потока на 102–178 %. Модель XGBoost обеспечила наибольшую точность вне выборки (R² = 0,850). Выявлен низкий уровень использования потенциала на рынках Индии, Пакистана и Бангладеш.

e17e448d62a75f27e1b7dd94366f6a8e608655e9.abstract: The article assesses the impact of inbound tourism on the national economy using Tourism Satellite Account indicators and develops a probabilistic forecast up to 2030. It argues that gross value added of tourism industries must be distinguished from tourism direct gross value added: in 2024 their ratio was 3.8. A formula for the effect of extending the length of stay is proposed; extending the stay by one night raises inbound tourism consumption by UZS 3.19 trillion (9.4%). Because the annual national series is short and has structural breaks, a dynamic panel gravity model based on 2,134 observations for 194 countries is used. Out of sample, the model with an error of 1.0% outperformed ARIMA (33.6%) and a random walk with drift (5.4%). The number of inbound tourists is forecast to reach 18.9 million in 2030, and the probability of achieving the target of 20 million tourists is 47.6%.

title: MULTILINEAR PETG MATERIAL MODEL IDENTIFIED WITH A NONCONTACT EXTENSOMETER
container-title: MM Science Journal
dc0b6aa0ed946495062feba69783d569a80107eb.abstract: This paper presents the identification of a multilinear isotropic hardening material model for PETG produced by fused filament fabrication (FFF) using a noncontact computer vision extensometer. A tensile test was performed on flat specimens with surface line markers, and the marker displacements were measured without contact by tracking them in recorded images. Strain was calculated from these displacements and combined with the measured force to obtain true stress and plastic strain, and ten points of the curve defined the model. The model was implemented in ANSYS Workbench and calibrated against the measured reaction forces of five specimens. The average absolute deviation of the calculated forces was 3.51 %. The results show the procedure provides an effective macroscopic description of the global tensile response of the tested PETG. The model assumes a homogeneous, isotropic material, and its applicability is limited to comparable printing parameters, specimen geometry and loading conditions.

title: Study on predicting double cracks coalescence behavior based on hyperparameter optimization of the kernel extreme learning machine classification model
container-title: International Journal of Structural Integrity
16ba3f3d6360c73cb9d25a14ee95b53158d64597.abstract: Purpose The study aims to develop an intelligent prediction framework for dual-crack coalescence behavior and enhance the prediction accuracy and generalization performance of crack state judgment under multiple crack morphologies. Design/methodology/approach Four typical machine learning classifiers including LR, KNN, SVM and KELM are comprehensively compared on datasets of linear, elliptical and circular dual cracks. The Kernel Extreme Learning Machine (KELM) with the best overall performance is selected as the base model. A Reinforced Multi-strategy Parrot Optimization (RMPO) algorithm is employed to globally optimize KELM's hyperparameters, taking regularization coefficient C and RBF kernel parameter as optimization variables. The negative average validation-set accuracy from inner-fold cross-validation is adopted as the fitness function for adaptive searching within a nested stratified cross-validation workflow. Findings KELM outperforms other machine learning models in predicting three types of dual-crack coalescence. After hyperparameter tuning by RMPO, the hybrid RMPO-KELM model achieves prediction accuracies of 0.973, 0.911 and 0.824 for linear, elliptical and circular dual cracks respectively. Compared to grid search (GS) and the Parrot Optimization Algorithm (PO), the optimized model achieves a more accurate nonlinear fit between crack geometric inputs and coalescence labels, and maintains reliable prediction accuracy on independent test subsets. Research limitations/implications This study only considers dual cracks in homogeneous plates under predefined loading conditions. The dataset is derived from numerical simulations, and further physical tests are required to validate the model. Future work can extend the model to heterogeneous materials, multiple cracks and complex load cases. The feature selection strategy may be further refined for broader engineering scenarios. Practical implications This proposed RMPO–KELM model enables fast identification of dual-crack coalescence states in homogeneous plates, avoiding heavy finite-element iterative computation. It offers an efficient auxiliary tool for structural safety assessment. The feature screening scheme also provides a reference for selecting dimensionless crack parameters. Engineers can adopt this framework for preliminary crack risk evaluation in similar plate structures. Social implications Accurate and rapid prediction of crack coalescence helps prevent sudden structural failures in infrastructure, reducing safety hazards and casualties. Reliable structural risk assessment extends service life of engineering components, cuts maintenance costs and lowers resource consumption. This predictive framework supports safer civil and mechanical infrastructure, benefiting public safety and sustainable asset management. Originality/value An RMPO–KELM hybrid intelligent prediction model is proposed for multi-morphology dual-crack coalescence prediction. The RMPO algorithm realizes efficient global searching of KELM hyperparameters, which significantly improves prediction precision and generalization capacity. This work supplies a data-driven solution for structural safety assessment involving crack propagation and coalescence.

title: RFI-to-Field Impact Analytics for Mega-Terminal Structural Packages: A Traceability Model Linking RFIs, Revisions, and Schedule Impacts
container-title: International Journal of Sustainability and Innovation in Engineering
1214e5bbf85062555d986fc284602b533dc4fb70.abstract: Requests for Information (RFIs) can delay and complicate large construction projects, yet their downstream effects on design revisions, field rework, and schedule are rarely traced. This paper proposes an RFI-to-field traceability framework for airport Project Management/Construction Management (PMCM) teams. The framework links each RFI to the resulting drawing revisions, field change orders (FCOs), Non-Conformance Reports (NCRs), rework, and critical-path delay across four project systems (Procore, Oracle Unifier, Primavera P6, and Bluebeam), and adds a leakage-aware classifier that assigns each RFI to a low, medium, or high impact class using only information available at submission. Because the logs of the motivating airport case are confidential, the framework is evaluated on a synthetic benchmark of 2,400 RFIs over 48 months with known ground-truth links; the results therefore validate the pipeline and are not empirical findings about real projects. The tiered linkage recovered 89%–99% of true links at each stage, with precision of 57%–96% (lowest for NCR and schedule links), and linkage-derived impact labels agreed with ground truth (Cohen's κ = 0.88). With a time-ordered split, the best early-warning model (random forest) reached a macro-F1 of 0.39 (95% CI 0.36–0.43) and ROC-AUC of 0.62 against a macro-F1 of 0.26 for a majority-class baseline, i.e., weak discrimination under the assumed noise. No cost or schedule saving is claimed; replication on anonymized real logs with a manual link audit is required.

title: Configuration-Aware Aircraft Maintenance Program Bridging: Data Model, Decision Rules and Scheduling Optimization Illustrated with FAA Airworthiness Directives
container-title: International Journal of Sustainability and Innovation in Engineering
7dda0bb5ba387d7b1c0adf38fe35cedcf803866d.abstract: This design-science paper specifies the IMPB-TDO framework: a relational data model with explicit limit anchors and evidence links; seven ordered decision rules that assign each requirement–aircraft pair to one of seven disposition classes, including an engineering exception that is never defaulted to “not applicable”; flight-hour, flight-cycle and calendar forecasting with “whichever occurs first/later” logic; and a network-flow mixed-integer program that schedules only approved tasks. Four Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Airworthiness Directives (ADs) from 2024–2025 serve as illustrative cases, and the framework is demonstrated on a synthetic 14-aircraft fleet and on randomly generated capacity-constrained fleets. The ADs differ in what determines applicability (all serials, in-service embodiment, repair method, certificate date) and in costing unit; two published fleet cost totals are ceilings, not expected costs. In the worked example on AD 2025-16-06, production embodiment, a planned modification and an undocumented configuration each changed the disposition. On a fleet built to contain these situations, an SB-aware tracking comparator still differed on 3 of 14 configuration-sensitive pairs, all traceable to provenance or coupled actions; a model-level filter differed on 10. On 18 generated instances with fleet-wide inspector capacity, the optimization lowered the common objective by a mean of 15% (up to 22%) relative to the best of two planner heuristics wherever a heuristic found a plan, found compliant plans on 5 instances where both heuristics failed, and proved infeasibility on 1; no run was proven optimal within 180 s, so gaps are reported. The paper contributes a specified, reproducible artefact; the synthetic results demonstrate mechanisms rather than operational effect sizes, which require the validation protocol provided.

title:
Research on Front-End Intake Performance Based on a Standardized
                    Aerodynamic Model for Electric Vehicles
container-title: SAE Technical Paper Series
8cd14ec5a100e2b22a04128138a8bc3808e77110.abstract: <div class="section abstract"><div class="htmlview paragraph">The front-end intake flow field of an electric vehicle and its control exert significant influences on the vehicle’s aerodynamic drag and heat dissipation performance. In this paper, a standardized aerodynamic model for electric vehicles was developed, providing a reusable benchmark platform for coupled investigations into vehicle aerodynamic and thermodynamic performances. Based on this model, the effects of the installation inclination angle of the cooling module and the opening degree of the active grille shutter (AGS) on the vehicle drag coefficient, the intake airflow rate of the cooling module, and heat dissipation performance were investigated. The results demonstrate that the inclined arrangement of the cooling module can reduce the height of the motor compartment, while the incoming air velocity and flow rate decrease obviously, which deteriorates the heat dissipation performance of cooling components. Regulating the opening degree of the AGS imposes remarkable impacts on the intake flow field, vehicle aerodynamic drag, and heat dissipation performance. As the AGS opening gradually increases within the range of 0° to 45°, the drag coefficient and cooling intake air volume vary in an approximately linear manner. Once the grille opening exceeds 45°, further increasing the opening angle produces a weaker effect on the intake flow field and aerodynamic drag.</div></div>
