title: AI anthropomorphism, emotional attachment and verification behaviour in GenAI use
container-title: Online Information Review
69181986ddbed0224e43f9b1fb18cf320f342860.abstract: Purpose With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), AI is increasingly perceived not merely as a tool but as a conversational partner. This study examines how AI anthropomorphism is associated with users’ verification of AI-generated information through emotional attachment. Design/methodology/approach A survey was conducted with 430 adult GenAI users in South Korea. The proposed mediation model was analysed using structural equation modelling. Findings Within the proposed structural model, AI anthropomorphism was positively associated with emotional attachment to AI, which was in turn positively associated with AI-generated information verification behaviour. AI anthropomorphism was also directly and positively associated with verification behaviour. The significant positive indirect association along the anthropomorphism–attachment–verification pathway suggests that the findings are more consistent with a cognitive vigilance pathway than with a cognitive illusion pathway. Rather than indicating that anthropomorphism and attachment reduce scrutiny, the results suggest that they are associated with greater verification effort. Originality/value This study narrows its empirical contribution to a mediation model linking AI anthropomorphism, emotional attachment and verification behaviour. It shows that emotional attachment to AI is not necessarily associated with reduced scrutiny, but may instead be linked to greater verification effort. Building on this finding, AI verification fatigue is repositioned as a promising theoretical extension for future research on the possible longer-term cognitive burden of repeated AI-generated information verification, rather than as an empirically demonstrated outcome of the present study.

title: Generative AI Literacies and Discipline-Specific Knowledge: Preservice Teachers Planning Task-Based L2 Lessons with GenAI
container-title: Digital Studies in Language and Literature
49cfa4edc8a86155f27305dd81b772f6f0a87a1a.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to support Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT)-oriented lesson planning in a preservice teacher education context, examining the extent to which LLM use can contribute to the mobilisation of TBLT-related competencies. The case study draws on triangulated data from surveys, interaction logs with the LLM, lesson plans produced by preservice teachers and their reflections. The module required participants to generate a lesson plan with an LLM and to compare the resulting plan with a previously created lesson plan developed without AI support. The analysis focuses on knowledge of TBLT principles and their implementation during lesson planning, and the GenAI competence activated through the interaction with the LLM. The findings reveal considerable variation in how the dyads interacted with the LLM. Some dyads formulated more precise prompts and prompt iterations, provided more contextualised input, engaged more critically with the LLM-generated output, and iteratively refined their lesson plans in ways that appeared more consistent with TBLT principles. The data suggest an association between a stronger conceptual understanding of TBLT and more purposeful interaction with the LLM. This association indicates that disciplinary knowledge may facilitate the effective use of LLMs for TBLT-oriented lesson planning. Rather than replacing pedagogical expertise, LLM use appears to be most productive when preservice teachers are able to critically evaluate and adapt the generated output in light of established TBLT principles.

title: Synergistic Effect of Hybrid Polarized Spin Currents Enables Sub-Nanosecond and Energy-Efficient Field-Free Switching on a Wafer-Scale Platform
container-title: ACS Applied Materials & Interfaces
c827389fb64f2c43d8fbcd310bdcb5e7e4331741.abstract: Abstract Spin–orbit torque magnetoresistive random access memory (SOT-MRAM) exhibits intrinsic potential for next-generation magnetic memory, whereas robust wafer-level field-free switching (FFS) of nanosized perpendicular magnetic tunnel junctions (pMTJ) remains a critical challenge for practical applications. Here, we present a robust FFS of 90 nm pMTJs on 300 mm wafers driven by the synergistic effect of y- and z-polarized spin currents generated at the antiferromagnetic (AFM)/nonmagnetic (NM) interface. Experimental results demonstrate that an appropriate combination of both y- and z-spin polarizations is able to significantly improve the FFS performance. 90 nm pMTJ arrays are fabricated on 300 mm wafers, where a mean tunnel magnetoresistance ratio (TMR) of 140%, an endurance of exceeding 1012 cycles, and a robust field-free SOT switching at sub-nanosecond (down to 0.2 ns) are simultaneously achieved. Robust FFS is observed at temperature up to 100 °C, and the switching polarity remains unchanged after 1T magnetic field disturbance. With the assistance of the voltage-controlled magnetic anisotropy (VCMA) effect, the switching current density is reduced by 20% and the switching energy can be as low as 0.35 pJ/bit. This work paves the way for SOT-MRAM toward commercialization.

title: Encouraging the use of generative AI for closed-book test preparation: effects on student assessment performance and perceptions
container-title: Microbiology Australia
a89131b7b8180b129ba0fc050cf8b5278dbad42d.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being used by university students to support learning. However, evidence from authentic classroom settings examining whether GenAI-assisted revision influences closed-book assessment performance remains limited. This study evaluated the educational use of Microsoft Copilot in a third-year undergraduate immunology course. Student performance was compared between the 2025 and 2026 cohorts using comparable closed-book assessments of identical format and similar difficulty. Before Test 2 in 2026, students were encouraged to use Copilot during structured revision activities. Following Test 2, students completed an anonymous survey examining their perceptions of using Copilot to support learning. No statistically significant differences were observed in Test 1 or Test 2 marks between cohorts. Although a higher proportion of students achieved higher grades in 2026, a similar trend was evident before the intervention. Survey results showed that 78% of students agreed that GenAI could support learning of complex scientific concepts when used appropriately. However, only 53% reported improved understanding of immunology concepts, 39% reported improved knowledge recall, and 71% expressed concerns regarding inaccurate or misleading Copilot-generated information. These findings suggest that although students recognise the educational value of GenAI, encouraging its use during revision alone may not improve subsequent closed-book assessment performance.

title: Use and perceptions of AI tools among Australian general practice registrars: a national survey
container-title: Journal of Primary Health Care
c3efd0b3647649ef143335193afd580c770d2a16.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used in health care, yet little is known about how often Australian general practitioner trainees (GP registrars) use them or how they perceive the impact of AI on training and clinical care. Aim This study aimed to examine how frequently registrars use AI tools for clinical care and education, types of AI used, the perceived benefits and risks, and training needs. Methods A national cross-sectional online survey conducted from 7 May to 4 June 2024 invited 3743 Australian General Practice Training or Fellowship Support Program registrars to participate. The survey assessed frequency and context of AI use, practice-level adoption, perceived impacts, training exposure, and ethical-legal concerns. Analyses were descriptive. Results Among the 727 respondents (19.5%), frequent use (weekly or more) was uncommon; 7.3% for clinical tasks, 5.0% for education. Practice-level adoption was low, with 10.8% reporting subscription to AI tools. Most registrars anticipated benefits, particularly learning efficiency and administrative workload reduction. However, 25.0% perceived increased medicolegal risk. Formal training was rare, with most relying on self-directed learning, though many rated AI education as important. Among clinical users, common tools included large language models (32.5%), remote patient monitoring devices (28.6%), and voice-to-text tools (26.2%). Large language models predominated in education (63.5%). Discussion In May–June 2024, AI tool use among registrars was limited, although most perceived potential benefit. Enthusiasm was tempered by concerns about safety, ethics, and legal risks. Structured training and guidelines are needed to support safe, effective integration into GP registrars’ practice and education.

title: Responsible AI and Structural Justice
da1087c38814e959c4bfbff69e0e4db0180d2fd1.abstract: This Element presents challenges of attributing responsibility for AI harms through political theories of structural injustice, where fault is broadly diffused and difficult to establish. I argue that AI systems feature complex structural entanglements between humans and machines-in computational architectures, organizational workflows, and societal data collectives-that pose problems for conventional liability where direct causal links are necessary for blame. I develop two modes of structural responsibility that address unjust AI outcomes from these entanglements. Thin structural responsibility traces where power and accountability lie in the processes of developing unjust AI systems. Thick structural responsibility enlists deployers, users, and broader publics alongside developers in collectively repairing unjust social conditions that produce and rely on AI systems. I show that many Responsible AI initiatives remain thin by demanding disclosures without systemic repair. Incorporating thicker reforms makes responsibility for just AI a living political practice rather than a managerial task. This title is also available as open access on Cambridge Core.

title: Performance-Driven Generative Design for Daylighting Optimization in a Tangerang Aerotropolis Office Building
container-title: DIMENSI: Journal of Architecture and Built Environment
faf1caa5c1813ed003b847519530da6d67dff4c7.abstract: Daylighting in tropical climates may increase glare risk in office buildings. This issue is particularly relevant in the Tangerang Aerotropolis area, where humid tropical conditions and airport operational safety regulations constrain building development. This study optimized daylighting performance in an office building using a Performance-Driven Generative Design approach. The workflow integrated Rhinoceros 3D, Grasshopper, ClimateStudio, and Galapagos to evaluate six envelopes and building mass variables. The optimization evaluated 950 design alternatives across 18 generations using UDI₁₀₀–₃₀₀₀ as the objective function. A maximum UDI₁₀₀–₃₀₀₀ of 95.5% was achieved with a WWR of 0.47, window height of 2.53 m, shading spacing and depth of 0.40 m, building width of 12 m, and orientation of 76°. Best-performing configurations converged within WWR 0.40–0.47, window height 2.50–2.60 m, shading spacing 0.30–0.50 m, shading depth 0.30–0.40 m, building width 12–13 m, and orientation 72°–84°. The results identified a high-performing configuration and recurring parameter ranges among the best-performing solutions.

title: Severe caffeine intoxication after sustained nonsuicidal caffeine use requiring hemodialysis: a case report
container-title: Renal Replacement Therapy
2ed5673dd9e70936642782fdf4a626d144aa7bda.abstract: Abstract Background Severe caffeine intoxication is well described after acute high-dose ingestion, whereas cases associated with sustained nonsuicidal caffeine use have been less frequently reported. We report a case of severe caffeine intoxication requiring hemodialysis in a patient who reported taking 400 mg/day of caffeine for 16 consecutive days. Case Presentation A previously healthy 26-year-old man developed nausea, vomiting, palpitations, marked sinus tachycardia, hypokalemia, hypophosphatemia, hyperglycemia, and lactic acidosis after 16 days of reported caffeine tablet use without suicidal intent. His serum caffeine concentration was 84.4 μg/mL. Emergency hemodialysis was followed by rapid clinical and metabolic improvement. Conclusions Severe caffeine intoxication should be considered even when the reported history does not suggest an acute overdose. A marked discrepancy between self-reported caffeine intake and serum caffeine concentration should prompt consideration of unrecognized additional exposure or atypical caffeine pharmacokinetics. Hemodialysis may be considered in selected patients with severe cardiovascular or metabolic manifestations.

title: Characterizing University Students’ Geometric Thinking Through Dialogues with Generative Artificial Intelligence in Geometry Transformation Learning
container-title: Jurnal Pendidikan Progresif
1c4a91710bc877408490a03a7a003f2d6291c53a.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has emerged as a promising technology for supporting mathematical dialogue, feedback, and reasoning in mathematics education. However, research has paid limited attention to how university students’ geometric thinking develops through sustained interaction with GenAI, particularly in geometry transformation learning. This study aims to develop a Dialogic Geometric Thinking Framework that characterizes the dimensions and progression of university students’ geometric thinking during sustained dialogue with ChatGPT. A qualitative exploratory design was employed involving undergraduate mathematics education students enrolled in a Geometry Transformation course at an Indonesian public university. Data were collected from student–ChatGPT dialogue transcripts, students’ written solutions, and reflective interviews. The data were analyzed thematically using reflexive thematic analysis to identify recurring characteristics and relationships among dimensions of geometric thinking and to synthesize them into an integrated framework. The findings identified five interrelated dimensions of geometric thinking: conceptual reasoning, representational coordination, procedural justification, reflective regulation, and mathematical elaboration. These dimensions illustrate how students progressively articulate mathematical concepts, coordinate representations, justify solution procedures, evaluate their reasoning, and extend mathematical ideas during AI-mediated dialogue. The study resulted in a Dialogic Geometric Thinking Framework that provides a process-oriented perspective on the development of university students’ geometric thinking during interaction with GenAI. The framework offers an initial theoretical foundation for understanding and further investigating geometric thinking in AI-mediated mathematics learning. Keywords: geometric thinking, generative artificial intelligence, chatGPT, geometry transformation, mathematical dialogue.

title: Designing Critical Human–AI Learning in Higher Education: The SC-AIM–FAVIC Framework for Analytical and Logical Reasoning
container-title: JPI: Jurnal Pustaka Indonesia
4ce99b9a5976c3c25eb4ecff905eaf4a200752ca.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now routine in university study, yet unstructured use risks cognitive offloading, surface learning, and uncritical acceptance of fluent but unreliable output. This article aimed to develop and specify the Symbiotic Critical Human–AI Learning Model (SC-AIM), operationalised through the five-stage FAVIC framework (Formulation, Augmentation, Verification, Integration, Creation), and to set out the assessment instruments and evaluation design that accompany it. Following the Analysis and Design phases of the ADDIE research-and-development approach, we synthesised recent experimental, meta-analytic, and survey evidence to derive design requirements, translated them into a stage-by-stage instructional specification, built a process-sensitive assessment rubric, and defined a quasi-experimental and qualitative validation plan for Indonesian higher education. The results are the model and its components: an evidence-to-design mapping, the FAVIC stage specification, a three-level process-sensitive rubric, and an evaluation design with hypotheses. Conclusion: SC-AIM offers lecturers a concrete, theory-grounded sequence that places human reasoning before and after AI assistance and makes verification an assessed activity, giving higher education a ready-to-use pedagogical model for developing analytical and logical reasoning in the age of generative AI.

title: A systematic review of theoretical perspectives frameworks and research gaps in AI localization for customer service
container-title: Discover Artificial Intelligence
9cf518f20dd7715f77bd6e5d242126f4273a5c11.abstract: Abstract Integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into the operations of customer service has become an important strategic task for organizations aiming to improve their service quality, increase efficiency, and raise the level of customer satisfaction. However, the effective localization of AI technologies within organizational contexts continues to be a challenge especially in Arab countries due to certain contextual challenges such as organizational culture, infrastructure, and human capital. This paper provides a systematic review of the literature on AI localization in customer service by synthesizing the findings of 150 peer-reviewed articles published between 2015 and 2025 in Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore. The review uses the PRISMA framework to ensure methodological rigor and reveals four key theoretical perspectives that underlie AI localization: Resource Dependence Theory (RDT), Resource-Based View (RBV), Continuous Improvement (CI), and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The synthesis reveals three categories of localization frameworks – governance-focused, collaborative adoption, and service improvement – as well as the key challenges across the dimensions of technical, organizational, cultural, and ethical. Three important research gaps emerge: (1) integration gap – the absence of the comprehensive frameworks addressing technological localization and its relation to service quality outcome, (2) mediation gap – the limited insight into the mechanisms of translation of AI into quality improvements, and (3) contextual gap – the lack of the research on AI localization in the Arab organizational context. The paper concludes with the research agenda for future studies in this field.

title: Hybrid Markov Regime-Switching and Hurdle modeling of last-mile livestock logistics in Ukraine under systemic volatility
container-title: Scientific Reports
44d27a692d2844d8c9620a9ead75624da98c4033.abstract: Abstract This study examines the transformation of last-mile logistics in Ukraine’s livestock supply chains under conditions of prolonged systemic volatility and infrastructure disruption. A hybrid analytical framework is proposed that integrates Random Forest Recursive Feature Elimination (RF-RFE) for preliminary predictor screening, a two-state Markov Regime-Switching (MRS) model for identifying latent logistics regimes, and a two-part Hurdle model for separately estimating disruption probability and conditional freight-cost intensity. The empirical analysis uses a verified monthly panel dataset covering 2023–2025 across three contrasting regional logistics nodes - Kyiv, Vinnytsia, and Lviv - and incorporates energy, security, market, transport, and infrastructure-related indicators. The MRS results identify two statistically distinct and persistent freight-cost regimes, with the systemic-crisis regime characterized by a 21.8% higher mean Freight Cost Per Ton and a longer expected duration than the operational-stability regime. The Hurdle estimates show that Security Alerts and Power Outage Hours are positively associated with the probability of logistics disruption, while Power Outage Hours and Fuel Price Volatility are positively associated with conditional freight-cost intensity; regional comparisons further reveal heterogeneous exposure to systemic shocks. Counterfactual technological scenarios further indicate that combining AI-assisted dynamic routing with decentralized autonomous and light electric transport solutions could reduce the estimated sensitivity of freight costs to energy disruptions by approximately 24.2%. The findings demonstrate the value of combining latent-regime identification, sequential disruption modeling, and technological scenario analysis for assessing the resilience of livestock last-mile logistics under persistent infrastructure and security shocks.

title: Designing AI-Agents with Personalities: A Psychometric Approach
ae67dae61c1d5baabd320d982987df901ef9df36.abstract: We introduce a methodology for assigning quantifiable and psychometrically validated personalities to AI-Agents using the Big Five framework. Across three studies, we evaluate its feasibility and limitations. In Study 1, we show that large language models (LLMs) capture semantic similarities among Big Five measures, providing a basis for personality assignment. In Study 2, we create AI-Agents using prompts designed based on the Big Five Inventory-2 (BFI-2) in different format, and find that AI-Agents powered by new models align more closely with human responses on the Mini-Markers test, although the finer pattern of results (e.g., factor loading patterns) were sometimes inconsistent. In Study 3, we validate our AI-Agents on risk-taking and moral dilemma vignettes, finding that models prompted with the BFI-2-Expanded format most closely reproduce human personality-decision associations, while safety-aligned models generally inflate ‘moral’ ratings. Overall, our results show that AI-Agents align with humans in correlations between input Big Five traits and output responses and may serve as useful tools for preliminary research. Nevertheless, discrepancies in finer response patterns indicate that AI-Agents cannot (yet) fully substitute for human participants in precision or high-stakes projects.

title: LLM4NL2BQS: using generative AI to transform natural language in BQS
container-title: Artificial Intelligence for Security and Defence Applications IV
e922e9c9fbadc8f0c31019b8bb50fbc66f3018cb.abstract: Complex query languages such as Boolean Query Syntax (BQS) are powerful tools for information retrieval within NATO’s Coalition Shared Data network. Their effective use generally requires substantial technical and domain specific expertise, restricting high quality query formulation to a limited number of specialised analysts and creating bottlenecks in information gathering and decision making. In this paper, we investigate three complementary approaches to translating natural language information needs into syntactically correct and semantically appropriate BQS queries. These are fine-tuning a small, open source language model, few-shot prompting and Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) using schema context drawn from the Allied Engineering Documentation Publication AEDP-17 specification of the Standardization Agreement(STANAG) 4559. Training data for fine-tuning is synthesised directly from the specification and validated both grammatically and against a live Coalition Shared Data (CSD)-Server. All three approaches are evaluated on a separate benchmark stratified by difficulty under three cumulative prompting conditions and compared against several general purpose language models, including commercial ones. The fine-tuned model achieves statistically significantly higher semantic accuracy than every comparison model at baseline prompting and higher syntactic and execution accuracy at every prompting condition, with the advantage widest on the most structurally complex queries. Fine-tuning already captures most of this benefit before any few-shot examples or RAG are added, while the commercial models depend far more on prompting strategy to reach their best results. This indicates that for a narrow query language tied to a specific schema, targeted fine-tuning of a small model is a more effective and more robust strategy than relying on few-shot prompting or RAG of a larger general purpose model, while lowering the barrier to entry for users without specialised expertise and reducing organisational reliance on highly specialised staff.

title: AI Driven Talent Management and the Performance of Agri Based Enterprises in Central Region Cameroon
container-title: Journal of Economics, Management, Entrepreneurship, and Business (JEMEB)
9a45a01f3f197d9b0c87ceca92e874eb272d0293.abstract: Purpose: This study examines the relationship between artificial intelligence (AI) driven talent management practices and the performance of agri based enterprises in the Central Region of Cameroon, focusing on the mediating roles of workforce productivity and employee resilience. Research Methodology: A quantitative cross sectional survey design was employed, targeting 250 managers and human resource professionals. Data were collected with a structured questionnaire and analyzed with SPSS and AMOS through descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation, and mediation analysis with 5.000 bootstrap resamples. Results: AI driven talent management was positively and significantly related to enterprise performance (r=0.523, p<0.01). Workforce productivity (β=0.18) and employee resilience (β=0.14) significantly mediated this relationship. Both the total indirect effect (β=0.32, p<0.01) and the direct effect (β=0.29, p<0.01) were significant, indicating partial mediation, with about 52 percent of the total effect transmitted through the two mediators. Conclusions: AI driven talent management enhances the performance of agri based enterprises both directly and indirectly through improved workforce productivity and stronger employee resilience. Enterprises should integrate AI strategically into talent management and support employees through change management. Limitations: The cross sectional design, self reported data, purposive sampling, and focus on a single region limit causal inference and generalizability. Contributions: The study provides empirical evidence from an underresearched African agricultural context and clarifies the mechanisms through which AI driven talent management translates into enterprise performance.

title: Robot cops on patrol: police officers' perceived effectiveness of AI-powered humanoid robots
container-title: Policing: An International Journal
399ffbef301f680d3c80797a3999bd5c26c9c5cb.abstract: Purpose The main purpose of the study is to examine how organizational justice, artificial intelligence (AI) literacy and perceived risks shape officers' attitudes toward AI-powered service and crime-fighting robots. Design/methodology/approach This study used survey data collected from 959 police officers in a major metropolitan area in Southwestern China. Two regression models were estimated to analyze correlates of police officers' perceived effectiveness of service and crime-fighting AI robots. Findings Results show that supervisor support for AI is a strong and consistent predictor of positive attitudes toward AI-powered robots, whereas supervisor justice is negatively associated with AI acceptance. AI training and AI knowledge also significantly enhance perceived effectiveness of AI tools, underscoring the saliency of technological familiarity. Perceived risks play a more limited and task-specific role. Originality/value The present study is among the first attempts to assess police officers' attitudes toward the application of AI in policing. This study provides evidence-based recommendations for the ethical and effective integration of AI into law enforcement practices.

title: AI governance as co-regulation: a practitioner-informed framework for defense-sector small and medium-sized enterprises
container-title: Digital Policy, Regulation and Governance
567df46acd778f8be8494c9ae84f8e44b8ec75da.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to examine how practitioners supporting defense-sector small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) place artificial intelligence (AI) governance within the coregulatory regime of National Institute of Standards and Technology Special Publication 800-171, the cybersecurity maturity model certification program, contracts and assessors. Design/methodology/approach An exploratory survey of 38 practitioners, recruited through a public LinkedIn post, combined a risk-to-control-family mapping task, artifact feasibility ratings and open-ended responses. Analysis was descriptive, with exploratory correlations adjusted for multiplicity and one researcher coded the open text. Findings Respondents concentrated AI risk on a few evidence-bearing control families, led by audit and accountability, risk assessment, access control and system and information integrity. Perceived compliance strain was high and readiness low. Artifacts resembling existing evidence, such as audit trail exports, were rated most feasible. Guidance ambiguity was the leading barrier. No exploratory association survived adjustment for multiplicity. Research limitations/implications The purposive sample and self-reported perceptions support pattern identification, not population estimates or claims about implementation outcomes. Practical implications Assessors and prime contractors could reduce SME burden by publishing exemplar AI evidence artifacts mapped to existing control families. Originality/value The study develops coregulation as a lens on the evidence burden of small firms at the base of regulatory chains, reports the full risk-to-control matrix and derives a seven-module framework that separates survey-supported elements from design choices.

title: AI Assessment of Heterogeneous Histopathologic Brain Tumor Sub-regions: the RANO MICCAI BraTS-Path 2024 Challenge
container-title: Neuro-Oncology
33be48153e50bcd0943f8c6fa42c207057d4b088.abstract: Abstract Background Automated classification of glioblastoma (IDH-wt, WHO CNS Gr.4) histopathologic sub-regions in whole slide images (WSI) is essential for quantitative tumor characterization, but faces substantial challenges from intra-tumoral heterogeneity and inter-observer annotation variability. The AI-RANO & RANO-Pathology working groups organized BraTS-Path 2024, representing the first international benchmarking environment and publicly available spatially annotated dataset, towards promoting the development and fair evaluation of Artificial Intelligence (AI) models to classify specific sub-regions: cellular tumor, pseudopalisading necrosis (PN), microvascular proliferation, geographic necrosis, infiltration into the cortex, and white matter penetration (WM). Methods Multi-institutional H&E-stained WSIs had reference standard samples generated by eight expert neuropathologists, following a rigorous peer review protocol, resulting in 309,118 data samples (training/validation/hold-out testing: 96,485/62,387/150,246). Quantitative performance evaluation of six AI approaches was conducted based on multiple metrics, including Accuracy and Matthew’s correlation coefficient (MCC). A robust statistically-aware ranking strategy offered statistical significance of the final rankings. Results Top-performing approaches employed common strategies, including large pre-trained models, ensembling, and extensive data augmentation, reporting Accuracy=0.69 and MCC=0.58. Key challenges included severe class imbalance, hampering minority class performance, and inter-annotator variability, especially for ambiguous sub-regions such as PN or WM. Conclusions BraTS-Path represents a valuable public resource for glioblastoma histopathologic sub-region assessment. Our findings indicate the specific task remaining an open research problem, highlighting the influence of rare sub-regions, the absence of a consistent “gold standard” annotation protocol, and the potential of foundation models to improve generalization, guiding future research toward developing more reliable AI tools for quantitative neuropathology.

title: A review of predictive maintenance strategies for Industry 5.0: AI, digital twins and human–machine collaboration
container-title: Journal of Quality in Maintenance Engineering
24d188956295cd9e7430988639ed3dfafe01a783.abstract: Purpose The purpose of this article is to provide a comprehensive review of predictive maintenance (PdM) strategies within the emerging Industry 5.0 paradigm, emphasizing the shift from automation-centric maintenance to human-centric, collaborative systems. The study aims to synthesize model-based, data-driven, artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled and hybrid PdM approaches, examine the role of key enabling technologies such as digital twins and edge computing and highlight human–machine collaboration in maintenance decision-making. By proposing a unified taxonomy, the article seeks to identify research gaps and guide the development of resilient, sustainable and explainable PdM systems. Design/methodology/approach This study adopts a structured systematic review methodology to analyze PdM strategies in the context of Industry 5.0. Peer-reviewed journal articles, standards and authoritative reports were identified through major scientific databases using predefined keywords related to PdM, condition-based maintenance, AI, digital twins and human–machine collaboration. The selected literature was critically examined and classified based on maintenance approach, enabling technologies, deployment architecture and degree of human involvement. Comparative analysis was employed to identify research gaps, challenges and emerging trends, culminating in the development of a novel taxonomy for Industry 5.0-oriented PdM systems. Findings The review reveals that PdM in Industry 5.0 is evolving toward hybrid frameworks that integrate data-driven intelligence with physics-based models and human expertise. While AI-based approaches improve diagnostic and prognostic accuracy, challenges related to data quality, interpretability and workforce acceptance persist. Digital twins, edge computing and collaborative robots emerge as key enablers for real-time, resilient and human-centric maintenance systems. The analysis highlights a lack of unified frameworks addressing human–machine collaboration and resilience, underscoring the need for explainable, lifecycle-oriented PdM solutions tailored to Industry 5.0 environments. Research limitations/implications This study is limited by its reliance on published literature, which may underrepresent proprietary industrial implementations and emerging practices not yet reported in academic sources. The review does not include empirical validation or quantitative benchmarking of PdM methods, focusing instead on conceptual and methodological synthesis. Nevertheless, the proposed taxonomy and identified research gaps provide a foundation for future empirical studies, experimental validation and large-scale industrial case analyses aimed at developing resilient, human-centric PdM frameworks aligned with Industry 5.0 principles. Practical implications The findings of this review offer practical guidance for industrial practitioners seeking to implement PdM within Industry 5.0 environments. The proposed taxonomy assists decision-makers in selecting appropriate PdM strategies based on system complexity, human involvement and technological readiness. Insights into digital twins, edge computing and human-in-the-loop AI support the design of maintenance systems that enhance reliability, reduce unplanned downtime and improve workforce acceptance. The study also highlights the importance of explainable and collaborative maintenance solutions to facilitate successful adoption in real-world manufacturing settings. Social implications By emphasizing human-centric and collaborative PdM, this study highlights the social impact of Industry 5.0 on the industrial workforce. The integration of human-in-the-loop decision-making and collaborative robots can improve workplace safety, reduce physically demanding tasks and support skill augmentation rather than job displacement. Transparent and explainable maintenance systems foster trust between workers and intelligent technologies, facilitating organizational acceptance and long-term adoption. Ultimately, Industry 5.0-oriented PdM contributes to more inclusive, resilient and sustainable industrial environments that align technological advancement with human well-being. Originality/value This article provides one of the first comprehensive reviews that explicitly situates PdM within the Industry 5.0 paradigm, moving beyond automation-centric perspectives. Its originality lies in the integration of PdM, condition-based maintenance, diagnostics and prognostics through a unified, human-centric lens. The study proposes a novel taxonomy that incorporates digital twins, edge computing and human–robot collaboration, offering a structured foundation for future research. By bridging technological, organizational and human factors, the article delivers both conceptual clarity and practical value for advancing next-generation maintenance systems.

title: Perceived fairness, accountability and transparency toward ML-based AI service delivery: conceptualization and measurement
container-title: Journal of Service Management
32ac1dcbe2ea84a31686f268ded2a0b816c7e9ab.abstract: Purpose This study conceptualizes and validates a multidimensional framework of consumers' perceived fairness, accountability and transparency (FAT) in machine learning (ML)-based AI service delivery. Addressing inconsistent conceptualizations and limited service-oriented measures, it examines how FAT perceptions emerge across goal-setting, coding and developing and implementation stages. A formative FAT scale is developed and tested for its predictive validity on trust and usage intention. Design/methodology/approach A multi-stage scale development process was used. Items were generated through literature review and 20 interviews, and face validity was assessed via an expert focus group. Two surveys (n = 448; n = 535) supported exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) validation of a reflective–formative FAT structure. A third survey (n = 455) established convergent and nomological validity with established FAT scales, trust and intention to use. Findings Results confirm FAT as a multidimensional construct shaped across goal-setting, coding and developing and implementation phases. All nine first-order factors significantly form the three higher-order FAT dimensions. The scale demonstrates strong reliability and validity, and fairness and transparency exhibit the strongest effects on trust and intention to use. Findings support a stage-based view of ethical perception in AI service delivery. Originality/value This research provides the first stage-based conceptualization and validated scale of perceived FAT in ML-based service AI. It integrates attribution theory with a socio-technical lens to disentangle how ethical judgments form throughout the AI lifecycle. The study advances theoretical clarity and offers actionable guidance for designing, developing and deploying ethically aligned AI services.

title: Exploring human–AI collaboration for management control in public healthcare
container-title: International Journal of Public Sector Management
14284e15945044815c9bcf6fc0c839ff33cdb032.abstract: Purpose This study examines how controllers in public healthcare envision human–AI collaboration in management control when dealing with uncertainty, complexity and equivocality, focusing on anticipated advantages and implementation challenges in an early-adoption setting. Design/methodology/approach We conducted an exploratory qualitative study with 14 controllers from Italian public healthcare organisations. Four closed-ended questions provided a preliminary picture of current AI adoption, while three scenario-based open-ended questions elicited prospective assessments. The framework method was used to analyse the data. Findings AI adoption remains limited and uneven, and is rarely embedded in everyday management control. Under uncertainty, controllers link AI to better forecasting and faster access to information, but worry about data quality, privacy and overreliance. In complex settings, they expect AI to help integrate diverse information and enable more systemic control, provided processes are standardised and human oversight remains. In equivocal situations, AI may support interpretation and communication, but its impact is limited by limited hands-on experience and the difficulty of codifying contextual nuances. Originality/value Based on the Jarrahi (2018) decision-making scenarios, the study develops a tentative conceptualisation of how public healthcare controllers envisage AI collaboration. The concerns of the participants inform three proposed arrangements: validation, recursive integration and contestable sensemaking. Their formulation and the accountability-augmentation principle are theoretical elaborations informed by prospective evidence and accountability research.

title: AI anthropomorphism, emotional attachment and verification behaviour in GenAI use
container-title: Online Information Review
69181986ddbed0224e43f9b1fb18cf320f342860.abstract: Purpose With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), AI is increasingly perceived not merely as a tool but as a conversational partner. This study examines how AI anthropomorphism is associated with users’ verification of AI-generated information through emotional attachment. Design/methodology/approach A survey was conducted with 430 adult GenAI users in South Korea. The proposed mediation model was analysed using structural equation modelling. Findings Within the proposed structural model, AI anthropomorphism was positively associated with emotional attachment to AI, which was in turn positively associated with AI-generated information verification behaviour. AI anthropomorphism was also directly and positively associated with verification behaviour. The significant positive indirect association along the anthropomorphism–attachment–verification pathway suggests that the findings are more consistent with a cognitive vigilance pathway than with a cognitive illusion pathway. Rather than indicating that anthropomorphism and attachment reduce scrutiny, the results suggest that they are associated with greater verification effort. Originality/value This study narrows its empirical contribution to a mediation model linking AI anthropomorphism, emotional attachment and verification behaviour. It shows that emotional attachment to AI is not necessarily associated with reduced scrutiny, but may instead be linked to greater verification effort. Building on this finding, AI verification fatigue is repositioned as a promising theoretical extension for future research on the possible longer-term cognitive burden of repeated AI-generated information verification, rather than as an empirically demonstrated outcome of the present study.

title: Generative AI Literacies and Discipline-Specific Knowledge: Preservice Teachers Planning Task-Based L2 Lessons with GenAI
container-title: Digital Studies in Language and Literature
49cfa4edc8a86155f27305dd81b772f6f0a87a1a.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to support Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT)-oriented lesson planning in a preservice teacher education context, examining the extent to which LLM use can contribute to the mobilisation of TBLT-related competencies. The case study draws on triangulated data from surveys, interaction logs with the LLM, lesson plans produced by preservice teachers and their reflections. The module required participants to generate a lesson plan with an LLM and to compare the resulting plan with a previously created lesson plan developed without AI support. The analysis focuses on knowledge of TBLT principles and their implementation during lesson planning, and the GenAI competence activated through the interaction with the LLM. The findings reveal considerable variation in how the dyads interacted with the LLM. Some dyads formulated more precise prompts and prompt iterations, provided more contextualised input, engaged more critically with the LLM-generated output, and iteratively refined their lesson plans in ways that appeared more consistent with TBLT principles. The data suggest an association between a stronger conceptual understanding of TBLT and more purposeful interaction with the LLM. This association indicates that disciplinary knowledge may facilitate the effective use of LLMs for TBLT-oriented lesson planning. Rather than replacing pedagogical expertise, LLM use appears to be most productive when preservice teachers are able to critically evaluate and adapt the generated output in light of established TBLT principles.

title: Encouraging the use of generative AI for closed-book test preparation: effects on student assessment performance and perceptions
container-title: Microbiology Australia
a89131b7b8180b129ba0fc050cf8b5278dbad42d.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being used by university students to support learning. However, evidence from authentic classroom settings examining whether GenAI-assisted revision influences closed-book assessment performance remains limited. This study evaluated the educational use of Microsoft Copilot in a third-year undergraduate immunology course. Student performance was compared between the 2025 and 2026 cohorts using comparable closed-book assessments of identical format and similar difficulty. Before Test 2 in 2026, students were encouraged to use Copilot during structured revision activities. Following Test 2, students completed an anonymous survey examining their perceptions of using Copilot to support learning. No statistically significant differences were observed in Test 1 or Test 2 marks between cohorts. Although a higher proportion of students achieved higher grades in 2026, a similar trend was evident before the intervention. Survey results showed that 78% of students agreed that GenAI could support learning of complex scientific concepts when used appropriately. However, only 53% reported improved understanding of immunology concepts, 39% reported improved knowledge recall, and 71% expressed concerns regarding inaccurate or misleading Copilot-generated information. These findings suggest that although students recognise the educational value of GenAI, encouraging its use during revision alone may not improve subsequent closed-book assessment performance.

title: Use and perceptions of AI tools among Australian general practice registrars: a national survey
container-title: Journal of Primary Health Care
c3efd0b3647649ef143335193afd580c770d2a16.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used in health care, yet little is known about how often Australian general practitioner trainees (GP registrars) use them or how they perceive the impact of AI on training and clinical care. Aim This study aimed to examine how frequently registrars use AI tools for clinical care and education, types of AI used, the perceived benefits and risks, and training needs. Methods A national cross-sectional online survey conducted from 7 May to 4 June 2024 invited 3743 Australian General Practice Training or Fellowship Support Program registrars to participate. The survey assessed frequency and context of AI use, practice-level adoption, perceived impacts, training exposure, and ethical-legal concerns. Analyses were descriptive. Results Among the 727 respondents (19.5%), frequent use (weekly or more) was uncommon; 7.3% for clinical tasks, 5.0% for education. Practice-level adoption was low, with 10.8% reporting subscription to AI tools. Most registrars anticipated benefits, particularly learning efficiency and administrative workload reduction. However, 25.0% perceived increased medicolegal risk. Formal training was rare, with most relying on self-directed learning, though many rated AI education as important. Among clinical users, common tools included large language models (32.5%), remote patient monitoring devices (28.6%), and voice-to-text tools (26.2%). Large language models predominated in education (63.5%). Discussion In May–June 2024, AI tool use among registrars was limited, although most perceived potential benefit. Enthusiasm was tempered by concerns about safety, ethics, and legal risks. Structured training and guidelines are needed to support safe, effective integration into GP registrars’ practice and education.

title: Responsible AI and Structural Justice
da1087c38814e959c4bfbff69e0e4db0180d2fd1.abstract: This Element presents challenges of attributing responsibility for AI harms through political theories of structural injustice, where fault is broadly diffused and difficult to establish. I argue that AI systems feature complex structural entanglements between humans and machines-in computational architectures, organizational workflows, and societal data collectives-that pose problems for conventional liability where direct causal links are necessary for blame. I develop two modes of structural responsibility that address unjust AI outcomes from these entanglements. Thin structural responsibility traces where power and accountability lie in the processes of developing unjust AI systems. Thick structural responsibility enlists deployers, users, and broader publics alongside developers in collectively repairing unjust social conditions that produce and rely on AI systems. I show that many Responsible AI initiatives remain thin by demanding disclosures without systemic repair. Incorporating thicker reforms makes responsibility for just AI a living political practice rather than a managerial task. This title is also available as open access on Cambridge Core.

title: Designing Critical Human–AI Learning in Higher Education: The SC-AIM–FAVIC Framework for Analytical and Logical Reasoning
container-title: JPI: Jurnal Pustaka Indonesia
4ce99b9a5976c3c25eb4ecff905eaf4a200752ca.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now routine in university study, yet unstructured use risks cognitive offloading, surface learning, and uncritical acceptance of fluent but unreliable output. This article aimed to develop and specify the Symbiotic Critical Human–AI Learning Model (SC-AIM), operationalised through the five-stage FAVIC framework (Formulation, Augmentation, Verification, Integration, Creation), and to set out the assessment instruments and evaluation design that accompany it. Following the Analysis and Design phases of the ADDIE research-and-development approach, we synthesised recent experimental, meta-analytic, and survey evidence to derive design requirements, translated them into a stage-by-stage instructional specification, built a process-sensitive assessment rubric, and defined a quasi-experimental and qualitative validation plan for Indonesian higher education. The results are the model and its components: an evidence-to-design mapping, the FAVIC stage specification, a three-level process-sensitive rubric, and an evaluation design with hypotheses. Conclusion: SC-AIM offers lecturers a concrete, theory-grounded sequence that places human reasoning before and after AI assistance and makes verification an assessed activity, giving higher education a ready-to-use pedagogical model for developing analytical and logical reasoning in the age of generative AI.

title: A systematic review of theoretical perspectives frameworks and research gaps in AI localization for customer service
container-title: Discover Artificial Intelligence
9cf518f20dd7715f77bd6e5d242126f4273a5c11.abstract: Abstract Integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into the operations of customer service has become an important strategic task for organizations aiming to improve their service quality, increase efficiency, and raise the level of customer satisfaction. However, the effective localization of AI technologies within organizational contexts continues to be a challenge especially in Arab countries due to certain contextual challenges such as organizational culture, infrastructure, and human capital. This paper provides a systematic review of the literature on AI localization in customer service by synthesizing the findings of 150 peer-reviewed articles published between 2015 and 2025 in Scopus, Web of Science, and IEEE Xplore. The review uses the PRISMA framework to ensure methodological rigor and reveals four key theoretical perspectives that underlie AI localization: Resource Dependence Theory (RDT), Resource-Based View (RBV), Continuous Improvement (CI), and Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). The synthesis reveals three categories of localization frameworks – governance-focused, collaborative adoption, and service improvement – as well as the key challenges across the dimensions of technical, organizational, cultural, and ethical. Three important research gaps emerge: (1) integration gap – the absence of the comprehensive frameworks addressing technological localization and its relation to service quality outcome, (2) mediation gap – the limited insight into the mechanisms of translation of AI into quality improvements, and (3) contextual gap – the lack of the research on AI localization in the Arab organizational context. The paper concludes with the research agenda for future studies in this field.

title: Trust Conditions and Regulatory Protection in AI Based Agricultural Information in Bangladesh
a2c5337801e170792c22bf8d97b0ff776a38bf12.abstract: Abstract AI-supported agricultural information may provide useful guidance while raising concerns about local suitability, accountability and oversight. This study examines stated trust conditions and perceptions of regulatory protection in a Bangladesh survey. The 385 adult, AI-aware records comprise law students, graduates, legal professionals and other respondents; 60 report a location classified as upazila or rural. The file does not identify farmers or establish that respondents use agricultural AI, so findings concern a mixed sample rather than representative rural users. The analysis retains separate questionnaire items and compares paired endorsement of statements on source/provider clarity, regulatory oversight and accountability. It also explores correlations between AI awareness items and two trust-related statements. Of 385 respondents, 310 (80.5%) agreed that clear sources and a responsible provider would increase trust, 255 (66.2%) agreed that regulatory oversight can increase confidence, and 317 (82.3%) agreed that strong accountability increases willingness to use agricultural AI. Source/provider clarity exceeded oversight endorsement by 14.3 percentage points; 210 respondents endorsed both statements. These are differently worded hypothetical propositions, so their contrast is not a ranking of interventions or evidence of causal effects. Associations between awareness and trust conditions were small and do not establish that training changes reliance. The study contributes an item-level distinction between provider transparency, institutional oversight, local adaptation and accountability, and proposes a future design that evaluates specific advisory systems with actual agricultural users.

title: Learning Philippine History with Generative AI: College Students’ Reported Experiences of Verification, National Identity, and Civic Responsibility
container-title: Journal of Educational Research and Practice
4bd6b70499ec4c8ef8048fb4eb892941ab6c2ed6.abstract: This qualitative descriptive study examined the experiences of college students with historical learning, information verification, and civic formation in the context of generative AI. The research involved 315 students from 14 academic programs at a private higher education institution in Laguna, Philippines. Data collection was conducted using an expert-validated written interview guide administered via Google Forms, and the data were analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. Participants indicated that readings in Philippine history facilitated connections between past and present issues, recognition of persistent national problems, comprehension of historical accounts, and reflection on Filipino identity. They perceived AI as a tool for facilitating information access, clarifying concepts, and enabling exploratory enquiry, while also expressing concerns about inaccuracies, biases, fabricated claims, and dependency. The participants' verification practices included comparing accounts, consulting academic sources, examining authorship, and exercising caution before accepting online content. Historical learning was linked to reflection on civic responsibilities and freedoms, as well as intentions to engage in public affairs and defend rights. Participants recommended responsible AI use, source evaluation, misinformation detection, interactive activities, and connections with current issues. This study provides a contextualized account of students' perceptions of historical learning, AI use, verification, and civic orientations. These accounts do not establish changes in historical competence, verification performance, or civic behaviour. The findings underscore guided source evaluation and critical examination of AI-generated historical information as areas for instructional consideration; their effectiveness requires further evaluation.

title: A Review of Image-Based and AI-Driven Water Level Monitoring: Methods, Datasets, and Deployment Considerations
745caff33a0707f7b7d53673f331735c10b76ece.abstract: Abstract Accurate and continuous water-level monitoring is essential for agriculture, flood management, and water resources planning. However, many rivers and agricultural canals remain ungauged because conventional sensing infrastructure is costly to install and maintain, limiting basin-scale water accounting and conservation policies such as water banking and leasing. Computer vision enables water-level estimation from ground-based cameras, unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and satellites, offering a low-cost, non-contact alternative to conventional sensors. This review synthesizes 93 studies selected from 168 articles retrieved from five databases, following PRISMA 2020 guidelines. We summarize contact-based and non-contact sensing methods and examine image-based approaches, including traditional image processing, classical machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL), alongside their imaging modalities and datasets. DL methods, particularly object detection, semantic segmentation, and transformer-based models, are more robust than earlier approaches under low light, reflections, and cluttered backgrounds, with several studies reporting field errors of approximately 1–3 cm. However, these results are not directly comparable because studies differ in datasets, reference measurements, and evaluation metrics. Three major research gaps emerge: (1) fragmented datasets and inconsistent evaluation protocols; (2) limited cross-site validation and model generalization; and (3) insufficient long-term field evaluation and robustness to illumination changes, reflections, and camera displacement. Future research should prioritize standardized, publicly available multi-site datasets, common evaluation protocols, cross-site and seasonal testing, and adaptive models that maintain reliability under changing field conditions.

title: Designing brackish-water desalination plants beyond the range of real data: AI methods and a physics-structured surrogate compared
d4774303f7de8dc83e6cec7f789204314c73d49c.abstract: Abstract Brackish-water desalination plants of 100,000–600,000 m³ d⁻¹ are being planned, yet the largest operating brackish plant with published costs we found is about 68,000 m³ d⁻¹, so AI-assisted designs at this scale extrapolate. On a physics-based model with Egyptian feed-water presets, NSGA-II and multi-objective Bayesian optimisation gave equal cost–energy hypervolume, and Bayesian optimisation covered brine-pond area better than 40-member NSGA-II in all 26 runs. Reinforcement learning allocated capacity across four sites better than random but not better than a greedy rule. Data-driven surrogates failed silently beyond their training range; a hybrid that fits a capacity scaling law cut the error from 3.2% to 0.2% but not when the true scaling changed. Against few large-scale references, the model’s capital cost was 51% low to 129% high; an element-by-element membrane simulation (unvalidated) gave 1–118% lower energy use, most at high recovery. Re-optimised with the simulated energy, the cheapest design needed 50–59% less evaporation-pond area. In a value-of-information analysis, once ponds were costed, none of eight uncertain cost inputs changed the best recovery, which was set by the feasible limit. In this study, model uncertainty and missing large-plant data, not the choice of algorithm, limited how far designs can be trusted.

title: Bridging textile design and AI: An innovative methodological approach for the Ghanaian Textile Designer
container-title: Fashion and Textiles Review
c995ab099d5cca3d19b1b98354cb0d9ab855376e.abstract: Purpose: The study aimed to investigate the feasibility of employing selected artificial intelligence (AI) software to generate contemporary textile designs. Focusing on bridging textile design and AI, with a methodological approach for the Ghanaian Textile Designer. With AI emerging as a transformative force in multiple industries, including textiles, the research sought to assess its capacity to enhance design processes and meet consumer preferences. Methodology/Design: Three AI software programs, including Playground, Leonardo, and Lexcia, were selected for the study. Each was provided with identical prompts to generate contemporary textile designs. The outputs were then systematically analysed to identify similarities, differences, and overall design quality. Findings: The results showed that while the software received identical prompts, the generated designs displayed notable variations, alongside some shared visual features. The AI-driven process proved significantly faster and more efficient than traditional methods and yielded designs consistent with consumer specifications. Practical and Social Implications: The findings suggest that AI tools can substantially improve productivity, creativity, and responsiveness in textile design. Introducing AI-based design tools to textile designers in Ghana could enhance competitiveness, foster innovation, and better align production with evolving market demands. Originality: This study offers an early exploration of the comparative application of multiple AI software tools for contemporary textile design, contributing novel insights into their feasibility, efficiency, and adaptability within the Ghanaian textile industry context.

title: Generative AI in the Taiwan medical laboratory scientist examination: Performance and educational utility
container-title: Journal of the Chinese Medical Association
b55e5be68ed0ab95ea64db8ec0ab939c6de068e5.abstract: Background: The rapid evolution of generative artificial intelligence (GAI), particularly large language models (LLMs), offers transformative potential for health professions education. However, their performance in specialized clinical domains, such as medical laboratory science as well as educational utility, remain insufficiently characterized. This study evaluated multiple LLMs on the Taiwanese Medical Laboratory Scientist Examination (TMLSE) and investigated the effectiveness of AI-generated assessments in undergraduate-year (UGY) medical laboratory training. Methods: Four LLMs—GPT-3.5, GPT-4o, GPT-5.2, and Gemini 3 Pro—were evaluated using six TMLSE administrations from 2021 to 2023. Accuracy was assessed across 10 disciplines and image-based items, with incorrect responses categorized into informational, logical, or statistical errors. Additionally, 180 AI-generated items were validated by experts and administered to 30 UGY students. Student satisfaction and correlations between assessment performance and clinical internship outcomes were analyzed. Results: All the models surpassed the 60% passing threshold, with clear generational improvement. GPT-5.2 (93.5%) and Gemini 3 Pro (92.1%) significantly outperformed GPT-4o (85.8%) and GPT-3.5 (67.1%). An error analysis indicated that informational deficiencies were the predominant failure mode, accounting for more than 95% of the incorrect responses across all the models. Although image-based items were more challenging than text-based questions were, GPT-5.2 demonstrated superior multimodal capability, achieving an image-based accuracy of 73.3%. In the educational evaluation, UGY students rated AI-generated items significantly higher than authentic TMLSE questions did in terms of overall satisfaction ( p = 0.0089) and perceived utility for examination review ( p = 0.0405). The performance on AI-generated assessments was positively correlated with clinical internship outcomes (Spearman’s r= 0.3662, p = 0.0465), whereas no significant association was observed with traditional TMLSE scores. Conclusion: Modern LLMs demonstrate high performance in specialized medical laboratory knowledge, although image interpretation remains a limitation. Integrating AI-generated assessments into UGY curricula represents an effective and scalable approach to competency-based education, with demonstrated alignment to real-world clinical performance.

title: The AI Response to the 2025ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes: A Comparative Evaluation of Five Large Language Models
05f391b792eb8872b2b4f1706ece168f383d3e38.abstract: Abstract Background and Aim: Cardiovascular diseases, particularly chronic coronary syndromes (CCS), remain a leading cause of morbidity and mortality. Large language models (LLMs) have emerged as promising tools for processing medical information and supporting clinical decision-making. However, systematic comparative evaluation of their performance on current cardiology guidelines remains limited. This study aimed to comparatively evaluate the quality, guideline adherence, and clinical applicability of responses generated by five LLMs to clinical questions derived from the 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP/NAEMSP/SCAI Guideline for the Management of Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes. Methods This was a cross-sectional, observational, methodological simulation study. A pool of 20 open-ended clinical questions was developed based on 2025 ACC/AHA/ACEP /NAEMSP /SCAI Guideline for the Managementof Patients With Acute Coronary Syndromes, covering diagnostic and therapeutic domains, and validated by a panel of three independent cardiologists with over 15 years of clinical experience. Questions were submitted to five LLMs Gemini, DeepSeek, Claude, Copilot, and ChatGPT using identical Turkish-language prompts via publicly available web interfaces in April 2026. Model identifiers were removed to ensure evaluator blinding. Five independent expert cardiologists scored each response on five domains Comprehensiveness, Guideline Appropriateness, Understandability, Clinical Applicability, and Overall Scoreusing a 5-point Likert scale. Interrater reliability was assessed via intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) and Cronbach's alpha. Group comparisons were performed using linear mixed-effects models with Bonferroni correction. Results Interrater reliability was acceptable to good across all domains (ICC range: 0.632–0.762; Cronbach's alpha > 0.80 for all domains). The LLM variable exerted a statistically significant effect across all five evaluation domains (all p < 0.001). DeepSeek achieved the highest estimated marginal means in all domains, including Overall Score (EMM = 4.87 ± 0.22), significantly outperforming all other models (p < 0.05 for all pairwise comparisons). Gemini demonstrated the lowest performance across all domains (Overall Score EMM = 2.75 ± 0.24). ChatGPT and Claude showed comparable performance in all domains (Overall Score: EMM = 3.79 ± 0.22 vs. 3.61 ± 0.23; p = 1.000). Diagnostic questions yielded significantly higher Understandability scores than treatment questions (EMM 3.736 vs. 3.512; mean difference = 0.224, 95% CI: 0.067–0.381; p = 0.005), while no significant model × question category interaction was observed in any domain. Conclusion Although the DeepSeek model demonstrated superior performance specifically within the context of the 2025 AHA Guidelines, this could be attributed to Chain of Thought reasoning. Nevertheless, the overall reliability of large language models in clinical applications remains variable, and future studies should focus not merely on information retrieval, but on their impact on clinical patient management.

title: Who Perceives Work Performance Improvements from Generative AI Use in Government, Early-Stage Diffusion? Exploring the Roles of Organizational Power and Motivation on Work Performance
container-title: Public Organization Review
f9d3a1870f796a8cac7fafb98bb5aa8602b92ab5.abstract: Abstract This study examines which civil servants perceive performance improvements from using generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) and why, drawing on the Ability-Motivation-Opportunity theory and the reinforcement politics model. Using the Korea Institute of Public Administration survey data, we analyzed responses from 1,608 Korean civil servants. Results indicate that civil servants who frequently use generative AI and are intrinsically motivated perceive greater benefits from AI-assisted work than those with organizational power. These findings suggest that, early in the adoption of generative AI tools in government, these tools influence performance by shaping motivation and usage, not hierarchy.

title: Fluent but unfounded: generative AI, cue–evidence decoupling and founder judgement
dfd79287042a4a3f498d9bdfd7f122b53d7e68d0.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) can now produce, within minutes, a venture risk assessment that reads like the work of an experienced analyst. Whether founders, and the investors who read their documents, can still tell how much such an assessment rests on is an open question with consequences for entrepreneurship, finance and the governance of AI. This article develops a theory of cue–evidence decoupling. People judge the strength of evidence from cues such as fluency, structure and agreement, and generative AI supplies these cues whether or not the evidence is there. Because founders act when the uncertainty they perceive falls to a level they can accept, decoupling lowers perceived uncertainty without lowering actual uncertainty. It also weakens written venture materials as costly signals to investors. Because feedback in entrepreneurship is slow and noisy, founders should learn to correct for decoupling only slowly. To make the theory testable before outcomes are known, the article draws on risk science to define the knowledge-strength gap: the number of strength-of-knowledge criteria on which a founder rates an AI-assisted risk assessment as better supported than blind raters judge a normalised version of it to be. Eight propositions specify when the gap widens (novel ventures; estimating rather than listing risks), when it narrows (an AI critic; feedback on past estimates), how it raises resource commitment and how disclosure of AI use shifts investors' errors. Each proposition is paired with a randomised test and a result that would refute it. The theory implies that AI may mislead founders most where they need it most. It recasts the debate on AI and Knightian uncertainty as a question about founders' beliefs, and it suggests that safeguards for AI-assisted decisions, including transparency rules, should target the grounds of confidence and not only the accuracy of AI output.
