title: Perceived fairness, accountability and transparency toward ML-based AI service delivery: conceptualization and measurement
container-title: Journal of Service Management
32ac1dcbe2ea84a31686f268ded2a0b816c7e9ab.abstract: Purpose This study conceptualizes and validates a multidimensional framework of consumers' perceived fairness, accountability and transparency (FAT) in machine learning (ML)-based AI service delivery. Addressing inconsistent conceptualizations and limited service-oriented measures, it examines how FAT perceptions emerge across goal-setting, coding and developing and implementation stages. A formative FAT scale is developed and tested for its predictive validity on trust and usage intention. Design/methodology/approach A multi-stage scale development process was used. Items were generated through literature review and 20 interviews, and face validity was assessed via an expert focus group. Two surveys (n = 448; n = 535) supported exploratory factor analysis (EFA), confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) and partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) validation of a reflective–formative FAT structure. A third survey (n = 455) established convergent and nomological validity with established FAT scales, trust and intention to use. Findings Results confirm FAT as a multidimensional construct shaped across goal-setting, coding and developing and implementation phases. All nine first-order factors significantly form the three higher-order FAT dimensions. The scale demonstrates strong reliability and validity, and fairness and transparency exhibit the strongest effects on trust and intention to use. Findings support a stage-based view of ethical perception in AI service delivery. Originality/value This research provides the first stage-based conceptualization and validated scale of perceived FAT in ML-based service AI. It integrates attribution theory with a socio-technical lens to disentangle how ethical judgments form throughout the AI lifecycle. The study advances theoretical clarity and offers actionable guidance for designing, developing and deploying ethically aligned AI services.

title: Understanding quality management in Indonesian Madrasahs from principals' and teachers' perspectives
container-title: International Journal of Quality & Reliability Management
6cb278206685b86ad11cadc329edc8d41c6332a8.abstract: Purpose This study examines how educational quality is conceptualized, enacted and sustained in Indonesian Islamic schools (madrasahs) through principals' and teachers' lived experiences. Design/methodology/approach A phenomenological case study, informed by total quality management and school effectiveness and improvement theory, was conducted using semi-structured interviews. Findings Educational quality was holistic, integrating academic, moral, spiritual and social development. Quality management emphasized continuous evaluation, mentoring, collaboration and Islamic values. Resource constraints, policy instability, bureaucracy and resistance to change prompted adaptive strategies, including creative pedagogy, peer learning, community engagement and gradual reform. Originality/value The study highlights quality as purpose-driven in faith-based education.

title: Knowledge management and project performance: a quasi-experimental study in EPC oil and gas projects
container-title: Engineering, Construction and Architectural Management
f8cbbe212626d6ac74d5d865040acd6ebe2c8c02.abstract: Purpose This study addresses two interconnected gaps in project-based knowledge management (KM) research: the absence of prescriptive, stage-specific intervention frameworks for Engineering, Procurement and Construction (EPC) projects, and the lack of causal evidence linking digital KM interventions to objective operational outcomes. Design/methodology/approach An integrated practical framework for knowledge transfer in EPC projects is developed by embedding Szulanski's knowledge transfer model within the EPC disciplinary structure; its Stage 2–4 mechanisms are validated through a quasi-experimental Difference-in-Differences design using longitudinal administrative data from 12 welders over eight weeks in an international oil and gas EPC project in Iraq. Findings The framework's prescribed mechanisms produce a 4.4% increase in production efficiency, a 21% reduction in defect rates and a 17% decrease in safety incidents simultaneously (p &lt; 0.001). These findings are consistent with infrastructural barriers playing a substantial role in fragmented EPC environments, and all mechanisms are operationalisable through an easy-to-deploy, cloud-based platform requiring no specialist development. Originality/value First, the study develops an integrated practical framework that transforms Szulanski's descriptive typology into a prescriptive design tool specifying stage-specific and discipline-specific knowledge management system mechanisms. Second, it provides causal validation of a KM framework using objective operational data, an evidentiary standard that perception-based studies cannot achieve. Third, it demonstrates that the framework's prescribed mechanisms are fully operationalisable through an easy-to-deploy, cloud-based platform requiring no specialist development, closing the gap between framework validity and framework adoptability that has historically limited the practical impact of KM research.

title: How information sufficiency and perceived CSF criticality relate to employees' ESG awareness in Hong Kong logistics
container-title: The International Journal of Logistics Management
a7d3bdaaa46896d254f1600438c0420e147415de.abstract: Purpose The environmental, social and governance (ESG) disclosure and governance regimes may not automatically translate into employee understanding. This study examines whether employees' perceived sufficiency of ESG information and perceived criticality of implementation factors are associated with reported increases in ESG awareness and industry-transition optimism in Hong Kong logistics. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected through a single-wave, cross-sectional survey of 213 employees working in logistics-related roles in Hong Kong, of which 212 cases were listwise complete for the regression models. The hypotheses were tested using ordinary least squares (OLS) regression with HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors and case-resampling bias-corrected bootstrap confidence intervals. Given the cross-sectional design, the results are interpreted as conditional associations rather than causal effects. Findings Perceived information sufficiency and perceived critical success factor (CSF) criticality were each positively associated with reported increases in ESG awareness, and increases in ESG awareness were positively associated with industry-transition optimism. Positive indirect associations were reproduced for both predictors. However, statistical support for the residual direct association between information sufficiency and optimism differed between OLS and ordered-logit specifications; the result is therefore estimator-sensitive and is not described as full mediation. The residual direct association for CSF criticality is control-sensitive: it remains positive across adjustment sets but varies in statistical significance. Originality/value The study provides a bounded employee-level account of how perceived ESG-information sufficiency and perceived implementation requirements relate to reported awareness and transition expectations. It distinguishes these perceptions from firm-level materiality assessment, objective ESG implementation and ESG performance.

title: Innovators and Transformers: When supplier counts mislead about pharmaceutical supply resilience
container-title: International Journal of Physical Distribution & Logistics Management
db3340f1cb96215395409cbd0378fb2bc3b4e9ce.abstract: Purpose Approved supplier counts are used as signals of supply capacity in pharmaceutical markets. This article shows that such counts record administrative visibility, measure the gap between administrative and operational visibility in the US drug shortage records, and show that neither count is a valid measure of operational redundancy without normalization by market type and volume. Design/methodology/approach The analysis links United States Food and Drug Administration (FDA) drug shortage records, Orange Book approvals, drug listing records and inspection classifications for 3,344 active ingredient-by-dosage form markets in a cross-section. It tabulates the share of approved applications with no active listing and no linked firm. A temporally aligned comparison measures approved applicants for shortage markets at shortage onset and for comparison markets at pseudo-onset dates drawn from the same onset distribution. Findings Across markets, 12.8% of approved applications that are not formally discontinued are absent from the drug listing directory and 59.6% of all approvals are either discontinued or unlisted; the shares are nearly identical in shortage and comparison markets. Under temporal alignment, shortage markets have a median of seven approved applicants at onset against a pseudo-onset median of one for comparison markets and the count of linked firms shows the same inversion: markets with no linked firm are the least likely to be in shortage. Among approvals that predate onset, the median lead is 20 years (83% of approvals in shortage markets). Practical implications Shortage-risk classification should not rest on approval counts, and a count of linked firms is not a substitute without normalization by market type and volume; a low linked-firm count in a high-volume generic market is the configuration to watch. Originality/value The article separates administrative visibility from operational visibility as distinct constructs. It quantifies the wedge between the public approval register and the active counts that the regulator and the Government Accountability Office build internally. It documents that statute, policy metrics, guidance and published studies use register counts as the count of competitors.

title: Exploring human–AI collaboration for management control in public healthcare
container-title: International Journal of Public Sector Management
14284e15945044815c9bcf6fc0c839ff33cdb032.abstract: Purpose This study examines how controllers in public healthcare envision human–AI collaboration in management control when dealing with uncertainty, complexity and equivocality, focusing on anticipated advantages and implementation challenges in an early-adoption setting. Design/methodology/approach We conducted an exploratory qualitative study with 14 controllers from Italian public healthcare organisations. Four closed-ended questions provided a preliminary picture of current AI adoption, while three scenario-based open-ended questions elicited prospective assessments. The framework method was used to analyse the data. Findings AI adoption remains limited and uneven, and is rarely embedded in everyday management control. Under uncertainty, controllers link AI to better forecasting and faster access to information, but worry about data quality, privacy and overreliance. In complex settings, they expect AI to help integrate diverse information and enable more systemic control, provided processes are standardised and human oversight remains. In equivocal situations, AI may support interpretation and communication, but its impact is limited by limited hands-on experience and the difficulty of codifying contextual nuances. Originality/value Based on the Jarrahi (2018) decision-making scenarios, the study develops a tentative conceptualisation of how public healthcare controllers envisage AI collaboration. The concerns of the participants inform three proposed arrangements: validation, recursive integration and contestable sensemaking. Their formulation and the accountability-augmentation principle are theoretical elaborations informed by prospective evidence and accountability research.

title: Next-generation family business leaders: antecedents and behavioral mechanisms of succession intention
container-title: Journal of Family Business Management
b2823ddbe63cff1d6c8c880dbfd42f30d539ec4a.abstract: Purpose Building upon the theory of planned behavior and family business research, this study examines entrepreneurial family background (prior family business exposure and family business self-efficacy) as an intergenerational influence on the succession intention of next-generation family business leaders. Addressing a gap in succession intention research, the study assesses two mechanisms (attitude toward family business succession and perceived family support) that explain the relationship between entrepreneurial family background and succession intention. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative survey-based research design was employed to examine a sample of 278 next-generation family business leaders from Austria, the United States and other countries. Findings Attitude toward family business succession significantly explains the relationship between prior family business exposure and succession intention, whereas perceived family support does not. Family business self-efficacy is strongly related to succession intention directly and indirectly through attitude toward family business succession and perceived family support. Practical implications We discuss future research directions for family business scholarship and the practical implications for family business firms, including the development of succession management capabilities that provide next-generation leaders with positive early-career developmental experiences. Originality/value The study contributes to succession intention research by showing that prior family business exposure and family business self-efficacy are associated with succession intention through different mechanisms. Prior family business exposure is linked to succession intention through attitude toward family business succession, whereas family business self-efficacy demonstrates a strong direct relationship with succession intention and significant indirect relationships through both attitude and perceived family support.

title: Clinical Features and Management Framework for Refractory Hypophysitis: A Cohort Study
container-title: The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism
761f25522dd1130793b944c84945964da18cd5f1.abstract: Abstract Background Glucocorticoid (GC) therapy is the cornerstone therapy for primary autoimmune hypophysitis (PAH), yet treatment failure and relapse are common. The concept and optimal management of "refractory" PAH remain undefined. Objective To define the clinical entity of refractory PAH, identify its distinguishing features, develop an exploratory screening model, and propose a structured management pathway based on treatment outcomes. Methods A retrospective cohort study of 100 PAH patients was conducted. Refractory PAH was defined as primary GC resistance or recurrence during tapering (GC-dependent). Twenty-two patients met these criteria. Baseline characteristics were compared between groups, and a exploratory screening model developed. Results Among 100 patients with hypophysitis, 22 (22%) met the criteria for refractory disease, including 19 with GC-dependent and 3 with GC-resistant hypophysitis. Compared with the non-refractory group, GC-dependent refractory hypophysitis was characterized by a lower prevalence of pregnancy-associated hypophysitis (5.9% vs. 41.7%, p=0.006), higher serum prolactin levels (median 30.2 ng/mL vs. 17.8 ng/mL, p=0.021), a higher prevalence of hypogonadotropic hypogonadism (82.4% vs. 55.4%, p=0.040), and a larger median pituitary stalk diameter (5.5 mm vs. 3.7 mm, p=0.043). No significant differences were observed between the GC-resistant group and the non-refractory group. Combination therapy with immunosuppressive agents (e.g., mycophenolate mofetil) or rituximab was effective in achieving radiological control. Glucocorticoid-related adverse events occurred in 40.9% of patients, most commonly hyperlipidemia and hyperglycemia. Conclusion This study defines and characterizes refractory PAH. The distinct clinical characteristics and the proposed structured diagnostic-therapeutic pathway offer a framework for managing this challenging condition.

title: Drivers and outcomes of harmonious environmental passion: a self-determination theory approach in the hotel industry
container-title: International Journal of Contemporary Hospitality Management
99f4164cf632e7fda00598b6f4fdea87db502743.abstract: Purpose Despite growing interest in employee-driven environmental sustainability in hospitality, limited research explains how personal, social and organizational factors jointly shape harmonious environmental passion (HEP) and how this passion translates into diverse green work outcomes. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), this study aims to develop and test a conceptual model that examines key antecedents and consequences of HEP among hotel employees. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from frontline and supervisory employees working in four- and five-star hotels. A structured questionnaire was used, and the proposed model was tested using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). Findings The results indicate that individual green values, personal environmental norms, nature connectedness (NC) and corporate environmental ethics positively influence HEP, while green psychological climate shows no significant effect. HEP positively affects in-role green behavior, extra-role green behavior, green voice behavior and green recovery performance. Proactive personality (PP) moderates the relationship between NC and HEP, such that the relationship is stronger among highly proactive employees. Practical implications Hotel managers can enhance employee-driven environmental sustainability by recruiting and developing employees with strong green values, reinforcing ethical environmental practices and strengthening employees’ connection with nature. Nature-related sustainability initiatives may be particularly effective among employees with higher PP. Originality/value This study applies SDT by integrating personal, social and organizational antecedents of HEP and by demonstrating its impact on both behavioral and performance-based green outcomes in hospitality settings.

title: AI anthropomorphism, emotional attachment and verification behaviour in GenAI use
container-title: Online Information Review
69181986ddbed0224e43f9b1fb18cf320f342860.abstract: Purpose With the rapid advancement of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI), AI is increasingly perceived not merely as a tool but as a conversational partner. This study examines how AI anthropomorphism is associated with users’ verification of AI-generated information through emotional attachment. Design/methodology/approach A survey was conducted with 430 adult GenAI users in South Korea. The proposed mediation model was analysed using structural equation modelling. Findings Within the proposed structural model, AI anthropomorphism was positively associated with emotional attachment to AI, which was in turn positively associated with AI-generated information verification behaviour. AI anthropomorphism was also directly and positively associated with verification behaviour. The significant positive indirect association along the anthropomorphism–attachment–verification pathway suggests that the findings are more consistent with a cognitive vigilance pathway than with a cognitive illusion pathway. Rather than indicating that anthropomorphism and attachment reduce scrutiny, the results suggest that they are associated with greater verification effort. Originality/value This study narrows its empirical contribution to a mediation model linking AI anthropomorphism, emotional attachment and verification behaviour. It shows that emotional attachment to AI is not necessarily associated with reduced scrutiny, but may instead be linked to greater verification effort. Building on this finding, AI verification fatigue is repositioned as a promising theoretical extension for future research on the possible longer-term cognitive burden of repeated AI-generated information verification, rather than as an empirically demonstrated outcome of the present study.

title: Financial strength and ESG participation: evidence from Thailand's tax-incentivized ESG policy
container-title: Journal of Work-Applied Management
a407cd828715c2b15355d82561daaf9236a8c3c3.abstract: Purpose This study reconceptualizes the environmental, social and governance (ESG)–finance nexus from an outcome-driven to an enabler-driven perspective by examining financial capacity as a boundary condition for sustainability participation. Using Thailand's 2023 tax-incentivized ESG policy as a natural experiment, the paper argues that institutional incentives alone are insufficient to drive adoption if firms fall below a critical financial resource threshold. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on institutional and resource orchestration theories, the study investigates the relationship between financial performance indicators and ESG rating attainment for 610 Thai publicly listed firms. Using Welch's analysis of variance and regression models, it identifies specific financial gatekeepers – grouped into valuation, profitability, liquidity and asset management dimensions – that determine a firm's ability to achieve recognition under the Stock Exchange of Thailand ESG (SETESG) rating framework. Findings The results show that firms with stronger profitability and valuation metrics – particularly return on assets, earnings per share and price-to-book value – were significantly more likely to obtain ESG ratings. Financially weaker firms remained largely excluded, revealing a sustainability gap that highlights the unequal effects of market-based policy interventions. Practical implications The study cautions that market-based ESG incentives may inadvertently reinforce financial asymmetries. To avoid siloing sustainability benefits among elite firms, policymakers should implement tiered disclosure frameworks and targeted capacity-building programs that assist resource-constrained firms in meeting institutional mandates. Originality/value This paper extends resource-orchestration and institutional-complexity theories by identifying financial capacity as a threshold mechanism rather than a mere outcome. It provides a sophisticated benchmark for international public policy, demonstrating how “inclusive” sustainability reforms can generate exclusionary effects in emerging economies if firm-level financial boundaries are ignored.

title: Generative AI Literacies and Discipline-Specific Knowledge: Preservice Teachers Planning Task-Based L2 Lessons with GenAI
container-title: Digital Studies in Language and Literature
49cfa4edc8a86155f27305dd81b772f6f0a87a1a.abstract: Abstract This study investigates the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) to support Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT)-oriented lesson planning in a preservice teacher education context, examining the extent to which LLM use can contribute to the mobilisation of TBLT-related competencies. The case study draws on triangulated data from surveys, interaction logs with the LLM, lesson plans produced by preservice teachers and their reflections. The module required participants to generate a lesson plan with an LLM and to compare the resulting plan with a previously created lesson plan developed without AI support. The analysis focuses on knowledge of TBLT principles and their implementation during lesson planning, and the GenAI competence activated through the interaction with the LLM. The findings reveal considerable variation in how the dyads interacted with the LLM. Some dyads formulated more precise prompts and prompt iterations, provided more contextualised input, engaged more critically with the LLM-generated output, and iteratively refined their lesson plans in ways that appeared more consistent with TBLT principles. The data suggest an association between a stronger conceptual understanding of TBLT and more purposeful interaction with the LLM. This association indicates that disciplinary knowledge may facilitate the effective use of LLMs for TBLT-oriented lesson planning. Rather than replacing pedagogical expertise, LLM use appears to be most productive when preservice teachers are able to critically evaluate and adapt the generated output in light of established TBLT principles.

title: Visibility management and profile construction on Tinder
container-title: Online Information Review
e7debc01313f065857fb39a2a59cb8e3923473b0.abstract: Purpose This article examines how visibility and recognizability are configured through self-presentation on Tinder. It conceptualizes visibility management as a framework for examining the degree and form of exposure through which users become available for recognition and evaluation within a platform environment. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on digital ethnography and qualitative analysis of 100 Tinder profiles, the study examines recurrent configurations of facial and bodily recognizability, visual concealment and other forms of visual and textual disclosure. The corpus consists of female profiles presented to two research accounts in the Barcelona area in 2023. Findings The findings identify three modes of profile presentation: concealment, negotiation and integration. These modes capture different configurations of exposure and recognizability. Concealment substantially restricts physical recognizability while retaining varying forms of visual or textual disclosure; negotiation combines recognizable and obscured elements within the same profile; and integration combines comparatively high physical recognizability with curated lifestyle representation. Rather than operating through a simple opposition between visibility and concealment, these modes indicate a continuum in which bodily exposure, facial recognizability and other forms of disclosure vary independently and in combination. Research limitations/implications The findings are based on qualitative analysis of 100 profiles visible within a specific demographic and geographic configuration of Tinder. The corpus consists exclusively of female profiles presented within a 10 km radius in the Barcelona area in 2023 and should not be interpreted as representative of Tinder users more broadly or as evidence of gender-independent patterns. Future research could combine profile analysis with interviews, comparative platform studies or cross-cultural approaches to further examine visibility management across digital environments and across different gender and sexual-orientation configurations. Originality/value The article reframes Tinder self-presentation as a form of visibility management. It distinguishes visibility management from self-presentation and impression management by foregrounding how different degrees and forms of exposure make users available for recognition and evaluation. The three empirically derived modes contribute to this framework by conceptualizing visibility as a continuum of recognizability and disclosure rather than a binary condition.

title: Project Management and Consultancy in Urban Planning and Civil Engineering
1babf1319273db650254ff13af2fa81e9d0f6c57.abstract: Project Management and Consultancy in Urban Planning and Civil Engineering addresses the relationship between technical expertise, coordinated project delivery, and professional advisory services in shaping the built environment. It provides an overview of project planning, implementation, monitoring, and evaluation within urban development and civil engineering contexts. Central themes include defining project scope, scheduling activities, estimating costs, allocating resources, managing risks, maintaining quality, and coordinating stakeholders. The book considers the role of consultancy in translating development objectives into feasible and actionable projects through technical assessment, strategic advice, and informed decision-making. It highlights the importance of integrating infrastructure requirements, environmental considerations, community needs, and long-term sustainability into project management practices. By connecting management principles with the challenges of urban planning and civil engineering, the volume offers a framework for understanding how multidisciplinary teams can support effective project outcomes. It is intended for students, researchers, planners, engineers, consultants, and professionals engaged in infrastructure and urban development.

title: Connecting landscapes, communities and knowledge: lessons from organizing the INSAKA symposium on participatory conservation
container-title: Frontiers in Sustainable Resource Management
ddcc02494543513c77361973a19e3999c8655f7c.abstract: Participatory conservation is widely endorsed as policy, yet the deliberative platforms through which it is enacted are seldom examined as research objects. This article studies a three-phase international symposium convened in Namibia in November 2025 by the University of Namibia under the INSAKA Consortium. It asks what such a platform reveals about the conditions under which participation in conservation becomes substantive rather than procedural. The study uses a single embedded case design in which the symposium functioned as both an authentic practice and a research site. Data comprised thematic presentations delivered across the three phases, rapporteur records of plenary and panel discussions and a moderated community panel at the ≠Gaingu Conservancy. Participant observation at all three locations and a closing reflective session completed the corpus, which was analyzed through reflexive thematic analysis. Five themes were constructed. Knowledge moved through iterative dialogue rather than one-directional transfer. Community participants articulated place-based ecological knowledge that reframed the questions posed to them. Adaptation practices reported by conservancy members operated across land-use boundaries, supporting planning at the landscape rather than unit scale. Existing compensation instruments marked the limits of procedural participation. Informal relational settings generated the event's most concrete institutional commitments. Cutting across these themes, the itinerant design made visible an asymmetry between Namibia's mature terrestrial participation architecture and its comparatively closed marine governance arena. The article contributes empirical evidence on how convening design shapes participatory outcomes. It argues that transferring the conservancy model to the coast is first a legislative question and only then a participatory one.

title: The Legal Responsibility of the Bengkulu City Government in Waste Management Based on the Principle of Sustainable Development
container-title: Journal of Multidisciplinary Science: MIKAILALSYS
16e4421c69d4faaf876d8338f1424b420f2051f7.abstract: Waste management is a local government responsibility that connects environmental protection with sustainable development. This study analyzed the legal framework governing the Bengkulu City Government’s responsibility for waste management and examined its alignment with sustainable development principles. The study employed a normative legal method with statutory and conceptual approaches. Legal materials were collected through library research and examined qualitatively using a descriptive–analytical approach. The findings indicate that the government’s responsibilities derive from national legislation and local waste management regulations. These responsibilities encompass policy formulation, the provision of facilities and infrastructure, waste reduction and handling, coordination, public participation, and supervision. Viewed through sustainable development principles, these responsibilities require consideration of interrelated environmental, social, and economic dimensions. The study concludes that sustainable waste management requires regulatory coherence, a clear allocation of governmental authority, and integrated policies addressing these three dimensions. By clarifying the scope of local governmental responsibility, the study provides a normative basis for aligning waste management governance in Bengkulu City with environmental protection and sustainable development objectives.

title: Encouraging the use of generative AI for closed-book test preparation: effects on student assessment performance and perceptions
container-title: Microbiology Australia
a89131b7b8180b129ba0fc050cf8b5278dbad42d.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being used by university students to support learning. However, evidence from authentic classroom settings examining whether GenAI-assisted revision influences closed-book assessment performance remains limited. This study evaluated the educational use of Microsoft Copilot in a third-year undergraduate immunology course. Student performance was compared between the 2025 and 2026 cohorts using comparable closed-book assessments of identical format and similar difficulty. Before Test 2 in 2026, students were encouraged to use Copilot during structured revision activities. Following Test 2, students completed an anonymous survey examining their perceptions of using Copilot to support learning. No statistically significant differences were observed in Test 1 or Test 2 marks between cohorts. Although a higher proportion of students achieved higher grades in 2026, a similar trend was evident before the intervention. Survey results showed that 78% of students agreed that GenAI could support learning of complex scientific concepts when used appropriately. However, only 53% reported improved understanding of immunology concepts, 39% reported improved knowledge recall, and 71% expressed concerns regarding inaccurate or misleading Copilot-generated information. These findings suggest that although students recognise the educational value of GenAI, encouraging its use during revision alone may not improve subsequent closed-book assessment performance.

title: Protocol for a UK-based feasibility randomised controlled trial evaluating the BabblePlay app intervention to encourage vocalising in infants with Down syndrome
container-title: Pilot and Feasibility Studies
c2b1770706b3e15125c6d2915dcf1fba35c4f4ff.abstract: Abstract Background Down syndrome affects around 1 in 893 live births in the UK and is the leading cause of intellectual disabilities. Children with Down syndrome experience delays in speech, language and communication, which increase with age. This delay is associated with negative social, emotional and economic outcomes in adulthood. Previous research has found that early, frequently delivered language intervention in infants with Down syndrome may be effective at improving early language skills. However, there are limited high-quality, evidence-based interventions for early speech development. This study is a feasibility randomised controlled trial (RCT) for evaluating the feasibility of an app, BabblePlay, as an intervention tool for increasing vocalisations in infants with Down syndrome. Method The study is a UK-based, remotely-delivered feasibility RCT. Online recruitment will take place July 2024 to January 2025. Children will be randomly allocated to the BabblePlay intervention group or a control group. The intervention group will be asked to use BabblePlay with their child for 5 min twice a day for 6 weeks (split into two 3-week periods). The control group will be asked to use a mirror with their child for 5 min twice a day for 3 weeks, followed by 5 min twice a day with the app for 3 weeks. We aim to recruit 40 children with Down syndrome aged 7–15 months. Data will be collected by BabblePlay, questionnaires and 2-day-long audio recordings at baseline and after the first and second 3-week activity periods. We will run focus groups with caregivers to explore the acceptability of the app. Feasibility (including recruitment and retention) will be assessed through progression criteria using a traffic light system. Discussion This feasibility RCT will allow us to evaluate progression to a definitive RCT to examine whether use of the app results in changes to infant babbling and word production. This study will highlight any necessary adjustments to the protocol. It will also add to the limited research on early speech and language intervention for children with Down syndrome. Trial registration This trial is registered with the OSF registry (registration DOI: https://doi.org/ https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/V2DNH ) registered on 10 August 2024. The study was prospectively registered prior to participant enrolment and data collection (which began mid-August 2024). Study advertising began in July 2024; however no participants were enrolled in the study or carried out study procedures prior to the OSF registration.

title: RAPID-2 study: a feasibility randomised controlled trial of a midwife-facilitated intervention for pregnant women with symptoms of mild to moderate anxiety
container-title: Pilot and Feasibility Studies
da45d7470a30c0fe0595c8ace3b49dbc76b40dea.abstract: Abstract Background Anxiety symptoms during pregnancy can escalate and adversely affect women and babies. Support is needed to prevent escalation and help women develop coping strategies. This study aimed to investigate the feasibility of a definitive trial examining the effectiveness of the RAPID-2 intervention for pregnant women with symptoms of mild to moderate anxiety. Methods A two-arm, parallel, open, pragmatic feasibility randomised controlled trial compared usual maternity care plus the RAPID-2 intervention with usual care alone. The study was conducted in 2023 across two NHS maternity services in England. Participants were nulliparous women at 16–20 weeks of pregnancy with symptoms of mild to moderate anxiety, assessed using the seven-item Generalised Anxiety Disorder scale (scores 3–14). RAPID-2 was a 12-week group-based intervention comprising four midwife and maternity support worker-facilitated sessions, two peer-led sessions and access to self-help resources. Four midwives and four maternity support workers were recruited and trained to facilitate the intervention. Objectives were to assess recruitment, retention and completion rates; women’s and facilitators’ experiences; and estimation of anxiety score parameters to inform a future sample size calculation. Results The recruitment target of 50 participants was achieved within 5 weeks, compared with the planned 16-week recruitment period, although study reach was lower than anticipated. Of 101 women provided with study information, 90 (89%) completed eligibility screening and 60 (67% of those screened) were recruited and randomised (31 intervention, 29 control). Post-intervention questionnaires were provided by 18 (30%) participants. Of the 31 intervention participants, six (19%) withdrew before intervention commencement and 15 (48%) attended at least one group. Of those who attended, 11 (73%) attended four or more sessions. Women who attended valued peer support and professional reassurance. Conclusions Women were recruited over a shorter timespan than planned, although recruitment reach, intervention attendance and questionnaire completion were lower than anticipated. Limited outcome data prevented reliable estimation of anxiety score parameters to inform a future trial. The current study design is not feasible for progression to a definitive trial without refinement. Strategies to strengthen inclusive recruitment, intervention accessibility and outcome data collection were identified. Trial registration ISRCTN12834758. Registered 18 March 2022.

title: Use and perceptions of AI tools among Australian general practice registrars: a national survey
container-title: Journal of Primary Health Care
c3efd0b3647649ef143335193afd580c770d2a16.abstract: Introduction Artificial intelligence (AI) tools are increasingly used in health care, yet little is known about how often Australian general practitioner trainees (GP registrars) use them or how they perceive the impact of AI on training and clinical care. Aim This study aimed to examine how frequently registrars use AI tools for clinical care and education, types of AI used, the perceived benefits and risks, and training needs. Methods A national cross-sectional online survey conducted from 7 May to 4 June 2024 invited 3743 Australian General Practice Training or Fellowship Support Program registrars to participate. The survey assessed frequency and context of AI use, practice-level adoption, perceived impacts, training exposure, and ethical-legal concerns. Analyses were descriptive. Results Among the 727 respondents (19.5%), frequent use (weekly or more) was uncommon; 7.3% for clinical tasks, 5.0% for education. Practice-level adoption was low, with 10.8% reporting subscription to AI tools. Most registrars anticipated benefits, particularly learning efficiency and administrative workload reduction. However, 25.0% perceived increased medicolegal risk. Formal training was rare, with most relying on self-directed learning, though many rated AI education as important. Among clinical users, common tools included large language models (32.5%), remote patient monitoring devices (28.6%), and voice-to-text tools (26.2%). Large language models predominated in education (63.5%). Discussion In May–June 2024, AI tool use among registrars was limited, although most perceived potential benefit. Enthusiasm was tempered by concerns about safety, ethics, and legal risks. Structured training and guidelines are needed to support safe, effective integration into GP registrars’ practice and education.

title: Responsible AI and Structural Justice
da1087c38814e959c4bfbff69e0e4db0180d2fd1.abstract: This Element presents challenges of attributing responsibility for AI harms through political theories of structural injustice, where fault is broadly diffused and difficult to establish. I argue that AI systems feature complex structural entanglements between humans and machines-in computational architectures, organizational workflows, and societal data collectives-that pose problems for conventional liability where direct causal links are necessary for blame. I develop two modes of structural responsibility that address unjust AI outcomes from these entanglements. Thin structural responsibility traces where power and accountability lie in the processes of developing unjust AI systems. Thick structural responsibility enlists deployers, users, and broader publics alongside developers in collectively repairing unjust social conditions that produce and rely on AI systems. I show that many Responsible AI initiatives remain thin by demanding disclosures without systemic repair. Incorporating thicker reforms makes responsibility for just AI a living political practice rather than a managerial task. This title is also available as open access on Cambridge Core.

title: Public–Private Partnerships in Defence Manufacturing: Performance,Risk Sharing and Accountability
container-title: International Journal of Engineering Technology and Management Sciences
d67878e396a617ad3d59e43da40a9ddb45938eab.abstract: World military expenditure reached US$2,718 billion in 2024, a real rise of 9.4% and the steepest annual increase since at least 1988, and governments now ask private manufacturers to expand defence output faster than state arsenals can. Public–private partnerships (PPPs) are the main contractual vehicle for this, yet the evidence on whether they deliver value, how they share risk, and who answers for failure is scattered across audit reports, policy documents and a thin academic literature. This review synthesises 101 sources published up to October 2026 on PPPs in defence manufacturing and support, drawn from the United Kingdom, the United States and India. It then develops a Performance–Risk–Accountability (PRA) framework that links a risk-adjusted value-for-money test, an optimal cost-sharing rule and an accountability condition for contestability. Four findings stand out. The UK National Audit Office could not conclude that the £10.5 billion, 27-year tanker PFI achieved value for money, and negotiations took over nine years. The UK government-owned, contractor-operated reform of defence procurement collapsed in 2013 with one bidder. India's private sector raised its share of defence production from 21% to 23% in FY2024-25, while only 14.5% of Rs 74,756 crore of corridor investment commitments had been grounded by April 2026. The framework implies that high-uncertainty development work should carry low private cost shares, mature serial production high shares, and that accountability fails when the state cannot credibly replace its partner.

title: العوامل المؤثرة في التأخر الدراسي في المراحل الأولى من التعليم الأساسي وآليات التدخل العلاجي للحد منه
Factors Influencing Academic Underachievement in the Early Stages of Basic Education and Remedial Intervention Mechanisms to Mitigate It

b3bd123d93f9392b965108983a677d73e07b0bbd.abstract: يهدف البحث الحالي إلى التعرف على العوامل المؤثرة في التأخر الدراسي لدى تلاميذ المراحل الأولى من التعليم الأساسي، والوقوف على أبرز الأسباب التي تسهم في ظهور هذه المشكلة ، سواء كانت أسباباً ذاتية ترتبط بالتلميذ من حيث الجوانب العقلية والجسمية والانفعالية، أم أسباباً أسرية ومدرسية واجتماعية تنعكس بصورة مباشرة أو غير مباشرة على مستوى تحصيله الدراسي. كما يتناول البحث مفهوم التأخير الدراسي وأنواعه وخصائص التلاميذ التأخرين دراسياً، مع تسليط الضوء على وأساليب الكشف والتشخيص التي تساعد على تحديد طبيعة المشكلة والعوامل المرتبطة بها، بما يسهم في اختيار أساليب التدخل العلاجي المناسبة لكل حالة. واعتمد البحث على المنهج الوصفي التحليلي، من خلال تناول الأدبيات والمفاهيم المرتبطة بموضوع التأخر الدراسي، وتحليل العوامل المؤثرة فيه، واستعراض أبرز الأساليب الطبية والنفسية والتربوية التي يمكن الاستعانة بها للحد من هذه المشكلة. وتوصل البحث إلى أن التأخر الدراسي ظاهرة متعددة الأبعاد، لا يمكن إرجاعها إلى عامل واحد بل تنتج عن تفاعل مجموعة من العوامل الفردية والأسرية والمدرسية. كما أشار إلى أن استمرار هذه المشكلة قد ينعكس سلباً على الحالة النفسية للتلميذ ويؤثر في ثقته بنفسه ودافعيته نحو التعلم وتوافقه الاجتماعي والمدرسي . وفي ضوء ذلك، أكد البحث أهمية الاكتشاف المبكر لحالات التأخر الدراسي، وضرورة تكامل الأدوار بين الأسرة والمدرسة والاخصائي النفسي والطبيب المختص إلى جانب توفير برنامج إرشادي والعلاج التربوي والنفسي، ومراعاة الفروق الفردية بين التلاميذ، بما يساعد على تحسين مستوى تحصيلهم الدراسي والحد من تفاقم هذه المشكلة.

title: Sorbates from 1,1-Dialkylsubstituted Alkenes and 3-Haloacrylic Esters via Pd(II)-Isohypsic Catalysis: Focus on Terpenes
container-title: The Journal of Organic Chemistry
fb7a20448d8165c47ec175a43e0dfbf793591e7a.abstract: Abstract Limonene and other 1,1-dialkylsubstituted alkenes undergo a regioselective Pd(II)-catalyzed C–H/C–X coupling with (E) and (Z)-3-bromoacrylates affording 4,4-disubstituted sorbate derivatives as mixtures of geometrical isomers (16 examples). This coupling, unknown to date for the synthesis of 1,3-dienes, follows a mechanism distinct from the well-known Mizoroki–Heck, and works where the Mizoroki–Heck fails. Density functional theory (DFT) computations allowed to propose a plausible mechanism for this transformation.

title: Knowledge Management Capabilities and Performance of Tier 1 Deposit-Taking SACCOs in Kenya
container-title: International Journal of Social Science and Humanities Research (IJSSHR) ISSN 2959-7056 (o); 2959-7048 (p)
92f5dfbbf464ec5b4492a76d713f3e42f888fa6e.abstract: The main objective of this study was to determine the influence of knowledge management capabilities on the performance of Tier 1 Deposit-Taking SACCOs (DT-SACCOs) in Kenya. Knowledge management capabilities were conceptualized as a second-order dynamic capability comprising knowledge acquisition, knowledge sharing and knowledge application. A mixed methods approach was applied, drawing data from finance, audit, credit, Front Office Service Activity (FOSA), marketing, and Information and Communication Technology (ICT) management staff across the 42 Tier 1 DT-SACCOs licensed by the Sacco Societies Regulatory Authority (SASRA) in Kenya. A census approach was adopted, and data were collected using structured questionnaires and analyzed using the Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS), with descriptive statistics and simple linear regression guiding interpretation. The descriptive findings indicated moderate adoption of knowledge management practices, with item means ranging from 2.09 to 3.46. Knowledge management capabilities were found to enhance collaboration, information sharing and decision-making, although limited knowledge application and weak knowledge-tracking mechanisms restricted optimal performance gains. Simple linear regression established that knowledge management capabilities had a statistically significant and positive influence on performance, explaining 56.8% of the variance in performance (R² = .568, Adjusted R² = .566, F(1, 249) = 327.248, p < .001; B = .719, β = .754, t = 18.090, p < .001), leading to rejection of the null hypothesis. The study recommends strategic prioritisation of knowledge management systems, particularly knowledge application and knowledge-tracking mechanisms, to improve competitiveness, operational resilience and sustainable performance among Tier 1 DT-SACCOs.

title: Financial Inclusion and Financial Empowerment among Women in Baringo County, Kenya
container-title: International Journal of Business Management, Entrepreneurship and Innovation
4bff16e9edb26b56dda32e3cd95f5cd362c3e5b6.abstract: Financial inclusion is gaining consideration for its possibility to foster financial development and promote inclusive growth and income equality. New financial services designed specifically for women are frequently the focus of efforts to reduce gender disparities in financial inclusion. Women's contact to high-quality financial services is critical to economic growth because it enables families to improve their standard of living. This study’s purpose was to examine the connections amongst women's financial empowerment in Baringo County, Kenya, financial access, the qualityand the use of financial services. Using a descriptive research design and a positivist philosophy, Economic and system theory were used to. Women who were registered with women's groups and key informants like representatives from financial institutions, area chiefs, and the Baringo County Social Services department made up the target population. Information was gathered utilizing organized polls and key witness interviews, utilizing straightforward irregular testing to choose members. The aim of the research was academic, and participants participated voluntarily. Information investigation included information altering, coding, order, classification, and show involving Measurable Bundle for Sociologies (SPSS). Descriptive statistics likefrequency distributions, percentages, and proportions were used to summarize the data. Quantitative analysis used descriptive as well asinferentialstatistics. Findings from thisstudy emphasized the significance of financial inclusion in increasing financial independence of women, the government's and social service agencies' roles in promoting financial inclusion, the importance of givingwomen in rural areas with financial information, and the need for legislative interventions to make easy access to financial services by women were among the recommendations. Loaning foundations were urged to survey their approaches to more readily oblige the rural women monetary necessities.

title: Developing and Evaluating Digital School Asset Management for Accountability in an Indonesian Island District
container-title: International Journal of Studies in International Education
225331262325aee898fc9f0d5bb423f6bb3ca9e4.abstract: Elementary schools require reliable asset information to account for infrastructure and coordinate district oversight. This study developed and evaluated a digital School Asset Management Information System (SIMA) in Tinangkung, an Indonesian island district. An ADDIE research-and-development process combined baseline interviews and surveys, model design, expert review, pilot testing, and an expanded one-group pretest–posttest evaluation. Four experts judged the model fit for implementation with minor revisions; 30 users completed an 18-item practicality questionnaire; and 14 schools contributed paired accountability measurements. Preliminary responses showed manual records in 10 of 11 schools (90.9%) and no direct district data integration in seven (63.6%). The initial practicality score was 75.51% of the possible total. After implementation, mean data accuracy increased from 74.2% to 98.2%, reporting timeliness from 0.0% to 92.3%, and digital asset traceability from 75.4% to 100.0%. Mean normalized gains were 0.94, 0.92, and 1.00, respectively. Primary paired comparisons were statistically significant at the 5% level. The findings indicate promising short-term administrative improvements associated with a three-axis school–cloud–district system, while the absence of a comparison group prevents exclusive causal attribution. The analysis concerns operational governance indicators, not student achievement, long-term financial savings, cybersecurity assurance, or external audit judgments, none of which were measured directly.

title: Topical 15% trichloroacetic acid versus silver nitrate cauterization in the management of idiopathic childhood epistaxis: a prospective randomized clinical trial
container-title: European Journal of Pediatrics
9a5276abcda5376bf892cd4f0d04e97b50be0f4e.abstract: Abstract The purpose of the study is to compare the outcomes of trichloroacetic acid (TCA) to silver nitrate chemical cauterization in managing pediatric epistaxis. In this prospective randomized assessor-blinded clinical trial, of 172 randomized patients, 157 pediatric patients with idiopathic anterior epistaxis were divided into 2 groups in a ratio 1:1, where group (A) was treated with silver nitrate 25% after local anesthesia application and group (B) was treated with 15% TCA locally applied to the bleeder. Patients were assessed upon recurrence, pain, and crusting at 1st, 2nd, 4th, and 12th week post-intervention. The incidence of epistaxis was not significantly different between the two groups. Pain was significantly greater in the TCA group ( P = 0.008*). Nasal crusting was slightly greater in the TCA group, but the difference was not statistically significant. Conclusion : Although not widely utilized in the management of pediatric epistaxis, TCA is considered an effective chemical cautery agent for the management of childhood epistaxis, with results comparable to those of silver nitrate in terms of recurrence but was slightly worse in terms of pain after intervention. Trial Registration : Number NCT06836791, Date of registration 02/19/2025. What is Known: • Epistaxis is a very distressing complaint in pediatric otorhinolaryngology. • One of the utilized modalities nowadays that proved efficacy in the management of epistaxis is the chemical cauterization of the prominent vessels in Little’s area. What is New: • This is the first study to compare the efficacy of silver nitrate to TCA in epistaxis treatment. • TCA is considered an effective chemical cautery agent for the management of childhood epistaxis, with results comparable to those of silver nitrate agent.

title: Nationwide Claims-Based Trends in Surgical Management of Rectal Prolapse and Rectocele in Korea, 2009–2024
b8822bd13a306847a087d9ff10b0ca3a0866d699.abstract: Abstract Rectal prolapse and rectocele are pelvic floor disorders requiring diverse surgical approaches, but long-term nationwide trends remain poorly characterized. We analyzed de-identified Korean Health Insurance Review and Assessment Service claims from 2009 to 2024 for patients with rectal prolapse (K62.3) or rectocele (N81.6) who underwent predefined procedures. Surgical episodes were classified into rectal prolapse-only, rectocele-only, and concurrent-diagnosis cohorts; procedures were grouped as perineal, abdominal, or rectocele repair. Among 47,614 episodes, 19,663 were rectal prolapse-only, 19,431 rectocele-only, and 8,520 concurrent diagnoses. Perineal procedures accounted for 84.9% of rectal prolapse operations, whereas rectocele repair accounted for 97.3% of rectocele procedures. In the rectal prolapse cohort, abdominal procedures increased from 6.1% in 2009–2014 to 20.0% in 2020–2024. Of 4,652 abdominal procedures, 95.5% had claims for laparoscopic instrument materials. Rectocele surgery increasingly shifted toward clinics, whereas abdominal rectal prolapse procedures were concentrated in higher-level hospitals. These nationwide claims data demonstrate divergent patterns in pelvic floor surgery and increasing claims-defined laparoscopic material use among abdominal procedures for rectal prolapse in Korea.

title: Designing Critical Human–AI Learning in Higher Education: The SC-AIM–FAVIC Framework for Analytical and Logical Reasoning
container-title: JPI: Jurnal Pustaka Indonesia
4ce99b9a5976c3c25eb4ecff905eaf4a200752ca.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is now routine in university study, yet unstructured use risks cognitive offloading, surface learning, and uncritical acceptance of fluent but unreliable output. This article aimed to develop and specify the Symbiotic Critical Human–AI Learning Model (SC-AIM), operationalised through the five-stage FAVIC framework (Formulation, Augmentation, Verification, Integration, Creation), and to set out the assessment instruments and evaluation design that accompany it. Following the Analysis and Design phases of the ADDIE research-and-development approach, we synthesised recent experimental, meta-analytic, and survey evidence to derive design requirements, translated them into a stage-by-stage instructional specification, built a process-sensitive assessment rubric, and defined a quasi-experimental and qualitative validation plan for Indonesian higher education. The results are the model and its components: an evidence-to-design mapping, the FAVIC stage specification, a three-level process-sensitive rubric, and an evaluation design with hypotheses. Conclusion: SC-AIM offers lecturers a concrete, theory-grounded sequence that places human reasoning before and after AI assistance and makes verification an assessed activity, giving higher education a ready-to-use pedagogical model for developing analytical and logical reasoning in the age of generative AI.

title: Childhood Exposure to General Anesthesia for Surgery: Identification of a Subtle Postoperative Cognitive Phenotype
container-title: Anesthesiology
bd2d5293ea5b2cf3a3290d324042562ada1a7b3e.abstract: Background: Early-life exposure to general anesthesia has not been consistently associated with overall cognitive deficits, yet its impact on executive functions and visuo-spatial processing remains unclear. The primary objective was to assess executive function performance, according to general anesthesia exposure for surgery. The secondary objectives were to explore distinct cognitive profiles and their associated factors, as well as to examine visuo-spatial attention as a complementary domain. Methods: In this ambidirectional cohort study, 77 children aged 9 to 11 yr, with or without previous general anesthesia exposure for surgery, completed a cognitive battery yielding eight cognitive measures assessing inhibitory control, cognitive flexibility, working memory, and visuo-spatial attention. Measures were analyzed using a linear mixed-effects model. Exploratory latent profile analysis was used to identify cognitive performance profiles. Results: No significant main effect of general anesthesia exposure for surgery was observed (chi-square[1] = 0.01; P = 0.92), indicating comparable overall executive function performance between exposed (mean age at exposure, 4.47 ± 3.00 yr) and nonexposed. Latent profile analysis identified two executive function profiles: efficient and vulnerable executive control. General anesthesia exposure was associated with slightly higher odds of belonging to the vulnerable profile group (odds ratio, 1.16; 95% CI; 1.151 to 1.159; P < 0.001). Regarding visuo-spatial attention, general anesthesia–exposed participants showed higher global–local precedence measures (estimate, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.04 to 1.01; P = 0.036). Conclusions: Early childhood exposure to general anesthesia was not associated with reduced overall executive function. However, a potential postoperative cognitive phenotype is suggested by a higher likelihood to belonging to a vulnerable executive control profile, together with greater visuo-spatial global–local precedence.

title: Growing Up With AI
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
1d0a243b804e5bc15a1d345307a3a8edd75d8671.abstract: This chapter examines the psychological implications of AI-curated digital environments on child consumers with a focus on cognitive development, screen engagement and mental well-being. Drawing on developmental psychology and consumer socialization literature, it explores how algorithmic personalization reshapes children's digital experiences and influences their ability to process information, regulate emotions and interpret persuasive content. The chapter moves beyond traditional notions of screen time by situating digital engagement within immersive, continuously adaptive environments. It further highlights the developmental vulnerabilities of pediatric consumers in navigating such spaces. In response, a developmentally informed framework for digital well-being is proposed, integrating technological design, user characteristics and contextual mediation. The chapter contributes to interdisciplinary discourse by offering a conceptual foundation for understanding child and AI interactions also informing ethically responsible digital practices.

title: Growing Up Algorithmic
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
bc9ada7a4d5842d7a6680ed7fef502edeb4bc9ea.abstract: The chapter critically examines how artificial intelligence has transformed children into consumers within the realm of online platforms, toys, and learning systems. It discusses the impact of AI-driven marketing strategies, including recommendation engines and synthetic influencers, on children's preferences and behaviors. The analysis is grounded in theories related to consumer socialization, media psychology, and digital surveillance, exploring how these technologies affect children's cognition, emotional attachments, and decision-making. It highlights concerns over hyper-personalized content, parasocial interactions with AI, and ethical governance regarding data privacy. Additionally, the chapter reviews existing regulatory frameworks, identifies gaps in protecting children, and proposes a holistic approach to understanding the interactions between children and AI. Finally, it advocates for ethical AI design, corporate responsibility, and enhancing AI literacy among parents, contributing to the broader conversation on child rights and digital well-being in an AI-driven era.

title: Juvenile Consumer in the Age of AI-Marketing
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
0a33e87f8dba8d3f37c618103c802b6a9bf7d949.abstract: In this chapter, the authors further develop on the changing face with regard to the juvenile consumer within the fast-growing realm of artificial intelligence. It also shows how AI technologies, including smart devices, social networking recommendation systems, and the Internet of Toys are shifting children as passive participants of the marketing process to active and data-generating participants in the digital economy. The paper is interdisciplinary and combines the knowledge of marketing, developmental psychology, digital ethics, and public policy to discuss four key issues, such as AI-enabled marketing practices, privacy, data ownership, digital well-being, and regulation. The authors state that, as much as AI presents opportunities of personalized learning and creative play and enhances connectivity. The growing popularity of gamification, influencer marketing, and emotionally adaptive systems makes the distinctions between entertainment and advertising and makes children less aware of when they are being sold a product.

title: Algorithmic Childhood Future-AI Prediction Systems and the Pre-Emption of Choice in Young Consumers
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
56005ba933d1e6bd7711a958429702ad6438517e.abstract: The fast adoption of Artificial Intelligence in the child-facing digital ecosystem has changed marketing into a reactive personalization model to a predictive and pre-emptive model of shaping choice. This chapter envisions an algorithmic childhood futures, in which AI technologies predict preferences and restructure the choice environment of children prior to the desire developing consciously. Based on the interdisciplinary theory and the latest case studies provided in the educational platforms and smart toy ecosystems, the chapter proves how predictive architectures may promote engagement and gradually reduce exploration and redistribute agency. This analysis puts the concept of algorithmic influence in a new perspective, as temporal harm, with its long-term developmental consequences, that are still poorly dealt with in existing governance models. To create a balance between innovation, commercial goals and digital well-being, the chapter ends with the suggestions to child-centered design and managerial principles.

title: Algorithmic Persuasion in the Age of AI
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
1c12aff4be2cfcce0ade40218bae9d4af7c74978.abstract: The architecture of marketing persuasion has undergone a structural change as a result of the quick adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in children's digital environments. AI-driven systems, in contrast to conventional exposure-based advertising, use real-time personalization, adaptive feedback loops, and predictive analytics to shape behavioral trajectories rather than just discrete consumption decisions. The AI-native child is conceptualized in this chapter, which also makes the case that modern marketing strategies increasingly function through embedded commercial intent in gaming platforms, educational technologies, smart devices, and conversational agents. The Child-Centered Ethical AI Marketing Model (CCEAMM), a normative but implementable framework based on developmental appropriateness, transparency, proportional data use, autonomy preservation, and long-term well-being orientation, is the chapter's response.

title: The Child Consumer in the AI Era
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
5ad4e55952093a68f81d3250e2c934b4b91cc2ed.abstract: This chapter examines how AI-driven marketing environments operate as algorithmically engineered choice architectures for child consumers. Rather than treating digital marketing as a set of isolated advertisements or promotional messages, the chapter conceptualizes contemporary child-facing platforms as adaptive environments that organize attention, structure choices, shape consumption pathways, and influence patterns of platform engagement. These environments operate through defaults, rankings, recommender systems, gamified rewards, push notifications, consent frictions, privacy settings, social proof cues, influencer content, in-app prompts, and interface-level behavioral signals. In such settings, marketing is not only communicated through visible persuasion. It is embedded in the design of the digital environment itself.

title: Algorithmically Objectified
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
b1b34dce36668c601e693340ade565960f440df2.abstract: This chapter examines how AI-driven marketing systems transform children's digital activities into datafied consumer profiles. It develops the concept of the datafied child consumer to explain how behavioral traces, contextual signals, inferred vulnerabilities, and attention patterns are captured, profiled, targeted, and monetized within platform-based marketing ecosystems. Using a structured thematic conceptual review, the chapter maps the recursive cycle linking child digital interaction, data capture, algorithmic inference, marketing activation, behavioral feedback, and commercial value extraction. It also evaluates the implications of this process for children's autonomy, privacy, consumer socialization, and digital well-being. The chapter concludes by proposing a rights-based, child-centered framework for responsible AI-driven marketing grounded in developmental appropriateness, data minimization, inference limitation, transparency, auditability, and limits on exploitative personalization.

title: Datafication of Childhood in the AI Era
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
552347525ce7b2f954b9e84ea5ecd812d16aa08e.abstract: Children have become data-creating consumers in algorithmic markets due to the proliferation of artificial intelligence in digital markets. The interactions between children are being constantly tracked, scanned, and sold, be them smart toys and educational applications, biometric-enabled platforms, and so forth. The chapter is a critical analysis of the lifecycle of data of the child, starting at birth to adolescence, and contains ethical dangers of biometric surveillance, algorithmic non-transparency, and behavioral profiling. It assesses the shortcomings of the regulatory frameworks like the Children Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in terms of their effectiveness in the response to the consent issue and transparency issue. The chapter develops a child-centered AI data governance framework to safeguard the digital well-being through theoretical issues, case study evaluation, and balancing innovation and autonomy.

title: Women and Youth Entrepreneurship as a Driver of Sustainable Development Goals

4d3ff4fc072f7074118c7fac6af20e3c9c9680aa.abstract: Entrepreneurship has emerged as a powerful catalyst for economic development, social innovation, and inclusive growth across global economies. In particular, women and youth entrepreneurship have gained increasing attention as key drivers of sustainable development and social transformation. By empowering underrepresented groups to participate actively in economic activities, entrepreneurship can contribute significantly to achieving the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs). However, traditional approaches to entrepreneurship development often fail to consider the complex and interconnected systems that shape entrepreneurial ecosystems. This chapter adopts a systems thinking perspective to explore how women and youth entrepreneurship can accelerate progress toward sustainable development. The chapter examines the structural, social, economic, and institutional factors that influence entrepreneurial participation among women and young people.

The analysis shows how communication supported the creation of a common language among entrepreneurs, financial institutions, incubators, public entities, the judiciary community and universities, contributing to the practical appropriation of knowledge, the reduction of perceived risk and the strengthening of financial literacy as an applied capacity.

It's an exploration of the successes achieved, 24×7 services, as well as ongoing issues in the field, including a lack of empathy and data protection. Some of the ethical challenges, along with future trends such as emotionally intelligent systems, multimodal interfaces and hyper-personalised approaches for service delivery, are also discussed in the chapter. This chapter offers real-world examples and research to illustrate how AI can benefit customer service and the factors to consider when considering AI-powered tools.

a7a264083703838cc8b600a740747b6bd7d805f2.abstract: One of the most impactful employee experiences that a firm can provide is corporate travel, but it is not a priority issue in human resource management. The customer journey mapping technique, which has been created in the service marketing sector to map and optimise the overall experience of the customer, has become an important tool of comprehending the employee traveller as an internal customer of the travel management system. The chapter focuses on how AI is used to improve the journey mapping of corporate travelling and discusses the HRM implications. Three sources of HRM value are analysed: employee experience and talent engagement, duty of care and risk management, and strategic workforce analytics. The chapter then proceeds to address challenges, ethical considerations, and privacy considerations and governance implications followed by providing illustrative examples and a research agenda. The main point is that AI-inspired journey mapping will transform corporate travelling into a type of procurement into a strategic HRM tool of engagement, safety, and organisational learning.

title: AI-Driven Recommendation Systems for Travel Planning

ba7554b3d7fdd7ea465fef06feb52f850f4cc265.abstract: Artificial-intelligence-driven recommender systems have become a pervasive part of the travel-planning experience, helping consumers filter vast inventories of flights, accommodation, and activities. Yet the finance dimension of travel remains comparatively under-theorised in the recommender-systems literature. This chapter integrates tourism informatics, recommender-systems research, FinTech scholarship, and behavioural economics to examine AI-driven travel recommendation through a personal-finance lens, with a particular focus on budget-sensitive and cost-aware travellers. The chapter argues that treating the traveller's budget as a first-class design parameter produces systems that are more useful to consumers and more defensible from a consumer-protection standpoint. It reviews the evolution of AI in travel recommendation, develops a budget-aware design space spanning constrained optimisation, price prediction, FinTech integration, contextual flexibility, and group budgeting, and considers the behavioural, ethical, and regulatory implications of this integration. Three illustrative cases: fare prediction, payment-aware recommendation, and explainable recommendation ground the arguments in existing practice, and a research agenda is outlined for the next generation of financially literate travel recommenders.

With the help of smart algorithms and scale capabilities to process data organizations can deliver extremely personalized experiences that are closely in line with the preferences activities and situational demands of contemporary travellers (Valeri, 2023; Gaur et al. 2021).

cab53579f6f706d2b096f9f8e1ef7047728972da.abstract: The introduction of the artificial intelligence (AI) into the travel marketing is a game changer in the way the industry will interact, retain, and serve the customers. This chapter discusses how AI-driven personalization approaches have evolved and are used in the travel industry and how technologies like machine learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics, and recommendation systems are helping to transform customer experiences. It also touches upon the ethical issues of privacy of data, algorithmic discrimination and customer permission. This chapter provides a theoretical context and practical data to travel marketers, technologists and policymakers who must work within the rapidly evolving AI landscape by looking at current applications and forecasting trends.

c40dd4dfa0f215bb2f130e973858a9a9331b2121.abstract: Pricing and revenue management has been the core of tourism and hospitality marketing since the perishable and capacity-limited nature of these services means that all unsold seats, rooms or tours are forever lost. AI can now enable tourism companies to predict demand, segment consumers and price them with the speed, resolution, and personalisation that would have been unimaginable in the classical yield management days. This chapter explores tourism services based on AI-driven pricing and revenue optimisation using the marketing perspective. It combines the existing revenue management literature with the current work on AI in marketing. The chapter plots AI potentials along the pricing and revenue lifecycle, which include demand forecasting, customer segmentation, price optimisation, distribution and channel management, personalisation, and post purchase recovery and then examines five dimensions of marketing that define whether AI-based pricing creates or destroys value: customer experience, perceived price fairness, trust and relationship quality, brand equity and customer lifetime value. It states that AI-based pricing is only successful in tourism when it is perceived as a marketing tool within the broader customer relationship, not a stand-alone revenue generator and concludes by discussing ethics, governance and a research agenda.

Coming on to create a polished and sleek experience across various channels, AI is quickly changing the mechanisms and techniques used in its marketing strategies. Taking modern insights and their examples, it further explains new techniques of natural language operation in delivering a more customised and good experience. There are also some mandates and challenges on the way, which include algorithmic bias, personal data security and limited access to digital technologies. Additionally, this book chapter also discovers the growing patterns and trends of AR, voice-enabled search and up-to-date pricing frameworks. Ultimately, it highlights that adoption of AI in cross-channel marketing is not an option but a mandate for travel portals that want to be there in the marketing; it has become a sign of competitive advantage for their customer fulfilment.
