f56fe25bbfdc23fa7b1ad75e4c574300c396c669.abstract: The growing computational demands of artificial intelligence (AI) are challenging conventional electronics, making photonic computing a promising alternative. However, existing photonic architectures face fundamental scalability and reliability barriers. This article introduces SKYLIGHT , a scalable 3D photonic in-memory tensor core architecture designed for real-time AI inference. By co-designing its topology, wavelength routing, accumulation, and programming in a 3D stack, SKYLIGHT overcomes key limitations. Its innovations include a low-loss 3D Si/SiN crossbar topology, a thermally robust non-micro-ring resonator (MRR)-based wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) component, a hierarchical signal accumulation using a multi-port photodetector (PD), and optically programmed non-volatile phase-change material (PCM) weights. Importantly, SKYLIGHT enables in-situ weight updates that support label-free, layer-local learning (e.g., forward-forward local updates) in addition to inference. With comprehensive system-level modeling, we show that a single 144× 256 SKYLIGHT core achieves a peak compute capability of 342.1 TOPS at 23.7 TOPS/W under a high-reuse tensor-core operating point. For end-to-end ResNet-50 inference, where the same physical core is reprogrammed across layers and tiles, SKYLIGHT reaches 1212 FPS with 60.9 mJ/image after explicitly accounting for PCM programming energy. System-level evaluations on four representative machine learning tasks, including unsupervised local self-learning, demonstrate SKYLIGHT ’s robustness to realistic hardware non-idealities (low-bit quantization and signal-proportional analog noise capturing modulation, PCM programming, and readout variations). With noise-aware training, SKYLIGHT maintains high task accuracy, validating its potential as a comprehensive solution for energy-efficient, large-scale photonic AI accelerators.

title: Assessing Socioeconomic Bias in AI-Powered Maternal Health Messaging: Evidence from Jacaranda Health’s PROMPTS Platform in Kenya
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
74c166ac509cfea4c48079f22557195c8417a57b.abstract: ABSTRACT Background In many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), mothers lack timely, accurate health information, which can delay lifesaving care. Jacaranda Health’s PROMPTS platform reaches 3 million+ mothers in Kenya via SMS, using artificial intelligence (AI) to triage questions, provide rapid responses, and connect urgent cases to human agents. While AI can expand access, if not carefully designed it may reinforce inequities. This study examines whether PROMPTS’s AI models perform differently across socioeconomic groups. Methods We applied a four-phase bias assessment framework. First, we surveyed 4569 PROMPTS users across 22 counties and assessed socioeconomic vulnerability using a validated typing tool. Second, we examined whether training datasets reflected users across vulnerability strata. Third, we evaluated AI performance in classifying question topics. Finally, we audited AI-generated outputs for medical accuracy, grammar, and thoughtfulness, stratified by vulnerability. Results PROMPTS engages women across vulnerability levels. The most vulnerable mothers were less likely to ask questions, suggesting underrepresentation in training data. The AI model correctly classified 90% of questions, with no significant differences by vulnerability, though confidence was lower for messages from more vulnerable mothers. AI-generated responses were equally accurate across groups, but answers to more vulnerable users were sometimes rated as less thoughtful. Conclusion PROMPTS demonstrates a fair application of AI for maternal health, with strong performance across diverse groups. However, underrepresentation of vulnerable mothers and subtle differences in response quality highlight areas for improvement. Engaging vulnerable voices, embedding safeguards, and routine monitoring will be critical to ensure AI advances health equity in LMIC contexts.

title: Research and Development of AI-Powered Task-Shifting for High-Quality Obstetrics Ultrasound Services in Community Healthcare Settings: Real-World Implementation Experiences from an LMIC
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
58396b4e3bef28d032518e1ac8e1f795a769257d.abstract: Abstract Blind Sweep Obstetric Ultrasound (BSOU) paired with artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed as a scalable approach to expand antenatal screening in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). However, limited evidence exists on how to implement BSOU-AI systems within real clinical environments, where infrastructure, workflows, and human resource constraints differ substantially from research settings. This study reports implementation experiences from a multi-center BSOU-AI project across tertiary hospitals and community health facilities in Nepal. We collected more than 3000 BSOU datasets using minimally trained providers and handheld ultrasound devices, developed and iteratively refined a nine-sweep BSOU protocol, and coordinated with national stakeholders to ensure alignment with the Rural Obstetrics Ultrasound Program. Real-world deployment revealed major challenges including machine incompatibility, inadequate digital infrastructure, annotation bottlenecks, workflow mismatches in high-volume hospitals, and difficulty capturing rare complications which required continuous adaptation of protocols, staffing, and data-management systems. Engagement with Nepal’s Ministry of Health prompted the addition of an evaluation arm comparing BSOU-AI performance not only to radiologist scans but also to nurse-led rural ultrasound, reflecting the true standard of care. Our experience demonstrates that AI readiness in LMICs depends as much on implementation science as on algorithm development. We provide methodological insights and practical recommendations for designing BSOU-AI studies that are scalable, contextually grounded, and responsive to health-system realities.

title: An AI conversational assistant to support self-managed medication abortion in Colombia: development and early testing in a telemedicine pathway
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
c230a21c79bab4fca674bce9f837badae975e723.abstract: Abstract Colombia continues to face unsafe and informal abortions, with elevated risks in the Pacific region, where structural inequities and stigma persist despite a liberalized legal framework. Profamilia, a major sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) provider, is expanding telemedicine to reduce these gaps. This case study describes the development and feasibility testing of an AI WhatsApp assistant for Profamilia’s medication-abortion telemedicine pathway to provide trusted information and navigation. Using Research-through-Design, Design Thinking and Agile sprints, we built an assistant grounded in local legal/clinical guidance, privacy-by-design (no identifiers), and human-in-the-loop escalation for risk and out-of-scope cases. After iterative internal validation, user-testing in three Pacific departments (Valle del Cauca, Cauca, Nariño; n=40; 605 questions) achieved 86.4% task success—defined as no Level-1 (high-risk) or Level-2 (service-flow) errors in responses—with 2.1% Level-1 errors. Users valued speed, clarity, trust and privacy. Priorities centred on interface/navigation microcopy and safety hardening to reduce Level-1 errors. Findings suggest early feasibility, safety and acceptability for a locally grounded assistant, with potential to bolster knowledge, support decisions and ease access to care. This case offers transferable insights for developing AI-enabled, rights-based SRHR tools. Next steps include a pilot to measure service-level and user-centred outcomes for equity-oriented scale-up.

title: Growing Up With AI
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
1d0a243b804e5bc15a1d345307a3a8edd75d8671.abstract: This chapter examines the psychological implications of AI-curated digital environments on child consumers with a focus on cognitive development, screen engagement and mental well-being. Drawing on developmental psychology and consumer socialization literature, it explores how algorithmic personalization reshapes children's digital experiences and influences their ability to process information, regulate emotions and interpret persuasive content. The chapter moves beyond traditional notions of screen time by situating digital engagement within immersive, continuously adaptive environments. It further highlights the developmental vulnerabilities of pediatric consumers in navigating such spaces. In response, a developmentally informed framework for digital well-being is proposed, integrating technological design, user characteristics and contextual mediation. The chapter contributes to interdisciplinary discourse by offering a conceptual foundation for understanding child and AI interactions also informing ethically responsible digital practices.

title: Growing Up Algorithmic
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
bc9ada7a4d5842d7a6680ed7fef502edeb4bc9ea.abstract: The chapter critically examines how artificial intelligence has transformed children into consumers within the realm of online platforms, toys, and learning systems. It discusses the impact of AI-driven marketing strategies, including recommendation engines and synthetic influencers, on children's preferences and behaviors. The analysis is grounded in theories related to consumer socialization, media psychology, and digital surveillance, exploring how these technologies affect children's cognition, emotional attachments, and decision-making. It highlights concerns over hyper-personalized content, parasocial interactions with AI, and ethical governance regarding data privacy. Additionally, the chapter reviews existing regulatory frameworks, identifies gaps in protecting children, and proposes a holistic approach to understanding the interactions between children and AI. Finally, it advocates for ethical AI design, corporate responsibility, and enhancing AI literacy among parents, contributing to the broader conversation on child rights and digital well-being in an AI-driven era.

title: Juvenile Consumer in the Age of AI-Marketing
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
0a33e87f8dba8d3f37c618103c802b6a9bf7d949.abstract: In this chapter, the authors further develop on the changing face with regard to the juvenile consumer within the fast-growing realm of artificial intelligence. It also shows how AI technologies, including smart devices, social networking recommendation systems, and the Internet of Toys are shifting children as passive participants of the marketing process to active and data-generating participants in the digital economy. The paper is interdisciplinary and combines the knowledge of marketing, developmental psychology, digital ethics, and public policy to discuss four key issues, such as AI-enabled marketing practices, privacy, data ownership, digital well-being, and regulation. The authors state that, as much as AI presents opportunities of personalized learning and creative play and enhances connectivity. The growing popularity of gamification, influencer marketing, and emotionally adaptive systems makes the distinctions between entertainment and advertising and makes children less aware of when they are being sold a product.

title: Algorithmic Childhood Future-AI Prediction Systems and the Pre-Emption of Choice in Young Consumers
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
56005ba933d1e6bd7711a958429702ad6438517e.abstract: The fast adoption of Artificial Intelligence in the child-facing digital ecosystem has changed marketing into a reactive personalization model to a predictive and pre-emptive model of shaping choice. This chapter envisions an algorithmic childhood futures, in which AI technologies predict preferences and restructure the choice environment of children prior to the desire developing consciously. Based on the interdisciplinary theory and the latest case studies provided in the educational platforms and smart toy ecosystems, the chapter proves how predictive architectures may promote engagement and gradually reduce exploration and redistribute agency. This analysis puts the concept of algorithmic influence in a new perspective, as temporal harm, with its long-term developmental consequences, that are still poorly dealt with in existing governance models. To create a balance between innovation, commercial goals and digital well-being, the chapter ends with the suggestions to child-centered design and managerial principles.

title: Algorithmic Persuasion in the Age of AI
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
1c12aff4be2cfcce0ade40218bae9d4af7c74978.abstract: The architecture of marketing persuasion has undergone a structural change as a result of the quick adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in children's digital environments. AI-driven systems, in contrast to conventional exposure-based advertising, use real-time personalization, adaptive feedback loops, and predictive analytics to shape behavioral trajectories rather than just discrete consumption decisions. The AI-native child is conceptualized in this chapter, which also makes the case that modern marketing strategies increasingly function through embedded commercial intent in gaming platforms, educational technologies, smart devices, and conversational agents. The Child-Centered Ethical AI Marketing Model (CCEAMM), a normative but implementable framework based on developmental appropriateness, transparency, proportional data use, autonomy preservation, and long-term well-being orientation, is the chapter's response.

title: The Child Consumer in the AI Era
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
5ad4e55952093a68f81d3250e2c934b4b91cc2ed.abstract: This chapter examines how AI-driven marketing environments operate as algorithmically engineered choice architectures for child consumers. Rather than treating digital marketing as a set of isolated advertisements or promotional messages, the chapter conceptualizes contemporary child-facing platforms as adaptive environments that organize attention, structure choices, shape consumption pathways, and influence patterns of platform engagement. These environments operate through defaults, rankings, recommender systems, gamified rewards, push notifications, consent frictions, privacy settings, social proof cues, influencer content, in-app prompts, and interface-level behavioral signals. In such settings, marketing is not only communicated through visible persuasion. It is embedded in the design of the digital environment itself.

title: Algorithmically Objectified
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
b1b34dce36668c601e693340ade565960f440df2.abstract: This chapter examines how AI-driven marketing systems transform children's digital activities into datafied consumer profiles. It develops the concept of the datafied child consumer to explain how behavioral traces, contextual signals, inferred vulnerabilities, and attention patterns are captured, profiled, targeted, and monetized within platform-based marketing ecosystems. Using a structured thematic conceptual review, the chapter maps the recursive cycle linking child digital interaction, data capture, algorithmic inference, marketing activation, behavioral feedback, and commercial value extraction. It also evaluates the implications of this process for children's autonomy, privacy, consumer socialization, and digital well-being. The chapter concludes by proposing a rights-based, child-centered framework for responsible AI-driven marketing grounded in developmental appropriateness, data minimization, inference limitation, transparency, auditability, and limits on exploitative personalization.

title: Datafication of Childhood in the AI Era
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
552347525ce7b2f954b9e84ea5ecd812d16aa08e.abstract: Children have become data-creating consumers in algorithmic markets due to the proliferation of artificial intelligence in digital markets. The interactions between children are being constantly tracked, scanned, and sold, be them smart toys and educational applications, biometric-enabled platforms, and so forth. The chapter is a critical analysis of the lifecycle of data of the child, starting at birth to adolescence, and contains ethical dangers of biometric surveillance, algorithmic non-transparency, and behavioral profiling. It assesses the shortcomings of the regulatory frameworks like the Children Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in terms of their effectiveness in the response to the consent issue and transparency issue. The chapter develops a child-centered AI data governance framework to safeguard the digital well-being through theoretical issues, case study evaluation, and balancing innovation and autonomy.

title: Implementing AI-CDSS in Low-Resource Maternal Care: Lessons Learned from the Preeclapp Deployment
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
c21285c26160f9ad7d7028e61962eee68a329a9e.abstract: Abstract Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are one of the leading causes of maternal morbidity and mortality in Colombia, particularly in rural regions with limited access to specialized care. In this context, Preeclapp was developed as a clinical decision support system grounded in expert-system logic, designed to provide guideline-based support for maternal care in settings with limited resources and connectivity. This proof-of-concept implementation study analyzes the integration of Preeclapp into clinical practice and the factors that influenced its adoption. The main barriers identified included unstable connectivity, lack of data interoperability, high staff turnover, and initial skepticism toward AI-based technologies. Nevertheless, the project showed preliminary feasibility of use by non-specialized personnel in obstetrics and gynecology, even in low-connectivity environments. To overcome these challenges, the project relied on training sessions, embedded educational resources, continuous technical support, and iterative software adaptations. Our implementation suggests that these strategies were perceived by users as supporting adherence to obstetric protocols, reinforcing clinical decision-making, and enhancing staff confidence, particularly in facilities with limited specialist availability. As a proof-of-concept implementation study, this work did not evaluate diagnostic accuracy or clinical effectiveness; instead, it focused on early implementation feasibility, usability, acceptability, and perceived usefulness. The findings suggest that sustainable adoption of AI-CDSS systems requires strengthening digital literacy and promoting a culture of innovation. Our experience with Preeclapp indicates that adoption and implementation benefited from a modular design, low-connectivity functionality, flexibility, and co-creation with local teams, which helped adapt the tool to each institution’s context.

7618ca5b91c52b831750f40d2a59ffd17dd1de82.abstract: The landscape of the customer service domain has been fundamentally transformed by rapid technological advancements and the rise of artificial intelligence (AI). Sophisticated AI-based chatbots are capable of providing personalised and real-time support at an unmatched level. The chapter discusses the internals of how AI can be integrated into customer service, its design and implementation (natural language processing (NLP), machine learning and conversational interface design). It's an exploration of the successes achieved, 24×7 services, as well as ongoing issues in the field, including a lack of empathy and data protection. Some of the ethical challenges, along with future trends such as emotionally intelligent systems, multimodal interfaces and hyper-personalised approaches for service delivery, are also discussed in the chapter. a7a264083703838cc8b600a740747b6bd7d805f2.abstract: One of the most impactful employee experiences that a firm can provide is corporate travel, but it is not a priority issue in human resource management. The customer journey mapping technique, which has been created in the service marketing sector to map and optimise the overall experience of the customer, has become an important tool of comprehending the employee traveller as an internal customer of the travel management system. The chapter focuses on how AI is used to improve the journey mapping of corporate travelling and discusses the HRM implications. Three sources of HRM value are analysed: employee experience and talent engagement, duty of care and risk management, and strategic workforce analytics. The chapter then proceeds to address challenges, ethical considerations, and privacy considerations and governance implications followed by providing illustrative examples and a research agenda. The main point is that AI-inspired journey mapping will transform corporate travelling into a type of procurement into a strategic HRM tool of engagement, safety, and organisational learning.

ba7554b3d7fdd7ea465fef06feb52f850f4cc265.abstract: Artificial-intelligence-driven recommender systems have become a pervasive part of the travel-planning experience, helping consumers filter vast inventories of flights, accommodation, and activities. Yet the finance dimension of travel remains comparatively under-theorised in the recommender-systems literature. This chapter integrates tourism informatics, recommender-systems research, FinTech scholarship, and behavioural economics to examine AI-driven travel recommendation through a personal-finance lens, with a particular focus on budget-sensitive and cost-aware travellers. The chapter argues that treating the traveller's budget as a first-class design parameter produces systems that are more useful to consumers and more defensible from a consumer-protection standpoint. It reviews the evolution of AI in travel recommendation, develops a budget-aware design space spanning constrained optimisation, price prediction, FinTech integration, contextual flexibility, and group budgeting, and considers the behavioural, ethical, and regulatory implications of this integration. Three illustrative cases: fare prediction, payment-aware recommendation, and explainable recommendation ground the arguments in existing practice, and a research agenda is outlined for the next generation of financially literate travel recommenders.

cab53579f6f706d2b096f9f8e1ef7047728972da.abstract: The introduction of the artificial intelligence (AI) into the travel marketing is a game changer in the way the industry will interact, retain, and serve the customers. This chapter discusses how AI-driven personalization approaches have evolved and are used in the travel industry and how technologies like machine learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics, and recommendation systems are helping to transform customer experiences. The chapter discusses how personalization affects consumer decision-making, brand loyalty and revenue generation based on the existing empirical research and case studies in the industry. It also touches upon the ethical issues of privacy of data, algorithmic discrimination and customer permission. This chapter provides a theoretical context and practical data to travel marketers, technologists and policymakers who must work within the rapidly evolving AI landscape by looking at current applications and forecasting trends.

c40dd4dfa0f215bb2f130e973858a9a9331b2121.abstract: Pricing and revenue management has been the core of tourism and hospitality marketing since the perishable and capacity-limited nature of these services means that all unsold seats, rooms or tours are forever lost. AI can now enable tourism companies to predict demand, segment consumers and price them with the speed, resolution, and personalisation that would have been unimaginable in the classical yield management days. This chapter explores tourism services based on AI-driven pricing and revenue optimisation using the marketing perspective. It combines the existing revenue management literature with the current work on AI in marketing. The chapter plots AI potentials along the pricing and revenue lifecycle, which include demand forecasting, customer segmentation, price optimisation, distribution and channel management, personalisation, and post purchase recovery and then examines five dimensions of marketing that define whether AI-based pricing creates or destroys value: customer experience, perceived price fairness, trust and relationship quality, brand equity and customer lifetime value. It states that AI-based pricing is only successful in tourism when it is perceived as a marketing tool within the broader customer relationship, not a stand-alone revenue generator and concludes by discussing ethics, governance and a research agenda.

AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
c588ddd8d5996746e14ae10690a2cc7988fa5134.abstract: This book chapter comprises new AI-powered tools such as machine learning, data analytics, and personalisation, which together shape improved customer involvement across physical touchpoints and the digital travel industry. Coming on to create a polished and sleek experience across various channels, AI is quickly changing the mechanisms and techniques used in its marketing strategies. Taking modern insights and their examples, it further explains new techniques of natural language operation in delivering a more customised and good experience. There are also some mandates and challenges on the way, which include algorithmic bias, personal data security and limited access to digital technologies. Additionally, this book chapter also discovers the growing patterns and trends of AR, voice-enabled search and up-to-date pricing frameworks. Ultimately, it highlights that adoption of AI in cross-channel marketing is not an option but a mandate for travel portals that want to be there in the marketing; it has become a sign of competitive advantage for their customer fulfilment.

b9e613bd3df85b54f82e072d3978910d175bafa3.abstract: This chapter examines how artificial intelligence reshapes personalization and recommendation systems across next-generation travel management across global travel markets. It integrates recommender-system theory, smart tourism research, customer-experience design, and predictive analytics into an implementation-oriented framework for airlines, hotels, online travel agencies, destination managers, and corporate travel programs. The chapter explains how collaborative, content-based, context-aware, knowledge-based, and generative models can orchestrate offers, itineraries, service recovery, sustainability choices, and duty-of-care interventions. It also evaluates data governance, privacy, bias, explainability, organizational readiness, and interoperability barriers that limit adoption. Six practical tables and four TikZ figures translate the discussion into architecture, metrics, risk, and roadmap tools. The chapter concludes that successful AI personalization depends less on algorithmic novelty than on trusted data, measurable value, ethical design, and cross-functional execution.

title: Talking to Travellers

AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
439ad8df55c01c5fbfb7f73acae8fad387788276.abstract: With chatbots and conversational artificial intelligence (CAI), the travel brands are transforming the way they connect with prospects and customers throughout the booking process. The argument among marketing scholars is that customer engagement is a multidimensional construct that encompasses cognitive, emotional and behavioural interactions with a brand and that these interactions are becoming mediated by intelligent technologies. Using the literature of marketing, service research, and tourism-informatics this chapter explores the creation of marketing value by chatbots and CAI in regards to travel services. It assesses the theoretical background of customer engagement and conversational AI, the history of chatbots in the travel industry, and their functional placements through the pre-purchase, purchase, and post-purchase processes. It then evaluates three main sources of marketing value including personalisation of the customer experience, brand communication and voice, and real-time marketing intelligence through conversational data. The chapter also takes into account the issues of challenges, such as hallucinations, channel fragmentation, and escalation failure, as well as the ethical, privacy, and trust issues. Arguments are based on three exemplary cases, and a research agenda is presented in the future of conversational-AI-based travel marketing. The main argument is that, when intelligently combined with the broader marketing stack, chatbots and CAI cease to be viewed as a cost-saving service channel, but rather as a strategic platform of relationship-based, data-rich interaction with customers.

title: Predictive Analytics for Consumer Behaviour in Tourism and Hospitality
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
a0716bed81d520e0c418e6f30cd54cc6dc83f45a.abstract: The forecasting of consumer behaviour and its associated response makes an exciting prospect in the tourism and hospitality industry, and can largely be attributed to predictive analytics. This chapter focuses on the use of data-driven methods to gain insights and predict users' trip preferences, booking behaviour, and expectations for the service (e.g., machine learning, AI, or big data analytics)—important topics such as Demand forecasting, Personalisation Strategies, Sentiment analysis, and revenue management in the latest research. Elsewhere in the chapter, the ethical dilemmas involved with consumer data usage, including privacy concerns and issues regarding the transparency and accountability of algorithms, are addressed. In this chapter, the authors tie together theory and practice, offering researchers and providers in the hospitality sector practical insights into how they can use predictive instruments to gain a competitive edge, enhance customer experiences and reach sustainable performance in their organisation in a fast-paced and changing tourism environment.

title: Behavioral Biases in AI-Driven Pricing and Revenue Optimization
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
ed174c4b4ed08f10fd6ad59224497a10a8aaa670.abstract: The intersection of artificial intelligence and behavioral finance presents an underexplored but commercially significant terrain for reimagining how tourism firms design and implement their pricing strategies. While revenue management in travel and hospitality has long depended on demand-based algorithmic models a persistent gap between what these systems predict and what consumers actually do reveals a structural blind spot the systematic cognitive biases that shape purchase decisions in ways that rational utility models simply cannot capture. This chapter develops a behavioral-AI pricing framework by synthesizing prospect theory mental accounting reference price anchoring and social proof mechanisms within the architecture of modern machine learning revenue management systems. Drawing on secondary evidence from major online travel platforms and published booking behavior studies we demonstrate that tourism consumers exhibit consistent loss aversion effects when exposed to dynamic price fluctuations that reference price anchoring significantly modulates willingness to pay at different stages of the booking funnel and that AI pricing engines which ignore these behavioral dimensions routinely suppress conversion or trigger demand destruction. Our proposed framework integrates behavioral signals into AI feature engineering arguing that affective pricing cues cancellation-loss framing and social validation mechanisms can be systematically deployed to improve both conversion rates and revenue per available unit without exploiting consumers in ethically problematic ways. The chapter contributes to the growing literature on neuroeconomic applications in hospitality management while offering practical direction to revenue managers who seek to humanize not merely automate their pricing decisions.

title: Chatbots and Conversational AI in Customer Engagement for Travel Services

AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience

Based on marketing, service research, and tourism-informatics literatures, this chapter explores how travel service chatbots and CAI can generate marketing value. It discusses the theoretical basis of customer engagement and conversational AI, the history of chatbots in the travel sector, and outlines their operational applications throughout the pre-purchase, purchase, and post-purchase processes. It subsequently examines three key bases of marketing value, which include customising the customer experience, brand communication and voice, and real-time marketing intelligence based on conversational data. Challenges, such as hallucinations, channel fragmentation, and escalation failure, as well as ethical, privacy, and trust considerations are also taken into account in the chapter. The main argument is that, designed appropriately as part of the broader marketing stack, chatbots and CAI no longer represent a cost-reduction service channel but rather a strategic customer engagement platform, full of data.

title: Chatbots and Conversational AI in Travel Customer Service
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
11cc7490a63085742c3525aa62522b3da243f5c1.abstract: Artificial intelligence has revolutionized customer service in the travel sector. This chapter explores the role of chatbots and conversational AI in travel customer service systems, from early rule-based chatbots to advanced large language models (LLMs) that can engage in long, multi-step interactions. The chapter draws upon recent empirical studies, case studies and theoretical perspectives to examine prominent use cases such as booking support, travel disruption management, personalisation and multilingual interactions. It also highlights key challenges including integration with existing systems, bridging the gap between language understanding and domain expertise, and ethical issues related to privacy and bias in conversational AI. The chapter also assesses human-AI interaction approaches and provides insights into future directions such as agentic AI and multimodal interfaces. Insights for industry practitioners and avenues for future research are explored.

title: Harnessing Generative AI and Large Language Models for Intelligent Travel Planning
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
c44e15ad738f4a32fc2a61c562801bad0d22ace2.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming how travellers discover destinations, plan itineraries, and engage with tourism service providers. This chapter provides a systematic and theoretically grounded examination of these technologies within intelligent travel planning. It traces the evolution of AI in tourism and explores key applications, including conversational trip planning, hyper-personalized recommendations, real-time adaptive guidance, and sentiment analysis. The chapter highlights opportunities to enhance accessibility, improve operational efficiency, and support data-driven destination management. It also examines critical challenges, including hallucinations, information reliability, algorithmic bias, data privacy, workforce disruption, and fragmented regulatory frameworks. The chapter concludes by addressing governance and policy needs while identifying future directions, including multimodal AI, sustainable AI, interoperable ecosystems, and interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the responsible adoption of AI in global tourism.

title: Artificial Intelligence Application in Travel and Tourism

AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
558186d5df62e0b9dff9bc4c709c75f520727051.abstract: The fast development of artificial intelligence (AI) is essentially transforming the sphere of travel and tourism. In this chapter, the author provides an in-depth discussion of AI application in key sectors of personalization, customer service automation, revenue management, destination management, hospitality management, transportation and sustainability. According to the current studies and industry dynamics, the chapter is very useful in studying the development of technology in the tourism industry- starting with primitive Global Distribution Systems to the current machine learning systems. Nevertheless, the transformative potential of AI cannot be undervalued, and so is the ethical issue related to its implementation, including the privacy of data, replacing people with a machine, and the biases of the algorithm. Exploring and analyzing challenges, especially in the developing world.The chapter ends by presenting new trends which include generative AI and augmented reality and the metaverse as a research framework that scholars and practitioners can use to study.

title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Large Language Models as a Digital Assistant for Power System Operators
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
43f02e9dd2362d62f0781c1271492951a9157aa0.abstract: Power-system operation is safety-critical: personnel integrate data, alarms, outages, switching requests, contingency analyses, grid-code rules, and cybersecurity constraints. This review assesses evidence, rechecked through May 31, 2026, on GenAI and large language models (LLMs) for operator support. It covers research, reports, standards, regulations, preprints, and industry initiatives, distinguishing retrieval-grounded systems, domain-adapted LLMs, time-series foundation models, tool-using agents, and digital-twin verification. It proposes a supervised assistant in which the LLM orchestrates and explains but is not operational truth. Near-term uses include document retrieval, regulatory interpretation, training, summaries, and explanations of approved calculations. Evidence does not support autonomous transmission-level actions. Deployment requires traceable sources, current models, restricted tools, cybersecurity boundaries, adversarial testing, human approval, and audit trails.

title: AI-Driven Distributed No-Wait Flow Shop Scheduling for Sustainable Energy-Aware Manufacturing Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
d9b0f4862ffea1e45716990a59652306558d70c3.abstract: The rapid evolution of smart manufacturing and Industry 5.0 has heightened interest in sustainable and intelligent scheduling approaches. The distributed no-wait flow shop scheduling (DNWFSP) problem is a complex combinatorial optimization problem that simultaneously involves assigning jobs to plants and sequencing them on machines. This problem becomes even more challenging when energy and environmental objectives are incorporated. This chapter proposes an AI-based distributed flow shop scheduling framework for energy-efficient manufacturing systems. The objective is to minimize total energy consumption. The approach relies primarily on deep reinforcement learning, specifically the Deep Q-Network (DQN), to learn an optimal decision-making policy in a dynamic and uncertain environment. The DQN model allows scheduling decisions to be adapted in real time based on the state of the production system. Experimental results show that the proposed approach significantly improves energy efficiency and resource utilization compared to conventional scheduling methods.

title: Machine Learning–Driven Carbon Emission
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
7c511103dc7bb5d22ff06c9abc63879ce415e340.abstract: Since the building sector contributes significantly to carbon emissions worldwide, sophisticated methods are required for precise forecasting and efficient reduction. The use of machine learning (ML) approaches for carbon emission prediction across the construction lifecycle—including material manufacturing, transportation, on-site activities, and operations—is examined in this chapter. Regression, artificial neural networks, support vector machines, and ensemble learning are among the machine learning models that are rigorously examined, with an emphasis on how well they can handle complicated, nonlinear datasets. In order to facilitate real-time monitoring and decision assistance, the chapter delves deeper into the integration of machine learning (ML) with digital technologies, such as building information modeling (BIM), the Internet of Things (IoT), and digital twins. Supported by case examples, a conceptual framework is put forth to direct ML-driven carbon mitigation methods. Future research directions and challenges are also covered.

title: Machine Learning in Hydrogen Production and Combustion
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
396533e60035866b42defb080e313a182f64fdcf.abstract: The transition to a green hydrogen economy is impeded by two computational and physical challenges: huge overpotential losses in water electrolysis and thermoacoustic/flashback instabilities when hydrogen combusts directly. The use of conventional high-throughput screening of electrocatalysts relying on Density Functional Theory is computationally infeasible in large compositional spaces, while H flame direct numerical simulation suffers from extreme multi-scale turbulence-chemistry interactions. In this chapter, we offer a combined machine learning method, integrating material-level electrocatalyst discovery with system-level combustion control. Firstly, we test ensemble tree models and Graph Neural Networks for forecasting adsorption free energies at transition metal hydroxides, alloys and high-entropy surfaces. Then we describe reduced-order surrogate models, like CNN-LSTMs, Autoencoders and PINNs to combust hydrogen-fueled internal combustion engines and gas turbines for prediction of flashback, identification of thermoacoustic modes, and reduction of NOx emissions in real time.

title: AI-Driven Lightweight Conductive Materials for Energy-Efficient Embedded IoT Electronics in Aerospace
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
a55b89f2fb3987d422ba86cb68582ebdb3cdab08.abstract: In the evolution of aerospace systems, the integration of lightweight conductive materials in embedded Internet of Things (IoT) electronics plays a pivotal role in enhancing performance. These materials are essential for optimizing electronic devices used in monitoring, control, and communication systems under space and airborne conditions. The aerospace sector demands weight reduction while maintaining high-performance properties, driving advancements in conductive materials. This chapter reviews the design, fabrication, and application of lightweight conductive materials for aerospace IoT electronics, with a focus on optimizing energy efficiency. Various categories of conductive materials, such as composites, thin films, and nanomaterials, are examined in terms of their electrical conductivity, mechanical properties, thermal stability, and weight percentage values. Additionally, the chapter explores the challenges and opportunities of incorporating these materials in aerospace IoT applications that aim to meet the unique demands of the aerospace industry.

title: AI-Driven Battery Health Monitoring and Predictive Analytics for Sustainable Electric Vehicle Energy Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
9d588e9311f2c0a9cd7ce1921d91a51a458080cd.abstract: This chapter presents an artificial intelligence-driven battery health monitoring framework for sustainable electric vehicle applications. It discusses battery parameters including State of Charge, State of Health, degradation characteristics, and Remaining Useful Life together with data acquisition, preprocessing, feature extraction, and normalization techniques for battery health prediction. Machine learning approaches such as Random Forest, Artificial Neural Networks, and Long Short-Term Memory networks are reviewed for degradation analysis and predictive maintenance. An experimental case study demonstrates the effectiveness of the developed framework in accurately estimating battery states and tracking degradation behavior. The chapter also explores intelligent battery management, fault diagnosis, digital twins, smart grids, Internet of Things, and Vehicle-to-Grid integration for future energy systems.

title: Electric Vehicle Smart Charging Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
8e4f2ec5067466af773c092cab5826b145ff82be.abstract: The rapid growth of Electric Vehicles is transforming modern transportation while creating major challenges for power grid stability, including peak load demand, energy imbalance, and renewable energy integration. To address these issues, smart EV charging systems have emerged as intelligent solutions capable of optimizing charging operations according to grid conditions, electricity pricing, and user needs. This chapter presents a comprehensive review of Artificial Intelligence and optimization techniques applied to EV smart charging systems. It analyzes machine learning, deep learning, deterministic, stochastic, and heuristic optimization methods, as well as hybrid AI–optimization frameworks. The study highlights their benefits in improving charging efficiency, reducing operational costs, enhancing load balancing, and supporting grid stability. Furthermore, current limitations such as scalability, computational complexity, and data dependency are discussed, alongside research gaps related to renewable energy integration, decentralized control, and real-time adaptive management.

title: How to Optimize Electric Vehicles Using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML)
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
7136bf72ac9299b116ba5c8813a99f469355cc31.abstract: Optimizing electric vehicles (EVs) through Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) is critical for addressing adoption barriers such as range anxiety and battery degradation. This chapter explores the transition from static, rule-based systems to dynamic, self-learning frameworks across Battery Management Systems (BMS), Predictive Energy Management (PEM), and Eco-Driving and Auxiliary (EDA) systems. By leveraging advanced methodologies like Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks, and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), these intelligent systems can enhance energy efficiency by up to 30% and extend battery life by nearly 40%. The discussion highlights how predictive analytics optimize real-time power allocation, regenerative braking, and thermal regulation. Despite challenges like high computational costs and cybersecurity risks, the integration of edge computing and V2G technology positions AI as a cornerstone for modernizing automotive operations and achieving a sustainable, software-defined transportation ecosystem.

title: Hybrid TCN-ExtraTrees Framework for Lithium-Ion Battery State-of-Health Classification in Indian Electric Vehicles
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
e9afe305db4f44eeadf11aafb47f5676e6b636dc.abstract: The rapid growth of Electric Vehicles (EVs) in emerging economies of the world, such as India, has created a pressing demand for Battery Health Monitoring Systems. While Lithium-ion batteries, being the most common power source for EVs which operates in a range of environmental and operating conditions, their performance is affected by various environmental factors. Therefore, estimating the State of Health (SOH) is crucial to evaluating the aging of the batteries. This chapter proposes an artificial intelligence–based framework to address the heterogeneous conditions of the Indian EV ecosystem by utilizing a Temporal Convolutional Network (TCN) and the ExtraTrees ensemble classifier. In addition to conventional battery parameters, environmental stress factors are also incorporated into the framework using meteorological data obtained from the NASA POWER database. Experimental evaluation was carried out and obtained an accuracy of 91.50% and a value of 0.9772 for the AUC-ROC metric, proving the effectiveness of the proposed framework for reliable battery health estimation.

title: AI and Machine Learning Approaches to Address Cybersecurity Challenges in Smart Grid Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
0b9ba87f4a19e4d12b8440a82ac46d2c3f3b2901.abstract: Smart grid systems have been utilized with artificial intelligence (AI) which has substantially improved their efficiency and reliability. Nevertheless, with the development of smart grids into more intricate, networked, and data-intensive systems, a smart grid is becoming more susceptible to cybercrime. The chapter handles the problem of cybersecurity available within smart grid systems shedding light on the especial vulnerabilities that lies in the fact that they are digital and automated. It talks about the application of AI-based solutions to deal with such risks and it focuses on approaches that include anomaly detection, real-time threat responsiveness, and forecast risk. Besides, the chapter is also about AI aimed at protecting the communication network and providing more effective identification processes, and autonomic safe work. Through interpretation of case studies and projections in the real world, this paper gives a holistic idea of how AI can enhance the cybersecurity infrastructure in smart grid infrastructures.

title: Detection of Anomalies and Electricity Theft in Smart Grids Using Variational Autoencoders (VAE) and Time Series Analysis
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
1733456c27aaf37eee6c7d368568452fec41f37d.abstract: The proposed approach to detecting electricity theft and abnormal consumption in smart grids using a variable-parameter autoencoder is presented. With the introduction of smart meters, traditional verification methods struggle to handle large volumes of data and often miss instances of fraud disguised as normal consumption. The proposed model combines convolutional and LSTM layers to capture both local patterns and long-term dependencies, feeding the data into a variable-parameter autoencoder that models the probability distribution of normal consumption behavior. Experiments were conducted on open datasets containing labeled hourly consumption data with various theft types, including mechanical tampering and data manipulation. Preprocessing included normalization and extraction of dynamic features, such as volatility and interphase correlations. Detection performance was evaluated using precision-recall curves and the F-score due to strong class imbalance.

title: Investigation of Vulnerabilities of Machine Learning Models to Adversarial Attacks in Smart Grid Forecasting Systems
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Sustainable Energy Systems
a4c69d2d3f388b09d23e5a415fd3321cd4c255fd.abstract: This article examines how the use of machine learning in Smart Grid forecasting turns predictive models into targets of cyberattacks. Small, carefully chosen distortions of telemetry, training data, or federated updates can shift forecasts of load, renewable generation, reserves, and grid stability without clear signs of failure. The review systematizes adversarial attack scenarios by model access, impact goal, lifecycle stage, and implementation level in digital infrastructure. It also highlights what makes energy time series different from images and ordinary tabular data: temporal structure, cross-channel consistency, and physical plausibility must be preserved. The paper analyzes resilience measures — anomaly detection, adversarial training, secure aggregation, physics-informed hybrids, and data integrity monitoring — with attention to computational cost and real-time use. Further research should focus on realistic black-box attacks, cascading effects, and engineering criteria for trusting predictive services.

title: Algorithmic Persuasion and the Commodification of the Indian Child Consumer

7ef08bed984a79d99131ec55e78d0e3fafb5c13c.abstract: Artificial intelligence has reshaped digital persuasion, placing children at the center of AI-driven consumption in India's platform economy. Gamification, recommender systems, and synthetic influencers exploit cognitive immaturity and emotional vulnerability in ways existing consumer and advertising laws cannot address. This chapter argues that AI-driven child-targeted marketing constitutes a distinct unfair trade practice, commodifying childhood itself. Grounded in consumer law and constitutional principles under Articles 14, 19, and 21, it advances a case for statutory limits prioritizing child dignity and autonomy.

title: Algorithmic Childhood
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Governing Childhood in the Age of AI
24a3c19b0daa4623298ba63af7df9b13718df0f6.abstract: This chapter looks at the idea of Algorithmic Childhood, which looks at how AI-driven personalization, algorithmic exposure, datafication, and behavioural nudging transform children online experiences and consumer identities. The digital platforms are relentlessly gathering and analysing data on children in order to customize their content, ads, and interactions and in the process, there are no sharp lines between play, learning, and commercial persuasion. Although the advantages of personalization are educational and age-related, they also contribute to making children more vulnerable because of their poor cognitive and emotional development. The chapter is a synthesis of interdisciplinary literature that identifies ethical issues, asymmetry of power, and the gap of the currently existing regulatory frameworks. It calls to the child-cantered policies of governing aimed to guarantee transparency and accountability, digital well-being, the safety of children, and safeguarding of child rights through AI-mediated markets.

title: Algorithmic Entrapment
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Governing Childhood in the Age of AI
9a1a337e1b2937ac4af2d2775b27805a3ce8499b.abstract: Artificial intelligence has transformed social media into adaptive persuasion systems that learn from and optimize for each child's behavior. This chapter shows how AI-driven curation undermines parental authority through qualitative analysis of Slovenian parents. Based on 14 in-depth interviews with parents of 22 children, we identify “algorithmic entrapment,” where engagement-maximizing systems override parental boundaries, exploit developmental vulnerabilities, and foster dependencies resistant to intervention. Parents recognized addiction-like symptoms but had a limited understanding of underlying AI mechanisms such as recommendation systems, predictive analytics, variable rewards, and personalized optimization. A “Surveillance Capitalism and Childhood” framework is proposed to explain how data extraction and attention monetization conflict with children's developmental needs. Protecting children requires shifting beyond parental responsibility toward governance solutions, including transparency mandates, limits on persuasive AI targeting minors, and independent audits.

title: From Digital Safety to Digital Flourishing
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Governing Childhood in the Age of AI
03a959e7ca0c73de400bfd81a13b9caeff54cbf1.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming children's digital environments, reshaping how they learn, interact, and participate as consumers. While existing scholarship and regulation largely emphasize digital safety—focusing on privacy protection and risk mitigation—there is limited attention to how AI can actively promote children's developmental well-being. This case study–based chapter advances a shift from digital safety to digital flourishing by examining how child-centered AI systems can support cognitive growth, social-emotional development, and ethical agency. Drawing on interdisciplinary literature and empirical case analyses of socially assistive robots, adaptive learning platforms, and conversational AI systems, the chapter develops a Developmental Flourishing Framework integrating developmental psychology, children's rights principles, and ethical marketing considerations. The analysis highlights both opportunities and structural risks, including algorithmic bias, surveillance practices, and persuasive design.

title: AI Literacy as Consumer Immunity in Children
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Governing Childhood in the Age of AI
9551deacb2f585906f3298c74c3b05f1921605f7.abstract: Whether driven by regulation or the market, pure protective responses are becoming less tenable as AI systems become more integrated into commercial ecosystems surrounding children. The future of child digital well-being will hinge on not just stronger regulations and more ethical platform design, but also critically aware young users capable to interpret and navigate algorithmic environments with informed scepticism and reflective agency. This chapter advances the notion of AI literacy as consumer immunity, putting forward a timely and actionable framework for educators, designers, policymakers and researchers interested in aligning technology innovation with ethical responsibility to children. Protecting the child consumer in the age of A.I. ultimately means pursuing both solutions: Creating safer systems while also fortifying the young brains that make their way through them.

title: AI Literacy
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Governing Childhood in the Age of AI
87a810168d220e42586510068471834bc1db6970.abstract: Children in contemporary school settings are daily consumers of AI-generated content — whether they know it or not. Recommendation feeds, synthetic images, AI-drafted text, and algorithmic advertising have become routine features of childhood digital experience, yet most K–12 curricula offer little preparation for navigating these environments critically. This chapter argues that schools bear a genuine responsibility to address this gap through deliberate, grade-appropriate AI literacy education oriented not merely toward using AI tools, but toward questioning and evaluating what those tools produce. Drawing on recent empirical work and theoretical scholarship across AI literacy, media education, and ethics, the chapter traces a developmentally staged curriculum pathway from early childhood awareness through secondary-level civic and ethical reasoning, while also highlighting key challenges in implementation such as teacher readiness, assessment alignment, and the limited geographic distribution of existing research.

title: Curriculum Development for AI Literacy in Schools
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Governing Childhood in the Age of AI
48f5f323ea3fb2f7789d2937410b6f74e253e184.abstract: Artificial intelligence has infiltrated the digital landscape of children at an extremely fast rate, affecting the way children learn, communicate and access information. This chapter in the book makes a case in favor of an all-encompassing curriculum in AI literacy that will help children understand how to critically analyze the systems of algorithms, defend against subtle persuasion, and identify fake media. Based on the Critical Media Literacy Theory, Persuasion Knowledge Theory, Socio-Technical Systems Theory and the Digital Resilience Frameworks, describes a modular, age-based curriculum between primary-level and secondary education. Experiential learning, gamification, and project-based assessments are some of the pedagogical strategies favored with the help of teacher training and alignment of policies. Finally, the chapter makes AI literacy a key factor to creating digitally resilient citizens who are capable of operating in algorithmically mediated spaces in a responsible, reflective and ethical manner.

title: Curriculum Development for Schools to Teach Children How to Recognize and Critically Evaluate AI Content
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Governing Childhood in the Age of AI
eabdf13bce65d9c835bad254e966a1d5672132c4.abstract: Children today are growing up in digital environments where Artificial Intelligence (AI) plays a central yet often invisible role in shaping their experiences. From personalized recommendations and AI-generated academic assistance to targeted advertising and algorithmically curated content intelligent systems influence how children access information, form preferences, and make decisions. This chapter argues that AI literacy must be recognized as an essential component of contemporary school education. Drawing on an interdisciplinary review of literature in AI literacy, media studies, and education, the chapter proposes a curriculum-oriented framework based on three interconnected dimensions: operational, sociocultural and critical literacy. In response, it introduces a practical pedagogical approach centered on “questioning the machine,” encouraging students to develop habits of inquiry, reflection and ethical awareness in their interactions with AI-driven content.

title: Play, Screen, and Sensibility
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Governing Childhood in the Age of AI
419ae53555cf9525f8072bd48eced60adce44aa6.abstract: This chapter examines how early childhood digital literacy should be understood not merely as technical skill, but as an ethical, relational, and pedagogical process. Focusing on children in their first years, it explores how screens increasingly shape curiosity, play, attention, and emotional development. The chapter argues that ethical sensibility must be nurtured alongside digital engagement through adult mediation, reflective dialogue, and balanced forms of play. It highlights the roles of parents and teachers in guiding children to interpret digital stories, games, and apps with empathy, patience, and moral awareness. Ultimately, it proposes that ethical digital literacy in early childhood begins not with control, but with care, conversation, and thoughtful participation.

title: Exploring AI-based teleorientation for the sexual and reproductive health of Spanish- and Quechua-speaking adolescents: a technology acceptance study
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
ca7fe9a8f94e5435dd342dbff7db0c6fd98892e4.abstract: Abstract Background Geographical, sociocultural, and confidentiality-related barriers continue to limit adolescents' and young people's access to sexual and reproductive health information. Objective To evaluate the acceptance of an AI-based teleorientation chatbot for sexual and reproductive health using the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted with 113 Quechua-speaking high school students in Ayacucho, Peru, who interacted with a bilingual (Spanish/Quechua) AI chatbot over a three-months period. Data collected using an extension of the Technology Acceptance Model 3 (TAM 3) were analysed with PLS-SEM. Results Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU) was the main determinant of Behavioral Intention to Use (BI; β = 0.53, p &lt; 0.001), confirming the role of Ease of Use in technology adoption. Perceived Trust (PT) had a significant positive effect on PEOU (β = 0.56, p &lt; 0.001) and a significant negative effect on Perceived Risk (PR; β = -0.69, p &lt; 0.001). The negative correlation of PR and the other constructs indicated that reducing perceived risk is important for technology adoption. Contrary to TAM theory, Perceived Usefulness (PU) was not a significant predictor of BI (β = 0.13). Conclusions This study demonstrates that trust and ease of use are key factors influencing adolescents’ acceptance of AI-based health chatbots in multilingual environments. The findings suggest that culturally adapted digital tools can help reduce barriers to accessing sexual and reproductive health information when they prioritize simplicity, cultural relevance, and user trust. These results provide valuable insights for the design of youth-centred digital health interventions in diverse contexts.

title: BeamGAN: a physics-informed conditional generative adversarial network for Monte-Carlo-free portal dose image prediction from incident fluence maps
container-title: Physics in Medicine & Biology
1d3458461752e4c44513c7343bf432f2d6ff6f27.abstract: Abstract Objective. To develop and validate a Monte-Carlo-free deep learning framework that predicts EPID portal dose images directly from treatment-planning-system (TPS) exported incident fluence maps, enabling real-time patient-specific quality assurance without Monte Carlo (MC) simulation or empirical per-machine commissioning. Approach. We propose BeamGAN, a physics-informed conditional generative adversarial network. A three-channel input—TPS incident fluence, its Sobel gradient map, and a beam’s-eye-view (BEV) target-thickness projection ray-traced through the planning CT with the PTV mask—embeds geometric and edge-scatter priors into an eight-level U-Net generator with a PatchGAN discriminator and an auxiliary registration network. The framework was trained on 91 head-and-neck IMRT patients (split 64/15/12) from one Elekta Versa HD linac, benchmarked against a Brownian-Bridge diffusion baseline (BiBBDM), and evaluated by input-channel ablation and error-injection sensitivity tests (12 patients, nine gamma criteria). Main results. BeamGAN achieved gamma passing rates (GPR) of 97.40 ± 0.67% (3%/3 mm), 95.42 ± 0.99% (3%/2 mm) and 87.00 ± 1.63% (2%/2 mm; 10% threshold), outperforming BiBBDM (83.32 ± 2.43%, 77.08 ± 3.20% and 67.20 ± 2.45%). On the held-out test set ( n = 12), the median GPR was 95.47% (IQR 94.86–96.27) at the TG-218 primary criterion 3%/2 mm; 8/12 cases met the institutional ⩾95% acceptance threshold and all 12 exceeded the 90% action level. Ablation identified the fluence-gradient channel as the dominant contributor, with the anatomical prior providing complementary gains. Sensitivity analysis established a criterion-dependent error hierarchy: systematic multileaf collimator errors were most detectable (ΔGPR up to 21.23% at 1%/1 mm), followed by collimator rotation (10.31%), whereas monitor unit scaling and setup errors produced marginal effects. BEV computation required 0.3–0.5 s per beam and inference under 50 ms. Significance. Embedded geometric priors can substitute explicit MC scatter modeling in portal dose prediction, removing a principal computational barrier to real-time electronic portal imaging device-based verification. Multi-institutional validation is warranted before clinical deployment.

title: Microwave dielectric property reconstruction of healthy and tumor rat breast tissues from in vivo measurements using generative AI
container-title: Physics in Medicine & Biology
6f396cb1a9a95edbc7d663997357931373fe0546.abstract: Abstract Objective. Rapid identification of suspicious breast lesions remains challenging, since pathological analysis following biopsy requires hours to days, limiting real-time decision-making, particularly during surgical procedures. Open-ended coaxial probe (OECP)-based methods have shown promise for characterizing target tissues through estimation of dielectric properties (DPs) from the measured reflection coefficient ( S 11 ). Conventional DP calculation from OECP measurements S 11 is commonly performed using iterative methods, while recent studies have also explored artificial intelligence (AI)-based approaches for DP estimation. In these studies, AI models were developed using either synthetic datasets or limited ex vivo measurement data. In contrast, this study presents a generative AI approach for direct estimation of frequency-dependent DPs from in vivo measurements of healthy and tumor rat breast tissues. Approach. Measurements were acquired over the 0.5–6 GHz frequency range. Conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN) and conditional variational autoencoder (cVAE) were employed to learn the nonlinear mapping between the measured S 11 responses and the corresponding relative permittivity ( ε ′ ) and dielectric loss factor ( ε ′ ′ ). Furthermore, model performance was evaluated using dependency-preserving metrics, including copula log-likelihood and Kendall’s τ , together with regression metrics such as root mean square error (RMSE), symmetric mean absolute percentage error, weighted mean absolute percentage error, and coefficient of determination ( R 2 ). In addition, the estimated DP responses were fitted to a one-pole Cole–Cole model using median normalized nonlinear least squares optimization to extract the corresponding parameters ( ε s , ε ∞ , τ , α , σ ). Main results. The lowest RMSE values for healthy and tumor tissues were 0.98 and 2.90, achieved by the cVAE and cGAN models, respectively. The mean absolute percentage deviations, Δ ( ε c ) , between the Cole–Cole-fitted and reference DPs were 2.99% for healthy tissues and 5.05% for tumor tissues. Significance. These findings demonstrate the feasibility of generative AI-based, non-iterative DP reconstruction directly from in vivo OECP measurements.
