title: Novelty or eeriness? Investigating consumer responses to AI-generated product images through expectancy violation theory
container-title: Journal of Research in Interactive Marketing
887864754512a1ae8f592d2397ed290befbca8bd.abstract: Purpose Drawing on Expectancy Violation Theory, this study examines how product image creator identity (AI vs. human) influences purchase intentions and the underlying psychological mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach Three online experiments examined consumers' attitudes toward AI-generated product images and purchase intentions toward the featured products, assessed how these evaluations deviated from expectations associated with human-created images, and identified conditions under which artificial intelligence (AI) imagery was more or less effective in shaping consumer responses. Data were analyzed in Statistical Package for the Social Sciences using Multivariate Analysis of Variance and Multivariate Analysis of Covariance, with serial and moderated mediation analyses conducted using the PROCESS macro. Findings Consumers consistently prefer human-created product images and perceive them as more novel, whereas AI-generated images evoke greater eeriness. Perceived novelty, eeriness, positive and negative expectancy violations, and attitudes mediate the relationship between image creator identity and purchase intention. Product type serves as a boundary condition, with AI-generated images evaluated more favorably for search products than for experience products. Originality/value This research identifies positive and negative expectancy violations as central psychological mechanisms shaping consumer responses to AI-generated product images. By highlighting product type as a boundary condition, it helps reconcile mixed findings in the AI-generated marketing literature and provides actionable guidance for the strategic use of AI-generated product imagery.

title: Explainable AI-based framework for 3D structural as-built modeling of aging buildings in Korea using laser scanning
container-title: Engineering, Construction and Architectural Management
9d0f972f52a37add6c936521dbd3ddf06dde8a83.abstract: Purpose This study proposes a framework for automatically generating 3D structural as-built models of aging buildings by predicting the structural dimensions of members concealed behind finishes using laser scanning and machine learning, particularly when original construction drawings are unavailable. Design/methodology/approach Laser scanning captures building geometry but includes both structural components and non-structural finishes (e.g. plaster), making it unsuitable for directly extracting structural dimensions. To address this, the proposed framework extracts geometric features from point clouds and employs machine learning techniques to predict structural dimensions of columns, beams, walls and slabs. Six machine learning models – Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM, CatBoost, Linear Regression and Support Vector Regression (SVR) – were trained using data collected on 1,560 column elements, 2,875 beam elements, 870 wall elements and 148 slab elements across 50 buildings and validated through two real-world case studies. Findings The best-performing model achieved MAPE of 10.51% for column width (95%CI: 8.47–12.71), 12.98% for column depth (95% CI: 10.86–15.41), 14.91% for beam width (95% CI: 13.63–16.15), 18.91% for beam depth (95% CI: 17.94–19.90), 10.42% for walls (95% CI: 8.89–12.00) and 10.70% for slabs (95% CI: 7.11–14.50). The predicted dimensions enabled reconstruction of 3D structural as-built models without relying on original drawings; the estimates are intended for planning-stage use. Practical implications The framework provides a non-destructive, full-coverage estimate of structural member dimensions that would otherwise require original drawings or local removal of finishes. In practice, it is intended to reduce reliance on destructive investigation and, through the SHAP analysis, indicates where confirmatory openings could be prioritized, thereby supporting planning-stage decisions for the maintenance and retrofitting of buildings whose drawings are missing or outdated. Originality/value This study is among the first to formulate the discrepancy between laser-scanned surface geometry and concealed structural dimensions as a prediction problem and to propose a framework that returns the predicted dimensions to a 3D structural as-built model. Machine learning provides the enabling component, and explainability is used to direct in situ verification rather than as a methodological contribution in itself.

title: Enhancing the Industrial Metaverse With Extended Reality
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Enhancing the Industrial Metaverse With Extended Reality
8c9989343b1d8ff24876fc27926ed580f327cbc9.abstract: The convergence of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Extended Reality (XR) is transforming industrial work by integrating intelligent decision-making, immersive technologies, and digital twins into human-centered workplaces. This review synthesizes research from Industry 4.0/5.0, digital twins, XR applications, and organizational studies to develop a unified understanding of AI-XR convergence. It proposes three frameworks—Industrial Metaverse Work Architecture (IMWA), AI-XR Industrial Transformation Framework (AXITF), and Human-AI-XR Integration Continuum (HAXIC)—to explain technological, operational, and organizational transformation. The chapter further presents theoretical propositions, governance imperatives, implementation strategies, and future research directions, providing a comprehensive foundation for responsible, human-centric industrial metaverse adoption.

title: Integrating XR, AI, Digital Twins, and IIoT in the Industrial Metaverse
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Enhancing the Industrial Metaverse With Extended Reality
fbf2ccf62346b15568a02d6b5e5729370294b911.abstract: This chapter examines the Industrial Metaverse as the convergence of Extended Reality (XR), Artificial Intelligence (AI), Digital Twins, and the Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) into persistent, immersive, and intelligent industrial ecosystems. Based on a structured narrative review, the chapter proposes a five-layer integration architecture and positions it against RAMI 4.0, IIRA, ISO 23247, and cyber-physical system models. It specifies synchronization requirements for XR-enabled Digital Twins, maps threats and security controls to each architectural layer, and reviews applications in manufacturing, energy, healthcare, and logistics. The chapter also examines generative AI, industrial foundation models, edge AI, and blockchain, together with their risks, and addresses governance, regulation, and human-machine collaboration. It concludes with an implementation pathway and research directions for secure, trustworthy, and human-centric Industrial Metaverse ecosystems aligned with Industry 5.0.

title: XR-Enabled Moodle Learning Ecosystems for the Industrial Metaverse
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Enhancing the Industrial Metaverse With Extended Reality
02afab14813059458f1c623082082cd38c0ca92f.abstract: This chapter, per the authors, presents a conceptual framework for using Moodle as the learning orchestration layer for XR-enabled workforce training in the industrial metaverse. It synthesizes recent research on extended reality, digital twins, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and cybersecurity awareness to identify a gap between immersive industrial training prototypes and LMS-based evidence, assessment, and governance. The chapter proposes the XR-Moodle Industrial Learning Ecosystem (XMILE), which links Moodle courses, XR scenarios, digital twin states, AI-supported analytics, and cybersecurity controls. It explains the model's layers, data flows, use cases, evaluation metrics, and implementation roadmap for universities, technical training centers, and industrial organizations. The contribution is a practical structure for designing measurable, secure, and role-based training that supports skill transfer, cyber hygiene, and instructor decision-making.

title: AI as therapist or assistant? Opportunities and boundaries of artificial intelligence in mental health care
container-title: Mental Health and Social Inclusion
d8ff61e9a4fc5950274fbbae98c4af08416fbf29.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine where generative artificial intelligence (AI) may add value in mental health care, where its clinical limits remain and how human oversight should change as AI assumes greater responsibility. Design/methodology/approach This opinion piece draws on recent randomized trials, systematic reviews, safety evaluations and international guidance on conversational AI in mental health. The evidence is interpreted through a three-level framework: supportive self-management, clinician-augmented care and autonomous clinical care. Findings AI-supported interventions can improve symptoms of depression and anxiety in some settings and may widen access to low-intensity support. However, evidence remains heterogeneous and important concerns persist around suicide-risk responses, privacy, bias, over-reliance and accountability. Current evidence supports AI more strongly as an adjunct than as an autonomous therapist. Social implications Access alone should not be mistaken for inclusion. Safe mental health AI also requires attention to digital access, language, culture, affordability and routes to human care. Originality/value The paper proposes a practical clinical hierarchy in which the evidence threshold, regulatory scrutiny and human oversight increase with the clinical responsibility assumed by AI.

title: Practice Briefing: From automation to delegation – governing generative AI in property investment
container-title: Journal of Property Investment & Finance
0d8441e184bb520c85f45164a8740e5739b4e1e5.abstract: Purpose Most real estate organisations approach artificial intelligence with the question “what can we automate?” This paper argues that the framing is wrong for generative AI, whose highest-value uses in property investment are not the automation of known processes but the delegation of judgement-laden work – and that the industry's default safeguard, “a human in the loop”, is not a governance strategy. Design/methodology/approach A practice briefing combining the management literature on delegation and recent evidence on human–AI complementarity with the authors' experience of three years of executive education and advisory work with senior real estate professionals. Findings Generative AI creates most value where neither the process nor the output can be fully specified in advance – precisely where automation-era governance fails. Uniform human review predictably degrades into rubber-stamping as volumes grow. Effective governance separates two questions: what kind of work is being transferred, and how much the outcome matters. Practical implications A two-axis classification (is the process known? Is the output verifiable?) Sorts any task into one of four working modes – automate, assist, structure, delegate – and an accountability ladder scales oversight from logging to full human decision-making. Investment teams can apply the framework immediately by classifying tasks rather than jobs and reallocating scarce review capacity to where consequence is genuine. Originality/value The paper reframes AI adoption as a delegation-design problem continuous with management skills the industry already possesses, separates task classification from governance intensity and names the failure mode – accountability theatre – that uniform human review creates.

title: PixelVision: A Modular Web-Based Framework for AI-Assisted Biological Image Analysis Across Diverse Microscopy Modalities
container-title: Microscopy
d82f057493b9d8b5c12e3a6ea042659bef8ebfbc.abstract: Abstract The increasing volume and heterogeneity of microscopy data in biomedical research present challenges for automated image analysis and the integration of assay-specific computational methods. We developed PixelVision, a modular, web-based framework that integrates deep learning models, quantitative image analysis, and expert review across diverse biological imaging modalities. The framework supports single-organism imaging, two- and three-dimensional cell culture analysis, whole-slide imaging, and interactive annotation through a shared infrastructure for model deployment, version management, and data processing. Quantitative evaluations demonstrated application-specific classification and segmentation performance, with inference throughput of approximately seven high-resolution images per second on a single GPU. In a prospective zebrafish screening study, iterative model refinement using expert-reviewed classifications was associated with an increase in macro-averaged F1 score from 0.867 to 0.967 across three screening rounds. PixelVision provides a framework for integrating automated image analysis and expert assessment across heterogeneous microscopy workflows.

title: scHiCGNN: Per-Chromosome Graph Attention for Single-Cell Hi-C Clustering
container-title: Bioinformatics Advances
4a93d6669776147fe6874ee9c846b19120eaa6de.abstract: Abstract Motivation Single-cell Hi-C measures three-dimensional chromatin organization in individual nuclei, revealing cell-to-cell variability in genome folding that bulk Hi-C cannot resolve. The central computational task is to cluster cells by chromatin state, but each cell yields a sparse, high-dimensional contact matrix poorly suited to linear principal component analysis pipelines or to hand-designed multi-stage neural pipelines. Results We present scHiCGNN, a graph attention framework that encodes each chromosome's contact matrix as a weighted graph, applies multi-head graph attention to learn node-level features, and fuses per-chromosome embeddings into a compact cell-level representation through a lightweight self-attention block. The resulting embedding is consumed by standard unsupervised clustering. We evaluate scHiCGNN on six public datasets: Flyamer, Collombet, Nagano (mouse) and Ramani, Lee, 4DN (human), spanning 171 to 19,388 cells. scHiCGNN consistently improves over principal component analysis baselines on all six datasets and matches or exceeds the published Higashi and MRscHiC numbers on the three larger human datasets, reaching Adjusted Rand Index values of 0.944 (Ramani), 0.674 (Lee), and 0.875 (4DN); on the smaller mouse datasets, MRscHiC's engineered pipeline retains an advantage. Direct graph representation learning is a practical and conceptually clean alternative to flattened-vector approaches for single-cell Hi-C clustering. Availability and implementation https://github.com/changlabtw/schicgnn

title: AI-personalised recommendations and brand trust: a dual-appraisal account of perceived diagnosticity and algorithmic persuasion awareness
container-title: Asia Pacific Journal of Marketing and Logistics
4e4ebf3bb779260b6b54d8220a10009d115eef87.abstract: Purpose This study examines the joint associations of perceived AI-personalised recommendations, perceived diagnosticity and algorithmic persuasion awareness with trust in the recommended brand. Design/methodology/approach A cross-sectional survey of 412 consumers in China who recalled a recent recommendation they perceived as AI-personalised was analysed using partial least squares path modelling. Findings Perceived personalisation was positively associated with diagnosticity (β = 0.472) and algorithmic persuasion awareness (β = 0.353). Diagnosticity was positively associated with brand trust (β = 0.413), whereas algorithmic persuasion awareness was negatively associated with it (β = −0.194). The corresponding indirect associations were 0.195 and −0.069. Research limitations/implications The cross-sectional, self-reported design limits causal and temporal interpretation. Experiments, observed exposures and longitudinal studies can test the proposed relationships and boundary conditions. Practical implications The findings suggest potential applications in recommendation design involving decision support, transparency and consumer control alongside behavioural performance. Social implications Consumer education could help consumers distinguish product relevance from the data use and commercial purpose underlying personalised recommendations. Originality/value The study extends recommendation research by examining perceived diagnosticity and algorithmic persuasion awareness jointly in relation to trust in the recommended brand. This focus complements work on recommendation-agent trust, trust in ad information and AI-related information disclosure.

title: Challenges and solutions for cross-regional collaboration in the construction industry of the GBA: using a human-AI collaborative qualitative analysis framework
container-title: Engineering, Construction and Architectural Management
1a83813a43c88812fb2906be886642e2b042cf38.abstract: Purpose Under the “One Country, Two Systems” framework, cross-regional collaboration in the construction industry of the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area (GBA) faces multiple barriers arising from institutional, managerial and cultural differences. Drawing on institutional theory, boundary-spanning theory and a project governance framework, this study systematically identifies challenges and solution pathways for cross-regional collaboration from the macro external environment to the micro project level. Design/methodology/approach The study examines eight representative cross-regional projects using a multi-case study design. The formal qualitative coding and cross-case analysis drew on 27 anonymized interview records from 23 unique participants across the eight cases. The broader body of primary interview material comprised approximately 200,000 Chinese characters, supplemented by field notes, project materials and secondary documentation to support contextual understanding and triangulation. The study developed a human-AI collaborative qualitative analysis framework in which ChatGPT and Google Gemini assisted axial coding and pattern identification, while researchers retained responsibility for open coding, contextual validation, final codebook decisions and theoretical interpretation. Findings The study identifies a three-level structural model of barriers and responses. Institutional heterogeneity and fragmented governance at the macro level constitute primary structural bottlenecks. These constraints increase resource costs and generate conflicts in organizational routines at the meso level, ultimately producing authority-responsibility imbalances and localization dilemmas at the micro level. To address these, the study proposes a three-level solution framework comprising macro-level institutional integration, meso-level strategic innovation and micro-level refined governance. Originality/value This study provides a comprehensive multi-level analysis of cross-regional collaboration specific to the GBA construction industry, linking macro policy research with micro-level project management. Methodologically, it documents a human-AI collaborative qualitative analysis framework in which AI assists axial coding and pattern comparison, while researchers retain responsibility for contextual interpretation and theoretical development. The findings suggest that qualification recognition, organizational capability building and project-level responsibility arrangements should be developed in concert.

title: The motivational gain control effect: mechanisms of predictive load and brand signal-to-noise ratio on danmaku interaction with AI advertising
container-title: Online Information Review
08c4b1b05bc220d127972f129a2868abce8ea41c.abstract: Purpose This study develops the motivational gain control model, examining how dual cognitive demands of AI-generated advertising – internal decoding burden from structural transitions and external attributional ambiguity from executional convergence – jointly influence real-time audience interaction. Predictive load captures expectation-updating demand across adjacent stages; brand signal-to-noise ratio (BSNR) captures attributional clarity relative to competitors, constituting two dimensions of cognitive decoding valence whose evaluative meaning depends on product involvement. Design/methodology/approach Using panel data from 248 AI-generated advertisements and their danmaku interactions – synchronous viewer comments overlaid on video – on a major Chinese video platform, each divided into five periods, a panel vector error correction model estimates short-run and long-run effects and product involvement's moderating role. Findings For low-involvement products, content-level predictive load suppresses danmaku interaction while BSNR enhances it across both horizons. For high-involvement products, the positive effect of BSNR is significantly attenuated, whereas the negative effect of predictive load is only marginally attenuated, mainly in the long run. The BSNR attenuation provides strong evidence against a pure resource-depletion account; the predictive load attenuation, though marginally significant, is directionally consistent. Together, these patterns support motivation-dependent valence reassessment. Cross-modal congruence exhibits non-monotonic temporal patterns distinct from content-level features. Originality/value This study provides evidence against the fixed valence assumption shared across processing fluency, competitive interference and elaboration likelihood frameworks, proposing motivation-dependent valence reassessment as an alternative mechanism. It jointly models internal narrative dynamics and external competitive similarity through predictive load and BSNR and employs danmaku interaction as a real-time behavioral trace of evaluative response in AI advertising research. Peer review The peer-review history for this article is available at: Link to the website.

title: Governing AI with Kaizen: technostress and continuous improvement in Italian public organizations
container-title: The TQM Journal
471d6e01bdd62b3801646b8171e69e48d0bcd109.abstract: Purpose The growing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into Italian public administration raises a central question: can person-centred human resource management practices turn technology from a source of psychosocial strain into an enabler of continuous improvement? This paper explores how formalized and participatory governance of AI adoption, structured around three Kaizen principles, is associated with employee participation in digital change and with the technostress reported by public employees. Design/methodology/approach A theory-informed qualitative multiple-case study was conducted in five organizational cases, namely Italian public administrations engaged in digital transformation projects funded by the Piano Nazionale di Ripresa e Resilienza (PNRR). In each organization, a manager–officer dyad (10 participants in total) took part in narrative interviews held between October and November 2025, focused on lived experiences of AI adoption, perceptions of human resource management and professional engagement. Transcripts were analysed through deductive, theory-driven content analysis based on the three Kaizen principles (process orientation, step-by-step improvement and human capital orientation) and on the technostress dimensions, followed by within-case and cross-case comparison. Findings Across 10 participant accounts embedded within five organizational cases, practices consistent with Kaizen were associated, within the accounts, with distinct narrative profiles of technostress and engagement. Accounts reporting all three principles described active co-authorship, professional empowerment and emerging roles; accounts reporting none described persistent techno-anxiety, disengagement and eroding professional identity. Among the creators, techno-insecurity is the one most closely tied to how adoption is governed, and is typically accompanied by techno-anxiety as an affective strain response, while overload, invasion, complexity and uncertainty appear in association with specific operating conditions. Intermediate accounts varied with the missing principle and its hierarchical level. Originality/value This paper develops the joint Kaizen–STS framework as an original analytical lens for AI governance in public administration. It provides qualitative evidence that Kaizen-consistent HR governance is associated with less salient technostress, particularly in the governance-related dimensions emerging from the analysis, and with stronger reported participation, professional agency and more favourable organizational conditions for continuous improvement. The study therefore contributes to organization and human resource management research by proposing the vertical governance gap between managerial design and operational experience as a sensitizing concept and offers public managers a diagnostic framework for PNRR-funded digital transformation across heterogeneous public-sector settings.

title: Transforming Rural Youth Learning through AI-Driven Agricultural Extension: A Conceptual Framework and Proposed Evaluation Protocol
container-title: Journal of Scientific Research and Reports
a0125c9a442e43fd8282a47f2a7682cd22740915.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly being explored as a means of supporting rural youth in accessing agricultural knowledge, public services, education, and livelihood opportunities. However, access to a smartphone or internet connection does not necessarily provide the ability to locate reliable information, evaluate digital advice, communicate safely, or use online services independently. This paper develops a design-oriented conceptual framework for integrating AI-supported learning into agricultural extension to strengthen these practical digital competencies among rural youth. The framework combines baseline task-based assessment, adaptive learning recommendations, local-language microlearning, agricultural task-based exercises, peer support, and human facilitation by extension workers. The manuscript is conceptual and protocol-oriented; no primary dataset was supplied, no field intervention was conducted, and no empirical outcomes are claimed. The framework is informed by literature on digital competence, digital agricultural extension, and AI adoption in extension services. It also specifies a proposed mixed-method evaluation protocol involving baseline and post-intervention tasks, follow-up assessment, learner interviews, and subgroup analysis where feasible. The paper outlines implementation components, measurable indicators, ethical safeguards, and priorities for future field validation. It argues that AI may help personalise and extend agricultural learning, but equitable and trustworthy implementation requires local-language design, accessible infrastructure, human verification, privacy protection, and continued face-to-face support.

title: AI Versus Human Recommendation: Effects on Decision Switch Under Conflict
container-title: Proceedings of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society Annual Meeting
6bd58fcd780d0c7f65a3c8106d3f424cfe04fb82.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly integrated in everyday decision-making, understanding how individuals respond to AI versus human advice is critical. The present study examined whether individuals are more likely to revise their initial decisions based on recommendations’ source (AI vs. Human) and stance (Agree vs. Disagree), while holding recommendation content constant. Fifty-nine participants completed eight game scenarios from popular casino games. After each initial choice, participants received a recommendation and were prompted to re-make the same decision. Mixed-effects logistic regression revealed that there is a strong tendency for participants to switch their selection when presented with disagreeing recommendations, regardless of its source. No significant differences were found in switching behaviors between AI and human-disagree conditions, though confidence increased in presence of decision switch when the opposing recommendation came from AI. Future research should explore how individual differences and contextual factors influence adoption of AI advice.

title: Investigating Context in How Clinicians Make Sense of AI: Qualitative Interview Study
container-title: JMIR Human Factors
2baa50bbde31bb925343221de386d00e34a3116c.abstract: Abstract Background AI-driven clinical decision support systems (AI-CDSS) are increasingly being introduced to enhance clinical decision-making, yet their adoption in health care remains limited. Research has examined technical, organizational, and contextual barriers to adoption, but less attention has been paid to how knowledge, values, and responsibility around AI-CDSS are constructed and negotiated in practice. Objective This study examines how clinicians and AI experts make sense of AI-CDSS by reanalyzing qualitative interview data through a feminist and constructivist science and technology studies (STS) perspective. Whereas the original study examined informational needs, this reanalysis asks how participants construct relevant knowledge, evaluate the value of AI-CDSS, and negotiate appropriate use and responsibility in clinical practice. Methods The authors conducted a reanalysis of semistructured interviews held in 2024 with clinicians (n=8) and AI experts (n=8) in the Netherlands. The original study focused on informational needs for AI-CDSS. For this analysis, a deductive coding framework based on European Commission guidelines for trustworthy AI was first applied, and the material was then inductively reorganized into 5 empirical themes. Subsequently, feminist and constructivist STS concepts were used as sensitizing concepts in an abductive analysis, and these concepts were brought into dialogue with the empirical themes to examine the sociotechnical relations underlying participants’ accounts. Results Situated knowledge shows that the informational needs of clinicians are not universal but relate to their roles and specific clinical contexts, with understanding oriented less toward technical transparency than toward actionable guidance, relevance, and integration into decision-making. Standpoint theory illuminates differences between stakeholder priorities: clinicians emphasize information on how to use and act on AI outputs within existing workflows, whereas AI experts focus more on providing technical characteristics and performance metrics. Tinkering captures how clinicians experiment with AI systems in practice to develop situated, lay forms of expertise. Situated value highlights that perceptions of an AI-CDSS’s worth are relational, with clinicians valuing novel, context-sensitive insights and developers prioritizing performance metrics. Finally, response-ability reveals how trust and accountability are largely delegated to institutional structures, while clinicians report limited legal, organizational, and structural support to respond meaningfully to uncertainty or errors when using AI-CDSS. Conclusions Reanalyzing the same interview material through an abductive STS approach makes sociotechnical dimensions visible that were not the focus of the original analysis. Rather than treating informational requirements as universal or adoption as primarily a matter of technical performance and communication, the findings show how knowledge, value, and responsibility are constituted through situated professional practices and institutional arrangements. Processes and considerations regarding how clinicians make sense of AI-CDSS are not universal but are shaped by social, cultural, and institutional contexts. This analytical perspective underscores the need for context-sensitive, multistakeholder strategies to support meaningful and responsible AI adoption in clinical practice.

title: Unpacking the Adoption of AI Decision Support for High-Risk Pregnancy Detection by Health Workers in Morocco: Embedded implementation research
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
567428cbbe72269e0c30883f91c09798cb82ffcb.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) Clinical decision support systems (CDSS-AI) have proven useful for early screening, detection, and rapid diagnosis of maternal and perinatal morbidity and mortality, as well as for timely referrals of high-risk maternal cases. Only a few CDSS-AI have been implemented in maternal and neonatal health (MNH) in the Middle East and North Africa (MENA) region. In Morocco, reducing the maternal mortality ratio remains a significant challenge, particularly in remote rural areas. These high mortality rates are attributed to the first and third delays in the Three Delay Model. To address these delays, we co-developed a web-based and mobile app CDSS-AI, called “Oumoumati”, with the Ministry of Health, and implemented it in eight rural primary health centres in Al Haouz province. We adopted an embedded implementation design. We interviewed twelve purposefully selected stakeholders, including midwives and health managers. Data analysis employed deductive coding informed by a realist synthesis while remaining sensitive to emergent inductive findings. Thematic analysis was structured using the Context-Mechanisms-Outcomes heuristic. Our study findings showed that the utilisation and adoption of CDSS-AI is conditioned by systemic intertwined multilayered factors: The general context (e.g., resources), health system context (e.g. professional recognition), organisational context (e.g. managerial support), intervention characteristics (e.g. ease of use), and individual capacities (self-confidence). Our project highlighted that the ethical, responsible, and contextualised use of AI may contribute to alleviating gender issues and inequitable access to care for women residing in remote, underserved areas, provided it is co-designed with trained frontline workers and empowered local communities.

title: Towards Transforming Maternal Health in Pakistan Through Equitable, Context-Aware AI for Early Detection of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM)
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
1f4086ae3c5e353ecefcc1f5712755bd1e98ab84.abstract: Abstract This study presents AI-GDMP, an AI-enabled risk prediction tool developed to support early detection of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus (GDM) among pregnant women attending a tertiary hospital in Islamabad, Pakistan. GDM diagnosis relies on mid-pregnancy oral glucose tolerance testing (OGTT) performed between 24– 28 weeks of gestation. By focusing on the first trimester and utilising non-invasive, low-cost features, AI-GDMP offers a potentially equitable and accessible approach to early high/low-risk classification, particularly valuable in resource-constrained antenatal settings. By flagging high-risk women early in pregnancy, the tool opens a wider window for lifestyle modification, nutritional counselling, and closer follow-up before overt hyperglycaemia develops. The AI model was trained and validated on retrospective data from a JCI-accredited tertiary care hospital in Islamabad (2015–2024): eligible OGTT-linked pregnancies were digitized and screened (n = 3,748), yielding a final analytic cohort of 3,102 pregnancies (1,352 GDM; 1,750 non-GDM) with a stratified 80/20 train–test split (n = 2,481/621). A structured feature engineering pipeline reduced 93 candidate variables to 49 early-pregnancy predictors, with additional reduced feature sets (29 and 25 predictors) derived using Lasso- based selection. Among multiple machine learning approaches, the Random Forest classifier delivered the most promising results on the independent hold-out test set, achieving an AUC-ROC of 0.88, an accuracy of 77.9%, and a recall of 75.9%. Data collection followed ethical protocols, including IRB approval and anonymized patient records. The trained-model was integrated into a clinical software environment, enabling real-time high/low-risk output through a physician dashboard and provides a foundation for prospective validation and equity-focused evaluation in Phase 2.

f56fe25bbfdc23fa7b1ad75e4c574300c396c669.abstract: The growing computational demands of artificial intelligence (AI) are challenging conventional electronics, making photonic computing a promising alternative. However, existing photonic architectures face fundamental scalability and reliability barriers. This article introduces SKYLIGHT , a scalable 3D photonic in-memory tensor core architecture designed for real-time AI inference. By co-designing its topology, wavelength routing, accumulation, and programming in a 3D stack, SKYLIGHT overcomes key limitations. Its innovations include a low-loss 3D Si/SiN crossbar topology, a thermally robust non-micro-ring resonator (MRR)-based wavelength-division multiplexing (WDM) component, a hierarchical signal accumulation using a multi-port photodetector (PD), and optically programmed non-volatile phase-change material (PCM) weights. Importantly, SKYLIGHT enables in-situ weight updates that support label-free, layer-local learning (e.g., forward-forward local updates) in addition to inference. With comprehensive system-level modeling, we show that a single 144× 256 SKYLIGHT core achieves a peak compute capability of 342.1 TOPS at 23.7 TOPS/W under a high-reuse tensor-core operating point. For end-to-end ResNet-50 inference, where the same physical core is reprogrammed across layers and tiles, SKYLIGHT reaches 1212 FPS with 60.9 mJ/image after explicitly accounting for PCM programming energy. System-level evaluations on four representative machine learning tasks, including unsupervised local self-learning, demonstrate SKYLIGHT ’s robustness to realistic hardware non-idealities (low-bit quantization and signal-proportional analog noise capturing modulation, PCM programming, and readout variations). With noise-aware training, SKYLIGHT maintains high task accuracy, validating its potential as a comprehensive solution for energy-efficient, large-scale photonic AI accelerators.

title: Assessing Socioeconomic Bias in AI-Powered Maternal Health Messaging: Evidence from Jacaranda Health’s PROMPTS Platform in Kenya
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
74c166ac509cfea4c48079f22557195c8417a57b.abstract: ABSTRACT Background In many low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), mothers lack timely, accurate health information, which can delay lifesaving care. Jacaranda Health’s PROMPTS platform reaches 3 million+ mothers in Kenya via SMS, using artificial intelligence (AI) to triage questions, provide rapid responses, and connect urgent cases to human agents. While AI can expand access, if not carefully designed it may reinforce inequities. This study examines whether PROMPTS’s AI models perform differently across socioeconomic groups. Methods We applied a four-phase bias assessment framework. First, we surveyed 4569 PROMPTS users across 22 counties and assessed socioeconomic vulnerability using a validated typing tool. Second, we examined whether training datasets reflected users across vulnerability strata. Third, we evaluated AI performance in classifying question topics. Finally, we audited AI-generated outputs for medical accuracy, grammar, and thoughtfulness, stratified by vulnerability. Results PROMPTS engages women across vulnerability levels. The most vulnerable mothers were less likely to ask questions, suggesting underrepresentation in training data. The AI model correctly classified 90% of questions, with no significant differences by vulnerability, though confidence was lower for messages from more vulnerable mothers. AI-generated responses were equally accurate across groups, but answers to more vulnerable users were sometimes rated as less thoughtful. Conclusion PROMPTS demonstrates a fair application of AI for maternal health, with strong performance across diverse groups. However, underrepresentation of vulnerable mothers and subtle differences in response quality highlight areas for improvement. Engaging vulnerable voices, embedding safeguards, and routine monitoring will be critical to ensure AI advances health equity in LMIC contexts.

title: Research and Development of AI-Powered Task-Shifting for High-Quality Obstetrics Ultrasound Services in Community Healthcare Settings: Real-World Implementation Experiences from an LMIC
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
58396b4e3bef28d032518e1ac8e1f795a769257d.abstract: Abstract Blind Sweep Obstetric Ultrasound (BSOU) paired with artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly proposed as a scalable approach to expand antenatal screening in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). However, limited evidence exists on how to implement BSOU-AI systems within real clinical environments, where infrastructure, workflows, and human resource constraints differ substantially from research settings. This study reports implementation experiences from a multi-center BSOU-AI project across tertiary hospitals and community health facilities in Nepal. We collected more than 3000 BSOU datasets using minimally trained providers and handheld ultrasound devices, developed and iteratively refined a nine-sweep BSOU protocol, and coordinated with national stakeholders to ensure alignment with the Rural Obstetrics Ultrasound Program. Real-world deployment revealed major challenges including machine incompatibility, inadequate digital infrastructure, annotation bottlenecks, workflow mismatches in high-volume hospitals, and difficulty capturing rare complications which required continuous adaptation of protocols, staffing, and data-management systems. Engagement with Nepal’s Ministry of Health prompted the addition of an evaluation arm comparing BSOU-AI performance not only to radiologist scans but also to nurse-led rural ultrasound, reflecting the true standard of care. Our experience demonstrates that AI readiness in LMICs depends as much on implementation science as on algorithm development. We provide methodological insights and practical recommendations for designing BSOU-AI studies that are scalable, contextually grounded, and responsive to health-system realities.

title: An AI conversational assistant to support self-managed medication abortion in Colombia: development and early testing in a telemedicine pathway
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
c230a21c79bab4fca674bce9f837badae975e723.abstract: Abstract Colombia continues to face unsafe and informal abortions, with elevated risks in the Pacific region, where structural inequities and stigma persist despite a liberalized legal framework. Profamilia, a major sexual and reproductive health and rights (SRHR) provider, is expanding telemedicine to reduce these gaps. This case study describes the development and feasibility testing of an AI WhatsApp assistant for Profamilia’s medication-abortion telemedicine pathway to provide trusted information and navigation. Using Research-through-Design, Design Thinking and Agile sprints, we built an assistant grounded in local legal/clinical guidance, privacy-by-design (no identifiers), and human-in-the-loop escalation for risk and out-of-scope cases. After iterative internal validation, user-testing in three Pacific departments (Valle del Cauca, Cauca, Nariño; n=40; 605 questions) achieved 86.4% task success—defined as no Level-1 (high-risk) or Level-2 (service-flow) errors in responses—with 2.1% Level-1 errors. Users valued speed, clarity, trust and privacy. Priorities centred on interface/navigation microcopy and safety hardening to reduce Level-1 errors. Findings suggest early feasibility, safety and acceptability for a locally grounded assistant, with potential to bolster knowledge, support decisions and ease access to care. This case offers transferable insights for developing AI-enabled, rights-based SRHR tools. Next steps include a pilot to measure service-level and user-centred outcomes for equity-oriented scale-up.

title: Growing Up With AI
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
1d0a243b804e5bc15a1d345307a3a8edd75d8671.abstract: This chapter examines the psychological implications of AI-curated digital environments on child consumers with a focus on cognitive development, screen engagement and mental well-being. Drawing on developmental psychology and consumer socialization literature, it explores how algorithmic personalization reshapes children's digital experiences and influences their ability to process information, regulate emotions and interpret persuasive content. The chapter moves beyond traditional notions of screen time by situating digital engagement within immersive, continuously adaptive environments. It further highlights the developmental vulnerabilities of pediatric consumers in navigating such spaces. In response, a developmentally informed framework for digital well-being is proposed, integrating technological design, user characteristics and contextual mediation. The chapter contributes to interdisciplinary discourse by offering a conceptual foundation for understanding child and AI interactions also informing ethically responsible digital practices.

title: Growing Up Algorithmic
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
bc9ada7a4d5842d7a6680ed7fef502edeb4bc9ea.abstract: The chapter critically examines how artificial intelligence has transformed children into consumers within the realm of online platforms, toys, and learning systems. It discusses the impact of AI-driven marketing strategies, including recommendation engines and synthetic influencers, on children's preferences and behaviors. The analysis is grounded in theories related to consumer socialization, media psychology, and digital surveillance, exploring how these technologies affect children's cognition, emotional attachments, and decision-making. It highlights concerns over hyper-personalized content, parasocial interactions with AI, and ethical governance regarding data privacy. Additionally, the chapter reviews existing regulatory frameworks, identifies gaps in protecting children, and proposes a holistic approach to understanding the interactions between children and AI. Finally, it advocates for ethical AI design, corporate responsibility, and enhancing AI literacy among parents, contributing to the broader conversation on child rights and digital well-being in an AI-driven era.

title: Juvenile Consumer in the Age of AI-Marketing
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
0a33e87f8dba8d3f37c618103c802b6a9bf7d949.abstract: In this chapter, the authors further develop on the changing face with regard to the juvenile consumer within the fast-growing realm of artificial intelligence. It also shows how AI technologies, including smart devices, social networking recommendation systems, and the Internet of Toys are shifting children as passive participants of the marketing process to active and data-generating participants in the digital economy. The paper is interdisciplinary and combines the knowledge of marketing, developmental psychology, digital ethics, and public policy to discuss four key issues, such as AI-enabled marketing practices, privacy, data ownership, digital well-being, and regulation. The authors state that, as much as AI presents opportunities of personalized learning and creative play and enhances connectivity. The growing popularity of gamification, influencer marketing, and emotionally adaptive systems makes the distinctions between entertainment and advertising and makes children less aware of when they are being sold a product.

title: Algorithmic Childhood Future-AI Prediction Systems and the Pre-Emption of Choice in Young Consumers
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
56005ba933d1e6bd7711a958429702ad6438517e.abstract: The fast adoption of Artificial Intelligence in the child-facing digital ecosystem has changed marketing into a reactive personalization model to a predictive and pre-emptive model of shaping choice. This chapter envisions an algorithmic childhood futures, in which AI technologies predict preferences and restructure the choice environment of children prior to the desire developing consciously. Based on the interdisciplinary theory and the latest case studies provided in the educational platforms and smart toy ecosystems, the chapter proves how predictive architectures may promote engagement and gradually reduce exploration and redistribute agency. This analysis puts the concept of algorithmic influence in a new perspective, as temporal harm, with its long-term developmental consequences, that are still poorly dealt with in existing governance models. To create a balance between innovation, commercial goals and digital well-being, the chapter ends with the suggestions to child-centered design and managerial principles.

title: Algorithmic Persuasion in the Age of AI
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
1c12aff4be2cfcce0ade40218bae9d4af7c74978.abstract: The architecture of marketing persuasion has undergone a structural change as a result of the quick adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) in children's digital environments. AI-driven systems, in contrast to conventional exposure-based advertising, use real-time personalization, adaptive feedback loops, and predictive analytics to shape behavioral trajectories rather than just discrete consumption decisions. The AI-native child is conceptualized in this chapter, which also makes the case that modern marketing strategies increasingly function through embedded commercial intent in gaming platforms, educational technologies, smart devices, and conversational agents. The Child-Centered Ethical AI Marketing Model (CCEAMM), a normative but implementable framework based on developmental appropriateness, transparency, proportional data use, autonomy preservation, and long-term well-being orientation, is the chapter's response.

title: The Child Consumer in the AI Era
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
5ad4e55952093a68f81d3250e2c934b4b91cc2ed.abstract: This chapter examines how AI-driven marketing environments operate as algorithmically engineered choice architectures for child consumers. Rather than treating digital marketing as a set of isolated advertisements or promotional messages, the chapter conceptualizes contemporary child-facing platforms as adaptive environments that organize attention, structure choices, shape consumption pathways, and influence patterns of platform engagement. These environments operate through defaults, rankings, recommender systems, gamified rewards, push notifications, consent frictions, privacy settings, social proof cues, influencer content, in-app prompts, and interface-level behavioral signals. In such settings, marketing is not only communicated through visible persuasion. It is embedded in the design of the digital environment itself.

title: Algorithmically Objectified
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
b1b34dce36668c601e693340ade565960f440df2.abstract: This chapter examines how AI-driven marketing systems transform children's digital activities into datafied consumer profiles. It develops the concept of the datafied child consumer to explain how behavioral traces, contextual signals, inferred vulnerabilities, and attention patterns are captured, profiled, targeted, and monetized within platform-based marketing ecosystems. Using a structured thematic conceptual review, the chapter maps the recursive cycle linking child digital interaction, data capture, algorithmic inference, marketing activation, behavioral feedback, and commercial value extraction. It also evaluates the implications of this process for children's autonomy, privacy, consumer socialization, and digital well-being. The chapter concludes by proposing a rights-based, child-centered framework for responsible AI-driven marketing grounded in developmental appropriateness, data minimization, inference limitation, transparency, auditability, and limits on exploitative personalization.

title: Datafication of Childhood in the AI Era
container-title: The Algorithmic Child Consumer
552347525ce7b2f954b9e84ea5ecd812d16aa08e.abstract: Children have become data-creating consumers in algorithmic markets due to the proliferation of artificial intelligence in digital markets. The interactions between children are being constantly tracked, scanned, and sold, be them smart toys and educational applications, biometric-enabled platforms, and so forth. The chapter is a critical analysis of the lifecycle of data of the child, starting at birth to adolescence, and contains ethical dangers of biometric surveillance, algorithmic non-transparency, and behavioral profiling. It assesses the shortcomings of the regulatory frameworks like the Children Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) in terms of their effectiveness in the response to the consent issue and transparency issue. The chapter develops a child-centered AI data governance framework to safeguard the digital well-being through theoretical issues, case study evaluation, and balancing innovation and autonomy.

title: Implementing AI-CDSS in Low-Resource Maternal Care: Lessons Learned from the Preeclapp Deployment
container-title: Oxford Open Digital Health
c21285c26160f9ad7d7028e61962eee68a329a9e.abstract: Abstract Hypertensive disorders of pregnancy (HDP) are one of the leading causes of maternal morbidity and mortality in Colombia, particularly in rural regions with limited access to specialized care. In this context, Preeclapp was developed as a clinical decision support system grounded in expert-system logic, designed to provide guideline-based support for maternal care in settings with limited resources and connectivity. This proof-of-concept implementation study analyzes the integration of Preeclapp into clinical practice and the factors that influenced its adoption. The main barriers identified included unstable connectivity, lack of data interoperability, high staff turnover, and initial skepticism toward AI-based technologies. Nevertheless, the project showed preliminary feasibility of use by non-specialized personnel in obstetrics and gynecology, even in low-connectivity environments. To overcome these challenges, the project relied on training sessions, embedded educational resources, continuous technical support, and iterative software adaptations. Our implementation suggests that these strategies were perceived by users as supporting adherence to obstetric protocols, reinforcing clinical decision-making, and enhancing staff confidence, particularly in facilities with limited specialist availability. As a proof-of-concept implementation study, this work did not evaluate diagnostic accuracy or clinical effectiveness; instead, it focused on early implementation feasibility, usability, acceptability, and perceived usefulness. The findings suggest that sustainable adoption of AI-CDSS systems requires strengthening digital literacy and promoting a culture of innovation. Our experience with Preeclapp indicates that adoption and implementation benefited from a modular design, low-connectivity functionality, flexibility, and co-creation with local teams, which helped adapt the tool to each institution’s context.

7618ca5b91c52b831750f40d2a59ffd17dd1de82.abstract: The landscape of the customer service domain has been fundamentally transformed by rapid technological advancements and the rise of artificial intelligence (AI). Sophisticated AI-based chatbots are capable of providing personalised and real-time support at an unmatched level. The chapter discusses the internals of how AI can be integrated into customer service, its design and implementation (natural language processing (NLP), machine learning and conversational interface design). It's an exploration of the successes achieved, 24×7 services, as well as ongoing issues in the field, including a lack of empathy and data protection. Some of the ethical challenges, along with future trends such as emotionally intelligent systems, multimodal interfaces and hyper-personalised approaches for service delivery, are also discussed in the chapter. This chapter offers real-world examples and research to illustrate how AI can benefit customer service and the factors to consider when considering AI-powered tools.

title: AI-Enhanced Customer Journey Design for the Employee Traveller in Corporate Travel Management
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
a7a264083703838cc8b600a740747b6bd7d805f2.abstract: One of the most impactful employee experiences that a firm can provide is corporate travel, but it is not a priority issue in human resource management. The customer journey mapping technique, which has been created in the service marketing sector to map and optimise the overall experience of the customer, has become an important tool of comprehending the employee traveller as an internal customer of the travel management system. The chapter focuses on how AI is used to improve the journey mapping of corporate travelling and discusses the HRM implications. Three sources of HRM value are analysed: employee experience and talent engagement, duty of care and risk management, and strategic workforce analytics. The chapter then proceeds to address challenges, ethical considerations, and privacy considerations and governance implications followed by providing illustrative examples and a research agenda. The main point is that AI-inspired journey mapping will transform corporate travelling into a type of procurement into a strategic HRM tool of engagement, safety, and organisational learning.

title: AI-Driven Recommendation Systems for Travel Planning
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
ba7554b3d7fdd7ea465fef06feb52f850f4cc265.abstract: Artificial-intelligence-driven recommender systems have become a pervasive part of the travel-planning experience, helping consumers filter vast inventories of flights, accommodation, and activities. Yet the finance dimension of travel remains comparatively under-theorised in the recommender-systems literature. This chapter integrates tourism informatics, recommender-systems research, FinTech scholarship, and behavioural economics to examine AI-driven travel recommendation through a personal-finance lens, with a particular focus on budget-sensitive and cost-aware travellers. The chapter argues that treating the traveller's budget as a first-class design parameter produces systems that are more useful to consumers and more defensible from a consumer-protection standpoint. It reviews the evolution of AI in travel recommendation, develops a budget-aware design space spanning constrained optimisation, price prediction, FinTech integration, contextual flexibility, and group budgeting, and considers the behavioural, ethical, and regulatory implications of this integration. Three illustrative cases: fare prediction, payment-aware recommendation, and explainable recommendation ground the arguments in existing practice, and a research agenda is outlined for the next generation of financially literate travel recommenders.

title: AI-Powered Personalization in Travel Marketing
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
a76f410908c64fcb5afded73b8d65c2600197e9e.abstract: The world travel and tourism sector is undergoing a radical change based on the rapid developments in digital technologies especially artificial intelligence (AI) big data analytics and networked digital ecosystems. Out of all these advances one of the most significant agents of change that have been altering the design and supply of travel services is the use of AI to personalize the services. With the help of smart algorithms and scale capabilities to process data organizations can deliver extremely personalized experiences that are closely in line with the preferences activities and situational demands of contemporary travellers (Valeri, 2023; Gaur et al. 2021).

title: AI-Driven Personalization in Customer Engagement and Travel Marketing
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
cab53579f6f706d2b096f9f8e1ef7047728972da.abstract: The introduction of the artificial intelligence (AI) into the travel marketing is a game changer in the way the industry will interact, retain, and serve the customers. This chapter discusses how AI-driven personalization approaches have evolved and are used in the travel industry and how technologies like machine learning, natural language processing, predictive analytics, and recommendation systems are helping to transform customer experiences. The chapter discusses how personalization affects consumer decision-making, brand loyalty and revenue generation based on the existing empirical research and case studies in the industry. It also touches upon the ethical issues of privacy of data, algorithmic discrimination and customer permission. This chapter provides a theoretical context and practical data to travel marketers, technologists and policymakers who must work within the rapidly evolving AI landscape by looking at current applications and forecasting trends.

title: AI-Based Pricing and Revenue Optimisation in Tourism Services
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
c40dd4dfa0f215bb2f130e973858a9a9331b2121.abstract: Pricing and revenue management has been the core of tourism and hospitality marketing since the perishable and capacity-limited nature of these services means that all unsold seats, rooms or tours are forever lost. AI can now enable tourism companies to predict demand, segment consumers and price them with the speed, resolution, and personalisation that would have been unimaginable in the classical yield management days. This chapter explores tourism services based on AI-driven pricing and revenue optimisation using the marketing perspective. It combines the existing revenue management literature with the current work on AI in marketing. The chapter plots AI potentials along the pricing and revenue lifecycle, which include demand forecasting, customer segmentation, price optimisation, distribution and channel management, personalisation, and post purchase recovery and then examines five dimensions of marketing that define whether AI-based pricing creates or destroys value: customer experience, perceived price fairness, trust and relationship quality, brand equity and customer lifetime value. It states that AI-based pricing is only successful in tourism when it is perceived as a marketing tool within the broader customer relationship, not a stand-alone revenue generator and concludes by discussing ethics, governance and a research agenda.

title: AI and Omnichannel Marketing Strategies in Travel Platforms
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
c588ddd8d5996746e14ae10690a2cc7988fa5134.abstract: This book chapter comprises new AI-powered tools such as machine learning, data analytics, and personalisation, which together shape improved customer involvement across physical touchpoints and the digital travel industry. Coming on to create a polished and sleek experience across various channels, AI is quickly changing the mechanisms and techniques used in its marketing strategies. Taking modern insights and their examples, it further explains new techniques of natural language operation in delivering a more customised and good experience. There are also some mandates and challenges on the way, which include algorithmic bias, personal data security and limited access to digital technologies. Additionally, this book chapter also discovers the growing patterns and trends of AR, voice-enabled search and up-to-date pricing frameworks. Ultimately, it highlights that adoption of AI in cross-channel marketing is not an option but a mandate for travel portals that want to be there in the marketing; it has become a sign of competitive advantage for their customer fulfilment.

title: AI-Powered Personalization and Recommendation Systems in Next-Generation Travel Management

b9e613bd3df85b54f82e072d3978910d175bafa3.abstract: This chapter examines how artificial intelligence reshapes personalization and recommendation systems across next-generation travel management across global travel markets. It integrates recommender-system theory, smart tourism research, customer-experience design, and predictive analytics into an implementation-oriented framework for airlines, hotels, online travel agencies, destination managers, and corporate travel programs. The chapter explains how collaborative, content-based, context-aware, knowledge-based, and generative models can orchestrate offers, itineraries, service recovery, sustainability choices, and duty-of-care interventions. It also evaluates data governance, privacy, bias, explainability, organizational readiness, and interoperability barriers that limit adoption. Six practical tables and four TikZ figures translate the discussion into architecture, metrics, risk, and roadmap tools. The chapter concludes that successful AI personalization depends less on algorithmic novelty than on trusted data, measurable value, ethical design, and cross-functional execution.

title: Talking to Travellers
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics

439ad8df55c01c5fbfb7f73acae8fad387788276.abstract: With chatbots and conversational artificial intelligence (CAI), the travel brands are transforming the way they connect with prospects and customers throughout the booking process. The argument among marketing scholars is that customer engagement is a multidimensional construct that encompasses cognitive, emotional and behavioural interactions with a brand and that these interactions are becoming mediated by intelligent technologies. Using the literature of marketing, service research, and tourism-informatics this chapter explores the creation of marketing value by chatbots and CAI in regards to travel services. It assesses the theoretical background of customer engagement and conversational AI, the history of chatbots in the travel industry, and their functional placements through the pre-purchase, purchase, and post-purchase processes. It then evaluates three main sources of marketing value including personalisation of the customer experience, brand communication and voice, and real-time marketing intelligence through conversational data. The chapter also takes into account the issues of challenges, such as hallucinations, channel fragmentation, and escalation failure, as well as the ethical, privacy, and trust issues. Arguments are based on three exemplary cases, and a research agenda is presented in the future of conversational-AI-based travel marketing. The main argument is that, when intelligently combined with the broader marketing stack, chatbots and CAI cease to be viewed as a cost-saving service channel, but rather as a strategic platform of relationship-based, data-rich interaction with customers.

title: Predictive Analytics for Consumer Behaviour in Tourism and Hospitality
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
a0716bed81d520e0c418e6f30cd54cc6dc83f45a.abstract: The forecasting of consumer behaviour and its associated response makes an exciting prospect in the tourism and hospitality industry, and can largely be attributed to predictive analytics. This chapter focuses on the use of data-driven methods to gain insights and predict users' trip preferences, booking behaviour, and expectations for the service (e.g., machine learning, AI, or big data analytics)—important topics such as Demand forecasting, Personalisation Strategies, Sentiment analysis, and revenue management in the latest research. Elsewhere in the chapter, the ethical dilemmas involved with consumer data usage, including privacy concerns and issues regarding the transparency and accountability of algorithms, are addressed. In this chapter, the authors tie together theory and practice, offering researchers and providers in the hospitality sector practical insights into how they can use predictive instruments to gain a competitive edge, enhance customer experiences and reach sustainable performance in their organisation in a fast-paced and changing tourism environment.

title: Behavioral Biases in AI-Driven Pricing and Revenue Optimization
container-title: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
AI-Driven Transformation of Travel Marketing and Customer Experience
ed174c4b4ed08f10fd6ad59224497a10a8aaa670.abstract: The intersection of artificial intelligence and behavioral finance presents an underexplored but commercially significant terrain for reimagining how tourism firms design and implement their pricing strategies. While revenue management in travel and hospitality has long depended on demand-based algorithmic models a persistent gap between what these systems predict and what consumers actually do reveals a structural blind spot the systematic cognitive biases that shape purchase decisions in ways that rational utility models simply cannot capture. This chapter develops a behavioral-AI pricing framework by synthesizing prospect theory mental accounting reference price anchoring and social proof mechanisms within the architecture of modern machine learning revenue management systems. Drawing on secondary evidence from major online travel platforms and published booking behavior studies we demonstrate that tourism consumers exhibit consistent loss aversion effects when exposed to dynamic price fluctuations that reference price anchoring significantly modulates willingness to pay at different stages of the booking funnel and that AI pricing engines which ignore these behavioral dimensions routinely suppress conversion or trigger demand destruction. Our proposed framework integrates behavioral signals into AI feature engineering arguing that affective pricing cues cancellation-loss framing and social validation mechanisms can be systematically deployed to improve both conversion rates and revenue per available unit without exploiting consumers in ethically problematic ways. The chapter contributes to the growing literature on neuroeconomic applications in hospitality management while offering practical direction to revenue managers who seek to humanize not merely automate their pricing decisions.

title: Chatbots and Conversational AI in Customer Engagement for Travel Services

61f356e4896a0d512dee258558f6e2599b3911a4.abstract: Conversational artificial intelligence (CAI) and chatbots are transforming the way travel brands interact with the prospects and customers throughout the booking process. There has been a long-standing argument by marketing scholars that customer engagement is a multidimensional concept that includes cognitive, emotional, and behavioural interactions with a brand, and the interactions are becoming mediated by intelligent technologies. Based on marketing, service research, and tourism-informatics literatures, this chapter explores how travel service chatbots and CAI can generate marketing value. It discusses the theoretical basis of customer engagement and conversational AI, the history of chatbots in the travel sector, and outlines their operational applications throughout the pre-purchase, purchase, and post-purchase processes. It subsequently examines three key bases of marketing value, which include customising the customer experience, brand communication and voice, and real-time marketing intelligence based on conversational data. Challenges, such as hallucinations, channel fragmentation, and escalation failure, as well as ethical, privacy, and trust considerations are also taken into account in the chapter. The arguments are based on three illustrative cases and a research agenda is provided on the next generation of conversational-AI-enabled travel marketing. The main argument is that, designed appropriately as part of the broader marketing stack, chatbots and CAI no longer represent a cost-reduction service channel but rather a strategic customer engagement platform, full of data.

title: Chatbots and Conversational AI in Travel Customer Service

11cc7490a63085742c3525aa62522b3da243f5c1.abstract: Artificial intelligence has revolutionized customer service in the travel sector. This chapter explores the role of chatbots and conversational AI in travel customer service systems, from early rule-based chatbots to advanced large language models (LLMs) that can engage in long, multi-step interactions. The chapter draws upon recent empirical studies, case studies and theoretical perspectives to examine prominent use cases such as booking support, travel disruption management, personalisation and multilingual interactions. It also highlights key challenges including integration with existing systems, bridging the gap between language understanding and domain expertise, and ethical issues related to privacy and bias in conversational AI. The chapter also assesses human-AI interaction approaches and provides insights into future directions such as agentic AI and multimodal interfaces. Insights for industry practitioners and avenues for future research are explored.

title: Harnessing Generative AI and Large Language Models for Intelligent Travel Planning

c44e15ad738f4a32fc2a61c562801bad0d22ace2.abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs) are transforming how travellers discover destinations, plan itineraries, and engage with tourism service providers. This chapter provides a systematic and theoretically grounded examination of these technologies within intelligent travel planning. It traces the evolution of AI in tourism and explores key applications, including conversational trip planning, hyper-personalized recommendations, real-time adaptive guidance, and sentiment analysis. The chapter highlights opportunities to enhance accessibility, improve operational efficiency, and support data-driven destination management. It also examines critical challenges, including hallucinations, information reliability, algorithmic bias, data privacy, workforce disruption, and fragmented regulatory frameworks. The chapter concludes by addressing governance and policy needs while identifying future directions, including multimodal AI, sustainable AI, interoperable ecosystems, and interdisciplinary collaboration to ensure the responsible adoption of AI in global tourism.

According to the current studies and industry dynamics, the chapter is very useful in studying the development of technology in the tourism industry- starting with primitive Global Distribution Systems to the current machine learning systems. Exploring and analyzing challenges, especially in the developing world.The chapter ends by presenting new trends which include generative AI and augmented reality and the metaverse as a research framework that scholars and practitioners can use to study.

43f02e9dd2362d62f0781c1271492951a9157aa0.abstract: Power-system operation is safety-critical: personnel integrate data, alarms, outages, switching requests, contingency analyses, grid-code rules, and cybersecurity constraints. This review assesses evidence, rechecked through May 31, 2026, on GenAI and large language models (LLMs) for operator support. It covers research, reports, standards, regulations, preprints, and industry initiatives, distinguishing retrieval-grounded systems, domain-adapted LLMs, time-series foundation models, tool-using agents, and digital-twin verification. It proposes a supervised assistant in which the LLM orchestrates and explains but is not operational truth. Near-term uses include document retrieval, regulatory interpretation, training, summaries, and explanations of approved calculations. Evidence does not support autonomous transmission-level actions. Deployment requires traceable sources, current models, restricted tools, cybersecurity boundaries, adversarial testing, human approval, and audit trails.

title: AI-Driven Distributed No-Wait Flow Shop Scheduling for Sustainable Energy-Aware Manufacturing Systems

d9b0f4862ffea1e45716990a59652306558d70c3.abstract: The rapid evolution of smart manufacturing and Industry 5.0 has heightened interest in sustainable and intelligent scheduling approaches. The distributed no-wait flow shop scheduling (DNWFSP) problem is a complex combinatorial optimization problem that simultaneously involves assigning jobs to plants and sequencing them on machines. This problem becomes even more challenging when energy and environmental objectives are incorporated. This chapter proposes an AI-based distributed flow shop scheduling framework for energy-efficient manufacturing systems. The objective is to minimize total energy consumption. The approach relies primarily on deep reinforcement learning, specifically the Deep Q-Network (DQN), to learn an optimal decision-making policy in a dynamic and uncertain environment. The DQN model allows scheduling decisions to be adapted in real time based on the state of the production system. Experimental results show that the proposed approach significantly improves energy efficiency and resource utilization compared to conventional scheduling methods.

7c511103dc7bb5d22ff06c9abc63879ce415e340.abstract: Since the building sector contributes significantly to carbon emissions worldwide, sophisticated methods are required for precise forecasting and efficient reduction. The use of machine learning (ML) approaches for carbon emission prediction across the construction lifecycle—including material manufacturing, transportation, on-site activities, and operations—is examined in this chapter. Regression, artificial neural networks, support vector machines, and ensemble learning are among the machine learning models that are rigorously examined, with an emphasis on how well they can handle complicated, nonlinear datasets. In order to facilitate real-time monitoring and decision assistance, the chapter delves deeper into the integration of machine learning (ML) with digital technologies, such as building information modeling (BIM), the Internet of Things (IoT), and digital twins. Supported by case examples, a conceptual framework is put forth to direct ML-driven carbon mitigation methods. Future research directions and challenges are also covered.

title: Machine Learning in Hydrogen Production and Combustion
